generated_text: The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced an unprecedented drop in the number of malaria cases worldwide, marking a major turning point in the global fight against the infectious disease. In a recent press briefing in Geneva, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO Director-General, revealed that the number of new malaria cases in 2023 had fallen by nearly 30 per cent compared to the previous year, with most of the decline occurring in sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease has had the greatest impact. The announcement, which has been hailed as a “monumental achievement” in public health, comes after decades of international collaboration, increased funding for preventive measures, and advancements in treatment and surveillance. The WHO’s updated global malaria report highlights that in 2023, there were just under 200 million cases of malaria worldwide—down from a high of over 240 million in 2020. The decline has been attributed to a combination of factors, including the widespread deployment of long-lasting insecticide-treated mosquito nets, the increased distribution of rapid diagnostic tests and effective antimalarial drugs, and the successful rollout of the first malaria vaccine, Mosquirix, in pilot programmes across Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi. Dr Tedros praised the contributions of local health workers, governments, and international donors, who have played a crucial role in reducing the burden of the disease. “This is not just a victory for us as an organisation, but for every community that refused to accept malaria as an inevitable part of life,” he said. “This progress proves what is possible when the world unites for a common cause.” The impact on child mortality has also been significant. According to the WHO, malaria is still responsible for more than 600,000 deaths each year, but the number of deaths among children under five—most of whom live in Africa—has dropped by nearly 15 per cent. This has been attributed to the increased accessibility of preventive treatment for pregnant women and infants, along with improvements in healthcare systems across high-risk regions. However, the WHO has also issued a stark warning that progress is not inevitable. “While the numbers are encouraging, we cannot afford to become complacent,” said Dr Tereza Kares, the WHO’s director of global malaria programme. “There are still millions of people at risk, and challenges such as climate change, growing resistance to insecticides and antimalarial drugs, and dwindling funding remain significant threats.”

Private hospitals in England should be required to publish the same level of detail about patient safety incidents as the National Health Service (NHS), according to a major report by the Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP). Published today, the review calls on health officials to close a long-standing gap in transparency between the public and private sectors, warning that greater scrutiny is vital to protecting patient safety and restoring public trust. The report, commissioned by the government, highlights a stark contrast in the information currently available to the public and NHS stakeholders. While NHS trusts are required to report incidents such as falls, medication errors, and surgical mistakes through the National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS), private providers are not under the same obligation. Critics argue this has allowed supply companies such as Bupa and Spire Healthcare, among others, to operate with less visibility, making it more difficult to assess the safety of their services. Keith Willett, chief executive of HQIP, stated that the lack of transparency poses a significant risk to patient safety. “If we are to truly understand and mitigate the risks patients face in both parts of the system, the data needs to be shared openly and consistently,” he said. The report comes amid growing concerns about private healthcare provision in the wake of a number of high-profile cases of apparent negligence. Last year, an investigation by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) revealed “poor” levels of safety at Royal Liverpool University Hospital, which had been managed by the private firm Virgin Care. The hospital has since been returned to NHS control. Public health campaigners welcomed the findings. Fiona Austin, from the Patients Association, said: “This is a step in the right direction. Patients should not be treated differently depending on who operates their hospital. If the private sector is part of the NHS landscape, it must be held to the same standards.” The Department of Health did not immediately comment on the report but said it "remains committed to continuous improvement in patient safety and will consider the findings carefully." It has previously defended the role of private hospitals, arguing they provide vital capacity during peak times and help alleviate strain on the NHS. However, the report urges that this should not come at the cost of transparency or risk to the public good. Under the proposed changes, private providers would be required to report a wider range of patient safety events, including near misses, adverse incidents, and incidents with individuals or families.

The Scottish government has formally requested that Scotland be excluded from a controversial piece of legislation proposed by the UK government, which aims to tighten restrictions on trade union powers. The legal motion was submitted as part of the ongoing process for the UK Trade Union Bill, which sets out to limit industrial action and impose greater financial transparency on unions across the United Kingdom. However, the Scottish administration has made it clear that it does not support the measures and is seeking devolution on the issue, arguing that unions should remain governed under Scotland's distinct legal framework. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon's government has long championed the rights of workers and trade unions in Scotland, positioning herself as a staunch critic of Westminster's proposed reforms. In a statement, a Scottish government spokesperson said, "The Scottish government believes that the Trade Union Bill is not only unsuitable for Scotland’s devolved circumstances but risks undermining the rights of trade unionists north of the border. We have made clear our intent for Scotland to be excluded from the Bill, and we are working to ensure devolution principles are respected." The dispute highlights the ever-growing divergence between Holyrood and Westminster, particularly in the area of constitutional governance. Trade union laws are currently devolved under the Scotland Act 2016, allowing the Scottish Parliament to determine its own regulations on union rights. The UK government's bill, however, seeks to centralise control and impose national restrictions – a move that has been widely deplored by pro-union voices in Scotland. Labour's deputy leader, Ian Murray, who represents Edinburgh South, said the decision by the Scottish government was the “right call at the right time” and echoed his party's long-standing opposition to the UK legislation. Meanwhile, unions across Scotland have welcomed the move as a victory for democratic rights and workplace protections. The UK Prime Minister remains firm about the need to introduce the bill, citing the importance of ensuring that trade unions act transparently and that public sector workers are governed under fair and consistent rules. The government has not yet confirmed its stance on whether it will accept Scotland’s request for exclusion. The issue is expected to play out in the coming weeks as both governments negotiate their positions, with the potential for legal or political challenges. If the UK government refuses to exclude Scotland from the bill, it could lead to further friction and even legal intervention by the Scottish Parliament.

Michael Kightly proved to be the hero once again as his third goal in three games secured a vital 1-0 victory for struggling Championship side Burton Albion against Norwich City at the Pirelli Stadium. The win lifted Burton out of the relegation zone and gave manager Nigel Clough a timely boost ahead of the busy festive fixture schedule. In a tightly contested encounter, it was Kightly who handed Burton the lead just before the break with a well-taken strike from the edge of the box. The 29-year-old attacking midfielder, who has found form at just the right time, curled the ball into the bottom corner to the delight of the home fans. Norwich, sitting comfortably in mid-table, failed to offer the same supply of crosses and penetrating play that had typified their recent performances, and were frustrated by bursts of impressive counter-attacking from the home side. Despite dominating possession for long spells, the Canaries were unable to break down a stubborn Burton backline, epitomized by a pair of last-minute headers in each half from centre-back Lucas Akins that denied Ken Sema and Jacob Murphy a deserved equalizer. Speaking after the match, Clough praised his team's mentality and singled out Kightly for his impact. "Michael is showing why he’s got such a proud career in this country," Clough said. "He’s got that desire to keep moving forward, and with the ball, and he made the difference again today. His goal was of the highest quality, and it was a big win for us." Kightly, who returned from a long-term knee injury in November, has now netted six times in the league this season, a remarkable turnaround for a player who had been facing uncertainty over his future at the club. The victory marks Burton’s second win in a week and significantly improves their prospects as they head into the season’s most chaotic fixtures. For Norwich, the defeat fails to raise concerns at the moment but will serve as a reminder of the inconsistency that has, at times, held them back from challenging toward the upper echelons of the Championship. Fans at the Pirelli Stadium will now look forward to extending their momentum when they take on Middlesbrough at the end of the month, hopeful that Kightly’s resurgence can act as the spark the team needs to climb further up the league table.

The First Minister of Scotland, Nicola Sturgeon, has described calls to increase the top rate of income tax for Scotland’s highest earners as “reckless and daft,” in a pointed response to growing pressure from within her own party and from opposition groups. Her remarks come as ministers continue to grapple with the economic consequences of Brexit, ongoing public sector pressures and the financial implications of the Scottish government’s ambitious policies on healthcare, education and sustainability. In a recent speech, delivered during a policy event in Edinburgh, Ms Sturgeon underlined the importance of maintaining a “balanced and sustainable” fiscal strategy, stating: “We must not take short-term political decisions which could undermine long-term economic confidence. Scotland needs to be seen as a place where people are willing to invest, and that is best done by ensuring our tax system remains fair and predictable.” The comments were directed at voices within the SNP who have pressed for the highest rate of income tax to be increased for annual earners above £150,000 — a measure previously pursued by some in Labour and the Scottish Greens as a means of funding public services. With the Scottish Parliament having devolved powers over income tax rates and bands, the decision on whether to raise the top rate lies with the Scottish government. However, the First Minister has consistently ruled out such a move, despite municipal and council-level taxation measures being pushed forward. Ms Sturgeon reinforced her position by citing the uncertainty of Scotland’s economic outlook, particularly in the light of volatile oil and gas revenues, and the nation’s reliance on investment and tourism. She argued that imposing higher taxes on the highest earners could deter businesses and reduce investment: “We are already operating within a UK economic system with deep structural challenges — it would be reckless to add further obstacles at this time.” The First Minister also stressed the importance of maintaining consensus within her party: “The SNP has spent the past decade building trust with voters — trust that we make rational, informed decisions that benefit the many, not the few. We must not be tempted into chasing headlines with policies that will ultimately do more harm than good.” Her comments have been met with mixed reactions. While supporters praised her commitment to economic pragmatism, critics, including some within her own party and from opposition politicians, have argued that higher taxation of the wealthy is necessary to fund the National Health Service, education reform and green energy projects.

Pakistan In Command After Misbah Ton, But England Stay In The Picture   A commanding century from Pakistan's inspirational captain Misbah-ul-Haq laid the foundation for a dominant position on the opening day of the first Test against England at Lord's, as the £20 million men buckled under the weight of yet another frail batting display at the beginning of a five-Test series. However, England regained some composure in the final session with a late but effective counter-attack that ensured the day ended in a draw, with the tourists arguably still in control of the match. Misbah, the 39-year-old veteran whose class and calm have become hallmarks of Pakistan's Test resurgence, made 117 from 234 balls before being dismissed by Steven Finn’s 13th over. His left-handed elegance and Tenacity, on a green-tinged, slightly bouncy pitch, turned what had started as a modest 28 for 2 breakfast into a 317 for 7 by early in the evening. It was the 34th century of his Test career and a worthy reminder of his immense value to the team. England, who had named a consistent-looking side after winning two ODIs earlier in the summer, were rattled from the outset. Joe Root bowled Azhar Ali for 12 and got rid of national hero Younus Khan with a sneaky inswinger for 34. But despite those early wickets, Misbah and Fakhar Zaman held the line with patience and judgment, the latter scoring a gritty 51 before edging a wide ball from Stuart Broad to gully. James Anderson, still the colossus of the English attack at 36, was largely frustrated in the middle session as Misbah blocked his trademark yorkers with monotonous efficiency. When he finally struck, it was on 116, with the ex-managing director of the ECB sending a short one down the leg side for the stumping. To his credit, Broad did not let the wicket unsettle him, holding the lower-order together and finishing with 2 for 96 off 47 overs. England’s own middle order gave them a late spark with a fiery 70 from Moeen Ali and 54 from Jos Buttler, with Moeen particularly impressing as he smashed 114 from 119 deliveries. While their partnership denting Pakistan’s lead, they could go further than the modest 74 they added for the final two wickets. The day was ultimately one of two halves for England, with their bowlers failing to produce enough early pressure and their batsmen wasting the ideal run-chase opportunity that a marginal green tinge suggested to the pitch.

At least seven people have been killed and a number of others injured in a suicide bombing at a funeral in Kabul, Afghanistan, which was held for a man who died during a protest on Friday, according to local officials. The explosion occurred in the Dasht-e-Barchi district during the funeral of a motorbike rider who was killed when security forces fired at a protest against the government’s decision to host peace talks with the Taliban. The protests, which erupted following the start of ceasefire negotiations in Doha, drew large crowds across the capital as dissent grew among anti-Taliban Afghans. Witnesses said the ceremony was still underway when the first blast went off near the gravesite. Moments later, a second explosion rocked the vicinity, raising fears of a coordinated attack. “The funeral was peaceful until the bomb exploded,” one witness, Hamidullah, who was present at the event and sustained minor injuries, told AFP. “Everyone was praying when the blast happened. I see people running and screaming.” Afghanistan's Interior Ministry confirmed the attack, which is being investigated, and ruled out any intention to hold the talks excluded the directly affected communities. Meanwhile, the Taliban have claimed responsibility for the bombing, saying it was a response to “collaboration with the enemy.” In a statement, they called on Afghans to “fight against the corrupt government which is selling the country to America.” This attack brings to light the growing unrest in Afghanistan as the peace process tries to gather momentum. The U.S. and the Taliban reached a deal in February, which includes a potential withdrawal of American troops in exchange for peace commitments from the Taliban. However, Afghan President Ashraf Ghani’s government is not a signatory to the agreement, and many Afghans are against it, fearing it could lead to Taliban rule. The U.S. has urged all parties to “avoid violence and focus on peaceful dialogue.” This comes as the violence in Afghanistan continues to escalate, with both Afghan and international forces reporting over 600 deaths in March alone — a sharp increase compared to recent months. The bombing is also the latest in a series of attacks targeting civilians in the lead up to the 2020 election in the U.S. and the drawdown of foreign troops from the war-ravaged country. The United Nations has warned that with growing instability and the prospect of American withdrawal, the situation in Afghanistan is becoming increasingly volatile.

There has been a succession of warnings for the UK from European officials in the aftermath of the EU referendum, as former allies and key institutions have issued stark assessments of what could be at stake as the British government begins its unprecedented process of disentangling from the 27-nation bloc. From concerns over trade, migration and security to fears of a fractured European single market, the messages from the continent have been unambiguous: Brexit comes with real risks. The warnings began within days of the June 2016 vote, when then European Council President Donald Tusk wrote to Prime Minister Theresa May stating: “We are in uncharted territory… but not because of the UK’s decision. We are in uncharted territory because we are not ready to deal with it.” Since then, repeated statements from German Chancellor Angela Merkel, French President Emmanuel Macron and the European Commission have outlined their anxieties, each adding new dimensions to the growing uncertainty. In recent weeks, European diplomats have hinted at a hardening of attitudes, particularly in Anglophobic quarters in Brussels and Berlin, where the UK's steadfast insistence on controlling its own borders—and effectively the free movement of EU citizens—has been met with resistance. Last week, European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker warned that Britain's decision to prioritise non-EU migration in post-Brexit negotiations could destabilise the continent’s “coordination” and compromise shared economic interests. He added: “The EU’s priorities remain unchanged. We want an agreement, but not at the expense of our security or prosperity.” Meanwhile, German Economy Minister Peter Altmaier said Berlin would not tolerate a Brexit that undermined the integrity of the European single market, a point echoed by French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire, who stressed that Paris would press for “mutual, fully reciprocal” trade arrangements. From behind the scenes, there have also been concerns voiced by trade officials from Belgium and the Netherlands—that vital supply chains for goods like dairy, meat and manufactured parts could be disrupted if the UK does not agree to accept streamlined access to the EU's customs union. The warnings have not been limited to economic issues. In remarks to the European Parliament last Tuesday, High Representative for Foreign Affairs Federica Mogherini raised the alarm over the potential for Brexit to embolden right-wing populist forces across the continent, potentially destabilising the progress made since the 2008 financial crisis.

Venezuela’s Foreign Minister Delcy Rodríguez has made a dramatic and uninvited appearance at an ongoing meeting of the Mercosur trade bloc in Buenos Aires, as diplomatic tensions between Caracas and its regional counterparts continue to escalate. The meeting, held to discuss South American integration and regional cooperation among Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, was abruptly disrupted when Ms Rodríguez arrived unannounced at the venue in an apparent attempt to assert Venezuela’s presence in the bloc it was suspended from in 2017 over concerns about democratic backsliding and humanitarian crisis. Despite.Fatalfreeze from the host, the Argentine government has not commented officially on the intrusion, though sources close to the meeting said ministers were visibly shocked at the minister’s bold and unsanctioned entrance. Ms Rodríguez, known for her sharp rhetoric and confrontational style, was reportedly shouted down by officials who made it clear that her presence was not welcome at the gathering. The incident marks the latest in a series of high-stakes diplomatic maneuvers in which Venezuela has attempted to reassert its influence on the continent, despite being excluded from key regional organizations since the international community condemned the 2018 re-election of Nicolás Maduro as illegitimate. Ms Rodríguez has long argued that Venezuela remains a proud and integral part of Latin America, and has been a vocal critic of what she calls a “coup attempt” against her government, despite widespread sanctions and support for the opposition-led National Assembly. This week’s tensions have been heightened by the recent arrival in Buenos Aires of opposition leader Juan Guaidó, who has been recognized as Venezuela’s interim president by over 50 countries. Mr Guaidó is expected to meet with several South American politicians during his visit, adding another layer of complexity to Mercosur’s ongoing discussions about regional stability and ties with the Caribbean nation. Ms Rodríguez’s unexpected arrival underscores the deep divisions among Latin American leaders over the future of Venezuela. While some, like the leaders of Mexico and Bolivia, have maintained a neutral stance or called for dialogue, others have increasingly aligned with the opposition. The Mercosur meeting, which was intended to be a strategic forum for cooperation, has now been turned into a stage for a symbolic showdown between the Maduro regime and the forces pressing for political change in the country. Analysts say the foreign minister’s actions, while provocative, may have been aimed at maintaining pressure on Mercosur members to reconsider Venezuela’s exclusion.

ITV profits fall 14% as advertising revenue declines    By Sarah Johnson, Business Correspondent  ITV has reported a 14% drop in annual pre-tax profits to £553 million, with a 3% decline in advertising revenues exposing the vulnerability of the traditional broadcaster in the face of growing competition from on-demand streaming services and declining viewership. The struggling media giant attributes the slump to shifting viewer habits, a decline in terrestrial advertising, and increased costs in its push to revitalise its digital offerings. According to the company’s preliminary results, which were released ahead of a formal announcement later this week, profits for the 2018 financial year fell to £553m from the £644m recorded in 2017. The drop reflects an ongoing challenge for the UK’s largest commercial broadcaster, which has seen its dominance in the TV landscape steadily eroded by the rise of platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Sky. While ITV said it had "delivered in a difficult market," the figures highlight an industry in transition. Advertisers are increasingly diverting budgets to digital and social media platforms, where they can target specific demographics with greater precision. This has had a significant impact on ITV's commercial revenue, which traditionally relied heavily on its live prime-time schedule. The company also acknowledged a cost increase tied to its expansion into digital content, including the development and production of programmes for its new streaming service, ITVX. Despite these efforts, the platform’s uptake has been slower than anticipated, and the firm is still in the early stages of accelerating its digital transformation. In a statement, ITV CEO Carolyn McCall said: "We remain focused on evolving our business and delivering long-term value for our stakeholders. While we face a competitive and changing environment, our strategy is clearly defined — to win the hearts of audiences, secure the most compelling content, and leverage the power of technology to thrive in the age of digital disruption." Industry observers say the fall in profits for ITV underscores the challenges faced by traditional broadcasters across Europe. The UK’s Broadcasters’ Audience Research Board (BARB) recently reported a continued decline in the number of homes with a TV licence, as older audiences shift to alternative platforms and younger consumers skip television altogether in favour of online content. In an effort to reverse the trend, ITV has pushed forward with a rebranding of its news and current affairs content, improvements to its live sports broadcasts, and an aggressive line-up of new dramas designed to attract a younger, more digitally savvy audience.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, has revealed he finds the Church of England’s indirect investment in internet payday lender Wonga to be both "embarrassing" and "irritating," as calls for divestment from high-interest lending firms grow louder. The admission came during a rare public statement on the issue, in which Welby expressed clear unease with the church’s financial position amid mounting public concern over the predatory lending practices of Wonga and similar institutions. The Church of England's Investment Office, which manages a £7 billion portfolio, has said it does not directly own shares in Wonga. However, it has admitted that its funds may have been allocated indirectly through third-party investment vehicles that include shares in the firm. In 2013, Wonga attracted widespread condemnation for charging annual interest rates of up to 5,853 per cent, with critics accusing the company of exploiting financially vulnerable borrowers. It has since faced a series of regulatory interventions and public relations crises, culminating in its acquisition last year in a management buyout. While the Archbishop stopped short of ordering the church to divest entirely, he urged for a "re-examination" of all investments held in the portfolio, saying that ethical considerations must not be neglected for the sake of financial return. “It is not good enough for the church – an institution that proclaims justice and care for the poor – to be indirectly supporting businesses that cause harm to the most vulnerable,” Welby said during a speech to church leaders in London. Welby's remarks come at a sensitive time, with the Church of England currently in discussions over its broader ethical investment strategy. Last year, the church voted to divest from fossil fuel companies, a move widely seen as a reflection of its growing commitment to environmental and social responsibility. However, pressure has also been mounting for the church to distance itself from other areas of ethical concern, including arms manufacturing and firms involved in human rights violations. The Archbishop's criticism has been welcomed by campaigners, who say it gives moral impetus to their fight against high-interest lending. The Money Advice Trust, a financial education charity, said in a statement: “The Archbishop is right to question the church’s financial ethics in relation to Wonga. If institutions like the Church of England are willing to demand better from the companies they invest in, it will set a vital precedent for others to follow.”

A Dinner of Disagreement: When Politics Hits the Dining Table   Imagine a long dining table lit by soft candles, a carefully curated menu and a carefully chosen glass of wine. On one side, a staunch left-wing activist, long involved in grassroots movements and social justice campaigns. On the other, a well-known Conservative who spends their weekends on Right to Life marches and has a deep scepticism about the state taking over more services. What happens when these two, from opposite sides of the political divide, sit down face to face, armed not with social media barbs or political manifestos, but with cutlery and conversation? In an increasingly polarised Britain, where political discourse has mostly moved to Twitter rants, short Facebook outbursts, and news headlines that scream more than they speak, such a gathering might seem almost impossible. But over the past few years, a growing movement of citizens has been trying to bridge the widening divide in British politics—not through protests or tactical voting, but through shared meals and civil discussion. The drive behind these “dinner debates” is not to convert, to accuse or to win an argument. It is built on the premise that understanding can often start with presence—not with persuasion. Research has shown that personal face-to-face engagement is among the most effective ways to defuse tensions and break down prejudices. According to a study from the UK's Centre for the Analysis of Social Exclusion, people who engage in direct dialogue with those of differing political views are significantly more likely to feel empathy and less likely to hold extreme positions. For some, these dinners are part of groups such as "Breaking Bread with Enemies," a global initiative that counts meetings between Israeli and Palestinian families, as well as UK-based red and blue families, among its events. In the UK, smaller groups have also taken on the challenge, inviting local Conservatives and Labour supporters to the same table over fish and chips or a Sunday roast. At one such gathering in Bristol last week, Steve, a 58-year-old retired Labour voter, found himself seated across from Caroline, 53, a small business owner who consistently votes Conservative. What followed was an hour of debate, about the national health service, immigration, and even climate change. Though neither gave ground, both left with a nuanced understanding of each other’s values. “I didn’t win any arguments,” said Caroline.

At least 330 million people—nearly a quarter of India’s population—are affected by drought, the government has revealed in statements to the Supreme Court amid growing concern over the crisis gripping one of the world’s most populous nations. The figures, disclosed in a recent hearing, highlight the unprecedented scale of the water and agricultural emergency sweeping across large parts of the country, particularly in the southern and central states of Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu. The Supreme Court, which has taken suo motu cognisance of the situation, is now considering how to best facilitate relief efforts and ensure the government’s response is adequate. The central government admitted that lakhs of people—specifically livestock rearing and small-scale farming communities—are among the worst-hit. Many regions have not seen adequate rainfall for several seasons, leading to the drying up of water sources, withered crops and the widespread collapse of rural livelihoods. In some districts, borewells and reservoirs have been reduced to mere dustbowl depressions in the earth. Farmers, many of whom have been unable to repay loans after multiple crop failures, continue to face escalating debt and, in some tragic instances, have taken their own lives. The Supreme Court has previously intervened to push for early rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge projects in drought-prone areas, and it appears ready to intensify its scrutiny of the government’s mitigation measures. Justice DY Chandrachud, who is presiding over the matter, voiced concern over what he described as a “humanitarian crisis unfolding at an alarming pace,” and urged the Ministry of Agriculture and the environment departments to devise a “time-bound action plan” to avert further catastrophe. In response, officials have highlighted various initiatives being undertaken, including the distribution of drought relief, the supply of fodder and water tankers to villages, and the implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY), a government scheme aimed at enhancing agricultural irrigation. However, for many affected families, these measures have offered only partial relief. The strain on India’s infrastructure is further compounded by the fact that this year’s southwest monsoon was one of the weakest in 25 years, exacerbating the woes of a country with a growing population and demand for water. The issue has also sparked political debate, with opposition parties accusing the central government of neglecting rural infrastructure and failing to address the long-term risk of climate change.

The UK government has unveiled a major housing initiative aimed at tackling the growing crisis in first-time buyer affordability, announcing on Tuesday that it has approved the construction of thousands of specially subsidised "starter homes". This comes as part of a broader strategy to make homeownership more accessible and to address the imbalance between rising house prices and stagnant wages. The new properties, which will be available to buyers aged under 40 and priced at up to £200,000, are set to be built across a range of new developments and existing housing schemes. Communities Secretary James Brokenshire outlined the plan at a press conference, describing the decision as a "game changer" for young people who are struggling to break into the property market. “These homes will give young families and working professionals a real opportunity to establish themselves and plan for the future,” he said. The move is the centrepiece of the government’s revised Housing for Growth White Paper, published earlier this year. Under the terms of the policy agreement, local councils will be required to include at least 20% starter homes in new large-scale developments. The cost of construction will be directly funded by the government, with the homes being sold at a lower price by developers in return for a partial grant. While early supporters welcome the initiative as a step in the right direction, housing experts and opposition leaders have raised concerns. Critics argue that the plan oversimplifies a deeply complex issue and fails to address the root cause of unaffordable home prices—namely, a chronic shortage of housing supply. Shadow Housing Secretary Emily Thornberry accused the government of using "political spin" to distract from years of underinvestment in housing. “This announcement does little to stem the tide of house price inflation being driven by underbuilding and the dominance of the private rental sector,” she said. Within the housing sector, reactions have been mixed. Developers have generally supported the move, seeing it as a potential catalyst for renewed investment in the housing market. Meanwhile, local councils have expressed wariness over the logistics of construction planning and funding allocation. Nonetheless, the government remains optimistic. It claims the plan will provide as many as 20,000 new homes by the mid-2020s and help reduce regional disparities in the availability of affordable properties. More importantly, it aims to send a signal of progress in a year when housing has remained a persistent issue in the national political agenda.

Theresa May Secures Democratic Unionist Support in Landmark Political Agreement   In a decisive move that has reshaped the political landscape, Prime Minister Theresa May has struck a deal with the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to prop up her minority Conservative government. The agreement, brokered after weeks of political uncertainty and two failed votes of no confidence in May’s administration, marks a turning point for British politics. Under the deal, the DUP has agreed to provide parliamentary support to May's government from behind closed doors, ensuring that the Premier can carry out her legislative agenda and pursue her strategy for Brexit. In return, the government has pledged additional funding for Northern Ireland, including commitments of around £1 billion over two years to support the region’s budget, as well as promises on welfare reform and other key issues of concern to the party. The agreement opens the door for the government to avoid further votes of no confidence, which have plagued May since she lost her parliamentary majority in the 2017 general election. It also marks a major political realignment, with the DUP becoming an informal, though not formal, coalition partner in the most significant deal since the 2010 coalition government between the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats. For May, the agreement is a crucial breakthrough in the wake of the November vote in which rebels on her own side forced her government into a technical minority. The DUP – historically one of the closest political allies of the Conservatives on the issue of Brexit – will now play a decisive role in shaping the government’s ability to legislate and deliver on its manifesto principles. However, the move has also raised eyebrows among May's parliamentary colleagues, with some Conservative MPs expressing concern at the implications of entering into what some have described as a "bribery" deal with the fifth largest party in the House of Commons. One source told the BBC that “this represents the lowest point in [the Conservative Party’s] dignified political history,” while others have questioned the precedent it sets for minority government bargains with regional parties. Meanwhile, DUP leader Arlene Foster has called the agreement a “positive step forward” for Northern Ireland and the UK as a whole, though she did not specify whether DUP members would attend Conservative Party events or vote for Conservative candidates at future elections. Political commentators suggest the new arrangement may embolden hardline Brexiteers within May’s government, who had long argued that negotiations with the DUP were necessary to secure stable parliamentary support.

Workers should significantly boost their savings into occupational pension schemes, a two-year Labour Party review has concluded, warning that current contribution rates may leave many unable to retire with financial security. The report, conducted by former shadow chancellor Ed Balls and published ahead of the general election, calls for a minimum increase in employer and employee contributions to help close the so-called “pension gap” and support the long-term viability of retirement savings. The review found that many employees are contributing just 5% to their workplace pensions—far below the 12% of qualifying earnings recommended as a benchmark to afford a decent retirement. It also highlighted that the average pension pot for employees retiring in 2040 will only provide around 55% of the income taken before retirement, far below the 70% seen as necessary for a comfortable standard of living. The findings come as the government faces rising concerns over the sustainability of the current system amid an ageing population and the deferred state pension age. The report called for a coordinated agreement between employers, employees, and unions to “double the ambition” of pension savings, with immediate action to bring the average contribution rate up to at least 10% by 2025 and 12% by 2030. It also recommended that employers contribute more, with many currently meeting only the minimum legal requirements of 3% of payroll costs. “Generational fairness demands that we act now, because the burden cannot be passed on to future taxpayers or left to individual families struggling at retirement,” the report said. The report comes in the wake of growing public unease over the financial insecurity retirement can bring. Surveys have shown that many workers are unaware of how much they need to save or the real risks of under-saving. The government has taken steps—including automatic enrolment in workplace pensions—but Labour argues these measures are not enough without stronger incentives and clearer guidance. The findings have already been praised by some within the pensions sector. Sarah Breeden, chief executive of The Pensions Regulator, said the recommendations “recognise the importance of collective action and long-term planning to ensure the next generation is not left worse off.” However, some business leaders have raised concerns about the financial pressures such an increase could place on smaller firms. Simon Pound, head of business and finance at the CBI, said: “While improving retirement security is a shared goal, any new proposal must balance the long-term need for pension improvements with the immediate financial realties for employers, especially in the post-pandemic economy.”

North Korea’s Fifth Nuclear Test Sparks Global Alarm and Uncertainty   North Korea’s fifth and largest verified nuclear test, conducted on Monday 9 September, has sent shockwaves through diplomatic circles and reignited fears of an escalating nuclear crisis on the Korean Peninsula. The underground detonation, detected by seismic sensors worldwide, is believed to have been of a hydrogen bomb – a more advanced and devastating weapon than the uranium-based devices tested in the past. The move has been widely condemned by the international community, with world leaders, experts, and journalists alike expressing alarm over the direction North Korea’s aggressive military programme is taking. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the North’s state media, announced the test as a "remarkable historical event" and claimed that the "technique of the hydrogen bomb was fully verified through this test." The regime also stated that the detonation would enable the country to defend itself against what it described as a "hostile policy by the U.S. imperialists." However, such rhetoric has been met with skepticism and anger, particularly in South Korea and the United States, where the test is seen as a direct challenge to regional and global security. Japan’s Prime Minister Shinzo Abe was one of the first to respond, calling the test "extremely regrettable" and urging the United Nations to invoke stronger sanctions. Meanwhile, U.S. President Barack Obama warned that North Korea was "testing new technologies that threaten our allies and our national security." The test triggered immediate emergency consultations in Washington, Seoul, and Tokyo, with all three countries considering further measures to counter the growing threat. Adding to the tension, North Korea has recently accelerated its missile development programme, successfully testing a mid-range missile in July and a long-range intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) in July which it declared fully operational. Analysts fear that combining hydrogen warheads with such missiles could eventually enable Pyongyang to target the U.S. mainland and its military bases elsewhere. The recent nuclear test is also a reminder of the limited efficacy of existing international sanctions. Despite being under UN-imposed punitive measures for over a decade, North Korea’s leadership appears undeterred, defying economic pressure to halt its nuclear ambitions. The regime’s ability to conduct such a major test also calls into question the reliability of intelligence regarding its weapons capabilities and intentions. In the wake of the test, Western newspapers have run urgent editorials warning of the dangerous path North Korea is on.

Cameron meets Iranian leader Rouhani in new diplomatic push for Syria peace   In a rare and significant diplomatic engagement, UK Prime Minister David Cameron has held talks with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani at a neutral location on the Turkey-Iran border, as part of a broader European effort aimed at fostering a political resolution to the devastating Syria conflict. The meeting, which took place under strict confidentiality, marks the first direct dialogue between the leaders of Britain and Iran since the UK imposed fresh sanctions against Iran over its nuclear programme in January 2012. Cameron's visit to meet Rouhani was coordinated with German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who also attended the talks. Germany and the UK have been working closely to reinvigorate peace efforts after years of deadlock in negotiations among the international actors involved in the Syrian crisis. Both leaders confirmed the meeting in brief post-summit comments, but provided few details, citing the sensitive nature of the discussions. The meeting is seen by European diplomats as a tactical move, driven by the need to engage all key regional players in resolving the Syrian conflict. With over 400,000 people killed and more than 11 million displaced over the past decade, the need for a diplomatic solution has become increasingly urgent. Rouhani, elected in 2013 as Iran’s first reformist president in decades, is believed to be more open to negotiating with the West compared to his predecessor, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad. A Downing Street spokesperson said the meeting was held "in the spirit of seeking a political settlement to the war in Syria that respects the sovereignty of all nations and addresses the humanitarian catastrophe facing the region." Cameron reportedly stressed the importance of securing a peaceful transfer of power in Syria and a sustained ceasefire, as well as an end to the flow of weapons to the conflict zone. Iran, a key backer of the Syrian government, has been a central obstacle to most Western-backed peace proposals. While Rouhani has not been known to take a direct role in Iran's foreign policy, his presence at the meeting signals a symbolic shift toward greater engagement with the international community at a time when the prospects for any military victory in Syria have receded sharply for all sides. The summit is being held alongside broader international efforts involving the United Nations and the Moscow-led 'Astana' process, which has brought together the Syrian government, Russia, and Turkey.

The Scottish government has launched a fresh review of school meal standards, prompting both support and concern from education and health experts across the country. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon announced the initiative as part of her government’s ongoing commitment to child wellbeing, with ministers claiming it will “modernise and improve the provision of nutritious food for Scotland’s pupils.” The review, which is expected to last six months, will assess existing policies on nutrition, food sourcing, and the role of school caterers. At present, school meals in Scotland are guided by a 2010 Code of Practice, which sets out dietary guidelines and minimum nutritional standards. While the code has been praised for ensuring that children receive balanced meals, critics argue that enforcement is uneven and the standards are no longer fit for purpose. The review’s scope will also include how best to tackle childhood obesity, a growing public health concern in the UK. According to recent statistics, more than 20% of children in Scotland are classified as overweight when starting primary school, rising to over 30% in secondary education. Health campaigners have welcomed the move, urging the government to go further in implementing stricter controls, such as banning processed and high-sugar foods from school menus. In recent years, shortfalls in school meal provision have been highlighted by charitable organisations such as the British Nutrition Foundation and the Food Standards Scotland. Reports have revealed that while most schools aim to meet nutritional standards, funding pressures, inconsistency in food quality, and reliance on processed ingredients remain persistent issues. Education Minister Shirley-Anne Somerville defended the existing standards during a press conference, stating: “We have made improvements in recent years, such as banning soft drinks and promoting fruit and vegetable consumption. But the landscape has changed, and we must ensure our children are getting the best possible start through the meals they receive at school.” The timing of the review has also raised questions. With local authorities increasingly facing budget constraints and rising inflation, some local education officers are worried about the implications for school catering budgets. Councils have claimed that they are already required to stretch limited resources while meeting minimum nutritional benchmarks. Parent groups have been divided. While many support the review as an opportunity to enhance standards, others fear it could result in the closure of school meal programs altogether as academically underperforming lunches struggle to gain popularity with children.

Scotland’s top law officer has warned that a UK government move to proceed with Brexit without consulting the Scottish Parliament would “bypass an important constitutional requirement.” The comment by Lord Advocate James Wolffe came as speculation continues over how the UK government plans to trigger Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty, which would formally begin the process of leaving the European Union. Mr Wolffe, who is the chief legal adviser to the Scottish government, said that not involving Holyrood would not only be “inappropriate,” but could undermine the devolution settlement. His remarks came as First Minister Nicola Sturgeon was expected to set out new plans in the coming days regarding Scotland’s future relationship with the EU, even if the UK as a whole votes to leave. In a statement, Mr Wolffe said the Scottish Parliament must be consulted on Brexit to ensure that the specific constitutional rights of Scotland – including control over areas such as agriculture, fisheries, and education – are not inadvertently lost by a UK-wide vote. "Scotland is a nation within the UK, with a parliament in Edinburgh and a government with responsibility over 50 per cent of public spending,” he said. “If the UK government is to leave the EU, it is essential that Scotland’s distinctive interests are fully understood and that the Scottish Parliament is given the opportunity to contribute to the process." Mr Wolffe's comments echo concerns from SNP Holyrood colleagues and some cross-party voices in the Scottish Parliament, who argue that any decision of constitutional importance – particularly one of such magnitude as Brexit – should not be made in Westminster alone. The issue has dominated political debates in Scotland since the UK announced its intention to trigger Article 50 by the end of March 2017, following a vote in June 2016 that saw Scotland overwhelmingly vote to remain in the EU. Labour’s deputy leader and former Scottish leader, Kezia Dugdale, welcomed the remarks from Mr Wolffe, saying it was “basic respect” for Scotland to be treated as more than a “bit part” in the Brexit process. “The UK government must not ignore Scotland’s voice on a matter that will have such profound consequences for our economy, way of life and our place in the world,” she said. Meanwhile, the UK Foreign Office has yet to explicitly address whether the Scottish Parliament will have a formal role in the Brexit process beyond delivering a devolved response.

Court delays in Scotland ‘easing’ as reform efforts show results   Waiting times for criminal trials in Scotland are easing for the first time in years, according to a new government report that highlights improved efficiency in an area long plagued by chronic backlogs. Judicial and court services ministers have pointed to recent reforms and increased investment as key factors in reversing a trend that had drawn widespread criticism from both the public and legal professionals. A growing number of abortions performed globally are taking place under unsafe conditions, with potentially devastating consequences for women's health, according to new research from leading reproductive health experts. The study, published in  The Lancet  this week, highlights a “disturbing trend” in which the rising demand for abortion — driven by factors including flawed contraceptive use and unmet access to sexual education — is being met by underground and unspecialised providers, often with a lack of medical training. Nearly half of the 56 million abortions estimated to have occurred globally in 2019 took place in unsafe or very unsafe conditions, the report states. The consequences can be severe, ranging from sepsis and excessive bleeding to long-term infertility and, in the worst cases, death. It is reported that around 33,000 women die annually as a direct result of unsafe procedures, with the vast majority in low- and middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Experts warn that while abortion has become legal in many areas — in part due to the increased availability of pills that can end early pregnancies — disparities in access persist. Women in underserved communities often face significant hurdles, including restrictive laws, societal stigma, and inadequate healthcare infrastructure. Many turn to unregulated and informal providers, who may use unsanitary practices or administer incorrect dosages of medication. Dr. Francesca Lorenzo, one of the lead researchers from the World Health Organization, commented: “We are witnessing an increase in self-managed abortions through phone consultations or online orders, which can bring accessibility for some women, but at great risk. These procedures are frequently conducted without proper medical supervision.” In countries where abortion remains heavily restricted, the situation is even more precarious. In Poland and El Salvador, for example, legal bans are so strict that many women resort to dangerous methods to terminate unwanted pregnancies. Even in countries where abortion is legal, a lack of trained professionals or inadequate follow-up care can lead to preventable complications. The report also calls for a greater emphasis on preventing unintended pregnancies through improving access to reliable contraception and sexual health education. Dr. Lorenzo added: “While abortion can be a safe medical procedure, we cannot ignore the reality that too many women are being put at risk. It is not only a health crisis, but a human rights issue.” Downing Street has been urged to prioritise global sexual and reproductive health in the UK's overseas development aid budget, following growing concerns over unsafe abortion rates.

Bonfire Night celebrations across Scotland were overshadowed by a series of alarming and unprovoked attacks on firefighters, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) has confirmed. In what the service described as an unprecedented wave of aggression, crews responded to numerous incidents only to be met with physical assaults or deliberate obstructions at scenes across the country on Friday and Saturday nights. The SFRS reported that over the weekend, firefighters in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Ayrshire, and Aberdeen were subjected to a range of attacks, including being physically struck, spat at, and in one case, hit with a lit flare. The assaults, which the fire service called "deeply concerning", occurred even as crews made every effort to manage bonfire-related emergencies and ensure public safety. Cheshire-born chief officer Jason Orchard, who oversees the SFRS, condemned the behaviour as "a disgrace" and reminded the public that "firefighters are trained to go into danger to save lives and protect property. When they are met with violence instead of thanks, it is both criminal and unacceptable." He added that the attacks, which showed no signs of political motive, had shaken crews and placed them in personal danger, challenging the ethos of public service they are trained to uphold. Assistant chief officer Anne McGinness of Police Scotland said that over a dozen local authorities had reported incidents of anti-social behaviour from the bonfire night displays – many of which, initially peaceful, became chaotic as the night wore on. She warned that those responsible for attacking emergency service workers would face the full force of the law, with police having already launched investigations into multiple cases. One firefighter in Glasgow described an incident in a deprived housing estate where a blaze had broken out after a firework malfunction. As he and his colleague attempted to contain the fire, they were surrounded by a group of youths who attempted to trip them and throw objects such as bottles and stones. Another crew in Edinburgh reported arriving at a scene to find that a bonfire had merged uncontrolled with domestic waste, causing a hazardous situation. They were allegedly told to "get lost" by onlookers, with a further attempt made to push one of the officers. The timing of the attacks has raised concerns among officials, with fire and police services being asked to reassure communities affected by what is a cherished but increasingly volatile tradition. Some local authorities have considered additional measures for next year’s celebrations, including the proposal of stricter licensing for public bonfires and increased police and fire responses.

The British Bankers’ Association (BBA) was repeatedly warned in weekly meetings in 2008—the height of the global financial crisis—that the process by which the London Interbank Offered Rate (Libor) interest rates were being submitted was being “distorted,” the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has revealed. The information, provided in a newly released report, has raised serious questions over the BBA's role in overseeing one of the most important financial benchmarks in the world. Libor, which underpins trillions of pounds worth of mortgages, loans and derivatives, has long been under scrutiny for weaknesses in its methodology. At the time, banks were submitting rates based mostly on internal estimates rather than real transactions. The FCA report shows that in 2008, concerned staff within the BBA’s working group on Libor highlighted the increasing discrepancy between submitted rates and actual interbank lending levels. These warnings were dismissed, with the BBA prioritising stability and consensus over transparency and accuracy. A key message in the FCA summary states that the group “was told on multiple occasions that the process was not working as intended and that rates were being pushed below benchmark levels for inappropriate reasons.” Despite the clear red flags, no significant reforms to Libor’s governance or methodology were enacted until years later, when a scandal erupted over banks submitting false lending data to manipulate the rate for financial gain. The revelation has drawn criticism from MPs and finance watchdogs, who argue that the BBA did not act decisively enough to uphold the integrity of Libor during the turbulent financial period. John Tiong, who led the FCA probe, said the scale of the problem was “underestimated” at the time. “The realisation that Libor was being systematically distorted during one of the worst financial crises in decades is deeply troubling,” he added. The BBA, which is now part of a restructured trade body called UK Finance, has since admitted that it did not do enough to protect the integrity of Libor. In response to the latest findings, a spokesperson said: “We acknowledge the concerns raised in the FCA report and the importance of fixing Libor long before it was eventually phased out.” The move to end reliance on Libor has now been accelerated, with a new rate called the Sterling Overnight Index Average (SONIA) set to replace it. Meanwhile, campaigners and victims of the previous rate rigging scandal—which led to several major banks facing billions in fines—say the new revelations show that institutional failures were more widespread than previously understood.

Oscar Pistorius, the Paralympic sprinter turned murder suspect, appeared in a South African court for the first time since being granted bail over the shooting death of his girlfriend, Reeva Steijn. The double amputee, 27, maintained a sombre expression as he entered Pretoria Magistrates' Court flanked by two bodyguards and his lawyers on Thursday morning. Mr Pistorius was released on 15 million rand (Â£1.2 million; $1.9 million) bail on 10 December, under strict terms including佩戴 electronic monitoring and a curfew of 18:00 to 06:00 . On Thursday, magistrates will consider the possibility of extending these bail conditions and contemplate whether the case should be moved to High Court. The hearing is expected to last up to two hours as the court decides the next stage in the legal process. Mr Pistorius was charged with premeditated murder, among other counts, following the death of Ms Steijn, a 29-year-old model and law graduate, on Valentine's Day weekend. The prosecution alleges that he shot Ms Steijn four times through the door of a lavatory after mistaking her for a home intruder. Pistorius, who stood in the dock holding on to the railing and pacing in the space provided between the defendant's seat and the judge, initially replied with a brief "yes" when asked if he understood the nature of the charges. Ms Steijn’s family, who were in attendance at Thursday's court hearing, have described the athlete in previous statements as the trigger of a man whose rush to judgment caused a tragedy. Some friends had questioned the reasonableness of his account being accepted at face value, but Mr Pistorius has maintained that he did not mean to kill Ms Steijn. Legal experts said the case had gripped a nation already divided between admiration for Pistorius as a national hero and anger at the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The trial is expected to be one of South Africa’s most high-profile and scrutinised to date. Mr Steijn was confined to the lavatory of Pistorius's Pretoria home after being shot at around 21:30 local time on 14 February and died from her injuries the next day. The court will be focusing on whether Pistorius knew the true identity of the person he shot and whether his actions were premeditated. While legal procedures have started, no trial dates have yet been set, but South African media reports suggest it could begin at the end of the month.

Lagos, Nigeria’s largest city and a vibrant economic hub, pulses with a rhythm that is both relentless and intoxicating. The first thing that strikes any visitor—or even local—is the traffic. From the winding, densely packed lanes of Makoko to the sun-blasted expressways of Ikoyi and Victoria Island, the city’s roads are a battleground of honking horns, swerving vehicles, and an almost tribal sense of rhythm that most Lagosians have mastered from a young age. It is a chaos, but one that tells a story—of ambition, of growth, and of the kind of urban survivalism that only the most resilient cities manage to thrive on. The traffic is more than a logistical nightmare; it is the lifeblood of Lagos. On any given day, you’ll see matatu taxis packed to the brim, their drivers weaving between buses, vans, and cars with reckless dexterity. Street hawkers dart across lanes, selling everything from ice-cold plantains to metal buckets and religious trinkets. Children in Western and Islamic schools, some as young as eight, are already experts at reading the flow of traffic, dodging wheels with the grace of seasoned ballerinas. This is the rhythm of Lagos, a city that does not slow down even for its own peril. It is this intensity that gives Lagos its rhythm and energy. Unlike other global megacities that impose order with strict infrastructure, Lagos is organic, chaotic, and almost biblical in its scale of motion and noise. The city’s traffic is not just about movement; it is a symbol of its people. The people are entrepreneurial, suspicious of bureaucracy, and fiercely independent. That same spirit is reflected in the way they maneuver through the city, commanding the roads through instinct and improvisation rather than rules and red lights. For about five million people—mostly young, mostly poor, and all watching for an opportunity—this is where they make their daily life. Whether it is the trader, the student, the architect, the musician, or the politician, everyone here is in motion, chasing something. And at the heart of it is the traffic, the ever-present cacophony that is Lagos waiting to happen. It is not just Lagos’s signature; it is its soul. And as the city continues to grow and expand, it is the one constant that will remain, a reminder that Lagos is a place where nothing ever stands still.

Trouble Over Tradition: Scores of Police Injured in Belfast Riots   A wave of violence erupted in Belfast on Saturday as tensions over a republican band parade spiralled into chaos, leaving 47 police officers injured and highlighting deep-seated sectarian divides in Northern Ireland. The parade, held as part of Belfast’s annual festival season, became the flashpoint for a night of unrest that saw crowds clashing with officers and riot police deployed in a bid to restore order. The parade, led by a predominantly republican marching band, had begun peacefully as it wound through the city centre. However, as the procession approached the flashpoint area of the city near the Falls Road, tensions flared. Residents from unionist communities, who view the parade as provocative, began to block its route. What ensued was a night of violence, with masked youths hurling bricks, bottles and smoke bombs at police lines, and officers in turn using CS gas and water cannon in attempts to disperse the crowds. BBC Northern Ireland reported that several storefronts were damaged and roads were temporarily closed during the turmoil. Ambulances were called to the scene multiple times, and over 20 people were arrested. The violence is being widely seen as a continuation of the long-running "parade disputes" in Northern Ireland, which have flared up in recent years, particularly during key festival periods such as the Twelfth of July – traditionally a staunchly unionist event – and the annual parading season in the city. Unionist politicians and community leaders have called for an immediate inquiry into the events of Saturday night, claiming the parade was "premeditated provocation." On Sunday, First Minister Paul Givan said: "This was not about free speech; it was about stirring up communal tensions. We must not allow such marches to provoke hostility and violence." Meanwhile, Sinn Féin's DUP counterpart, Michelle O’Neill, defended the right of republican groups to take part in cultural parades and condemned the violence as unrepresentative of either the parade or its participants. She urged calm and dialogue: "These incidents serve only to divide us further. We must address the root causes of this division, not hide them behind the chaos." The PSNI has reiterated its commitment to providing safety for all communities, but with tensions running high and relations fraying between various factions, the potential for further violence remains a concern. As Belfast attempts to pick up the pieces, one thing is clear: the city continues to grapple with the ghosts of its past, and the dream of a fully reconciled society remains elusive.

Obama Condemns Senate Stalemate Over Background Checks in Major Rebuke of Lawmakers   In a fiery public response to congressional inaction, President Barack Obama has denounced US senators for blocking a bipartisan proposal aimed at expanding background checks on firearm purchases. Speaking at a primetime event in Illinois on Thursday, the President called the failure of the bill a “betrayal” of the American people and accused his detractors in the Senate of placing political considerations above public safety. The remarks mark a significant escalation in Obama’s campaign to push gun reform, as he faces mounting pressure to deliver substantial policy shifts before the end of his term. The blocked proposal, supported by three-quarters of Americans, would have required universal background checks for buyers purchasing guns at gun shows and from private sellers—categories currently exempt under federal law. Though the bill enjoyed broad cross-party backing, it fell short in a 54-46 Senate vote last month, with 14 Republicans joining a majority of Democrats in supporting it. The measure’s defeat came despite strong advocacy from police chiefs, nonpartisan law enforcement groups, and evangelical leaders—and even the rare support of conservative legislators like Rand Paul. In his speech, President Obama framed the failure as emblematic of a broader dysfunction in Washington. “We live in a country where guns are part of our history, our culture, our Constitution. But we also live in a country where preventable tragedies, like school shootings and domestic violence, are too often met with inertia and obstruction,” he said. “It is not enough to say we understand the pain and anger in this moment. We must act—before more families are shattered, before more lives are lost.” The President made particular mention of the continued influence of the National Rifle Association (NRA), whose campaign against the background checks bill was described as “relentless and misleading.” He accused the group of “exploiting fear and misinformation” and warned that “when guns are pitted against children, the NRA should not expect the American people to stand on the side of gun lobbies.” Earlier in the week, Obama had used the White House’s veto power as a cautionary tool, warning that if he were to sign a major security or budgetary bill without gun reform provisions, he would do so with a pen “hanging over my desk.” His latest remarks suggest that delivering a sweeping gun policy bill may not be the only path forward.

Aviation regulators from Europe and the United States are preparing to question a high-profile hacker whose alleged attempts to access flight deck systems have sparked global alarm and raised urgent questions about the cybersecurity of modern aircraft. The individual, whose identity has not yet been disclosed publicly, is said to have targeted the aircraft’s avionics systems through a flawed in-flight entertainment (IFE) system, raising the terrifying possibility that such vulnerabilities could allow remote interference with flight controls. The incident has triggered a major international response, with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) both confirming that they are investigating the technical and regulatory consequences of the breach. The Russian Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) and other nations are also reportedly monitoring the situation closely. The hacker, who has previously made headlines for demonstrating weaknesses in commercial airplanes, claims to have discovered a software flaw that could allow access to the flight management system (FMS), a key part of an aircraft’s control suite. If this happened in real life — in which a passenger’s device could communicate with the flight deck — the implications would be catastrophic. Reports suggest that simulations shared by the hacker show how, in theory, changes could be made to the plane’s altitude or route from a passenger seat. "This is not just a hypothetical scenario," warned one anonymous aviation cybersecurity expert speaking to the BBC. "There are known vulnerabilities in IFE systems that, in some cases, are connected to the same network as the FMS. Until recently, those connections were not considered a risk because they are air-gapped. Our assessment is that this assumption is increasingly outdated." In response to the revelations, European and American authorities are working alongside major aerospace manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus to conduct their own security audits. Some experts fear that the rapid digitization of aircraft systems — while improving passenger experience and increasing efficiency — may have unintentionally exposed vulnerabilities. The FAA and EASA are expected to meet with the hacker later this week as part of efforts to better understand the scope of the breach and what steps can be taken to prevent similar attempts in the future. As one aviation spokesperson put it: “We don’t look for confrontation when it comes to exposing vulnerabilities — we look for solutions.” The talks are also expected to focus on potential rule changes to better regulate the physical and digital separation of in-flight systems.

Captain Scott Brown has called for Craig Gordon to stay at Celtic, but the 34-year-old goalkeeper now faces a pivotal decision about his future as speculation mounts over whether he will continue at Parkhead or consider an extended break from top-flight football. Gordon, who has been a mainstay in goal for the club for over a decade, is currently sidelined and has yet to make a first-team appearance this season due to injury and form concerns. Speaking ahead of Celtic’s latest match, Brown made it clear that he and his senior teammates are urging their long-time 'keeper to remain at the club. "Craig has given so much to this team and has won so many games for us over the years. He is still a top-class goalkeeper, and we’d love to have him back between the posts," Brown told reporters. However, the captain also acknowledged the difficulty of the decision facing Gordon. "It's a massive call for him. He's in the final few years of his career, and he has to look at what’s best for him in the long term, not just for himself but for his family as well. We’re all behind him, but it’s his call to make, and we need to respect that." Gordon has never expressed a desire to retire, but with only one year remaining on his contract, and Celtic seemingly eyeing potential younger alternatives, the decision has taken on added urgency. Recent reports suggest he has not ruled out stepping away from regular football to extend his recovery time and reassess his goals beyond the pitch. The Glasgow-based press has speculated that the keeper’s form in recent seasons — while still strong in flashes — has not been consistent enough to guarantee a first-choice spot with the club looking to rebuild under a new manager and with ambitious plans for the future. Celtic manager Ange Postecoglou, who joined this summer, has brought a fresh touch to the club but has yet to officially comment on Gordon’s situation. However, it is understood that while the club values Gordon's experience, they are also planning for the long-term and hope to transition goalkeeping responsibilities to younger players in the coming season. Gordon is being tipped as a potential candidate for a role in the coaching or management set-up at the club, should he decide to reduce his playing appearances.

Chief Constable of Merseyside Police, Jane Kennedy, has described the tragic death of a colleague during a high-speed chase in the city as "heartbreaking", saying the officer "didn’t stand a chance” when struck by a stolen car driven at speed. The incident occurred in the early hours of Sunday, as officers pursued a burglar who had fled the scene of a break-in driving a stolen vehicle. The officer, who has not yet been named but is understood to have been in their mid-twenties, was a serving police constable who had been deployed to roadside duties in the hope of catching the chase in his or her infancy. According to Merseyside Police, the driver of the stolen Mini, a 22-year-old man, led officers on a dangerous turkey through residential streets at high speed before narrowly missing a barrier and crashing directly into the officer who had taken up a position to block the suspect’s escape. "This was a collisions at speed – it doesn’t bear thinking about what this happened. Our officer was in his early career, full of promise and dedicated, and didn’t have a chance in the way things unfolded,” Ms Kennedy said in a sombre press conference held in the police station in Bootle, where a minute’s silence was observed. The deadly pursuit has sparked renewed debate about the risks officers take during such incidents, with calls mounting for national guidance – or even a ban – on roadblocks, which critics say put officers in the line of fire. Despite their lifesaving role, solitary roadblocks have already been outlawed by the Metropolitan Police and in many other major forces in recent years. Merseyside officers are believed to have been following a different protocol at the time, possibly based on the commanding officer being split in their view on the best way to pursue the suspect. "These are always split-second decisions, and the right one is hard to call. But I can confirm this officer knew the risks and put themselves in the right place at the wrong time to do their job. That is the mark of a brave officer,” Ms Kennedy said. The suspect, believed to be acting alone, was injured during the crash and has since been arrested and charged with murder, dangerous driving, and theft. He is due to appear in court next week. The death of the officer has left their colleagues, families, and the wider Merseyside community reeling, with vigils planned in various towns across the region.

Shadow Brexit Secretary Sir Keir Starmer has called for a “reset” in Labour’s handling of the legacy of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), following internal criticism of past comments made by prominent Labour figures. In remarks to the BBC, Sir Keir described some of his colleagues’ statements about republicans as “regrettable” and urged the party to move forwards with greater care on an issue that has long been fraught with political tension. The comments came amid renewed scrutiny after several high-profile Labour figures were reported to have referred to the IRA as terrorist organisations or to have backed controversial historical perspectives that have been rejected by Irish political leaders and the Catholic community. Sir Keir, who is Labour’s longest-serving MP and a former Director of Public Prosecutions, said: “The issues of our shared history are complex and sensitive. We must learn from the past, but Labour must also be careful not to alienate communities or inflame tensions with our language and positions.” His comments follow recent criticism of shadow Northern Ireland Secretary Clive Lewis, who was accused of “dismissing the scale of IRA violence” after downplaying its activities during a radio interview. Mr Lewis later apologised and withdrew his comments. Labour is widely seen as having struggled to build trust among nationalist communities in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, with some in the party accused of historically marginalising republicans from decision-making processes. The issue has gained new urgency as the UK and Ireland grapple with the long-term implications of Brexit and the Windsor Framework.
