Sir Keir’s intervention is the latest in a series of efforts to mend fences in what Labour leader Sir Keir also acknowledged was a “sensitive time” for the party. “The Labour Party has to be a party that can talk with respect and dignity to all communities – in Britain and abroad,” he said. “That includes listening to the lived experiences of the Irish people and recognising the pain and progress that have gone into building peace.” The Northern Ireland Office is expected to be handled closely by Labour should they win the next general election, with officials warning that a stable peace process will require balanced and inclusive political dialogue. Sir Keir stressed that Labour was committed to a policy of “no normalisation of violence,” and that its approach to Northern Ireland would be guided by the principles enshrined in the Good Friday Agreement.

A "vicious" fox has sparked a wave of panic in a quiet seaside town in Devon after it herded eight people into a sports club and refused to leave them alone for more than six hours, sparking an unprecedented response from both local residents and authorities. The incident took place in the early hours of Sunday at the Torquay Sports and Social Club in Lower Brixham, with the club’s manager describing the event as “chilling,” a rare but alarming twist in the area's typically peaceful human-wildlife encounters. The fox was first spotted just before midnight near the car park of the club when a group of friends emerged from a late-night drinks session. Witnesses claimed the animal, apparently large and aggressive, began circling people, darting between parked cars and forcing the group to retreat back into the building. When the initial group of three was followed by five more, all trying to leave the premises, the fox appeared to take chase, forcing the entire eight into the club, where they then spent several hours behind locked doors for fear of being attacked. Club manager Elaine Moberley, who assisted those trapped inside, said: “It was like something out of a horror movie. We immediately called the police and the RSPCA, but as it turned out, only the RSPCA had the expertise to deal with the creature. Everyone was extremely distressed. You could hear the fox outside growling, knocking against the door, it was really frightening.” The animal, believed to be a male fox in its prime, was cornered and eventually captured after more than two hours by RSPCA officers using a humane trap. According to a spokesperson for the RSPCA, the fox was taken to a specialist facility for assessment and treatment. “It is extremely rare for a fox to behave in such a manner, and even rarer for it to cause the kind of fear this one did. It may be suffering from some kind of injury or neurological condition,” the spokesperson said. Animal behaviourists have since begun to assess the possible causes of the fox’s aggression. Dr. Matthew Bannister, a local wildlife expert, said such incidents are exceptionally rare but not unprecedented. “In most cases, wild animals become aggressive as a result of being injured or sustained trauma. This fox could have been attacked by another animal, or even shot, and is reacting in a defensive way,” he said.

The Trussell Trust, one of the UK’s largest food aid charities, has revealed that a record number of people required emergency food support last year, with more than 2.1 million three-day emergency food parcels given out to people in crisis across the country. The charity described the figures as a "stark warning" of the continued and deepening cost-of-living challenges faced by families and individuals across Britain. The 2023-24 statistics, published last week, show a 13% increase compared to the previous year, with the number of people supported by the Trust's network of nearly 1,300 food banks reaching three times the amount reported just a decade ago. The charity said the stark rise was driven by rising poverty and the growing number of people living in households where someone’s income is more than 50% below the average, a key threshold in measuring the depth of poverty. The report highlights the human cost behind the statistics, with hundreds of thousands of people, including a growing number of children, needing to turn to charitable food aid simply to survive. Caseworkers at food banks describe stories that are increasingly difficult to comprehend, from families going without heat to ensure they can afford food, to parents skipping meals to feed their children. Nina Jackson, chief executive of the Trussell Trust, said the crisis “is no longer just about food: it’s about people struggling to afford the essentials of life.” She added that the UK was experiencing “a deepening poverty crisis that is hitting the most vulnerable hardest” and called for urgent action from the government. The data also reveals a worrying shift in the scale and speed of the emergency support being provided, with some food banks reporting that they are now opening more frequently and handing out aid more quickly than before. In some communities, food parcels are now being distributed within 24 hours of a referral — a significant and troubling departure from the previous system, which allowed for more time to address underlying issues. The Trussell Trust report attributes the continued reliance on food banks to a range of interconnected economic pressures, including stagnant wages, rising energy prices, and the continued strain of council tax bills on household budgets. It also points to the end of the Universal Credit wait time allowance — which previously gave claimants an initial month’s rent — as having pushed many further into hardship.

The Ancient Egyptians are often remembered for their intricate and elaborate mummification rituals, painstakingly preserving the bodies of pharaohs and nobles in the hopes of ensuring their afterlife journey. But a far less known, yet equally astonishing, aspect of this civilization is the sheer scale of animal mummification — a practice that extended to millions of creatures, from cats and birds to crocodiles and snakes. New research and archaeological discoveries are shedding light on the reasons behind this massive ritual, revealing that these animals were not just pets but were integral to religious practices and spiritual beliefs. In temples dedicated to the gods, particularly during the Late Period and Ptolemaic era (around 664–30 BC), priestly communities mass-produced animal mummies in vast quantities. These creatures, often bred specifically for the purpose, were embalmed, wrapped in layers of linen, and placed in pottery or wooden coffins. Some were even presented by the public — worshippers would give offerings of mummified animals in exchange for divine blessings or to demonstrate piety and devotion. Cats, revered as sacred and associated with the goddess Bastet, were among the most commonly mummified animals, though other creatures — including falcons, baboons, fish and dogs — also featured prominently. Some were found in burial chambers, while others were arranged in enormous caches, such as the 300,000 mummified ibises uncovered in the necropolis of Saqqara. Dr. Salima Ikram, an expert in Egyptology at the American University in Cairo, explains that the commercialisation of the practice was not a sign of disrespect, but rather a reflection of the deep connection the ancient Egyptians held with the spiritual and symbolic significance of animals. “These mummies are not random remains,” she said. “They are the result of a highly ritualised and economically driven system meant to satisfy the religious needs of both the priesthood and the people.” The scale of the practice has also raised debates among Egyptologists. Some argue that it was an act of devotion, while others have suggested that the mass production could have been motivated by profit. Either way, it is clear that the Ancient Egyptians did not limit their mummification to humans — they extended their rituals to include a diverse and astonished array of animals, each with its own place in the intricate tapestry of their spiritual life. As more tombs are discovered and studied, our understanding of this phenomenon continues to grow, offering a deeper insight into the beliefs and practices of one of the world’s most enduring civilisations.

Sue Innes, the partner of the late motorcycle medic Dr John Hinds, has expressed the hope that the proposed emergency response unit in his name will serve as a fitting tribute to the man she described as an “incredibly courageous” and “incredible” individual. Dr Hinds, a 51-year-old paramedic and respected member of the community, tragically lost his life while on duty in 2021 after a collision with a delivery van. He was one of the pioneers of BURN – the Birmingham Urban Response Project, a crew of highly-skilled, rapid-response medics who attended ambulance calls on motorbikes to get through city traffic more quickly. “I believe there could be no better legacy for my incredible other half than saving lives,” Mrs Innes said, speaking at an event to mark the progress of the new Dr John Hinds Response Unit, which is being funded by the Blue Light Living Foundation in collaboration with the West Midlands Ambulance Service. Dr Hinds was much-loved not just for his professional dedication, but for the way he conducted himself off the back of the motorbike. Former colleagues describe him as a “ray of sunshine, a joker, a jokester,” who never failed to make those around him feel at ease. The proposed unit, named in honour of Dr Hinds, is set to be staffed by paramedics – likely to include other motorcycle medics – who will respond to emergencies in high-traffic areas of Birmingham and surrounding cities. The aim is to continue the legacy of fast, efficient, life-saving care in a way that Dr Hinds would have endorsed: innovation, compassion, and community. The memorial fundraising campaign for the unit is now over 80% of its £500,000 target, thanks in part to support from the public and statutory bodies. Mrs Innes, who continues to be a vocal advocate for the idea, said she is heartened by the outpouring of generosity and the recognition of her partner’s work. “The community has been amazing,” she said. “John gave so much of his time and heart, and it’s deeply moving to see people giving back in his name. That’s the kind of person he was. Selflessly trying to help others.” Dr Hinds’ death left a profound impact not only on his partner and family but on the emergency services community as a whole. The West Midlands Ambulance Service has since reiterated its commitment to supporting the line of work Dr Hinds was so instrumental in advancing.

If you find yourself rolling your eyes at the sight of potholes left unfilled for months, or watching crumpled up leaflets advertizing dubious 'services' blow around your local park, you're not alone. A growing number of residents across the UK are fed up with the way their local councils are running things — and for good reason. Complaints about disorganisation, bad communication, and a perceived lack of accountability are on the rise. A recent survey by the Local Government Association found that nearly 60% of people believe their local authority is failing to meet basic standards in areas like waste collection, street maintenance, and public safety. Some of these issues are down to funding shortfalls, as councils face ever-tighter budgets, but many people argue that inefficiency and poor management are also to blame. In places like Manchester, London, and Birmingham, incidents of fly-tipping and neglected open spaces have turned community forums into battlegrounds for residents demanding better service. "We've been asking for action for years. They always say 'we're aware, thanks for your feedback,' but nothing changes," said Claire Thompson, a resident of Walsall, West Midlands, who recently joined a public petition protesting the closure of local libraries. "It’s like they’re out of touch with what the people they’re supposed to serve actually need." The blame doesn’t just rest with national funding – many critics point to internal mismanagement and political infighting within local government. Town halls have been accused of awarding dubious contracts to firms with limited provenance, and at times been caught up in scandals involving questionable financial decisions. Meanwhile, the system of local elections, which are meant to provide a democratic check and balance, is struggling with a lack of engagement and an unattractive field of candidates in many areas. "It’s easy to vote in a general election, but when the real decisions are made closer to home, people don’t always know who to vote for or why it matters," said electoral expert Dr. Ruth Beaumont from the University of Nottingham. "That needs to change – people have to feel their local representative is holding the council to account." So, what can you do when you’re fed up? As one disillusioned resident put it: “We've been shouting into the void long enough – maybe the time has come to stop accepting things as they are.” Whether it's writing letters, joining community groups, or running for office, more citizens are considering taking action in the hope of turning the tide against the local council’s worst habits.

Shadow business secretary Chuka Umunna has hinted at the possibility of one day competing for the leadership of the Labour Party, though he stressed that he hopes no such vacancy will materialise in the near future. In an interview ahead of a major parliamentary debate on economic reform, Umunna, 43, suggested that while he has not ruled out the prospect, his priority remains fulfilling the role handed to him by the current leadership under Jeremy Corbyn. "I would not say I would ever definitively rule out participating in a leadership contest, but I hope that it is not necessary in the near term," he said. "There's still a lot of work to be done in rebuilding Labour's platform and bringing our party together around the values that have always united us." Umunna’s remarks come at a time of heightened speculation about Labour’s internal direction, following the general election in June, which saw the party gain seats but fall short of assembling a majority government. Many have been watching Umunna closely, as a moderate voice within the party, and his potential leadership bid is seen as a possible turning point for Labour’s political identity. A former economics graduate from the University of Edinburgh, Umunna entered parliament in 2010 as a rising star within the party. Hailing from London’s Bexleyheath, he has long been associated with the left-wing Fabian Society but is often cited as a rare figure who can bridge Labour’s traditional and more centrist wings. His experience as chair of the Select Committee on Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy, along with his involvement in Labour’s Shadow Cabinet, has given him a high public profile. He has been a vocal advocate for investment in technology and manufacturing, arguing that these sectors will be vital to the UK’s future in a post-Brexit economy. When asked whether he felt the current Labour leadership had achieved enough to prepare the party for what he described as “the next decisive political phase,” Umunna replied cautiously. “We have laid a strong foundation, and Jeremy has galvanised much of the party. But leadership is not a one-person show. It requires coherence, unity, and a clear mandate. I hope the party can continue to move forward in a stable and focused way without needing a leadership contest.” His comment was interpreted as both a show of support for Mr Corbyn and a slight repositioning of his own ambitions away from the spotlight on the leadership race.

Lincoln Leads Golden Globe Race as Spielberg's History Drama Emerges as Front Runner   The release of Steven Spielberg’s  Lincoln  has ignited a firestorm of critical and award-season anticipation, with the historical drama now emerging as a frontrunner at this year’s Golden Globe nominations. The film, based on the Pulitzer Prize-winning book by Doris Kearns Goodwin, chronicles the political and moral challenges faced by Abraham Lincoln in the final months of the American Civil War as he fought to pass the 13th Amendment, abolishing slavery in the United States. Currently, the film is widely seen as the strongest contender in the best drama category, with Oscar-winning screenwriter Tony Kushner earning strong praise for his adaptation and Daniel Day-Lewis delivering what critics are already hailing as a career-defining performance as the 16th American president. Lionsgate, which acquired the rights to distribute the film in the UK and Ireland, described the early response to  Lincoln  as “overwhelming” and has delayed its UK theatrical release to February, no doubt in anticipation of the building awards buzz. The film arrives hot on the heels of previous Golden Globe and Oscar successes like  The Social Network  and  12 Years a Slave , both of which went on to historic Oscar wins. At its core,  Lincoln  is a deeply political film, focusing on the intense power struggles within Congress and the executive branch, as well as the personal toll the presidency took on Lincoln and his family. Spielberg, who previously visited the American Civil War with  Saving Private Ryan  in 1998, has once again transformed history into a gripping cinematic experience. The Golden Globes, handed out by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association and announced later this month, have long served as a bellwether for the forthcoming Oscars. In recent years, Golden Globe winners have gone on to win key Academy Awards categories, and with  Lincoln  receiving early praise and industry support, speculation is rife that the film may dominate the ceremony. However, it will face stiff competition. The Oscar-winner  Zero Dark Thirty , the politically-charged  Argo , and Queen of the Arthouse Alfonso Cuarón’s deeply moving  Gravity  also feature among the early predicted nominees. British actor Daniel Day-Lewis, whose work in  There Will Be Blood  and  Lincoln  has already garnered three Oscars, is seen as a near-certainty for his Golden Globe trophy line in the Best Actor category.

Theresa May Makes ‘Strong Commitment’ to Rights of EU Citizens in Post-Brexit UK   Prime Minister Theresa May has made a "clear and direct" commitment to securing the rights of EU citizens living in the UK after Brexit, attempting to reassure thousands who have grown increasingly anxious about what the country’s exit from the European Union might mean for their livelihoods and futures. Speaking at the Conservative Party conference on Thursday, Mrs. May outlined a vision that sought to underpin policy with emotion as much as political pragmatism, calling EU nationals who have made their homes in Britain “a vital part of our national story, of our society and of our economy.” Mrs. May pledged that the UK government would go to “whatever lengths are necessary” to ensure that EU citizens currently living in Britain are not placed at risk following the formal Brexit process. Her comments came amid mounting pressure from pro-European and business leaders, as well as growing unease among the 3 million EU nationals currently residing in the UK. The Prime Minister reiterated a previous government statement that the UK would not require these individuals to reapply for residency after the UK leaves the EU, directly countering recent suggestions from some-quarters of the Leave campaign that unrestricted immigration from Europe should not be a post-Brexit policy. “Let me say clearly: we want to provide reassurance and clarity," Mrs. May said. "Once the UK leaves the EU, I want and I intend for these citizens to be able to remain in our country and to carry on their lives as they have done for years.” The announcement, which followed behind-the-scenes diplomatic efforts and a warning from the European Parliament that a rush to settle the rights of EU citizens in the UK could derail Brexit negotiations, marked a turning point in the government’s approach to one of the most contentious and human aspects of Brexit. It echoes similar assurances from Chancellor Philip Hammond, who recently said he expected no significant changes to the rights of EU nationals currently in the UK, provided negotiations run smoothly. Mrs. May’s speech was also notable for her acknowledgment of the emotional toll the ongoing Brexit debate has taken on EU citizens. She said the government had received numerous messages from them, many expressing “concern, confusion and fear over what might come next.” Her hope, she said, was that the government’s actions would do "more than simply set out a policy — this is a message of welcome and appreciation.”

What happened to Jacob Rees-Mogg's tax return? The big question swirling around government   A mystery is unfolding in Westminster that has drawn audible gasps from MPs, baffled journalists and prompted a hint of unease from Number 10. Where is Jacob Rees-Mogg’s tax return? The Conservative former Brexit Secretary and current member of the House of Lords is one of the most prominent figures among the so-called "Chipping Sodbury Tax Discrepancy" story from last year, where financial services firm Citizens Advice found a supposed "£2 billion black hole" in tax demand letters during the 2019 winter. At the time, the claim united politicians across the spectrum in outrage and the government scrambled to explain how HMRC appeared to have misplaced thousands of assessments for high-earning residents. Now, more than a year later, the question remains: Why has Rees-Mogg’s 2018 tax return never materialised? As details of prime ministerial decisions are frequently delayed for decades, and Statements of Financial Interest from MPs remain mired in discretion, the issue has been quietly excluded from public view—until now. Last week, under parliamentary questions tabled by Labour MP Sir Adrian Bailey, as well as cross-party transparency advocates, it has become clear: Rees-Mogg's tax return for the year ending April 2018—when he was a prominent and visible minister—was never submitted. His office confirmed he had not submitted one, and that he was not subject to the tax return requirement for that year. When pressed further, Spokesperson for the Exchequer Services Department could not give a clear reason why—only that the law at the time did not require it. But that answer has done little to quiet the chatter in government. Ministers are now reportedly questioning what such a lack of transparency says about the ability of a senior civil servant to maintain trust with the public and the press. The unavailability of Rees-Mogg’s tax documents is being treated by some in Whitehall as a case study in bad practice by a man who has long relied on his own arcane, aristocratic enthusiasm for tradition and procedure. Meanwhile, opposition leaders and commentators have seized on the apparent gap in the public record. "This is not the first time the government has failed to be transparent where it matters," said Labour's shadow chancellor, Rachel Reeves. "When prominent MPs and civil servants refuse or fail to submit tax returns in a timely manner, it sows further mistrust in a system that many already believe to be elitist and unaccountable."

Being overweight cuts dementia risk, major study finds   In a surprising twist to long-standing health advice, a groundbreaking study has found that being overweight may protect against dementia. The research, conducted by an international team of scientists and published in  Alzheimer’s & Dementia: the Journal of the Alzheimer’s Association , is the largest and most detailed examination to date of the relationship between body weight and cognitive decline. The findings challenge existing public health recommendations and raise fresh questions about the complex link between weight and brain health. The study, led by researchers from the University of Queensland and involving more than 1.3 million people from 19 different countries, concluded that individuals categorised as overweight had a 20% lower risk of developing dementia compared to those with a normal weight. The results showed no significant increase in risk for overweight individuals, and in some cases—even for those in the obese category—there was a marginal reduction in the likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s and other dementias. Dr. Claire McEvoy, lead author of the study and a researcher at the University of Queensland, said the results were both unexpected and thought-provoking. “Despite the well-known risks of obesity for cardiovascular disease and diabetes, we found that excess body weight did not correspond to an increased risk of dementia. In fact, being overweight may offer some form of biological resilience against neurodegenerative processes,” she said. The research team, which included scientists from institutions in the UK, Sweden, and the US, analysed data through a method known as Mendelian randomisation, which uses genetic variants to infer causality between risk factors and diseases. This approach helps to rule out lifestyle confounders such as diet and physical activity, offering a more accurate assessment of body weight’s direct impact on brain health. While the findings do not suggest people should gain weight to reduce their dementia risk, the study highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the disease. “This shouldn’t be taken as licence to ignore weight management entirely. Obesity, of course, comes with serious risks. Our work points to the possibility that metabolic health and fat distribution—alongside overall weight—play a role in cognitive outcomes,” explained Dr. McEvoy. Professor Simon Lovestone, of the Dementia Research Centre at University College London and one of the study’s co-authors, added: “The relationship between brain health and body weight is not as straightforward as we once thought.

Fifteen years have passed since a study published in the prestigious medical journal The Lancet by Dr Andrew Wakefield and his colleagues first linked the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine to the development of autism and bowel disease. Though the study was retracted in 2010 after it was revealed that Dr Wakefield had acted with “dishonesty and irresponsible” conduct, the damage had already been done. The research, though heavily discredited and widely condemned, has had a lasting impact on public health, contributing to declining vaccination rates and a resurgence of preventable diseases. Dr Wakefield's research claimed that some children showed signs of autism after receiving the MMR jab. The paper sparked global concern, prompting parents to delay or refuse the vaccine, which protects against three highly infectious and potentially fatal diseases. Ten of the 12 co-authors of the original study later withdrew their support for its findings, and in 2010, The Lancet formally retracted the paper after a formal inquiry found that the research was “fraudulent and ethically unacceptable.” The original claims were not supported by subsequent large-scale studies over the following decades, which have overwhelmingly shown no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Despite this, the fear persists in some communities, often due to misinformation perpetuated by anti-vaccination activists and unreliable websites. This has led to preventable outbreaks, such as the measles epidemic in Europe in 2018-2019, which was the worst in over two decades. The World Health Organization (WHO), the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the UK's National Health Service have all reiterated the safety and efficacy of the MMR vaccine. In fact, being vaccinated is still considered the best way to avoid the serious complications of measles, mumps and rubella, such as encephalitis, deafness and miscarriage. Public health officials are concerned that the misinformation era, fuelled by social media and distrust of scientific institutions, has made it even harder to convince parents to vaccinate their children. “The legacy of the Wakefield paper was not just the mistrust of the MMR vaccine, but mistrust of immunisation as a whole,” said Dr Zoe Metcalf, a public health expert speaking at a recent medical conference. As the 15th anniversary of this controversial publication passes, the wider implications go beyond one scientific paper. It serves as a stark reminder of the power of misinformation in the digital age and the need for strong, evidence-based communication to protect global health.

Hamilton Academical moved off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership after a gritty 1-1 draw with Ross County at New Douglas Park, despite being reduced to 10 men for more than an hour. The result preserved their unbeaten record in 2024 and allowed them to collect a vital point that elevates them above Kilmarnock in the relegation play-off battle. The hosts started brightly and took the lead in the 12th minute when captain Steven Lodwick volleyed in from Timon Wellens’ cross, pulling off a fine individual effort to send the home fans into raptures. The goal gave Hamilton a deserved lead, but it was short-lived. Ross County, riding high in the table, responded with resilience and equalised just seven minutes later through captain Barry Croom, whose clinical finish from a well-worked move levelled the score and ignited the visitors' supporters. What made the remainder of the game harder for Hamilton was an ill-judged challenge by defender Michael Devlin in the 34th minute, which saw him shown a second yellow card for a professional foul. The dismissal immediately changed the complexion of the match, and County had the better of the next half-hour, with Hamilton relying on their organisational strength to defend stoutly as they were pressed on the back foot. Despite being a man down, Hamilton's relentless spirit – particularly from skipper Lodwick, who led by example – allowed them to withstand a barrage of County pressure and remain in the match. Goalkeeper Brian Easton was called into action on multiple occasions in the second half, making a crucial double save in the 72nd minute to deny a potentially decisive goal from substitute Jordan Roberts. County, frustrated and with their energy beginning to wane, struggled to break down a resolute Hamilton side. The hosts, meanwhile, attempted to draw level themselves but lacked the cutting edge in the final third. Substitutes Billy McKay and Alan Dunne threatened late on but could not find a winner for the home side. As the final whistle blew, both sets of players were to the ground in celebration. For Hamilton, the point could prove crucial in their survival mission, while County extended their unbeaten run to five games. Manager Martin Canning praised his team’s resilience after the match. "This is the character we’ve shown all season, especially with 10 men," he said. "We were under immense pressure and our lads stood up to it.

The family of a man who died in police custody in Glasgow has raised urgent concerns about Scotland’s handling of such cases, backing calls for a full government review of all deaths in police custody across the country. The incident, which has sparked renewed debate over policing procedures and oversight mechanisms, has drawn widespread attention after the family claimed that systemic failures led to the preventable loss of life. The deceased, identified as Lee Ayres, was taken into custody on a mental health-related matter by Police Scotland earlier this month. His family has since said they were not informed of his condition prior to his death and that the police response was “woefully inadequate.” The family’s lawyer, Sharon Wilson, said they believe the system is failing vulnerable individuals and the government must act now to implement real change. Calls for a review have also come from members of Scotland’s Parliament and rights organisations, who argue that the current system is not transparent or effective enough to prevent future tragedies. Labour’s Caroline Lindsay highlighted the lack of public confidence in the current process, stating, “Families are left in limbo and too often we see no justice delivered for the victims or the people who loved them.” Despite repeated assurances from Scottish ministers that current investigations into such cases are thorough, critics say the independent reporting to the Procurator Fiscal and the use of inquests do not provide the level of accountability or reform that is needed. The family of Mr Ayres has called for the introduction of an independent national register of deaths in custody and an end to restrictions on families’ access to vital information. A spokesperson for the Scottish government said they are “listening carefully to the concerns being raised” and would consider all options to ensure justice is served. Meanwhile, the Police Federation is under pressure to explain why the incident did not trigger a call for reform sooner, given the string of similar cases over recent years. As the story continues to draw attention, it adds to a troubling pattern of deaths in custody across the UK. Advocacy groups have warned that without urgent action to improve transparency, accountability, and response protocols, incidents like Mr Ayres’ will continue to strain public trust in the justice system. The family said they want their loved one’s death to serve as a catalyst for meaningful reform, not just another number in a tragic series.

Ziggy Gordon admitted he was “gutted” not to sign off from Hamilton Academical with a late winning goal as he prepares to decide on his future after leaving the club. The forward, who was a cult hero among fans for his versatility and relentless work ethic, marked his final appearance for the Accies with a display of grit and determination at Newton Park on Saturday. However, despite his efforts, the team fell to a 2-1 defeat against Falkirk, and Gordon was left reflecting on what could have been. Gordon’s future lies in North America, where he has been linked with a move to the United Soccer League (USL), but details of his transfer have yet to be confirmed. Known for his no-nonsense style on the pitch and his lovable personality off it, Gordon has left a lasting impression during his time at the club. Speaking after the match, the 29-year-old said he had approached his final game with a combination of nerves and excitement. “It’s been an emotional week in a lot of ways. I wanted to finish on a high, obviously. I wanted that goal, but it just wasn’t to be,” he told BBC Alba. “I’m proud of the way the lads and I tried to give something back today. We went out there for the fans and gave it our all.” Gordon, who joined Hamilton in 2014 and became one of the club’s most consistent performers, confirmed he would be making his departure at the end of the season. “I’ve been here four great years, and I’ve made friends for life. That’s what it’s all about at the end of the day. The club will be in safe hands and it’s time for a new challenge.” Fans are already speculating about how Gordon will be remembered at the club. With 83 appearances and 23 goals to his name, he is among the most popular players in Hamilton’s recent history. His departure has left a void on the pitch and in the dressing room. Earlier in the week, players, fans and staff gathered for a farewell lunch at the club’s training ground, where Gordon was presented with a signed cap and a framed photo of himself in a Hamilton jersey. Captain Steven Fletcher described Gordon as “one of the best pros” he’d played alongside, praising his consistency and commitment.

A tragic love triangle may have played a role in the death of a young soldier at Deepcut Barracks in Surrey, an inquest has heard. The 18-year-old recruit, whose identity has not yet been released, was found dead in 1995 at the military base, a case that has long been mired in controversy and unanswered questions. The inquest, which recently resumed its proceedings, heard new evidence suggesting that the recruit had been involved in a romantic relationship with one fellow soldier, while recently ending a relationship with another, creating a complicated and emotionally charged situation inside the barracks. Lewisham Crown Court has been told that the girl had been part of a complex romantic dynamic during her short time at the base, which only lasted a few weeks before her death. One boyfriend, with whom she had left a relationship shortly before her arrival at Deepcut, had shown concern for her welfare in the aftermath of her transfer. Meanwhile, at the barracks, she had reportedly entered into a relationship with another soldier. The details emerged in testimony from a close confidante and from letters stored in the young recruit’s belongings, which offered insight into her inner turmoil and personal struggles. Coroner Jonathan Teverson presiding over the inquest said he was seeking to establish the full context surrounding the recruit’s death, including whether the pressures of military life, the emotional toll of the relationships – and the possibility of mistreatment or bullying – had contributed to her demise. The case has reignited calls for a full and independent investigation into what happened at Deepcut Barracks, which has already seen five other recruits found dead under suspicious circumstances over a 10-year period. The boyfriends mentioned in the court proceedings have not been named, as the investigation is ongoing. The incident has once again stirred public outrage and raised concerns about the treatment of young recruits in the British Army, particularly those who are vulnerable and unsure of where they fit in the brutal environment of basic training. The Ministry of Defence has issued a statement offering its ‘deepest condolences’ to the family of the recruit, while confirming that it is cooperating fully with the inquest. This tragic chapter in the long-running Deepcut saga highlights the emotional challenges faced by young recruits and raises renewed questions about what young people are asked to endure in the military system. As the inquest continues, families of all those lost at Deepcut remain hopeful that the truth will finally come to light.

A cargo ship that spent 19 days stranded in the Solent after developing a significant list has been found to have been in an “unstable” condition when it left port, according to a new report by the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA). The vessel, the  MS Létocart , became a focal point of concern and operation after it capsized on one side by nearly 50 degrees as it approached the Solent—a strait separating the Isle of Wight from mainland England—on 22 August, pulling into roadways and prompting extensive logistical efforts to stabilise the situation. The MCA revealed in its findings that the ship was already in a compromised condition when it departed fromバルセロナ, Spain. Onboard stability calculations had been miscalculated, and insufficient ballast had been loaded, contributing directly to the instability that led to the ship's dramatic lean. This raised serious questions about the safety procedures followed by the company and port authorities. The  Létocart , which was carrying scrap metal worth an estimated £20 million, became stuck near Cowes and necessitated a costly and complex salvage operation involving over 1,000 personnel and specialist equipment. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency confirmed that water entered the vessel as early as 14 August—five days before the ship reached British waters—despite no initial alarms being raised by the crew or operators. Government officials and maritime safety experts are now scrutinising the cargo ship's operators and the regulatory oversight in Barcelona. The report has called for greater vigilance in pre-departure assessments and for more stringent enforcement of international maritime safety standards. Environment Minister Andrew Griffiths said: “This is a sobering reminder of the dangers of inadequate safety checks in the maritime sector. We must ensure that such crises are never repeated, not just for the safety of our coastlines but for the sailors on board and the communities affected by such incidents.” The ship was eventually unmoored in early September and towed for dismantling. However, the incident has led to renewed calls for reform in maritime governance and increased penalties for breaches of stability and ballast guidelines. The report is expected to be used as a case study in future training of maritime engineers and port officials. Local authorities in the Isle of Wight have also raised concerns over the additional strain placed on emergency services and the environmental impact of the operation.environment ministers have pledged to work more closely with French and Spanish agencies to improve cross-border maritime safety protocols.

In a bold move to reshape the future of aviation in South Africa, South African Airways (SAA) has launched an online recruitment drive for cadet pilots, with the aim of bolstering the ranks of a struggling national airline. The initiative, launched in mid-August, constitutes the latest in a string of efforts by the government-owned carrier to revive its dwindling fortunes and restore public confidence in the organisation. The advertisement invites applications for basic flight training, with ambitious plans to groom the next generation of South African pilots to lead the country’s skies. With SAA currently under financial distress and the subject of extensive bail-out discussions with the South African government, the airline’s decision to invest in pilot training is seen as a long-term strategy to revitalise its human capital and secure its future. The move also underscores the importance placed by policymakers on protecting the national carrier, which has become a symbol of the country's post-apartheid history and its ambition to serve as a continental gateway. The recruitment drive comes at a critical juncture for SAA, which has been grappling with chronic financial losses, flight cancellations, and a declining fleet. Formerly a proud flagbearer of African aviation, the airline has faced a consistent erosion of competitiveness in recent years, partly as a result of mismanagement and escalating operational costs. The launch of a cadet pilot programme is a first of its kind for SAA – historically, new pilots have been sourced from commercial flying schools or foreign airlines – and signals an attempt to take matters into its own hands. Under the programme, successful candidates will be put through a structured training process that includes both theoretical and flight-based components. While financial details have not been made public, reports suggest that the government is supporting the initiative as part of its broader plans to recapitalise SAA, which is expected to receive approximately R15 billion in funding over the next 18 months. The pilot cadet initiative has been met with cautious optimism by aviation analysts and industry insiders. While many welcome the move as a step in the right direction, concerns remain about SAA’s broader challenges. “Training new pilots is essential for any airline, but it needs to be supported by wider reforms and strong management,” said one aviation expert. The National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa (NUMSA), which represents SAA workers, has also weighed in on the issue, saying that it supports any initiative that prioritises employment and skills development for young South Africans.

The suspended chief executive of Lancashire County Council, Nick Goddard, will not receive a financial settlement after it was confirmed that he had left the authority by “mutual consent” more than a year ago, the council has revealed. Mr Goddard, who had been the authority’s chief executive for over 11 years, was suspended in October 2023 amid an investigation into alleged misconduct. Since then, speculation over the terms of his eventual departure—and whether he would receive a financial package—has dominated local political discourse. In a brief statement released this week, the council confirmed that Mr Goddard had left the county council “in line with prior agreements” and that no additional payment had been made beyond the terms of his employment contract. The statement said the council had acted “in the best interests of the organisation and its residents.” Mr Goddard, a former senior officer of Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council, had been at the centre of a long-running saga involving allegations of poor financial decisions and lack of transparency in his management style. Councillors from both Labour, who hold overall control of the authority, and the Lib Dems—Lancashire’s official opposition—had called for clarity over the nature of his departure. A council source added: “At no point has there been any financial settlement paid to Mr Goddard, and the council is committed to ensuring that public funds are used appropriately, and that all actions are taken transparently.” The news of Mr Goddard’s departure under non-settled terms has been welcomed by the council’s leader, John Fitzpatrick, who said: “This resolution ensures that the council can move forward without unnecessary expenses and puts the focus back on delivering vital services to the people of Lancashire.” The decision to allow Mr Goddard to leave without a compensation package follows a period of increasing pressure on local authorities to demonstrate fiscal responsibility in light of budget cuts and rising demand for public services. Political activists and local media had highlighted concerns over potential precedents for senior executives being bailed out after controversial tenures. Mr Goddard’s exit marks the end of a turbulent chapter for Lancashire County Council, which has faced a string of financial crises and internal governance problems over the past decade. He has not commented on his departure or the nature of his relationship with the authority. The council has now entered a transition period, with an acting chief executive in place until a permanent replacement is appointed.

Young England stars ‘complacent’ and need to play more, says Harry Redknapp   England’s youth players may be technically gifted and physically strong, but former manager Harry Redknapp has warned that many lack the maturity and discipline to follow in the footsteps of past greats. Speaking in a recent interview, Redknapp urged the country’s most promising talents to treat their early success with humility and to use every opportunity to sharpen their skills. The ex-West Ham and QPR manager, who has served as an FA advisor, pointed to a worrying trend among emerging English stars, saying many “think they have made it.” Redknapp stressed that without extended experience at the top club level, these players risk slowing their development and falling behind international peers. “There’s no doubt our young lads are better now than they were a few years ago, but I still think there are too many of them who get the call-up to an Under-21 or England team and get complacent,” he said. “They need to keep working hard and not get distracted. Football doesn’t wait, and if you’re not careful, you’ll fall behind.” Despite their technical abilities, Redknapp highlighted a consistent theme: insufficient minutes in competitive matches. “They’ve still got to play more club games. You can watch a million clips, train every day in the best environments, but nothing beats the pressure of a Premier League or Champions League game,” he added. Redknapp’s comments come as England continues to grapple with producing a generational talent capable of leading the national team into the next era. While the Premier League offers a high standard of football, the former West Ham boss believes some clubs are still reluctant to give young players the starting roles they need. “We used to play our young players out of position and about five or six to a team, just to get the minutes in. It wasn’t always perfect, but at least it gave them experience and the chance to fail and learn,” he said. “Some clubs now put the development of players above winning at all costs. That’s great in principle, but if you don’t give them the run of the pitch, how can they expect to thrive on Saturday afternoons?” The issue of youth development has been a hot topic in the footballing world in recent years, with England's League Football Education board launching updated academies regulations aimed at improving player goalds.

Manchester United have already begun planning for a potential return of Paul Pogba, less than a year after the former midfield talisman departed for Juventus, according to sources close to the club. The revelation comes as United continue their rebuilding project under manager Erik ten Hag, who has stressed the need for consistent central midfield strength. Pogba’s £89m exit in August 2019 marked one of the most high-profile departures from Old Trafford in recent years, but speculation has since swirled about a possible reunion between the 29-year-old and his former club. With the Italian giants likely to face financial constraints under new ownership and Pogba’s contract set to expire in 2024, the possibility of re-signing the French international is being seriously evaluated by United’s board. “They’re starting to map out how they could bring him home,” one insider revealed to The Guardian. “It’s not in the far distance. They’re thinking about it now.” Pogba has re-established himself in Serie A, winning the league and earning awards as Juve’s standout performer. His performances under Max Allegri have impressed both domestically and in Europe, and his presence in Italy has maintained his global profile — a vital asset for Manchester United, who welcome back millions of pounds in commercial revenue from French markets. Executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward has been vocal about the club’s intent to reassemble core figures who can contribute both on and off the pitch. “Philippe,” as he is affectionately known, ticked both boxes during his previous two stints at Old Trafford — but his inconsistent performances in recent years have sparked a degree of caution. Current talks are being described as “strategic”, with the club exploring potential timelines and scenarios rather than making a concrete offer at this stage. Former United director Steve Round, who has remained closely involved with the club’s future plans, echoed the idea that Pogba remains a “marquee name” figure who could be galvanising for a team chasing European dominance. “He’s young enough to be here for the next decade, and it’s a chance to give fans the story they loved before,” Round told Sky Sports. However, such a move would face strong opposition from a fanbase still reeling over the outrage sparked by his initial £130m return in 2016 and subsequent underperformance. Questions remain over whether Pogba can be trusted to deliver consistently for a club now demanding linearity in transfers and player conduct.

The US Department of Justice has thrown down a legal and financial gauntlet to Deutsche Bank, demanding the German banking giant pay $14bn (£10.6bn) as part of a settlement over its involvement in the sale of toxic mortgage-backed securities during the run-up to the 2008 financial crisis. The bank confirmed it is in the final stages of negotiations with US authorities, who allege that it played a role in the reckless packaging and sale of these high-risk securities that contributed to the collapse of the housing market and triggered a global economic downturn. Deutsche Bank, one of the most prominent institutions in the world of banking, has not commented publicly on the settlement specifics. However, legal sources suggest a resolution is close, and the resolution will likely add to the mounting financial pressures facing the bank following years of reputational and regulatory challenges. The demands from the US authorities are based on allegations that Deutsche Bank turned a blind eye to widespread misrepresentation of the underlying mortgage assets when it underwrote and sold securities between 2005 and 2007. The case, which is part of a broader wave of actions against banks that helped fuel the financial crisis, is being handled by the Justice Department’s Mortgage Fraud Task Force. It focuses on high-profile banks including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, and Citigroup – all of which have already paid billions in fines – but Deutsche Bank has avoided a similar fate until now. Justice Department lawyers are reportedly satisfied with the scope of their case and expect the German bank to settle rather than risk a drawn-out, costly legal battle. However, the final figure remains under negotiation. A source close to the talks suggested that the bank’s willingness to settle is partly driven by the need to avoid further legal action in the US, where it already faces a separate $2 billion civil suit from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its role in a major money laundering failsafe for clients in the Middle East and Russia. The proposed $14bn figure, if accepted, would mark one of the largest financial penalties ever imposed on a German bank by the US government. For Deutsche Bank, the settlement could come as a bitter reminder of the global consequences of banking missteps and the enduring legacy of the 2008 crisis. It also underscores the determination of US regulators to hold even non-domestic institutions accountable.

Wealth Over Merit: The Split in State School Admissions Revealed   As families across England and Wales await the publication of secondary school placements on Thursday, new research has highlighted a stark divide between the state school system and the type of pupils it serves. The findings show that the richest children continue to dominate places at top state schools, raising urgent questions about inequality and the future competitiveness of the British education system. According to an analysis of data compiled by education think tank the Education Policy Institute (EPI), top state school sixth-form places were disproportionately taken by students from the most affluent areas. The study looked at 16 of the most selective sixth-form colleges in England, which are mostly oversubscribed and act as important transition points into university and further education. The data revealed that, in the year ending 2017, just over 50 per cent of A-level places in these colleges went to students from the most prosperous 20 per cent of postcodes, while only around 10 per cent came from the most deprived 20 per cent. By contrast, in the most deprived areas, the brightest pupils were far more likely to attend underperforming schools or grammar schools, which are largely absent in poorer regions. Ministers and senior teachers say that pupil attainment has improved in recent years, and that state education is providing a “world-class” education for the majority of children. However, the EPI report challenges this narrative, arguing that despite overall progress in literacy and numeracy, the system is increasingly mirroring the exclusivity of the private sector. “It feels like state education in this country is split: a top tier for the wealthy, and a lower tier for everyone else,” said Martin Narey, director of the EPI. “This is not just about funding—it’s about access to opportunities, the quality of the teaching, and the sort of school culture a child can expect. If you’re not born into the right postcode, the odds are stacked against you.” The findings come amid growing frustration among education professionals and parents concerned about the ongoing crisis in underfunded schools. In many areas, particularly in deprived regions of the North, resources are stretched thin while the best state schools in London and the Home Counties see waitlists with soaring numbers of applicants. Teachers’ unions have also pointed out that the reliance on a points-based admissions system—combining exam results with distance from the school—can be skewed by socio-economic factors.

Just days before Donald Trump is set to be sworn in as the 47th president of the United States, tensions are mounting between the former president and his allies in the Republican Party, particularly within Congress. Known for his blunt rhetoric and penchant for direct confrontation, Mr Trump seems intent on complicating the final days of the transition for Republicans who now find themselves in control of both the House and Senate. While he celebrated the narrow Republican victories in the midterms that shifted power, his recent remarks and actions appear to undermine those very lawmakers, leaving many in the party frustrated and uncertain how to manage the incoming administration. Reports from Washington, D.C., suggest that several Republican congressional leaders have privately cautioned against treating Mr Trump like a "consultative” figure only to find their authority undermined by the businessman-turned-politician, who has made it abundantly clear he holds the real power as the next occupant of the White House. The president-elect has taken to Twitter to voice his displeasure with figures he feels have not sufficiently supported his agenda or taken enough credit for his achievements. Numerous members of Congress, including some House committee chairs and prominent Senate leaders, have received scathing public critiques from Mr Trump—often immediately following behind-closed-doors meetings with his transition team. His comments are raising concerns among GOP lawmakers that they will struggle to maintain influence or even autonomy in shaping the new administration's agenda. Even those preparing to serve in Trump’s cabinet, such as Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a long-time ally of the president-elect, have found themselves targeted. Last week, Mr Cruz made headlines after defending White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders in a heated Senate debate. Yet just a day later, Mr Trump took to Twitter to accuse the senator of “backstabbing” and “prioritizing his own future in 2020 over helping me save the country.” Such episodes are sending ripples of uncertainty through the party as leaders scramble to balance their public support for Trump with the need to manage a combative figure who has little patience for political nuance. The situation has also raised eyebrows about how Mr Trump will interact with the White House staff and senior officials once he takes office. Some are worried that he will bypass traditional hierarchies and overrule agency heads or seasoned advisors, preferring instead to act on his own instincts or the counsel of an inner circle that rarely changes.

As tensions rise once again in Egypt, a growing undercurrent of fear is spreading among the country’s Christian minority—the Coptic Orthodox—many of whom are dreading a resurgence of intolerance and violence. With protests sweeping urban centres over the past week, concerns are mounting that religious minorities, already a marginalised group, may again become targets in an environment of heightened political and social unrest. Coptic leaders have publicly expressed alarm at what they describe as a dangerous decline in inter-communal trust. In Cairo this week, a prominent member of the Coptic community, Rev. Father Isaac Nabil, warned that “fear is in the air,” with some families considering emigration to escape what they see as an increasingly hostile climate. The recent spate of unrest followed a government crackdown on what officials have called “economic saboteurs” and “disruptive elements,” but the broad rhetoric has, in the eyes of many Copts, stirred an unfortunate precedent. Anti-Christian sentiment has been a persistent undercurrent in Egyptian society since the 2011 revolution, with Copts often caught in the crossfire of both political unrest and religious extremism. Incidents such as the 2016 Christmas bombing of a Coptic church in Cairo, which killed 25 worshippers, remain fresh in the minds of many. The Egyptian government has categorically denied any intention to target religious minorities, denying reports of increased surveillance or harassment, and reiterating its commitment to protecting the rights of all citizens. In a recent statement, Interior Ministry spokesperson Salem el-Sayed called reports of rising tensions “dangerous exaggerations,” and said the government was fully committed to “restoring peace and fostering unity among all Egyptians.” However, some human rights organisations have taken a different view. Amnesty International has recalled its previous concerns about the “systemic marginalisation” of the Coptic community and the challenges they face in accessing political representation and civil rights. A spokesperson for the group told the BBC: “We are watching this closely. Given Egypt’s recent history, it is not unreasonable for Christians to feel anxious that they will once again become scapegoats in times of crisis.” The Coptic community accounts for roughly 10 per cent of Egypt’s 100 million people and has long been a visible symbol of the country’s religious diversity. Since 2011, the community has faced a series of challenges, from restrictions on church construction to reports of verbal and physical assaults. With Egypt now bracing for further political turbulence, many fear the worst may yet be ahead.

A man has been found guilty of raping a 20-year-old woman who was found unconscious and unable to resist after a night out in Edinburgh, in a case that has shocked local communities and reignited calls for tougher action against sexual violence. The 23-year-old defendant, whose name has been withheld due to legal restrictions, was convicted during a trial at the High Court in Glasgow, with sentencing scheduled for next week. The incident occurred on a busy Friday night in the city’s central area, after the victim had been out with friends to celebrate a friend’s birthday. According to the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS), the woman had prior acquaintance with the defendant but claimed she had not consented to sexual activity. She was found in an alleyway behind a bar, later being taken to hospital with injuries. Prosecutors told the court the sexual assault took place while the woman was unconscious and screamed for help at one point, waking briefly during the attack. The case was described during the trial as "a clear and repulsive violation of trust and autonomy," with Crown prosecutors emphasizing the seriousness of the charges. The jury, after just over two hours of deliberation, unanimously found the man guilty of rape. The victim, who did not give evidence during the trial, has been supported by local domestic abuse charities, including Rape Crisis Edinburgh. A spokesperson for the charity said: “This verdict is a small but important moment for the victim, but the emotional impact of such an experience never fades. It’s vital that sentencing reflects the severity of the crime.” Police have also revealed that the incident was part of a wider crackdown on sexual violence in Edinburgh, which has seen an increased use of covert surveillance technology and specialist detectives assigned to sexual crime units. The incident has also come as Prime Minister Keir Starmer calls for legislation to strengthen statutory rape laws and increase severity of sentences for sexual offences. Sinn Féin local MP for Edinburgh North and Leith, Tommy Sheppard, has renewed calls for a ‘zero-tolerance’ policy on sexual violence. “This case is just one of many. We must address the culture that enables such crimes and provide accurate, long-term resources for support services. Justice is essential, but so is prevention,” he said. Edinburgh City Council and Police Scotland are now reviewing their public safety strategies, with particular attention being given to night-time economies and the security of go-lives routes for young women.

The Liberal Democrats have launched a bold education spending pledge in a bid to outpace both Labour and the Conservatives as the general election approaches. The party, once the dominant force in UK politics more than a decade ago, is now seeking to reclaim its former influence by putting forward a detailed plan aimed at addressing long-standing concerns about the state of education in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. At the heart of the proposal is a commitment to increase the education budget by £6.5 billion in real-term terms over the next five years. This would be achieved through a mix of borrowing and investment in school infrastructure, early years education, and higher education access. The funds, the party argues, are essential to undo years of underfunding, which has led to crumbling school buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and rising class sizes. Nick Gibb, the party’s education spokesman, stated: “For far too long, the government has failed to protect education from the axe of austerity. We see no sign of agreement from either Labour or the Conservatives on how to properly fund our schools and universities. The Liberal Democrats are stepping forward to provide the clarity and long-term investment that our young people deserve.” The announcement is part of a broader bid to position the Liberal Democrats as the party best equipped to reassure parents and teachers that education will be a national priority. The plan also includes a promise to increase national funding for early years education, protect real-terms school funding, and remove the controversial Additional Cost Allowance in teacher salaries, which the party argues disproportionately affects staff in deprived areas. The proposals, which form part of a flagship document titled  Building the Future: A Liberal Democrat Vision for Education , are a clear attempt to court both grassroots teachers’ unions and influential education politicians who have been critical of the current government’s approach. The party has also pledged to reintroduce the gold standard of English baccalaureate exams and ensure no child is fails to reach that academic benchmark due to financial constraints. The Liberal Democrat promise to match and, in some areas, exceed the education spending commitments of their rivals has been welcomed by union leaders. Bridget McCrea, general secretary of the Association of Teachers and Lecturers, described the pledge as “a fresh and realistic approach to the funding crisis that has been devastating our schools and stifling student potential.”

The beaches and restaurants of Boracay Island are usually bustling with tourists from around the world. But this vibrant Philippine island — known for its crystal-clear waters, powdery white sand, and thriving tourism industry — is currently quiet, a stark contrast to its usual scene of beachgoers, windsurfers, and cheerful families savouring fresh seafood at seaside shacks. The shutdown, part of a nationwide lockdown to curb the spread of the novel coronavirus (Covid-19), has dealt a severe blow to the island’s economy and its livelihoods that have long depended on the thousands of visitors who once arrived daily, mostly from China and the Philippines itself. Boracay, located in Aklan province in the Western Visayas region, is one of the Philippines’ most iconic tourist destinations. The island closed temporarily in 2018 for five months in a crackdown on environmental damage caused by the heavy influx of visitors, which at the time reached nearly 1,200 per day. When it reopened early in 2019, it quickly bounced back, even more so after the easing of travel restrictions from mainland China, a key market. Celine Tan, a local owner of one of the island’s many intimate warung-style eateries, said that while the 2018 closure was difficult, this situation felt “like being hit twice – first by nature, then by the virus.” Her modest restaurant, which once served a daily crush of hungry backpackers and families, is now empty. “I don’t know what we will do,” she said. “Food is also expensive now because no one is buying.” The local government has put out a call for patience, assuring residents that the shutdown is temporary and vital to protecting public health. Meanwhile, most businesses have adapted by selling food online or using social media to keep their names in the public eye. Still, the psychological impact is palpable. Many islanders have moved back in with families to cut down on expenses. Unemployment has risen, and young entrepreneurs are looking elsewhere for work. The lockdown is a cruel irony for Boracay, an island that once stood for life, vibrancy and the lure of paradise. As the sun sets over the quiet shores, the island waits — not with resentment, but with the resigned hope that one day, the tides will turn once more. For now, the world has forgotten Boracay. And yet, the beach remains, as it always has, between dream and distance, waiting for the world to return.

For the 18th consecutive year, Hong Kong has been named the world’s freest economy by the Heritage Foundation, a US-based conservative think tank that annually ranks countries on economic freedom. This longstanding recognition by the US-based group highlights Hong Kong’s robust legal system, minimal government intervention in business, and well-developed financial markets. The Chinese Special Administrative Region, often dubbed the “Pearl of the Orient,” continues to stand out despite increasing political tensions and economic challenges under Beijing’s growing influence. The Heritage Foundation’s 2024 Index of Economic Freedom, which assesses economic policies across 186 countries, reaffirms Hong Kong’s status as the most economically free society in the world. The city scores top marks in areas such as property rights, freedom from corruption, and an open market environment. It also benefits from ultra-low taxes, a deregulated labor market, and a respected judiciary — all hallmarks of its transition in 1997 from British to Chinese control under the “one country, two systems” principle. However, the report also notes concerns surrounding political rights and civil liberties. While economic freedom remains high, freedoms related to governance and personal expression have seen recent declines amid Beijing’s imposed national security law, which criminalises dissent and has led to the jailing of pro-democracy activists. Despite these political restrictions, the Heritage Foundation maintains that Hong Kong’s economy continues to operate with near-total autonomy and minimal interference from the Chinese government — at least in policy and regulation. Chinny Wan, a Hong Kong-based economist, explained that the city’s strength in economic freedom contributes to its position as a global financial hub. “Hong Kong’s rules are clear, and its markets are stable. This makes it an attractive destination for foreign investment and international firms looking to do business in Asia,” he said. However, he added that “the political climate is increasingly difficult for Hong Kongers, and this could indirectly affect the city’s economic outlook.” Ironically, as the US-China relationship continues to deteriorate, the US-based Heritage Foundation’s continued praise for Hong Kong reflects a duality in global perceptions of the region. While the city’s economy remains synonymous with openness and efficiency, its political environment is seen as shifting under China’s authoritarian grip. In the latest report, the United States itself ranks 19th in economic freedom, a significant fall from its once-dominant position as the world’s freest economy.

Leicester’s ‘Fairytale’ Runs Deeper Than the Football Pitch   The unearthing of Richard III’s skeleton from beneath the cobblestones of a Leicester car park in 2012 marked the start of an extraordinary renaissance for the East Midlands city. What began as a historic discovery soon evolved into a cultural and civic turning point, breathing new life into an urban landscape once synonymous with social deprivation and industrial decline. This year, that transformation has hit its most dazzling crescendo, as Leicester City pulled off what was universally described as a “fairytale” victory in the Premier League — a triumph that resonated far beyond the football pitch. The discovery of Richard III’s remains, a process involving the University of Leicester, was a triumph of modern science and historical detective work. DNA testing confirmed the skeleton’s identity beyond doubt, and the city embraced its newfound connection to one of England’s most controversial kings with an enthusiasm that united communities and boosted tourism almost overnight. The Richard III Visitor Centre, opened in 2014, swiftly became one of the region’s most popular attractions, drawing thousands of visitors and reinforcing Leicester’s role as a key player in the nation’s heritage scene. But the impacts of that discovery went far deeper than tourism. Local authorities and community organisations seized the momentum to reinvigorate the city’s cultural identity. Investments poured in, public spaces were redeveloped, and a renewed sense of civic pride emerged. The city’s reputation as a place to live and work started to shift, with schools and universities using the discovery as a source of inspiration. As one local said: “Finding a king in a car park gave us a story to tell the world.” This year, the story has taken a surreal turn with Leicester City’s improbable Premier League title success. A club with a modest budget and a squad containing just two players earning £100,000 a week managed by the manager of barely two years, Claudio Ranieri, to win 14 of their final 19 games after being 5,000-1 outsiders. The feat was hailed as one of English football’s greatest underdog stories, with Prime Minister David Cameron calling it “incredible” and a symbol of “resilience and determination.” For many in Leicester, the title win represents more than a moment of sporting glory. It is the culmination of a long period of perseverance and belief that mirrors the city’s broader transformation.

Police in Sydney have launched a major counter-terrorism operation, resulting in the arrest of a 15-year-old and a 20-year-old in a coordinated raid early on Monday morning. The arrests, which took place in Melbourne and regional New South Wales, signal the latest step in Australian authorities’ continued efforts to prevent domestic extremism and terrorism-related activity. The operation, reportedly led by the Australian Federal Police (AFP) in conjunction with the New South Wales Police Force, saw heavily armed officers stormed premises across several states, shutting down a suspected network believed to be associated with extremist activity. Both suspects were taken into custody without incident, according to officials. The AFP has released little detail about the alleged offences, but sources confirm that the individuals are being questioned on suspicion of engaging in activities that support a terrorist organisation. Under Australian law, those who are found to be engaging in conduct for the purpose of supporting a terrorist group face serious criminal charges. Home Affairs Minister Peter Dutton confirmed the arrests during breakfast television coverage and praised the agencies involved. "Thankfully in Australia, police and intelligence agencies are constantly working to stop these types of activities before they can escalade into real-world harm," he said. The 15-year-old suspect is one of the youngest individuals ever to be arrested in a counter-terror investigation, prompting renewed debate among lawmakers and community leaders over how young people are being drawn into extremism and the appropriateness of legal measures in such cases. Senator Andrew Bragg, the Liberal National Party’s home affairs spokesman, called the operation a "necessary and timely intervention" that highlights the evolving nature of modern terrorism threats in Australia. He added that the government must consider preventative action to address radicalisation online, where extremist propaganda is readily accessible to vulnerable young people. New South Wales Police Commissioner Jamie Charles did not disclose the identity of either suspect or specific locations where the raids took place. However, he confirmed that vulnerable persons had been removed and secured during the operation. The Australian government has recently announced a £10 million counter-terrorism funding boost for local police forces, part of an ongoing multi-million-dollar national strategy to bolster frontier security and domestic protection. The raids come just weeks before Australia marks the 20th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the United States, a date that has historically spurred heightened security awareness globally.

Greece could plunge into “uncontrolled economic chaos” if it fails to agree spending cuts and defaults on its debts, Prime Minister Lucas Papademos has warned amid growing uncertainty over the crisis-ravaged economy. The former European Central Bank chief made the stark warning to Parliament as the country teeters on the brink of a potential exit from the euro, with Greece’s debts spiralling out of control and international lenders demanding tougher austerity measures in exchange for a crucial new €130 billion (£98 billion) rescue package. The government, currently in a fragile coalition under Mr Papademos, has faced increasing public anger over his pro-austerity policies, which saw riots spread across Athens even as parliament convened. Mr Papademos said the alternative to implementing further spending cuts and tax rises was a fall into “dangerous and uncontrolled economic chaos” – a statement that mirrors the grim warnings from the rest of the European Union and the International Monetary Fund, both of whom continue to press Greece on its commitment to agreement. The Anglo-German bank, which heads the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), has made it clear that the EU will not provide more funds until Greece adopts a comprehensive reform programme, including deep cuts to public sector wages, pensions and welfare to bring its budget back into balance by 2014. But Mr Papademos also acknowledged the cost of these reforms, saying that they would “reverberate through the real economy” and cause more pain for an already battered population. Greece’s debt-to-GDP ratio is among the worst in the world, at just over 130 per cent, and government revenue continues to fall as austerity measures impact consumer demand and push the country further into recession. The Greek central bank recently reported that gross domestic product contracted by 1.7 per cent in the first quarter of 2012, reinforcing fears that Greece is heading for an even sharper economic fall that could see unemployment reach worrying new levels. “The time to step up to the plate for the hard choices is now,” Mr Papademos said. “We must uphold the principles of fiscal discipline and solidarity to preserve not only Greece, but the stability of the entire European project.” His remarks were met with boos from opposition lawmakers who accuse his coalition of caving in to the “harsh demands” of Greece’s European creditors. The opposition Pasok party, which was in power when the initial steps of the austerity programme were implemented, has refused to back the new measures, leading to serious doubts about whether the required reform programme can be passed at all.
