Lord Jonathan Janner QC, a former Labour MP and Jewish community figure who died in 2019, was the subject of a long-running investigation into historical child sex abuse allegations more than a decade before his death. Now, a former director of public prosecutions (DPP) has stated he was never informed about the investigation — a revelation that has reopened questions about the handling of historic sex abuse claims within the British justice system. Christopher Nokes QC, who served as DPP from 1996 to 1999, has confirmed that he was never made aware of the investigation into Janner during his tenure or after he left office. Nokes, who is now 86, made the remarks in the context of wider scrutiny of how institutions across the UK responded — or failed to respond — to serious allegations of abuse during the 1990s and early 2000s. The claims against Janner, a vocal advocate for victims of the Nazi Holocaust, emerged in 2011 in a criminal trial involving another accused man. Janner, who was 82 at the time, denied all allegations and was cleared of any wrongdoing. Nevertheless, the case raised concerns about how justice was handled. A subsequent independent investigation into the conduct of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) in the Janner case was launched by Tony Blair’s son-in-law, David Kennedy QC, and found that prosecutors had acted properly. However, no formal public inquiry has ever been held into the handling of the wider investigation. Nokes’ comments have sparked fresh criticism that key members of the justice system were not kept informed of extremely serious allegations that had the potential to damage public confidence and weigh heavily on the judicial and parliamentary process. Labour MP Luciana Berger, a vocal advocate for justice about child abuse, said: “It is deeply concerning that a senior figure in the prosecution service was never informed about an investigation that was running concurrently with his role. This case should be revisited with a view to uncovering exactly how such allegations were passed — or not passed — between institutions.” Historical child abuse has become one of the most intense political and legal issues in recent years, with the abuse scandal in Rotherham being one of the most high-profile examples of a failure by authorities to act. The Janner case, which predated the Rotherham revelations by several years, has been cited by survivors’ groups as another example of how powerful figures have been protected by a lack of transparency between law enforcement bodies, political parties, and the justice system.

The UK must have "full control" of its borders and territorial waters after Brexit, UKIP has said as it sets out six key demands for Prime Minister Theresa May as she prepares to begin formal negotiations with the European Union. The party's leader, Paul Nuttall, stressed the need for "tangible" deliverables from the government’s Brexit strategy and outlined a series of tests that he claimed must be met if Brexit is to "deliver on its promise". Speaking at a party policy event in London, Mr Nuttall said: “We are not here to be a political cheer squad for the government. We are here to represent the interests of the people who voted to take back control, and that is exactly what we will do.” One of UKIP's six tests is the immediate implementation of Operation Stack—a contingency measure to prepare for disruptions at the Eurotunnel between Calais and Folkestone—on the first sign of border delays in the event of a no-deal Brexit, rather than waiting for a major incident. Another demand is repatriation of the five EU agencies that have operations in the UK, including drug and customs enforcement bodies, which Mr Nuttall argued should no longer require approval from Brussels. UKIP also wants the UK to end the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice over British law and reject any trade deal with the EU that requires the UK to accept European arrest warrants or participate in the European Arrest Frame, instruments they claim facilitate unjust extraditions and fail to uphold British justice. Immigration and border control was a central theme in the UKIP manifesto, and the party reiterated that the full freedoms of movement between the UK and EU must end, with the UK instead operating its own immigration policies and quotas. “We want a Britain where our own people come first, not a passport-free Europe,” Mr Nuttall said. He added that the party would continue to “hold the government’s feet to the fire” to ensure that Parliament votes on the final Brexit deal, a promise that has faced significant uncertainty over the past year. The announcement comes at a time when public and political confidence in the government's Brexit strategy is under pressure. Prime Minister Theresa May is set to trigger Article 50 by the end of March, but recent months have seen her government face internal divisions and external criticism over the lack of clarity in the reform process.

Colin Kazim-Richards scored a dramatic late goal to send Blackburn Rovers into the FA Cup quarter-finals and heap further embarrassment on Arsenal, who were cruising towards victory before the 87th-minute twist. The Championship side stunned the Premier League leaders at Ewood Park, with Kazim-Richards netting a stoppage-time winner to ignite scenes of wild celebration among the home fans and leave Arsenal players in disbelief. Arsenal, who entered the tie as heavy favourites and having suffered a 4-0 drubbing by Chelsea in their last league match, had looked in control for most of the night. Olivier Giroud had given the north London giants the lead with a powerful header in the 47th minute, and only another towering display from Blackburn goalkeeper Paul Robinson, who made numerous vital interventions, denied them a deserved victory. Tottenham Hotspur fans, who had just witnessed their side lose a 3-2 thriller against Middlesbrough earlier in the day, suddenly had company in cricketing terms in their despair over the state of London football. Arsenal, who showed signs of unrest among the players over manager Arsène Wenger’s regime, looked rattled by the raucous Ewood Park atmosphere — a far cry from their typically controlled performances at home. Kazim-Richards, who joined Blackburn on loan from West Ham earlier this month, was a late substitute but made an instant impact. The 30-year-old former Manchester City and Burnley star exploited a defensive lapse from Arsenal to fire in a stunning winner — a moment he described as “one of the best of my career.” “We knew we had to give everything tonight,” he said in the post-match interview. “We believed in our ability and our manager’s plan. To do it at home, with the fans behind us — it doesn’t get any better than this.” Blackburn manager Paul Lambert praised his side’s resilience and called the result a “fair reflection” of their performance. “You always put the treble on the table at 2-0 up at home, but it wasn’t to be,” said Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who was visibly unimpressed. “We had numerous chances to win the game but always lack the final confidence. It’s a long season and we can’t afford to be complacent after results like this.” The victory is set to revive Blackburn’s hopes of staging another giant-killing in one of the country’s most storied competitions.

The Royal Bank of Scotland has confirmed that the new £5 note, to be launched later this year, will feature the image of Nan Shepherd, the renowned Scottish novelist and poet, whose literary contributions have long been celebrated within the UK and beyond. This announcement has been met with widespread admiration and pride as it marks a significant step in recognising Scottish women in the nation’s history and culture. Nan Shepherd is best known for her classic literary work,  The Living Mountain , a lyrical and profound reflection on the Cairngorm Mountains and the deep relationship between humans and the natural world. Published in 1977 when Shepherd was 78 – after many years of submitting it for publication and only finding a publisher with the help of writer and friend Lewis Grassic Gibbon – the book is now considered a modern classic and a milestone in nature writing. She was also an accomplished poet, a respected academic in the world of English literature, and for many years a member of the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Her philosophical explorations in literature earned her admiration across the academic and literary communities, even if many of her works went largely unnoticed in her own lifetime. The Royal Bank of Scotland’s new £5 note takes pride in celebrating the legacy of one of Scotland's greatest literary voices, with the design featuring an illustration of  The Living Mountain  and a quote from the novel. The reverse side of the new note will continue to feature the naturalist and artist Sir Alfred Gillett, as part of the bank’s ongoing commitment to reflect Scotland’s rich heritage through its currency. Jim Leisy, spokesperson for the Royal Bank of Scotland, said: “We are proud to feature Nan Shepherd on our new £5 note. Her life and work embody the spirit of Scotland – creative, thoughtful, and deeply connected to our landscapes. Her story is a powerful reminder of the impact one person can have, even when recognition is long delayed.” As the new note moves closer to circulation, it is expected to galvanise interest in Shepherd’s works and inspire a new generation of readers and writers. The choice to feature Shepherd on the £5 note also echoes recent efforts across the UK to highlight the contributions of women and underrepresented groups in cultural and national narratives. Educators and literary figures have already predicted a surge in the sales of  The Living Mountain , with schools and libraries looking to introduce it to a wider audience.

Three men from South Wales have been sentenced to prison for playing pivotal roles in assisting a Cardiff teenager to travel to Syria and join so-called Islamic State (IS) fighters. The group, who were arrested as part of an ongoing UK security operation, admitted in court that they had provided the young man—whose name has not been disclosed for legal and security reasons—with support, guidance and even funds to aid his journey to the terror group’s self-declared caliphate. The case, which has raised serious questions about community vulnerability and the effectiveness of counter-terrorism efforts in local areas, was uncovered by the Metropolitan Police's Counter-Terrorism Command. The accused—two brothers in their 20s and a 39-year-old family friend—were arrested in early 2023 after an investigation into suspicious activity linked to online radicalisation and extremist recruitment. Prosecutors said the trio, all of whom had no prior history of violent extremism, were described as “closet supporters” of IS and played an active role in encouraging the boy to leave the UK, using social media and messaging apps to disseminate propaganda and bolster his resolve to join the conflict in Syria. During the trial, it was revealed that one of the men had even advised the teenager on how to avoid detection by UK authorities when leaving the country. The others were implicated in providing financial assistance, travel advice and guidance on communication – all of which are considered serious facilitation offences under the UK’s counter-terrorism laws. Speaking outside court after the sentencing, a senior prosecutor said the case highlighted the growing concern that radicalisation is no longer limited to individuals in isolation, but can occur within seemingly unremarkable communities. “It is clear from this case that extremist ideology can spread quickly and insidiously, even among those with no prior links to terrorism,” the prosecutor said. “We are determined to stamp out such activity wherever it occurs.” The teenager in question, who had previously been known to school and local youth services as unassuming and well-behaved, had reportedly become increasingly interested in Islamic extremism after spending time online. The teenager was stopped by UK Border Force officials before he could reach the Middle East and is currently receiving psychiatric and de-radicalisation support from specialist security and mental health services. The three men were handed sentences of four to five years in prison, depending on the specific nature and extent of their involvement.

The Democratic Republic of Congo’s president, Joseph Kabila, finds himself at the heart of a deeply contested and uncertain political crisis following his narrow victory in the 28 November general election. Official results, announced by the Constitutional Court last week, declared Mr Kabila the winner by the slimmest of margins—just 12,000 votes out of more than 43 million cast. The outcome has cast doubt on the legitimacy of the widely anticipated re-election of one of Africa’s most enduring political figures, who has now arguably secured a third term in office despite mounting public pressure for him to step down when his previous mandate expired in December 2016. Opposition candidate Martin Fayulu, who led the vote in the first round, claims that the final results are fraudulent and has rejected the outcome outright. His campaign team has accused the election commission and the court of manipulating and discarding votes in key regions to ensure Mr Kabila’s victory. The logistics of the election—conducted across a sprawling, volatile country in which at least six electoral rounds failed to finish on time—have only fuelled suspicions. Reports of missing or misallocated ballots, and allegations of ballot stuffing, have further raised concerns about the accuracy of the results. Mr Kabila’s victory comes as opposition parties, civil society groups, and even some Catholic Church leaders demand a recount or a fresh election. Baptiste Kanyinda, head of Mr Kabila’s Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), has called for calm but warned that the results lack credibility. Mr Fayulu’s coalition, Alliance of the Presidential Candidates for the Republic (APCR), insists it will pursue legal action through international avenues if the Congolese judiciary refuses to respond to its demands. The international community has taken note. Prime Minister Bruno Tshisekedi—whose Lulua coalition finished second in the voting—has expressed "deep concern," though he has so far refrained from outrightly declaring the election invalid. The African Union, meanwhile, has called for calm and urged all parties to seek dialogue. However, with distrust at a high and tensions mounting, it remains unclear whether Mr Kabila can consolidate his power or whether the country is drifting toward deeper political instability. For millions of Congolese citizens weary of Mr Kabila’s prolonged rule and frustrated by delays in democratic reforms, the latest development has left the nation at a crossroads. Whether the election result stands or not, one thing is certain: the stability of the Democratic Republic of Congo remains alarmingly fragile.

The UK government has written to a number of high street retailers, urging them to make significant improvements to better accommodate disabled customers, following a BBC London investigation that exposed a “depressing” lack of accessibility across several popular stores. The findings, which follow months of covert filming and interviews, reveal consistent failures in basic accessibility measures, from step-free access to clear signage, prompting ministers to issue an urgent call to action. In a letter addressed to a range of major retailers, including clothing stores, supermarkets and chain pharmacies, the Department for Business, Energy, and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) cited the Equality Act 2010 and highlighted the legal responsibility of businesses to ensure disabled people are not unjustifiably disadvantaged. The letter also stresses the importance of treating inclusivity not just as a legal obligation, but as an opportunity to reflect the diverse needs of the population. The BBC investigation focused on locations across London and the south-east of England, assembling a damning picture of barriers faced by disabled shoppers. Filmmakers documented stores where wheelchair users were forced to turn back, ramps were oversized and unusable, and entrances were inaccessible during store hours. One store was filmed where staff waved a visually impaired woman into inappropriate changing areas, while another left visually impaired signage obscured by promotional posters. Campaigners welcome the government's intervention but demand much more than letters. Disability charity Scope, which provided support to the BBC for its research, said the report underlines the need for a long-overdue nationwide audit of retail accessibility. “What we saw was not an isolated issue confined to a few stores — it’s systemic,” said spokesperson Lucy Spilsbury. “This is not just a problem of bad management; it’s a failure to prioritise disabled people in the way the sector is designed.” Retailers contacted by the BBC responded with a mix of defences and goodwill promises. One major chain said the findings had “caught us off guard” and admitted some stores are “in transition” as they handle lease renewals and refits. Another chain pledged to begin an internal review and “ensure all staff are adequately trained” to better support disabled visitors. Government sources confirmed that while the letters are non-binding, enforcement action will be considered if repeated inspections reveal a failure to act. A spokesperson for BEIS said: “We expect businesses to uphold the law and the spirit of inclusion set out in the Equality Act.

The mother of a Scottish man who has gone missing in Amsterdam has claimed he sent her a text message just an hour before he vanished, saying he was “very homesick.” Peter Stewart, 28, from Edinburgh, disappeared last week after arriving in the Dutch capital for a short trip. His mother, Ruth Stewart, told BBC Scotland that the message was out of the ordinary for her usually cheerful son and had left the family deeply concerned. "We knew he was only in Amsterdam for a few days, and he had said he’d call when he got there,” Ruth said. “But the last thing he sent me was just an hour before he went missing — a simple message that said, 'Mum, I just miss home and I'm not sure why I came here.' My heart sank when I read it. It didn't sound like Peter.” Peter had gone to Amsterdam to meet up with friends and was expected back in the UK at the end of the week. He had breakfast with his companions on the morning of his disappearance and was last seen at a centrally located café in the Jordaan district. Shortly after, he was reported missing when he failed to return to his hotel. Authorities have launched a full missing persons investigation, with local police in Amsterdam working to trace Peter’s movements in the city. A search of local CCTV footage has so far failed to confirm his whereabouts after he left the café. Officers have also visited his last known accommodation and gathered details from the friends he was staying with. Ruth Stewart has described her son as “a very independent young man” who had no known mental health issues or history of running away. “This is just so out of character,” she said. “He had a good job, a circle of friends here in Edinburgh, and no problems that we are aware of. I just want him to know he's safe here, and that we're waiting for him.” Friends and family have set up a Facebook page to share information and have called on anyone who may have seen Peter to get in touch. A local guesthouse owner told reporters that Peter had been staying with a group of young people and was described as sociable and in good spirits on the day he disappeared. Dutch police have not commented beyond confirming they are treating Peter’s disappearance as a missing persons case and are working with their UK counterparts.

AUSTRALIA ELECTS NEW RIGHT-WING POLITICAL FORCE AS SENATOR DEFIES GOVERNMENT   In a dramatic and unexpected shift on the Australian political landscape, Senator Cory Bernardi has launched a new political party, the Australian Conservatives, after defecting from Prime Minister Tony Abbott’s centre-right Liberal Party. The move marks the emergence of a vocal new force on the right, one that puts policies of economic liberalism and free speech at the forefront of its agenda. Bernardi’s announcement in Adelaide has sent ripples through both government and opposition circles, as it underlines growing divisions within the Coalition and brings new uncertainty to an election year. The senator, a long-standing critic of both major parties—the Liberal Party and the Australian Labor Party—has accused them of moving too far to the left, particularly on issues such as mass immigration, multiculturalism, and the cost of living. Addressing a crowd of supporters, the 51-year-old senator declared: “We have been told, often by prime ministers and shadow leaders, that Australia cannot afford another political party. But Australia cannot afford not to have another political party when our national identity is under threat and when our key institutions are being undermined.” The Australian Conservatives is set to challenge the status quo by advocating for a patriotism-based platform that promotes colourblind multiculturalism, lower taxes, less regulatory intervention, and a stronger national defense. The party already has three parliamentary representatives: Senator Bernardi, along with Nick Xenophon and Moti URI, both of whom have long held their own political initiatives outside the major party framework. The coalition’s leader, Mr. Bernardi, has also invited other defectors to consider joining the new party, a move likely to provoke further internal fractures within the Liberal Party and potentially split the right across the country. Mr. Abbott, whose government has been struggling to unify a fractured voter base, has publicly supported his former colleague. In a statement, he said he “respects” Bernardi’s decision, even as he acknowledged that the formation of a new party will create challenges for the election campaign. Prime Minister Tony Abbott’s government has already shown signs of ideological strain, particularly among younger, more conservative voters who have been increasingly alienated by compromise on immigration and economic policies. With a general election expected next year, a new political competitor could shift the balance of power in unpredictable ways. The launch of the Australian Conservatives also coincides with a growing unease on the right about the influence of identity politics and the ideological direction of the major parties.

Amid the recriminations that so swiftly followed America's third successive Ryder Cup defeat two years ago, there seemed to be a consensus that a fresher approach was needed to halt the US decline in these biennial matches. That consensus has since driven sweeping changes to the team's strategy and selection process, but with this year’s clash against Europe on American soil at Illinois' Congressional Country Club, the question remains: have they turned the tide in time? The last meeting in Hazeltine in 2016 was a bruising defeat for Team USA, with Europe romping to a convincing victory and underlining the growing chasm between the two sides. For the three previous editions of the competition, dating back to 2010, European golf had triumphed in what many observers saw as a new era of dominance. It was a dramatic reversal of fortune for the US, whose last win had been in 2008 in Ireland — a victory that still resonates with American fans as a golden era of transatlantic competition. In the aftermath, the American golfing establishment, led by PGA Tour Commissioner Jay Monahan, determined that fundamental changes were necessary. A new captain was appointed — Davis Love III, who had previously led the US to victory in 2008, returned in 2023 — and a data-driven approach was introduced to player selection and team tactics. The traditional reliance on star power and natural star charisma gave way to a more strategic, analytical methodology, incorporating depth charts, performance analytics, and team dynamics as critical components of the selection process. “In 2016, we were not just a team of individuals but a collection of star players who didn’t always play well as a unit,” Love recently told Golf Digest. “Now, there is a clearer focus on how our guys compete not just head to head, but how they support and uplift one another.” That vision becomes evident when looking at the team's latest crop of up-and-coming talent. The inclusion of rising stars like Russell Henley and Matthew Fitzpatrick (now converted to the American side) is a sign that the US is not only revising how it selects players but also who. There is an evident effort to diversify not just in skill but in playing styles and temperaments to mirror the European side, which prides itself on a broad bench and adaptable play. The European team, meanwhile, appears to be experiencing something of a shake-up of its own.

Survivor of 7/7 Attack Shows Her Remarkable Recovery to the World   Five years after her life was changed in an instant by the devastating 7/7 terror attacks in London, Gillian Gibbons has taken a courageous step forward — unveiling the new face she has painstakingly rebuilt through a series of world-leading reconstructive surgeries. The 48-year-old teacher, who was just one of 121 people killed and a further 770 injured in the attacks when a double-decker bus caught fire following a terrorist bomb in Tavistock Place, has rarely spoken publicly about her ordeal. But now, with the support of the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) and a team of pioneering plastic surgeons, she is emerging from years of private treatment to show the world who she has become. Gibbons, who was left with severe burns covering more than half of her body and her face, has undergone 28 surgical procedures at specialist units in London and Birmingham to restore her appearance and quality of life. Today, thanks to advances in facial reconstruction, skin grafting and prosthetic techniques, she is now walking the streets with a new face and a new sense of confidence. Speaking in a controlled media briefing in London, she said: “For years, I’ve hidden from the world. I used to be a healthy, active woman. After the attacks, I often felt invisible, and sometimes it was easier to stay that way. But I don’t want to be forgotten. I want to live again and show others that healing, even in the most unimaginable circumstances, is possible.” The 7/7 attacks, carried out by four Islamist extremists in 2005, remain one of Britain’s most tragic acts of terrorism. A bomb exploded on a number 30 bus while Gibbons was standing on the top deck, engulfing her and other passengers in flames. She was among the most seriously injured and survived thanks to emergency care at University College Hospital. Her recovery path was treacherous. Doctors told her family early on that she would suffer lifelong disfigurement. But Gibbons refused to give up, and through a pioneering blend of pioneering medical treatments and sheer willpower, she began a journey to reclaim her identity. Her new face includes facial skin transplants and 3D-printed implants designed around her original facial structure, with the goal of creating a map that is visibly her own — yet dramatically transformed. Professor Mark Birch, the lead surgeon on her team, said: “This case has been one of the most complex I’ve ever been involved in.

The International Criminal Court is to open a new preliminary investigation into alleged abuses by UK military personnel of Iraqi detainees during the Iraq War, according to a statement released from The Hague. The announcement comes after months of speculation by human rights groups and legal experts that the UK’s Chilcot Inquiry and domestic courts would not pursue criminal proceedings against British soldiers or officials for the alleged war crimes committed between 2003 and 2011. The ICC said that the preliminary examination would investigate claims of ill-treatment, arbitrary detention, and other potential war crimes as part of a larger probe into the legality and conduct of the Iraq War. The decision underlines the growing role of international justice in holding states accountable for conduct in military conflicts and marks a significant step for victims and activists who have repeatedly urged the court to intervene. Human rights organizations, including Amnesty International and the British-Supported Dignity Centre for Peace in Baghdad, have long documented cases of alleged abuse at facilities such as Camp Bucca and the notorious “Havana Club” – a former Ministry of Justice building in Basra where British troops, according to testimonies and leaked Army documents, detained and mistreated Iraqi civilians. In 2016, the Chilcot Inquiry condemned the Iraq War as a “tragic failure of leadership” but stopped short of recommending criminal prosecutions against any individuals in the UK. Meanwhile, national courts – citing parliamentary immunity and statute of limitations – have ruled they cannot prosecute British personnel unless triggered by an international body. The potential ICC investigation will focus on the chain of command at the time, including the involvement of senior military and political figures in the abuse of prisoners. The court will assess whether UK forces failed to implement adequate safeguards to prevent torture or cruel treatment and whether their actions under international law constitute war crimes as defined by the Rome Statute. UK Foreign Secretary Dominic Raab has yet to comment officially on the news. However, previous statements from the UK government have been reluctant to accept the jurisdiction of the ICC in cases involving British nationals. In 2020, then-Prime Minister Boris Johnson announced the UK’s formal initiative to withdraw from the Rome Statute, although no formal steps have yet been taken. The decision to begin an investigation raises renewed questions about the accountability of Western forces in conflicts abroad and the ability of international law to redress historical wrongs.

The rollout of the UK’s future 5G mobile network must learn from the shortcomings of the previous 4G launch if it is to be successful and meet public expectations, according to a new report by a parliamentary committee. The inquiry, conducted by the House of Commons Science and Technology Select Committee, has highlighted a number of serious concerns surrounding how 5G infrastructure is being deployed across the country, citing lessons that need to be heeded from the past. The report notes that the 4G network’s rollout, which began in 2012, was plagued by problems including insufficient investment, slow deployment in rural areas, and a lack of public engagement. Many communities, particularly in rural parts of the UK, were left without reliable connectivity for years, exacerbating the digital divide between urban and rural areas. The new inquiry warns that failing to address these issues now could result in a repeat of these failures in the transition to 5G. “This is a pivotal moment for mobile communications, and the UK must not allow its historic shortcomings in 4G to undermine the future of 5G,” the report states. “If the government and telecom providers continue to treat the rollout as piecemeal and commercially driven without addressing regional disparities, the UK risks falling further behind in the global race for faster, more reliable connectivity.” The committee has called on both the government and mobile network providers to improve collaboration with local authorities and communities, and to take a more strategic, national approach to 5G deployment. It also stresses the importance of ensuring that no part of the country—particularly rural areas—misses out on the benefits of the next-generation mobile technology. Without action, the UK could face what the report describes as a “dangerous communications gap,” with vulnerable communities and businesses left behind in the digital economy. Ministers are being urged to take a proactive role, using the National Infrastructure Strategy to set clear targets for 5G coverage and to explore the use of public funding to support areas where commercial interest is limited. The report also highlights the need for greater transparency around 5G technology and its health and environmental implications, a concern that has already prompted significant public debate and, in some cases, opposition to the installation of new mobile masts. The report comes at a time of growing urgency, with the UK eager to demonstrate leadership in the development of faster, more adaptable mobile networks.

The first victims of the devastating St Petersburg metro explosion have been officially identified as part of an ongoing investigation into the attack, which has left Russian authorities and the public searching for answers. The blasts, which occurred at the metro station of Sennaya Ploshchad during the morning rush hour, killed 14 people and injured more than 100, marking one of the deadliest acts of terrorism on Russian soil in recent years. Among the confirmed victims is Yulia Slavina, a 32-year-old mother of two who worked as a marketing executive in the city. Her husband and young children arrived at the hospital shortly after the explosion to search for signs of her. Nearby, the body of Roman Pavlov, a 29-year-old security guard well-known to his colleagues for his dedication and calm nature, was also identified by his partner. The emotional toll on the victims' families has been immense, with many making public appeals for information about their loved ones. As details emerge, the community has rallied to offer support in every way possible, from setting up memorials at the metro entrance to national outpourings of grief expressed on social media. Russian investigators, meanwhile, are working tirelessly to determine the identity of the attacker. According to Interfax, early reports suggest the suicide bomber was a female suspect carrying explosives in a handbag. Video from the scene is being pored over by forensic teams, along with CCTV footage from the surrounding area, while the FSB (Federal Security Service) has taken over the inquiry. Chechen President Ramzan Kadyrov hinted at involvement from someone within the Chechen diaspora, a claim that has already sparked concern over regional tensions. Some reports suggest the blast was a suicide attack, and it is feared that the incident could be linked to separatist groups in the North Caucasus. However, no group has yet publicly claimed responsibility. In the wake of the tragedy, the Russian government has reiterated its stance that the attack is a reminder of the persistent threat of terrorism. President Vladimir Putin has described it as an act of "barbaric criminality," and ordered increased security measures across all public transport systems. As St Petersburg grieves, the hunt for the attacker continues and questions remain as to what triggers would lead someone to carry out such an act in the heart of the city. The road to delivering justice will be long, but the names of the victims—ones who were simply going about their day—will not be forgotten.

A Muslim teacher who was denied entry to the United States during a school trip last month has revealed he was still in the dark about the reason behind the decision, more than a week later. The incident, which has raised concerns over potential discrimination and inconsistencies in US border control policies, has puzzled both the teacher and his colleagues. Deen Baig, a 43-year-old teacher from the UK who has worked at a school in Dubai for the past decade, was stopped by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport as he and his students were arriving for a planned educational visit. While the students were waved through, Mr Baig was detained for over two hours and then informed he would not be allowed into the country. “I’m still waiting to know why I was refused entry,” Mr Baig said during a short London press conference on Wednesday. “I was given no paperwork, no explanation—just a simple statement that I would not be allowed in. I was treated as a criminal, when I’m just a teacher trying to do my job.” Mr Baig’s group had planned a week-long trip to visit historical and cultural sites in Texas, a common practice among international schools. After the short meeting with a CBP official, he was sent back to the UK on an unexpected flight, while the students continued with their planned itinerary. The school at which Mr Baig works has since expressed concern, noting that the teacher has a clean background and no prior travel restrictions. A school representative said the incident “has left our community deeply unsettled and has led many to question the policies governing who is allowed into the United States.” This case is not the first to raise eyebrows following the Trump administration's former travel ban and ongoing reports of increased scrutiny at US borders, particularly for individuals from Muslim-majority countries. While the Biden administration has since taken steps to roll back some of these measures, reports of confusion and uneven application of new guidelines persist. Mr Baig, who has travelled to the US for previous school trips without issue, said he believes his name flagged up some kind of red tape—possibly something to do with an old spell of US-based education when he studied at a US university in the early 2000s.

Switzerland’s parliament has approved a controversial new bill that prioritises local jobseekers over EU citizens during periods of high unemployment, deepening tensions with European Union member states and reigniting concerns about the rise of inward-looking policies in the Alpine nation. The legislation, passed with a narrow majority in the lower house of parliament on Tuesday night, is set to face a final hurdle in the upper house and, if approved, could mark a significant shift in Switzerland’s traditionally flexible approach to European integration and free movement. The bill, supported by the right-leaning Swiss People's Party (SVP), was backed by 134 of 200 lawmakers in the National Council, with a sizeable number of cross-votes from centrist and socialist members. Opponents have raised concerns that the measure will not only undermine Switzerland’s long-standing agreement on the free movement of people with the EU, but also place the country’s economy at risk by making it less attractive to skilled foreign workers during times of low domestic unemployment. Under the proposed policy, local residents would be given preference for non-European job applicants during periods when the Swiss national unemployment rate exceeds 8 per cent. If approved, the move would allow cantons and local authorities to restrict hiring in certain sectors to Swiss nationals and non-EU migrants, effectively sidelining those from EU member states during economic downturns. Swiss media have highlighted the growing – and deeply polarising – debate between Swiss citizens who support self-preservation and those who fear the impact of restrictions on Switzerland’s traditionally open economy and highly competitive job market. The SVP and its supporters argue that the measure would protect Swiss jobs and prevent a situation where nationals struggle to find work amid an influx of foreign labour. Critically, however, the politicians failed to define a timeline for when exactly the threshold would be implemented, nor did they detail a comprehensive plan for the transition beyond job market controls. The Swiss government is already engaged in difficult negotiations with the European Union over the future of their complex relationship, following the 2019 vote to limit guest worker numbers. The EU has flagged the new proposed bill as further evidence of Switzerland retreating from the free movement agreement, which is currently one of the cornerstones of its relationship with European partners. The International Labour Organization has warned that such policies could exacerbate existing inequalities and do little to address the root causes of unemployment.

There is no doubt that Kenya has been deeply scarred by the attack on the University in Garissa, in which at least 148 people were killed. The brutal assault, carried out by al-Shabaab separatists on April 2, 2015, marked one of the deadliest incidents of terrorism in the nation’s history and has since left a lasting imprint on the collective consciousness of the country. Almost a decade later, the echoes of that day still resonate within the halls of Kenya's educational institutions, its communities, and its political landscape. The Garissa University was targeted for its predominantly Muslim student population, a calculated decision by the jihadists to not only instil fear but also to send a chilling message of division and hatred across ethnic and religious lines. It was a stark reminder that no corner of the country’s richly diverse demographic was truly safe. Following the coordinated attack, which involved gunmen opening fire and beheading those who survived the initial onslaught, the campus fell into a gruesome silence that resonated across the nation. In the days that followed, the country united in mourning, as vigils and moments of silence were held nationwide. The brutal nature of the killings, and the chilling coldness of the attackers, ignited a strong reaction both from within Kenya and the international community. Political leaders from across the country, including those from opposition parties, put aside their differences to show solidarity with the victims and their families, and to reaffirm the nation’s commitment to unity and peace in the face of terrorism. The government was quick to blame al-Shabaab, a Somali-based militant group that has long been designated a terrorist organisation. Yet, the attack raised uncomfortable questions about security protocols, intelligence sharing, and the continued threat from extremist elements within the East African region. Following the incident, Prime Minister Raila Odinga condemned the attack as "a condemnable violation of human rights" and called for unity among Kenyans to defeat the threat of terrorism. As the nation grapples with the trauma, efforts to commemorate the victims and provide support for the bereaved remain ongoing. A memorial was established at the university, serving as a place of reflection and remembrance for all those who perished. As such, the attack on Garissa University stands not only as a dark chapter in Kenya’s history but also as a call to action for a country striving to heal and protect its future.

The government is moving to clarify its plans for an English votes for English laws (EVEL) system, as former Commons leader Chris Grayling confirmed the decision to delay progress on the reform to September. Speaking in the House of Commons, Grayling, who now serves as secretary of state for transport, said the legislative process would be put on hold during the upcoming summer recess to allow for further consultation and parliamentary scrutiny. The move comes as concerns over the complexity of the reforms continue to grow, with critics from all sides of the House expressing unease over how the system would operate and whether it was likely to exacerbate tensions during the legislative process. Grayling confirmed that a revised timetable would avoid a vote on the bill before September, adding that the department responsible for overseeing the changes had received more than 130 written representations and held dozens of meetings with stakeholders, including MPs, parliamentary staff, and officials. “We are determined to deliver an English votes for English laws system that works for all, but we must get this right,” he said. The reform, which was initially designed to give English MPs more influence over laws that affect only England, has been complicated by disagreements over how to define English and Welsh legislation and how to ensure fair representation in a House of Commons that includes members from devolved nations such as Scotland and Wales. The current system, which came into effect after the 2015 general election, has been widely regarded as flawed, with many MPs frustrated by the convoluted procedures and ambiguity over what constitutes an English or Welsh issue. The reforms seek to replace the existing ad hoc process with a full and sustainable system. However, the complexity of the proposals has been met with scepticism, with some law officers and legal experts warning of unintended consequences and legal challenges. Conservative MP Neil Hamilton, who has been among the most vocal critics of the reform, said: “This delay is welcome given the lack of clarity surrounding the proposals. Parliament deserves a straightforward solution, not a patchwork that could be found legally unsound.” Labour, meanwhile, has passed up an opportunity to press the government on the issue during a debate on the general principles of the bill, with shadow leader Angela Eagle citing a lack of clear opposition. As the government delays a decision, questions remain about the political and constitutional implications of the reforms, and whether the delays will satisfy those who believe the entire principle of the proposal is flawed.

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has dismissed speculation surrounding his willingness to shake hands with rival Jose Mourinho ahead of Monday’s pre-season clash between the two Manchester clubs in Beijing. Speaking ahead of the eagerly anticipated friendly fixture, the Spanish tactician categorically denied any suggestion that he would refuse the gesture, as such a decision had been greatly exaggerated in some media reports. “Of course I will shake his hand,” Guardiola said at a press conference in Manchester. “I have always respected Jose and I have every reason to treat him with courtesy. It's a game of football. We compete on the pitch, and when the whistle blows, that’s what we do.” The friendly, which is part of both clubs' pre-season tour in the Far East, marks the fourth time the rivals have met on Chinese soil in seven years and is expected to draw a massive crowd to the Workers’ Stadium in the Chinese capital. Despite the warm words from Guardiola, the handshaking controversy has been a talking point following comments made by Mourinho earlier this week. The Portuguese manager, currently in his first season as United’s head coach, had suggested Guardiola might refuse to meet him by hand over personal disagreements, a notion Guardiola swiftly refuted. “There are frustrations in every rivalry, and Mourinho and I have had our moments, but this is not about us. It is about our clubs and our fans,” Guardiola added. “Let’s not make personal stories out of football games. We are here to prepare our teams and to enjoy the match.” Guardiola and Mourinho’s rivalry has long been a source of fascination for football fans. Since Mourinho returned to the Premier League in 2013, the pair’s encounters have often been overshadowed by their mutual barbs, intense body language, and post-match exchanges that have at times flared into full-blown public disputes. Their touchline battles, particularly during key matches in recent seasons, have gone viral on social media and have only heightened the drama between the two clubs. Mourinho, however, has always maintained a level of respect for Guardiola and has publicly acknowledged the Catalan manager’s credentials as one of the very best in world football. The question of whether the pair’s on-field and off-field rivalry will evolve in the coming season remains to be seen. For now, both men are focused on building for what promises to be another intensely competitive Premier League campaign.

A damning review into the deaths of three people at the hands of a prolific killer has revealed that the tragedy may have been averted if police had investigated complaints made against him. The findings, published by an independent inquiry, highlight serious failings in the response to warnings about the individual, whose background as a violent aggressor had been brought to the attention of law enforcement on multiple occasions prior to the incident. The killer, whose identity has been withheld for legal reasons, was found by police last month after a fatal house-to-house search concluded a horrifying case in which he confessed to three murders and was linked to further attacks. The inquiry, led by retired senior police officer John Carlisle, said it had uncovered “systemic gaps in the handling of domestic violence complaints and coercive relationships that could have provided an early warning of his dangerous behavior.” One specific concern highlighted was the failure to check the suspect’s past and the lack of communication between local authorities and police, despite a history of reported threats and abusive conduct. The review noted that between 2013 and 2022, there were at least 12 separate complaints made to local councils and the police force over the suspect, many of them relating to controlling and violent behavior in personal relationships. “A coordinated response and a more thorough investigation of these reports could potentially have saved the lives of these victims,” the report said. The inquiry also pointed to a “culture of under-reporting” and “insufficient training” within certain departments in handling domestic abuse cases. Earlier this month, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it was urgently reviewing the policies for dealing with abuse and threats in the home, following the deaths. The families of the victims, some of whom had worked closely with their loved ones during the years leading up to the crimes, have been vocal in their condemnation of the police’s handling of the case. “We were told there was nothing they could do,” said one relative. “If it had been up to us to do something, we would have acted.” The chief constable of the area has apologized and pledged urgent reforms. “This is something we all deeply regret,” he said. “Our failings exposed by this report are clear and cannot be ignored. We are committed to learning the lessons and making the necessary changes to ensure such a tragedy is never repeated.”

A man who admitted raping a 12-year-old girl has walked free from court after prosecutors decided not to pursue a criminal case. James Smith, 28, of Birmingham, admitted the offence before a judge had been appointed, and was released immediately. His victim has since described the trauma as “the worst day of my life”. The case, which has sparked outrage among campaigners and members of the public, has raised serious questions about how the justice system protects children from sexual predators. The incident occurred in a residential area in Nechells last October, where Smith, a man with no prior criminal record, targeted the girl, whose identity is being withheld for legal and safety reasons. The girl’s family reported the assault to police the following morning, and Smith was swiftly arrested and taken into custody. When first interviewed by West Midlands Police, Smith gave a detailed account of the offence, including details of how he targeted the area and approached the child in the early hours of the morning. However, when the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) reviewed the case, it concluded that there was insufficient evidence to proceed to trial. In a statement, the CPS said that while Smith had admitted the crime, the available evidence did not meet the threshold for a criminal conviction. The decision has been met with widespread condemnation. A local MP, John Howell, called the release of Smith “shocking and indefensible – this man should be behind bars, not walking free on the streets of Birmingham”. Children’s charities have also voiced their concern. Janice Nasci, chief executive of the NSPCC in the West Midlands, said: “No amount of shame or embarrassment should have stopped justice from being done. Every child deserves to be protected, and the way this case has been handled demonstrates a glaring failure in the system.” The girl, now aged 13, has required ongoing psychological support since the attack. Teachers and neighbours have described her as a “bright and well-behaved child” who was left in tears after the incident. Her parents, who described the assault as “overwhelming and terrifying”, have been demanding a review of the case and called for an urgent investigation into why it was not proceeded with. Legal experts have weighed in on the situation as well. Professor Simon Daly, a criminal law expert at the University of Birmingham, said the case highlighted a “critical flaw” in how admissions are treated within the CPS.

Labour Pledges ‘Credible’ Immigration Plan Within 100 Days of Office, Says Miliband   Labour has set out its clearest timeline yet for reforming immigration policy, with leader Ed Miliband vowing to publish a “credible” set of measures within 100 days of taking office after the next general election. The pledge, made in a major party speech on immigration and integration, signals a decisive shift for a Labour party long accused by critics of having no coherent stance on one of the most divisive issues in British politics. Speaking at a private event in London, Mr Miliband called immigration “a test of our values as a country” and said Labour would act quickly to address concerns over border control, integration and the treatment of foreign workers and asylum seekers. “We must have an immigration system that is not just effective, but one that commands the trust and support of the British people,” he said. “That is why, if we are in government, Labour will present a plan within 100 days — a plan built on shared principles and delivered with common sense.” The statement was a direct challenge to the current coalition government’s approach, particularly the controversial “EU freedom of movement” rules that have become a focal point for both Remain and Leave campaigners in the EU referendum debate. Mr Miliband also sought to distance Labour from the perception that it is too tolerant on immigration: “This isn’t a question of being soft or hard — it’s about being realistic and responsible.” He outlined four main principles for the party’s future immigration policy: securing the border, improving integration into communities and the workforce, treating migrants with dignity and fairness, and managing future flows responsibly. On the issue of EU migration, Mr Miliband acknowledged the public’s concerns but stressed that any changes must be developed in line with international obligations and human rights commitments. Labour has come under fire in recent years for a perceived lack of clarity on immigration, particularly during the election campaigns of 2010 and 2015. Party polls suggest that immigration is now one of the top issues among voters, and the timing of Mr Miliband’s speech coincided with a renewed political focus on the EU referendum. As such, the speech was seen as a bid to reframe the debate ahead of what is likely to be a defining election in 2020. The opposition leader also placed emphasis on improving the integration of existing immigrants, suggesting measures such as language training and better access to education and employment.

Disgraced former world snooker champion Stephen Lee is hoping to turn a new leaf by inspiring young players in China, where he is working to promote the sport despite the tarnished reputation he brought to it in the UK. The 50-year-old, who was jailed in 2010 for match-fixing and banned for life from the World Snooker Tour, has recently embarked on a tour of Chinese snooker academies with ambitious aims to mentor up-and-coming talent and help foster a new era of competitive players. Lee, once a household name in the snooker world for his tactical brilliance and aggressive style at the table, now faces considerable scrutiny as he seeks to reinvent himself as a sports educator in the nation where the game is booming. China, which has invested heavily in developing snooker talent in recent years, has seen the rise of young stars such as Ding Junhui and Yan Bingtao, and Lee is eager to play a role in that expanding community. Speaking to a local audience in Qingdao, Lee said: “I have made mistakes in my past, and I accept the full consequences of my actions. But I truly believe that snooker is a special sport that can change lives. If I can share the lessons I’ve learned — both on and off the table — and help young people from humble beginnings achieve their dreams, then I have something positive to contribute still.” Lee's journey to China marks the latest chapter in his life since his downfall in the UK. In 2008, he was found guilty of five charges of fixing matches during the 2006 UK Championship and European Open, a scandal that shattered his career and led to his imprisonment. While many in the snooker community remain wary of his presence, Lee argues that his years of experience — both as a player and as someone who has faced and learned from adversity — make him uniquely suited to guide younger athletes. In China, snooker is not just a sport but part of a strategic education initiative aimed at developing soft skills, perseverance, and discipline among students. Lee is being employed as a coach and mentor, helping to run training camps and working closely with academy coaches and students. His comments have also sparked debate about redemption and whether figures from the UK's sporting scandals can play a constructive role beyond their borders. World Snooker, the sport's governing body, has not officially commented on Lee’s involvement but has been advised of his activities in China.

Tony Pulis, the West Bromwich manager and former Wales international, believes the nation’s historic successes on the European Championship stage could inspire a new generation of Welsh footballers. Speaking at a recent coaching seminar in Cardiff, Pulis praised the progress made by the Welsh national team under manager Chris Coleman and called for the FA to capitalise on the current momentum. Welsh football has enjoyed one of its most successful international periods in living memory, with a memorable run to the semi-finals of Euro 2016, where they defeated England on their way to becoming the first British nation to reach that stage of the competition outside of their home continent. Recent campaigns have shown continued signs of progress, with Wales securing strong results in World Cup and European Championship qualifiers. Pulis, who made over 500 appearances for his country between 1976 and 1993, stressed the importance of translating the excitement of success into long-term development at the grassroots level. “When you see a nation playing with belief and heart, and getting results against the best, it leaves an impression, especially on young players. That could be the catalyst for something special,” he said. He also highlighted the need for consistent support for coaches and young players, ensuring that the structures in place allow for continuous growth. “It’s not just about the players trotting out for the national team. It’s about the people who are coaching them, and the environment they’re being given to develop. Success on the pitch has to be backed up by success off it.” Pulis also praised the role of the current Welsh squad in setting an example for the future. He pointed to the professional attitude and determination shown by figures such as Gareth Bale, Ashley Williams and Aaron Ramsey as qualities that could shape the next wave of talent coming through the Welsh system. Welsh football fans have long bemoaned the fact that many of their brightest stars leave for clubs abroad at young ages, often barely aware of the culture and passion for the national game. But Pulis believes the recent surge in success can change that. “More and more young players will say, ‘I want to be part of that team, I want to play for Wales one day.’ And that’s something we as players, coaches, and supporters can all be proud of,” he said. As the next European Championship cycle begins, Pulis’s message is clear: Wales has entered a new era on the international stage, and there is real optimism that this surge in success could lay the foundations for a golden age in

Blair-Bush Memos Reveal Closeness of Relations Pre-Iraq War   A series of confidential memos sent by former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair to then US President George W. Bush in the lead-up to the 2003 Iraq War has revealed the deep level of trust and co-ordination between the two leaders during one of the most controversial periods in modern political history. The documents, released in full for the first time in a parliamentary committee report, underscore the unique and often unprecedented nature of the Blair-Bush relationship, which has frequently been referred to as the “special relationship” between the UK and the US. The memos, dated prior to the invasion, show Blair seeking clarification and reassurance from Bush, reflecting the gravity of the decision that the two leaders jointly pursued. They also highlight the significant role Blair played in shaping the justification for the war, based on then-premier assessments of Iraq’s alleged possession of weapons of mass destruction (WMDs). The prime minister’s repeated diplomatic overtures to Bush suggest a close, almost familial bond, with Blair often writing in an informal tone that went beyond protocol. Among the most notable examples is a memo from March 2003 written in short, personal form as Blair asked for Bush’s certainty on the military objectives in Iraq and on whether the invasion would indeed lead to the “liberation” of the country. This level of openness, and the apparent comfort in exchanging such sensitive information, has led critics to question whether Blair was overreliant on American assurances at the expense of independent UK judgment. The documents have now been published as part of an ongoing investigation into the political and ethical responsibilities of the Blair government in the Iraq inquiry. Sir John Chilcot, the lead investigator, has requested access to Prime Minister Gordon Brown about the content of these memos, highlighting the significance of Blair’s communications during the run-up to the war. The timing of the release has also sparked renewed debate about the invasion, with some MPs, including from the opposition Labour Party, calling for further transparency about the intelligence and advice available to the government at the time. The Iraq War, which ended in failure to find WMDs and ultimately contributed to years of instability in the Middle East, has been one of the most divisive legacies of the Blair-Bush alliance. Political analysts say the memos serve not only as a historical record but as a case study in how personal relationships between heads of state can influence major international decisions.

Poland Surpasses India as the Largest Foreign-Born Population in the UK, ONS Reveals   For the first time on record, the Polish community has overtaken the Indian-born population as the largest group born outside the UK, figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveal. The announcement follows years of steady migration from Poland and marks a significant milestone in the shifting demographic landscape of Britain. The ONS report highlights that over 535,000 people in England and Wales were born in Poland, eclipsing the Indian-born community, which now numbers just under 530,000. The figures underpin the impact of Polish migration, particularly since Poland’s accession to the European Union in 2004, which brought greater ease of movement between the UK and other EU member states. The Polish community, often referred to as the A2 group of EU citizens, has grown rapidly in the last decade, drawn by economic opportunities and a thriving workforce in sectors such as hospitality, agriculture, construction, and transport. Many Polish migrants have settled in areas such as London, the West Midlands, and Northamptonshire, where strong networks and employment prospects have facilitated integration and growth. While the news of Poland’s shift as the leading non-British birth origin will come as no surprise to many, it raises important questions about the future of the national identity – particularly as the UK navigates the uncertainties of post-Brexit life. Polish migration has been a source of political and social debate for years, with fluctuating sentiment at times clashing with the realities of someone who, in London alone, over 100,000 children are now born to Polish parents. Despite continued immigration figures from Poland being lower in recent years, the existing population remains stable, and many have become long-term residents or even citizens. Employers still rely heavily on Polish workers to fill roles where domestic labor is scarce, and small businesses and local economies have benefited significantly from their presence. In a response to the ONS figures, a spokesperson for the Polish community group Wypoznan said it was a proud moment for Poles living in the UK. “This recognition is a testament to how hard our people have worked to contribute to British society,” the spokesperson said. “From construction to care work, the Polish community has played a vital role in this nation.” Conversely, the go-down of the Indian-born population as the number one nationality is a notable development.

Fulham maintained their remarkable Championship form with an emphatic 2-0 victory at Barnsley on Saturday, extending their unbeaten away record in the division to an impressive 12 matches and securing their first triumph at Oakwell since 1970. The result marked a strong start to the new year for Slavisa Jokanovic’s side, who continue to impress as one of the promotion contenders in the second tier. A first-half strike by substitute Ryan Sessegnon, followed by a composed finish from Paul Lang’s cross by Tomas Kalas in the second half, proved the difference in an absorbing encounter. The victory not only extended Fulham’s unbeaten league run to five games, but also sent a powerful message to their rivals about their credentials as a team capable of challenging for the top two. Barnsley, meanwhile, suffered their third consecutive league defeat and find themselves hovering just above the relegation zone, with the Cats now looking increasingly vulnerable as the season progresses. The Serbian manager has once again demonstrated his ability to extract consistent performances from his squad, with the team’s attacking flexibility and defensive resilience drawing particular praise from pundits. Indeed, Fulham’s recent Championship campaign has been the antithesis of their relegation scrap last season and has sent shockwaves through the table. The Craven Cottage side have scored in all of their last 10 league games and have now picked up 33 points from a possible 45, earning comparisons with the form they showed when winning promotion from the Championship in 2001. Former Fulham forward Marcus Bettinelli, who celebrates his 30th birthday this week, was a surprise inclusion in the starting XI and continued his fine form in goal, replying to questions after the game by saying, "It's been a great campaign so far, and the lads are playing with real belief and freedom. We’re not resting on our laurels—every week it gets tougher, but we’re up for the challenge." With just over 20 games remaining in the season, Fulham are well on course to secure an immediate return to the Premier League via the play-offs or direct promotion. However, Saturday’s result over Barnsley sent out a clear message: Jokanovic’s team are serious contenders, and their consistent away form is a key factor in their bid for the top tier once more. The final day crowd of more than 11,000 at Barnsley, which was a record for Championship encounters involving Fulham due to restrictions at smaller grounds, only added to the sense of occasion, with fans from both clubs soaked by the rain as they celebrated the thrilling contest.

The South Carolina House of Representatives has voted to remove the Confederate flag from the state capitol grounds, following an intense and often contentious debate that divided lawmakers and citizens alike. The flag has flown atop the State House in Columbia since 1961, symbolizing the heritage of the Confederate States during the American Civil War. Over recent years, it had become a source of deep controversy, representing to many the legacy of slavery and racial oppression. The pivotal vote came in the wake of the tragic death of 9-year-old Tamir Rice, a Black boy fatally shot by a Cleveland police officer, which once again reignited national debates about race and symbolism in the United States. However, even prior to this tragic event, pressure had been mounting in South Carolina for change. The flag had endured protest, violence, and condemnation, most notably following the 2015 Charleston church shooting, when a white supremacist who killed nine Black congregants displayed the flag at his trial. Speaker of the House Joseph Neal framed the motion as one of unity and progress. “It’s time to move forward as a state and not remain anchored to a symbol of division,” he said during the debate. The House passed the motion overwhelmingly, with 71 in favor and 35 opposed. The Senate, which had previously resisted calls for removal, had also repealed a measure in 2015 that would have banned the display of the flag, but now it appears the political climate is shifting. Governor Nikki Haley, a strong advocate for removing the flag, tweeted in response to the vote, “It is time. Let our state move forward. Let’s fly a flag that represents all South Carolinians.” The symbolic removal is expected to take place in the coming weeks. While the decision has been hailed as a step towards reconciliation, it has also drawn sharp criticism from some lawmakers and constituents who view the flag as a representation of southern heritage and pride. One dissenting member, Rep. Steve Gregory, argued that to remove the flag was to erase the state’s history. “We are not erasing history,” he said. “We are choosing to live in the present and embrace a future where all people are valued equally.” Supporters of the vote welcomed the decision as a long-overdue acknowledgment of a painful chapter in American history. Civil rights leaders in South Carolina and beyond praised the lawmakers for taking a stance against a symbol that continues to inflict deep wounds on the Black community.

European retailers including Hennes & Mauritz (H&M) and Inditex, the parent company of Zara, have announced they will sign the Bangladesh Fire and Building Safety Accord, a legally binding agreement aimed at improving safety in thousands of Bangladeshi garment factories. The move comes in response to growing concern over the working conditions in the factories that supply fast fashion to global markets, particularly in the wake of the 2013 Rana Plaza disaster, in which 1,134 workers died. The Accord, which was first signed in May 2013 by over 200 brands, requires participating companies to pay for safety assessments, inspections, and necessary retrofits in factories producing clothes for the signatories. H&M and Inditex have now confirmed their decision to join the Accord following significant pressure from campaign groups, ethical investment bodies, and consumer outrage over the exploitation of garment workers in the developing world. The two major fashion brands had been among the few leading retailers that had refused to sign the agreement in recent years. Critics had accused them of prioritising profits over the well-being of workers, many of whom earn less than £50 a month and work in poorly maintained buildings. Emma McCrea, deputy director of Clean Clothes Campaign, welcomed H&M and Inditex’s decision, stating: “This is a major breakthrough. It sends a clear message that brands must take responsibility for the conditions in their supply chains and support the right to safe and healthy workplaces.” Under the Accord, independent experts are tasked with overseeing compliance with safety standards, and the contract is designed to last beyond any individual brand's participation. This approach aims to eliminate the so-called “cherry-picking” strategy, in which some brands attempted to avoid legal responsibility by slipping out of the agreement when it became legally binding. The news follows the recent rejection of the Accord by the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the country’s powerful garment industry body. BGMEA has argued the Accord places an unfair burden on local manufacturers and fails to respect Bangladeshi law. However, the initiative is backed by trade unions and relied upon by thousands of Bangladeshi garment workers who hope to see an end to dangerous conditions. With H&M and Inditex now on board, campaigners have called for other major global retailers to follow suit. The latest development marks a pivotal moment in the push for greater accountability in the global fashion industry, where clothing is often made at the cost of human lives.

Plans to introduce a ‘soft opt-out’ system for organ donation in Scotland have been formally published by the Scottish government, marking a significant shift in the country’s approach to transplantation and organ availability. Under the proposed model, individuals will be presumed to have agreed to donate their organs unless they have explicitly opted out — a system known as ‘presumed consent’. The Scottish government has defended the move, stating that it is designed to reduce the number of patients on the waiting list and save lives by increasing the number of available organs. The Scottish government has announced its intention to introduce a 'soft opt-out' system for organ donation, a proposal that suggests individuals under the new presumption would be considered willing donors unless they have opted out. The plan has been submitted to Holyrood and now invites public and parliamentary debate before legislation is formally developed. The announcement has reignited the ethical and moral debate around organ donation, with proponents arguing that the opt-out system will encourage a cultural shift and increase donor numbers. Health Secretary Shona Robison has previously stated that Scotland currently has one of the lowest rates of organ donation in Europe and that changing the system could save more than 500 lives over the next decade. Under the current system, individuals must register as donors, a process that many experts say only a minority of the population has completed. With the proposed model, families will still be consulted following a loved one’s death, but their views will not be able to override the presumed consent. This is designed to avoid situations where family objections prevent the use of viable organs. The Scottish government’s proposals align with the systems already in place in Wales, which implemented a similar model in December 2015. Early figures from Wales suggest that while immediate increases in donor numbers have not been substantial, public awareness and registration rates have improved. Figures about how many people have updated their status since the change came into force are still being collected. Opponents of the system, including some religious and community groups, have raised concerns about the implications of presumed consent. They argue that it places pressure on families at a time of grief and could erode the principles of personal autonomy and informed consent. The publication of the proposal comes as part of a wider review of organ donation and transplant services in Scotland.

England were on the wrong end of a 30-3 hammering at the hands of Wales on Sunday, yet they know first-hand that the red rose can bloom again against the best teams in world rugby — provided their A game turns up for the right match. On Saturday, England face Australia at Twickenham in a key autumn international and, if they can summon the same determination they displayed in their 21-16 win over the Wallabies at the same venue last season, this could be their day. The stark differences between their performances in Cardiff and a potential performance in London present a puzzle for fans and analysts alike. Wales made them look disorganised, jaded and lacking in direction, with the national side seemingly struggling to find form after missing out on the Grand Slam. But history tells a different story. England have beaten Australia 13 times since the Wallabies last recorded a victory in the 1998 World Cup, and they have been a formidable force in major international fixtures in recent years. Speaking in his pre-match press conference on Friday, England captain Owen Farrell showed no signs of despair. “If we play like we can, we can beat anyone on our day,” he said. “Last Saturday wasn’t one of those days and we need to take the learning from that and apply it tomorrow against Australia.” Farrell was alluding to the national side’s defensive lapses, a lack of ball control and the poor discipline that cost them a string of tries against Wales. But the players will know that the Wallabies, despite their 2015 World Cup success, are not the same dominant side they once were. Australia have been inconsistent in the autumn internationals this year, losing three of their last four games under head coach Joe Schmidt. They arrive in Twickenham with a 50-50 chance — the kind of uncertainty England will be hoping to exploit. “Against Wales, we were barely up to it. Against Australia, we’re not just going to hang on for dear life,” explained Eddie Jones, England's head coach, in a rare show of public optimism. “This is a different team, a different game. We have a game-plan and we have the ability to execute it if the attitude is right.” The match will also serve as a litmus test for Jones' management style after a turbulent week following the defeat against Wales.

Ukrainian military forces have been placed on high alert along the de facto border with Crimea and on the frontlines facing separatist rebels in the east, amid growing concerns over potential escalations in the ongoing conflict. The recent move, confirmed by Ukrainian officials, appears to be a strategic readiness response to intelligence reports indicating possible movements of Russian-backed forces and weapons in the Black Sea peninsula, which was annexed by Russia in 2014. The alert affects multiple military units deployed in the disputed regions, including those in the Luhansk and Donetsk oblasts, where pro-Russian rebels have been locked in a drawn-out stalemate with Kyiv’s armed forces since 2014. According to a military spokesperson released on Sunday, Ukrainian troops have intensified patrols and surveillance operations, particularly near the Bakhmut and Kupiansk fronts, where the fighting has been most intense in recent months. A statement from the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces highlighted the readiness of troops to respond to any unauthorised incursions or hostile activities across the front lines and in Crimea, which, although not internationally recognised as part of Russia, continues to be a flashpoint for tension.
