This heightened state of alert comes at a time of renewed international concern as the war in Ukraine approaches its deadly third year. Western military and intelligence sources have reported a significant build-up of Russian troops along the border – a prelude often associated with major offensives seen in previous years. While Kyiv and its Western allies have long warned that Russia was preparing for a new phase of the invasion, Moscow has consistently denied any intent to escalate hostilities. Instead, it has focused on justifying its so-called "special military operation" by citing continued "fascist" threats in eastern Ukraine. The situation in Crimea adds another layer of complexity. Though physically separated from the rest of the mainland, the peninsula remains an area of active military posturing. Ukrainian forces maintain a cautious but firm presence along the unrecognised administrative border, with satellite imagery over the past few weeks showing unusual vehicle movements near occupied Sevastopol. These reports have fuelled fears that Russia could once again attempt to expand its control or carry out cross-border incursions into Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions. Local officials in the eastern oblasts have also raised concerns over the additional strain being placed on already overstretched communities. "Our people go to bed with the sound of artillery in the background," one mayor in the line-of-contact zone said.

A former aide to former Prime Minister David Cameron has appeared in court in London accused of possessing and downloading indecent images of children, marking a high-profile case that has drawn attention due to the defendant’s political background. The individual, whose name was not disclosed during the initial hearing at the Old Bailey, is alleged to have accessed and stored prohibited material on electronic devices over a prolonged period. The trial, which is expected to last several weeks, has already sparked questions about the personal conduct of those in positions of public trust. The charges stem from an investigation by the National Crime Agency (NCA), which began after an anonymous tip-off led to the discovery of the material during a routine digital check. The accused, who served in a junior advisory role during Cameron’s time in government from 2010 to 2016, is said to have deleted the evidence soon after the agency’s involvement was confirmed. A prosecution witness later recovered most of the files, according to court documents. During the brief initial hearing, Judge Mr Hain QC addressed the defendant’s bail application, noting that due to the nature of the charges and the accused’s access to electronic devices while out of custody, bail would require restrictions. The individual was released on stringent conditions, including the surrender of electronic devices for monitoring and regular check-ins with police. The Crown Prosecution Service has confirmed it will proceed with the trial, citing the seriousness of the allegations, and has emphasized the priority of protecting vulnerable victims. 知情人士透露，被告在聆讯中对指控不认罪。辩方律师专注于案件的事实细节，同时试图限制在审判过程中透露任何可能对被告造成声誉损害的信息。另一方面，反对派议员已对内政部提出批评，要求更加彻底审查高级官员的背景调查程序，并建议将类似罪行的刑期增加，以示警戒。 This case has reignited public debate over how thoroughly civil servants and political advisors are vetted and whether the screening process should be independently reviewed to ensure transparency. The Cameron era, often described as relatively light-touch in approach to personal and political conduct, is now under a different spotlight as it becomes entwined with legal rather than political scrutiny. Public reaction has been mixed, with some calling for a fair trial and others urging swift justice. The trial is expected to resume next week, with additional witnesses, forensic experts, and potentially recovered files set to play a central role in determining the defendant’s culpability. Meanwhile, the former aide's name, once known within Westminster circles, has now become synonymous with what one commentator described as "an uncomfortable reminder that lives spent in the public eye can conceal private horrors."

The future of how Europeans' data is shared with US companies such as Facebook and Google is set to be considered by the EU's highest court, in a case that could have sweeping implications for digital privacy and transatlantic data flows. At the centre of the legal review is a long-standing agreement known as the Privacy Shield, which was established in 2016 to replace the invalidated Safe Harbour framework and govern how personal data shared between the EU and the US is protected under European regulations, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The European Court of Justice (ECJ) was asked to rule on the case by Austria's data protection authority, which argued that US surveillance practices are incompatible with EU privacy laws. The court's upcoming judgment could determine whether the Privacy Shield is sufficient to safeguard Europeans' fundamental rights when their data crosses the Atlantic. The case stems from the Guardian journalist Schrems and his challenge to the data practices of Facebook, which at the time operated under the Safe Harbour agreement. The agreement was found wanting by the ECJ in 2015 and later discarded, leading to the formation of the Privacy Shield. However, concerns continue to persist over the lack of clear legal protections in the US for EU citizens' data, particularly in the context of foreign intelligence surveillance programmes such as those revealed by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden. The EU's stance remains firm that national security justifications must not override the requirement to protect individual privacy, a position that puts the bloc at odds with US agencies that maintain the right to access large volumes of data for counter-terrorism and intelligence purposes. Despite this, major US technology firms rely heavily on the legitimacy of the Privacy Shield to justify transferring user data freely between the US and their European subsidiaries and customers. Any ruling that undermines the agreement could compel companies—including tech giants such as Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft—to find alternative, and potentially more cumbersome, means of managing data transfers. The Danish data watchdog has already raised concerns over the scale of unregulated data access to EU users, arguing that European regulators cannot enforce their laws against foreign intelligence agencies. The ECJ's decision will likely send a strong message about the EU's commitment to data sovereignty and the limits of global cooperation on security and privacy.

At a time when compassion and dignity should be front and centre, concerns are growing over reports of angry reprimands and a string of aggressive outbursts directed at vulnerable patients dining at a mental health hospital in the south of England. Staff and patient advocates have expressed alarm that such behaviour, reminiscent of a strict hostel for troubled youth, has become normalized in an institution designed to support the mentally unwell. The allegations have sparked an internal inquiry and renewed calls for institutional reform in how mental health services approach patient care, particularly in inpatient settings. According to a whistleblower among the nursing staff, the incidents occur most prominently during mealtimes when the slow movement or delayed actions of residents seem to provoke tempers. "It's as if the people in charge have forgotten that these are not children to be scolded, but adults in need of care and understanding," the source said. "These aren’t schools: they’re hospitals where fear and frustration must be met with calm, not condemnation." The hospital in question has not officially commented, though its management has confirmed that an internal investigation is underway following anonymous concerns raised through both national and local mental health support forums. The Home Office and the Care Quality Commission (CQC) have also been informed of the allegations. One patient, who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions, described watching a nurse scold another inpatient for “pushing too slowly through the food queue.” The same patient said, “It’s frightening. You come here because you don’t feel safe in the world, and then you’re told you’re not acting right in the very place that’s supposed to protect you.” This is not the first time staff have been implicated in poor handling of vulnerable patient cases. A 2017 CQC report rated the facility as "good" overall but noted "areas for improvement" in the "tone of interactions between staff and patients." At the time, the hospital had committed to training that would reinforce "a culture of kindness and respect." The most recent rebukes appear to contradict those promises. Mental health charities such as Mind and Rethink Mental Illness have issued statements urging transparency and accountability. “Words are powerful when dealing with those who are already hearing negative and harmful messages every day,” said a spokesperson for Mind. “Such conduct from those in positions of care is not only damaging but a serious breach of best practice.”

A man has been sentenced to life imprisonment after admitting the murder of a Glasgow shopkeeper whom he claimed had “disrespected” Islam, in what prosecutors have described as a racially and religiously motivated attack. The victim, Masud Uddin, 56, was the owner of a convenience store in the south of the city when he was shot at close range outside the shop on the evening of 21 August 2023. During the trial at the High Court in Edinburgh, the defendant, identified only as “Abdul” (not his real name), admitted the murder under the Crown’s direction of joint enterprise. He claimed that he acted in response to what he perceived as an insult to the Prophet Muhammad, although prosecutors have stressed that there is no evidence the shopkeeper had made any such statement or gesture. The victim, a British Bangladeshi, was respected within the local community and had run the shop for over 20 years. The incident has sent shockwaves through Glasgow’s Muslim community and broader society, with calls for greater efforts to combat hate crime and prevent radicalisation. Local leaders and religious figures have condemned the murder as an act of terrorism, inappropriate and unwarranted. A short, handwritten note found at the scene and purportedly written by the killer included references to Islamic texts, further deepening concerns about the role of extremist ideology in the crime. Depute fiscal principal, Rachael Farley, said the victim had no connection to any of the tensions or tensions the defendant was responding to. “This was an unprovoked attack,” she said during the sentencing hearing. “It was a targeted, religiously motivated act of violence that was carried out with fury and intent.” The prosecution requested a whole-life tariff, which the judge agreed to, meaning the man will serve at least 25 years before being eligible for parole—if ever. Masud Uddin was survived by his wife and two young children. Tributes poured in for the community-minded entrepreneur, with many local residents calling for education and understanding to help prevent such attacks in the future. Speaking outside court, Mr Uddin’s wife, Farzana, described her husband as a “quiet, hard-working man who loved his family and always treated everyone with respect.” The case is being closely monitored by the Home Office and anti-terrorism units, as it raises troubling questions about the extent to which religiously inspired violence is growing in the UK.

The Hatton Garden jewel raid, already a source of national fascination and mystery, has been described as the “largest burglary in English legal history” in ongoing court proceedings. The case, centred on a £14 million heist in 2015, continues to draw attention as it unfolds in central London, with new details emerging about the audacity of the crime and the scale of its potential fallout. The theft, which took place in April 2015, targeted a high-security vault in the heart of Hatton Garden, one of the UK’s most important centres for the diamond trade. At the time, it was dubbed the "Great Diamond Heist", mostly because the thieves bypassed heavy security to penetrate a locked safe behind a false wall inside the office of jeweller Leslie C. Rosenthal. It is now being cited in court as the most valuable property crime in English legal history — matching up to £25 million worth of stolen goods, when the full value of the loot is likely to be taken into account. Christopher Tse, QC for the Crown, told the Old Bailey that the crime demonstrated meticulous planning and was executed with the help of individuals who had long-standing experience in the criminal underworld. The raid was as much a feat of engineering as it was of deception. It is believed that the perpetrators used a digger from the basement of a public car park to tunnel into the vault, and operated it remotely during the Easter Bank Holiday, when staff had gone to their families and the building was empty. The case has already led to convictions and ongoing investigations, with at least four men found guilty of conspiracy to commit burglary. Those sentenced have included a retired police officer and a scaffolding contractor, both of whom provided their skills under the guise of legitimate work. Meanwhile, most of the stolen goods remain absent, frustrating police and the victims of the heist. Paul Condon, 83, is among the most notable suspects still at large. Despite extensive surveillance efforts, he has evaded capture and has been described in police statements as a key figure in the planning and coordination of the raid. His supporters, comprising family and close friends, maintain that he is “an honest man unfairly treated by the media and the system.” Legal experts have begun to consider the long-term implications of such a high-value crime, noting that if the court’s current assessments are accurate, the Hatton Garden case may rewrite the benchmarks for property crime in England.

Victor Moses’ remarkable resurgence at Stamford Bridge has defied all expectations, with the 28-year-old former Chesterfield player now lying at the heart of Chelsea’s surprise Premier League charge. Just over a year ago, Moses found himself on the transfer market with only 11 Premier League appearances to his name since the start of the 2014-15 season. However, under manager Thomas Tuchel, the winger has become a pivotal figure in Chelsea’s attacking philosophy — a 3-4-3 formation that has propelled them to the top of the league table after a stellar start to the season. Since the Blues made the tactical switch midway through last season, Moses has transformed from a forgotten man into the most impactful wide player in the division. His blistering pace, sharp decision-making, and left-foot finishing have brought a new dimension to the team, with his recent performances drawing widespread acclaim. Last weekend’s 4-2 win over Manchester United saw Moses shine once again, playing a key role with a goal and two assists as the London side looked every bit like serious title contenders. The story of Moses’ revival is one that blends tactical innovation with personal determination. After spells on loan at Middlesbrough, West Ham, Inter Milan and Fenerbahçe since 2015, many considered it unlikely that he would rediscover his form at Chelsea – particularly with Antonio Conte initially preferring other options on the left flank. But when the former Italy coach departed after Euro 2020 and Tuchel arrived with a fresh blueprint, Moses found himself at the perfect place at the perfect time. In the 3-4-3 system, Moses' dual ability as a winger and a forward has been central to Chelsea’s attacking success. Deployed as a false nine in certain phases of play or a wide forward when the shape demands it, his adaptability and energy have impressed both fans and pundits. Notably, the former Liverpool star has shown a willingness to press, track back and put in the defensive work often overlooked in discussions about flair players. Moses’ effectiveness has been further bolstered by his bond with forward Kai Havertz, whose performance has also risen to new heights as he benefits from being played behind the striker or with Moses to his right. The partnership has helped regulate the play in midfield while stretching opposition defences with pace and precision. Going into the heart of the Premier League season, Moses’ resurgence offers a compelling subplot in a title race that suddenly seems wide open.

Former Prison Governor Calls for Army to Restore Order in Prisons   A former chief prison officer has sparked fresh debate over the state of Britain’s prison system, suggesting the government should consider deploying the Army to take control of correctional facilities in order to restore order and security. Andrew Shaw, who served as a governor at multiple high-security prisons across England, made the comments during a recent policy forum in Westminster. With his career spanning nearly three decades, Mr Shaw has witnessed a sharp decline in the conditions and functioning of many of the country’s most challenging prisons. He said: “We are in crisis. Prisons are run-down, understaffed, and in many cases, entirely unmanageable. The level of violence, drug use, and disorder is at levels we haven’t seen since the 1990s. The system is unable to contain the problem itself.” Mr Shaw, who now advises on correctional policy for an independent think tank, argued that the armed forces must be brought in if the government is serious about restoring authority in prisons. “The Army has discipline, structure, and the capability to bring about a rapid improvement. They can provide order while long-term reforms are put in place.” His comments come as the justice secretary has faced increasing pressure to address chronic overcrowding, staff shortages, and rising levels of self-harm and assaults in prisons. Earlier this month, a report by the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman found that nearly half of all incidents of violence in prisons occurred in the worst-run facilities. Mr Shaw’s call for military involvement, however, is not without controversy. Critics argue that the Army is not trained or equipped to run prisons, and that such a move would be a tacit admission of systemic failure. Paul Burstow, the shadow justice secretary, said: “Bringing in the Army is not the solution to broken policy. We need to properly fund and reform prisons, not militarise them.” Others, including some retired Ministry of Justice officials, have warned that using the Army could create new problems, including tensions between civilian and military staff and a lack of effectiveness in long-term rehabilitation efforts. Despite the controversy, Mr Shaw maintains that waiting for a slow-moving reform process is not an option. “We are talking about people with complex needs living in unacceptable conditions. Something has to be done, and done quickly, before the situation deteriorates any further.”

A criminal investigation into the case of a father accused of sexually assaulting his 13-month-old daughter shortly before her sudden death must be reopened, according to former UK Justice Minister Sir Simon Hughes. The comments come amid growing public outrage and a renewed inquiry into whether the process surrounding the child’s death—initially recorded as an accident—was properly and transparently handled. The girl, from an unnamed town in the north of England, was found dead in a field in December 2019. In the days prior, her father was reportedly arrested and taken to a police station in connection with the alleged sexual abuse. Although he was later released under suspended police investigation, the girl’s death was initially attributed to suspected accidental asphyxiation, with no further action taken against the parent. However, following years of campaigning by the child’s mother and a growing body of evidence suggesting the true cause of death could not be ruled out without further scrutiny, urgent calls for an independent review of the case have been made. Sir Simon Hughes, a former Liberal Democrat MP and long-time advocate for victims of sexual abuse and domestic violence, has called for a full criminal investigation to be reinstated. “This case is deeply troubling and raises serious concerns about how vulnerable children are protected in our legal and social systems,” Hughes said. “If this father is innocent—and I have seen no evidence of that—I want to know the truth. But equally, if he is guilty, the system must respond. This case simply cannot end with ambiguity.” The original medical cause of the child’s death was listed as unascertained, with no confirmation of whether the alleged assault contributed. Local authorities have since declined to discuss the case publicly, prompting criticism from campaigners and members of the public who say the silence is deeply disrespectful to the child and unjust for the family. Central to the controversy is the fact that the father was seen by officers during the alleged incident and was released without being held for further questioning. Questions are now being raised as to whether there was adequate communication between the local police force, social services, and child protection agencies. A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said: “We are aware of the public interest in this case and are looking at whether a full investigation can be reopened.

Two recent business surveys have raised fresh concerns that the Scottish economy is spiralling deeper into decline, casting a shadow over economic recovery in the wake of the pandemic and Brexit-related challenges. The reports, published by separate research bodies, indicate that a previously observed slowdown may now be accelerating, with businesses reporting reduced confidence, falling investment levels, and weakening demand across key sectors. According to the latest report from the   Scottish Chambers of Commerce   (SCC), businesses are facing a "perfect storm" of external and domestic pressures. Headline data from the survey suggests that over 60% of firms are reporting a drop in sales, with the worst performance seen in sectors like hospitality, retail, and construction—those still heavily reliant on consumer spending and small business activity. Energy and manufacturing sectors, which had shown early signs of resilience following post-pandemic reopening, are now also showing signs of strain, with firms citing increased energy costs, supply chain bottlenecks, and continued skills shortages. Concurrently, a separate survey conducted by the   Economist Intelligence Unit’s Business Monitor International  , a respected global economic forecasting group, has corroborated these findings. The index—measuring business sentiment, investment intent, and growth—fell below the critical 50-point threshold for the first time in two years, indicating a deepening pessimism among Scottish businesses. The decline was particularly sharp in the public sector and among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which now face the dual challenge of shrinking orders and inflation-driven operating costs. These findings have already begun to stir alarm in Holyrood, where Labour leader Anas Sarwar warned that the government must “wake up to the crisis on its doorstep.” Meanwhile, the Scottish Greens have called for urgent intervention through targeted support for energy-intensive sectors and a renewed focus on green investment to stimulate jobs and innovation. The Scottish government has so far offered cautious responses, with a spokeswoman stating that “a robust recovery is still underway,” and that support packages, including wage subsidies and business-rate relief for SMEs, are already in place. The growing consensus among business leaders, however, is that existing measures are not enough. With the Bank of Scotland restricting lending to small businesses and regional unemployment figures quietly ticking upwards, the call for sustained economic stimulus and a nuanced approach to regulatory easing is becoming ever more insistent. Whether Edinburgh is prepared to take bold action or will continue to rely on go-slow austerity policies remains to be seen, but for now, Scotland’s economic headwinds show no sign of abating.

Nigella Lawson Claims Ex-Husband Charles Saatchi Threatened to 'Destroy' Her with Drug Use Allegations   Nigella Lawson has told a court that her ex-husband, advertising tycoon Charles Saatchi, threatened to “destroy” her with “false” allegations of drug use, as the long-running high-profile legal battle between the couple continues. The British television chef and author, known for her culinary expertise and charismatic on-screen presence, delivered a poised and detailed account during the ongoing High Court hearing into claims she was involved in controlling child sex abuse rings. Lawson denied the allegations, called “wholly untrue and outrageous,” as she provided evidence in a claim she is seeking millions in compensation for mental distress, damage to her career, and defamation. During cross-examination by lawyer Jonathan Sumption QC for Saatchi, Lawson described how the couple, who married in 1986 and divorced in 2001, had a long history of arguments and emotional instability. She revealed that after their marital breakdown and the split of the London home they once shared, Saatchi was unhappy that she had sold off shared property. According to her, this led to a spiral of acrimony and, eventually, what she described as a vengeful campaign. “It was something to do with getting back at me, destroying me professionally,” she said. Lawson claimed that Saatchi became fixated on spreading false information about her, including the idea that she was taking and dealing drugs. “He said he could make that stick, and he could destroy someone with that,” she testified. “He made it a very clear threat.” She also said he made other bizarre and unsubstantiated claims, including that she was part of a “pedophile ring.” The trial, which has gripped the public for weeks, follows years of speculation and unsavoury press coverage. In 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron unreservedly apologised to Lawson, after she made allegations against National Crime Agency (NCA) officers that they had suggested to the media she was involved in child abuse. At the time, NCA officers were investigating Saatchi, who was later arrested over claims of historical abuse involving two girls but was not ultimately charged with any offence. Lawson, who has sold millions of cookbooks and headlined some of the UK's most-watched cooking programmes, has consistently maintained her innocence and dignity in public, even in the face of brutal media scrutiny. The trial continues, with further testimony from both parties expected to provide deeper insight into the turbulent and ultimately destructive relationship between two of Britain’s most recognisable public figures.

Lewis Hamilton believes his record-equalling seventh world championship is the foundation for "something special" between himself and Mercedes in the years to come. The seven-time champion clinched the title at the final race of the season in Abu Dhabi, a dramatic finale in which title rival Max Verstappen faded as Hamilton picked up yet another crown for the Silver Arrows. For Hamilton, who tied with Michael Schumacher on the all-time list of F1 champions, the triumph is not just another feather in his cap but a catalyst for building something even greater. "This victory is the start of something special between me and Mercedes," said the 38-year-old Briton during his post-race interview. "We’ve had some incredible years and I feel like we’ve only just scratched the surface of what we can do together. I left nothing on the table this season, and I’m excited for what lies ahead." Hamilton’s world title came amid an intense and at times controversial conclusion to the 2024 season, which saw close rivalries in both the championship and the constructors' awards. The Briton’s final victory was a fitting end to a campaign that saw him bounce back from mid-season struggles, showcasing the resilience and skill that have defined his career. Mercedes, for their part, proved that they can still compete at the highest level, reclaiming both titles from Red Bull after a competitive – at times contentious – battle. Hamilton and Mercedes have had a long and storied partnership, with the English driver making his debut with the team back in 2013. Since then, they have dominated F1 in a way that few teams and drivers have achieved, building a legacy that will outlast them both. Now, with the world title wrapped up, Hamilton is setting his sights beyond the numbers and the records, on legacy and impact. "I want to do more than just win titles," he said. "I want to inspire young people, to make a difference on and off the track. This title is a beginning for us, not an end. We can keep building something that represents more than just a Formula 1 team or a driver. We can show what is possible when you believe in what you're doing and fight for it every day." Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff echoed Hamilton’s sentiments, calling the partnership with the driver “unfinished business” as they head into 2025.

Luis Suarez has lost a major sponsor following his continued disciplinary issues on the pitch, with his latest transgression—the biting of Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini—provoking a swift response from brand partners. The Uruguayan international, already banned for biting two opponents since the 2010 World Cup—Deerlijk’s Otman Bakkal and Netherlands’ Georginio Wijnaldum—has once again drawn global condemnation with an incident that occurred during last week’s international friendly match in Ohio. The attacking midfielder was shown a red card and is now facing the possibility of further disciplinary action from UEFA, but the decision has not only cost him three matches of upcoming European qualification games but also a high-profile sponsorship deal with U.S.-based sportswear giant, Under Armour. Under Armour confirmed the termination of its association with Suarez, citing the player’s “undesirable and unbecoming conduct” as incompatible with the brand’s values. In a brief statement, the company said: “We are disappointed by Luis’s recent actions and, as a result, we will no longer be working with him.” This marks the second time that Under Armour has severed ties with a high-profile athlete over repeated controversies, following the controversial departure of American NFL star Richie Incognito in 2014. The move also reflects a wider trend among sponsors of distancing themselves from athletes whose off-field conduct causes reputational risk, particularly in an age of heightened social media scrutiny. Suarez’s agent, Fernando Huanini, was unavailable for comment at the time of publication, but the striker is said to be in receipt of legal advice regarding the circumstances of the incident and potential disciplinary procedures. Some reports suggest that the Uruguayan Football Association and Barcelona—where Suarez plays—are analysing the broader implications of the incident, with Barcelona’s vice-president Javier Faus having already publicly supported the striker during past controversies. The 35-year-old forward was widely regarded as one of the most talented players in world football, having helped Barcelona win four La Liga titles and the Champions League, as well as guiding Uruguay to the 2011 Copa América final. His personal achievements have long been overshadowed by his on-field acts of aggression, which have resulted in sustained bans from the game and a cloud of criticism from the international footballing community. Club president Josep Maria Bartomeu has publicly defended his position on the player in the past, although the recent incident could now prompt action from the club in the form of a transfer.

In a harrowing firsthand account from one of the darkest days in British sporting history, a former police officer has revealed the grim reality he faced during the Hillsborough disaster in 1989. As thousands of fans flooded into Sheffield Wednesday's ground for the £3 FA Cup semi-final between Nottingham Forest and Liverpool, the Leppings Lane end became an impossible, overcrowded nightmare. Forty-nine lives were lost, and hundreds more were left with injuries that would follow them for the rest of their days. At the heart of a new police review, which is once again casting fresh questions over the handling of that fateful April afternoon, the officer has spoken of the moment he carried a 16-year-old boy from the terraces, blood still wet on his clothes and life already slipping from his grasp. Citing the overwhelming tide of bodies and the desperate demands on rescue efforts, he revealed he and others present did not see the point in assembling the fan into the standard recovery position. "You look at them, and you know... there's not a lot you can do," he said, his tone still heavy with the weight of memories over 30 years old. The officer, who served in South Yorkshire Police at the time and did not wish to be named, recounted the chaos as emergency services tried in vain to treat the wounded. "It was dark, the crush was relentless, and people were just fading away around us. We had to act quickly, but the reality was many of those we found were beyond help," he explained. The recovery position, normally used to keep airways open for unconscious but breathing victims, was not a priority in a scenario where medical staff had no clear access and were themselves overwhelmed. The officer’s account has been released as part of an ongoing independent review, Operation Hyacinth, which is reassessing all evidence connected to the 96th man and the 49 lives lost. This fresh scrutiny comes barely a week after the unearthing of previously secret police files that suggested senior officers were aware of the danger at the stadium long before the final whistle was blown. Those files have intensified calls for full accountability and deeper transparency about the decisions made that day. Speaking to the BBC, Dr. Richard Dawkins, a renowned independent criminologist and long-time Hillsborough campaigner, said the officer’s reflection was a deeply human glimpse into a man’s struggle to go on with his life while grappling with actions he could never undo.

The extensive private art collection of renowned Peruvian-Peruvian-born fashion photographer Mario Testino is set to go on public display in the UK for the first time, offering a rare glimpse into the passion and eclectic tastes of one of the world's most celebrated lensmen. The exhibition, which will be unveiled at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, promises to be a landmark event in both the art and fashion worlds. Testino, whose work has graced the covers of major fashion magazines and whose portraits have captured the likes of the British Royal Family, is as distinguished as a private art patron as he is as a photographer. Over the past three decades, he has accumulated a collection of over 100 works spanning classical masterpieces, modern art, and contemporary pieces from across the globe. The exhibition showcases everything from Renaissance paintings and Impressionist works to works from the likes of Andy Warhol and Anselm Kiefer. This is the first time Testino has been willing to share the personal treasures that fill his homes in London and New York. Organized in collaboration with the Royal Academy, the show is the result of years of planning and was only made possible with the full cooperation of Testino, who has always been known for guarding his private life and collection with great discretion. “I have always believed in surrounding myself with the best work I can find from the best artists,” Testino said in a Royal Academy statement, expressing both pride and a sense of obligation. “I’m incredibly grateful to the Royal Academy for giving the public the opportunity to see the pieces that live in the walls of my home. It is also a way of sharing the visual world that has inspired me through my career.” The exhibition is expected to draw art lovers and fashionistas alike, as it promises to offer not only visual treats but also insights into Testino’s motivation and appreciation of the broader arts. “Testino’s collection is unique and very diverse,” said Dr. Karen Livingstone, the Royal Academy’s head curator. “It reflects his extraordinary eye and gives us a window into the mind of a true visionary.” The exhibition will run for three months, opening to the public in early November. Tickets are already selling fast, as art and fashion enthusiasts prepare to see behind the curtain of one of the world’s most private and powerful art collections.

Leaked Briefings Expose Ed Miliband’s Attack Strategy for PMQs   The veil was torn off the opposition’s strategy when Labour leader Ed Miliband’s classified briefing notes for the upcoming Prime Minister’s Questions were leaked last night, revealing a full arsenal of planned lines aimed at Prime Minister David Cameron. The documents, reportedly passed to a member of the press during preparations for today’s Commons showdown, outline a series of targeted questions suggesting Miliband intends to focus on Cameron’s policy inconsistencies, the economy, and Tory record on public services. Critics are already panning the strategy as “predictable and underwhelming,” while Labour allies claim it underlines the party’s renewed focus on holding the government to account. In the notes released, Miliband is advised to push hard on the prime minister’s controversial decision to implement the so-called “bedroom tax,” the National Health Service winter crisis, and the government’s handling of the economy—particularly in light of the UK’s slow post-referendum recovery. The plan suggests he will also raise concerns over the apparent lack of progress in forming a coherent Brexit strategy, despite the original June 2016 referendum promise of one. Notably, Miliband is briefed to press Cameron on two core issues said to reflect public dissatisfaction: the real-terms cuts to public services and the Tory-led government’s response to domestic violence. “It is clear the government is failing to protect vulnerable people and is making life harder for hardworking families,” reads an internal line to be used when referring to the bedroom tax and benefit changes. The notes reveal a measured, fact-based tone in an apparent departure from the often volatile style of previous Labour opposition leaders. One point underlines a planned emphasis on policy over personality: “Be calm, assertive, but not confrontational.” The leak has been met with swift condemnation from the Conservative Party, with one senior Tory MP suggesting it showed a “lack of discipline among Labour’s inner circle,” and even hinting at a calculated leak. “This isn’t the work of a united party,” the MP added. “It shows confusion and a leadership in crisis.” However, Labour insiders have dismissed the leak as a minor setback, insisting the content of the briefings reflects a mature critique of government policy. “This is a new phase of opposition,” said one party aide. “We’re delivering serious scrutiny with real purpose.”

The BBC has revealed the lineup for its series of election programming, as the nation prepares for a general election set to take place in early 2024. Among the highlights are two eagerly anticipated Question Time special editions, where Prime Minister Theresa May and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn will answer questions from the public on the key issues facing the country. The announcement has been met with both excitement and some controversy, with political commentators already predicting a tense and fiery exchange. The flagship BBC One show will serve as a key battleground for both leaders to outline their visions for the future of the UK and to defend their records in office. Question Time, known for its engaging and often combative format, is expected to draw large audiences, with fans and critics alike tuning in to witness the politicians put on the spot by a panel of everyday voters. In addition to the Question Time specials, the BBC’s election schedule includes a range of in-depth documentaries, live debates, and coverage of the major party manifestos. The coverage will be broadcast across the BBC’s radio and online platforms, with social media also playing a central role in engaging younger viewers and first-time voters. A full schedule was released on the BBC website, with each programme offering a detailed platform for each party to articulate its policies to the public. The prime minister’s participation in the Question Time special follows recent speculation over her future in politics. May has remained resolute about standing in the upcoming election, and the appearance will offer her a chance to reiterate her conservative positions and reassure her base at a time when the party is facing mounting pressure from both inside and outside Parliament. Sources in May’s office have confirmed that she is determined to demonstrate her leadership qualities on one of the country’s most respected political programmes. On the other side, Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has been a frequent figure on the public stage in recent months, as he continues to rally the party around its progressive agenda. The Question Time appearance will be another chance for Corbyn to highlight Labour’s key policies, including healthcare, education, and environmental issues. His response to difficult questions will be closely watched, especially as Labour seeks to recover from recent by-election losses and gain ground in traditionally Conservative heartlands. The BBC has also confirmed that other major party leaders will participate in the live coverage, with the first of a series of election debates scheduled for the following week.

Hearts’ Neilson Stresses Big Opportunity for Muirhead to Rebuild Career   Hearts head coach Robbie Neilson has publicly backed midfielder Robbie Muirhead after the player switched to Tynecastle on a season-long loan from Celtic, stating that the move gives him the chance to "get his career back on track." The Scottish Premiership side confirmed the arrival of the 23-year-old on Monday, with Neilson voicing his belief that Muirhead, once hailed as one of Scotland's top young talents, is ready to prove himself again under the light of the Tynecastle spotlight. Muirhead, whose career has been marred by injuries and inconsistent performances since breaking into the Celtic first team, is the latest in a line of young players brought in by Hearts as they look to strengthen an already youthful squad. Neilson, who has overseen a dramatic transformation at the club since taking charge in 2018, described the move as a tactical and psychological opportunity for both the club and the player. “I think he’s a very talented player,” Neilson told reporters on Tuesday. “He has the ability to change games, and I believe he knows he needs to come here and show us – and everyone – what he can do. It’s a real opportunity for him to get his career back on track, and I’m sure he understands how important that is – not just for his development, but for the team as well." Muirhead, capped at under-21 level for Scotland, was signed by Celtic from Dunfermline Athletic in 2014 in a £500,000 deal, but has made only seven senior appearances for the Glasgow giants. His move to Hearts comes amid intense competition in the Scottish top flight, where the Jambos are currently sitting in a play-off position but have the ambition of challenging for European qualification. Neilson admitted that Muirhead is not currently in the first-team plans but insisted he will have every opportunity to fight for his place. “He will train with the first team and will have to work hard to earn any minutes,” said the Hearts manager. “But I am not bringing him in just to sit on the bench. He has to know that this is his chance.” The loan arrives at a crucial point in the season, with Muirhead's senior career seemingly at a crossroads. Hearts supporters will be hopeful that his experience of playing at a higher level could provide a spark, while the midfielder's representatives will likely be watching closely for what could be a turning point in his rise.

A driver accused of causing a fatal crash that took the life of a five-year-old boy has told a court he cannot remember anything about the collision, as his trial opened in a case that has gripped a local community mourning the loss of a young life. The incident, which occurred during the early hours of the morning on a remote section of a rural road, left the child dead and raised serious questions over the circumstances leading up to the head-on collision. The defendant, a 37-year-old man from Manchester, appeared before magistrates in Rochdale as the preliminary hearing took place. Prosecutors allege that the man was driving at excessive speed under the influence of alcohol prior to the crash, which also left two other people injured. The child, who was among a group of friends returning from a local basketball event, had left the road shortly after the game to look for their mobile phones, which one of the children had dropped. It was in that brief moment that the horrific collision occurred, tragically taking the boy’s life. The boy’s mother, who was driving the group in a second vehicle, has described the moment as “a living nightmare”. She told reporters outside the court, “It is impossible to put into words how much we miss him. He was joyful and full of life. Nothing should have taken him so suddenly.” The accused, who was found unconscious at the scene and later taken to hospital, initially denied any recollection of the events leading up to the crash. He told the court, “I have no memory of the road, the car, the impact—nothing. I just don’t remember. If I had known my actions caused this, I would not be here.” The court was told that toxicology tests revealed the presence of alcohol in the defendant’s system, as well as a number of prescription drugs. However, the Crown Prosecutor stressed that the severity of the incident meant the exact state of the defendant at the time was not as important as the outcome—the death of an innocent child. The fatal crash has reignited local discussions about vehicle safety, road conditions, and the dangers of driving under the influence. Community leaders said the incident has left a deep scar on the area, with the child remembered as a “bright light in a dark space”.

Former US President Makes Bold Promise to Eradicate Tropical Disease in Three Years   Dr. Paul Henderson, former president of the United States, has made a dramatic pledge to the global health community, stating that a devastating tropical disease — long considered one of the world’s most persistent public health challenges — will be eradicated within three years. Speaking during a high-profile address at the International Health Summit in Geneva on Wednesday, Dr. Henderson, who founded a leading global health initiative under his administration, outlined a renewed strategy to bring about a disease-free world. "This is not a distant dream or an impossible hope," he said during his keynote speech. "Today, I can stand before you and say with confidence that we will eradicate this disease by 2028 — and that is a promise I will not only make, but also deliver." The disease in question, known for its crippling effects and high mortality rate in underprivileged regions of Africa and parts of South Asia, has resisted centuries of attempts to fully eradicate it. Despite significant progress in recent decades — including the introduction of mass treatment programs and increased public awareness — it remains a major cause of death and disability, particularly among children. Dr. Henderson’s remarks have sparked both excitement and skepticism in the international health community. While many experts applaud the ambition, some caution that global eradication initiatives require not only financial and political will but also broad national cooperation and infrastructure development in often the most under-resourced regions of the world. "I admire his vision and his conviction,” said Dr. Silvia Nogueira, a leading epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO). “But to achieve eradication in such a short time will require an unprecedented scaling up of resources and coordination at a global, national, and community level. That is no small task.” According to recent WHO estimates, approximately 15 million people are living with the disease today, with an estimated 800,000 new infections reported annually. Dr. Henderson’s initiative, launched in partnership with a consortium of global health bodies, pharmaceutical firms, and developing nations, aims to accelerate treatment, increase access to vaccines, and expand surveillance and monitoring systems across affected regions. The former president pointed to the successful eradication of smallpox in 1977 as proof of the feasibility of such an ambitious goal. “We have done it before,” he said. “And the science is even more advanced today.

Apple Pay, the mobile payment service launched by the tech giant Apple, will face spending limits of £20 in the UK when it is introduced later this month, according to the BBC. The restriction will apply to the majority of transactions, as security systems developed with banks and payment providers require safeguards against potential fraud. The new system relies on contactless card technology, designed to enable users to make purchases by tapping their iPhone or Apple Watch on a payment terminal. It is positioned by Apple as a more secure and convenient alternative to traditional contactless bank cards, which are already widely used in the UK. However, this new service adds another layer of encryption via Apple’s own chips, making it even more difficult for payment data to be intercepted. Despite the promise of a seamless and secure payment experience, the imposed £20 cap is expected to draw criticism from consumers, especially from those who use contactless cards and are used to spending up to £30 in a single transaction. The cap is, however, standard for new contactless payment systems in the UK and is usually reduced over time as trust builds between the customer and the service. Apple Pay will initially be supported by major banks including Barclays, Lloyds, HSBC, and NatWest, as well as prepaid card providers and mobile phone operators such as EE and Vodafone. The company has worked closely with UK regulators and financial institutions to ensure the system is robust before launch, with further features such as higher transaction limits expected to be phased in as the service matures. The launch will mark Apple’s latest foray into financial services, following the success of Apple Wallet in the US and the rapid adoption of mobile payments globally. While the UK market is relatively advanced in terms of contactless payments, Apple Pay is expected to accelerate the shift away from cash and traditional card payments. Retailers are reportedly excited about the technology, which promises to speed up transactions and reduce queues at major stores and airports. The technology is also seen as a key step towards Apple’s goal to become a key player in the digital financial ecosystem, competing against major fintech startups and international players eager to shape the future of payment systems. Critics have, however, questioned why the UK limit is so low compared to other countries. In the US, for example, the first-time spending limit for Apple Pay is $100 (roughly £75).

Douglas Carswell, the only UKIP MP and a prominent voice in the Brexit campaign, has said that the UK Independence Party must be willing to “work with anyone” to win the upcoming EU membership referendum, calling for a broad coalition to achieve a “clean break” from the European Union. Speaking in a wide-ranging interview, Carswell warned that if UKIP continued to act alone, it risked being sidelined by the wider public mood, a position that would not serve the party—or the cause—well. The former Conservative, who defected to UKIP in 2014, made his comments during a debate hosted by the think tank Policy Exchange, where he said it was vital for the Leave campaign to offer the public a clear alternative to the “hopeless status quo.” Although UKIP has long taken the lead in the Eurosceptic movement, the rise of Labour and Conservative MPs within the campaign has raised concerns within the party that its influence may be waning. Carswell argued that working across party lines was a necessary step if the Leave cause was ever to succeed. “I’m not saying we have to compromise the fundamental principle of leaving the EU,” he said, “but we need to listen to the people who are with us and not to push away those who share our aim, even if they don’t agree with every point of our manifesto. This is a national campaign – it’s not about party politics, and it never was.” His comments are the latest sign of growing unease within UKIP over its electoral prospects. Last year, the party made a strong showing in the European elections but failed to translate that momentum into parliamentary success, with leader Paul Nuttall losing his Cleethorpes seat. Meanwhile, UKIP’s share of the vote has continued to fall, with recent polls suggesting about 10–12 per cent support nationwide. Carswell’s suggestion that UKIP should consider collaboration with others is not new. Last year, it was reported that the party had secret talks with the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats about shared messaging and campaigns, though these were abandoned after a backlash. However, as the EU referendum approaches—and with no accurate way to assess public opinion—many within UKIP believe unity could offer the best chance of securing a decisive 'Leave' vote. The leader of UKIP, Paul Nuttall, has not yet commented on Carswell's proposal, though party sources confirmed it was a growing topic of internal discussion.

A new survey has revealed that a majority of the LGBT+ community in the UK feel they have to conceal or lie about their gender identity or sexual orientation in some contexts, often due to concerns about discrimination, rejection, or negativity. The findings, released by the Equality Network and polling over 1,000 individuals across the country, highlight the ongoing challenges faced by the community even as legislative and societal support for equality continues to grow. The data comes amid a broader conversation about the progress made in LGBT+ rights, including the legalisation of same-sex marriage and increasing visibility in media and public life. However, the survey adds an important caveat: for many, these advances have not yet translated into full acceptance in everyday life. Almost half of respondents said they had to hide or lie about their identity at work, with others reporting similar feelings in their families, friendships, and even in specialist LGBT+ support groups. The survey also found that younger members of the community were more likely to feel "safe enough" to be open about their identity, but in other cases, particularly for non-binary and transgender individuals, the fear of rejection was stark. One respondent, Sam, a 28-year-old woman who is part of the transgender community, said: "I’ve had to lie to colleagues about who I am because there was a possibility they would treat me differently or, worse, decide I’m not reliable." According to the report, the main reasons for lying were: fear of discrimination (34 per cent), fear of confidentiality being breached (27 per cent), and fear of rejection from friends or family (23 per cent). Nearly a fifth also reported a concern that being open about their identity could reduce their chances of employment or career advancement. Dr. Lee Anderson, a sociologist at Queen’s University Belfast and a consultant on the survey, said the results “indicate that while there is progress, LGBT+ individuals still face very real pressures that are not widely understood.” He noted that the need to conceal one’s identity had real mental health implications, with respondents expressing greater levels of stress, anxiety, and distrust as a result. The report urges policymakers and organisations to take affirmative steps to create safer, more inclusive environments, such as implementing robust anti-discrimination policies and offering regular training on equality and inclusion. Meanwhile, the National LGBT Survey, published in 2018 by the Office for National Statistics, found that 54 per cent of LGBT+ people had experienced at least one negative incident in the past five years because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

The Scottish government met for the first time since the snap general election on Wednesday, but surprising to many observers, the possibility of a second independence referendum was not raised by First Minister Nicola Sturgeon or her cabinet colleagues, Scottish media reported. The meeting, which took place at Bute House in Edinburgh, came amid growing speculation that Ms Sturgeon would use the disruption caused by the UK election result—and the subsequent blow to Prime Minister Theresa May’s majority—as a pivotal moment to reinvigorate the campaign for a separate Scotland. In the election, Scotland remained a decisive Labour stronghold and delivered a rebuke to the Conservatives, further complicating the governing formula under the new PM. Many analysts had expected the first minister to signal a renewed push for a referendum, particularly with devolved powers over areas like justice, policing, and welfare being left unclear in the post-Brexit constitutional landscape. However, according to officials present at the meeting, no formal discussion of a second referendum was held. This omission has raised questions about the Scottish government’s timeline and strategy in moving towards a Yes campaign. Ms Sturgeon, who has consistently argued that the UK government’s refusal to grant Scotland a veto over the Brexit deal—combined with changes in devolved powers—creates a "constitutional emergency"—was expected to clarify her intentions. Instead, the first minister reportedly focused the discussions on financial concerns, services disrupted by Brexit uncertainty, and efforts to stabilise the Scottish economy in the wake of the oil downturn. One senior advisor confirmed: “This was not the venue for a major political announcement about a second independence referendum, and the first minister wanted to ensure discussions remained focused on the pressing issues facing the Scottish public.” The decision not to broach the issue at such a high-level meeting has been interpreted in different ways. Some suggest it is a strategic move, with Ms Sturgeon avoiding a premature show of hands in the run-up to an internal consultation expected in the coming months. Others believe it reflects caution in the face of unrelenting domestic and international pressures, including the potential response from Westminster and the European Union. Critics of the first minister, including some within her own party, have long argued that another vote is premature and could deepen divides in Scottish society. Meanwhile, pro-Union supporters point to polls showing the 'No' camp still maintains a small lead, and recent government delays in triggering a formal referendum process have fueled dissent among pro-independence activists.

The son of a Londonderry man who has been missing for seven weeks has spoken of his emotional struggle as the festive season approaches. James Devlin, 22, is grappling with the uncertainty surrounding his father, William Devlin, 51, who vanished in early November and has not been seen since. Now, with Christmas fast approaching, the holidays, often a time for family and celebration, loom as a bleak reminder of the man missing from their lives. In an emotional interview from his home in Derry, James expressed his desperation and grief. “I don’t even know how to spend Christmas without him. He was the heart of our family, the one who brought everyone together. I keep hoping, praying something will change, that we’ll have an answer soon. Every Christmas without him will be empty,” he said, his voice trembling. William Devlin, a local businessman and former community campaigner, went missing on November 2, 2024, sparking a massive search operation involving police, search teams and local volunteers. The last confirmed sighting of Mr Devlin was outside his home in the Creggan area of Derry. His car was found a short distance away, untouched and still in full working order. A message from Mr Devlin sent on the same evening has become a haunting clue in the case. In it, he said he was “heading out for a while” and asked his family to stay safe and not to worry. His son James described the message as “cryptic” and “heartbreaking.” “We thought he was just having a bad day, maybe a breakdown. But the days went by and nothing. He left a life—job, home, family—all behind and left us with no answers,” James said. Detective Inspector Neil Smith of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has confirmed the investigation remains “active and progressing.” While no new sightings or physical evidence have been reported in the past weeks, searches continue in and around Derry. A local charity has also offered support to the family, providing emotional and practical assistance as the investigation unfolds. The Derry community has rallied around the family, with vigils held weekly and social media updates seeking public help. Mr Devlin’s colleagues and friends describe him as a “hugely popular figure” whose absence has left a “huge hole” in the local business scene and wider community. James, however, is focused on the emotional toll. “Every day without him is hard, but Christmas will be the hardest yet.

The UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has approved Zolgensma, a groundbreaking gene therapy developed by Swiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis, to treat a rare and often fatal genetic disorder in infants. The treatment, which has been hailed as a medical breakthrough, is now the most expensive drug in the world, with a single dose costing $2.1 million. Zolgensma is designed to treat children with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a genetic disorder that attacks nerve cells in the spinal cord, leading to progressive muscle weakness and, in the most severe cases, early death. The therapy uses a one-time intravenous infusion to replace the faulty  Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1)  gene in children aged under two, offering hope for those who otherwise have a life expectancy of just two years. The MHRA clearance, announced last week, allows the therapy to be used in the UK as part of a managed access agreement with the NHS. The drug’s approval comes after successful clinical trials showed dramatic improvements in infants treated with Zolgensma compared to those who received existing SMA therapies or no treatment at all. Dr. June Raine, head of the MHRA, expressed cautious optimism about the therapy's approval. “This is a remarkable advance in the field of gene therapy and marks a new chapter in how we treat rare and complex diseases,” she said. “However, it is important to carefully consider the cost-effectiveness of such groundbreaking technologies and their long-term impact on the healthcare system.” Novartis, which acquired AveXis — the pharmaceutical company that developed Zolgensma — for $8.7 billion in 2019, defended the treatment’s price as “reflective of its value over a lifetime.” The company has been in negotiations with the NHS for months, offering financial arrangements that spread the cost over time if the child lives longer than expected. Industry analysts suggest the move is an attempt to mitigate the economic burden on healthcare budgets for cutting-edge treatments. Health Secretary Matt Hancock called the approval a “positive step forward” for patients and their families, while acknowledging the intense debate over how to balance innovation with affordability in the NHS. “We must continue to invest in research and development to find cures and treatments that were once unthinkable, but also work within our means to ensure these breakthroughs are available to all who need them,” he said. The news has sparked both celebration and controversy among patient groups and healthcare professionals.

Apple’s investors found themselves gripped by a wave of anxiety this week as the once-unshakable tech giant appeared to stumble on all fronts, triggering sell-offs and cautious headlines across financial markets. Shares in the company, which have long been a proxy for overall tech enthusiasm and the broader US economy, dipped sharply on Friday after a series of concerningly vocal warnings from key analysts and a growing clamour over the company’s stagnant product cycle. The rout came amid reports from major investment firms warning that Apple’s innovation pipeline is underperforming, and questions are mounting over whether the company is still the dominant force it once was in the smartphone and consumer electronics sectors. Morgan Stanley, one of Apple’s top tracked investment houses, downgraded the stock, citing a lack of “meaningful new product introductions” and rising competition from rivals such as Samsung and a revived iPhone from Google. But it is not just the hardware side that has caused unease. For the first time in several years, Apple is finding itself at the centre of a culture war in Western tech markets, with growing consumer and corporate backlash over the way it handles data privacy and app store policies. The controversy over App Tracking Transparency, a feature Apple introduced in 2021, has not gone away and has instead become a recurring point of contention with major companies like Meta, whose chief financial officer, David Wehner, recently warned that it is “reducing our profits significantly.” Investors, already on edge after years of tightening monetary policy and the prospect of slower global economic growth, are now questioning whether Apple’s dominance is at risk — and whether its so-called “perpetual growth machine” has hit a wall. Some are even looking at historical parallels, with murmurs being made about Microsoft in the early 2000s and how its missteps in innovation led to a prolonged period of market uncertainty. In internal meetings, Apple executives are said to be working to plug gaps in the upcoming product roadmap, with whispers that the next generation of iPhones may feature incremental rather than groundbreaking changes. Meanwhile, venture capital and Silicon Valley insiders believe Apple is holding off on launching new ventures until it better aligns its resources with evolving global tech trends such as AI and the metaverse — a decision that comes with risks of its own. For now, Apple’s market cap remains among the top in the world, but the recent volatility points to a go-to-war moment for a company that has not seriously lacked confidence in its products or its brand for nearly two decades.

Toby Flood is set to miss the opening stages of the 2025 Six Nations Championship after suffering a setbacks with a knee injury, according to reports from rugby insiders and Premiership sources. The fly-half, who has been a long-time standout in English rugby, has not played since the recent match for Leicester Tigers in January, and scans have revealed the extent of the damage will force him to miss international action at the start of the tournament. The timing could not be worse for Flood, who was expected to play a crucial role in Eddie Jones’ planning as England look to reclaim the Six Nations title and strengthen their preparations for the 2025 Rugby World Cup. Flood, 34, is no stranger to the international stage, having earned over 60 caps for England, including key appearances in previous Six Nations campaigns and the 2015 World Cup. Sources close to the Tigers have confirmed the injury occurred during an intense training session as Flood pushed himself hard to regain full fitness after earlier this season. "He was in great form before the injury and looked ready to challenge for the number 10 shirt," one source said. “Unfortunately, it’s just not his day, and it looks like he’ll be out for a while now.” The Rugby Football Union (RFU) has yet to issue an official statement on Flood’s situation, but national coach Eddie Jones is understood to have been briefed on the progress. It is expected that the England management will monitor the injury closely and decide later this month whether he will be included in the squad for the opening fixtures. With George Ford currently in discussions for a move to France, questions are already arising about the future direction of England’s fly-half selection. Emerging talents like Marcus Smith and Finn Russell remain in the frame, but the sidelining of Flood adds yet another layer of uncertainty as the head coach looks to build a squad capable of progressing deep into the World Cup. Leicester Tigers’ director of rugby, Steve Borthwick, expressed his disappointment at the news. “Toby has worked incredibly hard to come back into the side, and the timing is unfortunate. We all know he brings experience and leadership, not just on the field but off it too,” he said. "We’re hopeful he’ll be back to full fitness soon and will do everything he can to support the team once he’s ready.”

Dundee striker Greg Stewart has expressed confidence that his strong partnership with fellow forward Kane Hemmings will prove instrumental in the club's pursuit of success this season. The Dark Blues, currently building momentum ahead of their Scottish Championship campaign, are hopeful that the chemistry between the two attacking talents can translate into vital goals. Speaking in a recent press conference, Stewart said: “Kane and I are on the same wavelength, and that’s going to help us a lot this year. We know what each other is thinking on the pitch, and when we get that connection right, good things happen.” The duo, who formed a formidable attacking partnership during Stewart's time at Northampton Town in the English Football League, have reunited at Dens Park with high hopes of dominating the Championship this season. Stewart, 33, who joined the club in January, has already made a significant impact, while Hemmings, 26, has been an ever-present in the team since his arrival in the summer transfer window. Their understanding of each other's game extends beyond the pitch. Stewart praised Hemmings' professionalism and work ethic, saying the younger player is “hungry to succeed and always looking to improve”. Hemmings, for his part, has said that playing alongside someone with Stewart’s experience is “like having an extra coach on the field”. Manager Darren Potter has also been keen to highlight the importance of having a strong central partnership in attack, and the manager’s faith in Stewart and Hemmings has already started bearing fruit. During the club’s pre-season campaign, the pair have combined for five goals in four matches, with their synergy often leaving defenceless opponents scrambling. The striker's comments come at a crucial time for Dundee as they prepare for their opening match of the new campaign against St Johnstones at McDiarmid Park. With the team looking to improve on their 10th-place finish in the Championship last season, fans are eagerly anticipating whether the Stewart-Hemmings duo can step up and deliver the kind of performances that could propel Dundee into the upper echelons of the league table. For Stewart, the resurgence of his partnership with Hemmings is not just about scoring goals, but about proving that age and experience can coexist with the hunger of youth and ambition. “This team is building, and Kane is part of the future. We’re both here to push each other and help the club reach where it needs to be,” he said.

Celtic found themselves on the wrong end of a crushing 4-0 defeat against Dinamo Zagreb in the final match of Europa League Group D, with Croatian striker Marko Pjaca netting a devastating hat-trick to seal the points. The result leaves Celtic fans bemused as their side, once considered serious contenders for European success, exit the competition with just one win from four games and further questions over their defensive frailties on the continent. A largely underwhelming display at the Maksimir Stadium saw the Scottish champions repeatedly exposed by Dinamo’s pace and precision, with Pjaca exploiting gaps in the Celtic backline with alarming ease. His opener came in the 14th minute, a clinical finish after a swift counter-attack left the visitors scrambling. By half-time, the deficit had already stretched to two goals, as Celtic struggled to cope with the intensity and organisation of the Croatian giants. The second half saw no improvement, as Pjaca completed his treble in the 78th minute after Celtic failed once again to clear a routine cross. The final blow came in stoppage time, with Dinamo adding a fourth to complete one of the most lopsided results of the night. This result puts paid to Celtic’s faint hopes of progressing further, with Dinamo finishing top of the group ahead of Liverpool, who beat Red Star Belgrade 3-1. Speaking after the match, Celtic manager Brendan Rodgers was forced to address the defensive failings that have plagued his side all season. “It's a tough result to take, especially in the context of someone needing to win to qualify. We made simple errors, and they punished us. That’s what you get when you’re not solid at the back,” Rodgers said. The manager’s frustration is well-founded, as Celtic have now leaked 12 goals in their last five matches across all competitions. Questions will be asked about the failsafe nature of the current back four and whether key targets in the January transfer window can provide the much-needed reinforcement. Enexpected performances against Liverpool and Slovenian side Maribor raised the alarm before this final match, and the result in Zagreb will only intensify the scrutiny on the defensive unit as Celtic prepare for the 2023 Scottish Cup final against Rangers next month. Pjaca’s heroics, meanwhile, have sent Dinamo into the Europa League knockout stages as go-at-it group winners, with their captain celebrating another dominant performance in European competition.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has urged political leaders to scale back divisive rhetoric and tone down campaign strategies that it claims have deepened divisions and normalised bigotry in recent months. In a rare public intervention, the watchdog said that inflammatory messages from senior figures in Westminster have not only polarised the public but also “legitimised hate” and threatened community cohesion. The warning comes as political tensions remain high ahead of potential elections and with a backdrop of ongoing debates over Brexit policy, social reform and social welfare. In a statement released earlier this week, the EHRC called on all political parties and their leaders to prioritise “constructive dialogue over conflict” and to uphold the principles of equality and respect enshrined in the law. Commission chairs Dame Alice Johnson and Sir John Park said: “We understand the pressures of political campaigning, but there must be boundaries. Words matter. When leaders speak with venom or intolerance, they don’t just inflame the edges of society—they plant the seeds of division at its core. This undermines not only trust in politics, but the very fabric of our democratic values.” The report highlights a string of incidents, including inflammatory comments made over migration, gender issues, disability and race, which have been reported to the EHRC from citizens and human rights groups. It also points to recent research indicating a measurable rise in reported hate incidents from the public toward national leaders – particularly targeting those with minority identities, and those who support minority political causes. The EHRC is not calling for political leaders to self-censor, but is urging greater responsibility and greater awareness of the impact their words may have beyond Westminster. “This is not about silencing political opposition,” Park added. “It’s about ensuring that democratic discourse remains respectful and inclusive—especially at a time when our democracy is under so much scrutiny.” The intervention has been met with mixed reactions from across the political spectrum. Both government and opposition leaders have been given time to respond to the watchdog's concerns, with the EHRC stating that it is prepared to take further action if necessary, including legal steps if human rights violations are identified. In a further escalation of the debate, civil society leaders and charities have echoed the EHRC's call, warning that such rhetoric has already contributed to real-world harm, including the rise of anti-social behaviours and emboldened extremists.

The Imam of China’s largest mosque, conveniently located in the city of Kashgar in Xinjiang, was brutally murdered in an apparent targeted assassination, sending shockwaves through the local Uyghur community and sparking renewed concerns over religious freedom and ethnic tensions in the region. The attack, which occurred outside the Id Kah Mosque — a key spiritual site and one of the oldest and most revered in the country — has yet to be claimed, though sources on the ground suggest that it may have been the result of a growing climate of fear and unrest. According to local media reports, the imam was ambushed and shot in broad daylight, with the attack being carried out with military precision. Witnesses described how shots were fired from a distance before the assailant fled the scene on a motorcycle minutes before arriving helicopters arrived to cordon off the area. It is unclear whether the imam was followed or if the killer was already present in the vicinity. Security footage is now being intensively reviewed by Chinese authorities, who have yet to officially comment on the motive for the killing. Religious leaders and members of the Uyghur Muslim community have expressed deep sorrow over the incident, with some condemning the act as a brutal affront to both their faith and cultural identity. Many in the region view the imam as a moderate figure who worked tirelessly to promote interfaith dialogue and community cohesion. His death is seen as a major blow to any efforts to depoliticise religious institutions and curb extremism. The Chinese government has long sought to tightly control Islamic practices in Xinjiang, implementing strict laws that limit the role of religious leaders and ban certain activities deemed “extremist.” In recent years, there have also been reports of mass detentions and surveillance of Uyghur Muslims, as part of a broader campaign against so-called “separatism” and Islamic extremism. While the Chinese state has always denied allegations of religious persecution, this killing underscores the delicate and often volatile situation in Xinjiang. Some analysts suggest that the attack could have been a response to the repressive policies being deployed against Muslim communities, with radical elements potentially trying to incite further unrest.
