Others, however, have speculated that rival groups or dissidents within the community themselves could be responsible. The incident also raises questions about the extent of security in a region long under tight state surveillance, and whose reach even stretches beyond Xinjiang.

The company that conducts most of America’s rocket launches, United Launch Alliance (ULA), has unveiled the specifications for its next-generation vehicle, the Vulcan Centaur, marking a pivotal shift in the US space launch industry. The disclosure comes as a direct response to the growing challenges posed by the rising dominance of SpaceX and the rapid advances in reusable rocket technology. ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, has long played a critical role in NASA’s deep space missions and national security launches, but this new rocket signals an attempt to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market. Officials at ULA announced the Vulcan Centaur during a press conference in Decatur, Alabama, the site of its production facilities. The new rocket is set to replace the Atlas V, a workhorse of the industry since 2002. Unlike the Atlas V, which uses Russian-made RD-180 engines, the Vulcan Centaur will be powered entirely by American technology, a move aimed at addressing lingering political and supply chain concerns following years of controversy over reliance on Russian components. Central to the Vulcan Centaur’s design are its new BE-4 engines, developed by Blue Origin—owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos—marking a rare instance of two major aerospace players in the US working in tandem. “This is not just an evolutionary step for ULA, it’s a revolutionary one,” said Tory Bruno, ULA’s president and CEO, in opening remarks. “For the first time, we are building a new class of launch vehicles for the future—leaner, more affordable, and better suited for missions that will help define this century.” The Vulcan Centaur is designed to carry both government and commercial payloads, with the ability to be configured for missions ranging from satellite deployment to crewed flight to Mars, in line with NASA’s Artemis programme. ULA has confirmed the first launch of the Vulcan Centaur will take place in 2021, pending final government and industry reviews. Despite these optimistic claims, the company faces stiff competition. SpaceX, with its Falcon rockets and Starship system, has slashed costs and dramatically increased launch frequency through reusable technology. Meanwhile, companies such as Blue Origin and Rocket Lab continue to push the envelope in both commercial and deep space applications. ULA’s move into the next generation of launch vehicles also coincides with growing interest from the US government in fostering a robust domestic space industrial base.

A Clergyman’s Condolence: Can Violence Ever Be Justified in the Fight Against Terror?   In a rare and controversial statement from a religious leader in the Middle East, Bashar Warda, the Chaldean Catholic archbishop of Irbil in northern Iraq, has spoken out on the use of lethal force against members of the so-called Islamic State (IS). Warda, whose archdiocese has been deeply affected by the extremist group, described the use of violence in this context not as a moral failure, but as a necessary response to a moral atrocity. “Irban,” said the 50-year-old prelate, using the Aramaic word for “human being," as he sat in the small, dust-choked stone chapel of St Moriof, near his monastery in the Nineveh plains. “When you treat a cancer, you have to use unfortunate measures.” These words—meant for a short conversation on the ground realities of faith in a land torn apart by war—have since dominated headlines across Europe, the Middle East, and, to some surprise, the United States. It is not that Warda is the first to defend the use of violence against terrorism. But in a land where both Christians and Muslims have historically upheld deadly non-violent traditions, and where many still mourn the Christian bloodshed of the Armenian genocide, the archbishop’s remarks cut through long-held taboos. Warda, a biblical scholar and former peace activist, has spent the past decade navigating the war-torn landscape of northern Iraq, which has seen some of the worst atrocities of the 21st century. His own community, the ancient Chaldean Christian minority, was nearly wiped out in 2014 when IS overran the city of Mosul and about half a million Christians fled the region. Many were slaughtered, many more had their homes and churches destroyed. In that context, Warda told me, it is impossible to advocate peace to those who have already suffered violence and treachery. “This is not about revenge,” he said, stressing the theological nuances. “It is about the protection of the innocent. It is about saving your sisters and brothers from annihilation. If IS is a virus, then the body of a just society must respond with whatever is necessary to heal.” The archbishop’s comments have caused a stir not only among Iraqi Christians, but also among his Catholic counterparts in Europe. Many religious leaders—especially in the Vatican—have emphasized non-violence, urging that even when faced with extreme terrorism, the Church must maintain its witness to peace and reconciliation.

In a dramatic finish that will live long in the memory of St Andrew's faithful, Birmingham City came from behind to snatch a 2-1 victory over Sheffield Wednesday thanks to a stoppage-time header from Lukas Jutkiewicz. The win lifted the hosts up the Championship table and added a touch of euphoria to a match that ebbed and flowed with tension and twists until the final whistle. The visitors had taken the lead in the 32nd minute when Adam Reach's curling effort from the edge of the box found the top corner of the net, leaving Birmingham's goalkeeper, Tomasz Kuszczak, with no chance. The Blades' goal was a moment of brilliance, and it appeared to offer the visitors a chance to secure a vital away point in their promotion push. Yet, Birmingham were not ready to give up. Just before half-time, Oliver Burke, the EFL Young Player of the Year, came close for the home side with a dipping shot that was pushed away by Barrie Dickinson. The early second-half period saw both teams trade chances, but it was not until the 68th minute that Birmingham were handed a golden opportunity. Substitute Micah Odubajo was fouled in the box, and as he made his grief known, referee Simon Hooper pointed to the spot. Up stepped Jutkiewicz, who had looked lively – but nervous – with the ball, and he made no mistake, sending Dickinson the wrong way with a composed finish. Jimmy Sirrel’s Stand erupted. The visitors collapsed at the back, and for the next ten minutes, Birmingham piled on the pressure. Yet, a late equaliser evaded them – until the 95th minute, when the hosts were awarded a set-piece from the left. Captain Neil Etheridge made a last-ditch clearance to deny Robby Panama, but the ball fell to Jutkiewicz, who met it with a thumping header that nestled into the bottom corner. The celebration that followed was chaotic and cathartic. Players, officials and supporters alike rushed onto the pitch, acknowledging the sheer magnitude of the moment. Birmingham had not only salvaged a point but had snatched all three from the jaws of defeat. Speaking after the match, Birmingham manager lunches Townshend praised the "mental strength and character of the lads", particularly Jutkiewicz, who had struggled with consistency in recent weeks. "Lukas does not get enough respect," he said. "What he contributed today – the goal, the energy, the leadership – was world-class."

Lewis Hamilton secured a commanding and almost flawless victory at the Mexican Grand Prix, continuing his dominance from pole position in a race that passed like a masterclass in precision and patience. The Mercedes driver extended his championship lead by overtaking Red Bull's Max Verstappen with relative ease and then managing the race at a steady pace to cross the line in first place and leave his rivals trailing in his wake. Hamilton’s performance was the kind of near-flawless display that has defined his career, and one this season he has delivered only a few times. From the start to the chequered flag, the seven-time world champion rarely looked troubled, maintaining a tempo that saw him lap consistently in the high 1:19s and low 1:20s and never forcing the issue when it wasn’t necessary. It left the rest of the field, notably Verstappen, who finished a distant second, unable to find a way past in the final 20 laps despite a brave and committed bid late in the race. While Hamilton's performance earned the admiration of the Mercedes pit wall, the real drama of the Mexican weekend unfolded behind him, where rival factions of the sport jostled for position in a tightly packed mid-field and frustrations flared as mechanical and strategic missteps punished otherwise strong contenders. Red Bull, watching closely from the sidelines, will have been heartened by Verstappen's second-place finish but concerned by Hamilton's level of control and the unflinching superiority of the Mercedes car. Verstappen was the closest challenger all race, but the gap Hamilton carved in the early laps proved difficult to close. His attempt to close the gap in the last few laps led to a thrilling, at times tense, stretch as the Dutch driver pushed hard – but not hard enough, or perhaps at the wrong points in the race. Behind the pair, the midfield battle raged. Lando Norris made an impressive fight from the back of the grid to finish in the points, while both Charles Leclerc and Carlos Sainz struggled with car balance and pace, ultimately finishing just outside the points. Mercedes’ other driver, George Russell, brought home a solid fourth for the team, but his race was more straightforward and lacked the sparkle of his podium rivals. The Mexican Grand Prix proved another chapter in the ever-unfolding tale of Hamilton's season, a race that was a reminder of the peaks he's still capable of reaching if the car continues to perform at this high level.

Dr Kate Granger, a 34-year-old Yorkshire-born doctor who was diagnosed with terminal breast cancer in 2011, used the time left to her after the diagnosis to make a lasting impact on the healthcare system and beyond. Five years later, on 23 July 2016, the medical professional passed away having raised over £1.2 million for the Yorkshire Cancer Research charity and played a vital role in reshaping doctor-patient communication across the NHS. Her legacy began shortly after she was diagnosed, when she started a Twitter campaign under the hashtag #hellomynameis. The idea was simple but powerful: to call out poorly introduced, unnamed hospital staff who rarely made eye contact with their patients. “It only takes a few seconds to smile and say hello,” Dr Granger famously said. The campaign quickly gained momentum, resonating with thousands of patients and prompting national conversations about the importance of dignity and respect in healthcare. In an exclusive interview last year, Dr Granger spoke about the motivation behind her drive. “When I was admitted to hospital for the first time after my diagnosis, I was treated more like a number than a human being. My care mattered, yes, but so did I as a person.” Her determination to improve the human element of medical care led to the launch of the national GIRFT – Getting it Right from the Start – national campaign – which aimed to improve the quality, safety, and sustainability of acute hospital services across the UK. Dr Granger’s efforts did not go unnoticed. She was invited to address the Department of Health, led public discussions at hospitals and universities, and was an articulate advocate for patient-centred care. Her TEDx Talk, “How a Cancer Diagnosis Made Me a Better Doctor,” delivered in 2014, has been viewed over half a million times and remains a powerful testament to her philosophy of care. Beyond her advocacy work, Dr Granger was passionate about fundraising and philanthropy. The charity she helped to create, My Name Is... Healthcare, has trained over 90,000 health professionals in improved patient communication. Her fundraising efforts raised hundreds of thousands of pounds, which were used to support medical research and to improve treatment and facilities for cancer patients. Dr Granger’s husband, Dr Louis Lee Granger, described her as “a trailblazer, a fighter, and a role model for so many in the medical profession and beyond.” Her untimely death at the age of 34 marked the end of a life dedicated to changing the world, one conversation at a time.

Sharp's strike secures Sheffield United a gritty South Yorkshire derby win against Barnsley   A first-half goal from Billy Sharp was enough to secure Sheffield United a hard-fought 1-0 victory over their cross-city neighbours Barnsley in a tense South Yorkshire derby at Bramall Lane. The match, played in front of a raucous and packed crowd, concluded with both teams reduced to 10 men each as tempers flared in the closing stages, but United's side proved resilient, picking up a vital three Premier League 2 points to keep their promotion hopes alive. Sharp, who has emerged as one of the standout performers in the division this season, opened the scoring just before the half-hour mark. The 34-year-old striker managed to get the better of Barnsley’s towering central defender Joel Marciejwicz, latching onto a well-delivered cross and heading the ball powerfully beyond the outstretched hand of goalkeeper Adam Davies. The goal was a moment of clinical brilliance in a match that otherwise featured a number of missed chances and a lack of clear-cut opportunities for both sides. The second half saw the tempo rise steadily, with both managers attempting to break the deadlock. Barnsley, controlled by Neil Warnock since early January, started to assert more pressure on the Blades’ backline, and it was little wonder when United's left-back – Matej Kovar – was shown a red card for a reckless challenge in the 57th minute. What followed was a heated period of play, with Barnsley matching their opponents’ intensity. However, the Blades remained solid in defence and made it difficult for the visitors to carve out clear chances. Just before the 80th minute, Barnsley’s defender Sam Morsy was sent off for a challenge on Sharp, significantly altering the balance of the game. From that point on, the match became more of a battle of wills than one of footballing finesse, with both teams absorbing heavy pressure but proving unable to create anything that came close to equalising. The final whistle sparked a wave of celebration among the home supporters, many of whom have long been desperate to see their team climb out of the lower half of the table. Speaking after the game, Blades manager Chris Wilder praised his team’s character and defensive organisation, praising Sharp for his crucial goal and leadership on the pitch. “Billy's a fantastic professional and a real leader for us,” Wilder said.

A prominent figure tipped as a potential leader of UKIP is likely "too extreme" to be permitted to stand in the leadership election, according to a senior party member in the Welsh Assembly. The comments, made by UKIP AM Darren Millar, follow mounting speculation about who might succeed the party as it grapples with a crisis in public perception and dwindling electoral influence. Millar, who serves on the party's national executive, told BBC Wales that while the individual in question would be free to declare an interest in the candidacy, the party would not be able to proceed with their nomination if the content of their past remarks was taken into account under the party’s rules. The unnamed candidate, who has gained a following among the party’s hardline activists, is believed to have made controversial statements in the past regarding immigration and left-wing policies—remarks that, while deemed acceptable in the more ideologically rigid corners of the UKIP base, are considered too far-reaching for the party’s central office to endorse. The prospect of such a candidate rising in prominence at a time when the party is striving to re-invent itself and avoid political irrelevance has sparked internal debate. Some within the party see a return to its original, more radical stance as necessary to galvanise support, particularly among younger, disillusioned voters. Others argue that such an approach would only deepen the perception of UKIP as a fringe outfit disconnected from mainstream concerns. Millar, who is seen as a more moderate voice within the party, did not name the individual but was clear in his criticism: "We are not in the business of someone who is beyond the pale. If a candidate has a record of making statements that are not in line with the law or acceptable in the real world, they won't be allowed to stand." He added that UKIP needed to maintain a "calm and considered image" if it had any chance of progressing beyond what he described as “the echo chamber of the far right.” The un-named candidate’s supporters, however, are unlikely to be deterred. They argue that UKIP was founded on uncompromising principles and that any attempts to moderate the party’s message amount to a betrayal of those origins. Millar’s remarks have already drawn sharp criticism from within the party, with one prominent backbench MP accusing the AM of "caving in to the mainstream media's narrative and watering down the very identity that makes us relevant."

Great Wall Motor eyes move on Fiat Chrysler as global EV race intensifies   In a bold move that signals the shifting tides of global automotive influence, Chinese automaker Great Wall Motor is reportedly considering a bid for Fiat Chrysler, the iconic Italian-American carmaker owned by Sergio Marchionne and best known for its Jeep brand. The potential interest comes amid an increasingly aggressive expansion strategy by Chinese automotive firms, who are looking to muscle in on Western markets and secure a stake in high-profile brand portfolios as the world rapidly transitions to electric vehicles (EVs). Great Wall Motor, China’s fourth-largest automaker and the manufacturer of the popular Haval and Ora brands, has already made waves in recent years by acquiring a controlling stake in the Swedish electric vehicle company, Polestar, and launching a luxury SUV under the new WoLong (Dragon) brand. Now, the company is said to be casting its gaze across the Atlantic, with whispers in the financial and automotive sectors suggesting it is considering a takeover of FCA — a company synonymous with the rugged ruggedness and American automotive heritage of brands like Dodge, Ram, and Maserati. According to informed sources, Great Wall Motor is currently conducting due diligence on Fiat Chrysler, which collapsed last year in a $43.5 billion merger with French giant PSA Group to form Stellantis, the world’s fourth-largest carmaker. While it is unclear whether Great Wall is looking to acquire the entirety of Fiat Chrysler’s pre-merger assets or just specific brands and technologies, the prospect of a Chinese investment in the American juggernaut — which produces the iconic Jeep Wrangler — has stirred both interest and controversy. The potential move would represent a massive gamble for Great Wall, as Fiat Chrysler’s legacy and manufacturing base in the US present both untapped opportunities and complex challenges. Marchionne, who ran the company with a “Berserk” mentality and an ability to turn around failing ventures, leaves behind an organisation that is now part of Stellantis, but still has a significant footprint in the American market. To acquire anything more than a sliver of that could represent a financial mountain for any investor, Chinese or otherwise. However, for Great Wall, the prize could be enormous. Given the Biden administration’s push for electric vehicles and the Biden-Xinjiang sanctions currently complicating trade, the recent easing of tensions and a potential investment in a major American brand could be aimed at softening diplomatic perceptions and deepening economic ties.

Chris Gayle Makes History with World Cup Double Century   Chris Gayle has etched his name further into cricketing folklore by becoming the first player to score a double century in a One Day International World Cup, leading West Indies to a dominant 53-run win over Zimbabwe in their Pool B clash at the Manuka Oval in Canberra on Tuesday. The West Indies opener blasted an unbeaten 215 not out off just 146 balls in a blistering innings that sparked a thrilling, record-breaking encounter and stunned fans in a stadium packed with spectators and colour. Gayle's feat immediately sent ripples through the cricketing world, not only because of its sheer scale—his knock is now the highest individual score in ODI history and the highest in a World Cup match—but also for its audacity in what was a must-win game for the Caribbean side, who had lost their opening match to Pakistan. “I was just going out there to perform when the opportunity was given,” said a humble Gayle after the match. “There’s no intention to chase records, just to win games and do the best I can for the team.” The innings, laced with 20 sixes and two centuries broken before stumps, was a masterclass in power-hitting and timing, reminiscent of the kind of rhythm West Indies cricket used to be known for – but hasn’t often demonstrated in recent years. At one point, Gayle hit a 36-ball fifty as he and Evin Lewis accelerated the innings from 80 for two to a formidable 349 for four in 50 overs. Lewis, West Indies' other opener, made a composed 90 in the top-order partnership, but it was Gayle who carried the bat and stole the show with his relentless assault on the Zimbabwean bowling attack. Zimbabwe, who lost a top-order wicket inside the first 10 overs, looked out of sorts against Gayle’s onslaught, and despite their response being led by captain Hamilton Masakadza (58), they were bowled out for 296 in 47.1 overs. The victory not only secured West Indies a much-needed win but also provided a timely reminder of cricketing firepower from one of the game’s greatest entertainers. The double hundred comes three years after the 37-year-old Gayle played his 100th ODI, and at a time when questions continue to be asked about his availability for the 2019 World Cup.

Harriet Harman, the acting leader of the Labour Party, has called for unity and reflection rather than finger-pointing in the wake of the party’s devastating defeat in the general election. Speaking at a post-election meeting of Labour MPs in London, Harman urged the party to avoid what she described as a “blame game” in analysing the result. The Labour Party suffered historic losses, losing nearly 60 seats and ending up with a smaller share of the vote than in the 2015 election, a result she described as a “wake-up call” for the party. Harman acknowledged the scale of the humiliation but underlined the need for solidarity as the party begins the process of recovery and re-election planning. “This is not the time for divisions or recriminations,” she said. “We need to be honest about what went wrong, yes, but we must also look ahead and work together to restore the trust of the British people.” The remark came as Labour MPs debate the future direction of the party following the leadership contest that will be triggered by Keir Starmer’s expected resignation. Shadow Cabinet members, including Angela Rayner and Emily Thornberry, have already called for a unity of purpose as the party puts itself back together. Harman, who took on the role of acting leader on a temporary basis, warned against internal battles. “We have no mandate – no mandate for any policy, no mandate for any programme, and certainly no mandate to fight amongst ourselves,” she said. Labour’s defeat was attributed to a number of factors, including a failure to connect with voters in traditional strongholds and the difficulties of running on a manifesto focused on Brexit. Harman did not specifically criticise either faction of the party but stressed the importance of collective responsibility. “We are all responsible for today’s result,” she said. “We all have a part to play in what comes next.” Her comments echo those of other Labour figures who have called for reflection rather than attack. The party now faces a difficult road to re-emerge as a cohesive force in British politics. As Harman concluded the meeting, she issued a rallying call. “We are not finished. We mustn’t be. We are a strong party with a proud heritage and a necessary vision for the country. Let’s get back to work together.” The next steps will involve the selection of a new leader, with negotiations set to begin in the coming weeks about who will be entrusted with leading Labour into the next election.

The European Commission has unveiled controversial plans to establish an EU-wide Border and Coast Guard agency as part of a sweeping strategy to tackle the unprecedented influx of migrants arriving on Europe’s shores. The proposals aim to increase coordination among national border forces, introduce rapid response systems, and implement stricter control over EU external borders in a bid to stem the flow of illegal migration and enhance security across the bloc. Under the new framework, the agency—still to be named—would be tasked with patrolling the EU's external land and maritime borders, coordinating joint operations, and managing asylum applications to ensure a more equitable distribution of responsibility among member states. The proposals come as EU leaders face mounting pressure from populist parties and security experts over the continued arrival of migrants from the Middle East and Africa, with over a million people arriving by sea in 2015 alone. The plan has already sparked fierce debate across the continent, with critics warning of increased militarisation of border zones and the risks of human rights abuses. Amnesty International and other humanitarian groups have voiced concerns over the lack of oversight and accountability built into the proposals, arguing that centralised control could lead to a harsher, more punitive approach to migration. The European Commission’s executive vice-president, Frans Timmermans, defended the plans, stating: “We must treat migration as a European challenge and not just a national one. This agency will help us act decisively – protecting our borders while safeguarding the dignity and rights of all individuals seeking refuge.” The new force would initially be modelled after the Frontex border agency, but with significantly more powers, including the ability to conduct joint surveillance and conduct maritime rescues. It would also have the authority to push back boats with migrants still at sea, a controversial move that has drawn sharp criticism from human rights organisations. Supporters of the plan argue that without binding cooperation and a unified response, the EU will continue to be overwhelmed by the crisis. Germany and Hungary, among others, have called for the swift establishment of the force, with the latter advocating for greater capacity to return migrants to countries of origin. However, many within the EU fear the initiative will further divide the bloc, particularly with France and Germany struggling to agree on a unified approach. France has suggested tighter control over Mediterranean entry points and has called for a no-go policy for unauthorised arrivals, while Germany has consistently upheld its commitment to processing asylum claims in accordance with international law.

Pakistan Sends Troops to Assist Citizens After Devastating Earthquake in Iran   In a gesture of solidarity and urgency, Pakistan has deployed a military rescue team to assist local communities across the border in south-eastern Iran after a powerful 6.5-magnitude earthquake struck the region early on Wednesday. The disaster, which has left at least 1,000 people dead and thousands more injured, has prompted cross-border aid efforts as both countries continue to cope with the aftermath of the quake. The tremor, centred near the town of Khash in Sistan and Baluchestan Province, hit during the early hours and caused widespread devastation. Entire districts were left in ruins, with collapsed buildings, severed communication lines and blocked supply routes making rescue operations immensely difficult. Myriads of unconfirmed reports suggest the numbers of displaced could be well into the tens of thousands, with entire villages cut off in the mountainous terrain. Despite being a neighbour often politically at odds, Pakistan, which shares a porous border in the region, swiftly responded by sending a contingent of soldiers and rescue workers, including emergency medics and engineering specialists. The operation, based out of Gwadar, is aimed at reaching remote Baloch villages near the border — many of which have significant Pakistani and Afghan populations, as well as nomadic communities unaccounted for in official demographics. Foreign Office spokesperson Zahid Haider confirmed the deployment, saying, “Our priority is to help affected communities — especially those of ethnic Baloch and other vulnerable groups — who may not have access to emergency services due to the geographic isolation of the area.” The decision to assist has been widely praised in the region, particularly amid sourer international relations and a backdrop of political instability in both countries. For many in the border regions, such aid is seen as a vital lifeline. Sana Ullah, the head of a relief organisation based in Turbat, said: “The people there are used to hardship, but this is beyond anything they've experienced. The Pakistan Army is the only rapid source of help at the moment.” Local health workers in Kerman province in Iran have confirmed that hundreds of injured remain in hospitals, some waiting for surgery or critical care due to a shortage of medical personnel. Websites and social media have begun to surface appeals for aid to the region, highlighting the desperate need for water, food, and blankets. Pakistan's involvement is set against the backdrop of deepening cooperation between the two countries on trade and connectivity, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which has already transformed infrastructure in Balochistan.

Rising Concussion Awareness Could See More Rugby Stars Retire, Warns Medical Expert   As the spotlight continues to shine on the long-term risks of brain injuries in contact sports, concerns are growing that a new wave of rugby players may be forced to retire early to protect their health. Dr Barry O’Driscoll, a former World Rugby medical adviser, has warned that the sport’s increasing understanding of concussion is likely to lead to more high-profile retirements in the coming years. Speaking in an interview, Dr O’Driscoll stressed that while awareness of the dangers of repeated concussions has improved dramatically in recent years, the consequences remain serious. “Rugby is a fantastic sport, but it’s inherently risky when it comes to head injuries. We have made great strides in protocols, education, and detection, but the reality is that more players are now being told the risk is too great to continue,” he said. O’Driscoll’s remarks come amid fresh calls for action following reports that several current and former players have left the game over concerns about chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head trauma. While CTE cannot always be definitively diagnosed until after death, the symptoms it can cause—including memory loss, mood changes, and early-onset dementia—have led to growing alarm among medical professionals and former players alike. “Dr Barry is right to point this out,” said Andy Hay, a former Scotland international and current campaigner for player welfare. “We’ve seen it already with some senior players leaving the game. More will follow. The problem is that retirement is often a very difficult decision, one that can impact not just a player’s career but their identity and way of life.” O’Driscoll, who spent over a decade in World Rugby’s medical advisory role, has been at the forefront of concussion reform in the sport. He pointed to the introduction of the “Head Injury Assessment” (HIA) protocols in 2009 as a turning point. “Before HIAs, concussions were often missed or downplayed. Now, any player who shows signs of a head injury is automatically taken off the field for assessment,” he explained. But despite these measures, sustained improvement in the identification and treatment of concussions has come at a cost. “More players are being sent for scans and assessments than ever before,” O’Driscoll said. “And some of them are told they’re simply not in a fit state to return.

A senior magistrate has resigned from his post following an investigation into his attempts to pay an asylum seeker’s bail in a controversial case that has sparked debate over the integrity of legal professionals and the ethical boundaries between justice and compassion. Mr David Feast, 55, who served as the deputy head of the South West division of the magistrates’ courts, was suspended in February after it was revealed he had tried to pay £200 of bail on behalf of Ake Julius, an asylum seeker from Cameroon, who was facing a minor motoring charge. Feast said he had done so to prevent the man from being immediately deported, arguing the decision was motivated by a belief that the justice system should act as a "last resort" and not a "barrier to access." But the Judicial Conduct Investigations Office (JCIO), which oversees complaints against magistrates, ruled the action was a clear breach of protocol and in conflict with the independence of the judiciary, leading to his suspension. Feast, a long-serving member of the magistracy in Somerset and Devon, stepped down from his role on Monday after weeks of mounting criticism from the public, legal experts, and senior members of the judiciary. In a statement, he said: “I did what I did to assist someone who I believed was being unfairly treated by the system. I never intended to overstep, but I now accept that I misjudged the situation.” He added that he had acted “in good faith” and hoped the public would not “dismiss the importance of compassion in the law.” The case came to light after Julius was arrested in Plymouth in January on suspicious driving charges. At a hearing, he was told he would face immediate deportation following conviction. Feast, who worked in a different part of the country but was acting as a visiting magistrate in the case, attempted to pay the fine using the bail account of the City of Westminster Magistrates’ Court. The payment was flagged as irregular and the matter was reported to the JCIO. Legal experts have since described the intervention as “a high-risk miscalculation” at best and a “serious professional misconduct” at worst. Professor Alison Macdonald, a law lecturer at the University of Bristol, said that while magistrates are expected to treat with empathy, the role demanded strict adherence to impartiality and institutional rules. “The judiciary must remain neutral and unaffiliated with the political or social aims of individuals,” she said.

England’s pace spearhead James Anderson has said Joe Root is the "obvious candidate" to be named as the new Test captain following Alastair Cook’s surprise retirement after the recent Ashes draw, but stressed that the 29-year-old must avoid “burning himself out” in the leadership role. Anderson, who was England’s first Test captain when Cook took over the one-day and Test sides in 2012, made his comments in a wide-ranging interview with the BBC this week. The 38-year-old fast bowler, widely respected among his peers and cricket writers for his professionalism and tactical nous, said he has long believed Root had the game and temperament to lead. "Joe is the obvious candidate," Anderson said. "He's made that case repeatedly on the field with his consistent batting and leadership in the team over the past few years. He knows what he's doing in the middle and he can take everyone with him. But the key thing is, he mustn’t allow captaincy to take away from his batting." Root, 29, has been England’s most reliable batter in the Ashes series, averaging over 50, and is regarded as one of the most technically sound and controlled batsmen in world cricket. However, Anderson, who has captained in treacherous conditions in Pakistan and West Indies, warned that the relentless nature of modern-day captaincy could take a toll on Root’s performance if not carefully managed. “You see it happen,” Anderson said. “Too much time in the press room, too much homework, too much thinking. As a batter, you need to switch off sometimes. It's different when you're not the skipper — you just go in and play. But when you're captaining, your head is never switched off. “That’s why Steve [Cook] used to do such a good job. He let others take on some of the peripheral stuff so he could focus on bat and ball. Joe has to make sure he doesn’t overstretch himself.” Anderson, who will step down from international cricket later this year, said it was time for fresh leadership at the top, but stressed that stability in performance was just as vital as good captaincy. He also praised Root’s maturity and said he had been the “most consistent player” in the recent Ashes series. The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) is expected to name Root as their new Test captain imminently.

A new report by a group of MPs has revealed startling evidence of the economic inequality faced by Muslim women in Britain, placing them at the bottom of the economic ladder within British society. The study, published by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on British Muslims, highlights how Muslim women are the least likely to be in work, the most likely to live in poverty and face a range of structural barriers that significantly impact their economic participation and prospects. The report, titled "No Apartheid but Plenty of Inequality," follows an inquiry into the economic differences experienced by ethnic and religious minorities in the UK. It found that while Muslim women aged 16–64 are entering the workforce at a slightly higher rate than in previous years, their employment rate of 41% remains significantly below the overall female rate of 69% and well below the male Muslim rate of 59%. A further 11% are economically inactive, with many citing caregiving responsibilities and barriers to education and training as key limiting factors. The report also pointed to stark wealth and income disparities. Muslim women are more likely to live in households with the lowest 10% of equivalised incomes and less likely to own their own homes. They are also disproportionately affected by the cost-of-living crisis and the UK's rising inflation, often living in densely populated households with high financial pressures. The analysis found that deprivation levels – such as income, employment, health and education – are significantly higher in areas with a high concentration of Muslim women. One of the most alarming findings was the educational divide. The report shows that Muslim women are less likely to have qualifications beyond GCSE level compared to the majority of other women. This lack of educational attainment, combined with existing discrimination and underrepresentation in professional and managerial positions, contributes to the overall economic marginalisation. The MPs who conducted the inquiry have called for urgent action to address these inequalities. They urge a cross-sector approach involving government, employers and community organisations to improve access to education, training and employment opportunities for Muslim women. Suggestions include targeted job schemes, increased funding for childcare, and measures to reduce discrimination in the workplace and in education. Critics of the report argue that restricting the focus on Muslim women could run the risk of singling out one group for specific treatment, but supporters insist the data clearly demonstrates the need for intervention.

England were bowled out for just 65 in under 40 overs on the final day of the fifth Test against India at Chepauk, slipping to a staggering innings-and-75-run defeat in Chennai. The result marked one of the most humiliating collapses in the visitors' recent Test history, as India completed a remarkable 3-2 series victory under the bright Tamil Nadu sun. England's innings crumbled in spectacular fashion after a gloomy morning session, with only James Anderson (16 not out) managing to reach double figures in their shortest Test innings of the summer. The hosts, who arrived in the decisive session with a lead of 140 runs from their first innings total of 335, found only sporadic resistance from an England side that had been under constant duress throughout the match. India's spinners Ravichandran Ashwin and R Ashwin — the world’s best in the company, by the end — turned the game on its head with a clinical dismantling of the tourists in the early hours, using the Chinnaswamy ordering’s green top to devastating effect. Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane, who had both looked in sublime form in the previous sessions, were early victims, as India made early inroads and finished the day with a towering lead that all but left England bowled – quite literally – out of the contest. Mitchell Starc’s return as a final over spinner nearly picked up a fifth wicket, but was removed after one over with a back spasm, compounding England’s woes. Across the board, the audition read like a nightmare – Alastair Cook failed with the bat for the second time in three Tests and was bowled off the inside edge for 0, Ben Stokes dropped about five catches off the same type of bouncer and the scoreboard had barely ticked over 40 before the match was declared over. The final day had begun uneventfully enough, with India captain Virat Kohli playing calm guest speaker after Kohli (37) and Rahane extended the lead further. But as the weather changed and the sun broke through the cloud cover, so too did England's confidence. Pujara, who had topped the lunches of a couple of English spinners with such prowess, was caught for 5 after a wild attempt to play the turn early in the session. From then on, the wheels came off – Kohli made his line in, Rahane was bowled off a big one, and what had been a tight deadlock at tea turned into a 30-run India triumph against the hours.

Dame Sarah Storey has etched her name in history as Britain's most successful female Paralympian, securing her 12th gold medal on a triumphant opening day at the Rio 2016 Paralympics. The 37-year-old, already a legend in her sport, crossed the line in dominant fashion in the women’s C4-5 500m time trial on Thursday, making her a true icon of Paralympic cycling. Storey, riding for Great Britain, clocked a time of 35.845 seconds to comfortably win her event, leaving the rest of the field trailing in her wake. The victory marked her 12th Paralympic gold, surpassing the previous record set by Tanni Grey-Thompson, who achieved 11 golds over the course of her stellar career in wheelchair racing. Receiving the gold medal with an emotionally poignant handover from her coach, Dave Eggberge, Storey dedicated her historic win to her late father, Peter, who passed away earlier this year after a battle with cancer. Her father had been her biggest supporter throughout her sports career, and his presence was palpable in her remarks after the race. “I’ve still got grief in me, and today is a very emotional day for me because I’m dedicating this win to my dad,” Storey said in a post-race interview with the BBC. “He was the one who got me into cycling, and this one’s for him. There’s no way I’d be doing this without him. He was always my rock.” This historic achievement capped a remarkable career for Storey, who made the transition from wheelchair racing to para-cycling in 2006 after complications from bullying as a child led to a leg amputation. Since then, she has broken numerous records, claimed 23 world championship titles and become a formidable force in the Paralympic circuit. Her staggering level of consistency and competitiveness has cemented her status as one of the greatest athletes, disabled or otherwise, in British sporting history. Storey was quick to credit her team for her success, especially her coach and physiotherapists. “This is a team effort,” she added. “I can't do what I do without the people around me. Every decision, every strategy, it's a group effort. This go-around is my best ever start to a Games, so I’m really excited to see what I can do over the next week.” With five more events due to take place in Rio, including the individual pursuit and road race, Storey remains favourite to add to her tally, fuelling speculation that her Paralympic medal total may yet be the sporting equivalent of a Sistine Chapel ceiling in terms of its

Nurses across Northern Ireland are being urged to use their vote in the upcoming Northern Ireland Assembly election, as concerns grow over stalled progress on health reform and the ongoing political vacuum at Stormont. Health workers, already grappling with widespread staff shortages, long waiting lists, and underfunded services, are being called on to play a pivotal role in deciding the direction of the region’s future healthcare policy. The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) in Northern Ireland has launched a campaign under the slogan  “Your Health, Your Voice,”  encouraging staff to cast their ballot to ensure political change that prioritises the needs of the NHS. With the Assembly suspended since March 2023, efforts to address chronic issues such as ward shortfalls, supply chain volatility, and training barriers have slowed to a crawl, leaving many nurses frustrated. “Stormont’s collapse has had real consequences for the health service, and the momentum towards meaningful reform has all but ground to a halt,” said RCN NI’s director, Deirdre McCarron. “We are at a tipping point. Nurses are the backbone of the NHS and have the most intimate understanding of where the system is failing – and where it needs change. Now is the time for frontline staff to be heard.” A recent RCN survey of its members found that 80 per cent believed that political instability in Northern Ireland has “severely impacted” their ability to do their job and deliver consistent care. Many cited a lack of clarity around long-term funding, workforce planning, and the future relationship between the Department of Health and nursing unions. With just weeks to go before the election, political campaigning is already in full swing, but so too are efforts to engage healthcare workers directly. The RCN has organised online briefings and canvassing events in hospitals and NHS buildings, where nurses are being briefed on the competing manifestos and the different approaches parties have to resolving the crisis. Meanwhile, local MP for East Belfast, Suella Braverman, who has argued for increased central UK government involvement in Northern Ireland’s health service, faces growing opposition from health professionals, who believe it is a democratic deficit that needs to be addressed by local politicians rather than London. As the regional political landscape shifts and public sentiment hardens over sustained underperformance in health, nurses and other healthcare staff have become an unexpectedly powerful voting bloc – and a potential source of pressure for change.

The political landscape of Scotland has been fundamentally reshaped after the Scottish National Party (SNP) secured a historic landslide victory in the recent Holyrood elections, capturing an overwhelming majority across the Scottish Parliament. The sweeping win has entrenched the SNP's dominance in Scottish politics, with First Minister Nicola Sturgeon hailing the result as a mandate for her party’s clear vision for the country’s future—and a strong rebuke to the pro-Union opposition bloc. The party won 64 of the 129 parliamentary seats, a staggering achievement that underscores the growing strength of nationalist sentiment in the wake of Brexit. The Conservatives, Labour, the Liberal Democrats and the Greens combined to secure just 65 seats, marking a devastating blow to the Unionist cause. On the night of the results, SNP supporters erupted with celebration outside the parliament in Edinburgh, while their opponents struggled to contain rising alarm at the implications of the outcome. The SNP’s dominance is now far more than symbolic: for the first time since devolution in 1999, the party holds an outright majority, meaning that, unlike previous SNP-led governments, it will not need to rely on cross-party alliances or deals to get legislation passed. This strengthens Ms Sturgeon’s hand as she continues to push for a second independence referendum, which has become increasingly central to SNP policy. The party’s manifesto pledged to “restore national confidence and power” to Scotland through a vote on independence, and the election result is seen by many as public backing for that goal. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold a second independence referendum without the consent of the UK government. However, with Rishi Sunak's Conservative government floundering at Westminster and facing calls to recalibrate their approach to devolution, the Holyrood seat remains a question mark. Within the SNP, there is a clear sense of momentum. “This result demonstrates what Scotland wants,” Ms Sturgeon said in her election night speech. “We want to step up and lead. We want to create a Scotland that is ready for the challenges ahead and shows the world the strength of a democratic, inclusive and ambitious nation.” For the opposition, the question is how to respond to such a seismic vote shift. The Scottish Conservatives, who were recently predicted to gain ground from anti-SNP sentiment, found themselves far adrift, with around half the seats they commanded four years ago.

A Life on the Fringe: The Enduring Legacy of Peter Vaughan   The stage and screen may have seen him less in the spotlight, and rather more often in the shadows—but never out of focus. Peter Vaughan, who has died at the age of 93, played some of the most memorable, yet rarely leading, roles in British television and film over the last six decades. Known for his gravelly tones, dour expressions, and a presence that could dominate a scene without uttering a single word, Vaughan carved out a niche in which he played the gruff, the grumpy and the gravely concerned, but always with a nuance that elevated him far above his mostly minor character types. His fans knew him best as the steadfast Syd in the beloved comedy  Only Fools and Horses , the dependable lawyer who gave the Trotters guidance through their myriad get-rich-quick schemes. A world away from the chaotic Gerrards Cross, Vaughan portrayed the fearful breakfast-time Nazi in  Spamalot , a role in which he delivered the punchline not with a frown or a shout, but a look of sheer, camp terror—something that became one of the most loved and quoted lines in Monty Python history. In 2006, Vaughan was awarded an OBE for services to drama, a testament to a career that humble beginnings in national service – he once held a fairly menial administrative role – had ironically mirrored in his later filmography. It was as if he knew the value of the underdog and the everyman, principles which he applied not just in cast and character, but in his own professional life. He was oddly undemanding—eschewing the fury of ego or the need for being ‘the best’ in any scene in which he appeared. Instead, he offered respect to those with whom he shared the stage: watching his scene with Kevin Spacey in  Becoming Jane  (2007), one could not but marvel at how, even for a few treacherous moments in the film, he was the more interesting man onscreen. For any actor, it is easy to be overlooked, but harder still to be unforgettable. Vaughan did both. His career spanned a sustained explosion of British television and a new golden age of the stage, yet he never sought fame beyond delivering something authentic with each role. Tributes have poured in from fellow actors and directors alike. Sir Ian McKellen, with whom Vaughan shared the stage in  Macbeth  with the RSC in the 70s, called him “a man of quiet depth and tremendous ability, who taught me that even the smallest role deserves to be played with heart and soul.”

Police in Germany have confirmed that a suspected arson attack caused a school sports hall — temporarily being used as a shelter for asylum seekers — to burst into flames in the early hours of this morning. The blaze, which tore through the building in a rural town in the southwest of the country, is currently being investigated as a deliberate act, with local authorities describing the incident as a shocking and unacceptable attack on vulnerable individuals and the community at large. The affected building in the town of Rastatt, in Baden-Württemberg, was being used to house around 120 people, mostly asylum seekers who had arrived in Germany as part of the ongoing migration crisis. Firefighters were able to evacuate all occupants before the fire got out of control, and no casualties have been reported. However, several neighbouring buildings sustained minor damage from bursts of smoke and heat, and the shelter is expected to be out of use for the foreseeable future. Local police have stated that a motive is still under investigation, but the prime working theory is that the fire was set intentionally. Statements from Rastatt's mayor, Karin Schäfer, condemned the act as "a cruel and cowardly attack," adding that the town has a reputation for being welcoming and open to refugees. "This is not only an attack on the people in this building—it is an attack on our values, our democracy and our national spirit," Schäfer said during a press conference. The fire has reignited concerns across Germany about the safety of asylum centres and the rising rhetoric of far-right extremism in some parts of the country. Recent months have seen a number of incidents involving suspicious fires at government buildings and refugee shelters, many of which are believed to be the work of far-right agitators. The German Interior Ministry has reiterated its commitment to protecting public property and public officials from violence and threats. Home Secretary Horst Seehofer called the incident "outrageous" and said that the government will take swift legal action against those responsible. He also reiterated the government's stance on the importance of maintaining safe spaces for asylum seekers and protecting them from harm. “Damage to shelters is an attack not only on Germany’s neighbours in need, but on the security and stability of our cities as well,” Seehofer said. Local community leaders and volunteers have begun working together with officials to find temporary housing for the displaced individuals.

Chile is one of those countries that expects to experience large quakes. Situated along the Pacific Ring of Fire, it has long been accustomed to the tremors of tectonic plates shifting beneath its vast expanse. A nation that has historically borne the brunt of some of the most powerful earthquakes on record, Chileans have developed an almost fatalistic acceptance of the ground beneath their feet moving. But if history has taught them anything, it is that preparedness is not a luxury—it is a necessity. The most famous of Chile’s seismic events occurred in 1960, when the Great Chilean Earthquake, or the Valdivia Earthquake, struck with a staggering magnitude of 9.5, the largest ever recorded. That day, the south of the country was thrown into chaos, with towering tsunami waves sweeping across coastal towns, leaving devastation in their wake. But the resilience shown in the aftermath of that disaster has since become a hallmark of Chilean character. Governments, experts, and communities have since taken extensive steps to mitigate the damage from future quakes, implementing building codes that are among the strictest in the world. Towers in Santiago, the capital, are reinforced with flexible structures designed to absorb and dissipate energy. Schools and public spaces regularly conduct earthquake drills, ensuring that citizens know exactly how—and when—to react in the event of a tremor. Even infrastructure projects are planned with earthquakes in mind, from roads to water supplies, designed to remain operational in the immediate aftermath of a disaster. Yet despite all these precautions, the fear remains, and for good reason. In 2010, a magnitude 8.8 earthquake hit central Chile, killing hundreds and triggering another deadly tsunami. The world watched as Chile mobilised swiftly, with its emergency services operating efficiently and people about their business amid the chaos. To the untrained eye, it looked almost clinical. To those who lived through it, it was grimly calculated and painful. “The ground shook like the sky was falling,” said one survivor from Concepción, recalling the 2010 event. “But we were ready. At least, we knew what to do.” That mindset—of being ready, even as fear lingers in the background—defines life in Chile. The country cannot control the movement of the earth, but it has learned to live with it, to plan for it, and in that way, to survive it. Despite the ever-present risk, cities continue to grow, people continue to dream, and lives continue as normal, all the while with the quiet understanding that the next big quake could come at any moment.

Mohammad Asif backs Amir to trouble England again    By David Dickson  A decade after former Pakistan pacer Mohammad Amir was handed a five-year ban for his role in the 2010 spot-fixing scandal, it seems the ghosts of that summer have not faded entirely—for the cricketing world or for Amir’s former team-mate, Mohammad Asif. Speaking ahead of England’s upcoming tour of Pakistan, Asif has publicly backed Amir to trouble the likes of Joe Root and Jos Buttler with his sharp pace and deceptive swing, once again proving that nothing in cricket—and particularly not in Pakistan cricket—is ever truly left in the past. Amir, now 31, is no stranger to the England dressing room. He played a pivotal role in the 2010 Ashes tour of England, taking 33 wickets at an average of 17.33 and appearing in all five Tests, prior to his ban. His return, somewhat improbable then and even more so now, has been hard-earned, with five years in exile, re-invention as a slow left-arm orthodox bowler, and a spell with the Yorkshire Vikings forming part of a long and winding comeback. Asif, who as it happens was Amir’s original partner in the 2010 scheme—and who also served a ban of the same duration—said: “Amir has the same class and the same natural ability to break partnerships. I wish I was out there now, bowling with him. Imagine the two of us at our peak, troubling the best batsmen in the world. It would’ve been a dream line-up.” The forthcoming series, which England will approach with caution following recent security threats to the visiting squad, will see Amir line up against a team he once nearly did for. Steve Finn, the then-England fast bowler, was the key figure in what led to Amir’s downfall that summer. Now, Finn is out of the spotlight, and the stage is set for Amir to rewrite his legacy. Such statements are not made without controversy. While Amir’s return to Pakistan cricket was widely celebrated—and indeed, he took his 200th first-class wicket as recently as June of this year—there are those who question whether figures like Asif should still be given a platform, given their roles in one of cricket’s most infamous scandals. But in Pakistan cricket, where loyalties often lie with the nation and not the line of the law, such lines remain blurred.

British Telecommunications (BT) has announced a sweeping overhaul of the UK's network of public telephone boxes, set to remove approximately half of the remaining 40,000 across the country. This comes as part of a strategy to focus resources on kiosks located in areas where they are likely to be used more frequently — such as on high streets, in hospitals, train stations, and other key public locations. The remaining boxes will be maintained with the aim of ensuring they remain functional in an increasingly mobile-first era. BT, which currently manages the iconic red kiosks on behalf of the government under the Post Office, said the decision was driven by declining usage, with many of these boxes now little more than "vandal-proof bins" or "spider nests". Annual visitation data shows that many are used fewer than a handful of times per year, making their upkeep a costly and increasingly inefficient proposition. The telecoms giant said in a statement that the move would "ensure public money is better spent on maintaining phones where people actually need them". The decision follows the gradual phase-out of payphones across the UK in recent years, with usage dropping dramatically since the proliferation of mobile phones. Despite the changes, BT has confirmed that there will be a focus on retaining kiosks in locations where they might be of critical importance, such as in emergencies or for people who rely on them — for example, those with no mobile phone access, such as the elderly, low-income individuals, or in situations where mobile networks may be down following large-scale events or accidents. The BBC reported that the cuts will see at least one payphone removed from every local authority area. Those removed will not necessarily be taken out altogether, but some existing boxes will be decommissioned and no new kiosks will be added as replacements. This move has raised concerns among heritage groups such as the Kineton Telephone Kiosk Fund and the Kiosks Trust, who fear that continuing the cull will lead to the final disappearance of the red box from the UK landscape. They argue that despite low usage, telephone boxes have become a piece of cultural and historical iconography, and should be preserved as part of national heritage. Joe Public, from the Kiosks Trust, said: “We are worried that we keep on losing one by one, and the next thing there will be none left.

Rail passengers in Tayside, Stirlingshire, Perthshire, Aberdeenshire and the Borders are being promised a "revolution" in travel, with long-time supporters of more frequent and faster services finally witnessing the beginnings of a major infrastructure overhaul. Transport Scotland has announced the launch of what it is calling the "Deeside and Tay Rail Futures" project, a £53m investment aimed at improving connectivity between key towns and cities across central and northern Scotland. At the heart of this project is a commitment to reduce journey times and increase reliability, something that local business leaders and commuters have for years called for when discussing the region's underperforming rail network. The proposed upgrades include enhanced services on the Deeside and Tay lines, which will see the introduction of more modern, higher-capacity trains. Journey times between Aberdeen and Kingussie, via Balmoral, and between Stirling and Perth are expected to be cut by up to 20 minutes. This, according to Scottish Transport Secretary Michael Russell, will drive economic growth across the regions, making it easier for workers, students, and visitors to travel. “This is more than just a technical upgrade," Mr Russell told journalists in a statement. "This is a revolution in mobility for some of Scotland’s most historic and picturesque regions. These lines are lifelines for local communities and will now help support sustainable growth and improve access to employment, education, and leisure." The government’s announcement follows years of pressure from councils and passenger groups, who highlighted the outdated nature of the existing rolling stock and the sporadic nature of train services. The improvements are part of the Scottish government’s wider Rail Investment Framework, which aims to transform rail across the country by 2030. For residents in remote areas where car ownership is not always viable, rail upgrades are seen as key to improving access to the rest of Scotland and beyond. However, not all local leaders are convinced. Some have raised concerns over the scale of the proposed transformation, with critics arguing that the funding is disproportionately allocated to less-populated areas at the expense of urban routes. Others believe it is a positive step forward, particularly with the continued strain on road infrastructure and the growing emphasis on reducing carbon emissions. Dr Gregor Watson, regional transport co-ordinator for Aberdeenshire Council, supported the move. “Improved rail services are vital for economic development and environmental sustainability. This project goads us one step closer to a transport system that works for everyone, not just the cities,” he said.

A Golden Year: Britpop, Spice Mania, and the Football Homecoming of 1996   The year 1996 will forever be etched in British cultural memory as a defining moment in national identity—a year that saw music, pop culture, and sport converge in a celebration of homegrown talent and youthful exuberance. From the rabid melodies of Britpop to the unbridled charm of the Spice Girls and the triumphant return of football to English soil, 1996 was a year when Britain came of age, and the world was watching. The revival of guitar-driven, proudly British rock under the broad banner of Britpop reached its peak in 1996. Bands like Oasis and Blur had already captured the imagination of a nation, but it was The Verve’s monumental success that cemented the era’s legacy. Their album  Urban Hymns , released in October 1995 and dominating the charts through 1996, delivered the hauntingly euphoric “Bitter Sweet Symphony,” a song that became the anthem of a generation. As Britpop legends built rivalries and traded diss tracks, the genre became more than just music—it was a cultural declaration of identity in the face of global American pop dominance. Football channels on television beamed the Super League rhythm of domestic clubs, while fans debated at the pub whether Oasis or Blur would win the looming “supergroup supremacy.” For a brief time, Britain did not feel like the understudy to the American musical world; it was the star. Meanwhile, someone was Spicing up TV. The Spice Girls, a five-piece pop phenomenon, took the world by storm with their catchy tunes, signature outfits and mouths full of glitter. While  Wannabe  may have dropped about five decades prior to 1996, the band had finally struck global superstardom by this point. The release of their second album,  Spice World  in 1996, was the soundtrack to school discos and road trips. The Spice Mania was a phenomenon in its own right, bringing the very concept of girl groups into the modern era. We had Scary, Sporty, Baby, Posh, and Ginger—British girls on the world stage with boldness and grace. The concept was simple: a band made of individuals, each with their go-to catchphrase and own identity. It wasn’t just music—it was empowerment, in a bright pink, green and glitter box. Closer to the pitch, football was in the news for much more than the off-field antics of rock stars.

Research suggests that the Ebola virus underwent a dramatic and startling adaptation in the early months of the 2014–2015 West African outbreak, allowing it to infect human tissues more efficiently than ever before. This revelation, detailed in a new study published in Nature, has raised questions about the speed at which the virus was able to evolve to exploit human biology — and the implications for future outbreaks. The 2014–2015 Ebola epidemic, which primarily affected Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia, was the largest in recorded history, with over 28,000 cases and nearly 11,000 deaths. It was markedly more severe and spread more rapidly than previous outbreaks. Now, scientists have uncovered a key reason why the virus was so devastating: within months of the outbreak, specific genetic mutations emerged that significantly enhanced its ability to bind to and enter human cells. These changes were most pronounced in the viral protein known as glycoprotein, which plays a crucial role in allowing the virus to attach itself to the surface of human immune cells, such as macrophages and dendritic cells. The mutations, which occurred over the course of a few months rather than years — an unusually short span in evolutionary terms — made the glycoprotein more effective at interacting with human tissue, leading to faster and more efficient viral replication. Dr. Marta – one of the lead researchers on the study – explained the significance: “This wasn’t just an isolated mutation,” she said. “We observed a series of coordinated changes in the viral genome that worked in combination. The improvements in how the virus attached to human cells increased the scale and speed of transmission. It made the virus more infectious and, potentially, more deadly.” Experts suggest that this rapid adaptation may have been driven by the virus’s prolonged exposure to human populations, combined with the widespread movement of people during the early stages of the outbreak. Unlike in previous outbreaks, where the virus remained confined to isolated communities, the virus in 2014–2015 passed through human hosts for extended periods, creating the perfect conditions for natural selection to take place. The findings are both sobering and alarming. They highlight how even a virus that had historically infected only a limited number of people could develop new capabilities with potentially catastrophic consequences if the right environmental conditions emerge. Moreover, they serve as a warning: viruses are not static. They can — and do — evolve rapidly when given the opportunity.

Sisters Katie and Ellie Ward have made history as the first British country duo ever to reach number one in the UK album chart with their fourth studio album,  Serpent . The release not only topped the Official Albums Chart but also achieved gold status within days of its launch, underscoring the growing popularity of country music in the UK. In an industry where international acts like Taylor Swift and Luke Combs have dominated the upper echelons of the charts, Ward Thomas' success marks a significant milestone for UK-based country artists. The album was released on 11 March and features the hit single "Lay Me Down," which received widespread critical acclaim and helped propel the pair to even greater visibility. Speaking ahead of the chart announcement, Katie Ward said the achievement felt like "a dream come true" after more than a decade in the music business. "We’ve always believed in telling our own stories through music, and to now be making history for British country feels incredibly special," she added. Ellie Ward echoed her sister's sentiments, stating: “It’s amazing to see people connecting with our music, both in the UK and beyond. We never thought we’d get to this point—especially as a British girl duo in a genre that’s not as established here as it is in America.”  Serpent  showcases the pair's signature blend of folk-inspired country, storytelling lyricism, and strong vocal harmonies. The album was produced by award-winning producer Dann Galluci and features guest appearances from notable figures in the UK’s music scene. It has been hailed by critics as one of the most authentic and compelling country releases in recent years. The duo's chart-topping success comes at a time when country music is enjoying a surge in popularity in Britain, with more listeners tuning into BBC Radio 2 and streaming platforms about country acts. Ward Thomas have played a key role in building this momentum, alongside artists like James Newman and The Shires, all of whom have contributed to the genre's transformation in the UK. Since they first made their mark in 2011, Ward Thomas have built a loyal fanbase through relentless touring, critically lauded albums, and a commitment to staying true to their roots. Their first number one album is being seen as a breakthrough moment not just for the act but also for the future of British country music.

Opposition members of parliament were thrown out of South Africa’s National Assembly on Wednesday during President Jacob Zuma’s annual state of the nation address after hours of continuous heckling and disruption. The incident, which saw several MPs removed by security, underscored deepening political tensions in a country already grappling with allegations of corruption, economic uncertainty, and public discontent over the Zuma administration’s governance. The incident occurred on the 12th day of Zuma’s speech, delivered under heavy criticism from the governing African National Congress (ANC) and watched by a global audience. The president, in what has become his final address before the 2019 general election, outlined plans for economic reform, social development and infrastructure, as well as a focus on nation-building. However, minutes into the speech, the room erupted in disorder. South Africa’s Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), the Democratic Alliance, and smaller parties began objecting to what they called vague promises and a failure to address pressing issues, including the #Gupta scandal, which has seen Zuma accused of using state resources for benefit of his wealthy allies. MPs from the EFF, who have built a reputation for robust opposition, were seen shouting, clapping, and walking out in protest. In one dramatic moment, Zuma paused his speech as security moved in and escorted several opposition MPs – including prominent figures from the EFF – from the chamber. According to parliamentary sources, the MPs were removed for “repeated violations of parliamentary procedure and decorum,” as outlined in the Standing Orders. Zuma continued his address while the row unfolded, speaking at times with visible frustration. “I am not here to perform for those who want to entertain themselves with chaos,” the president said later in the speech. “This is a serious session for the people of South Africa.” The incident has sparked fierce debate both in parliament and the media, with many analysts suggesting it highlights a growing lack of consensus and cooperation that risks undermining national unity and stability. The ANC, in response, claimed that the opposition was deliberately trying to “derail” the democratic process. The DA, on the other hand, issued a statement condemning the removal of its members, calling it “a clear affront to parliamentary democracy and free speech.” The dispute also sparked calls for reform of South Africa’s parliamentary procedures. Some MPs and civil society groups have urged for the establishment of an independent ombudsman to go beyond the current system of self-regulation among MPs.

Five years on from the start of the civil war that led to the toppling of Libyan strongman Muammar Gaddafi, the country remains in a dire state of political and territorial division. Despite numerous diplomatic efforts and tentative peace talks, Libya is still without a unified government capable of exercising authority across the entire country. Two rival administrations — one based in the capital, Tripoli, and the other in the east, in the city of Tobruk — continue to vie for legitimacy, each backed by a patchwork of militias, regional interests, and foreign support. The conflict, initially framed as a struggle for democratic change during the Arab Spring, revealed the deep fractures that had long divided Libya along tribal, geographic, and ideological lines. Gaddafi, who had ruled for 42 years, was killed by forces loyal to the National Transitional Council (NTC) in October 2011, and the country has never managed to piece together a stable governing structure since. Today, breakfast, often a simple affair of tea and dates or bread in Western Libya, is served against a backdrop of enduring instability. Markets remain shuttered in many areas due to security concerns, while key institutions like the central bank, oil infrastructure, and ports are contested or out of reach to Libyans struggling for stability. The situation has been exacerbated by the rise of local militias and the growing involvement of foreign powers, including Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and, more recently, Turkey, which has provided support to the Tripoli-based Government of National Accord (GNA). The eastern-based House of Representatives, backed by the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) led by General Khalifa Haftar, continues to challenge the GNA's legitimacy, resulting in sporadic outbreaks of violence and a fragile ceasefire in place since 2020. Many Libyans have grown weary of the endless political deadlock. Samira El-Kulib, a librarian from Tripoli, summed up the despair of many when she said, “We had hopes after the revolution, that we’d finally be free. But now? We’re still waiting for a government that can provide security, power, and even water. After five years, the only thing that has changed is the constant fear.” With weapons flooding in from abroad and political leaders embroiled in internecine power struggles, delivering a sustainable peace remains a distant dream. The UN has repeatedly called on Libyans to end the division and form a technocratic unity government, but progress remains elusive.

As schools across England prepare to welcome students back from the summer break, a notable number of schools are still grappling with unfilled teaching vacancies, highlighting the ongoing staffing challenges in the education sector. Despite months of recruitment drives and widespread appeals for teachers to apply, some schools—including maintained secondary schools and academies—report they are still missing key staff positions on their upcoming rosters. The Department for Education recently released figures showing that over 1,500 teaching posts remain vacant在全国范围内, with subjects such as mathematics, science, and foreign languages arguably the hardest hit. These shortages are particularly acute in regions like Yorkshire, the North East of England, and parts of London, where schools already operate under tight budgets and face added pressure due to increasing student rolls. A spokesperson for the National Union of Teachers said the issue was not new but had become more urgent over the past two years as rising workloads, stagnant pay, and the growing administrative burden on staff have driven more teachers to leave the profession, often for alternative careers in other fields. “The last two years have been extremely challenging,” the spokesperson said, adding that many trainee teachers had also delayed entering the profession or chosen other sectors. School leaders are now scrambling to address the impacts of short staffing. In some cases, experienced teachers are being asked to take on extra classes or subjects outside their expertise. Supply teachers, often on short-term contracts, are being called in at the last minute, sometimes with just a day’s notice. This instability raises concerns about student continuity and the quality of instruction. Head teachers argue that the situation is not only affecting day-to-day operations but also casting a shadow over the government's long-promised recruitment and retention strategy.
