Some principals have questioned the strategy's effectiveness and called for more immediate action, such as increased funding for recruitment incentives and better pastoral support for staff. With the new academic year having already begun, officials at the Department for Education say they are monitoring the situation closely and working with local education authorities to provide emergency support where needed. But for many schools, the lesson is clear: filling the vacancies is not just about getting teachers into the classroom before the bell rings—it's about ensuring the long-term stability of the country's education system. As one school administrator put it: “We’re always trying to catch up.

To understand the outpouring of elation and relief Wales football fans feel after their team qualified for Euro 2016, you must understand a little bit of the country’s football history. For decades, Wales has existed on the periphery of international football, often scrapping for respect as a nation with proud tradition but little recent success on the global stage. The qualification for their first major tournament since the 1958 World Cup has not just been a sporting triumph—it has been a moment of emotional catharsis, a long-awaited renaissance for a country deeply connected to the beautiful game. Wales' footballing heritage is rich and passionate, often referred to by pundits and historians as "the Welsh Golden Age" of the 1950s and '60s. Yet, since Terry Yorath qualified for Spain '82, their teams have mostly been used as convenient goals for more dominant European nations in qualifier after qualifier. The raw disappointment when, year after year, Wales found themselves returning from early qualifiers empty-handed was palpable. For many fans, the hurt was both national and personal. Former player Gary Speed once described the Welsh footballer as a “giant in a small suit,” embodying the struggle of their position in the global hierarchy. But everything changed in 2013. Chris Coleman took charge of the national team, replacing the long-serving boss Gary Neville, with a clear vision and fiery determination. The former Premier League defender had already proven his mettle at club level and now found himself with the opportunity to reshape the fortunes of a nation at full international level. What followed was a remarkable transformation. Coleman's emphasis on a physical, attacking style—combined with a strong sense of unity and identity—allowed Wales to evolve from perennial also-rans to contenders on the international stage. The Euro 2016 qualification campaign was especially emotional. The final qualifying group included England, Belgium and Slovakia—a group many considered cruelly tough for Wales to have drawn. But instead of being overwhelmed, Wales stepped up. A 3-0 victory in Wembley over England was a defining moment. For the first time in 58 years, Wales had beaten England at home. It was more than just a win; it was a symbolic rejection of long-standing inferiority and a declaration that Welsh football was no longer content to play second best. Qualifying for France 2016 is more than just a ticket to a tournament—it is a statement that Wales deserves to be there, that the spirit and passion of its fans and players have earned their place.

PSNI Fuel Passport Scheme Under Fire Amid Claims of Red Tape Obstruction   A controversial pilot scheme by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) aimed at tackling the rising problem of anti-social drivers who leave petrol stations without paying for their fuel has sparked outcry from businesses and community leaders. The so-called  Fuel Passport Scheme  has been accused of being more harmful than helpful, with critics arguing that its implementation is mired in unnecessary bureaucracy and fails to address the real issue. The scheme, launched last month, requires drivers who are reported as unpaid fuel offenders to voluntarily hand over their relevant documents to petrol station attendants when refuelling. This data is then passed to the PSNI who can use it to pursue prosecution. However, many small independent fuel station operators across Northern Ireland say the process is impractical and overly complex. One shopkeeper in Craigavon who wished to remain anonymous stated: “We’re meant to be running an assembling, not a police station. Why are we now supposed to act as a front for the PSNI?” According to the PSNI, 4,287 incidents of so-called “white van crimes” were reported in Northern Ireland last year—many of them involving vehicles leaving petrol stations without payment. In one particularly high-profile case last month, a lorry driven by a Russian national was caught filling up in Omagh and fleeing without paying £189 in fuel. Local businesses and police have linked the increase in these crimes to an influx of Eastern European truckers operating under informal contracts and slipping through the radar of financial record-keeping. The scheme follows a similar one-year pilot in Donegal, which reportedly resulted in a 65 per cent drop in the number of cases. However, the Northern Ireland version is considered crude in its execution, with no guidance provided about how petrol station staff are to manage such procedures without the assistance of law enforcement. Concerns have also been raised about potential discrimination and data privacy breaches, with fears unscrupulous drivers could be unfairly targeted for background checks. Northern Ireland’s Business Alliance called for an explanation and urgent revision to the initiative. Speaking on behalf of the group, spokesperson Ciaran Doyle said: “While we fully support the PSNI in its efforts to tackle sustained criminal activity, this scheme is not fit for purpose. It risks alienating legitimate customers and places an undue burden on small businesses who are already struggling to go about their daily operations.”

The first human trials of a promising new vaccine designed to prevent rotavirus, a leading cause of severe childhood illness, have shown encouraging results, according to a team of scientists. The trial, conducted in the UK by researchers at the University of Oxford, marks a significant step forward in the fight against a disease that affects millions of infants worldwide each year and claims the lives of more than 200,000 children annually—most of them in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Rotavirus is a highly contagious virus that causes diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever. In young children, the illness can quickly lead to dangerous dehydration and even death if not treated promptly. Current vaccines are already used in many countries, but researchers say the new formula could offer broader and longer-lasting immunity, particularly in regions with high infant mortality. The trial involved 120 healthy adult volunteers, who were given either the new vaccine or a placebo. Early data, published in the journal The Lancet, showed that the vaccine prompted a strong immune response without raising safety concerns. Researchers are now preparing to test the vaccine in infants before moving towards large-scale clinical trials. Dr. Sarah Waterhouse, one of the lead researchers on the project, said: “These results are very promising and give us the confidence to take the next step in developing a vaccine that works in infants. If all goes well, we aim to have it ready for wider use in five to six years.” Currently, global health organisations recommend the use of two existing rotavirus vaccines, which are highly effective in high-income countries. However, the vaccines appear less effective in low-income areas, where rates of rotavirus illness and death remain high. Experts believe this is due to a combination of factors, including poor healthcare infrastructure, malnutrition, and the presence of other infections in young children that may interfere with the body’s ability to build immunity. The new vaccine from Oxford is based on a purified form of the virus and is designed to trigger a stronger immune response to the most dangerous strains. Uniquely, it requires only one dose, which would make it easier to administer in areas where access to healthcare can be limited. Dr. Simon Clarke, a virologist from the University of Reading who was not involved in the study, commented: “This is a significant advancement. If the next stage of trials is successful, this vaccine could truly make the difference we’ve been hoping for in the developing world.”

Mark Bridger, the man found guilty of abducting and murdering five-year-old April Jones in a brutally disturbing and sexually motivated attack, has been sentenced to a whole-life term in prison by a judge at Mold Crown Court. The 58-year-old, who maintained a respectful appearance in court before the sentencing, will now spend the rest of his life behind bars without the possibility of ever being released. The case, which has left a deep scar on the communities of Machynlleth and Powys, was marked by its horrifying brutality. In October 2012, April Jones set off from outside a supermarket to visit a friend’s house just a short distance away. She was never seen alive again. Bridger, who had shown a long-standing interest in children and had been under police investigation for years for other indecent and criminal behaviour, was eventually identified as the killer through forensic evidence and his own DNA. April was found dead the following morning in woodland a mile from her home, her skull crushed with a rock in what the police later confirmed was not an accident, as Bridger had initially claimed. The coroner ruled her death a murder and noted that the sexual motive behind the attack was paramount. A short time later, April’s family were grief-struck once more as they were informed that Bridger had tried to kill another little boy just hours after April’s death. At his trial, the prosecution depicted Bridger’s actions as “callous and calculated.” Despite his bizarre and pretentious attempts to win the sympathy of the court by acting as a “model prisoner” during the trial, the judge was unforgiving. Sentence remarks described the crime as “a monstrous and despicable act” and stated that the only appropriate punishment was a life sentence with no opportunity for parole. April’s family, who have endured unimaginable suffering since the tragedy, were present in court and received an apology from Bridger that was widely seen as insincere. Despite this, they have urged for time to grieve and for continued reflection on how such a case could have been allowed to escalate. The case has raised concerns about how authorities monitor and act on individuals with a proclivity to violence and child sexual abuse. Bridger had been investigated by police on multiple occasions but was never arrested for such crimes. His conviction serves as a stark reminder of the importance of vigilance and thorough safeguarding protocols in protecting vulnerable children.

Surrey Police have revealed that former BBC presenter Sir Jimmy Savile was questioned in 2007 in relation to allegations of historical non-recent child sex abuse. The confirmation comes after months of calls by campaigners and media figures for a full independent inquiry into the late broadcaster, whose death in 2011 sparked a national outcry and led to more than 100 allegations being made against him. In a statement, Surrey Police said that Savile had been “interviewed under caution” during an investigation into claims of sexual abuse dating back to the 1980s and early 1990s. However, they added that no criminal charges were brought at the time. The force declined to comment further on the nature of the allegations or the outcome of the investigation, citing legal advice. The revelation has reignited calls for the Home Office to launch a full inquiry into Savile’s actions. In an exclusive interview with the BBC, one of the complainants, who has remained anonymous, said she was in disbelief at the news. “If he was interviewed, then why wasn’t he arrested? Why was he allowed to walk away with no consequences, while other victims were left to suffer in silence?” Savile, who hosted high-profile BBC programmes such as Top of the Pops and Jim’ll Fix It, was posthumously stripped of his knighthood in 2012 and other honours were also removed. His case became emblematic of institutional failures in the handling of historic abuse allegations, particularly in the public sector, and led to a series of internal reviews at the BBC. In response to the latest disclosure, Metropolitan Police Commander Mary Jackson said: “This is a matter for Surrey Police and their investigation at the time. We are aware of the recent statements about Sir Jimmy Savile and the ongoing calls from the public for a full inquiry. The police and other public bodies will continue to learn from the past and handle future allegations as they arise to ensure justice for victims.” Campaigners have described the news as further evidence of a culture of cover-ups and a failure to take allegations against Savile seriously during his lifetime. Sara Corbet, chief executive of the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, a child protection charity, said: “This revelation underscores the fact that we must not only examine the past but learn from it. Historic abuse must be taken seriously, and victims should always be believed.” As of now, there are no indications that Surrey Police will reopen the 2007 investigation, but the force has confirmed it is prepared to provide evidence to any future independent inquiry.

The Australian government has revealed that it has referred approximately 40 foreign nationals for investigation over suspected breaches of the nation’s real estate investment laws, according to a senior government official. The move comes amid growing concerns over the impact of overseas property speculation on the domestic housing market and as the government continues to scrutinise compliance with strict foreign ownership rules. The individuals in question, whose nationalities have not yet been disclosed, are believed to have potentially violated the Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) guidelines, which strictly regulate offshore investors’ access to residential property in Australia. These include prohibitions on foreign buyers acquiring new homes or auctioned properties. According to the official, the Australian Business and Investment (ABIC) unit, part of the Australian Federal Police, will now assess whether these cases warrant formal action under the   Residential Land Acquisitions Act  . If the investigations lead to substantiated evidence of misconduct, the implicated parties could face financial penalties, fines, or even be ordered to sell the property in question. The FIRB has been under increased pressure in recent years to ensure compliance with its regulations, particularly in property hotspots such as Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, where demand from international investors has driven up prices and limited housing availability for local residents. Minister for Immigration and Border Protection, Peter Dutton, reiterated the government’s stance, stating: “We are determined to ensure that Australian residential property is not being unfairly accessed by foreign investors who fail to comply with the law. Any breaches of these restrictions will be met with swift and decisive action.” The suspected violations are said to have occurred in both metropolitan and regional areas, with suspicious property activity including unauthorised purchases at auctions, the use of straw buyers, and failure to lodge statutory declarations and related documentation. A spokesperson for the Department of Homes, Local Government and Social Inclusion said: “We are committed to protecting the Australian housing market for our own citizens. Any illegal activity will not be tolerated.” This latest development marks the most significant crackdown in several months and could signal a broader push to enforce existing laws more rigorously. With ongoing political debate around housing affordability and rental shortages, enforcing strict penalties against non-compliant investors is increasingly seen as a necessary step. Audits and data from property agencies suggest that overseas buyers are responsible for a significant proportion of recent property transactions, particularly in the luxury and developer-new housing sectors.

Microsoft and Barnes & Noble team up in $300m digital books venture   In a major move to strengthen its presence in the digital reading market, Microsoft has announced a $300 million (£185 million) investment in a new venture with US bookseller Barnes & Noble. The collaboration will see the two companies create an eBook publishing and retail platform, combining Barnes & Noble’s long-standing expertise in book retail with Microsoft’s global technology reach and cloud-based capabilities. The joint venture will be headquartered in Ohio and is expected to create hundreds of jobs as it seeks to challenge the dominance of Amazon’s Kindle in the digital books space. Barnes & Noble already owns the Nook brand, which made a name for itself in the early years of the e-reader boom but has struggled to maintain traction against Amazon’s formidable platform. Microsoft is not just investing financially but is also expected to provide access to its Azure cloud services and global infrastructure to support the venture’s scalability and performance. This marks the tech giant’s latest step into the publishing industry, following previous moves into digital media and gaming. In a statement, Microsoft’s Chief Operating Officer, Kevin Turner, said that the new venture "presents a significant opportunity to reshape the digital reading experience for consumers around the world". He added that the venture "aligns with Microsoft’s broader strategy to build platforms and services that empower people and businesses in the digital age". Joe Fiore, Barnes & Noble’s President and Chief Executive Officer, said the new partnership was "a bold and exciting proposition for the future of books and reading". He described the venture as “a strategic transformation for Barnes & Noble, allowing us to focus more effectively on building a world-leading digital reading ecosystem.” The new company will have the rights to use both the Microsoft and Barnes & Noble brands, and it remains to be seen whether the Nook brand will be integrated into the new venture or rebranded entirely. Analysts have suggested that the new venture could lead to a more tightly integrated experience between Windows-based devices, like tablets and PCs, and digital books. Microsoft’s investment follows a series of high-profile deals in the publishing and media sectors, including content partnerships with media groups like The Wall Street Journal and the BBC. The latest partnership with Barnes & Noble also suggests a broader strategy to expand the company’s ecosystem beyond traditional software and hardware offerings.

Home Secretary Amber Rudd has come under fire from critics and journalists alike after she sharply defended her government’s proposals to limit the use of non-British workers, responding with the now widely reported line: “Don’t call me a racist for talking about immigration.” Speaking to Sky News, Mrs Rudd rejected accusations that her stance on immigration was discriminatory and instead framed the issue as one of fair treatment for British citizens and the need for employers to "look first at home" before recruiting from abroad. The comments sparked a social media frenzy, with many users expressing concern that her tone crossed a dangerous line in the difficult and emotive debate over immigration policy. Mrs Rudd’s remarks came in the context of new plans to increase pressure on firms to offer opportunities to British workers first. These proposals are part of a broader review of visa systems and employment laws aimed at prioritising home-grown talent amid ongoing public concern over high levels of immigration. The government’s approach has drawn both praise and criticism. Supporters argue that British workers should be given preference in employment, particularly in sectors dominated by foreign workers, such as hospitality, healthcare, and agriculture. They see the proposals as a long-overdue correction to a system that, in their view, has not done enough to protect the domestic workforce. However, opponents and think tanks have warned that such policies risk damaging productivity and risking economic growth, particularly in industries where skills shortages remain a pressing challenge. Critics also argue that equating discussions about immigration policy with racism is dangerously reductive and could stifle much-needed conversations about fair employment practices. During the interview, Mrs Rudd was pressed on whether her statement — in which she also said “I read some of the letters from people [who] think that talking about this is racist” — would send politicians down a slippery slope where any reform in immigration or welfare policy could be blocked by accusations of racism. She responded: “It’s very difficult [to talk about immigration]. We have to know that we can make the changes we need to make for this country. My job is to protect the British people.” Mrs Rudd passed off her response as a reaction to a frequent criticism she has faced over the years. Since becoming a prominent figure in Theresa May’s cabinet, the former minister has consistently defended a hardline stance on immigration, with her comments often drawing fiery responses from the left and accusations of racial insensitivity from opposition figures.

Wales prop Gethin Jenkins has announced his continued commitment to international rugby, vowing not to retire as he aims to reclaim his place in the starting XV. The 37-year-old, known for his longevity and consistency on the international stage, has faced increased competition in the forwards in recent seasons but remains determined to prove his worth again on the Test circuit. Jenkins, one of the most capped players in Welsh rugby history, has earned a staggering 147 caps for his country since his debut in 2002. Despite a successful career spanning over 15 years, and playing a pivotal role in Wales' triumph at the 2005 Rugby World Cup, Jenkins has been absent from the international scene in recent seasons. His last appearance came in 2017, but the veteran forward is not ready to walk away from the game just yet. Speaking to the media, Jenkins emphasized that he feels in the best physical and mental shape of his career and is eager to step back into the Wales setup. "I love playing for Wales and I'm not ready to hang up the boots," he said. "There's still more I want to achieve and I believe I can contribute at the highest level. Right now, my focus is on getting back into the starting line-up and helping Wales succeed." His comments come as Wales look ahead to a crucial upcoming season that includes matches in the Six Nations and potential Tests against top-tier international sides. With new coaching staff aiming to rejuvenate the team’s dynamic, Jenkins sees an opportunity to prove his value and help lead the side forward with his wealth of experience. Jenkins has a long career at club level with Cardiff Blues and Ospreys under his belt and continues to be an influential figure in the Welsh domestic game. However, it is on the international stage where he has left the most significant mark — and he is determined to make one final impact. Wales coach Warren Gatland has not publicly commented on Jenkins' future in the squad, but sources indicate that the forward will undergo a rigorous trial period with the national team. Jenkins will need to show both physical readiness and the ability to adapt to modern rugby's increasing demands. If successful, Jenkins could become the oldest player to start for Wales in a competitive international game. The veteran prop's ambition highlights the enduring passion that drives top-level rugby players.

The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has ruled that a website did not breach copyright law by linking to photos from  Playboy  magazine that had been published on another site without permission, in a landmark decision that could have wide implications for internet law. The ruling, delivered by the EU’s top court, clarifies the legal status of  deep links —links that direct users to specific files on a website rather than a homepage—and whether linking to copyrighted material hosted elsewhere constitutes a copyright infringement. In its judgment, the court stated that linking to a photograph or other protected content that has already been uploaded to the internet by a third party does not, in itself, infringe the rights of the original copyright holder. The case was brought after  Playboy  turkey, a local edition of the adult entertainment magazine, claimed that a rival website had infringed its copyright by linking directly to images extracted from  Playboy  photoshoots that had been illegally uploaded to a third-party site. The company argued that the act of republishing, even indirectly, amounted to a violation of its intellectual property rights. The CJEU, however, rejected this argument, ruling that a website is not legally responsible for linking to content that has already been placed on the internet by other users. “The mere action of placing a link to a protected file, without the website provider itself carrying out any act of reproduction or making the work directly available to the public, does not amount to an act of infringement,” the court said in its ruling. The judgment has been welcomed by digital rights advocates, who argue that the decision affirms the foundational principles of the open internet and protects the rights of users to freely access and share information. Sam Jordison, a digital rights campaigner, told the BBC, “This ruling is about ensuring that the web continues to function as the interconnected network of links we have come to depend on. If every link was governed by the same strict rules as direct reproduction, the internet as we know it would collapse.” However, copyright holders have expressed concern that the ruling could make it easier for unauthorised content to be widely disseminated. A spokesperson for the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry said, “While we support innovation and a thriving digital economy, this ruling could allow infringing content to be perpetuated with no accountability for those who spread it.”

White British pupils in England are making less progress at school than children from most other ethnic backgrounds, according to a new report that has sparked fresh debate about the performance of the country’s dominant ethnic group in education. Published by the UK’s Office for Standards in Education (Ofsted), the study highlights what it describes as a "complex picture" of educational outcomes and warns that the gap between White British students and other groups is growing in some cases. The findings show that children from Asian and Black ethnic backgrounds across all social classes tend to outperform their White British counterparts in terms of academic progress. The report also notes that White British children are the most likely to not meet expected levels of achievement in both maths and English by the end of primary school, and are also disproportionately represented in the group of students who fall behind year-on-year. In secondary school, the trend continues, with the report revealing that young Black and Asian students are more likely to take and pass A-levels and achieve better GCSE grades overall. The data adds nuance to a long-standing discussion about underperformance, which is often linked to factors such as poverty and area deprivation. However, the report suggests that even among White British pupils from well-off households, progress levels are faltering — a phenomenon that defies easy explanation. "This is not as simple as saying poverty is the only barrier to achievement," said Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Hilton. "White British students from affluent backgrounds, where all other factors support success, are still not performing as well as children from other ethnic groups. This is a worrying development that we urge schools and policymakers to urgently address." The report also points to a number of contributory factors, including cultural attitudes towards education, parental involvement, and a possible lack of engagement with the curriculum among some White British pupils. There are also concerns about how schools are resourcing support for White British children, who may not be considered vulnerable groups in the same way as others are. Education ministers and child education experts have long argued that progress in the system should not be measured only against ethnic benchmarks. "It’s about giving every child the opportunity to reach their potential," said a spokesperson for the Department for Education. "Our focus must always be on the individual needs of students, not on comparing them to others."

Smuggling Hidden Passport: A Dark Underground Runs Between Deportation and Return   A BBC investigation has uncovered a deeply troubling pattern: illegal immigrants facing deportation from the United Kingdom are being smuggled out of the country via the port of Dover and then mysteriously “reappeared” in the UK—some within days. The revelation has sparked alarm within immigration and border control services, with officials conceding that an underground network is facilitating the illegal re-entry of those who were officially removed. According to the findings, a complex web of human traffickers and corrupt officials is exploiting the UK’s departure and repatriation procedures. The port of Dover, one of the principal entry and exit points of the country, has become a hub for this illicit activity, with individuals being discreetly transported across the English Channel before being returned under the cover of darkness. The process typically involves the misuse of vans, ferries, and even legitimate transport routes to spirited deportees back into the UK. In several cases, migrants intercepted at British airports or found living without valid status in towns across the South East have been later identified as people who had already been flagged as having left the country. Phil Carter, a former Home Office immigration officer, described the practice as “a full-scale game of cat and mouse, and the system is losing more often than not.” He added that it suggests a serious flaw in the way the national database – which records who has been deported, and who is subject to an exit check – is being used in practice. What makes the situation even more alarming is the fact that the same people, in some cases, have been found in receipt of welfare benefits or working in the agriculture and construction sectors shortly after their supposed removal. One migrant profiled in the BBC’s investigation, recently intercepted at an East London train station, claimed he had been picked up by an individual who had “promised safe passage back” for £3,500. The Ministry of Home Affairs has confirmed that it is aware of the issue and has begun a review of operations at processing centres and points of departure across the UK. A spokesperson for the Home Office stated: “We take all reports of irregularity within our immigration system very seriously. We are currently examining the procedures that have allowed this to occur and are working closely with law enforcement to identify those responsible.”

Sport at the elite level, even for those few geniuses who can routinely do what others can only dream of, typically appears to be about obvious effort and relentless industry. Whether it's the early morning runs, the punishing gym sessions, or the sleepless nights spent refining technique, the public image of elite athletes is one of unflinching dedication and single-minded purpose. It is an image that is rarely far from the media spotlight, with fans and commentators constantly hailing the “grind,” the “work ethic,” or the “professionalism” of the world’s greatest sportspeople. And for the most part, this perception is well deserved. But what often goes unnoticed is the invisible machinery that supports this visible effort. The real genius of elite performance lies not just in what you see, but also in what remains unseen. It is the art of knowing when to push, when to rest, and when to trust your instincts. It is the science of nutrition, sleep, and mental preparation—often more nuanced and delicate than the physical training itself. And, perhaps most importantly, it is the deep, intellectual mastery of a sport, the kind that allows even the greatest talent to truly understand the game in ways that set them apart. Take, for example, the greats of the past and present: Lionel Messi, Serena Williams, Cristiano Ronaldo, and Muhammad Ali. What is most obvious is their talent: footwork, power, speed, and finesse. But what often gets overlooked is the mental acuity and awareness that underpin their greatness. These athletes understand the principles of the game at a strategic level beyond their opponents. They read the field, the pitch, the court, or the ring as naturally as a seasoned general studying a battlefield. This is knowledge that does not always come from coaching, but from intuition developed over years of experience. The story of elite sport is not just about physical superiority or tireless work. It is about learning to trust the instinct that is forged in the furnace of those early, gruelling hours. It is about understanding that even for the exceptional few, true greatness is not just a matter of effort—it is a matter of balance, wisdom, and knowing when to rely on the unseen forces that have shaped champions long before they ever take to the field. And that, perhaps, is the greatest lesson of all. Talent, as much as it dazzles, is only part of the equation.

Tens of thousands of mourners packed into Auckland’s iconic Eden Park on Wednesday for a public memorial service for former All Blacks star Jonah Lomu, who passed away earlier this month at the age of 40 after a long battle with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The event, held on the rugby field where Lomu once electrified World Cup crowds with his blistering pace and ferocious power, was a fitting tribute to a man widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the game. The Eden Park pitch, normally reserved for elite competition, was transformed into a stadium of remembrance, with the crowd stretching far beyond the usual stands as fans from across New Zealand and the wider rugby world came out to pay their respects. From the front rows of the stadium to the fervent supporters squeezed into the aisles, the atmosphere was one of love, admiration, and deep sorrow. The ceremony began with an assembling of All Blacks jerseys from across the decades, laid out on the ground in memory of Lomu’s legendary career, before the All Blacks Haka, the team’s traditional challenge dance, was performed with immense emotion by past and present members of the national team. Sir John Kirwan, one of New Zealand’s all-time rugby legends, delivered a heartfelt eulogy, recalling Lomu’s impact on and off the field. “Jonah was a man of extraordinary ability, but more than that, he was a beacon of humanity,” Kirwan said to thunderous applause. “He gave so much joy to so many people, and he did so with a smile and a humility that never left him, even as the world watched in awe.” The memorial also featured speeches from family, former teammates and politicians, as well as tributes from key figures in global rugby, including World Rugby’s CEO Brett Gosper, the English Rugby Football Union and prominent South African players. There was also a tribute to Lomu’s role as a unifying symbol in post-apartheid rugby, particularly after playing for South Africa against his former All Blacks team in 1995 – a gesture that helped bridge divides in a country still healing from the scars of racism and segregation. Lomu, who represented New Zealand in three Rugby World Cups, including the 1995 final where he scored two tries, was a global ambassador for the sport, known not only for his physical dominance but his kindness and generosity.

Ex-News of the World editor Rebekah Brooks described herself as feeling "vindicated" after her acquittal on all charges in the high-profile phone-hacking trial, which had gripped the nation for years. Brooks, once one of the UK’s most powerful media figures and a former government minister, was formally cleared of conspiracy to hack phones and conspiracy to misconduct in public office on Tuesday. The verdict marks the end of a legal battle that has haunted her career and personal life since the phone-hacking scandal brought down News International and led to sweeping reforms in the press. The former News International chief denied the Crown’s allegations that she had known about or sanctioned the hacking of voicemails at the now-defunct  News of the World . Throughout her trial in south London, Brooks maintained her innocence, with her defense portraying her as a victim of rumour and political animus. Speaking outside the Old Bailey, she said: "Today is a great day for justice. I have always said I was innocent, and now the court has agreed. I profoundly thank the jury for their service, which was delivered with the utmost care and professionalism." The trial, which began over three years ago, had drawn widespread public and political interest due to the scandal’s impact on both the media and political landscape. Among the parties affected was former Prime Minister David Cameron, who was accused of improperly staffing his Downing Street operation with individuals with questionable conduct, and who had faced calls to step down during the crisis. The phone-hacking scandal also led to the establishment of the Leveson Inquiry, which looked into the culture, practices, and ethics of the press. Brooks' acquittal has been met with mixed reactions. Conservative MP and former minister Sir Edward Garnier described her verdict as a "triumph of truth", while critics, including victims of the hacking, have expressed disappointment. Hacked-off campaigner Glenn Mulcaire, a former private investigator who was jailed for intercepting voicemails, said in a statement that while the law may have exonerated her, history would not. "Rebekah Brooks will go down as the person who was the very heart of the culture that destroyed trust in the press. Today’s verdict cannot erase that," he said. Legal experts have suggested that Brooks' acquittal does not necessarily signal the end of her woes. Although the jury accepted her denial of the charges, she has still been heavily criticized for her role in the broader scandal.

Plain Packaging Could Cut Hundreds of Thousands of Smokers in UK, Government Review Suggests    By [Your Name], Staff Writer  A landmark government review is today revealing that the introduction of standardised, plain cigarette packaging could lead to   300,000 fewer smokers   in the UK within a single year. The findings, compiled by the Department of Health and handed to ministers this week, offer compelling support for a policy that has been heavily debated by both public health advocates and the tobacco industry. The review marks a pivotal moment in the UK’s long-term strategy to drastically reduce smoking rates, which remain the largest preventable cause of death in the country. The report is based on data from the past five years, combining clinical research, behavioural insights, and international comparisons, especially from countries like Australia, which was the first to implement plain packaging in 2012. According to the findings, making cigarette packs devoid of brand logos, colours, and promotional imagery significantly reduced their appeal, particularly among young people. “It’s not about punishing smokers but about protecting the next generation from the drug that kills over 80,000 people in the UK every year,” said one senior official familiar with the report. Under the proposed system, cigarettes would only be sold in   featureless, olive-green boxes  , with all branding removed. Large health warnings and graphic images depicting the long-term effects of smoking would dominate the packaging. The idea is to curb the allure of smoking through visual dissociation, making it harder for tobacco companies to market their products in a way that lures new customers. The government has faced pressure from opposition parties and the medical profession to implement the law quickly. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt was reported as saying in private meetings that the review provides “unequivocal” support for plain packaging. However, the Department of Health has not yet set a formal date for introducing the policy. Opposition has come largely from the tobacco industry, which claims the move is anti-business and infringes on free enterprise. A spokesperson for British American Tobacco said in a statement: “We fundamentally reject the assumption that this policy will lead to a reduction in smoking. We are concerned about the overreach of government into consumer choice.” Political allies of the new legislation argue that the cost of the review—estimated at £1.7 million—is a small price to pay for the long-term health benefits it could produce.

Embracing ‘Bad’ Emotions May Boost Wellbeing, New Study Reveals   A new study suggests that people may be happier if they are able to experience the full range of emotions they desire— including negativity such as anger and hatred— challenging long-held assumptions that being happy all the time is the key to good mental health. In a paper published in the journal  Emotion , researchers from the University of British Columbia and the University of California, Riverside, argue that emotional authenticity—how well a person’s emotional experiences align with their emotional goals—plays a significant role in psychological wellbeing. “We often think of happiness as the ideal emotional state, but this research shows that people also want to feel fear, anger, and even hatred in certain situations,” said Myriam Ouweneel, a co-author of the study. “When people feel what they want to feel, they tend to feel more satisfied with their emotional lives—even if those emotions are not pleasant.” The study involved more than 1,700 participants across the United States and the Netherlands, who were asked to self-report the emotions they experienced over the course of a week and the emotions they desired under various life circumstances—such as in response to injustice or as part of joyful celebrations. For instance, while people generally want to feel joy during happy events, they may also desire anger in response to being wronged or sadness during a loss. Results showed that individuals who experienced emotions that aligned with their desired emotional goals reported greater life satisfaction and better psychological wellbeing, regardless of whether those emotions were labelled as 'positive' or 'negative'. This held true even when people desired and therefore felt strong negative emotions like hatred or anger. “This challenges a common narrative in both psychology and popular culture that all negative emotions are harmful or should be suppressed,” said Dr Steve Martines, another lead researcher. “In reality, people often seek out what might be termed unpleasant emotions because they see them as meaningful or validating.” One striking finding was the desire among participants for hatred—despite it often being socially unacceptable. Many reported feeling hatred in response to acts of political dishonesty, corruption, or intense personal betrayals. The study authors pointed out that such emotions, when acknowledged and experienced in line with personal values, can foster a sense of justice and purpose. The research also highlights the importance of emotional freedom.

Polish investigators have uncovered a shocking new detail in the case of the 2010 plane crash that killed former President Lech Kaczynski and more than 90 other prominent Polish figures. According to a recent police report, the coffin of the late president was found to contain what appear to be the remains of two additional individuals during a routine exhumation procedure prior to the transfer of his remains. The revelation has thrown fresh light on the long-standing circumstances of the crash, in which a Tupolev Tu-154 aircraft struck the Smolensk Cathedral in Russia while en route to a memorial ceremony for the 1940 Katyn massacre of Polish officers. The tragic event, which sparked considerable political and diplomatic tension between Poland and Russia at the time, has never been satisfactorily closed for many families of the victims. Leciej Dąbrowska, a spokesperson for the National Institute of Forensic Research, confirmed to the BBC that DNA testing was currently underway to determine the identities of the additional remains and their relationship, if any, to President Kaczynski. “We are treating this with the utmost gravity,” Dąbrowska said, adding that the findings might take several weeks to confirm. A number of grief-stricken relatives expressed shock and confusion at the news. "It’s unimaginable that after all these years, there is still something new to discover," said Elżbieta Grabowska, the sister-in-law of a staff member aboard the ill-fated flight. "What were they doing in the president’s coffin? Who made the decision to include them? All my family wants is the truth." The Polish government has not yet commented on the findings, though officials from the Office of the Prime Minister have requested time to fully review the forensic data. Some have speculated that the presence of the remains may point to chaotic or unplanned circumstances in the immediate aftermath of the crash, with emergency responders and local authorities potentially sending bodies back to Poland without proper identification. The re-examination of the bodies arose as part of ongoing efforts to compile a complete and accurate record of the crash for the families of the victims. A 2016 report from the Polish prosecution service concluded that the crash was the result of pilot error and failure to identify the low visibility path to Smolensk airport, with no evidence of a criminal conspiracy or foreign involvement. However, Russian officials continue to deny any wrongdoing.

Teachers should be valued "through their pay packet", according to Liberal Democrat schools minister David Laws. In a speech marking National Teacher Placement Day, Mr Laws argued that one of the most important ways to show respect for the teaching profession is by rewarding it with fair financial recognition. Speaking at the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) conference in Birmingham, he highlighted concerns that the current pay system fails to reflect the demands and responsibilities of the profession, a decline that has contributed to recruitment and retention crises across the education sector. Mr Laws, who was appointed to the role as part of the minority Liberal Democrat government under the coalition agreement, called for a rethinking of how teachers are compensated, including the potential for performance-based incentives and more transparent pay structures across schools. "If you want the best people to be teachers, you must pay them like you value them," he said. "Pay should not be used as a blunt instrument to push people out of the profession, but as a reward for the expertise and commitment they bring to our classrooms." The remarks come at a time of growing concern over the state of the teaching workforce. Recent government data shows over 100,000 teachers have left the profession in England since 2015, with many citing high workloads, low pay, and poor mental health support as the main reasons. Mr Laws also praised “the relentless dedication of teachers” who often go above and beyond, but warned that long-term reliance on goodwill and passion was not enough to sustain the profession. He announced the Liberal Democrats’ education policy, which includes a commitment to freezing non-essential government expenditure in order to increase investment in teacher salaries and professional development. "The Liberal Democrats are not going to accept the idea that being a teacher means living in financial uncertainty," he said. "It’s time we stopped asking teachers to work for the love of it and instead gave them the recognition they deserve.” The speech was met with applause and support from delegates, many of whom highlighted that pay is a key issue for the sector. However, officials at the Department for Education have refrained from commenting on the political debate over teacher pay, with one source noting that the current Conservative government remains focused on reducing administrative costs and improving school efficiency. Ms Laws’ statements have also prompted a wider conversation about the value of education and the role of government in delivering a sustainable teaching career.

Hundreds of New York City police officers turned their backs in defiance as Mayor Bill de Blasio passed by during the funeral of Officer Rafael Ramos on Thursday, the second of two officers killed in a jihadist-inspired ambush last month. The dramatic gesture, a stark show of anger and frustration toward the mayor, underscored the deepening rift between law enforcement and de Blasio, and highlighted growing tensions over the use of the phrase “Black Lives Matter” in public discourse. The funeral took place in Brooklyn, where hundreds of fellow officers, many clad in black, watched as Ramos’s coffin was brought to the chapel inside the Metropolitan Correctional Center. Immediately, the image went viral: as the mayor approached, uniformed officers collectively turned away, some with eyes lowered, others standing silently with their backs to de Blasio. It was a powerful, non-violent act of dissent from a community that has become increasingly estranged from the mayor following the deaths of Officers Rafael Ramos and Wenjian Liu on December 20. The officers’ killings — the deadliest for NYPD since 9/11 — have galvanised law enforcement, who accuse de Blasio of showing insufficient support for them since the fatal shooting of Eric Garner, a black man, in 2014, and the subsequent mass protests. Many officers believe the mayor has been overly aligned with protest movements, including the “Black Lives Matter” movement which they see as undermining their work and mistaking them for adversaries. In the wake of the murders, de Blasio faced widespread criticism from within the police community following his remarks toward the end of the previous year, in which he said cops in one area of the city were “not a good bunch.” He later walked back the comment, saying it was “unacceptable,” but it did little to repair the damage to trust, particularly when he also did not attend the funeral of the first slain officer, Wenjian Liu. The mayor denied any link between the officers turning their backs and political tensions, telling reporters, “That’s nonsense to suggest that, but for the record, no guest speaker will be asked to remain on the stage for a photo opportunity if a funeral was not happening.” However, the Associated Fraternal Order of Police (AFOP), a group that represents uniformed officers, has called for de Blasio’s resignation and accused him of “disrespect” toward the men and women of the NYPD. Ramos, 40, was a 14-year veteran of the force and a devoted family man.

The world's biggest conference on species protection has begun in Mafikeng, South Africa, promising to set the tone for global efforts to protect and preserve some of the planet’s most iconic and endangered creatures. But as heads of conservation agencies and wildlife experts from over 180 countries gathered at the 19th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), the atmosphere is anything but harmonious—particularly when it comes to the fate of elephants. With the African elephant population having dwindled to an estimated 350,000 from over 3 million prior to the 1960s, the species remains a stark symbol of both the success and the fragility of conservation work. CITES, the international body responsible for regulating international trade in wild animal and plant species, has long been a battleground between nations with diverging interests—those advocating for a total ivory trade ban and those seeking to reintroduce controlled trade for economic benefit and conservation incentives. This year's conference, which runs through 20 October, has opened with warnings that without strong and enforceable actions, elephants may slip beyond recovery. Conservation groups have expressed alarm at rising poaching levels and the apparent reluctance of some African nations to commit to banning the domestic ivory trade—which, they argue, is a major driver of poaching and illegal trafficking. In opening remarks, the host nation’s Environment Minister, Barbara Creecy, stressed the importance of a unified response: “The elephant is not just a concern for Africa. It is an emblem of global biodiversity. If we are unable to protect it, we are failing our responsibilities as stewards of the natural world.” Tensions are high as proposals are expected to be tabled on whether to lift the 1989 international ivory trade ban, currently in place to help elephant populations recover. While southern African nations such as Botswana and Namibia—the world’s two largest elephant populations—have long advocated for regulated ivory sales, others like Kenya, which burns its ivory stockpiles as a statement of principle, are firm in their opposition. The outcome of these discussions could shape the future of elephant conservation for decades to come. As the clock ticks and the world watches, the question remains: will the 5,000 delegates around this Mafikeng dinner table rise to the challenge, or will the elephant's plight drift into irreversible decline?

MSP Claire Baker is calling on the Scottish government to provide free feminine hygiene products in schools and colleges, highlighting the issue as a question of basic dignity rather than a political or financial debate. In a motion delivered at Holyrood last week, Baker, a Scottish National Party (SNP) member from Aberdeenshire, described the financial burden of period products as a “relic of the past” and an “affront to basic human dignity” that affects girls and women from low-income backgrounds. The motion, supported by cross-party backing, argues that the cost of sanitary products – which can account for up to 6% of a weekly food budget for the most vulnerable households – places unnecessary stress on young women, often forcing them to make impossible choices between essentials like food and hygiene. Baker referenced numerous stories from women left having to scavenge for napkins, use inappropriate substitutes, or skip school altogether because of an inability to afford basic products. In an exclusive interview with The Scotsman, Baker said: “This isn’t about handouts – it’s about human rights. No girl should have to miss out on education, work, or social inclusion simply because she cannot afford the basics of her own body. It impacts attendance in schools, it undermines their self-esteem and sense of worth.” The motion has been backed by third-sector organisations including the Royal College of Nursing and the national charity for women’s health, the Eve Appeal. Statistics from the Food and Poverty Report 2014 showed that 800,000 people in Scotland are living in households where the cost of essentials is in constant jeopardy, with sanitary products often missing from the list of essentials because of their out-of-sight nature. The Scottish government has so far categorised the motion as “pro-inflammatory debate,” and remains in discussion with ministers about the feasibility of funding such a scheme. Although currently projected to spend £840 million on welfare-related initiatives in the new financial year, ministers have not yet committed to the funding required for free period products. However, Baker has passed on a growing tide of public support to the initiative, with dozens of supporters taking to social media to share their personal experiences. One young woman, who wished to remain anonymous, said: “I once used a handkerchief and paper towel to hold me together through a class. That’s not something a girl should have to do.”

Ukraine’s acting President Olexander Turchynov and the newly appointed Prime Minister-designate Arseniy Yatsenyuk have issued stark warnings that significant and potentially unpopular measures will be required to stabilise the country’s crisis-hit economy and restructure its fragile political system. Speaking in Kyiv on Tuesday, the two leaders urged public patience and support as they outlined the difficult road ahead in restoring stability to the nation following months of political turmoil and economic uncertainty. The comments come just days after the dissolution of Ukraine’s parliament and the collapse of the Antanaslav coalition government, which was formed in the wake of the ousting of former President Viktor Yanukovych in February. Turchynov, who has been the interim leader since January, stressed that reforms would be necessary on all levels, including austerity measures and significant changes to the structure of the state administration. “We are entering a very difficult but necessary phase of rebuilding the country,” Turchynov said. “These steps will not be easy for the Ukrainian people or for our politicians. They will be painful and unpopular, but they are absolutely essential if we are to restore trust in our institutions and attract the foreign investors and aid we need.” Yatsenyuk, a former deputy prime minister with a reputation for pragmatism and reformist policies, backed his interim leader’s comments, describing the situation as “the most complicated moment since the fall of the Soviet Union.” He pledged to push forward with urgent economic and political reforms upon taking office as prime minister, but warned that this could include painful budget cuts, pay freezes for politicians, and structural improvements in transparency and accountability. Yatsenyuk is expected to be approved by the new parliament, following this week’s general election, and will be under immense pressure to deliver reform in a nation facing a deepening economic crisis. Ukraine has been hit hard by the Russian annexation of Crimea and ongoing conflict in the eastern Donbas region, both of which have contributed to a sharp decline in economic output, devaluation of the hryvnia, and high inflation. Western leaders have voiced support for the reform agenda, with the European Union pledging further financial assistance if Ukraine meets key performance benchmarks. However, there are concerns over public reaction to the proposed austerity measures, with large pockets of the population already suffering from energy shortages and reduced purchasing power. Local opposition groups have reacted angrily to the warnings, accusing the interim authorities of maintaining a status quo that has kept Ukraine mired in crisis for decades.

Welsh actress Angharad Rees, who has died of cancer at the age of 63, was one of the best-known faces of the 1970s thanks to her memorable role in the hit BBC drama  Poldark . Her performance as the fiery and charismatic Demelza Carne opposite Ross Poldark, played by Aiden Quinn, made her a household name and earned her widespread acclaim. Now, fans of the show and the wider acting community have paid tribute to Rees, who passed away earlier this week surrounded by her family. Born in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, in 1959, Rees grew up in a family that nurtured her love for the arts. Her talent for acting brought her to prominence during a golden age of British television drama.  Poldark , based on the novels by Winston Graham, was a particular standout for her career. It aired in 1975 and incorporated historical details with emotional intensity, while Rees’ portrayal of Demelza’s resilience and quiet strength resonated with audiences across the UK and beyond. In an interview earlier in her career, Rees reflected on being part of such a transformative production. “Demelza was a woman of few words but immense strength. I felt in many ways we were not so different,” she once told a Welsh national publication. Her understated performance helped bring depth and authenticity to the character, standing in contrast to her co-stars’ more outwardly dramatic portrayals. Beyond  Poldark , Rees continued to build a varied career in both television and theatre. She auditioned extensively in London and appeared in a number of esteemed stage productions, displaying a versatility that extended far beyond her most famous role. While  Poldark  may have made her a national celebrity, her colleagues and fans recall her for her intelligence, generosity and warmth. Angharad leaves behind her husband, Brian, and their two children, who have asked for privacy at this difficult time. A statement from her family read: “Angharad was a gifted actress, a loving wife, mother and friend. Her passion for her work and those around her will live on in the hearts of all who knew her.” Fans and fellow actors have flooded social media with messages of condolence, with many praising  Poldark  and celebrating Rees’ legacy as a pioneer of on-screen womanhood rooted in strength and grace. As tributes continue to pour in, it's clear that while Angharad Rees may be gone, her contributions to British television will not soon be forgotten.

A tragic migrant shipwreck off the coast of Libya last week — in which more than 300 people are believed to have died — was sparked by a surge of excitement aboard the vessel as survivors caught their first glimpse of rescue boats, according to testimonies from those who lived to tell the tale. The incident has drawn widespread condemnation and raised urgent questions about the risks of migratory journeys and the policies that allow them to continue. The distressed vessel was reported missing by aid organisations before being located off the coast of Misrata, where it was found to have capsized in the early hours of the morning. Rescue teams from the Italian coast guard and a number of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) were involved in the chaotic operation to save survivors from the wrecked boat, which was said to have been severely overloaded. Eyewitness accounts, collected from five survivors who reached hospitals in Tripoli and Misrata, describe an emotionally explosive moment when the migrants first saw a fleet of rescue boats approaching. “People were jumping for joy,” said one survivor, who is being treated for hypothermia and dehydration. “They clapped, they cried, they waved with both hands. We were thinking we were saved. But in that moment, as people moved to the front of the boat, we lost balance and it tilted violently. The rhythm of the sea got us.” Other survivors spoke of panicked chaos as the water poured in, swamping the vessel. “It was like an earthquake on that boat,” said Sila, a 28-year-old Eritrean woman. “Everyone was in one direction, trying to see the boats. It just tipped over.” The incident adds to the grim toll of the Mediterranean crossing, which is among the most perilous routes in the world for migrants and refugees. According to the United Nations, nearly 2,000 people have drowned in what is described as Europe’s deadliest border. Many of the migrants aboard the upturned boat came from Eritrea, Ethiopia and Nigeria, fleeing war, persecution and extreme poverty. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) confirmed it had documented 345 people missing following the accident, while 178 survivors have been accounted for so far. Dozens of bodies are still thought to be trapped in the wreckage, which has been identified as a trawler that had been repurposed for smuggling routes. Italian Foreign Minister Angelino Alfano has called the incident “a deep tragedy that demonstrates the human cost of the current crisis.”

In a quiet corner of Newry, a red deer stood frozen in the headlights of an approaching car, her antlers silhouetted against the moonlit sky. For the locals, it was an unexpected, almost surreal moment — a stark reminder that nature and urban life are increasingly intersecting in ways few anticipated. While deer are a familiar and even comforting sight in the hills and woodlands of rural Northern Ireland, their appearance in town centres is a phenomenon that is gaining attention. This event in Newry follows a growing trend: deer sightings in built-up areas across the country. In the past few years, farmers outside Belfast, residents of Derry, and hikers near Lisburn have reported encounters with red deer, roe deer, and occasionally even fallow deer wandering well beyond their traditional habitats. Experts suggest several factors are behind the shift — climate change, environmental conservation efforts, and, perhaps most significantly, the rapid expansion of green corridors in and around urban spaces. Dr. Eleanor Gale, a wildlife biologist at Queen’s University Belfast, explained: “Many people might think of deer as being purely rural, but they are highly adaptable. As green spaces in cities become more connected, deer are able to move more freely. They are opportunistic animals, and if their food and shelter needs can be met in a new area, they will move in.” This was certainly the case in Newry, where recent afforestation projects along the River Nanny and the expansion of public parks and nature walks have created new habitats within the city’s boundary lines. The deer seen in the town, she said, was likely part of a small dispersing group from a nearby woodland — not an outlier, but an example of a broader pattern. However, while these encounters can be surprising and occasionally charming — such as when children spot a deer about to cross a quiet footpath — they can also be problematic. City deer often venture into gardens, scaring residents or damaging plants. In more worrying cases, untrained individuals have attempted to capture them, leading to distress for the animals. There have even been instances of collisions between deer and cars — a particular concern on the city’s main arterial roads. Local councilor Mary Glass pointed out the need for a balanced approach. "We must appreciate the wonder of seeing wildlife in our towns, but we also need to consider the safety of both people and animals. This is a new challenge for urban planning and wildlife management."

Environmental activist and former environment minister Marina Silva has unexpectedly found herself at the heart of Brazil’s presidential election campaign, thrust into the national spotlight following the tragic death of Eduardo Campos, the rising candidate for the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB). The 49-year-old politician and former naval aviator died in a plane crash on August 13 during a campaign stop in the northeastern state of Pernambuco, his wife and daughter also among the victims. Within days, Mrs Silva, the vice-presidential candidate on Mr Campos’ ticket, was put forward as the new nominee by the PSB. The move has surprised political analysts and voters alike, not only because of her relatively low profile in recent years but also due to the polarised political climate in Brazil, which has been rocked by a sprawling corruption scandal and an economic downturn. Mrs Silva, 58, who served as Brazil’s environment minister under Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva between 2003 and 2008, has built a reputation for her hardline stance on environmental and social issues. She is widely credited with helping to reduce deforestation in the Amazon during her time in government, often challenging powerful agricultural and mining interests. Her campaign in the 2014 elections famously collapsed after allegations that her husband had illicitly transferred municipal contracts to private firms in the 1990s – a claim she denies. Now, with the death of Mr Campos, she is once again on the national stage, representing the Socialists in what looks to be a tight and unpredictable race. Current opinion polls suggest that the PSB may now split the progressive vote, with Mrs Silva oddly positioned as an anti-establishment alternative to both Dilma Rousseff of the governing Workers’ Party (PT) and Aécio Neves, the leading candidate from the largest opposition party, the Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB). However, not all are optimistic about her chances. Political commentator Mario Andreazza noted that the PSB’s move could backfire if voters perceive the change as a calculated political ploy. “Marina is a strong figure, but the party is trying to change the game at a time when the country is looking for stability and clarity,” he said. In the coming weeks, the focus will shift to how well the 54-year-old lawyer can run an independent campaign and whether she can rally the supporters of the late Eduardo Campos without falling into the fray of Brazil’s divisive political discourse.

Michael McIntyre can breathe a sigh of relief—his official title as Britain’s grumpiest man on Twitter—the droll, pith-helmet-wearing stalwart of conservative angst—remains entirely unthreatened by his political counterparts. Or at least that appears to be the view of those close to the infamous comedian, who has become a kind of accidental symbol of dry British wit—and Brexit confusion—online. In an era when social media has turned everything from policy announcements to policy blunders into fodder for memes, few have embraced the role quite like McIntyre. His irreverent, occasionally.Fatalf, take on political missteps and public policy blunders has earned him legions of fans—and made him a go-to figure for MPs, journalists, and even politicians needing a reaction to a particularly controversial statement or an eccentric government announcement. The recent turbulence surrounding the chancellor’s attempt to reassure beleaguered voters has turned out to be an unwitting scene in the latest McIntyre-themed breakfast, but those in the know insist he has no intention of ever donning the black suit and desktop hides of Number 11. “I feel certain,” as one well-placed source put it, “that he can rest easy—content that his droll role as the unchallenged voice of bemusement remains entirely in good hands.” British politics may be in a state of “constant national emergency,” but it is often the experts in bewilderment who seem to be thriving. McIntyre, of course, never intended to enter the political observer ranks, but his blend of exasperation and bemused sarcasm has found a perfect home in an increasingly surreal political landscape. Even the chancellor, whose ambition and ability to out-speak his former self has been well documented, has found himself inadvertently in competition with a man who, technically, is employed to play piano. But such is the bizarre rhythm of modern British politics that the line between public servant and public school-style jester is growing increasingly blurred. And if the joke, as many suspect, is always on the politicians—well, perhaps that is the real legacy the country is holding on to as it struggles to find its way through the thick fog of policy and parliament. One thing is certain: as of now, Michael McIntyre’s role is not one currently being applied for—from the opposition benches, nor from the corridors of Whitehall. He remains the grumpy guardian of British snark, and none more so than at the breakfast table.

French officials have revised their account of a deadly police raid last week, revealing that a woman previously believed to have blown herself up in a hail of bullets was not responsible for the explosion. Hichem Koubriti, cousin of suspected Paris attacks ringleader Chérif Kouachi, died in the raid on a hideout in Saint-Denis on 18 November. Initially, French authorities described the 32-year-old as a suicide bomber who detonated a vest just before police stormed the building, killing herself and a police officer. But in a dramatic correction, Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve announced on Thursday that the explosion was not caused by a suicide vest, but by shots fired during the firefight between officers and the terror suspects inside. "The explosion that took place during the Saint-Denis operation was not generated by a belt of explosives," Cazeneuve told reporters, adding: "A woman was indeed present in the scene, but died from the combination of gunfire and the detonation of a likely explosive device caused in part by police gunfire." The reversal has raised questions about the initial narrative and the intelligence that led to Koubriti’s inclusion as a suicide bomber. President François Hollande, whose administration has faced mounting pressure over both the attacks and the transparency of its response, defended the action of the police during the raid. "The services got what is most important – eliminating the threat," he said, referring to the deaths of Kouachi’s brother, Saïd, and other suspects. Earlier this week, the French press published conflicting reports about Koubriti’s role in the terror cell. Le Monde described her as a key plotter, while L'Express had questioned the claim that she had been a suicide bomber. Margot Walls, a colleague of Hichem in a Berlin-based Islamic charity group linked to the Kouachi brothers, had claimed to journalists that "Hichem had no bomb vest" and barely left the house. The new information has also prompted fresh scrutiny of the European response to terrorism, with officials warning that intelligence gaps remain. German Interior Minister Thomas de Maizière confirmed that Koubriti was known to German intelligence, but did not share details about her apparent radical shift to militant violence before the Paris attacks. Analysts say the revised account highlights the risks of rapid, speculative reporting in moments of high tension and underscores the need for careful verification in the coverage of counter-terrorism operations.

The UK government has published a list of 15 Scottish companies found to be in breach of the national minimum and living wage, accusing them of "exploiting workers by underpaying them." The move comes as part of a wider government campaign to ensure low-paid employees are not the victims of wage theft — a problem the government claims has become “too common.” According to data released by the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS), businesses across Ayrshire, North Lanarkshire and Edinburgh top the list. The list names companies ranging from small family-run businesses to firms operating in the hospitality and logistics sectors, but the government has not disclosed the number of workers affected or how much tax is still owed to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). Publicly naming the firms, BEIS has sent a clear message that the government will not tolerate wage underpayment, regardless of geography or sector: “We are determined to take action against businesses breaking the law and prioritise fairness, ensuring every worker is paid the wage they are legally entitled to.” Statements from the department also highlighted that, in the past year alone, £238 million has been recovered for over 8,600 workers across the country. For many, the move is to be welcomed. Unite, the largest trade union in Scotland, praised the government for taking a stronger stance. “It is totally unacceptable that in 2024, some employers still see wages as something they can cut rather than a basic right,” said their spokesperson. “By ‘naming and shaming’, they are also sending a powerful warning to any other rogue firms: this is a red line.” Yet, the backlash from some quarters has been swift. Industry representatives have argued that while underpaying staff is wrong, the government is not doing enough to support smaller businesses struggling with inflation and the rising cost of living. “This isn’t just about bad actors,” said Steve Birtles, chair of the Federation of Small Businesses in Scotland. “Some business owners are being pushed to their limits and are making tough calls just to keep their doors open. What is desperately needed is support, not just condemnation.” The 15 named companies are now subject to prosecution if they fail to rectify the wage violations. Affected workers are urged to come forward with evidence, as delays in reporting are said to be a major barrier to recovery. Meanwhile, the government has confirmed it is ramping up its auditing efforts, with more inspections in the pipeline, especially in sectors with a history of non-compliance.

The brutal death of Italian graduate student Giulio Regeni in Cairo has reignited international concerns over Egypt's human rights record, casting a spotlight on the country exactly five years after the uprising that led to the ousting of longtime leader President Hosni Mubarak. Mr Regeni, 28, a Cambridge University researcher, was found on 3 February with severe signs of torture along the River Nile. The circumstances of his death have sparked a diplomatic uproar and raised questions over the government's human rights practices, particularly its treatment of political dissent. Italy has formally demanded an independent international investigation into Mr Regeni’s death, arguing that the Egyptian authorities have failed to provide adequate answers. The Italian Foreign Minister, Paolo Gentiloni, described the case as "a tragedy that must be resolved with full transparency and justice." The Egyptian government has denied any involvement in the student’s death, with officials maintaining that Mr Regeni’s body was "desecrated" and that the circumstances do not prove murder or systematic human rights abuses. The student, originally from Modena, was in Egypt as part of his doctoral research into trade unionism. Reports from Egyptian and international human rights groups suggest he may have been seized by security forces after being seen with anti-government leaflets and expressing human rights concerns on social media. His body, found 30 miles south of Cairo, showed signs of severe beatings, strangulation, and possible electrocution. Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have long highlighted the erosion of civil liberties in Egypt since the 2013 military coup that brought President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to power. Mr Sisi, a former army chief, has presided over a sweeping crackdown on dissent, with thousands of opponents arrested under anti-protest and counter-terrorism laws. His government has often dismissed such criticisms as interference in domestic affairs. The Regeni case has deepened the unease among foreign governments and European institutions, many of which have close economic and strategic ties with Egypt. The European Parliament passed a resolution calling for an international investigation and expressed concern over the state of political freedoms in the country. The incident has also been a wake-up call for activists and opposition groups inside Egypt. Though the landscape for dissent has become increasingly dangerous, some local rights advocates are calling for renewed calls for justice, demanding that Mr Regeni’s death not be forgotten or ignored.
