Vallance noted that while global efforts to reduce emissions remain crucial for the long-term future of the planet, the next two decades will be shaped by the legacy of already emitted carbon. “Our ability to mitigate the worst effects of climate change beyond this period will depend on rapid global action, but for the coming years, what matters most is how well we adapt and build resilience here at home,” Vallance added. The government has been under increasing pressure to strengthen its climate adaptation strategies, particularly from environmental groups and local councils. Some critics argue that while the UK has been ambitious in setting net-zero targets, it has lagged in investing in flood protection, water management, and resilience planning for high-risk areas. Vallance’s remarks are likely to fuel further debate over the pace and scale of national adaptation efforts. The Environment Agency has already warned that 1.4 million homes in England are at high risk of flooding, and demand for drought-resistant infrastructure is expected to grow as water scarcity becomes a recurring problem.

Neil Hamilton, UKIP assembly group leader, has sparked controversy by claiming that Britain does not have a problem with Islamophobia and that there are no reliable statistics on hate crime. Speaking at a meeting in Cardiff, Mr Hamilton suggested that reports of rising hatred towards Muslims were exaggerated and that the data used to support these claims was "largely speculative". His remarks have been met with sharp criticism from politicians, community leaders, and anti-racism organisations who argue that Islamophobia remains a significant and growing issue across the UK. Hamilton, a long-standing critic of asylum policy and multiculturalism, said the lack of accurate statistical evidence called into question the true scale of anti-Muslim sentiment in Britain. “People talk about an Islamophobia epidemic as though it’s a scientifically proven fact,” he said. “But when you look at the statistics, they’re either not available or they contradict the narrative.” He added that the absence of reliable hate crime data made it difficult to formulate appropriate policy responses. However, opponents of Hamilton's position pointed to a series of high-profile incidents involving Muslims over the past five years, including attacks on mosques, schools, and community leaders. Reports from the Runnymede Trust and the Anti-Islamophobia Alliance have highlighted the impacts of Islamophobia on Muslim communities, with many individuals reporting discrimination, hate speech, and in some cases, physical violence. The government's own hate crime reporting websites show a steady rise in anti-Muslim incidents, although some argue the figures remain underreported due to public mistrust of authorities. Shadow Welsh Secretary Jenny Rathbone condemned Hamilton’s comments as “blatantly out of touch with the reality faced by Muslim communities in Wales and beyond”. She said his claim that there was no meaningful data was “astonishing in the face of increasing hate crime statistics and countless anecdotal reports from Muslim constituents”. Rathbone called on UKIP to reflect on “how such views undermine the promotion of unity and tolerance in society”. Similarly, Sarah Needham, director of the Wales Muslim Support Centre, said that Islamophobia was “very real and insidious”. “To deny its existence is not just false, it’s harmful,” she said. “This kind of rhetoric only emboldens those who target our communities. We need politicians to acknowledge the issue and work constructively towards solutions.” The Home Office has acknowledged the challenge of accurately measuring hate crime, noting that underreporting is a major issue.

Newcastle United found themselves at the summit of the Championship on Sunday evening as they claimed a hard-fought 2-0 victory over Barnsley at Oakwell. Dwight Gayle emerged as the hero with a brace, underlining his growing importance in boss Eddie Howe’s side, and propelling the Magpies to a fourth consecutive league win and top spot in the division. The win was a testament to the confidence that has surged through Newcastle since a difficult January, with Howe’s policy of player recruitment and a revitalised approach to attacking football clearly bearing fruit. The journey from bottom-half strugglers to league leaders has surprised even the most ardent Tyneside supporters, but this latest success only reinforces the belief that a return to the Premier League may not be as far-fetched as it once seemed. Gayle, who left the club in the summer of 2016 following a high-profile transfer to Crystal Palace, made an emphatic return to the St James’ Park fold, and his performance at Oakwell was no less impressive. The versatile forward’s first goal came in the 28th minute after a sweeping counter-attack, with Jamaal Lascelles doing the heavy work in midfield before playing the ball wide to Gayle, who swept it into the net off the underside of the bar. The second, just before half time, was a composed finish after a clever through-ball from Ki Sung-Yu, and it made the headlines: Gayle had scored 39 goals in all competitions for Newcastle since his return to the club in August. The victory also served as a statement of intent in a race for promotion that is already heating up. West Bromwich, Brighton, and Wolves are all close behind in the table and will look to close the gap in the weeks ahead, but for now, Newcastle are sitting pretty at the top. With 58 points from 29 games, the Magpies are starting to look like serious contenders. Ironically, the transformation has come at a time when confidence in the ownership of Mike Ashley has passed its lowest ebb. Recent weeks have seen further reports of salary-cap restrictions and the continued reluctance of the owner to invest in the transfer market. Yet, as supporters of the club know only too well, the ashes of a difficult January may well have become the building blocks of promotion. Howe, now in his first full season in charge, has succeeded in maintaining the spirit of the team while introducing a more modern and effective line-up.

For the first time in Northern Ireland’s history, a majority of Assembly members have voted in support of same-sex marriage, marking a significant shift in the region’s often divided political and cultural landscape. The vote came after years of campaigning by LGBTQ+ groups, civil rights organisations and individual politicians from across the political spectrum. The motion passed by 56 to 51 votes on Tuesday, making Northern Ireland the only part of the United Kingdom not to legalise same-sex marriage under self-governance. The devolved administration had historically blocked progress due to opposition from unionist and some nationalist parties, reflecting broader societal tensions shaped by decades of the Troubles. Among those backing the motion were Ulster Unionist MEP Jim Allister and the Democratic Unionist Party’s (DUP) Myra Thompson, both of whom have faced criticism from within their own parties for the move. Thompson, who voted in support of same-sex marriage for the first time in 2019, said she stood by her position and said the vote "recognises the humanity and dignity of all our citizens." Sinn Féin’s Máirtín Ó Muilleoir, one of the key advocates for the reform, highlighted that the vote showed "progress in a land where division has too often dominated the headlines." He added that the decision was not just about marriage equality but about moving towards a “fairer and more compassionate society.” Supporters of the reform celebrated the result as long-overdue. Gary Dobson of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions said the vote was a “landmark” step towards equality in Northern Ireland. Spouses who have already tied the knot in the Republic of Ireland or England, where same-sex marriage has been legal for years, have faced being split from their partners simply because their marriages are not legally recognised in their home communities. Opposition parties had urged the Executive to pass legislation legalising same-sex marriage as part of the Stormont House Agreement in 2014, but the DUP blocked the proposal, arguing for local legislation rather than relying on Westminster. Since then, calls have grown for a pragmatic solution to end the status quo. The vote is non-binding, meaning the passing of a bill would still require support from the Executive. With a regional government currently in place, following the return of devolution in January 2020 after a prolonged hiatus, opposition parties have started pushing the DUP go further on the issue.

The UK government is set to revise official alcohol consumption guidelines for the first time in two decades, promising clearer and more scientifically informed advice on how much the public should drink. The review has sparked widespread anticipation, with health campaigners, scientists, and alcohol manufacturers all watching closely to see whether the long-standing guideline of six to seven drinks a week for women and up to 14 for men will be significantly adjusted—or if it will remain as the benchmark for a "low risk" level of drinking. The current advice, issued in 2016, came under scrutiny as new research into the long-term and short-term effects of alcohol emerged. Experts now argue that the previous guidance downplayed the risks of even small amounts of alcohol and may not fully reflect the dangers of regular drinking on the liver, heart, and mental health. The Department of Health and Social Care confirmed the move as part of a push to address what it described as a “public health priority,” highlighting the growing concern over alcohol-related hospitalisations and deaths across the country. In recent years, studies have suggested that non-drinkers, on average, have a longer lifespan than those who consume alcohol, even in moderation. This, combined with increased understanding of cancer risks linked to alcohol, has put pressure on the government to reconsider the wording and implications of its guidance. The review also comes amid a broader public debate on alcohol culture in the UK. With drinking often deeply embedded in social, work, and family life, the revised guidance is expected to not only outline safer limits but also encourage more widespread awareness of the additives, principles and alternatives to drinking. Sources in Whitehall suggest the guidance may also shift the narrative from one that focuses on “a few units each week” to a more nuanced and personal approach based on individual health factors. The new advice is expected to be finalised by the end of the year, with the government aiming to publish it during a major public health awareness campaign. While the exact details remain under tight government control, one thing is certain: this review has the potential to reshape not only how much Britons drink, but how they think about it. MHCLG scientists and public health experts are currently consulting with stakeholders, including Public Health England, as well as bodies representing both health and the drinks industry.

Federer Makes Shock Exit as Berdych Steps Up in US Open Drama   The U.S. Open witnessed a stunning first upset of the tournament as Roger Federer was eliminated in the quarter-finals by sixth seed Tomas Berdych in a gripping three-set clash that left the tennis world reeling. The 17-time Grand Slam champion, who entered Flushing Meadows as one of the pre-tournament favourites, was dethroned by the Czech left-hander in a match that will be remembered for both its tension and the sheer tenacity of Berdych’s performance. Federer, who arrived in New York with a history of success at the U.S. Open, including five championship titles, was expected to easily navigate the draw. However, Berdych’s gritty display, marked by his towering left-handed serves and rally-stretching play, proved too much for the Swiss icon in a match that lasted 3 hours and 28 minutes. The final score—6-3, 4-6, 6-3—told the tale of a tournament turning point for both men. The defeat marked the end of Federer’s dream to become the first man in the Open Era to win two Grand Slam titles in the same year at the age of 34. Facing a watching brief during Wimbledon due to a knee injury, Federer seemed unstoppable as he won the Cincinnati Masters and reached the semis of the Rogers Cup. Yet his New York campaign unravelled as he failed to find his rhythm against a determined Berdych, who looked the more dangerous player throughout the afternoon. Berdych’s victory sets up a highly anticipated semi-final against Britain’s Andy Murray, who continued his red-hot form with a commanding win over Stan Wawrinka. This clash promises to be one of the key moments in the tournament, with the Wimbledon champion seeking to cement his place in New York history. For Federer, the loss will no doubt be a staggering blow to the legend, but for Berdych, it was a dream come true. The 29-year-old, who has long been tipped as a Grand Slam contender, will now carry the hopes of a nation as he steps onto the Arthur Ashe Stadium stage once more. In a post-match interview, Federer acknowledged the high standard Berdych set and praised the level of competition. “Tomas was better today. He didn’t give me anything. He served so well, made very few errors, and that’s what you need to beat the best players,” he said.

A Controversial Welcome: The Gaza Flotilla’s Daring Mission   In a move that has ignited fierce public debate and drawn strong reactions from both within Ghana and the international press, the West African nation recently announced its decision to offer refuge to two Yemeni nationals who have returned home after years in the infamous US detention facility in Guantanamo Bay. The controversial offer has been met with an uproar on the streets of Accra, with citizens divided between those who see it as an act of solidarity and those who suspect hidden motives and unintended consequences. Elizabeth Ohene, a prominent Ghanaian journalist, notes that the situation has become a test of Ghana’s international moral standing, as well as its growing confidence on the global stage. “This is not just about two men,” Ohene writes, “it is about who we are and who we want to be on the world map.” The news of the two Yemeni prisoners’ release had barely made it onto the international wires when it was revealed that Ghana had offered to resettle them after their repatriation. This came as part of a broader, still-evolving plan to provide housing, support, and legal help to over 80 individuals being held in Guantanamo—some cleared for release, others not. The US government had previously sent out non-binding requests to its allies to assist with resettlement, a task few have been willing to take on. In Ghana, the proposal has struck a nerve. For some, it is a bold move by a country increasingly unafraid to question global powers and challenge norms. For others, it has led to accusations of naïveté and suspicious timing: why now? Why not screen the individuals more thoroughly? And what are the potential security or political ramifications of being seen as a safe haven for those who spent years in a US prison considered emblematic of post-9/11 injustice? Demonstrations have erupted in Accra and Kumasi alike. On one side, protesters have chanted, “Free to be free, not for the US,” arguing that no one should be penalized for the excesses of the White House. On the other side, counter-demonstrators have demanded greater transparency, questioning the security clearances and the wisdom of opening Ghana’s doors without more information. Ohene highlights the complexity of the issue: “The Americans set this precedent of indefinite detention and disappearance. The notion of sending go-betweens to help us host those cleared for release is as much about easing their burden as it is about maintaining control over the narrative.”

Dr. Strangelove: The Timeless Satire That Still Chills and Chuckles   Fifty-eight years after its controversial debut,  Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb  remains a masterclass in dark comedy and biting satire — a cinematic warning bell for the madness of nuclear brinkmanship, as relevant today as it was in the height of the Cold War. Originally released in 1964, Stanley Kubrick’s film has now firmly cemented itself as one of the greatest film comedies ever made, praised for its audacious wit, surreal absurdity, and devastating commentary on the political failures of its era. At the heart of  Dr. Strangelove  is a scenario that feels more turkey than fiction: after a rogue U.S. air force general orders a nuclear attack on the Soviet Union, the rest of the world scrambles — to no avail — to avert global annihilation. The film plays out in a world of military incompetence, bureaucratic cluelessness and, most chillingly, uncritical adherence to the idea that technology and power alone will solve humanity’s problems. Kubrick, a careful and methodical director, carefully curated a cast of British actors to mock the bureaucratic and technocratic airs of American military life at the time. Peter Sellers delivers a career-defining performance in three roles – the twitching Royal Air Force Group Captain, the unhinged United States Air Force General Jack D. Ripper, and the eponymous Dr. Strangelove, a former Nazi scientist turned nuclear apologist. George C. Scott, playing General Buck Turgidson, is a towering figure of delusional patriotism, while Slim Pickens embodies pure, unthinking menace as the pilot in charge of the most powerful bombs on the planet. The film’s script, co-written by Kubrick and novelist Peter George (whose novel  Red Alert  was the film's source), is a tightly-woven web of tension, absurdity and irony. Lines that were considered shocking at the time — such as the line “Let’s all have a nice day!” delivered by Sellers as Strangelove at the climax — are now iconic, and the film’s constant jabbing at weapons of mass destruction and the “honor-bound” logic of military men has lost none of its bite. In an age where nuclear threats still go hand-in-hand with international diplomacy and tensions between global powers simmer,  Dr. Strangelove  continues to be a box office draw on streaming platforms and a staple at film festivals. Its legacy lives on not just in the comedy world, but in the halls of political science and international relations, where it is often used as a case study in the dangers of military escalation and bureaucratic myopia.

The British National Party (BNP) has announced the expulsion of its former leader, Nick Griffin, from its ranks, marking a significant shift in the party’s often-controversial history. Griffin, who led the far-right party from 1999 to 2014, has long been a divisive figure in British politics, and his removal has sparked speculation about the party’s future direction and internal dynamics. The BNP stated that a recent disciplinary meeting had voted to strip Griffin of all his affiliations with the party due to what it described as "serious breaches of conduct and conflict with the party’s current values." The exact nature of the breaches was not detailed in the official statement, but sources close to the party indicated that Griffin's recent public comments and activities had been deemed incompatible with the BNP's new strategy of rebranding as a "more moderate" political force. Griffin, who has repeatedly faced bans from broadcasting in the UK due to concerns over offensive language, has remained active in political commentary and has occasionally taken to social media to express views on immigration and national identity, often in ways that have drawn harsh criticism. His expulsion suggests a generational and ideological shift within the BNP, which has seen its support wane in recent years and has struggled to maintain relevance in the rapidly changing political landscape. The decision comes amid efforts by the BNP to distance itself from the extremist imagery of its past and to attract new members under the leadership of Adam Walker, its current leader. Walker, who has pursued a controversial approach to media engagement and collaboration with other right-wing groups in Europe, has previously called for a more “pragmatic” and professionalized political strategy. The expulsion of Griffin appears to be a step toward realigning the party under this new vision. Griffin responded to the news about his expulsion by calling it a "farce" and accused the party of betraying its roots. In a statement posted online, he claimed the BNP had lost its way and that the leadership was afraid to speak the "truth" about immigration and cultural identity. He also hinted at the possibility of forming a new political movement to continue his work. The BNP’s decision has been viewed by political analysts as both a bold move and a risky one. While it signals a new phase of attempting to shed the party’s image as a fringe, racist organisation, it also risks alienating members who see Griffin as the BNP’s most prominent and recognisable figure.

The Belfast Giants’ hopes of lifting the Elite League title were dashed on Saturday as they fell to a 2-0 defeat against the Sheffield Steelers in the semi-final of the play-offs, ending their season with a disappointing final chapter after a strong campaign. The Giants, who built their reputation as consistent championship contenders, were unable to make inroads on the Steelers’ goal, with the visitors dominating the game and securing an important away win in the best-of-seven series. The result leaves Belfast fans in a state of heartbreak, but admiration for their team’s resilience throughout the season. Despite the loss, the Giants had much to reflect upon with pride. Earlier in the play-offs, they defeated Edinburgh 4-3 in a dramatic and pulsating semi-final first leg and followed that with a gritty 3-2 win to extend the series. However, their hopes were halted as the Steelers, a physically imposing and disciplined side, adapted to the Belfast challenge by tightening their structure and limiting dangerous chances. Steelers forward Brad Larsen, a key figure in the side’s success, opened the scoring in the second period before a late insurance goal from Nick Brough sealed the victory for the Yorkshire-based team. Goalie Rhett Rakhshani was in commanding form to preserve the lead, making a string of vital saves in a game where the Giants struggled to create rhythm from the blue line. In a post-match interview, Belfast head coach Dean Smith expressed mixed emotions: “We had a lot of positives to take from this season, but today we weren’t at our best. Give credit to the Steelers — they executed their game plan and made it tough on us. It’s incredibly frustrating to fall short, but we’ll regroup and get ready for next season.” For the Giants, the future remains bright despite the disappointment. Their core group of players continues to show promise, and the club has consistently demonstrated its ability to perform under pressure. With another sell-out crowd at the SSE Arena, the passion for the team remains undiminished among supporters who have backed them through high and low. Meanwhile, the Steelers advance to the play-off final for the first time since 2015, waiting to see which of the two remaining semi-finalists — Edinburgh or Braehead Clan — will join them in the upcoming weeks. The path ahead is no less demanding, but after a commanding semi-final performance, their confidence is sky high.

The High Court has been told that requiring the UK Parliament to approve the Brexit process is of immense “constitutional importance,” as a landmark legal case challenging the government’s authority to trigger Article 50 without parliamentary approval reached a crucial stage this week. The case, brought by campaign group the Heathrow Residents Association among others, argues that allowing the government to begin the formal process of leaving the European Union by invoking Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty is a breach of parliamentary sovereignty. At the heart of the dispute is a legal interpretation of the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 and the relevant EU legislation, which the claimants argue empowers only Parliament—not the executive—to affirm the UK’s decision to leave the EU. The court heard detailed submissions from both sides on whether the government has the legal authority under existing statute to use prerogative powers to notify the EU of the UK’s intention to withdraw. The claimants’ QC, Sr James Eadie, told the court: "The significance of invoking Article 50 goes far beyond a routine constitutional matter. It involves not only the deepest, most profound constitutional questions about the nature of parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law, but also a foundational shift in the rights and obligations of two hundred million people as to their future and the future of their rights in the European Union." The hearing comes amid deep public and political debate following the 2016 referendum, in which 52% of voters chose to leave the EU. The government initially sought to trigger Article 50 by the end of 2017, although this was delayed indefinitely in the face of legal and political uncertainty. The Supreme Court has already ruled that the devolved legislatures will have a role in any future Brexit legislation, but the High Court case is the latest in a series about whether parliamentary vote is constitutionally required. The government has argued that the 2015 Fixed-term Parliaments Act gives Parliament the final say on whether the UK leaves the EU. However, the claimants insist that no existing legislation grants ministers the authority to begin the Article 50 process without a democratic vote. Speaking outside court, one of the campaign group’s chairpersons said: "This is not about stopping Brexit. It is about upholding the rule of law and ensuring that the Parliament, which is the voice of the people, has the authority to ratify the legal process that will redefine the UK’s place in the world."

Labour MP Naz Shah has described the remarks that led to her suspension from the party as anti-Semitic, saying her comments, which were first made in 2014 and recently resurfaced on social media, were taken out of context and misrepresented. Ms Shah, who represents Bradford West, has issued a fresh statement in response to renewed controversy over a tweet she posted more than six years ago, in which she joked: “I will not be a fan of AIPAC. If I had a problem with anti-Semitism, I would be concerned about the fact that the richest man in the world is Jewish.” Ms Shah was suspended from the Labour Party last week by the ruling National Executive Committee, accused of bringing the party into disrepute and breaching its anti-Semitism code of conduct. The tweet resurfaced after being shared by a far-left activist, prompting criticism from Jewish groups and some within Labour itself. In her latest response to the backlash, Ms Shah denied any anti-Semitic intent, saying her remark was a “poorly expressed joke” and not an endorsement of anti-Semitic tropes, particularly the idea that Jewish people disproportionately control global finance or power. “Ultimately, the tweet is anti-Semitic,” she admitted in written comments obtained by the press. “It's human of me to have made that mistake. I reject anti-Semitism in any form and have always stood up for Jewish communities – but I must also be allowed to speak plainly and to stand up for my own community." The comments have sparked renewed debate within the Labour Party over how best to address the issue of anti-Semitism, which has been at the heart of a crisis for the party in recent years. While some have praised Ms Shah for acknowledging the anti-Semitism in her remark, others have accused Labour of being inconsistent in its disciplinary approach. Shadow Chancellor Jonny Dunstone praised her for the "courage it has taken to finally admit that her comments were anti-Semitic" and called for her to be reinstated. But a number of Jewish Labour members and external anti-discrimination groups have maintained that her words passed the threshold for active anti-Semitism, citing the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) guidelines. Ms Shah is waiting on a full hearing to defend herself as part of the suspension process. Her case comes as Keir Starmer continues to implement tougher measures against anti-Semitism in the party, including the requirement for new members to affirm their agreement with the IHRA definition.

African Elephant: Beauty, Power, and Peril    By Farai Sevenzo, filmmaker and columnist  In recent decades, the African elephant has become a symbol of more than just Africa’s natural grandeur. It has come to represent the fragile balance between human development and the preservation of our planet’s biodiversity. These majestic creatures, the largest land animals on Earth, are an indelible part of the continent’s identity — yet they continue to be threatened by poaching, habitat destruction and a growing demand for ivory. As a filmmaker who has worked extensively in conservation and storytelling, I have witnessed the elephant’s plight up close, and I feel a deep responsibility to bear witness and act. The African elephant is more than just a tourist attraction. It is an ecological keystone, playing a critical role in maintaining the balance of savannahs, forests and water catchments. By uprooting trees, the elephants create clearings in which other wildlife can thrive. They plant seeds in the dung they leave behind, helping forests grow in barren patches. Their movements create pathways for smaller animals, and their presence is essential in the survival of entire ecosystems. To lose them would be to dismantle the very foundations of African biodiversity. But instead of protecting these ancient beings, we human beings have, for centuries, driven them toward the brink of extinction. The ivory trade, once central to African economies and even part of Royal ceremonies in places like Great Britain, has evolved into a ruthless and organized crime industry. Elephant carcasses are now found with their iconic tusks hacked off while the creature is still alive — a gruesome reminder of humanity’s indifference to the suffering of a species that has been around for millions of years longer than us. The statistics are alarming. Between 2006 and 2015, nearly 100,000 elephants were killed for their ivory in Africa. Despite a global ban and the fading of the legal ivory trade, poachers continue unimpeded in many regions. The problem is made worse by the increasing human population encroaching on elephant habitats, leading to frequent human-wildlife conflict. Elephants, which require vast tracts of land to roam freely, are now confined to shrinking pockets of wilderness, separated from their migratory routes and forced into conflict with the human settlements that now exist in their ancestral lands. In my work, I have met rangers who risk their lives to protect these animals. I have seen conservationists camping in the dust, armed only with satellite maps and a conviction that elephants matter.

Hammond warns EU treaty reform necessary to meet German demands   The UK’s hopes for a meaningful deal in Brexit negotiations may hinge on wider reform to the European Union’s treaty framework, Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond warned today. Speaking in a wide-ranging parliamentary statement, Hammond said that “treaty changes will have to happen” to align future EU arrangements with the “German requirements” that will inevitably shape any lasting agreement. In his most explicit indication yet that Britain’s divorce from the European Union may require a shift in the Union’s foundations, Hammond acknowledged that Germany—seen as one of the bloc’s most influential voices—has made it clear that new rules would need to be enshrined in European law to prevent no-deal scenarios and safeguard supply chains. “I stressed in my discussions with our European partners that we must not simply think of the Brexit process as a bilateral discussion between the UK and the EU,” said Hammond. “What we are considering is a far-reaching restructuring of the EU itself, and that must include treaty reform. Germany has made it clear that this is the only way to ensure fair, sustainable agreements for the future.” The Foreign Secretary, who recently returned from key talks in Berlin and Paris, outlined a growing consensus among EU leaders that the UK’s desire for full tariff-free trade, combined with minimal regulatory alignment, is incompatible with current EU rules. He said Germany, in particular, had insisted on new mechanisms to deal with so-called level-playing field issues, covering state aid, environmental standards and workers’ rights—key red lines for the bloc. “Germany and others believe those matters must be covered in full and included in the EU’s treaties to ensure they are binding and can be enforced,” Hammond continued. “If we accept that as a condition, then treaty change becomes not just desirable, but necessary.” Hammond did not rule out a two-track Brexit, where the UK remains in some single market arrangements on goods and fails to secure an arrangement on services and financial regulation. However, he insisted that the process must avoid creating “a new form of entanglement” that leaves Britain in a worse position than it is currently in. This comments come as intense speculation grows about the potential for a pro-Remain coup in the Conservative Party as well as sustained pressure from firms worried over a looming “cliff edge” if Britain leaves the EU without a deal.

The internet has become a “playground for paedophiles,” the NSPCC has warned in a sobering new report that highlights the growing risks children face online. As more young people spend increasing amounts of their time on social media, messaging apps, and gaming platforms, experts have raised the alarm over the ease with which predators can gain access and groom children. The charity has called on the government and tech companies to take stronger measures to protect vulnerable users. In a stark statement, NSPCC CEO Jason Cope said, “The online world is not as safe as many parents might hope. Children and young people are increasingly spending time in digital spaces where they can interact with strangers, including those who deliberately seek to exploit them. We urge all stakeholders to do more to stop predators from using the internet as a hunting ground.” The report, published amid growing concerns over online grooming and the risk of exposure to sexual abuse material, reveals that 38,000 children have been identified as being at immediate risk of harm from online sexual abuse in the past year alone. Many of these cases, the NSPCC says, could have been prevented with stronger safety protocols and better enforcement. Cope added, “We want the UK to be a world leader in online child protection and transparency. That means ensuring that platforms properly respond to reports of abuse and take action against users who break community guidelines. It also means giving children the tools, and adults the support, to stay safe online.” The NSPCC has already started pushing for legislation to make it a legal requirement for social media companies and app developers to implement age verification and safety checks. They have also called for greater investment in reporting systems and the expansion of support services for victims of online abuse. Parents and schools have been urged to play a key role in educating children about how to identify and respond to suspicious contact. Experts suggest that regular conversations about online safety and monitoring what children are viewing or sharing online are vital. Detective Chief Inspector Alan English, from West Mercia Police’s child abuse investigation unit, told BBC Radio 5 Live: “We have seen a huge increase in cases where children are being groomed online. These are scheming, manipulative individuals. It doesn’t matter how smart a child is—these people take great care to gain their trust.” As tech giants continue to face pressure over their safety policies, pressure is mounting on the government to act.

The brutal murder of Concepta Leonard and the attempted killing of her young son, Conor, have left the local community and wider public reeling, as newspapers across Northern Ireland highlight the shocking violence of the attack dubbed by the  Belfast Telegraph  as the “Maguiresbridge horror.” The incident, which took place in a remote section of County Fermanagh, has ignited a wave of anger and grief, particularly among residents in the small town of Maguiresbridge, where Ms Leonard had lived for many years. Initial reports describe how Ms Leonard, 51, was stabbed to death in what police have called a “targeted attack” outside her home on the evening of July 26. Her son, 12, was also violently attacked and seriously injured. A 43-year-old local man has since been arrested and charged with the murders, as well as with the attempted murder of the boy. Locals expressed disbelief, struggling to comprehend how such violence could unfold in a place known for its peace and rural tranquillity. Statements from the police and political leaders have underscored the gravity of the case. Police have praised the “quick thinking and bravery” of a neighbour, who came to the victims' aid, calling it “invaluable in the tragic circumstances.” Political representatives from across the divided community have spoken out against the violence, urging calls for national unity and calm. Naomi Long, MP for East Belfast, paid tribute to Concepta Leonard and her son in a moving statement: “This is a tragedy that splits the heart of our community, and the people of Fermanagh are united in grief and horror.” The details of the attack have left many shaken—particularly as the victim was a well-respected and community-minded individual. A former education worker, she was described as “a pillar of her community” by friends and colleagues. Local businesses and civic groups have expressed solidarity with the family, with flowers and toys laid outside the home as a mark of respect. As the case moves through the courts, many are calling for urgent action on domestic violence and the criminal justice system’s ability to address such heinous crimes. The Foundation for Peace and Reconciliation has already pointed to the need for greater support for rural safety initiatives, especially in areas with low population density and long police response times. The murder is not only a reflection of the deeply personal and tragic nature of the event, but also of the lingering shadows of violence in post-conflict Northern Ireland—still a region where community ties can be as fragile as they can be strong.

At least 31 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a suicide bomb attack outside the main Court Complex in central Damascus on Thursday, according to Syrian state media and local officials. The blast, which struck near the Criminal Court, where security trials are routinely held, is the latest in a string of high-profile attacks in the capital that have raised concerns over waning security even as the government claims regained control over most of the country. The explosion occurred in the Tariq al-Zaitar district, a bustling area known for its government offices and institutions. State-run media outlet SANA quickly blamed “terrorists” for the attack, a common descriptor used by the Assad regime for opponents of its rule. However, no armed group has yet claimed responsibility for the assault. Eyewitnesses described the scene immediately after the blast as one of chaos. Smoke billowed into the sky, and emergency personnel were seen swarming the site to assist the wounded while injured civilians lay scattered across the streets. The detonation heavily damaged nearby buildings, including a courthouse and police stations, and is being viewed as a direct challenge to the government’s security apparatus. The attack comes less than a week after the government announced the full recapture of the eastern Ghouta region, a last major opposition stronghold near Damascus that had been under siege for years. While Syrian forces and their allies from Russia and Iran have largely consolidated power in the capital and surrounding areas, incidents such as this confirm the persistent presence of extremist groups and dissidents. Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif condemned the attack in a statement, calling it an “act of terror” against peace and stability in Syria. Russia, which has repeatedly deployed military support to the Assad regime, echoed the condemnation and pledged to work with Damascus to “crush extremism.” The bombing also raises questions about the effectiveness of Damascus’s security forces in the capital, where prominent government and security figures operate. While rebel forces have been pushed out of the city, uncontrolled areas in suburbs have become hotbeds for sleeper cells and lone-wolf attacks. One survivor, speaking at a nearby hospital, described hearing the blast as he was walking home from work. “I heard a huge sound, like an earthquake. I came to see what had happened, and people were running and screaming,” he said. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitoring group, reported the death toll as 31 with more than 100 injured.

Liverpool earned a gritty 1-0 victory over Swansea City at Anfield thanks to James Milner’s 85th-minute penalty, a result that could not have come at a more crucial moment for both teams. For Brendan Rodgers’ side, it was a hard-fought win that extended their unbeaten league home record against the Swans and provided a welcome boost after a recent dip in form. But for Francesco Guidolin, Swansea’s beleaguered manager, the defeat only deepened the questions surrounding his position at the helm of a club currently languishing in the bottom half of the Premier League table. The game, played in front of a passionate Anfield crowd, was low on spectacle but high on tension, with the scoreline reflecting the difficulty both teams had in breaking down a resolute defensive display. Swansea left themselves vulnerable late on when Jordan Ayew missed a key clearance, allowing Firmino to be fouled just outside the box, earning a penalty for the visitors. Milner stepped up and sent Swansea goalkeeper Lukasz Fabiański the wrong way, sealing Liverpool’s first league win in four games and sending the home support into raptures. Swansea, who have now failed to win five of their last six league matches, were visibly frustrated as they struggled to create any clear opportunities in front of goal. Guidolin trotted out a 3-4-3 system that had been seemingly evolving week by week, but against a disciplined Liverpool side, his experiment yielded little fruit. The Italian boss, who was appointed in July after a short managerial career in Italy and China, has come under increasing fire from the Liverpool-born owner Steve Kaplan and sections of the club's supporters, who had questioned the hiring of a manager with no prior English top-flight experience. Guidolin’s struggles have been most evident on the training ground and in the dugout, where the severity of his Italian accent and a perceived lack of communication with his players have been cited as worrying signs. Swansea's transformation from a side that, under Garry Monk, routinely held their own against the league's elite, to one that now appears susceptible to any physical, well-disciplined opposition, has only intensified the pressure on the 61-year-old. While Liverpool’s victory provided a timely reminder of their capability to grind out results, it was also a sobering reflection of where they stand in the title race.

Barry McGuigan is calling for boxing’s governing bodies to play a more active role in supporting the mental health of fighters, following recent high-profile concerns and tragic cases in the sport. The former British featherweight champion, himself a vocal advocate for mental health awareness, believes that a specifically funded foundation would provide a vital lifeline for current and former boxers dealing with psychological distress. McGuigan, who has previously spoken candidly about his own struggles with anxiety and depression, stressed that mental health in boxing has long been neglected. “So many boxers are put under extreme pressure—physically, mentally and financially—and we rarely look at the cost,” he said. “We talk about conditioning bodies, but not conditioning minds. That has to change.” His comments come in the wake of several concerning incidents, including former world champion James DeGale revealing he was treated for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and the suicide of world title contender Michael Watson in 2020. Watson, who was paralysed in a match after being struck by a late, accidental punch, later took his own life, sparking national outrage and renewed debate over the mental toll of boxing. McGuigan’s proposal is gaining traction among both retired and active fighters. Many in the industry acknowledge that while charitable organisations such as Mind and Sport Against Substance Addiction (SASA) do provide services, more is needed at the top level of sport. He argues that boxing authorities, including the British Board of Boxing Control and the World Boxing Council (WBC), should allocate a percentage of licensing fees and prize money towards the foundation. “In football, cricket, and even rugby, mental health is part of the conversation. It should be in boxing, too,” continued McGuigan. “Boxing is a contact sport with a unique psychological burden. We have about 30 championship bouts a month in the UK alone. We can’t let this be an issue that fails to get the resources it deserves.” The foundation, if established, would offer confidential support, counselling for current and former boxers, and educational campaigns about the importance of mental health. It would also collaborate with sports psychologists and peer mentorship programs, helping reduce the stigma that still surrounds the topic in a sport that traditionally prioritises physical resilience. McGuigan’s call has sparked a mixed reaction from boxing officials. Some acknowledge the need for intervention, while others argue that the sport is already under pressure to reform its financial and safety policies.

In a country where freedom of expression is a vibrant and often chaotic reflection of its democracy, India has increasingly found itself at the crossroads of legal and political debate over what constitutes sedition. A British newspaper report has uncovered how, in recent years, Indian authorities have used the country’s colonial-era sedition law—Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code—to prosecute citizens for an array of seemingly trivial or culturally specific actions. From liking a Facebook post to not standing up in a cinema during the national anthem, the stretch of what constitutes dissent or treachery is expanding, raising concerns among human rights advocates and legal scholars alike. The use of sedition charges to suppress free speech has become a troubling trend, with individuals facing harsh consequences for expressing views on social media, drawing cartoons, or even voicing mild criticism of high-profile figures. Most recently, a university student in Karnataka was charged for allegedly asking a provocative question in an exam, while a young woman in Rajasthan faced a similar accusation for posting an online critique of a prominent yoga guru. Such cases, however unusual they may appear, are not isolated incidents. They indicate a growing comfort among authorities in India to invoke sedition, a crime punishable by life imprisonment, in increasingly expansive ways. In one particularly bizarre example, supporters of a rival cricket team in Mumbai were accused of sedition after rhythmically clapping in support of national pride – but ironically for another nation. Though no prosecutions followed, the incident prompted heated online debate and highlighted the difficulty of drawing lines between acceptable rhetoric and what authorities deem offensive to the state. Meanwhile, in Bengaluru, a man was temporarily detained for not standing during the national anthem in a cinema—a move that was described as “excessive” by the venue and later apologised for. India’s sedition law, introduced under British rule in 1870, was historically used to silence political dissent during independence movements and was rarely enforced after 1968 when the Supreme Court called it “highly dangerous”. Yet, in recent years, it has made a resurgence under state governments with active political agendas. Legal experts say this reflects both a broader strategy to maintain control over public narratives and a troubling shift in how free expression is treated. Advocacy groups, including the Indian bar association and international human rights bodies, have warned that the misuse of sedition laws is a direct affront to India's democratic values.

Rangers secured a vital 2-1 victory over Aberdeen at Ibrox Park on Saturday afternoon, lifting them to second place in the Scottish Premiership in a dramatic encounter that saw both teams reduced to ten men by the break. The clash, highly anticipated as one of the fiercest derbies outside of the Old Firm, delivered on drama and intensity, with red cards, goal-scoring flair, and a late surge from the Dons making for a compelling afternoon of top-flight action. Goals from John Fleck and Timofey Bazhenov gave Rangers the three points, while Sam Cosgrove netted a consolation for the visitors. The first half was a tense, tightly contested affair, with both teams feeling each other out and looking to establish control. It wasn’t until the 29th minute that the first major incident of the game occurred, when Rangers' Wes Dacres was shown a straight red card for a dangerous challenge in the box. Moments later, Aberdeen's Declan McDaid followed suit after committing a similar foul in his own half, leaving the teams 45 minutes to play with ten men apiece. Rangers took full advantage of their numerical advantage, and it was academy graduate John Fleck who broke the deadlock just after the hour mark with a composed finish after latching onto a through pass. The striker, who has been in fine form this season, showed calmness in front of goal, rounding the keeper and slotting the ball into an empty net. His goal sparked jubilant scenes among the home fans and injected fresh confidence into the Light Blue Army. Aberdeen responded well in the second half, displaying a mix of resilience and determination. Their equaliser came in the 68th minute through a well-worked move that ended with Cosgrove firing past Rangers goalkeeper Wes Foderingham. The Dons, now playing with intelligence and composure, began to control the tempo of the game and put the hosts under sustained pressure. However, in the 78th minute, the decisive moment came. A scramble in the box ended with Bazhenov, the Russian midfielder, scoring with a firm left-footed shot, giving Rangers a 2-1 lead. The goal sent renewed energy through the home side, with their supporters singing and chanting in celebration. In the final 10 minutes, Aberdeen threw everything forward but were unable to find an equaliser. Rangers, capitalising on their extra man, tightened at the back and held on for a vital win.

Local councils across England have sounded the alarm, insisting that care services for the elderly and disabled are “at breaking point,” with planned increases to the council tax falling dramatically short of the rising costs of providing essential support. The warning comes as a growing number of cash-strapped local authorities face the impossible dilemma of whether to cut frontline care, reduce eligibility criteria, or place a heavier burden on already stretched providers. The problems have been compounded by years of central government underfunding and a rapidly aging population that now sees more than 12 million adults in need of social care. A stark report published by the English Local Government Association (LGA) revealed a “financial cliff edge” is looming for councils tasked with funding adult social care. The LGA argued that the ring-fenced social care grant, which covers only 12% of the cost of adult social care, has failed to keep pace with inflation and the increased demands of an increasingly complex health and care system. Councils estimate that, collectively, an extra £8.9 billion per year is needed to preserve care services as they exist, with the government’s latest offer of increased funding over three years deemed insufficient. Council tax increases, which are expected to rise by up to 5% in many areas to help bridge the gap, have been described by some leaders as a “death by a thousand cuts” for families already struggling with the cost of living. “This isn’t just about numbers on a spreadsheet,” said Sue Eagles, leader of Hertfordshire County Council. “It’s about real people whose lives are directly impacted by cuts to someone being there in a time of need. Without investment, the scale of the crisis will spiral out of control.” The predicted shortfall in funding has already led to some councils announcing plans to reform eligibility policies, meaning only those deemed to have the highest level of need will qualify for publicly funded assistance. The most vulnerable — those with limited mobility, dementia, learning disabilities or physical impairments — face the most severe risks. Health professionals have echoed the concerns, warning that underfunding will further strain the health service, as the inability to access timely care leads to more hospital admissions and longer stays. The situation has ignited a fierce political debate as calls grow for a cross-party consensus to address the chronic underinvestment in social care. Shadow Health Secretary Jonathan Ashworth said: “The government must not wait until the system collapses to act.

When a new fitness coach joined England’s Women's Football team ahead of the 2015 World Cup in Canada, he was reportedly left "shocked" by the level of strength and conditioning work being carried out by the players. The coach, whose exact identity has not been disclosed, later revealed in a conversation with a BBC journalist that the squad was far behind the physical conditioning standards expected in modern international women’s football. This revelation has reignited questions about the investment in women’s football in England and follows ongoing criticism about disparities between the resources available to male and female athletes at the elite level. The 2015 World Cup, hosted by Canada, provided a relatively modest platform for the women’s game at the time and reflected a still-developing infrastructure in terms of coaching, facilities, and long-term planning. In the years since, there has been a noticeable shift in priorities, with the English Football Association (FA) investing heavily in the women’s game ahead of major tournaments, including the 2019 and 2023 World Cups. England’s Lionesses, as the team is known, have experienced unprecedented success, reaching the final of the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euro Championship and winning two major tournaments. However, this early disparity in strength and conditioning has been cited by insiders as a potential barrier to success in 2015. At the time, England finished third in Group B, barely qualifying for the knockout stages after a tight goal-laden match against Mexico and a solitary draw with Japan. The team ultimately failed to progress beyond the quarter-finals. John Spilsbury, the FA’s director of elite development, acknowledged the importance of physical conditioning in a 2020 interview, and it is understood that the appointment of a new fitness coaching team at that time marked a turning point for the women’s program. Officially, the FA said they "closely evaluate all aspects of player development and physical preparation to ensure the women’s team competes at the highest level." The development of the women’s game in England has continued to accelerate, with the English Championship entering its 10th season and continued investment from the national team's sponsors and the FA alike. Players such as Leah Williamson, Lucy Bronze, and Jodie Taylor have become household names, supported by an expanding fanbase and increased media coverage. But the tale of the 2015 World Cup camp serves as a reminder of how far the women's game in England, and indeed across Europe, has come in the last decade.

The UK Parliament has announced a formal inquiry into the widespread issue of sexual harassment and sexual violence in England's schools, with a dedicated Commons committee set to investigate the matter in depth. The move comes amid growing concerns by parents, teachers, and student advocates who have long argued that such incidents are underreported and often mishandled by school authorities. The inquiry is expected to scrutinise the procedures currently in place within schools, the effectiveness of government guidance, and the real-life experiences of those affected by this troubling issue. The announcement was made by education spokesperson for the Select Committee, Labour MP Kevan Jones, who said the inquiry aims to "ensure that every child can learn in a safe and supportive environment, free from fear or abuse." Jones, who chairs the Education Committee, said the investigation would cover "the extent of the problem, the responses of schools, the guidance provided by DfE [Department for Education], the experiences of victims and their families, and the role of Ofsted in tracking and addressing concerns." Recent reports highlighting a lack of consistency across schools, with some failing to address bullying, harassment, or assault appropriately, have added to the pressure for a formal inquiry. In 2021, a report by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) revealed that thousands of children are affected by such incidents each year, with most cases – particularly of harassment – going unrecorded. The inquiry is also expected to examine the impact of the current curriculum and how it equips students to understand and challenge inappropriate behaviour. Campaigners have welcomed the decision. Lucy Spilsbury, founder of the charity Children's Rights Alliance for England, praised the committee for taking the issue seriously. "This inquiry is a long-overdue step toward accountability and change," she said. "Too many children have been let down by a system that has failed to protect them. It is vital that this inquiry sheds light on the scale of the problem and leads to real transformation in school policies and culture." The Department for Education has not yet commented publicly on the inquiry, but it has been urged to provide full support and transparency during the process. The committee is expected to hear from headteachers, school governors, survivors of abuse, academies trusts, and independent schools to develop a comprehensive picture of the challenges and potential solutions. The inquiry is set to run throughout 2024, with the findings expected to inform future legislation and policy reforms.

Tanks and warplanes were deployed in a bid to dislodge the militants, with reports of heavy gunfire and explosions echoing through the ancient streets as government forces advanced. The operation, backed by the US-led international coalition and local Kurdish and Shia militias, marks a critical phase in the broader campaign to eradicate IS from Iraq and reclaim the city that once served as the group’s de facto capital. The Old City, a historic and densely populated area known for its narrow alleyways and centuries-old architecture, has been a stronghold for IS for nearly four years. Coalition forces and allied units reached the city’s outskirts last month, and the assault has now reached its decisive stage. While earlier phases of the liberation of Mosul, which began in late October 2016, saw significant progress, the Old City presented a unique challenge due to its urban terrain and the militants’ determined resistance. Despite the monumental effort, the operation has come at a human cost. Civilian casualties have been reported, and many residents remain trapped, with only limited humanitarian aid allowed to enter the district. The United Nations has warned of the potential for a “catastrophic” humanitarian crisis, with thousands feared to be in the crossfire of the fighting. Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi has hailed the offensive as a turning point in the fight against IS, stating that “freedom is knocking at the door.” However, military analysts caution that the battle for Mosul's Old City is being described as one of the most complex in the conflict, with IS employing suicide bombers, snipers, and suicide tunnels in an effort to disrupt the advance. The streets of Mosul have long been scarred by violence, and while the city has suffered immense destruction, the successful capture of the Old City would be a major symbolic and strategic victory. The UK's leading charities are facing a new wave of scrutiny after the BBC uncovered how they are using paid data lists to send mass letters to householders in a bid to raise vital funds. Campaigns by well-known charities such as Cancer Research UK, the NSPCC and the British Red Cross rely on these data sets — bought from third-party companies — to target homes where donors are statistically more likely to give money. In an effort to lift £5.5 billion from British households last year, these charities use computer algorithms and donor databases to identify patterns in giving history, household income and proximity to previous donors. The BBC found that the data revealed some families are receiving multiple appeals from different charities in the same month, regardless of whether the recipient had previously shown signs of being overwhelmed. These data lists cost charities thousands of pounds to purchase and are often accompanied by strict marketing guidance, including what tone and wording to use in the letters to maximise response rates. Internal documents reviewed by the BBC revealed that one data firm recommended using appeals that "appear compassionate in tone and visually appealing," and to "avoid any language that may elicit defensiveness." Concerns are surfacing among privacy advocates, who argue that the practice blurs the line between ethical fundraising and exploitation. "It's human nature for people to feel compassionate, but when you are bombarded by dozens of pleas from the same organizations, it can become invasive," said Sam Harrison, a spokesperson for the consumer watchdog Group. "The public deserves transparency about how their personal data is used and what choices they truly have in opting out." Despite the growing public unease, charities remain firm in their stance. "Our letters are carefully crafted to make an emotional and factual connection with our supporters," said a spokesperson for Cancer Research UK. "All our fundraising is fully compliant with UK law and binding charity legislation." Yet questions remain about the ethics of targeting grieving families or vulnerable individuals with tailored appeals. One campaign that triggered widespread controversy last year focused on a child homelessness crisis — the subject of a particularly emotional story about a lone parent forced to sofa-surf. The charity behind the campaign would not confirm whether the data scientists relied solely on demographic criteria or personal vulnerabilities to select recipients. Meanwhile, the Fundraising Standards Board (FRSB), which regulates the sector, says it is currently "monitoring the situation closely but has not received any formal complaints."

Calls are mounting for the government to introduce a tax on sugary drinks to combat rising childhood obesity and improve public health. Health campaigners and medical professionals argue that levying manufacturers of high-sugar beverages could curb consumption, encourage healthier choices, and generate funding for health initiatives. The idea, inspired by similar taxes in Mexico and the UK, has gained fresh momentum following new data from the National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP), which shows an alarming number of children in England are overweight by the time they enter secondary school. The figures reveal that 26% of 10 and 11-year-olds and 34% of 15 and 16-year-olds are classified as obese or overweight. Health charities, including the British Medical Association (BMA) and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH), have reiterated demands for action. Dwayne Fields, chair of the BMA’s junior doctors committee, stated: “We’re seeing the consequences of poor diet and sedentary lifestyles in our hospitals every day. A sugar tax on soft drinks is a necessary step to reduce the burden of obesity and diabetes, particularly in children.” The proposed levy, often referred to as a “sugar tax”, would see a charge placed on drinks with the highest sugar content, creating a financial incentive for producers to reformulate their products. The UK introduced a similar levy – the Soft Drinks Industry Levy – in 2018, which led to a significant reduction in the sugar content of many popular beverages. Proponents argue that a more robust tax, possibly expanded to include all sugary drinks, would have an even greater impact. However, opposition remains. Industry groups, including the Soft Drinks Association, have warned that additional taxation would unfairly target vulnerable consumers and could lead to price increases at a time of economic hardship. They argue that such measures should be accompanied by broader educational campaigns and a focus on balanced nutrition rather than singling out one product category. Critics also question whether a sugar tax, on its own, will significantly alter consumer behaviour. Dr. Sarah Jarvis, a GP and health commentator, told the BBC: “Policy needs to meet people where they are. A sugar tax is one part of the solution, but unless we also improve access to healthy food and provide better nutrition education in schools, the problem will persist.” The debate comes as schools and families grapple with the challenges of creating a healthier lifestyle for children in a food environment dominated by processed and high-sugar products.

Sajid Javid has ruled out a government takeover of the Port Talbot steel works, rejecting calls for nationalisation as a solution to the uncertainty surrounding the plant’s future. The Business Secretary made the comments following growing public and political pressure to intervene after Tata Steel, the current owner, failed to rule out mothballing two blast furnaces at the South Wales plant, which employs over 4,500 people. Speaking in Downing Street on Thursday, Javid stressed that policy must be based on long-term economic solutions rather than short-term political responses. “Nationalisation may seem like the easy answer when a situation appears desperate, but it is not the answer for Port Talbot or for British industry,” he said. Javid’s remarks come amid deepening concern across Wales and beyond, where the potential closure of the furnaces is seen as a devastating blow to the local economy. The steel plant is not only the largest of its kind in the UK, but also a vital component of the supply chain for other major industries, including automotive and aerospace. Prime Minister Theresa May is expected to meet with representatives from both Tata and the trades unions over the coming days to try and broker a compromise. Last week, UK steel unions written to MPs warning that a partial closure would result in the loss of hundreds of jobs and leave local communities in crisis. Critics of Javid’s stance have accused the government of failing to grasp the urgency of the situation. Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour leader, said the government was “out of touch” for not considering all possible options, including public ownership, to save jobs at Port Talbot. “This plant is not just a business asset — it’s the beating heart of a community. The government should be doing everything in its power to keep it open,” he said in a statement. Meanwhile, about 300 steelworkers held a protest outside the gates of Port Talbot on Thursday morning, demanding not only government intervention but also assurances from Tata. The mood among workers has grown increasingly anxious, with many fearing the possibility of unemployment in an area already hit hard by deindustrialisation. Tata has said the plant remains financially viable, but it is restricting overtime and reducing shifts in an effort to cut costs. The company has not ruled out mothballing the furnaces during the next maintenance shutdown, which is due in December.

Salmon Exports Rise in Value but Decline in Volume as Industry Faces Pressure   Exports of farmed salmon from Scotland rose by 17% in value in 2016 despite a significant drop in the volume of fish shipped overseas, according to new official figures. The data suggests that the industry is increasingly relying on higher prices and premium markets to offset declining production levels, reflecting broader challenges within the aquaculture sector. The Scottish government said that salmon exports by value reached over £1.3 billion last year, up from around £1.11 billion in 2015. However, the total volume of fish exported fell by nearly 9%, with around 165,000 tonnes sent to overseas markets. The biggest fall in volume was recorded in key export markets such as the United States and Canada, which together accounted for nearly half of all salmon sent abroad in 2016. Industry experts say the trend is driven by a combination of factors, including falling stocking levels in Scottish sea cages, a rise in production costs, and challenges linked to the UK’s decision to exit the EU. Farmers have struggled with rising feed prices, disease outbreaks such as sea lice infestations, and land-based operational constraints, all of which have impacted production capacity. At the same time, the move towards value-over-volume strategies has seen Scottish producers target high-end foodservice markets and premium branding initiatives, allowing them to secure higher prices even with fewer fish being exported. Calum MacLean, Chief Executive of the Scottish Salmon Producers’ Organisation, said in a statement that the findings highlight the need for a strategic shift in the industry. “It's clear that our ability to increase volume is now constrained by practical and environmental limits,” he said. “Our focus must now be on maintaining product quality, increasing marketing efforts, and securing sustainable premium prices to ensure the long-term viability of the sector.” The UK’s vote to leave the European Union is also sending ripples through the salmon industry. Producers are concerned about potential changes in trade regulations, export duties and the availability of the EU workforce that supports operations along Scotland’s rugged North Atlantic coastline. Environment groups have welcomed the decline in production volume as a positive shift in the context of environmental sustainability. Over the past decade, salmon farming has been linked to concerns over water quality, marine biodiversity, and the spread of diseases to wild fish.environment ministers have repeatedly called for more stringent regulation of the sector, and the reduction in fish stocks has been partly attributed to improved environmental controls.

Northern Ireland’s impressive three-game winning streak in their Euro 2016 qualifying campaign came to an end on Friday night as they were defeated 2-0 by Romania in Bucharest. The result saw their opponents leapfrog them to sit top of Group F, with only the group winners securing automatic qualification for the tournament in France. The match, played at the formidable Stadionul National, marked the end of what had been a most encouraging run for Michael O’Neill’s side, who had previously defeated Norway, Cyprus, and Georgia to climb as high as second in the table. The defeat leaves the Irish in second place with 12 points from six matches, two points behind Romania, and with a vital home fixture against Group F leaders Norway to come in October. Romania, managed by Edward Iordache, started the game with more intensity and control, their home advantage and recent good form in European qualifiers evident from the outset. The visitors, however, struggled to create clear-cut chances in the first half, with goalkeeper Vlad Ștefănescu making a couple of key saves to deny Northern Ireland a foothold in the match. The deadlock was broken just before half-time when Alexandru Chipciu calmly slotted in a 25-yard free-kick, curling the ball past a passive Michael McGovern. The goal was a hammer blow for the Irish – but it was seemingly the least of their worries. Belgium starlet Denis Suárez, on loan from Barcelona, completed the rout in the 70th minute with a powerful finish from the edge of the box, capping a strong individual performance. Suárez, playing just his second international match for Romania following his recent switch of international allegiance from Spain, was a constant threat with his energetic, unpredictable style. Northern Ireland, who had been expected to be a strong contender for a coveted European Championship spot, showed little of the resilience that had typified their recent performances. The midfield lacked the bite and composure that had been their hallmark, while the lone striker, Kyle Lafferty, was largely isolated by a严密 （tight）Romanian backline. Manager Michael O’Neill was visibly frustrated after the game, acknowledging that his side had "not taken our game to the next level when we needed to." "In the first 45 minutes, we were a shadow of the team we’ve been in previous matches," he said. "We lacked shape, lacked drive, and we just failed to match the intensity of the opposition."

Graham Dorrans fired Rangers to a vibrant start to their Scottish Premiership season with a decisive double as they brushed aside Motherwell 3-0 at Fir Park on Sunday. The Ibrox side, returning to the top flight after a three-year absence, made a bold statement of intent as they picked apart their lower-tier hosts in a display of composure, control and clinical finishing. Dorrans, 34, who has spent a significant portion of his career in Scotland, was the standout performer, netting twice in the first half to put the Light Blues firmly in the driving seat. His first arrived in the 18th minute after a sweeping move down the left, finished with a powerful left-footed strike into the top corner. Eleven minutes later, the experienced midfielder doubled the lead with a composed left-footed curler following a well-worked set piece. Although the rest of the half turned into a frustrating period for Motherwell as they struggled to stem the flow of possession, Rangers' second-half introduction of 20-year-old Josh Windass proved to be the spark needed to add a third. The young winger, on loan from Liverpool, capped a moment of individual brilliance with a solo goal in the 65th minute to seal the points and underline Rangers’ attacking depth. The victory was not without its moments of tension, as Motherwell fans, spoiling for a fight, saw their last-ditch appeals for a late equaliser fall flat. However, for Mark Warburton’s side, the three points served as a strong confidence booster and a clear warning that they are here to reclaim their place at the top of Scottish football. Speaking to the press after the match, Warburton praised the character and hunger shown by his players. “It’s a good start,” he said. “We’re a young team, but we showed today that we have the quality and the mentality to compete at this level. Graham was outstanding again, but the performance was about the whole squad. “There are areas we need to improve, but overall I was delighted. The players bought into the system, and it was nice to see us grow as the game went on.” The result sets the tone for an intriguing 2024/25 campaign as Rangers aim to bridge the gap with arch-rivals Celtic, who lost their opening match of the season to Livingston the previous day. With Dorrans in blistering form and new signings slowly bedding in, the early signs are encouraging that Ibrox’s return might not be as rocky as some had feared.

Tesco Mobile is set to shake up the UK’s mobile phone market with a bold new idea – offering customers monthly discounts in exchange for watching advertisements on their mobile devices. The move has sparked both intrigue and concern among consumers, as companies increasingly seek innovative revenue streams in a competitive industry. The discount scheme, which will roll out in the coming weeks, allows customers to select from various sponsored content options displayed on their phone screens. Adverts will not interrupt calls or texts, but will appear on the side of the screen, much like a digital billboard. By engaging with the content – whether that be watching a short video, viewing a product or image – users can build up a financial reward of up to £6 a month, which is then deducted from their mobile bill. Giles Littlejohn, chief executive of Tesco Mobile, said the initiative is about “finding new ways to help our customers save more and get more out of their mobile plans.” He added that the company is prioritising user choice and clarity: “We will be very upfront about what users are signing up for and will never hides any charges or commitments.” The service is the latest example of how mobile phone providers are turning to advertising as a way to augment income. Vodafone and EE have previously experimented with similar models, offering free streaming services such as Spotify in exchange for data-generated revenue. However, such services have drawn criticism from customer groups concerned about privacy, content quality, and the intrusiveness of the ads. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has previously warned that firms must ensure transparency and user consent when it comes to in-app advertising. Spokesperson for the ICO said: “We have made it clear that unnecessary or overly intrusive tracking of individuals’ data or device usage is being closely monitored under the Data Protection Act. Tesco would need to ensure its model is fully GDPR-compliant and the right of consumers to opt out is clearly explained.” Legal and consumer rights campaigner Dr. Sally Su, a lecturer at the London School of Economics, commented: “We need to be cautious. While the idea of earning money just by using your phone sounds appealing, it also raises concerns about how deeply companies are tracking our activity. There could be a fine line between useful discounts and being turned into a passive viewer with your data sold behind the scenes.”

Sri Lanka’s military faces fresh international scrutiny after a government-appointed judge confirmed that allegations of war crimes committed during the final stages of the country’s 26-year civil war are "credible", marking a rare and significant break from official denial. The judge, Justice Chaturanga de Silva, concluded his seven-month inquiry into war-time conduct earlier this week and has reportedly recommended that the government refer the matter to the International Criminal Court (ICC) for further investigation.
