A full report is expected to be released imminently, but leaked excerpts suggest a damning assessment of the conflict’s final days in 2009, when government forces launched a brutal offensive to destroy the Tamil Tiger Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). The conflict, which officially ended in May 2009, claimed more than 70,000 lives and displaced hundreds of thousands. For years, Sri Lankan officials have dismissed claims of widespread civilian killings, mass disappearances and torture, often labelling them as propaganda by foreign critics and Tamil exiles. However, the judge's findings, which were based on witness testimonies, video evidence, and international reports, suggest the truth may be far more troubling. Justice de Silva reportedly noted that "evidence presented during the inquiry supports the conclusion that grave breaches of international humanitarian law were committed", including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and attacks on civilians in conflict zones, particularly during the final months when the Tigers were cornered in the north-eastern province of Mullaitivu. The judge’s report comes amid growing international pressure for accountability. The United Nations has also launched its own probe into the conflict, and the UK, Norway, and other Western nations have continued to call for an independent review. Activists and human rights organisations, many of whom have long campaigned for justice for Tamil civilians, hailed the findings as a pivotal moment. However, there is deep concern that the Sri Lankan government will resist taking any meaningful action, citing domestic sovereignty. Last month, President Maithripala Sirisena passed a landmark amendment to the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), a controversial law once used to suppress Tamil political dissent. While described as a step forward, critics argue that its full repeal is still necessary to enable proper historical accountability and reparations for war victims. "The government must not let this moment slip away," said Vidya Rajah, programme director of the Sri Lanka Campaign for Peace and Justice. "This inquiry shows that the evidence is there.

Iran’s transformation into an Islamic republic in 1979 marked one of the most seismic political and ideological shifts of the late 20th century, ending decades of monarchical rule and ushering in an unprecedented era where religious authority would dominate the state. The Iranian Revolution, as it came to be known, saw the overthrow of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and the establishment of a system where Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the revolution’s spiritual leader, became the supreme guide of the nation under a new constitution. The revolution was born out of widespread discontent with the Shah’s Western-backed regime, his policies of rapid modernisation — known as the “White Revolution” — and his perceived alliance with the United States, which many Iranians blamed for entrenching inequality, repression, and cultural alienation. The Shah’s security forces, the SAVAK, were viewed as increasingly brutal in their suppression of dissent. As religious, political, and working-class opposition groups coalesced, the momentum for change grew unstoppable. Ayatollah Khomeini, exiled in Paris, emerged as the movement’s unifying figure. His fiery sermons against the Shah, the West, and what he called the “US-controlled putsch”, resonated with millions and galvanized a broad anti-regime coalition. On February 11, 1979 — just weeks after Khomeini’s triumphant return to Iran — the Shah fled the country, and within days, the new Islamic republic was declared. Under the new regime, the role of the clergy in governance was enshrined in the constitution. At its head stood the Supreme Leader, a position modelled on Khomeini, who combines religious, executive, and military authority. Below him, the head of government — the president — was created as a largely symbolic figure, chosen through popular vote but answerable to the Guardian Council, an unelected body of clerics and jurists who vet candidates for eligibility. Khomeini’s doctrine of  velayat-e faqih  — or the "Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist" — became the foundation of Iran’s political system, asserting that a senior Islamic jurist had the right to oversee the state to ensure it remained faithful to Islamic principles. The establishment of the Islamic republic brought with it far-reaching changes, including the redefinition of law, the closure of nightclubs and Western-style cafes, and the abolition of monarchical symbols. It also had global repercussions, most notably with the 1979–1981 seizure of the US Embassy in Tehran — the Iran hostage crisis — which symbolised the regime’s deep hostility to American influence and cemented its reputation as a radical power on the global stage.

The towering golden statue of three liberation soldiers—two men and a woman—dominates the skyline of Heroes' Acre in Harare, the solemn heart of Zimbabwe’s national memory. Standing over 30 feet tall, the striking figure is a symbol of the nation’s fight for independence and a tribute to those who gave their lives in the liberation struggle against colonial rule. The woman, placed at the center, is a potent reminder of the often-overlooked yet crucial role women played in the country's fight for freedom. The monument was unveiled in 2004 to replace the controversial statue of Ian Smith, the former Rhodesian prime minister, whose image had divided opinion even decades after independence. Herons' Acre, officially known as the National Heroes Acre, is a sprawling memorial site that honours the Zimbabwean heroes of the independence war, who fought under various guerrilla forces against the forces of British colonialism and white-minority rule. The monument is visited by dignitaries, schoolchildren, and foreign dignitaries on official state visits, particularly on 18 April—Zimbabwe Independence Day. It is here that the nation's annual ceremonies, including the laying of wreaths and special prayers, are held. The design and symbolism of the golden statue have sparked both admiration and debate. While many see it as a powerful embodiment of national unity and pride, others argue that its sheer size, and the choice to depict a unnamed woman at its heart, reflect wider questions about who gets remembered in the nation-building narrative. Historians and scholars have noted the importance of ensuring that the stories of ordinary fighters—both men and women—are preserved and acknowledged, preferably not just in symbolic form but through continued education and dialogue. The statue is part of a broader landscape of monuments and memorials in Heroes' Acre. Each plot of land within the grounds is marked by an inscribed stone or wooden slab, bearing the names of those who laid down their lives. Among them are well-known figures like Robert Mugabe, the country's first prime minister and a central figure in the liberation struggle, as well as lesser-known individuals whose names have not entered mainstream history but whose sacrifices shaped the nation. As Zimbabwe marks over 40 years of independence, the Heroes' Acre and its golden centerpiece remain a focal point of national identity and reflection. Yet, with growing calls for the country to reckon with the complexities of its post-independence history—including political strife, economic challenges, and the shifting tides of leadership—monuments such as this offer both a foundation and a challenge.

Mullah Mohammed Omar, the enigmatic leader of Afghanistan's Taliban regime, remained a shadowy and elusive figure throughout his public life—before vanishing altogether after U.S.-led forces toppled the Taliban in late 2001. Now, more than two decades since the fall of his government, fresh questions have been raised about his current whereabouts and role, as the Taliban regain control of key cities and his name re-emerges with a renewed sense of authority. Omar, who was born in 1959 into a poor family in Kandahar, was long regarded as the spiritual and political heart of the Taliban movement. Despite leading one of the most brutal regimes in modern history, Omar was known to rarely appear publicly, delegating authority to lieutenants and relying on messengers to communicate his decisions. This reclusive nature made him an object of fascination and speculation, even in the world beyond Afghanistan’s borders. After the 9/11 attacks, and the subsequent U.S. invasion, Omar's Taliban regime collapsed. He disappeared from public view, and, to this day, the whereabouts of Mullah Omar remain officially unknown. Over the years, a number of conflicting reports—some suggesting that he died in a Pakistan border area in early 2015, others placing him in hiding in Kandahar—failed to yield any conclusive evidence. Dr. Naomi Curry, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), said that Omar’s disappearance compounded the instability that followed the fall of the Taliban. “When the Taliban was first defeated in 2001, the loss of a leader who was so central to the movement’s identity and strategy created a void,” she said. “But Omar’s eventual return in a political leadership role in about 2006 shows that his image and authority were never truly diminished.” Last month, as the Taliban gained momentum in the south and east of Afghanistan, a statement appeared in Afghan media crediting ‘Mullah Omar’ for authorising strategic military campaigns. Analysts and observers have raised the concern that a figure removed from public life could still wield such influence from behind the scenes. That power, whether as figurehead or as hidden hand, suggests that the Taliban machine is more than just a war machine—it is also a well-organised structure with deep ideological roots. Omar is still revered as a symbol of resistance among many Taliban supporters. His name features regularly in propaganda and in the rhetoric of younger Taliban leaders, who invoke his legacy to legitimise their current rule.

A Scottish man who says he was a victim of abuse by former Crewe Alexandra coach Barry Bennell has warned that child sexual abuse in football may still be far more widespread than currently acknowledged, describing it as a “huge” problem that has been buried for too long. The survivor, who wishes to remain anonymous, spoke out after recent high-profile revelations in the UK, including the recent charges brought against Bennell himself. In an emotional statement released on Thursday, the man recounted how he was targeted in the 1990s while playing youth football in the north of England. “Barry Bennell held the lives of his victims in his hands,” he said. “As a child, you trusted coaches like a family member. When that trust is abused, it’s devastating. And when you grow up with those scars left behind, you constantly wonder how many others were affected, and whether the system is truly listening.” Bennell, who was charged this month with 29 counts of historical child abuse dating back to the 1990s, has long been a figure of controversy in English football. He was expelled from the game in 1994 after child sexual abuse allegations were made against him, but never faced criminal charges. The renewed interest in the case, sparked by book author Phil Cleary and the documentary "The Line of Beauty," has led to at least 40 new victims coming forward and authorities now seeking other suspects who may have facilitated or covered up Bennell’s actions through their own roles in the sport. The anonymous survivor said he is proud to share his story but added that the system has not changed enough. “There are still so many children out there playing football who are being watched and supervised by people who perhaps shouldn’t be in those roles,” he said. “There are whispers about certain clubs and certain individuals, and the fact is we have to be brave enough to shine a light into that darkness.” Sports minister Nigel Huddleston issued a statement to the press, reaffirming the government’s commitment to protecting children in all sports. “We are aware of the deep concern within the football community and have pledged continued support for victims and ongoing efforts to root out abuse at all levels of the game,” he said. Child protection agencies and sports organisations have also been contacted for comment, with Football Association representatives set to appear before MPs in a parliamentary inquiry into the handling of historical abuse in the sport.

The man, who is believed to have been part of a small group of Welsh-based extremists who travelled to fight in Syria, was identified by UK and Syrian government sources as having been killed in an RAF air strike on Sunday. It marks a dramatic escalation in the UK's military campaign against so-called Islamic State (IS) in Syria, and underscores the growing concern over returning foreign fighters. The man, who has not yet been formally named, was known to police but was not under active surveillance at the time of his death. He had previously been arrested in the UK on suspicion of terrorism-related activity, before later travelling to Syria in 2015. According to UK counter-terrorism officials, he was tracked through a combination of intelligence and surveillance, and was identified among a group of IS fighters when photographs emerged after the strike. The strike is believed to have occurred in the northern Syrian town of Manbij, a key IS stronghold that has seen heavy fighting in recent months. Manbij lies on the strategic highway between Raqqa, the de facto capital of IS, and the Turkish border. The UK has been part of the US-led coalition in the region for over three years, conducting hundreds of air strikes against IS targets in both Syria and Iraq. However, the killing of a British national is only the third such reported incident in recent months. The first occurred in September 2015 when a 16-year-old Royal Air Force airman, Farhad Azim, was killed by an accidental strike after being wrongly identified as an IS fighter. The second was Liam Mark Hughes, a 19-year-old Welshman who died in May 2016 after being killed during a joint military operation between UK and Jordanian forces in the eastern Syrian desert. The death of the Cardiff man is understood to have been confirmed by both the RAF and the Syrian government, the latter of which has increasingly allowed coalition air strikes on its territory as part of the fight to dislodge IS. The attack also highlights renewed calls within Parliament for greater scrutiny of British citizens who fight overseas. Concerns remain that some returnees could pose a threat on home soil, particularly in places like Cardiff, which has been identified by MI5 as one such area with a small but active extremist network. Locals in the Capital city have expressed mixed reactions to the news.

Two new polls have revealed that President Barack Obama is leaving office with one of the strongest approval ratings ever recorded for a departing U.S. president, highlighting a dramatic turnaround in public opinion toward the end of his eight-year term. A Gallup survey conducted in January 2017 placed Obama’s job approval at 60 percent — a significant increase from the 48 percent rating he was averaging just a year earlier. Another poll, from ABC News and the Washington Post, also showed him in a positive light, with 61 percent of respondents approving of his job performance. These figures mark the highest final approval ratings of his presidency and place Obama among the most popular presidents in American history who have exited the White House. The upward trend in Obama’s approval is largely attributed to the growing unpopularity of his Republican successor, Donald Trump, who had yet to be sworn in at the time of the polls. A wave of uncertainty and concern over the direction of the country under Trump appears to have pushed more Americans to look back with favor on Obama’s presidency. Additionally, the appeal for unity following the turbulent 2016 election, marked by intense division and high voter turnout, may have contributed to a more positive retrospective view of the outgoing president. Throughout much of his early years in office, Obama’s approval ratings were divided, with strong support from Democrats and resistance from many Republicans. His administration faced criticism over issues such as the Affordable Care Act, the handling of the economy, and the failed attempt to close the Guantanamo Bay detention facility. However, in his later years, Obama’s measured response to mass shootings, his climate accords such as the Paris Agreement, and his emphasis on racial justice — including prominent public speeches following police shootings and the Black Lives Matter protests — helped to reinforce a sense of leadership and moral clarity about which many Americans now feel nostalgic. Political analysts suggest the polls reflect not just a backlash against incoming policies and rhetoric, but also a deeper reassessment of Obama’s presidency as a whole. Historically, final approval ratings for departing presidents rarely exceed 55 percent. For example, Bill Clinton finished at 62 percent, while George W. Bush left with 55 percent. Barack Obama’s 60 percent mark now positions him among the upper echelon of those figures and underscores the complexity of gauging a president’s legacy in the run-up to a change of administration.

A US congresswoman has been shot in the head and six other people have been killed in a brazen attack in Tucson, Arizona. The perpetrator, a 22-year-old man, opened fire at a constituent meeting held by Democratic Representative Gabrielle Giffords, critically injuring the congresswoman as well as a number of unarmed civilians. The shooting, which unfolded at the congresswoman’s office complex on a quiet Saturday morning, has sent shockwaves across the country and raised urgent questions about political violence and gun control. The attacker, identified as Jared Lee Loughner, allegedly opened fire inside the lobby of the Talon gas station and the adjoining office of Rep. Giffords, located in the city’s Harrison Road neighborhood. Several people, including a federal judge and a nine-year-old girl, were also among those shot. The Arizona Daily Star reported that the victims who were not in frontline care and were in stable condition had been released from hospitals, while the congresswoman was taken to University Medical Center in Tucson for emergency surgery. Details emerged in the hours following the attack that painted a picture of chaos and fear. Casually dressed and armed with a semiautomatic pistol, the suspect is said to have calmly walked up to the congresswoman’s meeting as it was in progress. Witnesses described hearing gunshots and seeing people drop to the ground. One customer at the gas station told reporters that the shooter had been “just standing there” before he entered the office, while another described her “heart racing,” as she and other shoppers fled the building. Loughner was swiftly apprehended by local police approximately forty-five minutes after the attack. However, questions have already begun to mount regarding the ease with which the gun used in the shooting was obtained and whether mental health warnings had previously been raised about the suspect. His Apple computer was later revealed to contain a screenshot of the congresswoman’s resignation letter, suggesting a troubling obsession. Rep. Giffords is widely known for her advocacy on national healthcare reform and efforts to reduce the federal deficit. She has represented Arizona’s 2nd congressional district since 2006. Unconfirmed reports have suggested that the shooting may have been motivated by anger over a controversial bill being considered in Congress. As investigations continue, tributes to Rep. Giffords and the other victims have poured in from across the political spectrum. President Barack Obama swiftly condemned the attack, calling the shooting “a senseless act of violence that has left a nation shaken.”

Over the years I have spoken to more chancellors and shadow chancellors than most people of my age (that is not a boast, just a sad fact about my preoccupations). I have asked their opinions on everything from quantitative easing to the national debt to whether or not the furlough scheme worked. And yet, in all that time, there is one question that has never failed to provoke the same fascinated expressions — "What on earth is a ‘journalist’?" This is not a metaphor, nor is it a hyperbolic way of saying politicians find media coverage confusing. They really do seem surprised when, during the course of a gruelling financial interview, I produce my press card and ask them whether the government’s budget is working for ordinary families. Last week, during a particularly melodic session with the shadow chancellor, I was handed a Post-it note with the words "What is a press card?" scribbled in hand. I replied with something about it being a press card — a credential for a journalist in print and broadcast media — and swiftly wondered whether, in ordering puff pastry and a thick cappuccino for the man himself, I had gone a bridge too far. In the world of short attention spans and tweets from planes, it seems that something as basic as understanding who writes the headlines has gone by the wayside. Chancellors, shadow chancellors — often fairly young, and sometimes barely educated in political theory — are often simply not taught about the media ecosystem through which their policies are filtered and transformed. This might explain, in part, why someone recently apologised to me for not knowing my title. It might also explain why a hapless intern had to be quickly dispatched to Google to explain that “reporter” does not, in fact, make me a person with a tape recorder who hangs around railway stations talking to tramps. In fact, I once asked a very senior Treasury official whether he knew who journalists were. He said he thought we were just people who visited the Houses of Parliament and took notes. I did not correct him at the time. I did not want to give him an aneurysm. The lack of basic media literacy is not confined to the political sphere. A recent survey suggests that only 43 per cent of people in the UK can correctly identify that a journalist is a source of news or information, with the vast majority confusing us with public relations officers or opinion pollsters.

The UK’s probable EU referendum has sparked a vibrant and often impassioned debate, with many of the public turning to the BBC to get a clearer picture of what a potential Brexit would mean for their everyday lives. In the past week alone, thousands of messages have flooded in explaining concerns over jobs, trade, and the cost of goods — illustrating how deeply the issue has entered the national consciousness. From small business owners in the north to self-employed consultants in London, the question is the same: What happens if Britain votes to leave? The European Union is currently the UK’s largest trading partner, accounting for nearly half of all the goods and services it imports and exports. If the UK were to break away, trade agreements would need to be renegotiated, raising concerns among businesses about supply chain disruptions, higher tariffs, and an uncertain regulatory landscape. Paul Edgerton, who runs a food and beverage wholesaler in Manchester, contacted the BBC with concerns for his business. “Most of our imports come from continental Europe — France, Germany, the Netherlands,” he said. “We rely on that seamless movement of goods. If the cost goes up or delays start happening, that would hit both our company and our customers.” Equally troubling for consumers is the spectre of rising prices and food shortages, with many viewers speculating on whether British households would feel financial strain. The cost of imported food — estimated at £43 billion annually — and luxury items like wine and spirits are seen as particularly vulnerable. Questions are also being raised about the UK’s relationship with countries outside the EU, with worries that existing trade deals — or the lack of them — could affect global supply chains. Meanwhile, some are arguing that leaving the EU could offer fresh opportunities and greater independence. “I run a tourism agency that specialises in European holidays,” said Sarah Linwood from Norwich. “But the red tape of the EU is part of a bureaucratic nightmare. Leaving might give us the chance to simplify things and focus on what matters.” As the debate continues, the BBC’s response lines indicate a nation grappling with a complex choice. Signals are mixed, but one thing is clear: whatever the result, the way people trade, live, and work is unlikely to remain unaltered. With a decision looming, the public is watching and waiting with bated breath. What is not in doubt is that the outcome will shape the economic landscape for years to come.

A serial criminal who was tackled by a shop owner during a botched axe attack has been sentenced to six years in prison. The incident, which occurred in broad daylight in a quiet suburban high street, ended with the suspect being overpowered by the shop owner before police arrived. The man, identified as 34-year-old Liam Steele, had a long and troubling criminal history, including convictions for burglary, assault and previous violent offences. Steele was arrested a short time later after being treated for minor injuries from his struggle with the shop owner, who sustained a cut to his arm in the fracas. The attack on the convenience store, which took place in the north-west of England, had initially left locals reeling. CCTV footage later released by police showed Steele rushing into the store armed with a large hatchet, immediately heading to the till and demanding money. When the shop owner, Oliver Grant, 53, refused to hand over the cash, Steele raised the axe — a moment when, according to witnesses, Grant acted decisively to halt the rampage. Statements from inside the store later revealed how Grant tackled the attacker, sending the axe clattering to the ground and holding him until officers arrived. “He was a deranged man in there — out of control,” said one customer who remained on the premises. “I didn’t think Mr. Grant would make it out alive. It looked like a scene from a horror movie.” At Manchester Crown Court on Tuesday, Steele was found guilty of attempted arson, assault with intent and aggravated vehicle taking after it was revealed he had targeted the store as part of a series of planned attacks. He had previously been stopped in a stolen van outside the shop, which was reported to the police just minutes before the attempted raid. The prosecution highlighted that Steele had taken key precautions to make the crime appear as if it was a genuine gold heist — including carrying a pair of false beards and preparing a failsafe escape plan using the van. However, Grant’s readiness for such attacks, informed by local warning systems and gang intelligence reports shared between shopkeepers, ultimately foiled the plan. Speaking outside court, Grant was praised for his bravery by both his family and local traders. “Liam Steele had been planning this for days. He thought he knew the streets, the escape routes and the people. But the truth is, you can’t outsmart someone who truly believes the community is worth protecting,” he said.

And so a World Championships that began with metaphorical grey clouds over the sport ended with meteorological dark clouds spilling rain across the Bird’s Nest and Beijing beyond. The atmosphere was electric yet sombre, a fitting coda to a week where the sport of athletics seemed to grapple not just with the brilliance of its world-beaters but with questions of integrity, leadership, and the future of the organisation that governs it. The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) had faced unprecedented turmoil just days before the opening ceremony, with allegations of corruption and ethical breaches dominating headlines. The IAAF President, Lamine Diack, who had led the organisation for nearly three decades, found himself at the heart of a storm involving the handling of drugs testing and the repercussions of that secrecy. Just weeks before, he had appeared before the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), pleading for the organisation and the sport itself to be given time to reform from within. Now, with the world’s eyes on Beijing and thousands of athletes competing under the gaze of a profoundly split public and media, the weight of the scandal loomed ever larger. Inside the Bird’s Nest—renowned for its grandeur and for hosting the 2008 Olympics—the athletes did their best to rise above the noise. Records were broken, rivalries reignited, and new legends were born. Mo Farah added to his legacy with another double, showcasing his extraordinary endurance on the track. The Ethiopian distance squad, as ever, displayed brilliance and resilience, while the American sprinters, including the ever-dominant Usain Bolt, cast an air of gravity over the sprints with their dominance and celebrity. But beyond the tape and the roars of the crowd, the politicians, administrators, and board members of the IAAF navigated a very different kind of race: one of damage control and the fragile hope of redemption. The IAAF Ethics Commission had issued its report the day before the closing ceremony, unearthing more than two years of ‘irregular’ processing of Russian athletes’ biological passports, with Diack at the centre. As the athletes celebrated their achievements, the leaders of the sport stood on the precipice of a choice: whether to allow the governing body to continue unchanged, or to forcefully begin a new chapter with new leadership and sweeping reforms. The rain pouring down over the Bird’s Nest was a reminder—both literal and symbolic—that the day wasn’t just about ending a competition.

At first glance, it was a game jam like any other. A gathering of coders, artists and designers crammed into a university lecture theatre, whiteboards littered with scribbled ideas, laptops glowing under the dim lighting, and the hum of low conversation blended with the sound of keyboard strokes. But this was no ordinary night in the life of the UK’s burgeoning indie games scene. As the clock ticked toward midnight on Saturday morning, a hush fell across the room—something remarkable was about to happen. The event, organised by Code & Coffee, one of the UK's most dynamic independent game development communities, brought together dozens of participants from across the South East of England who had only 48 hours to create a functional game from scratch. From the get-go, the tone was one of excitement and collaboration. Teams were formed by chance encounters—strangers bonding over shared frustrations and ideas in the first 10 minutes of the event. By 10pm, no laptops had been closed, and no one was in a rush to leave. What made this particular jam stand out, however, was the theme: "The Last Night." It was intentionally open—games could take any form, be it short, narrative-driven experiences or action-packed adventures. For many participants, it tapped into something personal. "It got me thinking about endings," said Emma Carter, a 24-year-old game designer and part-time novelist who worked on a surreal puzzle game set in a dreamlike city dissolving into the void. "What’s the meaning of a last night? Is someone going to die, or is it a metaphor for a new beginning?" The theme also resonated with the broader challenges faced by the indie game community—time, resources, and whether their ideas would make it in an industry dominated by big-name studios and AAA titles. Many of the developers present were juggling day jobs and weekend projects alike. For some, the jam was their first real foray into the world of game design. By the end of the first 24 hours, players could be seen testing rough builds of their games, offering feedback, fixing bugs, or waiting for someone to come up with the missing mechanical piece they needed to finish their game. Some were battling technical issues, while others wrestled with the creative pressure of translating abstract ideas into something playable by Tuesday morning. Yet despite the pressure, the mood remained upbeat and friendly.

Two women have been jailed for their role in the tragic death of a seven-year-old girl who died after suffering a catastrophic brain injury. The aunt and grandmother, both from the North-West, were described by a judge as having been "wicked" in their treatment of the child, and were sentenced at Manchester Crown Court on Tuesday. The girl, named in court as “Molly,” was handed over to the pair for a weekend of supervision by her mother, who had struggled with caring for her due to ongoing personal and financial difficulties. During their time together, the child sustained severe head injuries which led to her death shortly after she was returned to her mother’s care. In a harrowing testimonial read out during the trial, a social worker detailed the “pattern of neglect and unchecked cruelty” that Molly had endured during her final days. The women had reportedly subjected the child to physical punishment and emotionally abusive comments, and failed to seek medical help when the girl began to show signs of distress following an earlier fall. Despite a lack of visible criminal intent, the court found both women guilty of child cruelty resulting in death, under Section 1 of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933. The aunt, 39, was sentenced to seven years and six months, while the grandmother, 58, received five years. The judge emphasized the “profound neglect and failure to provide any form of care” by the women, stating that while the jury found no evidence of deliberate intent to cause harm, the consequences of their actions were no less devastating. A family spokesperson said the mother was “devastated” by the loss and thanked the police and social services for their support following the inquiry. “Molly was a bright and loving child,” the statement read. “We mourn her deeply and are doing everything we can to support the rest of our family through this unimaginable tragedy.” Molly becomes another tragic case to highlight the worrying gap between unmet safeguarding concerns and the protection of vulnerable children. Advocacy groups have called for renewed focus on community-based support for families at risk, alongside improved training for those working with children in at-risk environments. An independent review into Molly’s case has been launched to determine what more could have been done to keep the girl safe before the weekend took place. Manchester City Council said it was “deeply sorry” for the tragedy and has pledged to conduct an internal investigation into its social care procedures.

The Tate Modern has unveiled the striking new addition to its South Bank home—a dramatic, pyramid-like tower that will house expansive gallery spaces—just days ahead of its official opening. The £167 million visitor extension, known as the Switch House, rises 32 storeys from the existing Turbine Hall, transforming the former Bankside power station into an even more formidable cultural landmark. Designed by architect Herzog & de Meuron, the same firm behind the original 2000 renovation of the Tate, the new building adds 60 per cent more gallery and exhibition space to the museum and features new viewing platforms, education suites, a public café, and three floors of brand new galleries. Visitors given a sneak preview of the extension described the Switch House as "a bold, modern vision that respects the industrial soul of the original building." The new tower, constructed using a special high-density concrete to withstand the heavy weight of the floors, is connected to the original building through a series of skybridges and stepped terraces offering panoramic views across the River Thames and London's skyline. Director of Tate Modern, Chris Dercon, described the project as "a monumental moment not just for the Tate, but for the future of art in the capital." He said the redesign would allow the gallery to display more of its extensive modern and contemporary art collection and to commission larger-scale works from international artists. “This new phase of the Tate Modern is about expanding our horizons, deepening our connections with new audiences, and reimagining what a modern art museum can be in the 21st century,” Dercon said in a statement. The Switch House is set to officially open on Saturday, and will feature an inaugural exhibition featuring major names from the modern art world, including Anselm Kiefer, Gerhard Richter, and Turner Prize-winning artist Lubaina Himid. The unveiling marks the latest chapter in the Tate Modern’s evolution since its dramatic transformation from a power station to one of Europe’s most visited art museums. Poised to guest nearly five million visitors a year, the new wing is expected to cement the Tate Modern as a global hub for contemporary art for decades to come. With the new galleries, learning facilities, and public spaces integrated into the London skyline, the museum has clearly set the bar high for the future of cultural architecture in the capital. As one art critic put it, “The Switch House doesn’t just house art—it is art itself.”

The London Fire Brigade has recruited an additional 60 counsellors to support firefighters affected by the traumatic aftermath of the Grenfell Tower fire, the Victoria Derbyshire programme has revealed. The devastating blaze, which engulfed the 24-storey building in Kensington on 14 June, claimed the lives of 71 people and left rescue crews grappling with the immense emotional toll of the incident. Firefighters have since spoken out about their mental health struggles, with many calling for greater psychological support from the brigade. The new counsellors were brought in as part of a significant increase in the brigade’s mental health resources in the aftermath of the tragedy. According to the programme, the fire service is now offering dedicated trauma support 24 hours a day, with counsellors working closely with affected crews to help them process what they witnessed. The fire, worsened by safety failures and flammable cladding, has turned Grenfell Tower into a symbol of both resilience and systemic neglect. Firefighters from London and other parts of the UK were deployed to Grenfell, with many of them required to re-enter the burning building multiple times in a desperate bid to save lives. Retired firefighter Bob Adie, who served for 27 years, has said that the sight of human remains in the street as he arrived on the scene was "unlike anything I’d ever seen". The national trauma – both for victims and responders – has prompted calls for long-term support for all involved. London Fire Brigade Chief Operating Officer James Leahy said the brigade was committed to looking after the wellbeing of those who served at Grenfell. "We are putting every resource into supporting our firefighters and their families following the Grenfell Tower incident,” he stated. “This includes access to expert trauma support and regular psychological assessments in the coming months and years.” The programme’s investigation also highlighted concerns that the scale of the fire’s impact on mental health is likely to grow in the coming months. Many firefighters are now experiencing insomnia, anxiety and vivid flashbacks, with some fearing the trauma may affect their ability to carry out their duties. As Grenfell’s victims await a full public inquiry into the disaster, the strain on emergency services remains evident. The 60 additional counsellors are part of sustained efforts by the Fire Brigade to demonstrate its commitment to the psychological wellbeing of its personnel – a reflection, perhaps, of growing awareness around the need to treat mental injury with the same seriousness as physical risk.

British cyclist Steve Cummings claims stunning victory in Tour de France stage seven with dominant solo performance   A delighted Steve Cummings made history on Sunday with a thrilling solo victory in stage seven of the Tour de France, storming up the final climb to win by a commanding margin of over a minute and bring pride to British cycling. TheDee-based rider, riding for Team Dimension Data, showed remarkable tenacity and form on the 216km route from Aire-sur-l'Adour to Hautefort, overtaking the leading group on arguably the most decisive ascent of the stage and maintaining his lead to the finish line. The decisive climb came late in the stage, but Cummings, 34, broke away from the peloton well before the foot of the final hill and set a blistering pace that many others found impossible to match. His dramatic solo escape was the moment the race turned, and as the lights turned green at the finish line, Cummings crossed with his hands raised in celebration—relieved and elated at securing a much-needed win in his long career. “My heart is pounding, to be honest. This is the pinnacle of my career, and I can’t tell you how proud I am of this victory,” Cummings said after the race. “It's a dream come true after so many years in the sport. I've worked so hard, and today everything just clicked.” Cummings' victory marks the first win of the 2019 Tour de France for Britain in the stage race and has sent ripples through the sport back home. The British cycling community has lauded his effort, which included a masterclass in readying a move just before the final climb—an element that had the race commentators惊叹 in awe. The stage, renowned for its hilly terrain in the rolling hills of southwest France, offered athletes the perfect setup for a daring breakaway. Cummings seized the opportunity and showed what can happen when timing, fitness, and courage align. He finished the stage in 5 hours 17 minutes and 19 seconds, crossing the line ahead of his nearest rival, Colombia’s Iván Sosa, who was more than a minute behind. Behind the winners, the overall standings remained largely unchanged, with defending champion Egan Bernal maintaining the lead in the yellow jersey thanks to the team time trial. However, for Cummings, the victory is a personal triumph after a career spent in the peloton chasing glory, and stage seven has confirmed his status as one of the stars of the Tour.

If your dream is to build a billion-dollar business, why not start with what you already love? That's the idea behind a growing number of entrepreneurs who are turning their interests in fantasy, science fiction, and superstardust into billion-pound markets. By building businesses based on imaginative storytelling and immersive worlds, these visionaries are proving that fantasy is far from the stuff of fairy tales — it's the stuff of real success. From role-playing games and online fan communities to NFTs and metaverse experiences, fantasy has become a powerful force in the tech and entertainment industries. One of the most notable examples is the video game company Epic Games, creators of the blockbuster title  Fortnite  — a game rooted in vibrant, fantastical world-building, now valued at over $30 billion. With fantastical battles, customizable avatars, and live virtual concerts, the game has redefined how young people interact with digital worlds — and how companies make money from them. But fantasy isn't just thriving in the digital space. Physical businesses are also tapping in. Multi-billion-dollar ventures like  The Lord of the Rings  intellectual property, now under Amazon Prime Video, continue to generate monumental returns long after the book series was first published in 1954. Meanwhile, global franchises like  Game of Thrones ,  Star Wars , and  Wandavision  have turned humble storylines into unstoppable money machines — with box office receipts, spin-offs, and merchandising fueling growth for decades. For new entrepreneurs, the key lies in what fans already love. Creating businesses inspired by fantasy taps into a deeply human desire — to escape, to explore, to believe in something bigger. As a result, investment in the sector is booming. In 2021 alone, venture capital funding in the "entertainment and media" sector hit $29 billion, the highest on record, with many startups capitalising on the imagination-driven economy. Of course, success isn’t just about imagination — it's also about innovation, business planning, and timing. But for those ready to mix entrepreneurial ambition with a healthy dose of daydreaming, fantasy is no longer a niche — it’s a waiting goldmine. So while you may not have mastered middle-earth academically, you just might conquer a new one with your next invention — forged, no doubt, from a world of your own making. The billion-dollar question becomes: Why not? After all, in fantasy, anything is possible — and increasingly in the real world, it is too.

Burkina Faso Stakes a New Beginning as Long-Suffering Nation Heads to the Polls   Burkina Faso stands on the precipice of a pivotal moment as it prepares for crucial general elections on 29 November, a year that has tested the fragile democratic foundations of a country long plagued by political instability and violent unrest. The elections, the first since the ousting of President Blaise Compaoré — a man who ruled for 27 years until a popular uprising forced him from power last year — represent not just a democratic milestone, but also a chance for the West African nation to reclaim its future under a democratically elected government. The transitional administration, which took over in the wake of the October 2014 unrest that led to Compaoré’s departure, has spent the past year attempting to stabilise the country, following violent riots and the assassination of the former president’s party leader, Zéphirin Diabré. The prime minister of the interim government, Isaac Zida — a former army captain and a figure linked to Compaoré’s regime — has been widely regarded as a strong and capable leader, overseeing the transition and ensuring that the country has not descended into chaos as many feared. “The people of Burkina Faso have shown remarkable resilience,” said one local observer in Ouagadougou. “They have endured a lot in recent years and now they just want peace, security, and jobs.” The presidential and legislative elections will see candidates from several political parties stepping forward, with the coalition in power led by President Pierre Sarkinado Kompaoré — no relation to the ousted former leader — hoping to capitalise on the stability they have maintained over the past year. Kompaoré, who took office as interim president, is widely expected to run for the presidency, though the field remains competitive. Security concerns remain high, however. The country has been hit by a worrying series of jihadist attacks, particularly in the east, where al-Qaeda-linked fighters have targeted security forces and civilian targets. The presidential guard, believed to be loyal to the former Compaoré regime, staged an attempted coup in September, underscoring the deep divisions that still run through the country. In the lead-up to the vote, security has been stepped up across the country, and a state of emergency remains in place. International observers, including representatives from the African Union and the European Union, have been invited to monitor the elections, whose credibility will be judged on whether they can be conducted in a free and fair manner.

For the first time since the massive global tax-avoidance scandal known as the Panama Papers broke in 2016, the secret whistleblower who leaked some 11 million internal documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca has spoken publicly. The individual, whose identity remains unknown, has now gone on record in an exclusive interview with a Swiss-based journalism collective, offering to provide further evidence to tax authorities in exchange for legal immunity. The whistleblower, who worked within the firm from 2006 to 2015, said the decision to leak was taken after witnessing what they called a “systemic disregard” of legal and ethical boundaries. “Mossack Fonseca wasn’t just facilitating tax avoidance—it was enabling money laundering, fraud, and even criminal enterprises under the guise of legitimate financial planning,” the source told the investigative team. The source revealed that the initial leak—spanning over 2.5 terabytes of data—was passed on to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) through encrypted means and carefully selected distribution channels, to protect both the documents and the whistleblower. The resulting international probe exposed over 200 politicians, corporate leaders, and high-profile figures from around the world using offshore structures to hide wealth, evade taxes, or obscure financial misconduct. Now, over five years later, the whistleblower is reaching out to law enforcement agencies with a proposal: in return for anonymity and legal protection, the individual is willing to share additional confidential files and phone recordings that could aid in ongoing investigations. “I’m not trying to make someone famous,” they said. “I’m trying to make sure that justice is served. That’s why I’d be willing to speak with prosecutors and politicians—so long as I’m safe from retaliation.” The leak has already triggered over 500 ongoing investigations across 50 countries, leading to resignations, civil and criminal prosecutions, and significant reforms in financial transparency laws. However, many of those implicated in the scandal have yet to face prosecution, often due to political immunity, jurisdictional challenges, or the complexity of piercing offshore secrecy. Critics have questioned whether the whistleblower’s motives are truly altruistic. Some have speculated that the renewed contact with authorities may be driven by a desire for recognition or financial compensation. However, the whistleblower denied any personal gain, stating they had already paid a “heavy price” in leaving their job and life in Panama. The responses so far from legal authorities have been cautious.

Chelsea captain John Terry is set to enter a new chapter of his glittering career, with manager Guus Hiddink suggesting that the 32-year-old could remain at Stamford Bridge beyond the summer, despite his current contract expiring this June. Terry, who has been a mainstay in the Blues’ defensive line since bursting onto the scene during the 2000–01 season, has long been synonymous with the club. Renowned for his leadership, aerial prowess and tenacity from the back, Terry has represented England over 100 times and is regarded as one of the most successful defenders in Premier League history. Hiddink, who was brought in on a short-term basis after the sacking of Jose Mourinho in December, has stressed the importance of continuity and calm during a transitional period. Terry left the starting XI back in September to play for England, following alleged racism and discrimination in a training ground incident with an assistant coach at the club. The FA cleared Terry of racially abusing Queens Park Rangers’ Anton Ferdinand in 2011, and he later apologised publicly to the Ferdinand family after a separate case involving Raheem Sterling in 2016. Speaking ahead of Chelsea’s next Premier League fixture, Hiddink said: “John has been an incredible captain and leader at this club, and we value his experience and presence. I’m not denying that we have to be careful with his future because of the age and his contract, but there’s no reason to rule out the possibility of him staying.” The sentiment has sparked speculation among Blues’ fans, many of whom are delighted at the prospect of Terry continuing in red and blue. Current players, including young defenders such as César Azpilicueta and John Mikel Obi, have spoken highly of Terry’s influence off the pitch as well as the impact he has had on their development. However, the exact nature of any new arrangement remains unclear. With Terry out of contract, Chelsea are not under any obligation to extend his playing days at the club. Moreover, Terry himself has refrained from commenting on his long-term plans, instead focusing solely on contributing to what has been a strong end to the 2016–17 campaign for the Blues. Terry’s potential continued involvement would come at a pivotal time as Chelsea set their sights on a top-four finish and the prospect of European success in various competitions. If Hiddink does eventually step down, as is expected in the summer, the inclusion of a box-to-box player with the experience and selfless leadership of Terry could prove crucial to stabilising the dressing room during any managerial transition.

In a bold move that has sent shockwaves through the world of football, David Bernstein — former chairman of the English Football Association — has called for the European football governing body, Uefa, to unite with national associations and break away from Fifa, in a bid to boycott the 2022 World Cup. Bernstein, a high-profile and influential figure in English football who served as FA chairman from 2011 to 2013, has dared to voice sentiments that have long been quietly debated behind closed doors. His remarks, which appeared in a BBC interview and were further detailed in an article for the  Guardian , mark one of the most definitive public calls yet for a reorganisation of international football governance and a rejection of Fifa's authority. Bernstein’s vision hinges on the idea that Uefa and national federations should sever ties with the world governing body, replicate the successful format of the European Championship (Euro), and establish a global alternative to the World Cup. He suggested that this alternative tournament could attract major footballing nations and, crucially, take place without the backdrop of many of the controversies that have stained Fifa in recent years — including accusations of corruption, inappropriate working conditions for migrant workers in host countries, and unedifying political and financial decisions on everything from stadium construction to broadcasting rights. “This is not something I’d like to see — it’s something that is becoming increasingly necessary,” Bernstein said, drawing on his long experience in the sport. “We have to ask ourselves: Is Fifa capable of cleaning up its act? And, if not, what is the alternative? We have the teams, the stadiums, the fans, and the talent. We don’t need Fifa to host the world’s biggest football tournament.” His call for a break away comes amid a backdrop of widespread dissatisfaction with Fifa's leadership and the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. There has been significant scrutiny of the small Gulf state's hosting of the tournament, both for its human rights record and the logistics of staging a summer event at a time when temperatures regularly exceed 40°C. While Fifa insisted it had fully addressed these concerns, critics remain unconvinced. Bernstein’s comments have already sparked heated debate. Some within English football circles have welcomed the idea of breaking free from Fifa, citing the organisation's opaque structure and history of corruption scandals. Others, however, have warned that such a move could risk fracturing the beautiful game and open the door for rival confederations to follow suit, thereby endangering the unity of football at the highest level.

The Public Services Minister Leighton Andrews is set to take a conciliatory approach when he addresses council leaders at their annual conference in Swansea today, as calls for greater collaboration between the Welsh Government and local authorities continue to grow. With a long-running dispute over funding and responsibilities still casting a shadow over local government in Wales, the timing of the conference and Andrews’ address could not be more critical. The minister is expected to use his speech to underline the Welsh Government’s commitment to a “working partnership” with councils, many of whom have argued that they are being increasingly stretched under a system of statutory duties without the funding to match. Recent months have seen a number of high-profile tensions, with some councils citing unsustainable financial pressures and difficulties in delivering key services ranging from social care and refuse collection to education and highways maintenance. An agreement reached last year on the Ten-Year Settlement for local government was seen by some as a positive step towards long-term clarity. However, many local government leaders continue to express uncertainty, particularly in light of this year’s budget announcement, in which a relatively modest real-terms increase was offset by rising inflation and the demand pressures posed by an aging population and increasing homelessness. Andrews, a key figure in the Welsh Government’s development of the well-being framework under the Well-being of Future Generations Act, is expected to reaffirm the importance of collaboration in delivering services. “Our national vision – that of a Wales of cohesive, empowered, and educated communities – begins and ends with local authorities,” he has previously stated. “We know the challenges are considerable, but our ability to meet them is what defines not just governance, but the future of our public services.” Council leaders have also raised concerns about the administrative burden placed upon them, with some claiming that their role is being conflated with those of health and fire services, without the necessary clarity or funding to match the expanded remit. A number of Welsh councils have already warned that local government may not be able to function as it does at present without urgent interventions. The tone for the day has been set by officials at the Welsh Local Government Association, who have welcomed the opportunity for dialogue but insisted that the focus must be on practical solutions rather than political rhetoric.

A café owner in Manchester has sparked a heated debate after claiming she will discipline children having tantrums herself if parents are unwilling or too nervous to do so. Sarah Collins, who runs a popular family-friendly café in the city centre, said she was tired of watching “chaos spread” during busy lunch hours as children threw food, screamed or lay on the floor uninterrupted. “I understand that today it feels like saying no to a child is like making a political statement," Collins said. “But if every time a child acts out, a parent just says, ‘we’ll do it later’, the child quickly learns that the outside world will always give in. I don’t like to interfere, but if it’s happening week after week and the parents are visibly stressed and stressed and yet doing nothing, then I have to step in.” Collins, who has run her café for five years, said she had used a gentle but firm approach in the past – for instance, distracting children with small breakfasts or toys if they were upset. However, she admitted she would not be afraid to speak directly to a child to restore some sense of structure. Her comments divide opinion. Lisa Waterhouse, a child behaviour counsellor, raised concerns about unsolicited discipline from adults outside the family. “Children need clear boundaries, but they also need to feel safe and understood. If a café staff member is taking on the role of a parent, it can be confusing and even intimidating for the child. The parent should be the one to manage the situation,” she said. On the other hand, social media has been abuzz with support for Collins. One Facebook user commented: “She’s just doing what so many parents are too scared to do. It shouldn’t be this hard to be a parent in society.” Others spoke of their own childhood experiences with firm discipline and argued it had “helped them become responsible adults”. Collins said she was not looking for praise but simply trying to find a solution. “We run a family café and we want to be welcoming to everyone. But if chaos becomes the norm, no one can relax. I’m just trying to create an environment where parents and children can enjoy their meal – without one being run over by the other.” The café has also updated its terms of service to allow staff to “intervene when necessary”.

Cuba is set to take a significant step into the digital age as Etecsa, the state-owned telecommunications agency, has officially granted approval for artist Vladimiro “Kcho” Reyes to launch the country’s first public wireless internet hub at his art and cultural centre in the capital, Havana. The initiative is considered a landmark in an island long known for its strict control over both the media and communications. The wireless hub will be based at a popular space known as La Cabaña, a contemporary art centre where Kcho, one of Cuba’s most internationally respected visual artists, has long hosted exhibitions and cultural events. While internet access in Cuba remains limited and often costly for the general public, this new public wi-fi station is expected to offer free web access and mark a symbolic shift towards increased digital connectivity—a sector the government has only recently begun to consider opening. Kcho, who is internationally renowned for his large-scale kinetic sculptures and subversion of everyday objects into politically charged statements, described the project as an extension of his mission to drive creativity and open access, even within the confines of Cuba’s socialist framework. “This isn't just about internet,” he said in a recent interview, “it is about connecting people, about culture and sharing ideas. It is a space for the voices of Cubans to be heard and to exist without limits.” The project was facilitated by Etecsa – historically one of the nation's most insular institutions – and reflects a small but telling movement towards modernisation and opening up within the government. In recent years, Cuba has seen the introduction of mobile internet at a state-subsidised cost and an increase in the number of cybercafés. However, internet access remains out of reach for many due to price, infrastructure limitations and government hesitation over the potential for unfiltered information about daily life to travel abroad. The wireless hub represents the first time a public cultural institution will be enabled to offer free wi-fi access to visitors and the wider community. Those who visit La Cabaña will now be able to access guest mail servers and browse the web—an opportunity many Cubans will seize with eagerness. Experts believe the development could be a precursor to broader internet liberalisation in the country, as state planners continue to navigate a balance between economic necessity and political control. “This is small, but it is meaningful,” said Dr. Luis Morales, a researcher at the Pedro Pan American Institute in Havana.

Six people have died after a whale-watching boat capsized off Canada's Pacific coast following a failed attempt to avoid a large breaking wave, in what emergency services described as a "tragic and sudden" incident. The vessel, which was carrying 25 passengers and seven crew, sank in winds of up to 55 km/h and high seas near Tofino on the west coast of Vancouver Island on Friday afternoon. According to local reports, the wave — estimated by survivors to be more than two metres high — struck the boat unexpectedly as it was sailing in a popular whale-watching area. The crew tried to steer out of the wave's path, but the vessel was caught off guard. Several passengers were thrown overboard and into the frigid waters, and despite the swift response from coastal rescue teams, six people could not be rescued and were later confirmed dead. Marine emergency responders, including the Canadian Coast Guard and local volunteer search and rescue units, launched an immediate operation. Twelve people were pulled from the water, with several taken to hospitals in Victoria, Nanaimo and Tofino to treat for hypothermia and other injuries. One of the crew members who survived, a tourism worker in his 30s, described the scene as "like a nightmare" in a televised interview. “It was chaos. The boat just got hit and then it flipped instantly. I remember the sound of people screaming and water everywhere,” he said. “There was nothing we could do — it was just too fast and too powerful.” Prime Minister Justin Trudeau expressed his condolences in a statement late Friday, saying the incident was a “heartbreaking reminder of nature's unpredictable power.” He praised the emergency workers’ efforts and said a full investigation into the cause of the wave and the incident would be carried out. Whale-watching is a flourishing tourism industry in British Columbia, with the area around Tofino and Clayoquot Sound being one of the most popular and accessible parts of the world to see humpback and orca whales. Safety regulations for guest vessels are strict, and boats are required to have life jackets and safety briefings on board. The National Marine Safety Centre is now waiting to see the findings of the Canadian Coast Guard and Transport Canada to determine whether any regulatory violations were involved. Local MP Susanna M. Lorenzo said the community was “deeply shocked” by the tragedy and thanked the first responders for their efforts on the water.

In a culture where long hours and relentless work schedules often define success, sleep — once a universal need — has become a somewhat taboo topic in boardrooms and city offices. For many in the corporate world, how few hours a person sleeps has long been equated with dedication and ambition, even when those hours come at great personal cost. The myth persists: the more sleep you sacrifice, the more committed you are to your career. This toxic narrative is a relic of a bygone era, where the macho culture of Wall Street or City of London trading floors admired the sleepless Wall Street banker who "napped" during a plane ride from New York to London, or the young corporate lawyer who bragged about surviving on four hours of sleep a night to meet a deadline. It has since been parodied numerous times in television and film, where protagonists destined for success shrug off exhaustion with a smirk and a double-shot espresso. But behind the bravado lies a very real public health problem, and scientifically, the idea that sacrificing sleep enhances productivity is not just misguided, it’s dangerous. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to a myriad of health issues, from depression and anxiety to heart disease, diabetes, and even early-onset dementia. Yet, in many corporate environments, admitting you need more than six hours of sleep is akin to confessing weakness. The message from the top has often been clear – if you're truly committed, you’ll work through the night and prove it the next morning with dark circles and a caffeine addiction. Even as global health experts and corporate wellness programs begin to champion the importance of rest, the lingering macho ethos remains. A 2022 UK study by the Centre for Mental Health found that over 40% of employees in high-pressure sectors reported suffering from sleep deprivation, with many attributing it to workplace expectations. "We are talking about a generation who have internalised a belief that rest equals laziness," says Dr. Suzy Carter, a workplace psychologist in Manchester. The tide may be turning, though. More young entrepreneurs are openly advocating for work-life balance, and some progressive firms have removed all-night coding sessions or late-night trading expectations. The question remains, however: how long will it take to convince a corporate world still hung up on a misguided idea of strength that sleep is not a luxury, but a necessity?

A prominent student leader accused of sedition in India has been released from prison following a court’s decision to grant him bail — just hours before his next court appearance. The news has sparked widespread relief among students, human rights activists, and critics of India’s controversial sedition law, who view the case as emblematic of the government’s alleged crackdown on dissent. Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) student leader Kanhaiya Kumar, a 23-year-old Ph.D. scholar from Bihar, was arrested in February 2016 following a speech he delivered during a protest at the campus in New Delhi, which the authorities claimed incited violence. The speech, reportedly in support of a banned insurgent group and critical of the nation’s security forces, resulted in Kumar being booked under numerous charges, including sedition, which carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. The alleged speech and the subsequent arrest turned Kumar into a symbol of resistance against government overreach into campus spaces, with universities and civil society organisations across the country holding protests in his support. However, as the legal case moved forward, many had feared that the charges would persist and that Kumar could remain jailed for some time. On Monday, a Delhi special court granted Kumar bail, ruling that he did not pose a risk to the public order. The court also noted that the prosecution had failed to produce “relevant evidence” to substantiate the sedition charge, and that it was “excessive and unreasonable” to hold him without sufficient grounds. Kumar was released on Tuesday morning and was immediately greeted by cheering supporters and media cameras at his residence in South Delhi. Speaking to reporters upon his release, Kumar expressed relief and praised the judiciary for upholding the rule of law and defending democratic values. “This is a victory for all those who have suffered in the name of nationalism and sedition,” he said. “No citizen should be penalised for expressing their opinion, no matter how critical.” Critics of the government have argued for years that the sedition law, first drafted during British colonial rule in 1870, is increasingly used as a tool to silence political opposition and marginalised voices. Since coming to power in 2014, the BJP-led government has been accused of employing anti-sedition laws against figures in academia, the media, and civil society, raising concerns about the erosion of free speech. Human rights law firm the Centre for Law and Political Education (CLPE) hailed Kumar’s release as a “breathing space” for civil liberties, while the JNU Students’ Union described it as a “momentous step forward in the fight for democratic rights in education”.

The man behind some of Britain’s most iconic and beloved television moments has passed away. Gareth Gwenlan, the former producer of the much-loved sitcom  Only Fools and Horses , has died at the age of 79. Known for his pivotal role in shaping one of the UK’s most enduring comedy programmes, Gwenlan’s death has been met with an outpouring of tributes from fans and industry professionals alike.  Only Fools and Horses , which first aired in 1981, became a cornerstone of British comedy during its 18-year run and has continued to be revered in the decades since. Gwenlan came on board in the show’s final years, serving as producer from 1993 until its conclusion in 2003. Although not the original creator, he played a vital role in maintaining the show’s high standards and ensuring that its signature blend of witty dialogue, character-driven storytelling, and the Del Boy/Terry dynamic remained intact. Gwenlan’s work with  Only Fools and Horses  helped secure awards and enduring popularity for the series. He was also involved in other notable television productions, including  Coronation Street  and  The Robin Williams Show , and was well-respected for his contributions to the industry as both a producer and script doctor. His passing marks the end of an era for those who worked alongside him and for audiences who grew up with his work. In a statement, the production company confirmed Gwenlan’s death but offered no further details. Tributes have begun to flow in from across the media landscape, with many remembering his affable nature and his commitment to quality storytelling. Fans have taken to social media to express their condolences and to share their favourite  Only Fools and Horses  moments, a testament to the lasting legacy of the programme and the people behind it. BBC presenter Sir David Attenborough and other broadcasting figures have also paid tribute to Gwenlan, highlighting the importance of his role in British television history. As tributes continue to flood in, the British public are reminded of the timeless charm of  Only Fools and Horses —a show that, thanks in part to Gareth Gwenlan’s stewardship, remains unassailable as one of the nation’s most treasured sitcoms. His passing leaves a void not only in the industry but in the hearts of millions who will remember his contribution to the art of British comedy. His legacy will live on, not just in the programmes he worked on, but in the joy they continue to bring to viewers today.

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has confirmed that Test openers Alastair Cook and Haseeb Hameed are available to play all of their county matches before England’s first Test of the summer against South Africa in July, ending recent speculation about their international commitments during the domestic season. The announcement comes after months of discussion between the ECB and the England players about scheduling, with particular attention paid to the challenging Test series against India in September and Pakistan in October. Both Cook and Hameed, who are expected to feature prominently in England's top order, can now prioritise their county cricket for Essex and Lancashire respectively during the ICC Cricket World Cup qualifiers and early part of the summer season. The ECB's decision marks a departure from recent policy in which key England players were rested for numerous county matches to maintain their workload ahead of international assignments. However, with the Ashes looming and the need to build continuity for upcoming tours in the Indian subcontinent, the governing body has opted for a more flexible approach. "We have worked hard to strike the right balance between county and international cricket," said ECB national director of cricket Paul Farbrace. "Alastair and Haseeb are available for all upcoming domestic fixtures, and we believe it is in their best interests to be as match-fit as possible going into the summer internationals." The news will be welcomed by both players – Cook preparing for his ninth Ashes series, and Hameed seeking to extend his growing reputation as a promising opening batsman. Cook, who recently announced his decision to keep his contract with Essex for this season, will hope to sharpen his technique in county cricket ahead of the daunting Test series. Meanwhile, Hameed is predicted to continue as England’s first-choice opener under new skipper Joe Root, and his performances in red-ball cricket for Lancashire will be closely watched. The ECB had previously faced criticism for a perceived lack of support for county cricket, with key players increasingly being absent during the domestic season to accommodate international fixtures. This development, though, suggests a recalibration of approach. The first Test against South Africa is scheduled for July 7 at Lord’s, with England then facing a three-Test series in Pakistan in October and early November. With a sustained workload necessary for Test cricket, the ECB’s balancing act between county and international commitments will be under further scrutiny as the season progresses.

Hague Claims Fiscal Reform Enables Tax-Free Pledge   Former Conservative leader William Hague has presented his party’s pledge to freeze income tax, VAT and national insurance as a victory for fiscal responsibility, claiming that by “putting finances back on track” the Conservatives can now afford the long-term commitment of a legislative guarantee on tax cuts. Speaking at a conference in London, the former Foreign Secretary argued that the government’s careful economic management over the past decade has laid the necessary groundwork for the party to eliminate uncertainty for both households and businesses. “With public finances stable and growth returning to the economy,” Hague said, “it is now possible – and responsible – to frozen key taxes in legislation, offering clarity and confidence to British families and employers alike.” The pledge forms a key part of the Conservative party’s platform for the next general election, and would be enshrined in what is known as a “Tax Stability Act.” The piece of legislation, which is expected to be introduced when the party is next in government, would require a majority in both Houses of Parliament to override it in order to raise the affected taxes. Prime Minister Theresa May, who was present at the event, praised the commitment as a continuation of the Conservatives' long-standing focus on economic certainty. “By locking in stability for the people of this country, we are protecting our long-term prosperity from the uncertainty that so often comes with political change,” she said, in reference to the Labour Party’s more ambiguous stance on tax. Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell quickly dismissed the plan as “a gimmick” which masks the Conservatives’ record on inequality and low wages. “This government has increased the cost of living for millions while giving tax breaks to corporations and the wealthiest,” he said. “Putting a stamp on the tax system as unchangeable ignores the crises that people are facing right now.” The pledge is also seen as part of a broader strategy to counter public discontent with the current rate of national insurance contributions, which many in the public and business sectors say have become a drag on growth. A recent survey by the British Chambers of Commerce found that over 60% of small businesses believe national insurance is restricting expansion. Hague, however, warned against rushed reactions to the pledge. He highlighted the caution of Chancellor Philip Hammond, who has made it clear that no specific timeline is attached to the introduction of the Act, and that it will only proceed on the basis of robust economic forecasts.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which vanished in March 2014 with 239 people on board, has entered what Australia’s Deputy Prime Minister Warren Truss described as a “new phase”, as officials admitted that the initial undersea operation in the southern Indian Ocean failed to provide any definitive answers. The announcement came after more than two years of one of the most extensive and costly air and sea searches in aviation history yielded no concrete evidence of the plane's resting place. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB), which has coordinated the search efforts, confirmed that the initial undersea search of 120,000 square kilometres near the last reported location of the aircraft had been abandoned. The focus now turns to a broader and deeper review of all available data, including revisiting the original flight path and satellite communications to refine the aircraft’s likely location. Prime Minister Tony Abbott said in a statement that while the search had been “inconclusive, it was not without value” and has provided “crucial information for future searches of this nature”. He stressed that Australia remains committed to the mission, but acknowledged that new funding would be required if a second phase is to be launched.
