For the families of the victims, many of whom have voiced frustration with the slow progress of the search, the move raises new concerns about the cost and duration of the operation. Laura Hinze, whose mother was on the flight, said: “It’s hard not to feel that they’re pushing the problem to the side and hoping it will disappear. We just want answers.” An international team of experts also weighed in on the situation. Richard Quest, CNN’s aviation correspondent, described the abandoned search as a “massive and frustrating chapter in one of aviation’s greatest mysteries”, while experts at the UK’s Air Accidents Investigation Branch hinted that the next stage of the operation might benefit from a fresh analysis of the aircraft’s possible data. Private consultants and satellite technology firms are also being considered as potential partners in the next phase. Ocean Infinity, a private company equipped with advanced sonar technology, had previously expressed interest in joining the search under a no-find, no-fee agreement, but its offer was turned down in 2016. With updated techniques and technologies becoming more accessible, the search team is now working to determine where and how the next operation might be carried out.

The Dutch team who have grown the world's first burger in a lab say they hope to have a product on sale in five years. It was the moment that changed the way the world thinks about meat: a few years ago, a group of scientists in the Netherlands unveiled the first lab-grown burger at a restaurant near London. Now, they are beginning to look towards the future of food production with optimism and ambition. In an exclusive statement released on Thursday, Mark Post, the lead scientist on the project and a professor at Maastricht University, confirmed that the journey from scientific innovation to commercial viability is under way. "This isn't just a scientific curiosity anymore," he said. "What we made back in 2013 was only the first step in a long process of refinement, cost-cutting and scaling up. We are now working directly with food technology companies, manufacturers and chefs to ensure what we create is not only nutritious and sustainable, but something consumers will truly want on their plates." The ground-breaking burger, which was made from cultured bovine muscle cells, cost around £230,000 to produce at the time. Today, the cost has plummeted by more than 99 per cent, with Post claiming that mass production could bring the price down to as little as £10 per patty. The team, now operating under the umbrella of the Maastricht-based startup Mosa Meat, aims to launch a commercial product within five years. This would mark a major turning point in global food systems and sustainability efforts. The principles behind the innovation are simple but revolutionary: instead of raising and killing an animal, lab-grown meat is cultivated from a few cells taken from a live animal and then multiplied in a controlled environment using nutrient-rich mediums. This eliminates the need for about 90 per cent of the land, 99 per cent of the water and dramatically cuts carbon emissions typically associated with traditional farming. The implications for global food security are immense. With the world’s population set to hit 9.7 billion by 2050, feeding the planet without further exhausting natural resources is an urgent challenge. Lab-grown meat could help reduce reliance on animal agriculture, which currently accounts for 14.5 per cent of all human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization. In the UK, the Food Standards Agency is already reviewing the future of lab-grown meat and other novel food products as part of its science-to-policy team’s forward-looking strategy.

The secret love affair of John Burgoyne, the aristocratic founder of the Fitzwilliam Museum, has emerged from archival shadows 200 years after his death. Known today more for his vast art collections and patronage than for personal scandal, Burgoyne maintained a remarkable and clandestine romance with a Parisian dancer named Marie-Louise Fournier during the early 19th century. Their correspondence, recently uncovered in a private estate sale, reveals a scandalous love story that has long been buried under Burgoyne's respected public legacy. Burgoyne was the son of an earl and, as the owner of one of the finest private art collections in Britain at the time, he became the namesake of Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam Museum in the early 19th century. However, beneath the surface of his carefully cultivated image as a refined cultural benefactor and nobleman, the letters reveal an intense and urgent passion for Fournier, a celebrated dancer in Paris during the early years of the French Revolution. In his letters, Burgoyne hides little of the desire he felt for the dancer. One letter, dated 1803, reads: “You are my soul, my obsession, the only one to whom my grief and joy can be directed. I would live in chains if it were only in your shadow.” The correspondence spans at least three years and often discusses plans to leave Britain, seeking a divorce from his estranged wife and fleeing to France to be with Fournier. Historians believe the affair may have influenced Burgoyne’s artistic tastes. Some of the French romances and works of art he later collected are thought to have been inspired by this period of his life. It was during his time in Paris that he amassed a collection of French art, including paintings by David and Lépere, that were later incorporated into the museum. Fournier, whose family fled to England during the revolution, is believed to have kept contact with Burgoyne for years after the affair, even after his return to England. However, no evidence suggests it was a lasting marriage; instead, it appears to have been a long-distance, emotional affair. She died in mysterious circumstances in 1820, with some records suggesting she may have been the victim of an accident or illness. The discovery of these letters by a Cambridge-based researcher has added a new dimension to the life of one of Britain’s most famous art patrons. “It’s fascinating that someone with such a public identity could lead such a private, romantic life.

The illegal use of Global Positioning System (GPS) jammers in the UK has been exposed in a groundbreaking new study that sheds light on a growing and potentially dangerous trend. Conducted by scientists at the University of Birmingham in collaboration with the Transport Research Laboratory, the research has revealed the widespread and often unnoticed deployment of GPS jammers — devices that interfere with signals from satellites, causing navigation systems, vehicle tracking units and even emergency services to malfunction. The study found that such jammers are commonly purchased online from overseas suppliers, often under the guise of “GPS blockers” or “anti-tracker devices.” They are marketed as tools for privacy or anti-theft protection, but in reality, they are mostly used to evade fleet monitoring, bypass vehicle tracking systems, or prevent location sharing. Alarmingly, the report also noted that some jammers are being installed in rental or commercial vehicles, posing a risk not only to the legitimate users of those vehicles but also to the public at large. Most concerning is the fact that these devices interfere with more than just private GPS equipment. When used, they can disrupt critical infrastructure, including the National Health Service (NHS) ambulance tracking systems, GPS-dependent rail networks, and even emergency response procedures. The impacts can be far-reaching; as the report warns, interference in GPS signals could delay emergency services and compromise national security. Professor Jan Macdonald, one of the lead researchers on the project, said: “This is a very serious and under-recognised problem. It’s not just about people misusing technology for convenience — we’re talking about the potential failure of systems that someone depends on in a life or death emergency. This is effectively digital pollution that can impact the entire country.” The law in the UK explicitly prohibits the use, sale, and possession of GPS jammers under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006. However, enforcement has been challenging due to the difficulty in detecting where and when jammers are being used. The study highlights the need for improved detection technology, alongside a public education campaign and stronger penalties for those caught using such devices. In response to the findings, the Department for Transport confirmed it was reviewing current guidelines and working with enforcement agencies to increase efforts to crack down on GPS jamming. "GPS interference is illegal and poses a serious risk to public safety," a spokesperson said. “We are taking this issue extremely seriously and are working with the relevant authorities to go after those who misuse these devices.”

Pig heads have been dumped outside a disused ambulance station in London, raising concerns over far-right activity and religious tensions, following claims that the building was being used illegally as a Muslim prayer space. The grotesque gesture, which has sparked outrage among local residents and Muslim groups, occurred in the Docklands area, where the former ambulance depot is now reportedly the target of anti-Islam rhetoric. The abandoned heads, left at the entrance on Saturday, are said to be a deliberate insult to both Muslims and Christians, given that pigs are considered unclean in Islam and the display evokes medieval Catholic iconography of animalistic mockery of humanity. Authorities revealed that local residents had previously raised concerns with council officials over the supposed use of the abandoned building as a place for Muslim prayers and gatherings. "While our investigation is ongoing, we are taking the incident very seriously," said a London Metropolitan Police spokesperson. A spokesperson for Hackney Council added that they were "aware of the situation" and working with borough officers and faith groups to address community concerns. "There is no evidence at this stage that the building is being used in contravention of the law," they said. The owner of the building, Thameside Developments, declined to comment directly on the reported use of the site, but confirmed it is currently on the market for redevelopment. The firm also noted that any such use would require official planning permission, which – if granted – could trigger further debate in an area marked by political and cultural sensitivity. Local politicians have voiced their condemnation of the act. Labour Assembly Member Rhoda Clark called it "abhorrent and dangerous," adding, "This kind of provocative activity only fuels division and contributes to the hostility that some communities in our area face." Meanwhile, the Muslim Council of Britain expressed shock at the incident, describing it as "a grotesque act of Islamophobia" and "a clear attempt to undermine the rights of vulnerable and minority groups." This is not the first time that far-right groups have attempted to provoke tensions in the Docklands, where issues of religious freedom, planning law, and community cohesion remain flashpoints. The incident will further inflame fears over the resurgence of anti-Muslim sentiment, which has increased since the Brexit vote. As such, calls are expected to increase for sustained community engagement and stronger policing of hate crimes in the area. The building, resembling an industrial relic, sits in a complex urban landscape where the lines between gothic architecture, neglected infrastructure, and contested social identity blur.

The secret behind Finland’s success in education has long intrigued educators, policymakers, and parents around the world. Despite spending significantly less time in school, facing lighter workloads, and being subjected to minimal amounts of homework, Finnish students consistently rank among the top performers in international assessments such as the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). In the latest results, Finnish students outperformed the majority of their peers across the globe in reading, mathematics, and science. At the heart of this surprising achievement lies a fundamentally different approach to education—one that prioritises quality over quantity, and well-being over academic pressure. Finnish schools operate on a shorter school day compared to many international counterparts, with students attending around 560 hours a year—roughly 200 hours less than in the United States. Moreover, many schools do not start the school day until 9 am, allowing children a full breakfast and extra sleep, which is believed to support mental alertness and learning. Class sizes are deliberately small, allowing for more personalised attention from teachers—many of whom are highly qualified and treated as respected professionals in society. All teachers in Finland are university educated and must complete a master’s degree, regardless of the educational level they are teaching. This puts strong emphasis on teacher training and autonomy, trusting educators to use their best professional judgment on how to teach and assess students, without the need for national standardised tests barring basic assessments in certain years. Equally striking is the amount of homework given to students. In Finland, children as young as eight are not assigned any homework at all. For those in higher grades, homework is kept to a minimum—just a few hours a week at most. Instead of cramming for tests, students are encouraged to explore and be curious. Play and creativity are valued in the learning process, and about an hour of the day is given over to unstructured recess, allowing children to recharge and socialise. What becomes evident when studying the Finnish model is that it does not focus solely on the accumulation of knowledge for the sake of academic performance. Rather, it fosters active and lifelong learning by building students’ confidence, independence, and love of learning. Students are evaluated not just on exam scores, but on their ability to think critically, work co-operatively, and solve problems. This holistic approach has helped Finland rank among the top countries in delivering world-class education, with a system that is as much about equity as excellence.

The start of the Easter holiday weekend is set to trigger one of the busiest car journeys of the year, as around 11 million vehicles are predicted to hit roads across the UK today. The annual trek, known as the “Easter Exodus,” sees millions of Britons travel from and to cities such as London, Manchester, Birmingham and Edinburgh on their way to coastal destinations, countryside retreats and family visits further afield. The expected congestion is a familiar but formidable challenge for drivers, with major motorways, including the M25, M1, M6 and M4, expected to reach capacity early in the morning. The National Rail and Highways Agency have issued advisories urging drivers to plan carefully, leave early and consider real-time traffic updates before setting off. Highways England has deployed additional staff and vehicles to assist with accident responses and traffic management, while the AA has warned of the potential for delays caused by heavy traffic and an increased risk of collisions. “With so many people hitting the road at once, patience is a virtue in these early hours, especially on stretches where motorways merge or narrow,” said a spokesperson for the AA. Despite the expected chaos, the Easter getaway is a much-anticipated event for many. Roadside services report rising demand for food and accommodation, with early bookings already maxing out at popular spots. Coastal towns such as Bournemouth, Southend and Torquay are often the most favoured destinations, but the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales and the Scottish Highlands are increasingly popular for those seeking a quieter break. The Department for Transport said it is monitoring the situation closely and working in partnership with local authorities and emergency services to ensure road safety is maintained. Meanwhile, the Police are reminding drivers to check their vehicles and be prepared in case of breakdowns. For those who would rather avoid the roads altogether, travel by rail has seen a significant increase in demand this year. Network Rail reported that trains between London and the South West and the North have been particularly busy, with additional services and overtime planned for drivers and staff to cope with the influx. As the country braces for one of the most intense periods of road travel, the Easter weekend is once again a reminder of the seasonal challenges faced by road users and the enduring British love of getting away from it all—no matter the traffic. Whether by car, train or even road trip via caravan, this week’s getaway is set to remain as chaotic as it is cherished.

Former Inverness Star Shocks Fans as He Steps Back into Manager’s Role with Caley Thistle   Inverness Caledonian Thistle manager John Robertson has revealed he is still pinching himself after taking the helm at the club for a second time. The 53-year-old, a club legend in his playing days and once regarded as a symbol of the club’s remarkable rise through the divisions, admitted returning to the dugout has been a surreal experience. Robertson, best known for his time as a player and former captain, had retired from football in 2017 and later pursued a career in the media. However, after a number of managerial changes at ICT over the past two seasons, he has been tempted back into football to guide the Highlanders through a challenging period in Scottish Premiership football. “It is absolutely shocking to be back – I never thought I’d be standing on the touchline again,” Robertson told the  Inverness Courier . “When I retired from football, I thought that chapter was closed. But when the opportunity came up, I thought, why not give it a go? This club means everything to me, and I wanted to see if I could give back something in return.” The return has surprised both fans and pundits alike. For years, fans had grown used to watching him pull on the green and yellow from the stands or commentate for live games. But the move, announced last week, has been met with a mixture of excitement and nostalgia. What makes the situation even more intriguing is the fact that Robertson now finds himself in the unusual position of being in charge of a club where his sons, Andy and Jason, have also played – with Andy still a key member of the squad. The younger Robertson recently played a central role in key moments in the most recent league games, prompting speculation about the challenges of the father-son dynamic on the training ground. “It's going to be different,” Andy admitted. “Having dad as a manager is something I have never experienced before. But I have always respected him as a player, as a man, and as a football man. If he's giving me advice, I'm going to listen.” Despite the sentiment, Robertson insists that he will treat every player, including his son, with professionalism and fairness. “There are no special rules when it comes to Andy or anyone else,” he said.

The number of requests for users' personal information from authorities in the UK surged sharply in 2015, with Twitter reporting a more than 100% increase, according to its latest transparency report. The social media giant said it received 5,664 requests from UK government agencies for data on users, up from just 1,988 the previous year. These requests were predominantly from the National Crime Agency and the Metropolitan Police. A total of 4,920 accounts details were handed over, representing a compliance rate of approximately 87% — the highest for any country outside the United States. Twitter's transparency report, which is published annually, reveals the growing reach of law enforcement agencies and government bodies into digital privacy. It highlights that the highest number of requests globally still came from the United States, followed by the UK and then Germany, with the company complying with approximately 60% to 85% of those cases. However, the spikes in British requests have raised concerns among digital rights groups, who argue that the ever-expanding scope of data sharing could threaten the freedom of expression and privacy of users. Despite Twitter's cooperation, the company reiterated its commitment to transparency and user rights in the report. It stressed that it only complies with legal orders and does not proactively share data. "We will continue to push back on national security requests that are overly broad or not based on individualised suspicion," said Twitter’s Head of Civil Liberties and Transparency, Naomi Johnson. However, critics argue that the volume and consistency of requests suggest a troubling normalisation of state surveillance in the digital age. In response to the report, a spokesperson for the UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) stated that all requests must be justified and adhere to legal frameworks, adding that the ICO "provides regular guidance to public authorities on the proper handling of personal data." Meanwhile, advocacy groups like Liberty have called for greater accountability and oversight. "The government should not be allowed to treat social media data requests like an open fishing ground. There needs to be more explanation and more checks to ensure it is not being abused," said an executive with the organisation. The report also revealed global trends, such as a 47% increase in data requests from firms elsewhere, including Microsoft and Apple, highlighting the broader issue of data privacy in the tech world. Yet, in the UK context, the go-to details on potentially millions of citizens have left many questioning just how private online conversations remain in today’s increasingly monitored digital landscape.

Drinking Overindulgence May Spark Skin Cancer Risk, Scientists Warn   A new wave of research has added yet another reason to reconsider heavy alcohol consumption, with scientists revealing that excessive drinking could trigger a cascade of biological events that may leave the skin more susceptible to cancer. The findings, published in a prominent medical journal, come amid growing public concern over the health implications of alcohol consumption, particularly as rates of heavy drinking continue to rise in many Western countries. The study, led by a team of researchers at King’s College London, suggests that alcohol is not just a passive risk factor but could actively alter the body’s ability to repair DNA damage caused by the sun’s ultraviolet (UV) rays. UV radiation is a known cause of skin cancer, damaging the DNA in skin cells and promoting mutations that can lead to cancerous growths. However, the research highlights how alcohol may interfere with the body's natural repair mechanisms, making the skin an even more vulnerable target. Dr Emily Hartley, one of the lead researchers, explained: “When someone drinks alcohol, particularly in excess, their liver begins to process the ethanol. This process generates reactive byproducts, including acetaldehyde and free radicals—substances that can damage DNA. This damage puts added strain on the body's DNA repair system, which is already busy coping with UV-induced mutations. If this system is already weakened by alcohol, the cells are less able to protect themselves, and cancer may be more likely to develop.” The study builds upon previous research linking alcohol consumption to a higher risk of skin cancer, particularly melanoma, the most dangerous form. While the findings are preliminary, they suggest a potential “domino effect” in the body—starting with the drink and culminating in cancer. Researchers are now calling for public education to highlight the skin-related dangers of alcohol, particularly among young people who are more likely to drink heavily and sunbathe simultaneously. The research also raises important questions about the cumulative effects of alcohol and sun exposure, particularly in social settings where drinking and sunbathing often go hand in hand. Dr Hartley warned: “If you drink a few glasses of wine during a day at the beach, you might not be doing your skin any favours. Alcohol could be making the damage sustained from the sun much worse.” Experts are currently urging the National Health Service (NHS) and health charities to revise public health messaging on sun protection to go beyond sunscreen and include warnings about alcohol consumption.

The British and Irish Lions will take to the field in their first Test against New Zealand with the same starting line-up that comfortably defeated the Maori All Blacks 32-10 at Whangārei on Saturday. A confident mood surrounds the squad as they prepare for the pivotal clash in Auckland on June 2, with head coach Warren Gatland making no alterations following the dominant midweek victory. The decision signals strong faith in the players who delivered a display of composure and physicality in the face of a spirited provincial challenge. It was a statement win that underlined the Lions’ readiness for the might of the All Blacks, the most successful team in Test rugby. Gatland revealed after Saturday’s match that regardless of the result, no changes would be made ahead of the series opener, saying: “We’re going to go in with the team that performed well against the Maori, and we’ll stick with the plan. These guys have earned the right to start.” The breakfast, as it is known to the Anglo-Irish playing group, features captain Alun Wyn Jones in the second row alongside Maro Itoje, with Northampton Saints’ Tommy Seymour and DTH van der Merwe offering consistent threats on the wings. In the backline, Stuart Hogg continues at full-back, while Glasgow Warriors' Finn Russell returns to the fly-half position after recovering from a minor knee knock. Russell’s inclusion has been a pivotal moment in the tour, as his creative flair and set-piece kicking add vital dimensions to the Lions’ tactical arsenal. The decision to keep the team unchanged has also sparked debate among rugby analysts, with some suggesting Gatland may consider reshuffling his pack should the All Blacks’ physicality prove a match for the Lions’ forward unit. However, given the team’s performance in recent matches and their ability to dominate key phases against the Maori, the coach has seemingly struck a balance of confidence and control. Gatland added that the key to the series is maintaining composure in the opening 20 minutes of the Test matches, saying: “They (New Zealand) have been great at capitalizing on any early weakness, and we have to start how we ended against the Maori. We have to be resilient.” The players, meanwhile, are relishing the opportunity to take on the world champions, with Johnny Sexton telling reporters: “We’ve done the hard work in the preparation, and now it’s time to show our character.

Hillary Clinton’s withdrawal from the 2016 US presidential election in the wake of the unresolved controversy over her use of a private email server while serving as secretary of state is now more than a political calculation — it is a full-scale retreat, with implications that will reverberate far beyond the Democratic party. The former first lady and former senator, who once appeared the clear frontrunner for the Democratic nomination, has now stepped aside in a dramatic reversal that leaves the field open for her more moderate rival, former Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, John Kerry. The decision comes days after FBI Director James Comey announced further classified documents had been uncovered relating to her use of a personal email account during her tenure in the Obama administration — the same issue that first sparked controversy in 2015. Despite numerous denials and assurances from Mrs Clinton and her team that the emails had been appropriately vetted and de-classified, public trust in her handling of the sensitive information continued to erode, particularly in an election cycle where transparency has been a defining issue. Statements from cybersecurity experts and bipartisan concern within Congress have only added fuel to the fire, reinforcing the perception that the issue was not just technical but deeply political in nature. Mrs Clinton’s decision puts pressure not only on her campaign but also on the Democratic National Committee, which must now reckon with the fallout of its most prominent candidate bowing out at the 11th hour. While her allies argue the decision was made in the spirit of “uniting the party” and focusing on defeating the “dangerous” Donald Trump, others have described it as a strategic surrender in the face of an unforgiving media narrative. The White House, which was initially cautious in its response, has refrained from endorsing Mrs Clinton publicly since the scandal broke in March — a departure from previous crises where President Obama often shielded his allies. Officially, the administration has denied any coordination in the timing of her exit, but sources close to the White House suggest the decision to not publicly rebuke the FBI’s new disclosures was intentional. For now, the focus shifts to Mr Kerry, a three-term senator and former secretary of state, whose own record on national security issues could come under increased scrutiny as he steps into the spotlight. With just two weeks remaining until the Democratic primary contest concludes, the path forward is clouded for both the party and voters who had hoped the race would remain as clear-cut as Clinton-v-Trump.

In a raw and poignant open letter that has begun to spark debate online, a Scottish teenager has addressed her parents, both of whom struggled with drug addiction, revealing how their choices shaped her more than she could ever have imagined. The 19-year-old, who only disclosed her name as “Emily” for privacy reasons, wrote the letter after years of dealing with the consequences of growing up in a household where addiction was the defining feature of daily life. The letter, posted by her on a social media platform, details both the pain and unintended lessons she learned as a result of her parents’ struggles. “I never wanted this life for them, but I don’t hate them for it. I’m grateful,” she wrote, adding that the experience gave her resilience, independence and a deep understanding of the fragility of family and life’s unpredictability. Emily, who now lives with her grandparents, stated that the emotional toll of growing up with an absent, unreliable presence at home was hard to articulate. “We never knew if dinner would be on the table at the right time, if we’d have a warm house or be left in the cold. I watched my parents fight over the next hit instead of fighting for a future for us,” she wrote. But as much as she griefs for what she lost, there was something else that she tried to convey in her letter. “I’m not denying the heartbreak, the fear, and the loneliness. But I’ve learned that life is not sunshine and rainbows. It’s messy. It’s uncertain. And it’s okay to carry the weight of someone else’s choices without letting it define you.” Her words have struck a chord with many across the country, with some praising her for her courage and maturity, while others have called for more systemic support for families struggling with addiction. One parent from Glasgow, who chose to share her own experience anonymously, said: "Emily's story isn’t unique. So many kids grow up like this, but not all are able to speak up. Her letter gives voice to those who might not know how to explain what they’re feeling." Addiction charities have also weighed in, with one national representative highlighting the importance of such stories in the wider conversation about substance misuse. "There’s a tendency to focus on the victim and the substance, but rarely do we consider the ripple effects on those who live with it every day," the spokesperson said.

Catalans Dragons delivered a stunning performance as they surged to the top of the Super League table with a commanding 42-6 victory over the struggling Hull KR at the Matmut Stadium. The Dragons ran in an astonishing seven tries, showcasing their class and putting to bed any notion that their recent success was a fluke. The result leaves them just two points behind league leaders St Helens, who suffered a shock defeat to Wigan Warriors on Thursday. From the first whistle, Catalans asserted their dominance, with Timani scoring the opening try in the 11th minute to set the tone for what would become a masterclass in rugby league. The Dragons' slick passing, electric pace, and clinical finishing left Hull KR reeling, with another four tries in the first half alone. Eliesa Katoa and Joel Tomkins both crossed the line twice, while Denny Solomona extended the lead with a solo effort that drew cheers from the home crowd. Hull KR managed only a late consolation through Brian Carney, in his emotional testimonial match, as the visitors found themselves overwhelmed by both the physicality and tactical precision of the Dragons. The defeat marks the third successive loss for Keli Ratuniyarawa’s side, who now sit deep in the relegation battle with only 12 points from 13 games. For Catalans, however, the match reinforced their credentials as genuine title contenders, and with key players in form and fitness, coach Laurent Frayssinous will be optimistic about their upcoming fixtures. The team’s blend of experienced internationals and emerging stars has created one of the most cohesive and versatile squads in the league. The victory also came with a personal milestone for hooker Sam Tomkins, who surpassed 200 career tries in the Super League. The 29-year-old pulled the strings for the majority of the match, orchestrating much of Catalans' attacking play and displaying the calm and composure that have long defined his game. With just a handful of matches left in the regular season, the race for the top four is heating up. Catalans will look to maintain their momentum as they prepare to host neighbours Toulouse on Saturday in what promises to be another highly anticipated clash of sides from the south of France. Hull KR, meanwhile, must regroup quickly if they are to avoid a prolonged run of misery. The Dragons' emphatic win is a stark reminder of the parity required to thrive at the highest level of rugby league, and it sets the stage for a thrilling finale to what has already been a thrilling 2024 campaign.

The future of a key UK-France border crossing point is under threat as the Brexit process looms, with former French prime minister and current presidential hopeful Alain Juppé now facing more questions over France’s stance on cross-Channel trade and security cooperation. A close ally of the centrist candidate has told the BBC that the border post in Calais is “definitely” set to close once Britain has formally left the European Union. The comments come amid escalating frustrations from French officials over the so-called “calais migrant crisis” and the perceived lack of control over the border post in the wake of Brexit. The situation adds yet another layer of complexity to the already tense relationship between the UK and France as both countries weigh the economic and security implications of Britain’s eventual exit from the EU. Calais, home to an infamous migrant camp on the edge of the Channel Tunnel terminal, has long been a focal point in the EU-wide migrant crisis. Despite numerous sweeps and removals by French authorities, the encampment has refused to disappear, inflating tensions between the two countries and putting extra strain on the port’s notoriously busy transport infrastructure. The closure of the UK border post would leave just three remaining posts available for UK-bound freight – in Dunkirk, Dieppe, and Le Havre – raising concerns among freight companies in both countries about potential delays and financial losses. For the UK government, which already faces the daunting task of negotiating border and trade arrangements post-Brexit, the prospect of an additional border bottleneck between Calais and Britain adds yet more complications to an already uncertain future. There are also fears that the full extent of the crisis has not yet been borne out, with local authorities in Calais pointing to the need for continued cooperation with UK and EU officials in dealing with the migrant influx. Stéphane Le Foll, a key figure in Juppé’s campaign and currently serving as French minister of agriculture, has not gone into specifics about the exact timing of the proposed closure but has insisted that the process will begin once the Brexit negotiations are underway. “It is a strategic decision that France must take as it is a sovereign country,” he said. “The border is a national issue, and after Brexit, we cannot allow that situation to continue as it always has.” Juppé, who currently leads in various polls among the centrist and centrist-left candidates vying for the presidency, has yet to officially comment on the statement from his close ally.

The father of a teenager whose life was cut short in the 1989 Hillsborough disaster was told in harrowing detail on Thursday how the “failures of others” ended his son’s future before it had fully begun. At the inquiry into the disaster, which claimed the lives of 97 fans during an FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest, the grieving father was visibly moved as he recounted the profound loss of his son. The inquest, now in its second week, has heard emotional testimony from families and former officials, pulling back the layers of blame and systemic failure that led to the tragedy. The man, who has not been named for legal reasons, described how his son, a passionate Liverpool fan and a bright young man with aspirations in engineering, was crushed during the match at Sheffield Wednesday’s stadium. “The dreams he had, the path he was on, all of that ended because of the failures of others,” he said, his voice breaking. "We lost not just a son, but a future — in a matter of minutes, the course of our lives was changed." The inquest has been examining the events of that April day in 1989, when a human crush developed in two standing pens at Hillsborough, leading to the tragic deaths of 97 fans, predominantly men, women and children from Liverpool. The inquiry is assessing the decisions made by South Yorkshire Police, emergency services, and the football authorities in the hours leading up to and after the disaster. Previously, the inquiry heard from senior South Yorkshire Police officers who, in some cases, gave conflicting testimonies about the flow of emergency services to the scene and their understanding of the unfolding tragedy. Much of the inquiry's focus has been on the delays in opening the gates that could have relieved the overcrowding in pen three at Leppings Lane end of the stadium. In his statement, the father said his family had not been adequately informed of the seriousness of the situation until long after the initial emergency. “We had to find out through the radio. No one called us. No one came with answers. We had a telephone call saying he had been taken to hospital, but when I got there I was told it was over. That’s how we learned our son was dead.” The inquest is expected to span several months, as it continues to deliver a comprehensive account of the disaster and the wider implications for stadium safety in the UK.

The collapse of BHS – one of Britain's most iconic high street retailers – accelerated on 25 April, when the company entered administration, leaving nearly 11,000 employees in limbo and triggering widespread outrage over years of mismanagement. The administration came as the latest twist in a saga that had depressed morale among staff and alarmed outsiders who had long questioned the ownership decisions that placed the company on an irreversible path to self-destruction. The day before the administration was announced, BHS’s administrator, Retail Acquisitions, penned a letter to customers that briefly outlined the company was facing "financial challenges" and would be consulting with employees. But by the following morning, it was clear that the store was not closing temporarily to restructure, but was effectively shutting its doors for good. Employees were told abruptly to leave the premises, and branches were handed to union representatives who locked them up, preventing administrators from opening the stores. In an emotionally charged statement, Steve Morgan – the former British Thai Restaurants chief and sole owner of BHS for the past seven years – admitted the role he had played in the retail group's demise. Morgan, who sold the firm to himself in 2009 for £1, and borrowed £125m as part of the complex deal, said he understood the frustration of employees and customers, but insisted it was a "path I had no choice but to take". He blamed poor trading and the aging store estate, as well as a lack of support from staff, for the company’s troubles. But Morgan’s admission did little to quell the fury of Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who branded him a "rogue businessman" and demanded urgent government action to save jobs and protect the £571m pension deficit. Trade unions reacted with fury, as did BHS employees, many of whom worked for the company for decades without receiving regular raises or job security. Members of the GMB Union held protests outside Parliament and Morgan’s former home, calling for justice for those left financially ruined by the collapse. The BHS crisis has drawn comparisons with the collapse of LL Bean and the recent insolvencies of Debenhams and Bensons for Beds, but the scale of the administrative disaster and the sheer number of lives affected has placed the company at the heart of a political firestorm. A prominent Muslim cleric is currently under investigation in connection with the murder of Qandeel Baloch, one of Pakistan’s most high-profile social media influencers and celebrities, Lahore police have confirmed. The cleric, who has not yet been named, is suspected of being linked to the 26-year-old’s husband, Noor-ur-Rehman, who has been identified as the prime suspect in her killing. The case has once again drawn attention to the pressures faced by women in Pakistan who challenge traditional norms, particularly through the use of social media. Qandeel Baloch, whose real name was Fouzia Azeem, gained national and international notoriety for her bold persona and open discussions on gender equality, arranged marriages and religious conservatism. Her death on 14 July 2016 sent shockwaves across the country and beyond. Her body was found in the district of Dadu, in southern Pakistan, after she was allegedly strangled by her brother-in-law. She had been missing for several days, with her husband initially claiming she was missing due to an “honour” issue, before admitting he had been involved in her killing. Despite the arrest and subsequent conviction of her killer in a lower court, many in civil society and women’s rights groups have called for a re-examination of the case, noting what they describe as a cover-up by local authorities. Now, with police alleging new links between the cleric and the murder, questions are being raised over whether wider networks of support were involved in Silencing her. Lahore police director Shafique Hussain stated that the cleric in question is also being investigated over claims that he provided advice to the killer on how to stage the murder and avoid detection. The cleric is being accused of using religious rhetoric to justify the act, a claim that, if proven, could spark further controversy given the role of fundamentalism in Pakistani society. Qandeel’s murder has been widely seen as emblematic of the cruel treatment women often face in the name of ‘honour.’ Her posts frequently challenged conservative values, making her a polarising figure. Yet her death has sparked a broader debate about women’s rights, press freedom and the limits of free expression in the country. As investigations restart, pressure is mounting on the government to ensure the case is handled with full transparency and that no powerful figures are shielded from accountability. For many, the case is not just about one woman’s tragic death — it is a symbol of the country's struggle to reconcile modern individual freedoms with entrenched social and religious traditions.

A Thai court has issued an arrest warrant for a senior Thai army officer over his alleged involvement in the trafficking of Rohingya migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh, in a case that has reignited diplomatic tensions and raised serious concerns about human rights abuses in the region. The officer, who has not yet been officially named by authorities, is accused of orchestrating or playing a key role in the smuggling of Rohingya people, who have long been victims of persecution in their own countries. The announcement comes amid growing international pressure on Thailand to confront reports of widespread human trafficking along its borders, where Rohingya and other migrant groups are often subjected to forced labour, sexual exploitation or detention in squalid conditions. The alleged involvement of a military official is particularly contentious, given the army’s powerful role in Thai politics and its previous dismissive response to accusations of complicity in such crimes. The warrant was issued following an investigation into a network of traffickers who allegedly turned migrants into commodities, assembling them onto boats and sending them out to sea—many of which have been intercepted by the Thai navy or have capsized, resulting in mass drownings. Survivors have told harrowing stories of beatings, confinement and ransom demands. The case is being handled in a closed-door special court in Bangkok, a procedural choice that has drawn criticism from human rights groups, who demand greater transparency. Justice for Migrants, a Thai NGO, has called for the trial to be made public, saying it is crucial for accountability and for preventing the cover-up of state involvement. The unfolding scandal also risks straining Thailand’s already sensitive relationships with Myanmar, which has accused Thailand of harboring refugees, and with Bangladesh, which has borne the brunt of a massive exodus of Rohingya following periods of violent crackdowns in Rakhine State under the previous regime. The arrest warrant is a rare move against members of Thailand’s elite military class, whose past links to human rights abuses have often been shielded by political impunity. It marks one of the first legal actions taken against senior officials over the migrant crisis, which the United Nations has described as one of the worst humanitarian and human rights disasters of the decade. The Thai military has yet to issue a formal response to the warrants, but previous statements from the agency have typically denied any systematic collusion with-traffickers.

A Celebration Like No Other: The Edinburgh Commonwealth Festival Steps Into the Spotlight   Under a sky promising rain but delivering only a string of sparkling moments, the heart of Edinburgh pulsed with music, colour, and an unmistakably Scottish sense of whimsy as the £1 million Commonwealth Children's Appeal kicked off in a riot of tartan, bagpipes, and self-deprecating good humour. The festival, hosted on the cobbled corners of the city with a backdrop of neo-Gothic grandeur and a nod to centuries of Scottish storytelling, wove together history, light-hearted banter, and heartfelt cause in a way only the Scots seem to manage. Pipers lined the walkways, their melancholic tunes mingling with the squeaks and giggles of dancing teacakes — a quirky nod to Scotland's eccentricities — while Scotty dogs, the beloved rescue charity emblem, wagged and barked alongside the crowd. One of the most talked-about moments of the evening was, predictably, the much-publicised "gay kiss." Though marketed with the same nonchalance as a bagpiped rendition of  "Close the Door, It's Cold Outside,"  the kiss, delivered between two dancers in kilted attendance, drew cheers and a few mock gasps from the onlookers — a reminder that Scotland, while known for its endurance, is also known for its unstoppable – and irreverent – spirit. Yet, beneath the bonhomie was the deep-rooted sense of purpose that has driven the appeal. The event, backed by a coalition of celebrity performers, politicians, and local businesses, is a direct effort to support children across the Commonwealth countries most affected by conflict, poverty, and environmental degradation. So far, the campaign has raised more than £750,000 in about four weeks, largely through the sale of the now-iconic tartan laces and a series of online auctions featuring Scottish art and memorabilia. Local singer-songwriter Kate Young kicked off the musical performances with a soul-stirring rendition of "A Man's A Man For A’ That," the traditional Robert Burns poem, bringing the audience to a rare, solemn silence. Other highlights included a rollicking chorus of "Flowers of the Forest," with Edinburgh locals joining the performers on stage in full Highland regalia, and a set by the Young Scots Piping Academy, their youthful energy lighting up a smog-violet evening. The event was also interwoven with Scotland’s history, past and present. A chronological storytelling session displayed the nation’s journey from the Wars of Independence to the 2016 Brexit fallout, delivered with the dry wit that has long defined Scottish political discourse.

The justice committee wants to ensure the new funding model is "as objective and proportionate as possible." A former judge and a university economics professor should sit on an independent panel to help the Home Office shape a new funding model for police forces in England and Wales, a parliamentary committee has said. The announcement follows a report by the House of Commons Justice Committee, which urged greater transparency and fairness in the distribution of police funding. The government plans to replace the existing A16 formula, which has sparked significant criticism for failing to reflect the differences in local policing needs. The committee said the formula "perpetuates inequities" and risks underfunding areas facing greater crime challenges. It argued that bringing in experts with no connection to political or policing structures would add an extra layer of impartiality to the process. In their report, the committee recommended the creation of an independent advisory panel, which should include a former judge, an economics professor, and a representative from the public. The panel would then advise the Home Office on a new funding formula and assess any transitional support needed for forces affected by the changes. "This isn't about adding red tape," committee chair Sir David Lammy told the BBC. "It's about ensuring that the funding model is as objective and proportionate as possible. Local needs vary, and so should the funding." The current A16 funding method, which blends factors such as population size, property value, and crime rates, has come under fire from police authorities and MPs alike. Forces in cities such as Greater Manchester and London have been advocating for a more nuanced approach that accounts for rising costs, such as inflation, increased crime rates, and demand on emergency services. The committee also highlighted the importance of clear and consistent dialogue between the government and police forces as the new model is developed. Ministers have yet to commit to a timeline for the review, but the Home Office said in response to the report it would "fully consider the recommendations and continue to work with local police and partners to improve the funding process." As debates over police funding grow more intense, the proposed independent panel initiative is seen as a potential breakthrough in addressing years of strain on local resources and public confidence in the policing system. With the general election looming, the issue is likely to remain a focal point of political discussion.

Luis Enrique accepts blame after Barcelona’s Champions League humiliation by Paris St-Germain   Barcelona manager Luis Enrique has taken full responsibility for his side’s catastrophic 4-0 defeat at Paris St-Germain in Tuesday’s Champions League clash — a match that has left the La Liga champions on the brink of an embarrassing early exit from Europe’s premier competition. The Catalan giants, who had long been considered among the bookmakers’ favourites for a clean sweep of all major trophies this season, were outclassed at the Parc des Princes, with PSG securing a commanding victory to take a 5-1 aggregate lead going into the second-leg at the Nou Camp next week. The result has sparked renewed talk of Barcelona’s transition period, with key players such as Neymar and Lionel Messi both missing due to injury and squad rotation concerns. Speaking in his post-match press conference, Enrique, who was appointed in the summer after a successful player career for the club and previous stint as manager, said: “This is a very difficult moment for me personally and for the whole team. I have to take full responsibility for the result. As a coach, I have to find the right solutions, and tonight we failed.” Enrique, who has previously guided Catalans to La Liga and Champions League glory as a player, was visibly frustrated as he elaborated on the tactical shortcomings. “It is clear that we did not show the same intensity and organisational structure that we need to compete at this level. We did not manage the match well, and the blame lies with me,” he said. The defeat was all the more alarming for Barcelona given the circumstances surrounding the squad. With European football returning after an international break, the players have continued to rotate as Enrique looks to manage fitness across all competitions. However, there is now a question mark over whether key players will be available to face the French side at the Nou Camp — or whether they should be rested for the league title race and upcoming domestic cup finals. Speculation has begun to mount over whether the treble-winning manager will retain his position should Barcelona fail to progress to the Champions League quarter-finals. With recent struggles in European competition — including a 2-0 defeat to Real Madrid in the 2014 final — fans and pundits alike have questioned whether the club have lost their grip on the trophy.

Ryan Day believes a strong showing at the World Snooker Championship could prove to be a decisive turning point in his career after earning a return to the world’s top 16 for the first time since 2015. The 38-year-old, who claimed the title in Sheffield in 2001, has enjoyed a resurgence in form over the past 12 months and regained the ranking he had previously lost due to a decline in results in recent years. Speaking ahead of the event, which begins next week, Day said a successful run at the Crucible was “a big plus” for his confidence and standing within the sport. "It’s been a long time coming, so getting back into the top 16 is a great achievement," Day said. "In order to establish yourself solidly there, you need to win titles – and what better place to pick one up than the world championship? It would give me a real springboard into the next stage of my career." The world’s top 16 players earned their automatic spots for this year’s championship, meaning Day’s qualification was a key goal over the last season. He currently ranks 16th in the world, up from outside the top 20 at this time last year. Day will fancy his chances in Sheffield, where he has previously progressed to the semi-finals and is no stranger to high-pressure situations at the iconic venue. However, the journey to the final is expected to be arduous as he will likely face off against some of the game’s biggest names, including defending champion Mark Selby, Ronnie O’Sullivan, and Judd Trump. "The level of competition is going to be very high, but I feel as prepared as I’ve been in years," he added. "That doesn’t mean I expect to walk away with the trophy, but the fact that I have the chance to be in this position is very satisfying." Day’s resurgence follows a challenging spell in which he dropped out of the top 16 and struggled to maintain consistency. He credited a change in mindset and a renewed focus on long-term success as key factors in his return to form. The Welshman pointed to his run to the semi-finals of the 2023 UK Championship as a sign of what he is capable of when he is at his peak. "It’s not just about the points on the board," he said.

In a rapidly evolving media landscape, the question of which organisation holds the most influence in shaping public perception and delivering news is increasingly complex. With the rise of digital platforms, the decline of traditional gatekeepers, and the growing power of social media, it is no longer certain that a single newspaper, television channel, or broadcast network can claim the title of the world’s most powerful media organisation. However, one entity that stands out in terms of reach, influence, and capacity to shape global discourse is Google. As the world’s search engine leader, Google wields unparalleled power in determining which news stories reach the public. Every day, billions of people turn to Google to find the latest updates on politics, conflicts, and world events, trusting the search engine to deliver relevant, reliable information. Google’s algorithms, which decide what users see at the top of their search results, play an immense role in shaping the narrative around global issues. In this way, the company is often regarded as the "gatekeeper of the internet" — a position with profound implications in the distribution of news. But is Google a news organisation in the traditional sense? While it does not produce news in the same way as The New York Times, The Guardian, or BBC News, it has become inseparable from the circulation of news. Google News, a feature within its ecosystem, aggregates and ranks headlines from all corners of the globe, effectively determining which stories are amplified and which are buried. This means that, while the raw content may come from other outlets, the power to determine what the public reads lies with Silicon Valley. When comparing this influence to that of traditional organisations, the contrast is stark. The BBC, for instance, has an esteemed reputation for journalistic integrity and a global audience, but it is funded by the public through a licence fee and is not nearly as pervasive as Google. Similarly, Bloomberg, the financial news giant, is powerful in its domain but lack the universal reach of Google. The power of the platform is unarguable. Google’s dominance in search gives it the ability to shape not just news consumption, but also the public understanding of the world. In democratic societies, access to accurate and diverse news is a cornerstone of informed decision-making. As such, Google's ability to prioritise which content comes to the fore can act as a de facto editorial policy — with no transparency for the public.

Glen Campbell — the golden-voiced country music icon whose smooth melodies and grinning charm made him a household name — passed away at the age of 81 after a long battle with Alzheimer’s disease. Throughout a career that spanned over five decades, Campbell maintained a remarkable consistency in both his music and public persona, becoming one of the most successful and enduring figures in American country music. Born on April 22, 1936, in concatenation with North Carolina and Tennessee’s backcountry pulse, Glen Milon Campbell emerged not as a rocker or a balladeer alone, but as a true chameleon of the American music scene. With three number one Billboard singles per decade from the 1960s to the 1980s, his career was marked by an almost uncanny adaptability. He captivated audiences with the twang and heartfelt lyrics of "Rhinestone Cowboy," an anthem for every free-spirited nomad, and wove tales of love and heartache in classics like “Wichita Lineman” — a song often hailed as one of the greatest in pop music. Campbell’s combination of effortless vocals and pleasant, approachable image helped him cross genres with ease. He was a member of the original  Nashville Sound , a production style that brought a more polished, mainstream feel to country music at a time when audiences were evolving along with their tastes. Yet, his appeal was not confined to the conservative heart of country radio; his work was embraced equally by rock fans and casual listeners, and he even co-starred in several Hollywood films, including his Oscar-nominated role in  The Rose  (1979). Despite his immense fame, Campbell remained remarkably grounded. Performing over 200 shows a year in his later decades, he often remarked that “people should come to listen to the music and not be bored.” That philosophy is perhaps best represented by the enduring series of  Goodtime Hour  television specials, where he hosted legends like Dolly Parton and Johnny Cash with his trademark humility and warmth. His stage show was a blend of country, rock, and even pop, always elevated by his crack band and his unassailable stage presence. In 2011, the world was touched by the release of the documentary  I’ll Be Me , which chronicled the man’s early decline as he struggled with early-stage Alzheimer’s. Instead of hiding from the public, Campbell and his family offered a deeply intimate portrait of a fighter who remained devoted to his fans and his music.

Two cyclists were taken to hospital after suffering injuries in separate crashes during the RideLondon-Surrey 100, an amateur cycling event that attracts thousands of participants from across the UK and beyond. The incidents, both of which are currently being investigated, occurred along the 100-mile route that winds through central London and into the Surrey countryside, and highlighted concerns about safety at one of the country’s most popular cycling events. The first crash happened in Wandsworth, when a male rider in his 30s fell off his bike while descending a slight incline. Emergency services were called to the scene and the cyclist was taken to St. Thomas’ Hospital for assessment. Witnesses described how the rider appeared to lose control before crashing into the gravel shoulder of the course. The second incident took place near Esher, where a teenage rider, believed to be in her early teens, was involved in a fall in a quieter section of the route near a forest path. Paramedics attended and, after assessing her condition, she was taken to a nearby NHS trust for observation. Her condition is reportedly stable, and family have been informed. RideLondon, organised by the charity organisers behind the Tour de France, is designed primarily for amateur cyclists and puts strong health and safety measures in place. Event officials confirmed today that there was no sign of third-party involvement in either incident and both crashes are being treated as isolated cases of rider falling. Lucy Mitchell, spokesperson for the event, said: “We are aware of the two incidents and are working closely with event partners and the cyclist families to provide all necessary support. The health and safety of our participants is always our priority.” There have been calls on social media for a review of the event's marshalling and signage, particularly at areas where the route includes uneven or narrow paths. Organisers have assured participants that all areas of the course are regularly inspected and considered safe for a recreational cycling event. As is standard for amateur events of this scale, all participants are encouraged to wear helmets, check their bikes before the start, and remain alert during the ride. Emergency response units are deployed at regular intervals along the route to deal with any incidents as swiftly as possible. Both riders who were injured are expected to make a full recovery, but the incidents serve as a reminder of the potential risks even in well-organised, road-closed cycling events.

The New Zealand government is preparing for a new kind of wilderness – one where tens of thousands of kiwi birds roam freely through native forests, far from the confines of predator-controlled sanctuaries. According to a newly released conservation strategy, there could be 100,000 wild kiwi on the mainland within 15 years, provided the plan is fully funded and implemented. Currently, kiwi populations are severely restricted due to threats from introduced predators such as rats, stoats and feral cats, which are responsible for the deaths of thousands of chicks and eggs each year. As a result, most kiwi conservation efforts have focused on offshore islands and fenced sanctuaries, where predator numbers can be kept to a minimum. However, these enclosures have now become the birds’ de facto home, limiting their numbers and natural dispersal. Environment Minister David Parker called the plan “the most ambitious in our history for a single native species.” He said the proposal – dubbed "Kiwifruit Freedom 2030" in initial drafts – aims to create safe corridors of land, or “kiwi highways,” that allow the birds to breed and forage without human intervention. “We need to move from small, managed pockets of land to large, self-sustaining wild populations,” Parker said in a statement. “If we can get this right, we will no longer be just trying to save kiwi from extinction – we will be restoring them as a keystone species of our ecosystem.” The plan involves a significant investment in predator control technology, including the use of automated traps, poison bait stations, and new biosecurity strategies. Local communities are already being invited to participate through hapū and iwi-led conservation projects, with some areas being identified as priority zones where kiwi translocations could begin as early as next year. The Department of Conservation (DOC) has also tapped into recent advances in genetic technologies, which could enable scientists to better identify and support the most genetically diverse kiwi populations to ensure long-term survival. However, the plan has sparked debate among conservationists. Some have welcomed the ambition as a bold step towards ecological recovery, while others have expressed concern about the feasibility of scaling up protection efforts to such an extent. “This is a very optimistic vision,” said Julianne Grigg from the Bird Life Society. “But without a vast increase in funding and public support, the risk is that we overextend the system and fail more birds.” Kiwi numbers have been in slow but steady decline since the 1950s, with estimates suggesting fewer than 70,000 birds remain in the wild today.

A senior Metropolitan Police officer involved in a high-profile operation during which a man was shot dead is to retire from the force, despite currently being under investigation in relation to the incident, it has emerged. The officer, whose identity has not yet been disclosed, is understood to be a long-serving commander within the force, with a distinguished record in operational and leadership roles. The revelation has sparked fresh calls for accountability within the Met and raised questions over whether the department is attempting to sidestep scrutiny before conclusions from the ongoing investigation are made public. The man, who was shot during a police operation in London earlier this year, had died from his injuries. The incident led to tense exchanges between residents in the local area and officers, with some members of the community expressing concerns about the use of lethal force and the conduct of the operation. The Met is currently conducting its own independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding the shooting and the roles played by individual officers. It is now being reported that the senior officer in question is being allowed to step down under terms which may be tied to his retirement, rather than being required to remain in post for the duration of the inquiry. Sources told  The Times  that the decision is being made in order to avoid impacts on morale or public perception as the investigation unfolds. However, critics have dismissed this as an excuse to remove the officer from active duty rather than ensuring full transparency. “If this officer is being allowed to leave while still under investigation, it sends a signal that the Met is not fully committed to the principle of accountability,” said one independent policing adviser. Questions remain about the officer’s role in the decision-making process during the operation, including whether they gave the go-ahead for the use of firearms, and whether existing protocols and oversight procedures were followed. In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “It is not unusual for officers to retire during the course of an investigation, depending on the nature of their role and the stage of the process. All ongoing investigations are being managed independently, and we do not comment on individual cases while they are ongoing.” The killing has added to ongoing scrutiny of the Met’s firearms procedures and use-of-force policies, particularly in the wake of a series of controversial incidents involving the police in recent years.

The Olympic Games have long been a global celebration of athleticism, unity, and national pride. However, one event—the sport of tennis—has always drawn a degree of controversy when it comes to its place on the Olympic calendar. Critics have long questioned whether a sport with its own lucrative Grand Slam tournaments—drawing millions in prize money and broadcast revenue—belongs in an event designed to transcend commercial interests and foster amateur ideals. Yet despite these concerns, tennis remains a popular and eagerly anticipated part of the Olympics, with the world’s top players vying for gold in a demonstration of their elite skills and international spirit. ATP and WTA Tour stars, including the likes of Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Serena Williams, have taken to the Olympic stage in recent years, often treating it as one of the most prestigious achievements in their careers. Tennis made its Olympic debut in 1896 in Athens but was dropped after 1924 and only re-introduced in 1988 in Seoul, after much behind-the-scenes negotiation. Since then, the sport has re-invented its Olympic presence, drawing huge crowds and immense global viewing figures. The decision to allow professionals to compete in 1988 was a significant one, and one that bridged the divide between amateurism and professionalism—principles central to the Olympics but often irreconcilable in modern sport. Many experts, and indeed fans, have long debated whether the Olympics should host tennis. The argument against it is rooted in the belief that the four Grand Slam tournaments—Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open—constitute the pinnacle of the tennis world. These events carry far greater financial stakes and prestige than any Olympic appearance, and top players often make it clear that they would not compete unless the timing fit with their Grand Slam schedule. However, the Olympics offer something else: a unique and unifying platform that cannot be matched by even the most glamorous tennis tournaments. The celebration of sport for the sake of sport, the shared experience of athletes from different nations and backgrounds, and the emotional intensity of representing one's country are reasons enough for many players to compete. As Djokovic said ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics: “Playing for your country wears a different hat. It's a huge honour.” The question around whether tennis truly belongs in the Olympics may go unresolved. But as long as the world’s best players continue to step into line in hopes of that green and gold medal, its place on the Olympic programme seems secure—for now at least.

The all-female Los Angeles trio Haim took an unconventional four-year break between albums — and they had an unusual answer when fans first asked where the follow-up to their acclaimed 2013 debut  Days Are Gone  might be. “Dinosaurs,” they responded, bemusedly at first, but the word stuck. As it turns out,  Dinosaurs  was more than just a clever punchline — it became the title of their eagerly anticipated second studio album, released this week. The band, composed of sisters Alana, Danielle, and Este Haim, has built a reputation for crafting shimmering indie-pop with a soulful undercurrent, but with  Dinosaurs , they seem to offer something different, something bolder — and perhaps a little more personal. Despite years of speculation and a string of much-anticipated singles, the path to  Dinosaurs  was not without its challenges. Haim spent much of the intervening years touring relentlessly, playing to sold-out crowds across the world, which made finding time to write and produce the new material incredibly difficult. The album’s gestation was also compounded by the immense pressure of following one of the most critically acclaimed debut albums of the 2010s. Danielle Haim, the band's primary songwriter, has spoken about the emotional toll of the silence in interviews. “I was so afraid of repeating ourselves,” she said recently, in reference to the self-doubt that crept in as the clock ticked and their fans waited. “I didn’t want to make a record just for the sake of music. It had to mean something to us, and to them.” The result is  Dinosaurs , a ten-track album that leans more into their blues and rock roots while maintaining the band’s signature harmonies and rich instrumentation. From the thumping drums and seductive guitar rifts of the first single, “Millis” — written as a tribute to the late producer Danger Mouse, with whom the band worked extensively on the album — to the defiant high-fashion anthem “Summer Girl,” the new material shows a band pushing beyond their comfort zone. The album’s title is symbolic as well. “Dinosaurs” as a metaphor for being out of place, trying to find your footing in a constantly shifting world, feels spot on in 2017 — not just for Haim, but for many artists seeking authenticity in a streaming-era music industry. And for fans, the wait was no disappointment. As one of the most successful breakout acts of the 2010s, Haim proves on  Dinosaurs  that growth comes with patience — and that sometimes, a four-year hiatus, metaphorically framed by the existence of ancient creatures, can produce the most unexpected kind of rebirth.

Boris Johnson has ramped up his campaign for the UK to leave the European Union, warning of what he described as a "slow and invisible process of legal colonisation" as EU influence spreads into all areas of British life. Speaking at a pro-Brexit event in London, the Conservative Party leader argued that the UK is becoming increasingly powerless on its own soil, with Brussels dictating the terms of policies that affect everything from food regulations to urban planning. "Just look at it — policy by edict, not by debate; laws formulated far from the public eye, often without the consent of elected representatives," Johnson said during his speech. "This is not what a free people should accept. We are losing control. That is the truth of it." The comments come ahead of a planned referendum on EU membership, with Johnson and other high-profile Brexit advocates calling for the vote to be held within the next year. The current Prime Minister, David Cameron, has steadfastly supported continued EU membership, but pressure from within his own party has grown after recent polls showed a tightening race, with opinions shifting in favour of the leave campaign. Johnson, the Former Mayor of London, painted a vivid picture of the EU’s grip on UK sovereignty, citing examples of legisla­tion regulating the size of bananas and the curvature of asparagus as evidence of an overreaching bureaucracy. "We are told these are negotiating ploys — they are not," he said. "These are the symptoms of a system that no longer respects national boundaries or democratic will." He also attacked the European Court of Justice (ECJ), comparing it to a "high-powered judge who dictates to every town mayor and every village councilor across the UK what they can and cannot do." Johnson called for the UK to repatriate all EU laws and place them in the hands of its national Parliament. "We must restore the right of our people to have laws they can understand, and not ones written by faceless officials in Brussels," he said. The remarks are the latest in a series of hard-hitting speeches by Johnson warning of what he calls the "irreversible" loss of democratic control under EU rule. His message resonated strongly with Conservative backbenchers and members of the public who have grown increasingly frustrated with the lack of tangible benefits from the EU while facing the cost of red tape and regulation.

Junior doctors marched through central London on Saturday in a show of defiance against proposed changes to their contracts in England, marking one of the largest demonstrations of the year in a long-running dispute that has gripped the healthcare sector. Organised by the British Medical Association (BMA), the protest saw thousands of medical professionals, trainees, and student supporters take to the streets, waving banners and chanting for the government to abandon what they claim are "dangerous and unrealistic" reforms to their working conditions. The proposed contract, which was first published last year by NHS Employers and the Department of Health, has been strongly opposed by junior doctors, who argue it undercuts their pay, erodes protections around working hours, and places them at greater risk of being forced to work during unsocial hours without proper safeguards. Central to the row is the so-called "night shift" bonus – an increase in pay for unsocial hours in exchange for giving up other entitlements, including the ability to opt out of on-call responsibilities if agreement is reached. Opponents say the deal would force junior doctors to work 11,000 extra hours a year, risking both their well-being and patient safety. Health Minister Ben Gummer, speaking earlier this week, reiterated the government’s stance that the new contract is "vital for the long-term future of the NHS" and will bring services into “the 21st century.” But he faced withering criticism from the protesters, who see the changes as an attack on their professional autonomy and their rights as workers. One participant, Dr. Sarah Smith, a junior doctor at St George’s Hospital in Tooting, told BBC Radio 4’s  Today  programme: “These are not just policy changes – these are being rammed through without our consent. We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for the same standards the public expect from their NHS.” The dispute has already led to strikes in several parts of the country, and it is feared that further industrial action could be on the way if the government and BMA fail to find a resolution. Emergency services have raised concerns about the potential for strain on already under-resourced hospitals, with some waiting times already creeping past the 11-hour threshold for accident and emergency departments. As the protest continued into the evening, the mood among the marchers remained resolute.
