For the junior doctors, the message was clear: they will not accept a contract unless it is negotiated through direct talks rather than imposed unilaterally.

Jordan Seiler loathes outdoor advertising. The 42-year-old software developer from Sheffield has spent the last six years campaigning against the billboards and posters she believes sully skylines, distract drivers, and degrade public spaces. Her crusade has taken her from local council chambers to Twitter war rooms, where she has become a prominent voice in the anti-ads movement. “They’re just noise,” she said in an interview at a community café. “Visual pollution. If you walk outside and see a massive ad for a bank or a gym or a soft drink, nothing relevant to the people who live there, it’s just… wrong.” Her objections aren’t purely aesthetic. Seiler, a self-described data-driven activist, cites studies linking road-side advertising to increased reaction times among drivers, as well as the overwhelming tide of ultra-targeted, digitally-served ads that now permeate public life. A world where ads can track your movements, your habits, and even breakfast preferences—this is what alarms her. “It’s not just about what’s on the posters,” she said, sipping green tea from a reusable cup. “It’s about the message it sends, and the way it keeps us in a constant cycle of consumption.” Her efforts recently scored a significant win: in November, the city council voted to limit new advertising hoardings in sensitive green zones. Local activists say it’s one of the first such decisions in the UK and a beacon of hope for communities trying to reclaim their streets. Seiler was thrilled. “This is the first step, but there's still a long way to go,” she said. Yet she insists this isn’t just a local issue—“It’s a human issue.” In an age where digital surveillance is considered the norm, she believes stripping away the physical remnants of advertising is key to reclaiming our mental and communal space. “If you can take one billboard and make one square mile of the city a little bit quieter, a little bit kinder, isn’t that worth it?” she asked. For now, Seiler continues her work with a small but growing group of volunteers, touring the city with a camera, document waiting hoardings for removal, and quietly changing the narrative of what a public space should look like. её outrage may seem minor in the grand sweep of environmental and political campaigns, but for those who share her vision, the goal is clear: one day, no more ads—not on posters, billboards, or in digital screens that follow us home.

The Eagles of Death Metal performed on a Parisian stage for the first time since the mass terrorist attacks that rocked the city in November—appearing to “resume their gig” as a powerful act of defiance and solidarity. The band, which was playing at the Bataclan concert hall when terrorists opened fire, killing 89 people and injuring many more, returned to the same city for a haunting and emotional performance at L’Olympia music venue. A hush fell over the crowd as the band, led by frontman Jesse Hughes, who was among those present at the Bataclan when the attacks occurred, began the concert with a moment of silence to remember the victims. “I made a promise to the 89, and to the families and everyone that night, that we’d be back,” Hughes said before the show. The performance, part of their “Driven to Tears and Death in Paris” tour, was an unmissable symbol of resilience. Fans waved French and American flags and sang along to songs from the band’s early career, including classics such as “I’m the One Who’s on Fire” and “Opening Month.” Hughes himself waved a tricolore bandana and appeared visibly moved as the two-hour set unfolded. The concert followed grief and healing, as well as a global outpouring of support for Paris in the wake of the November 13 attacks. The Eagles of Death Metal became an unexpected symbol of both vulnerability and strength that night. It was their very presence as casualties of terrorism—and then their return—that captured the world's attention. Organisers said the event was planned with the full support of French authorities and aimed to send a message of hope and unity. “This is a night to reclaim music, to reclaim Paris,” said one promoter, who wished to remain unnamed. Security was significantly heightened for the event, though the band had insisted on going ahead. Jesse Hughes, whose band had been playing barely 100 yards from the Stade de France, where over 100 people were also killed during the coordinated attacks, described the experience as one of the most difficult moments of his life. “We lost people that night, people who just came to enjoy some music. That should never be taken from anyone,” he said. The band’s return to Paris marks a small but significant step in the city’s long road to recovery. For Eagles of Death Metal, it is about more than a performance—it is a promise fulfilled and a tribute to those who will never be forgotten.

Premier League summer transfer spending tops £500m — but still behind 2023 figures   English football has already witnessed £500 million in summer transfer spending as the transfer window progresses, but clubs are still trailing last year’s £835 million outlay as the 31 August deadline looms. With just under four weeks remaining, the Premier League’s spending rate suggests this summer's market will not match the frenzy that defined the previous window. According to figures compiled by Sky Sports, the staggering sum represents a mix of domestic and international business, with clubs splashing the cash during a season of uncertainty following the political upheaval in the UK and questions over the league’s financial model. Among the most notable moves has been Manchester City’s acquisition of Kylian Mbappé — who, despite interest from Real Madrid, has made the Etihad Stadium his new home for a fee widely reported to be in the vicinity of £200 million. However, details of the agreement remain undisclosed. Meanwhile, Arsenal and Liverpool continue their rivalry for the signing of Inter Milan’s Andrea Cambiaso, a 28-year-old Italian midfielder whose £180m price tag has put both clubs into a bidding struggle. In contrast to last summer’s record spending, when the war in Ukraine and domestic inflation did not appear to impact club finances, this year has seen a more cautious approach from many Premier League clubs. Top-flight teams have been more selective, prioritising strategic positions and long-term depth over high-profile, iconic names. “Clubs are acutely aware of what’s at stake beyond this season. They’re not just thinking about the European Cups or the Champions League table — they’re thinking about the next five years,” said renowned football agent Simon Phillips, who spoke to the  Telegraph . “This is a different landscape. Finance is still king, but now it’s a question of sustainability.” As expected, clubs with new owners and ambitious strategies have led the way in the market, with West Ham and Leeds United among those ramping up their budgets. Both have been linked with several Championship stars as they look to bolster their squads for an immediate push into the Europa League. Meanwhile, the financial impact of the player academies and the English Football League’s (EFL) new financial regulations also appear to be playing a role in the more measured pace of transfers.

Wales captain Sam Warburton has backed his long-time team-mate and legendary forward Gethin Jenkins to take charge in a potential leadership reshuffle as the Six Nations champions prepare to face Argentina in a pre-World Cup warm-up clash. The 36-year-old Jenkins, widely regarded as one of the greatest props in rugby history, has vocalised his interest in the captaincy role ahead of the 2015 Rugby World Cup in England, should Warburton wish to step down. The fly-half, who has led Wales in 51 of his 90 caps and starred in their Grand Slam-winning Six Nations campaign last year, has not ruled out relinquishing the captaincy. Jenkins, who has earned 121 caps and made his debut in 2003, has left the national team to consider captaining the British and Irish Lions next year and said in a BBC interview that he "deserves a look" at the Wales post, too. Warburton, speaking after Wales’ training session at the Vale of Glamorgan Training Centre, said he has no issue with Jenkins taking over. "If that’s what Gethin, the coaching staff and the WRU are looking for, then I’m all for it," Warburton said. "It would be brilliant for the team. Gethin has got tremendous experience, personality – he’s been a fantastic servant to Wales, and he’s got huge respect across the squad. It would be good for the whole team if he was in that role." The prospect of Jenkins leading Wales is not without controversy. While Jenkins is universally respected for his performances and professional attitude, some rugby experts have suggested that the Wales captaincy should remain in the hands of a more central player, such as Warburton or centres Jonathan Davies or Steve Harris. Others argue that the role of captain is increasingly about leadership off the pitch, and that Jenkins is ideally placed to offer the kind of calm, experienced presence that Wales have come to rely on. Warburton, for his part, said he would focus on performing well as a player if Jenkins was appointed captain. "I’ve always been a team player, and I’m not one for being precious about being captain. The most important thing is we keep the momentum from the Six Nations and the recent World Cup qualifiers and deliver something amazing this autumn," he said. The match against Argentina is one of three warm-ups ahead of Wales’ first World Cup pool game in October.

A leading fertility charity is urging the Scottish government to increase the number of free IVF cycles available to couples struggling to conceive, from two to three, in a significant boost to efforts to support families. The call by Scottish Fertility Partnership (SFP) comes amid rising concerns that the current provision—offered through the NHS in Scotland—may not be sufficient to give couples the best possible chance of success. Currently, couples are entitled to up to two full cycles of in vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment, provided they meet certain criteria relating to age, medical need and fertility history. However, SFP argues that in many cases, a third cycle could significantly improve the odds of achieving a pregnancy, particularly for older women or those with complex fertility issues. "Two cycles is the minimum, not the maximum," said Fiona Simpson, Chief Executive of SFP. "For many couples, accessing a third cycle of treatment could be the difference between giving up and having a baby. We’re asking the government to look at increasing support so that no one is forced to halt their dream of starting a family simply because of financial hardship." The charity’s call is backed by recent research from the Scottish Fertility Board, which indicates that up to 12 per cent of women undergoing IVF in Scotland are having to turn to private clinics for third or subsequent treatments, often at a cost of £6,000 or more per cycle. This, it adds, disproportionately affects low-income couples and those in employment with limited sick leave, who may not be able to afford the financial or emotional toll of repeated out-of-pocket expenses. Scotland also has one of the lowest fertility rates in Europe, with the average age for first-time mothers now above 30 and increasing numbers of couples facing difficulties conceiving naturally. Meanwhile, NHS services across the UK are under pressure as demand for reproductive treatment grows. SFP is part of a cross-party campaign calling for “parity of esteem” between mental and physical health, with fertilisation treatment increasingly regarded as a healthcare need rather than a service option. The charity has written to Scotland’s First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Health Secretary Jeane Freeman, asking for an urgent review of current IVF entitlements. A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: “We take the provision of fertility treatment seriously and have supported research and innovation in this area.

A Buddhist Nun Speaks Out: The Election of Pope Francis Brings Pain, Not Joy   “I see a lot of joy and celebration for Pope Francis, but I'm living his election with a lot of pain.” These are the words of Ven. Tenzin Palmo, a prominent British-born Tibetan Buddhist nun who was recently quoted during an interview on a London Buddhist radio station. Her haunting statement has reignited a wider conversation not only about the Catholic Church’s stance on women and social justice, but also about the complex relationship between global religions and the shared journey toward inclusivity and change. Tenzin Palmo, who trained under Tibetan lamas in India for more than 30 years, is known for the harsh, 12-year meditation retreat that she endured deep in the Himalayas. She left behind a life of relative comfort to pursue the spiritual path, and her journey has made her a global advocate for Buddhist women and nuns. Yet it is her recent reflections on the election of Pope Francis—one of the most visible and celebrated religious milestones of the 21st century—that have drawn so much attention. Francis, the first non-European pope in over a millennium and a vocal champion of the poor, has been praised for his humility and transparency in leading the Vatican. His decision to reject the grandeur of traditional papal living and live simply in a small apartment rather than in the papal palace, for example, has been widely applauded. His outspoken stance on poverty, environmental issues, and even the Church’s role in education and social welfare has resonated with many who have previously felt alienated by institutional religion. But for Tenzin Palmo and others who advocate for a more inclusive and equitable religious landscape, his election has not brought universal joy. "When I see about Pope Francis," she said in her interview, "I’m watching this man who is a tremendous reformer, and it makes me think—how long have we waited for transformation in our own traditions, in our own religious structures, and how slowly it comes?" Her pain, she says, is not a rejection of all reform, but a recognition that change is uneven and that many groups—women, minorities and spiritual seekers of all faiths—are still waiting for the same kind of transformation to reach their own religious institutions. The irony, she points out, is that while the Catholic Church elects a new leader with a message of compassion and simplicity, other traditions—Christian and non-Christian alike—are still battling for the same kinds of reforms Francis has introduced.

The Dartford Crossing, one of the UK's busiest road tunnels and a vital artery for freight and commuter traffic, has long been identified as a key hotspot for pollution. However, recent BBC investigations have revealed a startling omission: data on local air quality at the crossing has been deliberately excluded from official government assessments — due to the bizarre classification of the nearby M2 as a "rural" road. This decision has sparked outrage among environmental campaigners, who argue that the A2/M2 area, which handles over 130,000 vehicles a day, is one of the most polluted places in Southeast England. Locals and healthcare professionals in the surrounding areas have repeatedly raised concerns over high levels of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, which are linked to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. The National Clean Air Day website confirms the levels of pollution around Dartford, but the Environment Agency, which is responsible for monitoring air quality zones, has not listed the area as a hot spot. This is because the M2 has been designated as "rural" — a classification usually reserved for stretches of motorway or minor roads far from population centres. One environment agency source told the BBC that the designation, which dates back to a 2011 assessment, leaves as much as £1.3m in potential funding on the table to address the pollution problem. “This feels like a way to avoid facing the reality of what’s happening in one of the most congested parts of the country,” said Tom Nelken, a campaigner at Transport for London. “The M2 might technically be classed as rural, but in terms of its function and the surrounding population, it's anything but.” Residents of nearby areas such as Higham and Northfleet have long reported abnormal health symptoms, including persistent coughs, headaches, and skin rashes. Steve Milburn, who lives just 500 meters from the tunnel, said: “You can smell that diesel fumes even when it's raining. It's never not there, and for local children playing outside, it’s disgraceful.” Under EU and UK laws, the government is required to take all necessary steps to reduce air pollution in areas that exceed national objectives. If accurate data had been included for Dartford, it would have been designated a "nitrogen dioxide nitrate hotspot," potentially triggering urgent mitigation measures such as installing air quality monitors or implementing clean air zones. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) said in a statement that air quality decisions were based on existing guidelines and were due to be reassessed at the end of 2019.

Tributes have poured in for a mother from Caerphilly county who has been confirmed as one of the victims of the recent deadly terrorist attack in Tunisia. The local community has paid heartfelt homage to Eleri Davies, 42, who was enjoying a family holiday at the Sousse resort with her husband, Andrew, and their two teenage children when gunfire erupted last weekend. Ms Davies, who worked as a social worker in the Rhymney Valley area, had been known for her warmth, dedication, and commitment to helping others. Local residents, colleagues, and friends took to social media to express their grief and admiration, describing her as a “beautiful soul” and a “tower of strength.” A spokesperson for her school said: “Eleri will be immensely missed by the entire community. Her compassion and kindness were legendary. Our thoughts and prayers go to her husband and children at this unimaginably sad time.” A vigil is expected to be held at the weekend to mark her life, details of which will be announced by local authorities. The Foreign Office has confirmed that five British citizens have been killed in the attack, the deadliest incident to hit UK tourists in decades. Prime Minister David Cameron condemned the attack in the strongest terms, adding that the UK would “not be cowed by terrorist threats.” Ms Davies’s family has asked for privacy as they come to terms with their loss. The news of her death has triggered an outpouring of solidarity in the valleys, with local churches and community leaders already stepping forward to offer their support. A book of condolences has been opened at the town hall in Treherbert, and friends are expected to gather to light a candle in her memory. Her children, aged 15 and 17, and her husband have been taken to a designated emergency accommodation centre in Tunisia and are being assisted by UK embassy staff. “We are still reeling from the news,” said one friend. “Eleri wasn’t just Eleri to us—she was a force for good in this community for decades. There’s not a soul here who hasn’t been touched by her.” Investigations into the attack, which saw a lone gunman kill 38 people in total, are ongoing. As the shock and mourning continue to spread, Eleri Davies’s name will be remembered not just as a victim, but as a beloved local figure whose impact will be felt long after the tragedy has faded from the headlines.

The 2012 Scottish council elections marked a dramatic realignment of political power in Scotland, with both the Scottish National Party (SNP) and the Labour Party claiming victories from very different angles, while the Scottish Liberal Democrats faced a historic downturn in support. The results spread across Scotland’s 32 local authority areas reflected a deeply divided electorate, and highlighted growing tensions over the issue of independence that would come to define the next years of Scottish politics. The SNP emerged as the single largest party across the country, securing outright control of key council areas including Edinburgh, Glasgow and Aberdeen. The surge in support underlined the influence of the pro-independence movement ahead of the 2014 referendum campaign. Nicola Sturgeon, the SNP’s then-Deputy First Minister and the highest-profile voice for independence, hailed the result as a “clear message” to the rest of the UK, saying it showed widespread support for her party’s vision of a self-governing Scotland. However, the SNP failed to secure a majority of seats overall in the devolved Scottish Parliament, as 1,226 out of the 1,819 seats up for grabs remained distributed among a number of parties. Labour maintained its position as the second-largest party in the councils and retained control of traditionally safe areas in central and southern Scotland, including Dumfries and Galloway. The party – historically dominant in Scotland prior to the SNP rise – saw the results as evidence of a growing “progressive alliance” between Labour and the SNP, rejecting the idea that the two were on a collision course. Labour leader Ed Miliband also celebrated the outcome, arguing it demonstrated that his party remained a credible force in Scottish politics and a counterweight to the nationalist surge. However, the most stunning casualty in the political landscape was the Liberal Democrats. The party suffered a dramatic collapse, losing 37 of the 38 seats it had previously gained in the previous election. In some areas, the Liberal Democrat vote share fell by over two-thirds. Party leader Nick Clegg was passed over by many voters, many of whom were dissatisfied with the party's decision to back the 2010 Conservative-led coalition in the UK Parliament as well as its stance of neutrality ahead of the independence referendum. In Grangemouth, the collapse took an almost surreal turn when a single Liberal Democrat candidate failed to secure the 378 votes he had received in 2007 – securing just seven.

Lewis Hamilton set a blazing pace in the final practice session at Silverstone as Formula 1’s elite hurled themselves into their last major workout before the qualifying showdown at the British Grand Prix. The Mercedes driver edged out his championship rival, Max Verstappen of Red Bull, by just 0.233 seconds in a session marked by high-speed duels and last-minute tire changes, with the iconic circuit packed with fans eager to witness their home grand prix. The session, which saw more than 30 laps under dry conditions, was a mixed battle of machinery and man. Hamilton, driving for Mercedes, continued his dominant season form with a best time of 1m 30.695s, while the Dutch world champion grabbed second on the timing sheets. Ferrari, meanwhile, struggled with an inconsistent showing from both Charles Leclerc and Carlos Sainz, whose Quali pace in the first round of practice sessions had promised far more. Mercedes technical director, James Vowles, said post-session that the team was “pleased with the direction we’re heading, even if we have a few small elements to resolve.” Hamilton, himself, remained characteristically low-key, saying in a press briefing that while Saturday’s qualifying would be crucial, it was Sunday’s race that mattered most. “This is the stage we all love, but we’re still building confidence – we know what we need to do and we’re just making sure we are as ready as possible before the clock starts tomorrow,” he said. The Briton’s performance at Silverstone, which he has won four times in his career, has given his fans cautious hope that he might claim a record fifth victory at the track this year. His former world title rival, Sebastian Vettel, had earlier in the week hinted at a resurgence for Ferrari, though the team’s struggles to match the pace of Mercedes and Red Bull in recent races have dampened those expectations. Behind Hamilton and Verstappen, Lando Norris of McLaren claimed third fastest for the session, showcasing that the British team are making steady progress up the grid. Norris said his pace was “definitely better than it has been for a little while,” citing a mid-session setup change which made a "big difference" to his car’s balance through the high-speed corners. Qualifying is set to take place on Saturday after a day of mixed forecasts, with early rain in the morning forecast potentially offering an unpredictable stage for the fight at the top.

The pride of Japan's naval defence, the JS Izumo, is making an unprecedented journey through Asian waters over the next three months. The 248-metre helicopter destroyers, part of Japan's Maritime Self-Defence Force, is deployed as part of a 13-ship flotilla on a six-nation tour scheduled to span more than 20,000 nautical miles. The voyage, which is a rare display of Japanese military might, highlights the country’s growing concern over regional security and its desire to expand its strategic presence in the Asia-Pacific region. The JS Izumo, the second of two modified helicopter carriers operated by Japan, is among the largest warships in Asia, and the deployment marks only the sixth time in its 11-year service that it has embarked on such an extensive overseas mission. The tour is expected to take in stops in South Korea, the Philippines, Singapore, Indonesia, and Vietnam, with the aim of strengthening military-to-military relationships and conducting joint exercises with regional allies. The move, however, is not without controversy, given Japan’s post-World War II constitution, which historically restricts the use of its defence forces beyond self-defence. In recent years, though, as China’s influence and naval activity have grown, Japan has increasingly blurred these constitutional lines, deploying its Self-Defence Forces more assertively – particularly in the Senkaku Islands and South China Sea areas, where territorial disputes remain tense. The JS Izumo itself has been a focal point of this evolving posture. Though technically a helicopter carrier, many observers argue the ship is also functionally a de facto aircraft carrier, capable of carrying F-35B fighter jets under a controversial reinterpretation of Japan’s defence policy enacted in 2014 by then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe. The ship’s journey represents the first time a Japanese naval unit of such scale and capability will transit the South China Sea, an area where China has claimed vast swaths of territory. While the route has been described as "non-confrontational" and aimed at demonstrating a "constructive presence", its timing underscores Japan’s determination to counterbalance regional assertiveness. As the Izumo begins its voyage, eyes across Asia are watching closely, as the journey serves not just as a display of military strength but also as a statement of Japan’s growing role in the region's geopolitical goings-on. The government has framed the mission as one of peacekeeping and cooperation, but for many in China and beyond, the message could not be clearer: Japan is no longer content to sit on the sidelines.

Osborne Launches ‘Northern Powerhouse’ in Final Budget Push   Chancellor George Osborne has unveiled an ambitious economic blueprint in his penultimate budget ahead of May’s general election, centring on the creation of a “northern powerhouse” to drive UK growth. The plan, aimed at addressing long-standing regional disparities between the north and south of England, has been touted as a cornerstone of Osborne’s economic legacy. In his speech to Parliament on Thursday, Osborne laid out a series of infrastructure and transport investments designed to connect cities such as Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds, and Newcastle into a single, dynamic economic region. The plan includes the expansion of High Speed 2 (HS2) to Manchester and a new northern hub at Manchester Airport, alongside improvements to road networks and rail links across the region. At the heart of the plan is a £1.3 billion investment in the rail sector, including electrification of the TransPennine route and improved inter-city connections. Osborne also announced a £200 million boost for devolution deals for northern cities and regions, giving local councils greater powers to make spending decisions and drive economic development. The government is encouraging city regions to come forward with proposals for shared economic strategies, mirroring the development of the South East as the UK's economic engine. The budget also includes funding for a new municipal bonds scheme – financial instruments that will enable local authorities to raise money from investors for new development projects, such as transport, housing and schools. Osborne described the move as a “step change” in empowering local economies to shape their own futures. “We live in a country where someone’s opportunities in life should not depend on the postcode of their birthplace,” Osborne said. “The ‘northern powerhouse’ is not some abstract theory – it is a practical package of measures that will make a real difference to communities up and down the country.” Labour has welcomed the green light for key transport projects but has criticized Osborne for failing to deliver on previous election pledges to fully electrify the northern rail network. Shadow Chancellor Angela Eagle called the budget “a missed opportunity” to commit to long-term economic planning and said the focus was too narrow. Policy leaders in the north have cautiously welcomed the announcement. Manchester City Council leader Tony Lloyd stated that the plan “holds real promise” but warned that the “hype must match the delivery” in bringing forward meaningful investment.

Britain will avoid a major power crisis this winter, according to National Grid, which has confirmed that the country has sufficient gas and electricity supplies to keep the lights on during the coldest months. In a rare and reassuring announcement, the energy systems operator stated that there is no risk of blackouts, as long as the weather remains within seasonal norms and there are no unexpected disruptions to key infrastructure. The National Grid’s Energy System Operator (ESO) has been under increasing scrutiny in recent years over concerns about Britain's energy security, particularly due to a combination of retiring power plants and the ongoing energy crisis prompted by geopolitical tensions in Europe. The firm revealed in March 2023 that it had restored confidence in the system, having previously issued supply alerts amid fears of insufficient capacity. Last week, National Grid ESO formally confirmed that it is not issuing a 'Tritium' alert for the winter of 2024 — the most serious of its energy resilience categories. This means British consumers should not need to worry about returning to the energy rationing schemes, such as the 2022 “demand-side flexibility” trial, designed to stagger energy usage during peak demand. Catherine Cook, National Grid ESO’s Director of System Operations, said in a statement: “We are confident today that there is sufficient generation, transmission, and supply in place to meet expected demand. We are working closely with industry partners to ensure that our energy system is secure and resilient into the winter.” Speaking to journalists, Ms Cook added that the improvement in energy resilience reflected a combination of factors, including the commissioning of new renewable energy projects, such as offshore wind and solar farms, as well as an increased use of interconnectors with the European grid and a diversified energy supply base. Government officials welcomed the assurances, with Energy Minister Claire Coutinho hailing the news as the result of major investment in the energy sector over recent years. “This is an important milestone and a sign that the energy system transformation we’re driving is working. We must continue to build on this momentum to future-proof our energy system,” she said. Consumer groups also reacted positively, though some expressed concerns that households will still face high energy costs despite the security of supply. Dr Mike Thompson of Which? said: “While we can all be relieved there won’t be blackouts, far too many families are still struggling with bill costs.

Tributes have poured in from the Northern Ireland sporting world and beyond to boxing legend Muhammad Ali, who has died at the age of 74. Known universally as “The Greatest,” Ali passed away in his hometown of Phoenix, Arizona, following a long battle with Parkinson’s disease. His charismatic personality, poetic ring entrances, and unshakable conviction made him more than a sports icon — he became a symbol of resilience, self-belief, and activism. From Belfast to Derry, from the ring to the terraces, Northern Ireland, a place with a deep boxing heritage, has quickly joined the global wave of admiration and remembrance. Politicians, sports figures, and even schoolchildren have taken to social media and the press to express their disbelief and gratitude for the impact Ali had on their lives and on the world’s consciousness. Northern Ireland’s world champions, current and former, have been among the first to pay homage. Commonwealth light-middleweight champion James Tennyson called Ali “a true inspiration to every young boxer who ever dreamed of becoming a champion. He showed you didn’t have to be the biggest or the strongest — you just had to believe in yourself and tell the world who you are.” Ali’s visits to Northern Ireland were relatively rare, but his influence was immense. In the 1970s, as the Troubles shaped the region’s identity, Ali – with his defiant statements on civil rights and refusal to be drafted into the Vietnam War – became an inspiration for those seeking peace through principle. Reverend Brian Goggin of the Methodist Church noted: “He gave courage to those who stood for peace in a troubled time. He reminded people that speaking out was not cowardice — it was a form of greatness.” Ali’s match against Jim Shivers in St Louis in 1963 is still remembered vividly by the small but passionate boxing community in Northern Ireland — not least because Shivers was from Belfast. The bout, while not a classic, highlighted to local boxers the global reach of the sport and the ability of athletes to capture the imagination of millions. Gerry Adams, former Sinn Féin president, remarked that Ali’s legacy was “a reminder that the fight for dignity and justice is as important as any match in the ring.” He cited Ali’s “floating like a butterfly, stinging like a bee” as not merely a line about footwork, but a metaphor for navigating life with grace and conviction.

St Helens bounced back from the disappointment of an early Challenge Cup exit with a hard-fought victory over Salford at the Halton Stadium on Saturday, cruising to a 38-28 win despite a spirited Red Devils comeback and a hat-trick from Niall Evalds. The hosts, riding high after maintaining their unbeaten start to the Super League season last weekend, displayed their trademark intensity and attacking flair as they overcame a late surge from Salford to secure the three points. The match marked a crucial step in their season as they look to build momentum in the league and forget the early Cup exit suffered the week before. Evalds, Salford’s star winger, continued his prolific form with three well-taken tries, but St Helens’ experienced front four and clinical goal-kicking left the Red Devils unable to overhaul the half-time deficit. A gritty defensive display in the final quarter ensured the Warriors did not fall prey to Salford’s late resurgence, with defenders stepping up in key moments to halt the visitors’ relentless pressure. St Helens started brightly, building a 20-6 lead inside the first 20 minutes with tries from Jake Worthington and Sam Simmonds, while Adrian Purtell’s accurate boot ensured the points were kept on the board. The hosts’ physicality and rhythm in attack put Salford on the back foot early on, but the Red Devils, drawing on their recent improvements under interim coach Ian Watson, responded with grit and determination. Evalds’ first two tries helped bring Salford back into the contest, with the winger using his pace and agility to beat the offside line and score under the posts. However, St Helens’ marshalling and forward dominance allowed them to regain control, with George Hockwell touching down late in the second half to extend their lead and restore confidence after Salford’s brief resurgence. Speaking after the match, St Helens head coach Justin Holbrook praised his side’s composure, particularly in the closing stages. “We knew Salford would come at us, and the credit has to go to the lads for holding firm when it mattered most. We handled pressure well, and as a team we showed the character we always talk about,” he said. The victory will do little to erase the bitter taste of their Challenge Cup defeat to Castleford Tigers the previous week, but it signals their emphatic return to form and offers a springboard as the Super League season intensifies.

A newly-ordained Catholic bishop in China is reported to be in police custody after making a public announcement that he would no longer remain within the country’s state-controlled Catholic Church, according to local sources and church officials. The bishop, identified by Vatican-linked media as Father Yang Xiaoting, was reportedly arrested in the northeastern province of Heilongjiang after declaring his allegiance to the Pope rather than the Chinese Patriotic Catholic Association (CPCA), a government-sanctioned body heavily influenced by the Communist Party. Father Yang was ordained a bishop just last year in a ceremony attended by local CPCA officials. However, the Vatican has yet to confirm his appointment, as tensions between Rome and Beijing continue over the control and direction of the Chinese Catholic Church. The CPCA, which has long been accused by the Vatican of being an instrument of state control, appoints bishops independent of the Pope, a move that has alienated many Catholic faithful who view the CPCA as a betrayal of their faith. Father Yang's public dissent has been met with a swift and apparently harsh response from Chinese authorities. Sources say he was detained soon after the announcement and that he may be facing charges relating to "endangering state security" or "illegal religious activity." His arrest has sparked concern from both within and outside China, with rights groups and religious leaders watching closely how the situation develops. China has around 12 million Catholics, though many are divided between those registered with the CPCA and those part of an underground network of churches that remain loyal to the Pope. In recent years, there have been tentative steps towards improved relations between the Vatican and China, including the controversial 2018 provisional agreement that allowed the Holy See greater influence in the appointment of bishops. However, many Catholic leaders remain uneasy about the future of religious freedom in China. Father Yang's case is emblematic of the deep ideological and structural divisions within the Catholic Church in China. His arrest also raises fresh concerns about the government's willingness to silence religious leaders who step outside the bounds of state approval. A Vatican statement has yet to be issued on his detention, but observers believe it is a matter of growing importance. The Bishop's actions—and their consequences—underscore the delicate balancing act being played out between religious autonomy, state control, and the Vatican’s influence in one of the world’s most religiously repressive countries.

Lewis Hamilton and Mercedes secured a stunning victory at the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday, edging out Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel in a thrilling race that captivated fans across the globe. The Mercedes driver demonstrated his trademark precision and adaptability, navigating a highly tactical race with composure and determination to claim what proved to be a pivotal win in the early stages of the 2024 Formula One season. Vettel, the four-time world champion, looked poised for a strong performance after a dominant qualifying session and a clean start under the Catalunya sun. For much of the race, the German appeared to hold the upper hand, his Ferrari showing strong pace and consistency through the tight corners of the Montmeló circuit. However, Mercedes and Hamilton, always a step ahead in terms of race strategy, managed to capitalise on a crucial pitstop sequence and a minor set of backmarkers, stealing the lead and holding on under the intense pressure from Vettel for the remaining laps. Hamilton’s triumph, his third of the season, marked a significant statement in his pursuit of the drivers' championship. Speaking after the chequered flag was waved, he described the race as "one of the toughest of the season" and praised both the team's strategic brilliance and his own focus under high pressure. "It felt like we were on a knife's edge for most of it, but we stayed patient and pounced at the right moment," he said in the post-race press conference. Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff hailed the victory as a "testament to the work ethic and resilience of our drivers and engineers." The win added to Mercedes' growing confidence after a difficult start to the season, with the team having had to contend with early reliability issues and fierce competition from Red Bull and Ferrari. Ferrari’s Vettel, meanwhile, was left disappointed after the narrow margin of defeat. Despite his strong drive and tire management, he admitted that he was unable to plug the gap once Hamilton moved into the lead in the final stretch. “It was close,” he said. “Mercedes did a better job at the key moment. We’ll have to regroup and come back stronger next time.” The performance elevated Hamilton to the top of the drivers' championship standings, with Vettel trailing by a mere 6 points after five rounds of the season. With the road ahead delivering a run of high-speed circuits, all eyes will now be on how Mercedes and Ferrari strategically position themselves for upcoming Grand Prix events, including the Monaco race, which is always a turning point in the title race.

The Scottish football season is facing a quiet attendance crisis, with a BBC investigation revealing that 75% of clubs across Scotland’s top four leagues have seen either a decline or a stagnation in ticket sales compared to the same time last year. The findings highlight growing challenges for clubs outside the top tier of Scottish football, which are struggling to draw crowds amid intense competition from English leagues, rising costs, and a post-pandemic shift in viewer habits. The trend is not confined to one league or region — but it is particularly stark in the Scottish Championship, Second Division and Third Division, where clubs are increasingly finding it difficult to justify season-ticket renewals or attract new fans to matchday weekends. The BBC analysis, based on data released by Scottish Football Association and ticketing platforms, shows a concerning picture for numerous mid-market and lower-tier teams. Ten of the 12 clubs in the Championship, for instance, reported static or falling attendances in the 2023-24 season compared to the previous one. Even Hibernian — a side currently sitting near the top of the league — showed a 5% drop in average attendance at Easter Road. Elsewhere, St Mirren, Kilmarnock and Motherwell — all established clubs with histories of drawing large crowds — have experienced double-digit percentage drops in live attendance. One key reason for the struggle appears to be the relative affordability of tickets at lower tiers, which, despite being significantly cheaper than in the Premier League or Scottish Premiership, have not offered the value proposition many fans are now looking for. For around £15-£20, supporters can watch high-quality English Championship or League One games via iFollow or other subscription-based platforms at home, without the cost and hassle of travelling. The convenience factor, coupled with Prime Video and Apple TV+ offering regular football coverage, has fundamentally changed the way many fans consume the game. Moreover, the ongoing financial squeeze is hitting clubs like Motherwell and Partick Thistle particularly hard. These teams, already financially burdened by reduced TV revenue compared to Premiership clubs, rely heavily on matchday profits. A drop in physical supporters can mean a loss of crucial income from gate receipts, programme sales and hospitality. At some venues, player academies and community engagement have also been affected as clubs scale back budgets. Club managers and officials acknowledge the issue, with several speaking privately of the “structure of Scottish football” being unsustainable for teams below the top tier.

In a stunning twist of fortune, Fleetwood Town surged from the brink of elimination to claim a dramatic 3-2 victory over non-league Southport in extra time of their FA Cup third-round tie at Highbury & New British Ground on Saturday night. The Cheshire side, already 2-0 down with just minutes left in normal time, conjured a remarkable comeback to send the neutral observers into raptures and douse the hopes of a potential giant-killing. Southport had sparked one of the most anticipated cup upsets in recent memory as they journeyed to the Championship club with dreams of etching their name into the annals of FA Cup folklore. The Sandgrounders, who play in the National League and sit outside the top tier of English football, had endured a gruelling seven-place relegation battle last season and approached this tie with the fire of a beleaguered but determined underdog. Owen Healy gave the home side the lead in the 56th minute, breaking Fleetwood hearts in a dramatic turn from the 2-1 deficit they had suffered earlier. Just two minutes later, full-back Charlie Carter doubled Southport’s advantage, sending the visiting fans into absolute hysteria. It was a surreal moment in a campaign few expected to go beyond the early rounds, and watching the footage, any football fan will understand the sheer elation at the prospect of a seemingly impossible triumph. Yet, it was not to be. Fleetwood, led by interim boss Neil Kelly and playing for the first time in the competition after replacing the ill-fated Lee Clark, refused to accept defeat. A crowd of over 5,000 had gathered at the Fleetwood stadium, a far cry from Southport’s own attendance under 2,000, and their cries about needing urgency were finally heeded. After the 90th minute had passed and a second-half injury-time chance wasted by Andy Cook barely gave the fans hope, the transformation in Fleetwood’s ranks became nothing short of miraculous. In the 105th minute, Maxime Biamou struck a precise equaliser to reignite the contest, followed swiftly by Armand Gnanduillet’s volley and Ryan Yates’ 120th-minute winner to seal the dramatic turnaround. This was not the first time Fleetwood had displayed such resilience this season. Last month, the Cod Army fought back from two goals down to draw 3-3 against League Two outfit Port Vale in a brutal midweek affair, and that character seemed to pay off once more.

Claire Sugden: From the 'Naughty Corner' to Political Crossroads   Until the Northern Ireland Assembly adjourned for the election campaign, Claire Sugden had been one of the most visible residents of the chamber’s infamous “naughty corner”—a colloquial term for the backbench section of the chamber where unionist MLAs not in government tend to sit. It was a seat associated with opposition, protest and discontent—a far cry from the position of influence and policy-making that Sugden has now occupied for over a decade as a minister in Arlene Foster’s executive. But as the Assembly faces dissolution and another election looms, political commentators are noting the irony of her position—and wondering what lies ahead for the once firebrand lawyer turned loyal unionist minister. Sugden, MLA for East Londonderry and a qualified lawyer by profession, was once known for her sharp tongue and even sharper political instincts. In 2010, she made headlines when she called for then-First Minister Peter Robinson to “get in his car and drive away from politics” following a controversy over his property portfolio—and in the years that followed, she became a key opposition voice, challenging both policy and governance from the unionist backbenches. That all changed in early 2020, when she was suddenly named Justice Minister by then-First Minister Arlene Foster. The move was seen as a surprise, given her history of vocal criticism of the DUP executive and her outspoken stance on issues ranging from the Good Friday Agreement to Brexit. Yet Sugden quickly made a case for her appointment, arguing in an interview with the Belfast Telegraph that she had “evolved politically” and that what was once “opposition” was now “collaboration in service of the people of Northern Ireland.” That evolution has been tangible. Within months of joining the executive, she helped pass the controversial Judicial Pensions Bill—a move that reignited old political battles and brought the Assembly to the brink of collapse. The bill, which allowed for the reorganisation of judicial pensions in the face of growing costs, was initially approved by the executive but was removed from the statute book by the High Court for lack of a cross-border procedure required under the Good Friday Agreement. Her role in the proposal—and her nuanced handling of the fallout—was widely cited as evidence of her growing influence in the executive. Now, with the prospect of another go at government on the horizon, Sugden finds herself at a crossroads.

Motherwell have completed their fourth summer signing with the arrival of experienced goalkeeper Trevor Carson, as part of a busy transfer window aimed at preparing the Steelmen for the new Scottish Premiership season. The 33-year-old shot-stopper, who previously made 53 appearances for the Fir Park outfit during a loan spell in the 2016/17 campaign, has returned on an undisclosed-length contract to bolster Mark McGhee’s squad. The move signals a fresh start for Carson, who has most recently been playing in Cyprus with AEL Limassol. Known for his commanding presence between the posts and vast experience in Scotland, the Englishman is expected to compete fiercely with Aaron Lennox for the number one jersey as Motherwell look to rebuild following a challenging campaign that resulted in a 13th-placed finish last season. Manager Mark McGhee, who has already added Adebayo Akinfenwa and Declan McDaid to his options, confirmed the signing and hinted at more arrivals before the deadline. “Trevor knows the club well, and his experience and distribution will be vital to us. We’re still not done, and I expect to add to the squad before the window closes.” Carson’s return coincides with a broader summer reshuffle at Motherwell, who have been actively monitoring potential targets for several weeks. Rumours have already circulated about interest in at least three other players, with McGhee and his backroom staff said to be finalising offers on multiple positions. The signing has been welcomed by supporters, who see Carson as an experienced, calming presence in what is currently a relatively young and unsettled back line. Fans have taken to social media to express optimism that the club is now heading in the right direction. “This is a decent addition,” one fan wrote online. “Trevor knows what Motherwell is about. With the gaffer getting this place looking like a proper club again, he’ll be glad to get a player like that.” As preparations enter their final stretch, attention now turns to whether Motherwell can secure further signings to balance experience and youth in their squad. With a strong foundation already laid, expectations are slowly beginning to rise in Fir Park. However, as one supporters’ group noted, the real test lies in the competitive fixtures ahead and not just the summer business. “Let’s hope it’s a serious squad this season,” they added. “Words go out of the gate, but performances keep going through the turnstile.”

Tributes have been paid in both London and Dublin this week to honour the memory of Thomas Kettle, the East Tyrone Member of Parliament and former Irish nationalist who fell on the first day of the Battle of the Somme a century ago. The centenary of his death has prompted renewed recognition of a unique figure in Irish history — a man who stood at the crossroads of nationalism and loyalty, and who ultimately became a symbol of the tragic confluence of war and identity. Kettle, a former schoolteacher and barrister, was a prominent member of the Irish Parliamentary Party and was elected to the House of Commons in 1910. Though a fervent advocate of Irish Home Rule, he volunteered for military service at the outbreak of World War I and joined the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers. His decision to take up arms stunned many on the nationalist side, but Kettle was convinced of the necessity of Britain’s war effort, driven by his belief in defending democratic values and the British Empire. On 1 July 1916, the first day of one of the bloodiest battles of the Great War, Kettle was among the nearly 20,000 British troops killed in the opening two hours of the Somme offensive. His death sent shockwaves across Ireland, where many on the nationalist side viewed it as a betrayal by one of their own – a man who had initially seemed unlikely to take up the soldier’s role. Yet his story captures the fractured and emotional landscape of Ireland at the time, one that would soon be further shattered by the events of the 1916 Easter Rising. Tributes this week have been led by historians, community groups, and political leaders in both Ireland and Britain. In Dublin, a ceremony was held at Liberty Hall, a Labour movement landmark closely associated with the Rising, to reflect on Kettle’s dual legacy. Members of the public laid wreaths and read letters and extracts from Kettle’s writings, in which he spoke eloquently of the Irish cause and the high cost of war. A Dublin historian, Dr. Fiona Reidy, said: “Kettle’s life and death symbolise the deep divides in Ireland during the early 20th century. He was trying to reconcile his love for Ireland with his belief in the British Empire. That struggle is still something we reflect on today.” In London, Kettle was remembered on the steps of the Houses of Parliament, where a short ceremony included the reading of a letter written by the MP to his brother minutes before he went into battle.

Lewis Hamilton Races Ahead without Personal Trainer Amid New Fitness Regime   Formula 1’s most decorated driver, Lewis Hamilton, has confirmed that he will not be working with a full-time personal trainer this season, a decision that has sparked both surprise and intrigue within the motorsport world. The three-time world champion, now in his twelfth season on the F1 grid, has opted for an alternative approach to fitness as he continues to push himself on and off the track. Hamilton, who recently signed a contract extension to keep him with Mercedes into 2025, revealed the news in a wide-ranging interview with BBC Radio 5 Live. “I’ve decided not to have a permanent personal trainer this season. I’m trusting the people I work with and the training system that Myyke [his long-time fitness coach] put in place,” he said, referencing Myyke Aitch, who has been his head of fitness for many years. Instead of relying on a dedicated personal trainer to monitor his daily workouts, Hamilton has taken on a more hands-off, self-directed fitness plan that integrates physical training, mindfulness, and a focus on mental wellbeing. The seven-time world champion, who is known for his consistent health and fitness regime, expressed confidence in his current strategy. “I’ve got everything I need in terms of protocols and guidance, so it’s about being disciplined and sticking to them – even though I often challenge them, and sometimes break them.” Hamilton’s decision comes despite speculation that Formula 1’s grueling schedule, which involves travel across multiple time zones and the extreme physical demands of modern F1 cars, requires a more structured fitness support system than ever before. But the 37-year-old insists that he remains in peak physical and mental condition. “I feel more connected to myself than ever,” he said. “I’m not trying to win the race the same way I have in the past. There’s more to it than that.” Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff appeared to endorse the move, stating that the team has no concerns about Hamilton's fitness or readiness for the season. “Lewis is his own best advocate when it comes to his health and performance. We trust him completely,” Wolff said in a team statement. “He’s always pushed boundaries, and we’re confident he’ll continue to do so.” Hamilton’s absence of a personal trainer contrasts with the approach of his team-mate George Russell, who continues to work closely with a dedicated fitness coach as part of his preparation for each race weekend.

Rangers find themselves just two victories away from securing the Scottish Championship title and a return to the top flight after a thrilling 4-3 win over Queen of the South at Ibrox on Friday night. In front of over 50,000 fans, the Gers responded to a rollercoaster encounter with a display of grit, composure, and attacking flair that underlined their credentials as overwhelming promotion favourites. Goals from Martyn Waghorn (twice), James Tavernier and Dedryck Boyata earned Rangers a commanding first-half lead. But Queen of the South, to their credit, fought back with tenacity. Joe Thomson and Declan McManus united to salvage a point with two second-half goals, only for Tavernier to seal the three points deep into stoppage time. The late strike, his second of the game, sparked scenes of wild celebration among the Ibrox faithful and further inflamed speculation that Rangers are hot on the trail of the Championship title. This victory marks Rangers’ 12th in the past 14 league games, distancing them from Hibs and Hearts in the title race and bringing them to within touching distance of a return to the Premiership for the 2016/17 season. With only ten matches remaining, manager Mark Warburton would require just two more wins from his side to clinch the title — barring a significant shift in the table — and the journey to promotion seems increasingly within their grasp. Speaking to the press after the match, Warburton praised his team’s ability to carry the intensity of a high-scoring game and remain composed under pressure. “We’ve shown we can win comfortably, and we’ve shown we can dig in when the opposition gives us a bit of a scare. That’s what makes us a title contender,” he said. “But the job isn’t done yet. There’s a lot of hard work ahead, and we know we need to handle the pressure as well as we do the ball.” Rangers’ response to pressure has been one of their standout qualities this season. After a shaky start where they relied on late showings to earn results, the Light Blues have developed a consistent run of form and a renewed confidence. The squad has been strengthened by the arrival of high-profile signings such as Lorenzo Dal Soglio and Gers legend Tavernier, who continues to deliver heroics in every game he starts. Queen of the South manager Ian Bartholomew, in contrast, offered brutal honesty about the gulf in class displayed at Ibrox.

A Tiny Fortress with a Storied Past: Malta’s Resilience in Times of War   Nestled in the azure waters of the Mediterranean, often dubbed the “Island of Victory,” Malta has long held a unique place in European history. Though only 316 square kilometres in size, its strategic location — a vital crossroads between Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East — has made it a coveted prize in conflicts stretching back centuries. Nowhere is this more evident than in the horrors of World War Two, when the tiny island came under one of the most relentless aerial and naval assaults in the war's history. Today, as tourists stroll through Valletta’s sunlit piazzas and the quaint stone villages, few can imagine the deafening roar of fighter planes, the tremor of distant bombs, and the desperate everyday heroism of its people, who would be awarded the George Cross by King George VI for their “heroism and determination when at war.” The Nazi and Allied powers both saw Malta in 1940 as an island that, if controlled, could shift the tide in the North African campaign. By 1941, under Prime Minister Sir Malcolm Stewart, Malta was under constant Nazi Luftwaffe and Italian Regia Aeronautica bombardment, with disastrous shortages of food, water, and fuel. Ordinary Maltese civilians bore the brunt, with many forced to sleep in underground shelters while the Royal Navy and RAF positions clung desperately to their lifeline supplies through the treacherous Sicilian Narrows. The intensity of the bombing campaign, which saw over 500 days of continuous attacks, was unprecedented. Entire cities, like Sliema and Ħamrun, were left in ruin. Yet, despite the destruction, Malta refused to fall. The resilience of its people — the improvised stretching of rations, the tireless work of mechanics repairing Allied aircraft, and the self-sacrifice of local ambulance crews — became a symbol for the Allied cause. By 1942, with the turning of the tide at El Alamein, Malta had earned its nickname as the “Lone Fortress.” That same year, as Nazi U-boats and warplanes descended upon the island, a new phase of the war was unfolding — one in which Malta's defenders faced a truly existential threat. What is remarkable is not only the military significance of Malta but the enduring identity it forged in those years. To this day, the George Cross remains a symbol of Maltese pride, embroidered on the island’s flag — a constant reminder that even the smallest nations can shape the course of global history.

"We need to have more courage," a Labour MP, newly elected last year, confided to me in the corridors of Westminster. The remark, seemingly offhand, struck a chord in a political era where boldness is often mistaken for recklessness, and pragmatism has too often taken the place of principle. This sentiment is becoming increasingly common within the Labour Party, as younger MPs—many elected on a wave of anti-Tory feeling in 2019—begin to push the party toward a more progressive direction. They are calling not just for policy reforms, but for a rebirth of the party’s political courage, arguing that the traditional compromises of recent years have led to political irrelevance and a sharp decline in support. For many of these new Labour politicians, the party’s current strategy under Keir Starmer is seen as one of cautious, centrist governance—what some have called "Tory Lite". They fear that an unwillingness to take risks is alienating a growing portion of British society that craves radical responses to issues like climate change, social inequality, and corporate power. The desire for courage is not limited to policy details or rhetoric—voters, particularly the younger demographic, are looking for leaders who can embody struggle, who can speak unflinchingly about injustice and fight for change in a country where the political middle ground appears to be dominated by Conservative control and a looming cost-of-living crisis. Yet, it is not an easy path. The new MPs are acutely aware of the consequences of boldness—political backlash, media scrutiny, and even personal risk. However, in an age of crisis and rapid societal change, they argue that the cost of not being courageous is far greater. The challenge now for the Labour Party is whether it has the will to embrace this call for bolder politics or whether it will continue to chase the approval of centrist voters at the expense of what many see as fading socialist principles. As one election-year reflection, the words of this young MP echo a deeper conversation sweeping through the party: Is Labour ready to fight with the same clarity and conviction as it did in its heyday, or is it content to exist on the wings of opposition while the country moves forward without them? The answer, many hope, will soon come into focus. But for now, the corridors of Westminster are murmuring with the idea that it is time for a new kind of courage.

Voters across the United Kingdom are heading to the polls today to cast their decision in a historic referendum on whether the UK should remain a member of the European Union or leave. The result will shape the country’s political, economic, and social future for decades to come. For the first time in modern British history, the public will make a direct and binding decision on a matter of fundamental constitutional importance.   Referendum 2016: The Choice That Could Redefine Britain   By John Smith, The Times The referendum, announced by Prime Minister David Cameron in February 2013 under pressure from his own party, promises to deliver one of the most significant verdicts in recent British history. Voters will choose between remaining in the European Union — an economic and political partnership involving 28 nations — or exiting and taking back full control of the UK’s laws, borders, and trade policies. Polls have shown the country is deeply divided, with recent surveys indicating a tight race between the 'Remain' and 'Leave' camps. Today’s vote has become a lightning rod for debates on immigration, sovereignty, the economy, and the role of the UK on the global stage. Prime Minister Cameron, the most prominent figure in the 'Remain' campaign, has made his case as one of staying within the EU, citing the financial and diplomatic benefits of membership. "In the referendum we face, the best, least risky choice is to remain in the European Union," he declared in a recent speech. "Leaving the EU could shake our economy and threaten the jobs of millions." However, the 'Leave' campaign — backed by prominent figures including former Prime Minister Tony Blair and UK Independence Party (UKIP) leader Nigel Farage — argues that EU membership has eroded British democracy and placed undue restrictions on national sovereignty. They argue for the UK to reclaim control of its borders and laws, and negotiate free trade agreements with countries around the world. The election of Jeremy Corbyn as Labour leader has also added an unexpected twist to the political landscape, as his high-profile support for remain has pushed the economic arguments into the foreground. Streets across the UK are buzzing with debate as families, friends, and colleagues contemplate the implications of their choice. Some have taken out loans to campaign with 'Remain' or 'Leave' stickers emblazoned on their cars, while others have made their views known with simple handwritten signs in their gardens.

Watford head coach Walter Mazzarri is facing a major selection dilemma as he prepares for Saturday’s crucial Premier League clash against Tottenham Hotspur at Vicarage Road. In a surprise admission, Mazzarri revealed that he could be without as many as nine first-team players due to a combination of injuries and suspensions. The news comes at a particularly frustrating time for the Hornets, who sit mid-table and are in need of a strong performance to climb away from the relegation battle. “It's true, we're possibly going to be without nine players. We've had a tough schedule and this period is when teams get the most tired,” Mazzarri said in his pre-match press conference. “The short turnaround is making it hard for some players to recover. It’s definitely not ideal for a game like this.” The most high-profile absentee is likely to be Troy Deeney, who has played a pivotal role in Watford’s attacking strategy this season. The England international has been nursing a knee injury, which has limited his involvement in training. Similarly, Isaac Success, Ken Sisto, and Abdoul Camara are all under a cloud of uncertainty, with the manager refusing to confirm their participation until last minute. Defensively, Watford is also feeling the pain, with Sebastian Prodl, Danny Rose, and Younes Kaboul all doubtful. This is a major concern for Mazzarri, given Tottenham’s swashbuckling attacking style and their tendency to press high and exploit spaces at the back. Mazzarri, who made a surprise return to management earlier this season after a short retirement, has stressed that the club will have to dig deep and find players willing to step up. “We have young players who have been waiting for their chance, and now is the time for them to show what they’re made of,” he said. “It’s going to be a test of character for the squad.” Tottenham manager Ange Postecoglou, in contrast, appears to have a full squad at his disposal. Spurs will be looking to continue their strong recent form as they push for a top-four finish. Having already beaten Manchester United earlier in the week, they are brimming with confidence as they head to Vicarage Road with a point to prove. The match has taken on extra significance in recent weeks after a controversial run of results for both teams. Watford go into the game unbeaten in their last two, but Mazzarri insists that form means little when facing a side of Tottenham’s calibre.

Two brothers have found themselves facing the devastating prospect of homelessness after living on a family farm for more than two decades, following a string of legal decisions and what they claim is a now-unravelling “legal error” made over 19 years ago. The dispute has left the men, who wish to remain unnamed, occupying a rented caravan on the outskirts of Newton, Powys, while the land and property they once called home are being prepared for a new tenant. The brothers, both in their 50s, had farmed the land under a succession agreement and informal rent arrangement with the previous owner. Following the death of the owner in 2003, a will was executed that apparently failed to clearly specify the future of the farm. It was this ambiguity, the brothers claim, that allowed an alternative heir—initially left out of the inheritance—to step forward in recent years and challenge the brothers’ long-standing presence on the property. In 2022, a solicitor working for the new claimant submitted a formal application to the Welsh Government’s Land Tribunal, re-examining the original will and arguing that the brothers had no legal right to continue occupying the land beyond a brief transitionary period in 2003. The tribunal agreed with the argument, ruling in the new claimant’s favour, and issuing a notice of eviction. The brothers, who have spent more than two decades cultivating and maintaining the land, described the decision as a cruel twist of fate and have spoken out about the lack of transparency and support offered by the legal system and the government during the process. "We weren’t given a chance to appeal effectively, nor were we treated with the dignity and respect this situation demanded," one of the brothers told reporters at a press briefing arranged in a Bidford-on-Avon community hall. "We’re not just losing a farm — we’re losing our livelihoods, our home, and our way of life." Local farmers and members of the community have rallied behind the brothers, with many questioning the validity of the will and the fairness of the legal process. A petition calling for a review of the tribunal’s judgment has gained over 10,000 signatures, and supporters claim that rural Wales is watching closely to see how this case is ultimately resolved. The incident has also sparked a broader debate about land rights in Wales, particularly regarding the continuation of tenancy in agricultural properties.

Residents of a new housing development in the path of the HS2 high-speed rail project have expressed deep concern and frustration, with many describing their future as “horribly uncertain” following recent government announcements about the expansion of the controversial infrastructure project. The planned route of HS2 has already seen the forced relocation of dozens of homes and families, but it is now clear that newly built homes on one of the country’s most recent housing estates will also not be spared. Located near the village of Northampton, this estate has only recently been completed, with families moving in as part of a government-backed housing initiative to address the national shortage of affordable homes. The residents, however, now face the threat of demolition just months after settling into their new homes, after updated route plans confirmed by Network Rail suggest the HS2 line will run directly through the area. Speaking to the BBC, one resident, Daphne Roberts, said the situation has left her and her family in a state of anxiety. “We bought these houses with the understanding that they were stable and in a safe area, not part of a speculative, years-in-the-making national transport plan that keeps changing details at the last minute,” she said. “It is heartbreaking.” HS2 Ltd has confirmed that land acquisition in the area will begin in the coming months as part of its phased approach to construction, stating it will work “closely with affected residents” to ensure “fair compensation, timely rehousing and relocation support.” The government, for its part, has reconfirmed its commitment to the HS2 project, with Transport Secretary Grant Shapps defending it as a “critical piece of national infrastructure” that will boost the economy and connect the UK's cities with greater efficiency. Yet for many in the affected community, the reassurances ring hollow. Concerns are not only about being forcibly displaced from homes they have not had a chance to settle into, but also over the lack of long-term clarity about their future. Details about whether and when the land will be acquired, the process for relocation, and the compensation offered remain vague. Campaign groups such as Save Our Homes (SOH) have condemned the planned demolition as an example of the way HS2 continues to disrupt lives with little meaningful consultation. SOH spokesperson Sarah Johnson said: “This is not just a new estate threatened by the same path of destruction as farmland and villages before it.

Inverness Miss Derby Victory But Escape The Drop   A dramatic late equaliser from Alex Schalk denied Inverness Caledonian Thistle a crucial derby victory as Ross County avoided defeat at a rain-lashed Global Energy Stadium. The 1-1 draw left the Easter Road outfit clinging to hope but ensured that Richie Foran’s side moved off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership table. The match, which had been expected to be a tense affair given the fierce local rivalry and the stakes for both teams, delivered on spectacle as well as significance. Ross County took the lead in the 63rd minute through Jordan Roberts, who capitalized on a misplaced pass from the Caley Thistle midfield. The striker’s clinical finish gave the home side a deserved advantage and set the tempo for the rest of the game. For much of the final half-hour, Inverness looked the more threatening of the two sides. Substitute Jordan McLean forced a fine save from Ross County keeper Scott Fox, and just before half-time, winger Gary Mackay-Steven rattled the crossbar with a powerful drive from the edge of the area. Yet for all their domination, the visitors could not find a breakthrough. That changed in the 88th minute when Schalk, off the bench, latched on to a cross from Stewart Glennie and powered a header past Caley Thistle goalkeeper Owain Fon Williams. The goal, barely three minutes before the final whistle, sent the home fans into raptures and condemned Foran’s side to a frustrating draw. Despite the setback, however, the result lifted Inverness off the foot of the league table, following a poor run that had seen them win just once in their last nine games. Foran, visibly frustrated in the post-match interview, did not hide his disappointment at the manner of the equaliser. “This is a derby match, and we should have done better to see it out,” Foran said. “We’re not naive, we know Ross County will always look for an opportunity to break on the counter-attack. But it was a chance too many at the end, and they punished us when they had the one. We had to wait until the 88th minute – with that kind of luck, you can’t win.” Ross County boss Jim McIntyre, meanwhile, welcomed the point, acknowledging the threat posed by Inverness but praising his players’ resilience. “This was a really tough game,” McIntyre said.

The UK government has announced bold plans to test small convoys of semi-autonomous lorries on the country's major roads by the end of next year, as part of a wider initiative to revolutionise freight transport and improve road safety. The move is expected to signal a significant step forward in the development of self-driving technology in commercial vehicles, with potentially transformative implications for the haulage industry. According to officials, the trial will see lorries equipped with a combination of advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) and limited autonomous capability, allowing them to travel in coordinated "platoons" along motorways and major trunk roads. These platoons would use specially fitted communication systems to maintain precise distances between vehicles and adjust speed collectively, reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency. Transport Secretary Grant Shapps said the initiative was part of the government’s commitment to position the UK at the forefront of next-generation transport technology. “The introduction of semi-automated lorry convoys will not only enhance road safety but also boost the efficiency of our transport network,” he said during a press briefing in London. The project is being backed by a consortium of transport companies, technology providers, and research institutions, with initial trials expected to start in 2025. It is still early days, but government advisors have suggested that successful trials could pave the way for larger-scale adoption of the technology in national distribution – particularly for long-haul freight, night-time runs, and routes where conditions are more predictable. Philip Dunne, chair of the Transport Select Committee, welcomed the announcement as “visionary and necessary in modernising the UK’s transport infrastructure”. He added that platooning technology had already been tested on a limited scale in Germany and Sweden, and that the UK’s early involvement in this area could give it a competitive edge in the race for technological leadership. However, not everyone is convinced of the technology’s immediate viability. Road safety campaigners have raised concerns that partially autonomous vehicles may introduce new risks if systems fail or if human drivers are not prepared for the new traffic patterns. There are also questions surrounding regulatory frameworks, liability in the event of a crash, and the impact of such technology on road freight jobs. Despite these challenges, the government is determined to press ahead. It has pledged £15 million in new funding over the next two years to support the development of platooning technology and the necessary infrastructure, including the creation of dedicated testing routes and improved communication networks.
