Samson Siasia, one of Nigeria's most celebrated football coaches, has announced his decision to walk away from the sport in his native country, citing what he describes as a "disrespectful system" that has failed to nurture talent and respect the sacrifices made by those who have served Nigerian football at the highest level. The 58-year-old is best known for guiding the Super Eagles to the semi-finals of the 1994 Africa Cup of Nations and for managing Nigeria's men's team at the 1996 Olympics, which brought them a historic gold medal. More recently, he led Nigeria to a bronze medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics. In a statement released earlier this week and shared widely across social media, Siasia said he had grown "deeply disillusioned" with the direction of football governance in Nigeria. "I am not leaving because I have failed the game. I am leaving because the game has failed me and countless others who have given their lives to it," he said in part. Siasia accused officials in the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) of corruption, erratic decision-making, and a failure to invest in youth development, saying that Nigeria's occasional successes in international tournaments are squandered by a system that "lacks vision". Siasia's decision comes amid a period of frustration for fans of Nigerian football. The country, once considered one of Africa's powerhouses, has failed to reach the Africa Cup of Nations final in the past decade and was edged out in the group stage of the 2021 edition in Cameroon. The men's team also struggled at the 2019 AFCON and had to contend with a controversial and late squad selection process. Critically, Nigeria's under-23 side, about whom high hopes were raised for gold at the 2016 Rio Olympics, have yet to replicate that success. The ex-coach's resignation is likely to be seen as a blow to the NFF, which is already under pressure to reform after a series of leadership disputes and governance scandals. Siasia's comments have sparked intense debate among fans, players, and journalists who share his concerns about the state of professional football in Nigeria. In his statement, Siasia also acknowledged the risks of stepping back from a career that has shaped so many careers in the sport. "I have always put the game first. This does not change. But I simply cannot support a system that undermines excellence and promotes mediocrity," he said.

Fresh anti-Japan protests have erupted across China as tensions flared on the anniversary of Japan’s 1931 invasion of north-eastern China, with demonstrators expressing anger over ongoing disputes over a chain of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea. The islands, known as the Diaoyu in China and the Senkaku in Japan, have been a flashpoint in Sino-Japanese relations for years, with both nations asserting territorial claims. The protests, reported to have taken place in major cities including Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, saw crowds clashing with police and smashing car windows at Japanese-owned outlets, including the well-known car dealership chain Toyota. Some protesters brandished Chinese flags and chanted slogans denouncing Japanese imperialism and demanding the "return of the Diaoyu Islands" to Chinese sovereignty. The bursts of anger come as China marks the 93rd anniversary of the Mukden Incident — when a minor explosion on a railway line near Shenyang was blamed by the then-Kwantung Army of the Empire of Japan and used as a pretext to invade China's north-eastern province of Manchuria. Chinese state media highlighted the anniversary with broadcasts and articles emphasizing Japan's historical aggression and the impacts of its wartime occupation. Japan has strongly condemned the violent demonstrations, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issuing a statement calling for dialogue and restraint from both protesters and authorities. The Japanese government reiterated its stance that the islands, located south-west of Okinawa and near Taiwan, are Japanese territory and have been administered by Japan under its jurisdiction since 1972. Chinese officials have not officially responded to the reports of violence but have increased their rhetoric around the islands. The Chinese Foreign Ministry has reiterated Beijing's claims and warned of being “watchful and vigilant” over any Japanese action it views as provocative. Analysts suggest the demonstrations are partly the result of deliberate government encouragement to rally nationalist sentiment in response to Japan's perceived encroachment and ongoing geopolitical maneuvering. Britain’s Helen Glover and Heather Stanning extended their remarkable unbeaten record to 28 consecutive races as they retained their women’s pair title at the World Rowing Championships in Aiguebelette, France. In a dramatic and tightly contested final, the duo displayed the composure, technical precision and raw power that have come to define their historic partnership, crossing the line triumphantly to the delight of British fans and reaffirming their status as the most dominant double scull partnership in women's international rowing. The 28-year-old Glover, who as part of the gold-winning pairs team at London 2012 became the first British woman to win an Olympic rowing gold, showed once again why she is regarded as a world-class performer. Partnered by Heather Stanning, 33, who made the switch from the team pursuit in the velodrome to rowing, the pair have forged a bond that seems unbreakable — both on and off the water. Their victory came against a fierce field, including teams from New Zealand and the Netherlands, as the final saw some of the closest racing of the championships. Britain edged ahead in the final 500m of the 2,000m course, a nail-biting finish that only underscored the level of competition in the sport. Glover and Stanning’s medal secured Team GB's second gold of the championships and highlighted the continued strength of British rowing on the global stage. Speaking after the win, Glover said: “We knew this was going to be a tight race — we just wanted to give it everything. It’s incredible to extend our unbeaten record and to have done it at the World Championships is the pinnacle of our season.” Stanning echoed her sentiments, adding: “This is a special team and we’ve worked incredibly hard to get here. We just wanted to leave it all out there and today we did that.” The victory marks the fourth World Championship gold for Glover, who has now won the most prestigious award for women’s pairs twice — in 2013 and now in 2015. For Stanning, it is her first world title, a testament to her extraordinary ability to cross-train from cycling to rowing and establish herself as a top-tier international competitor. Their record of 28 consecutive wins stretches back to the 2013 World Cup and includes the 2014 World Championships. If sustained, it is likely to stand for generations as one of the greatest in the history of the sport.

I recently met Greece's former finance minister, Yanis Varoufakis, in the lobby of a five-star hotel in Athens. It was the kind of quiet corner of the capital that still offers a sense of calm away from the financial chaos that has defined the country for years. Yet, as we discussed the state of Greece’s economy and its fraught relationship with its European partners, it was clear that peace remains an elusive concept in the nation’s political and economic life. Varoufakis, a former university economics professor and a figure of international controversy during his brief tenure in government in 2015, arrived in his role with a fiery political edge and a vision for Greece as a defiant participant in the eurozone crisis. Now, nearly a decade on from the peak of the debt crisis, the tone has shifted slightly. Yet the scars—from mass austerity, the collapse of public services, and the widespread disillusionment with Europe—remain palpable. We spoke at a time when, somewhat miraculously, Greece has managed to avoid another financial catastrophe. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has even hailed the country’s economic recovery, crediting years of painful reforms and the continuation of bailouts from the European Union and the European Central Bank. But as with many credit-based recoveries, the question remains: on what terms are these gains truly achievable? Varoufakis is no fan of this narrative of “recovery.” He sees it as a return to “business as usual,” where the underlying structural problems—inequality, the erosion of the welfare state, the dominance of banks in public life—are still in place. “People think they’ve seen the worst,” he told me. “They think the fury of the crisis has passed. But what they’ve seen is the future in reverse.” That future, he believes, is one where the same failures are repeated, dressed up in the language of "stability," "growth," and "integration." He cited the Greek public debt, still hovering around 170 per cent of GDP, as an example of a false peace. “The economy is not really ours any longer,” he said. “The way we manage resources, the way we make decisions—they’re not made for the people, but to satisfy the banks and the creditors.” The political landscape today is quieter, but far from resolved. The Syriza party—which Varoufakis once served under—has seen a decline in popularity, and Greece has returned to a more centrist, pro-EU alignment with traditional parties regaining power.

Llandrindod Wells, a once-prosperous spa town in rural Powys, has seen its storied wartime past brought vividly to life through an innovative digital initiative that is capturing the imagination of both local residents and history enthusiasts across the UK. During World War One, the town swelled with thousands of soldiers billeted in nearby buildings and converted homes, its tranquil setting making it an ideal base for troops on their way to the front. Now, through a series of QR codes strategically placed at key historical sites across the town, visitors are given instant access to a rich audio-visual account of the town’s military history. The project, led by the local heritage society in collaboration with digital historians, aims to preserve the memory of the thousands of men and women who once lived, trained, and rested in the area. Among the most dramatic stories to emerge is that of the 1st Battalion of the Welch Regiment, who were stationed in the town during the early years of the war. The QR codes allow users to hear testimonies from descendants of the soldiers and digitised letters, some never before shared publicly, offering intimate insights into life on the Home Front and the emotional toll of being so close to conflict yet so far from the land. One local resident, Margaret Davies, whose great-grandfather was stationed at the municipal baths, described it as a “moving way to reconnect with the past.” She said: “I had no idea the baths were used as a convalescent home for injured troops. Standing there and hearing the voices of the young men who stayed here is incredibly powerful.” The scheme also highlights lesser-known elements of the town’s role in the war effort, including its hospital for shell-shocked soldiers and the efforts of local volunteers who raised money and supplies for the trenches. Some of the codes even link to 3D reconstructions of the area as it appeared over 100 years ago, using archival photos and data to recreate the environment of the time. Councillor Rhys Williams, who championed the digital history project, explained its significance: “World War One often feels like a long distant event confined to the pages of history books. But in Llandrindod, it was very much a lived experience. This project gives the people of today the chance to hear the voices of the past and understand how this war shaped our town and our families.”

Fewer than One in Five Beggars Arrested in England and Wales Were Homeless    Exclusive findings reveal a stark disconnect between anti-begging laws and the housing crisis  Less than a fifth of those arrested for begging in England and Wales over the past 12 months were homeless, data analysed by  BBC Breakfast  has revealed. The figures, obtained through freedom of information requests sent to 121 police forces, cast fresh doubt on the effectiveness of provisions aimed at tackling street begging, and raise questions about whether current laws are being used as a tool to manage the appearance of homelessness rather than address its root causes. According to the data, of 8,906 people arrested for begging in the period from August 2023 to the same time in 2024, only 1,638 – less than 18 percent – were recorded as homeless by local authorities or in temporary housing. The majority – almost 72 percent – were either in employment, education or in permanent accommodation. This has sparked outrage among charities, who argue that many of the arrests are targeting vulnerable, working-class individuals rather than addressing the underlying issues of poverty and lack of housing. Santha Fobias, chief executive of the End Hunger Now charity, said: “It is not only heartbreaking but deeply worrying that people who are employed or in stable housing are facing arrest simply for asking for spare change on the street. These laws, supposedly drafted to protect and support vulnerable people, are instead being weaponised against the very same people they are meant to assist.” In recent years, a growing number of local authorities have brought in byelaws or passed Section 4 of the Vagrancy Act 1824 – which prohibits  “importuning for alms”  – as a means to control begging. Councils including Bristol, Manchester, and Warrington have all introduced measures giving officers the power to issue fixed-penalty notices for begging or removing individuals found ‘loitering’ for that purpose. Critics, however, argue that such measures do little to address the root causes of poverty or improve housing provision. Instead, they see these laws being used as a cost-cutting measure to make town centres appear 'tidier', and to reduce the visibility of begging – particularly in tourist hubs and near transport hubs. Jonathan Bate, a legal expert in housing law, said: “You don’t need to be homeless to be begging in the UK, especially with welfare cuts, low pay, and the rising cost of living.

A 16-year-old from south-east London has led his amateur football team to a historic milestone after they will take part in the FA Cup for the first time in the organisation’s more than 150-year history. The story of Oratory Youth FC, formed in the wake of the 2011 London riots, is one of community resilience, youthful determination, and an indomitable belief in the healing power of sport. The club was founded in 2011 by Jaleel Burrell, now 20, as a positive response to the chaos erupting on the streets of his local area. Burrell saw the spread of arson, looting, and violence and decided to channel the energies of disaffected youth into something constructive. With a group of friends, he began coaching boys in the backstreets of New Cross, using a donated set of polythene goals and a piece of astroturf as makeshift equipment. His mission, he said then and now, was to “give kids something to aim for, to stop them from being part of the problem.” Fast forward eleven years, Oratory Youth—renamed Oratory FC—has become a fixture in the Isthmian League Division One South, the eighth tier of English football. Their journey through local cup competitions has culminated in a first-ever FA Cup appearance, after a remarkable victory in their qualifying round last weekend. The club’s manager, Jaleel Burrell, has now fulfilled the dream he began when he held a plastic orange cone in one hand and led a group of boys in a game of football in the other. Oratory FC’s upcoming match will take place against a more established semi-professional side and comes with no illusions of glory or giant-killing ambitions. Instead, Burrell and his players see it as the culmination of years of hard work and a testament to the power of grassroots football. “We’re not worrying about the result,” Burrell said. “This is about showing the kids that no matter where you come from, no matter what challenges you face, you can chase dreams and make something of yourself.” The club’s story has touched a nerve beyond the football community. Local politicians, youth organisations, and even national media have praised Burrell’s leadership and the transformation he has helped bring to the community. For Burrell, the success of the club has never been about personal accolades. “It’s always been about the kids,” he said.

The sun had barely broken through the gray sky as we set off on a brisk afternoon walk through the windswept moorlands of Donegal, the cold wind cutting through the fabric of my coat like a blade. Accompanying Sinn Féin’s then-deputy First Minister, Martin McGuinness, and his loyal companion, a chunky and well-groomed dog whose name I was never privy to, I found myself in an improbable situation: walking shoulder to shoulder with one of Northern Ireland’s most prominent political figures beneath the brooding silhouettes of the ancient Inishowen peninsula. This was not, of course, a political fundraiser or a media stunt. No cameras followed us, no aides hovered nearby. It was simply another of McGuinness’s well-known, low-key engagements — a chance to step away from the spotlight and, perhaps, the pressures of a life lived in the political arena. The location was an unassuming one: an ancient hill fort, nestled in the rugged landscape just a stone’s throw from the border between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, where the history of the island thickens beneath the feet. McGuinness was in fine form, his presence as imposing as the stone ramparts we walked past. He moved with a measured pace, offering only brief observations on the country, the politics of it all, and the way the national conversation – about identity, legacy, and, still, peace – had evolved in his lifetime. His dog, equally unfazed by the weight of history and the weight of his owner’s reputation, sniffed at the damp earth with an air of indifference to the surrounding significance. The walk was oddly therapeutic. Here was a man who had spent decades in the frontline of conflict, overcoming a past that had once placed him at the heart of Sinn Féin’s militant wing. Decades of talking, of watching peace unfold slowly and unsurely, and yet he walked that day with a quiet confidence, as if the land itself had granted him a form of absolution. The wind howled around us, but his stride never wavered. For any onlooker unaware of who he was, McGuinness might have appeared to be nothing more than an older rural figure out for a bit of countryside exercise with a familiar companion. But the meaning of the scene was far more complex. In a nation still grappling with the divisions of its past, walking on that ancient Irish ground with one of its most controversial and respected figures was, perhaps, a small but telling act of reconciliation – with the land, with the border, and with time itself.

A Groundbreaking Discovery: Atmosphere Detected Around an Earth-Like Exoplanet   In a major scientific breakthrough, astronomers have identified an atmosphere surrounding an Earth-like planet for the first time, marking a pivotal step in the quest to find potentially habitable worlds beyond our Solar System. The discovery, published in  Nature Astronomy , was made using data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observatories. The planet in question, GJ 436b, is a terrestrial exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf star around 33 light-years away. While initially identified in 2004, it was long thought to be a hot Neptune due to its size. However, new observations suggest it has retained the rocky, Earth-like characteristics of its core and now offers the first evidence of an atmosphere surrounding such a planet. The team, led by Professor Kevin D. Koll and Dr. Aisling Locarnini of Harvard University, utilised spectroscopic analysis to detect the presence of hydrogen and helium in the planet's upper atmosphere. This finding is considered a major milestone, as it demonstrates that even small, rocky planets can maintain atmospheric conditions under certain circumstances. GJ 436b, while not in the "Goldilocks zone" and thus not considered habitable, is of critical interest because it is the smallest such planet yet found with an atmosphere detected – a finding that bodes well for future investigations into Earth’s planetary neighbours. Professor Koll said: “This result changes the way we think about the evolution of small exoplanets. We have known for some time that gas giants and ice giants can retain thick atmospheres, but we are now beginning to see that rocky planets can too. What we want to do next is find out if such atmospheres can support the conditions needed for life.” The implications for the search for extraterrestrial life are profound. If a rocky planet orbiting outside the habitable zone can retain an atmosphere, future missions may uncover similar conditions on planets where the balance of heat and pressure is right for liquid water – a prerequisite for life as we know it. The next phase of the research, supported by upcoming missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope, will focus on detecting more complex gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, which are essential markers in the search for habitable worlds. The discovery comes as interest in exoplanetary science has never been higher. With over 5,000 confirmed exoplanets, the detection of atmospheric signatures around Earth-like bodies could soon move from rare anomaly to routine science, bringing humanity closer to answering one of the most profound questions in science: are we alone?

John Higgins secured a commanding 10-7 lead over defending champion Mark Selby on day one of the World Championship final at the Crucible Theatre on Saturday, setting the tone for what promises to be a thrilling encounter in snooker's showpiece event. The world No 3 Higgins, a three-time Crucible champion, showcased his trademark composure and tactical prowess to take full advantage of erratic form from his English rival as the pair opened a best-of-35 clash in front of a captivated Sheffield audience. Higgins, who was in typically clinical form, moved to within three frames of victory at the midway point, but the former world number one saw his lead trimmed by Selby’s characteristically sharp break-building in the penultimate session. Higgins, 44, hit a century break in the third frame and another in the eighth as he made the most of a number of Selby errors in the first nine frames. But Selby, the 2016, 2014 and 2013 champion, fought back thanks to a 119 to move to 5-4. That would prove to be Selby’s peak, as Higgins immediately responded with a 91 in the 10th and followed it with a deadly double as he moved to within three frames of victory. Higgins converted a tight pot on the pink to take the frame and stretch his advantage. At the halfway stage of a gruelling day, the pair’s contrasting styles were laid bare: Higgins marshaled the table with his precise break-building and break-off, while Selby, about half his age, showed the same flashes of brilliance that have marked his career. Despite a late resurgence from the fading Selby, Higgins barely gave him a chance after the ninth frame to maintain his flawless record over the four decades he has competed in Sheffield. Higgins, who previously won world titles in 2007, 2009 and 2011, is seeking to reclaim the title that Selby took from him in 2016 and join the prestigious ranks of five-time world champions. For Selby, a win would see him equal his hero Ronnie O’Sullivan on four titles if he overturned the deficit on day two. With just six frames to go between them before the box office showdown on Sunday afternoon, all eyes will be on the Crucible for a conclusion to a final that has already seen one player step into the history books.

Rapper Invites Donald Trump to Chicago Amid Tense Election Rhetoric   In a bold and unexpected move, US rapper and Grammy Award-winning producer Che “Rhymefest” Smith has extended a public invitation to Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, urging him to visit Chicago in what the musician says is a challenge to the nominee’s negative portrayal of the city. In a statement shared online and since reprinted by local media outlets, he wrote: “If you want to see the real Chicago, Mr. Trump, I invite you to visit me here and tell me exactly what is failing.” Rhymefest, known for his lyrical activism and human rights advocacy, called out what he described as a “one-sided view” of the city. “Chicago is more than just violence and poverty. It’s a city rich in culture, resilience, and community. We don’t need outsiders coming through and trying to win political points by painting a narrative that isn’t the whole story. Let’s talk solutions, not insults.” The rapper, whose work has been featured on the Oscar-winning film  Chicago Blues , previously worked as a community advocate in underprivileged areas of the city, helping to establish centres for youth mentorship and education. He added: “If you’re going to speak for a city, you should be willing to learn from it. I’m not asking Mr. Trump to do charity, I’m asking him to engage.” Donald Trump has yet to respond to the invitation, but the initiative has already sparked a wave of support across Chicago and among music fans nationwide. Local politicians—including several from both major parties—have also praised Rhymefest for his nuanced take on the issue. This isn’t the first time that hip-hop artists have taken direct opposition to political rhetoric.

Women at high genetic risk of breast cancer could soon have a new treatment option other than undergoing a double mastectomy, with scientists heralding a potential breakthrough in preventive care using targeted drugs. Researchers have been investigating whether certain medications can significantly reduce the risk for women carrying high-risk genetic mutations, particularly BRCA1 and BRCA2, which are strongly associated with an elevated likelihood of developing the disease. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) is currently considering listing these preventive drugs, such as hormone therapies including aromatase inhibitors, as a standard recommendation for high-risk women. If approved, the move could offer a less invasive and less drastic alternative to the often life-altering decision of removing both breasts. Experts involved in the study, which has followed a cohort of high-risk women over several years, suggest that the drugs can reduce the chance of developing breast cancer by as much as 50 per cent. This is a significant step in offering options that retain physical well-being while still addressing the gravity of the risk. "This is a real game-changer," said Dr Emma Taylor, a breast cancer specialist at the University of Leeds, who has been working on the NICE review. “For many women, the choice between two breasts and a future with their health is incredibly difficult. Now, we may have another option that can significantly cut their risk, without requiring surgery.” The research – backed by health charities and genetic organisations – has gained momentum in recent months following the high-profile decision of Angelina Jolie to have a double mastectomy after discovering she carried the BRCA1 mutation. While Jolie’s decision helped spotlight the issue of genetic risk, it also sparked conversation around the lack of alternatives for prevention. Now, the prospect of a pill-based solution is considered a more palatable and manageable choice for many, particularly those who are not yet of surgical age or who wish to preserve their bodies for other personal reasons. Public Health England has also been keen to promote screening and early intervention for families with a known history of breast cancer. The National Health Service (NHS) has flagged the importance of individualised care plans for high-risk individuals, and this could soon include incorporating preventive medication into those strategies. While further trials and data analysis are being conducted, the hope is that by the end of the year, the drugs will be available as part of a national risk management protocol.

A newly promoted UK health minister has sparked a national debate by calling for people seeking help to end their lives to be allowed to obtain assisted dying in the UK. The comments came as he was appointed to his new role within the Department of Health and Social Care, and represented a bold stance on a highly sensitive and morally divisive issue. The minister, who has not yet been officially named in full, stressed that terminally ill individuals should be given the right to make decisions regarding their own end-of-life care, particularly in cases where suffering is deemed unbearable and pain cannot be adequately controlled. This marks the first time for several years that a senior government figure within the health department has publicly expressed support for reforming the UK’s strict laws around assisted dying. Currently, assisted dying is illegal across the United Kingdom, although the topic has been the subject of parliamentary discussions and several attempts to introduce legislation allowing the practice under tightly controlled circumstances. A law passed in 2022 legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults in England and Wales, but it was struck down by the Supreme Court five days later, on the grounds that it had not gone through the correct parliamentary process. Despite this recent setback, the new minister’s remarks are likely to reignite the struggle between legal, medical, and human rights voices on one side, and religious and ethical objections on the other. Leading medical groups have called for national guidance – rather than a blanket legalisation – and for death to remain a clinical decision, made carefully and in line with professional safeguards. The minister was quoted in a press briefing as saying, “When someone is dying, at the end of their natural life, they should have the choice to end their suffering on their own terms, with medical supervision.” He also cited examples from countries such as Canada and some US states, where assisted dying has been legalised and regulated under statutory frameworks. His statement has already drawn mixed reactions. Members of the public have praised it as a necessary and compassionate step forward, particularly in light of growing public awareness of the issues terminally ill patients face. However, others, including many within the medical profession and religious groups, have expressed concern that legalising assisted dying could lead to a “slippery slope” and put pressure on vulnerable individuals to end their lives prematurely.

I look forward to putting this behind me and focusing on my future, both on and off the pitch.” The case also reignited discussions surrounding the use of forensic evidence and the challenges of securing convictions in sexual assault cases. The jury was shown body-cam footage and DNA evidence which, despite being compelling for the prosecution, did not tip the scales in their favour. Court was told that the complainant had initially denied consent had been given but later admitted she had not been sure if Ranger had mentioned that she did not want to proceed with the encounter. The high-profile trial drew significant media and public attention, particularly given Ranger’s status as a former Premier League player and his recent personal and professional challenges. His case has been likened in some respects to that of Fabrice Muziya, the former West Bromwich Albion and Middlesbrough player, who was also cleared of similar charges earlier this year.

Hungary has found itself at the heart of an incendiary public debate over its actions during the Second World War, with historians, politicians, and citizens re-examining the role the country played in the Holocaust and its shifting alliances under Nazi influence. At the crux of the discussion is what many see as a long-standing failure to confront uncomfortable truths about Hungary’s wartime past—truths that have been increasingly difficult to ignore as government rhetoric on national identity and historical revisionism gains momentum. The debate has been reignited by a new education policy proposed by the ruling Fidesz party, which seeks to portray Hungary during the war as the victim of outside aggression rather than as a collaborator in the deportation and persecution of Jews. The government’s revisionist narrative suggests that Hungary was an unwilling partner in the war—a claim historians have swiftly dismissed as dangerous and inaccurate. Hungary was under a pro-Nazi government during the war and played a pivotal role in the deportation of more than 434,000 Jews to Auschwitz, a majority in just a few weeks in 1944, after the Arrow Cross Party took power. Historians stress that these deportations were not forced upon Hungary, as Fidesz claims, but were carried out as part of a deliberate and systematic campaign by the Hungarian state in collusion with Germany. "This latest move is deeply troubling," said Professor Balázs Apor of Budapest’s Central European University, one of the leading voices in the Hungarian historical community. "It’s not just rewriting history—it’s deleting it in a way that sets the stage for future intolerance. The Holocaust in Hungary was the result of government policy, and to suggest otherwise is a distortion of fact." The debate has spilled into the streets and parliamentary chambers alike. Opposition parties have condemned the government’s approach as a ploy to bolster nationalist sentiment ahead of the 2022 elections. Meanwhile, a growing number of citizens—young and old—have taken to social media to share personal family stories of wartime survival, many of which directly contradict the government’s narrative. Critics also point to the erosion of Holocaust education in schools and the defunding of initiatives that aim to document and preserve the memories of the survivors. At the same time, controversial Holocaust memorials have been erected in a new style that some claim inaccurately glorifies Hungary's pre-war defenders.

A man found guilty of causing the death of an 18-year-old university student while driving under the influence has been handed a seven-year prison sentence. James Harrison, 27, of Birmingham, was convicted earlier this month after a trial at Birmingham Crown Court. The crash, which occurred outside a bar near the University of Birmingham in November 2022, has left both the student’s family and his university community in mourning. The victim, identified only as a student from the West Midlands, was crossing a main road when she was struck by Harrison’s vehicle. Emergency services were called to the scene, but the woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Toxicology reports later revealed that Harrison had alcohol levels more than three times the legal limit. Judge Alice Johnson QC said the sentence took into account Harrison’s lack of prior convictions, but stressed the seriousness of the offence. “Driven by carelessness and intoxication, your actions had an irreversible and devastating impact,” she said during sentencing on Thursday. “This was a tragedy entirely avoidable if you had chosen not to drive in that condition.” Harrison showed no emotion during the hearing, and details of his remorse were not mentioned by the prosecution or defence. His defence barrister, Mark Sterling, said Harrison was still processing grief of his own since the incident but would comply with the sentence. The university has since launched a suicide prevention campaign in the student’s memory, while local MPs and council leaders have called again for improved road safety measures around campus areas. Campaigners for drink-driving awareness have welcomed the sentence, calling it a “just punishment for a preventable death.” Sarah Wilson, founder of the Mojo Foundation, said: “It is not just about the law, it’s about the real and lasting consequences of bad choices. No one should ever take another person’s life like this.” The victim’s family, who declined to comment publicly, have instructed their solicitors to pursue a fatal accident inquiry to examine whether more could have been done to prevent the crash. The fatal crash remains one of the most high-profile incidents of fatal drink driving in the West Midlands in recent years. Streets near the university have since been marked with new pedestrian waiting islands and speed-reducing road signs. But for the family of the student killed, no amount of new measures can undo the loss they have suffered.

Shakila Ghabring, the Afghan woman immortalised by National Geographic in a 2016 photo series that captured her haunting gaze and traditional face paint, has been denied bail after being arrested in the United Kingdom over allegations of passport fraud. The 26-year-old, who gained international recognition for her appearance in the "Afghan Women in Stealth" series by American photographer Lindsay Morris, is accused of using a forged UK passport to enter the country. Her arrest has stunned both the photography community and activists who had championed her story as a symbol of resilience and the quiet dignity of women under Taliban rule. Ms Ghabring gained notoriety not only for her striking appearance but also for the personal difficulties she and her family faced under Taliban restrictions in Helmand province, where women were forced to wear the all-covering chador and were barred from most public activities. Although the National Geographic features gave her global visibility, Ms Ghabring’s life after fleeing Afghanistan has, until now, remained largely unknown. Friends and representatives in the UK have confirmed that the charges relate to her immigration status, but have strongly denied that she had any involvement in criminal conspiracy or fraud. Ms Ghabring was arrested in the West Midlands two weeks ago and has since appeared in court. Her legal team has argued that she is a victim of exploitation by individuals who helped her flee Afghanistan and who allegedly misused her personal information. The case has raised concerns about the vulnerabilities of refugees and asylum seekers, particularly those with high-profile pasts who may become targets for exploitation. During her court appearance, the judge ruled that Ms Ghabring would remain in custody due to the risk of her absconding. Her representatives said they will appeal the decision and continue to gather documentation to support her case. A colleague of photographer Lindsay Morris told the BBC: “Shakila was not just a symbol of resistance but an incredibly kind and dignified person. She is not the woman some people are trying to portray in the media right now. This is complicated and deeply emotional for everyone involved.” Ms Ghabring’s story highlights the fragile balance between international recognition and personal privacy, particularly for those from conflict zones. Her arrest has ignited a wider debate about how media representations can alter lives, sometimes without offering the long-term support and protection that those in the spotlight require.

Amid growing concerns over the potential consequences of sweeping reforms to England’s probation service, MPs and criminal justice experts are calling for guarantees that public safety will not be compromised by the shake-up. The Ministry of Justice has confirmed plans to replace the existing network of 39 probation trusts, contracted out to private and charitable providers, with a smaller number of regional services run by the government. While the changes are described as “modernising” the system, critics argue that the hasty restructuring threatens to undermine rehabilitation and increase reoffending rates. The announcement, which forms part of a larger spree of public service reforms under the current government, has been met with resistance from frontline probation officers, who claim they are already stretched to capacity. Many fear the new model could lead to staff shortages and the loss of specialist roles, such as those working with sex offenders or young offenders. Lynne D处分, a probation manager in the North West of England, said: “We’re working with offenders when it matters most — at the time of release from prison, when they are most vulnerable and at risk of reoffending. With the current budget and staff pressures, we can barely keep up as it is. This reform doesn’t address the root problems; it just leaves us to pick up the pieces.” The opposition Labour Party has called on ministers to delay implementation until it can be proven the reorganisation will not weaken efforts to reduce reoffending, and has pledged to reverse the changes if the party wins the next election. At the moment, 42% of prisoners released after six months reoffend within a year — a problem probation services are tasked with helping to tackle. Those who have left the system with no connection to housing, drugs or mental health support are most at risk. Charities such as St Giles Trust and Nacro have also raised alarms, warning that a poorly planned transition could mean chaotic job roles and a lack of continuity for offenders. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson responded to the concerns by stating: “The proposed shake-up will put the public at the heart of the system by giving dedicated regional teams the tools and authority they need to focus on reducing reoffending. These changes will streamline the system, bring about greater operational control and ensure funds are used more effectively to support those who need it most.”

The Scottish National Party is pushing for further devolution of powers through the ongoing Scotland Bill, demanding tax and welfare levers that would significantly increase Scotland's autonomy from Westminster. However, the UK government has launched a sharp rebuke, with a senior minister urging the SNP to “stop talking and start doing” on legislative deliverables it was previously committed to. The row, which has reignited tensions between Edinburgh and London, highlights the deepening divide on the future of devolution under the provisions of the new Scotland Bill. The SNP is seeking sweeping new powers, including control over tax credits and the ability to set a separate income tax rate for the higher earners – a move its supporters argue is necessary to address inequality and tailor policy to Scotland’s distinct economic and social needs. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has framed the request as an urgent step forward in the journey towards independence, calling the current devolution settlement “stale and inadequate.” However, the UK government, represented by Deputy Prime Minister and Chancellor of the Exchequer Angela Rayner, has taken a hard line. Speaking at the House of Commons, she accused the SNP of “grandstanding” over powers it has not fulfilled previous agreements on, and accused the party of undermining the union by short-circuiting negotiations to push for early devolution on contentious issues. Rayner specifically referenced the SNP’s work on a draft bill on suicide prevention, which – despite being signed off by experts last year – has seen no progress in the Scottish Parliament. “It is not good enough for the SNP to demand more powers while failing to act on principles they claim to share. Stop talking and start doing,” she said, to a mix of applause from Labour benches and audible frustration from the SNP. The dispute over the Scotland Bill is part of a broader struggle over Holyrood’s legislative and financial authority. Within the bill, there are proposals to increase devolved powers to Scotland, but only within the overarching Union framework that London insists must be preserved. The UK government has suggested that the SNP should focus on local issues rather than “risking the future of the country” by inflaming the debate over independence any further. Critics of the SNP within Scotland, including Arbroath-based Tory MSP Ian McKee, have also joined the chorus of criticism, arguing that the party “hijacks Parliament with grandiose promises it can deliver on” while ignoring the everyday concerns of ordinary Scots.environment of the day-to-day concerns of ordinary Scots.

The UK government has unveiled proposals to grant new powers to regulators to fine mobile network operators and pornography website owners for failing to take sufficient action to protect children and vulnerable users from harmful material. The announcement, made in a statement by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), forms part of a broader crackdown on online harms aimed at creating a safer digital space for young people. Under the proposals, Ofcom will be given strengthened enforcement powers, including the ability to impose unlimited fines on companies that continue to allow under-18s to access age-inappropriate and potentially damaging content. The measure would particularly target mobile network providers who host or facilitate access to adult content without robust age verification checks, as well as operators of adult websites who fail to comply with block-listed domains or other regulatory directives. Culture Secretary Nadine Dorries said the government was "determined to hold platforms and service providers to account for the content they allow their users to access." She highlighted the "urgent need to protect children and vulnerable people from exposure to indecent material at a time when the use of smartphones and mobile data is growing at exponential rates." The announcement comes amid heightened public concern over the role of technology firms in failing to police their platforms effectively. Recent reports by child welfare charities and MPs’ select committees have pointed to a worrying rise in sexually explicit material being accessed by children via mobile networks and websites disguised as subscription-based services with misleading URLs, known as 'dark web' porn sites. The new proposals also include a call for stricter phone use policies among under-13s and greater transparency from mobile companies about how data is being shared and content accessed. The government is expected to publish full legislation on the proposals in the coming months, with a statutory consultation period being opened next month. Digital rights campaigners have welcomed the move but have urged caution over privacy concerns linked to age-verification systems. Meanwhile, trade bodies representing telecoms firms have expressed concern about the potential financial and operational burdens the new requirements could place on smaller mobile providers. The plan for the new powers is part of the wider Online Safety Bill, which has been undergoing revisions in Parliament. If approved, it would mark a significant shift in the UK’s approach to digital regulation, placing greater responsibility on providers to police what children can access with their mobile data and internet connections.

When I said hello to Rupert Murdoch outside the Manhattan headquarters of his media empire last month, he told me he was "not worried at all" about Ofcom. The tycoon, whose News Corp empire includes Sky, the Times, and formerly The Sun, exuded his trademark confidence as he brushed off concerns about the UK’s communications regulator preparing to extend its remit into journalism standards. He handed me a warm handshake and stepped inside his glass-fronted building on Eighth Avenue, just a stone’s throw from Central Park. The remark was as surprising as it was revealing. With the UK facing unprecedented scrutiny over press ethics in the aftermath of the phone-hacking scandal, and as Ofcom gears up to take over responsibility for broadcast and print journalism standards, many in the industry are watching closely how News Corp, with its vast holdings and political influence, will be affected. The Guardian, Labour, and even the Prime Minister have signalled support for Ofcom’s upcoming move to better regulate breakfast TV and local press, but Murdoch’s empire – and in particular his newspapers, such as The Sun and The Times – has always been a thorn in the side of regulatory bodies. Indeed, when the phone-hacking scandal broke in 2011, it revealed that journalists at News of the World had illegally tapped into the phones of not only celebrities and politicians, but also the suicide victim Milly Dowler. Although the News of the World was closed in 2011 and the Leveson Inquiry followed, the sector was left in limbo for years while the government debated the best way forward. Now, with Ofcom given new powers to monitor standards, many believe it will usher in a new era of transparency and accountability. But for politicians and powerful media figures like Murdoch, it also raises the question of how much influence they will maintain in shaping the media landscape. Murdoch’s dismissive attitude hints at deep-rooted resistance among media moguls to government and regulatory oversight. His global media empire has long been accused of using the press for political advantage, and he is widely reported to have forged close ties with Conservative politicians. His remarks come just as Ofcom is about to publish its updated regulatory framework, which is expected to include rules on how journalists treat public figures, how stories are investigated, and how the public can report concerns. Analysts say that the regulator’s new authority will place News Corp in the spotlight more than ever.

The planned privatization of the Forensic Science Service (FSS) is raising fresh concerns after a leading researcher warned that the true cost of winding down the government-owned organization could be more than three times the Ministry of Justice’s current estimate. Professor Paul Taylor, a criminology expert at the University of Leicester, has stated that flawed financial assessments and overlooked liabilities place the criminal justice system at risk and could ultimately cost British taxpayers billions. The government’s initial estimate for the closure, which would see the FSS devolved into private laboratories, was announced in December as part of a wider spree of public service cuts. The figure of £105 million was cited as the financial impact of handing over forensic services and winding down the national institution, which has provided specialist laboratory and scientific support to courts and police forces for more than 70 years. However, Professor Taylor has exposed what he describes as a “reckless underestimation” of the costs, based on his analysis of long-term contracts, redundancy settlements and the potential reconfiguration of regional forensic operations across the UK. Speaking to the Press, Professor Taylor said: “This isn't just about transferring functions from one entity to another. We're talking about a system that upholds the justice process itself. If the government is supplying only a quarter of the projected cost, they are not only misleading Parliament but also exposing the public to unnecessary financial and operational risks down the line.” According to leaked financial documents seen by journalists, the FSS has nearly 3,000 staff, a large portion of whom are senior scientists and laboratory technicians. Calculations by independent consultant firms suggest that paying off staff, clearing outstanding contracts and building up new private sector partnerships could push the total cost above £300 million—far exceeding the government’s current estimate. Prime Minister David Cameron, who has championed public sector efficiency, has yet to comment on the discrepancy. The move to privatize the FSS has been widely criticized by legal experts, who argue that it threatens the integrity of forensic evidence in the courts. There are also concerns that smaller private laboratories may not have the same technical capacity or independence as the FSS, which has long been a cornerstone of reliable forensic science. As Professor Taylor put it: “What we’re seeing here is a cost-cutting agenda that’s blind to the long-term consequences.

Lewis Hamilton secured a record-equalling seventh world championship in thrilling fashion after triumphing in an electrifying United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas in Texas on Sunday. The Mercedes driver extended his championship lead by overtaking Red Bull's Max Verstappen with two laps remaining, before fending off a valiant challenge from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc to clinch his third drivers’ title and his third overall victory at Austin. The win saw Hamilton surpass Ayrton Senna and join Michael Schumacher as only the second driver in Formula One history to claim seven world titles. As the chequered flag fell, the Brazilian crowd at the specially erected UK fan zone erupted in celebration, while Hamilton dedicated his victory to the people of Brazil, where he holds an adoring following, saying: “It’s my seventh title, and I can’t believe I’m still here. But this one is extra special.” Starting from third on the grid, Hamilton endured a tense opening when British rival and Mercedes teammate Valtteri Bottas made contact at the first corner, forcing him to fight back to the front. The Finn retired later in the race, but Hamilton powered into the lead and maintained composure under intense pressure from Verstappen, who had started alongside him and ran strong on the faster Red Bull machinery. Hamilton’s victory circle – where he was handed the famous trophy by reigning champion Mateo Lanfranchi, a young Italian kart racer – marked a surreal moment for the 35-year-old as he completed his win in front of a banner that read, “Lewis, this is your house.” Moments later, he unfurled a yellow flag emblazoned with the slogan “Equal is Equal”, a reference to the ongoing campaign he has led for equal pay in motorsport and beyond. He expressed his gratitude to his team, fans, and the Mexican and Brazilian fans who he said had supported him throughout his career. “You guys have always looked out for me, and to do something like this for you just means the world,” he told reporters after the race. Hamilton, who finished the season holding an unassailable lead in the drivers’ championship, now looks ahead to a winter of hard work and reflection. "I'm just so proud of this team and the fact that we’ve been able to keep pushing when things get tough. This win and this title, it's for everybody that believes in equality, in freedom of expression, and in respect for each other."

There was an unusual sense of anticipation in the corridors of the House of Lords this week, as the usual hum of political debate was replaced with a more electric, almost giddy atmosphere. Whispers could be heard in the grand Victorian chambers, where typically reserved peers and noble lords gathered over coffee and brandy to speculate about the biggest development in decades: the upcoming reform of the House of Lords—and the possibility that members might soon be elected rather than appointed. The prospect has rippled through Westminster like no issue has in years, with discussions spilling over from the debating chamber into the private salons, the London clubs, and even, of course, the political press. At the heart of it is a debate that has long been simmering: should the upper house remain an anachronistic relic of the past—a body composed largely of hereditary peers—or should it be modernised, with elected members and a more transparent structure? For decades, reform was deferred, postponed, or watered down—until now. The current Prime Minister, in a controversial and politically daring move, has introduced a bill that seeks to overhaul the House of Lords entirely over the next five years. The proposal involves the phased replacement of hereditary peers with elected members in a series of regional constituencies. It also calls for the abolition of the right of hereditary peers to sit automatically in the House, which is currently exercised by about 800 individuals, although only 92 are currently active. The new proposals suggest a new model: a reformed Lords with a mix of elected members and appointed experts—this in line with the Prime Minister’s vision of making the second chamber a more professional and accountable body. The bill, still in its early stages, has already sparked fierce debate. Conservative peers argue that reform is long overdue, and that the House must evolve to maintain the legitimacy of the British political system. “The aristocratic past no longer has a place in the governance of a modern nation,” remarked one prominent Conservative crossbench peer. But others are less sanguine. “This will undermine the stability that the House of Lords brings,” warned a high-profile former minister. “We are replacing calm, considered judgment with partisan politics. It is a dangerous path.” The unions, meanwhile, are staunchly in support of the reform, hailing it as a step toward equality and a voice for ordinary citizens.

Amid a year filled with unexpected twists, heartbreaks, and moments of pure joy, the final chapter has ended on a dreamlike high for Claire Thompson after her partner, Radek, proposed to her in a romantic surprise moments before Christmas. The 29-year-old from London shared the news with great delight, admitting the proposal during a quiet evening at home has made her already cherished festive season even more remarkable. "You never think it’s going to be you when those movies happen in real life, but somehow, Radek managed to pull it off. We’ve had such a strange year—some incredibly low points but also so many beautiful ones—and now to end it with this is just immeasurable." The pair, who have been together for four years and met while studying fine art at university, had left London for a countryside retreat, where Radek, a musician, used the opportunity to serenade her with an original song about the moment he first saw her, before slipping a ring onto her finger. "He got down on one knee, said the sweetest things, and even showed me a little map he made over the last few weeks of key places we’ve been together, marking them all up as memories," Claire said. Radek, 31, who has been playing in local jazz bands during the pandemic, said the idea came to him as a way to capture their journey in a unique and personal way. "I wanted something more personal than a grand gesture—something that felt like us. I spent weeks planning the song, the map, and the perfect moment. I just hope she’ll say yes. And she did. That’s the best part." The proposal had taken Claire completely by surprise, as the couple had recently been through a difficult period in their relationship, following a family bereavement and a health scare Radek experienced earlier this year. "I thought we were going to take a little break to regroup, and it just goes to show how powerful love is, even through the hard times," she explained. Now, as the couple prepares to celebrate their first Christmas as a formally engaged couple, Claire said it was a time for reflection and hope. "This is such a magical time of year as it is, but this? It’s a little Christmas miracle. I’m just thrilled, over the moon, and honestly, not sure if I can explain how grateful I am."

British Cycling has announced a comprehensive overhaul of its medical services following an independent review, in what the organisation has described as a ‘timely’ update to safeguard the welfare of its athletes. The announcement comes in response to growing concerns over athlete welfare and health systems within elite sports, and the governing body has pledged to introduce new procedures, additional staff and improved support structures to better serve its world-class riders. The decision to commission the review was taken in the wake of mounting pressure from athletes, parents and external sports bodies, who have questioned whether existing medical frameworks were sufficient to cope with the physical and psychological demands of modern elite cycling. Although no specific incidents were cited in the announcement, the review reportedly revealed shortfalls in emergency response, access to mental health professionals and communication channels between medical staff and athletes. Andy Harrison, British Cycling’s chief executive, stated that the findings of the independent assessment had been taken “seriously and in the spirit in which they were given.” He confirmed that new systems would be rolled out in the coming months, including enhanced medical supervision in training and competition, improved mental health support and clearer pathways for athletes to report concerns. “We are committed to providing the highest level of care and support for our athletes,” Harrison said in a statement. “This is as much about listening and learning as it is about action. We want to ensure that our medical services are world-class, not just in terms of infrastructure, but in the empathy, professionalism and expertise they offer to our riders.” The independent review was conducted by a panel of medical experts and former athletes, who were appointed to assess the effectiveness of current policies. Sources close to British Cycling said the panel made approximately 20 recommendations, ranging from the appointment of a dedicated medical liaison officer to the integration of more robust mental health assessments into routine athlete check-ups. The cycling body, which has enjoyed unprecedented success in recent years, boasts the highest number of Olympic and Paralympic medals among sports in the UK. However, the pressure to maintain that success has come under scrutiny, with questions raised about the long-term well-being of athletes. British Cycling’s announcement has been welcomed by Unite the union, whose sports sector representative expressed hope that the changes would lead to a cultural shift in how athlete welfare is prioritised.

Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has called on UK ministers to do more to involve people in Wales in the Brexit process, stressing that Welsh citizens must have a “bigger stake” in the outcome of the UK’s withdrawal from the European Union. Speaking ahead of a key EU withdrawal bill debate in the House of Commons, Davies said concerns remained over the lack of clarity and engagement on Brexit for Welsh voters and businesses. Davies, who is a vocal advocate for Welsh interests within the UK government, warned that without a clearer voice for Wales in the negotiations, there could be a risk of the nation losing out on vital opportunities, including access to EU funding streams and the ability to shape new trade agreements. His remarks come as the UK government prepares to set out its legislative framework that will pave the way for Brexit, including the Great Repeal Bill – legislation to transpose existing EU laws into UK law and allow for future changes to be made by parliament, rather than the European Commission. However, critics from both within and outside the UK Conservative Party argue that the process remains too opaque and lacks sufficient local input. Davies acknowledged that the devolved governments in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have a formal role in the Brexit process, particularly in matters that fall under their jurisdiction. However, he said that more should be done to ensure that the voices of ordinary citizens, from farmers and small business owners to healthcare workers and university students, are heard and considered. “We cannot allow Brexit to become an exclusive club for Westminster politicians and Whitehall officials,” Davies said. “The people of Wales, who will be just as affected as anyone else in the UK, deserve to have their voices heard at every stage of the process.” The call for greater stake and involvement has been echoed recently by Welsh MPs from across the political spectrum, as well as business leaders and civic groups. Many have raised concerns that Wales, which voted to remain in the EU by a significant margin of 51.1%, is unrepresented in the powerful rhetoric and decision-making that is now playing out at the top of British politics. Davies also raised the issue of funding for Wales, particularly the potential loss of European Structural and Investment Funds, which have long supported economic development and regeneration projects in the country.

A new government report has revealed that nearly 1,300 children and teenagers under the age of 17 in the United States die from gun-related injuries each year, highlighting the devastating toll of firearm-related violence on the nation's youngest citizens. The study, published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), marks one of the most comprehensive assessments yet of gun fatalities involving children and underscores the urgency of the national debate on gun control. The report found that, on average, more than three young people die each day due to gunshot injuries, whether by suicide, homicide or accidental discharge. The data spans from 1999 to 2020, a period during which firearm deaths among children increased significantly. The stark findings have reignited calls from advocacy groups and lawmakers for stricter gun laws, including universal background checks, limits on access to semi-automatic weapons, and improved firearm safety measures in the home. Dr. Shannon Frattaroli, one of the study's researchers and an assistant professor in the department of emergency medicine at George Washington University, said the report aims to provide a clearer understanding of the problem. “This is not just about violence in the streets, but about what is happening in homes, in schools, even in playgrounds,” she said. “The data shows we are losing a generation of children to gun-related tragedies, and we need to act now.” The CDC report also breaks down the causes, noting that suicide accounts for almost half of all firearm deaths among children aged 10 to 17, while homicide makes up the majority in younger age groups. Unintentional injuries, such as a child finding a loaded firearm at home or school, continue to contribute to a tragic but preventable proportion of deaths. Advocacy groups, such as Everytown for Gun Safety, have pointed to the importance of safe storage laws and firearm education to prevent accidental shootings. "These deaths are not inevitable," said Andy Pollack, national director of the student-led March for Our Lives, referencing his daughter who was killed during the 2012 Sandy Hook shooting. "They are the result of a lack of action." The report comes amid a national conversation on gun violence following high-profile school shootings and renewed pressure from young activists. While the Biden administration has pushed for stronger gun control measures, the recent overturn of New York’s "red flag" law by the Supreme Court has complicated efforts to implement federal reforms.

The heartbreak of families bereaved by the devastating effects of drug abuse is sharply in focus in Tuesday's newspapers, with real-life tragedies serving as a painful reminder of the ongoing crisis tearing through communities across the UK. The emotional toll on loved ones is laid bare in harrowing personal accounts and investigative reports that highlight the rise in drug-related deaths and the urgent need for a more robust response from government and healthcare bodies. In the wake of yet another record year for drug-related fatalities, newspapers have turned their attention to the personal stories behind the staggering statistics. One article details the journey of Sarah Johnson, from Bristol, whose son, aged just 21, died from a fentanyl overdose last year. In an open letter published in the  Daily Mirror , she writes: “I never imagined I would be writing these words. My son’s life was full of promise, music, and love. But he was lured into the nightmare of addiction, and now I live with the loss of a future he never got to see.” Her words are representative of countless others being shared across the country. The  Guardian  has also published a powerful feature on the impact of the opioid crisis, particularly the way illicitly manufactured fentanyl is now infiltrating the UK drug market. Citing coroner reports, the article points out that fentanyl, often mixed with other drugs such as heroin or cocaine, is estimated to be involved in more than 60% of all drug-related deaths. Experts warn that users are often unaware of the drug’s potency, making accidental overdoses increasingly common — a stark concern for public health officials. At the centre of the debate is the call for action. Advocacy groups are demanding greater investment in addiction services, expanded access to life-saving treatments such as naloxone, and a shift away from a criminalised approach to drug use. "This isn’t just about numbers on a page — it’s about real people, real families, and real communities in crisis," says Dr. Emily Wright, a senior advocate for the charity Action on Addiction. "We are running out of time." The stories shared in these pages are a grim reminder of how deeply entrenched the drugs crisis has become. For every article published, there are countless more being kept behind closed doors by those left to pick up the pieces of someone else’s life.

Morrisons layoffs to hit 720 jobs at Bradford headquarters   A significant blow has been dealt to the retail sector in West Yorkshire as supermarket chain Morrisons announced plans to cut 720 jobs at its headquarters in Bradford. The move, part of a broader strategy to streamline operations and reduce costs, has sent shockwaves through the local community and sparked concerns over the future of the company’s presence in the city. The affected employees work in non-retail roles across finance, human resources, marketing, and IT departments. Morrisons, which is headquartered in Bradford and is the UK’s fourth-largest supermarket chain, said the job losses would not result in store closures or reductions in frontline staffing. A spokesperson for the company released a statement expressing regret over the decision but insisted it was a necessary step in order to remain competitive in a rapidly evolving industry. “We are deeply sorry to have to take this difficult decision,” the spokesperson said. “These reductions are a result of a strategic review, and we are working closely with everyone affected to support them through this transition, including exploring options for internal roles, enhanced redundancy packages, and retraining.” Unions and local politicians have condemned the move, calling it a betrayal of both the employees and the city of Bradford. Steve Hutt, leader of Bradford Council, said the decision was a setback for a local economy already grappling with the impacts of national cost-of-living pressures and evolving retail challenges. “This is a devastating announcement for employees and their families,” Hutt said. “As one of the city’s largest employers, Morrisons’ decision is a major blow. We will be calling on the company to provide full details of how it is supporting those affected and to reaffirm its commitment to the city.” The news comes as Morrisons continues to face mounting competition from larger rivals such as Tesco, Sainsbury’s, and Asda, as well as from discounters Aldi and Lidl. The company reported a 12.2% drop in profits last year, despite launching operations in new markets, including the US. Critics have argued that Morrisons’ reliance on a traditional model, particularly its focus on regional stores, has left it exposed in a market dominated by online and convenience-based shopping. The decision to centralise operations and reduce back-office staff reflects the company’s effort to modernise its approach and reduce overhead. Meanwhile, union representatives met with Morrisons’ management on Monday to discuss the implications of the cuts and the timeline for affected employees, who are expected to be informed of their redundancy status within the coming weeks.

Calls have been growing for stronger legal measures to safeguard ambulance control room staff who face regular verbal abuse from members of the public when carrying out their vital and often life-saving work. Frontline workers at control centres across the UK are increasingly reporting a rise in threats, swearing, and even personal insults from those frightened or frustrated during emergencies. Incidents have ranged from vocal outbursts to outright threats, with some callers directing misogynistic or racist slurs at staff. Operation ARES, which documents the most serious and malicious incident reports, said last year was its worst on record. According to the figures, the number of abuse cases reported by 999 call-handlers increased to 839—a 45% rise compared to the previous year. Many of these reports resulted in police being called to investigate, but critics argue that the sanctions available under current laws are not enough to deter repeat offenders and do not adequately reflect the severity of the abuse endured by often-overworked staff. “Call handlers are professionals working under immense pressure, making split-second decisions that can mean the difference between life and death,” said Heather McEwen, the national lead for emergency services unions. “To be met with hatred, threats, or even occasional violence in the form of rude emails and abuse is absolutely unacceptable and needs to be taken far more seriously by the justice system.” Labour MP Wes Streeting has proposed new legislation that would see abusive callers face fines and, in the most severe cases, automatic criminal charges. It would also introduce a mandatory phone trace system to identify and prosecute individuals committing such crimes, which he described as “a full-blown public health issue affecting the morale and wellbeing of our emergency workers”. Similar proposals have also been backed by members of the cross-party parliamentary group on emergency services. Paramedics and ambulance control officers operate in a high-stress environment where the verbal abuse from the public is compounding an already difficult and emotionally draining role. Some are now experiencing symptoms of post-traumatic stress after repeated exposure to aggressive calls. The UK Ambulance Service has described incidents of verbal abuse as a growing occupational health risk, with the need for protection as urgent as it is long overdue. Currently, the most common charges brought against abusive callers are public order offences, which carry a maximum penalty of six months in prison and/or a fine.

A Breath Test That Could Detect Parkinson’s   In a breakthrough that could revolutionise early diagnosis and treatment, experts believe they may soon have a simple and non-invasive way to detect Parkinson’s disease using a breath test. If successful, this method could offer doctors a quick and cost-effective way to identify the motor disorder in its early stages—long before the visible symptoms of trembling hands, twitching fingers and unsteady gait appear. The test is based on the detection of specific volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in a patient’s breath, which are believed to be linked to the biological processes underlying Parkinson’s. Researchers, including those at the University of Edinburgh and the University of Manchester, have made significant progress in identifying unique “chemical fingerprints” that may serve as biomarkers for the condition. These findings suggest that the levels of these VOCs change significantly in the breath of Parkinson’s patients, and that these changes could be measurable even before symptoms develop. Parkinson’s affects almost 120,000 people in the UK alone, and the number is expected to rise as the population ages. With no single diagnostic test currently available, doctors rely on a combination of neurological exams and symptom monitoring, a process that is both time-consuming and leaves many patients without a definitive diagnosis for years. Early identification is crucial, as medication—and potentially future gene or brain-targeted treatments—would be far more effective when administered sooner. Dr. Sarah Farley, a leading researcher into neurological conditions at the University of Edinburgh, described the breath test as “one of the most exciting developments in the field in many years.” She added, “If we can establish this test as reliable, we can move away from the subjective assessment of symptoms and into an evidence-based method of diagnosis. That brings with it the opportunity for earlier intervention and, ultimately, better outcomes for patients.” One of the biggest challenges has been replicating and verifying these findings in larger clinical trials. So far, the studies have been small, often involving just a few dozen participants. Healthcare regulators will need to be confident that the test can be consistently accurate across a broader and more diverse population before it can be used widely in hospitals. The potential implications are huge. Not only would a breath test offer relief to doctors and patients trying to navigate the complexities of early Parkinson’s symptoms, but it also opens the door to earlier intervention, better disease management and the prospect of more tailored therapies.
