Ross County have found themselves at the heart of Scottish football this season after staging a dramatic 2-1 extra-time victory over Celtic in the Scottish League Cup semi-final — a result that sent shockwaves through the topflight. Now, with their European dreams within touching distance after booking their place in the Europa League qualifiers, the Dingwall-based club’s manager, Jim McIntyre, is setting his sights squarely on the league. The self-proclaimed “nobody’s” underdogs have stunned observers this term, riding a wave of attacking football and fearless performances that suggest a step change in the club’s standards. But for McIntyre, the triumphs in domestic cups are only part of the story. “Cups are great — the emotion, the impact on the fans, that’s special,” he said in a recent interview. “But what we’re really building is the ability to compete and push for the Premier Sports Championship title. That’s where the real test lies.” So far this season, Ross County have shown a marked improvement in their league form, currently sitting in the upper half of the table after a series of gutsy draws and wins against stronger opponents. They have weathered the early-season storm of fixture congestion and have faltered — quite rightly — to teams like Rangers and Hibernian. Yet there is a confidence now at Celtic Park that did not exist just 12 months ago. McIntyre, who took charge in the summer of 2013, has steadily transformed County from a team flirting with promotion to one capable of testing the top end of the league. His side now boasts a more direct yet structured style of play, with a strong emphasis on pressing high and playing from the front. Players like Nathan Austin and Lee Wallace have taken huge strides under his guidance, and key summer signings have added both depth and motivation to the squad. The manager is keen to ensure that this momentum is not lost now that the manager of the month and player of the month awards are coming the club’s way. “You can’t rest on your laurels, even if the players are performing at the top of their game,” he stressed. “The way I see it, we’re still building, we’re not at our peak yet. The league is the place to keep developing and showing consistency.” That path will not be easy. Next up for County is a grueling trip to Hearts away from home, followed by a fierce derby against Inverness Caledonian Thistle in the Highlands.

Andy Murray’s quest for a fourth Grand Slam title continued to elude him as he fell to a 6-4, 6-2, 6-2 defeat against Novak Djokovic in their Australian Open final clash on Sunday. The 31-year-old Scot, competing as a wildcard due to the timing of his Wimbledon breakthrough, extended his record of six runner-up finishes in major finals but was denied the scalp that would have rewritten the tennis history books. Murray, winner of the 2012 and 2013 US Open and the 2016 Wimbledon title, pushed his Serbian opponent with a resilient performance early on but was ultimately outclassed by Djokovic, who claimed the 10th Grand Slam of his career and extended his record for men with an Olympic gold and a calendar Grand Slam. Tennis fans had been hoping the match would serve as a nostalgic swansong for Murray, who is expected to leave the sport in the coming months after this season. However, for the second time in six Grand Slam finals, Djokovic proved to be the one man the Brit could not overcome, taking their head-to-head record in major finals to a 4-2 disadvantage. It was a masterclass from the world number two as he returned ferociously, dictated the rallies and rarely allowed Murray to settle. The relentless Djokovic won 30 out of 32 first serves and dropped only four points on his serve after completing the contest in under two hours and 40 minutes at Melbourne Park. Despite the loss, Murray said in his post-match interview that his experience in a Grand Slam final was a privilege. “It’s very emotional for me, and I want to thank the fans and all the team who’ve supported me,” he said. “I’ve had the chance to play in the Australian Open final, and I hope I can play some good tennis for the rest of the year.” Murray, who has battled numerous injuries, including hip operations that have hampered his ability to compete at the top level since 2019, was removed as a Wimbledon defending champion for the first time in his 18-year career earlier this week. He also becomes only the fifth man in the Open Era to lose a sixth Grand Slam final. The win for Djokovic, now with three Australian Open titles, leaves him goading Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer for the men’s record of 22, while adding to his legacy in a sport that has seen the ‘big three’ dominate for two decades.

The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation (Ofqual) has defended the integrity of the new GCSE combined science exam following a significant and unexpected spike in the number of candidates failing the qualification. Across England, nearly 45 per cent of students who attempted the 9 to 1-rated exams this summer were judged to have failed, defined as scoring a U grade or a very low grade of 1 or 2. This is a stark contrast to the previous modular science exams, under which failure rates hovered around 15 to 20 per cent. The new exams were part of the government’s sweeping education reforms, aimed at making GCSEs more rigorous and mirroring the A-level model with final exams assessing all content rather than modular assessments. But the results have ignited concern among teachers, parents and students, many of whom claim the exams were overly complex and not properly aligned with what was taught in the classroom. Ofqual, the watchdog responsible for regulating qualifications, has pushed back against this criticism. A spokesperson for the agency said the exam had been carefully designed to meet the requirements of the national curriculum and that the high failure rate was partly due to the "grades shifting" as a result of the introduction of the new 9 to 1 grading scale. "The exam has been subject to extensive moderation and considered against the standards of prior qualifications," said the spokesperson. "It is not unusual for results to vary significantly in the first year of a new qualification." Statistics released by Ofqual revealed that the new combined science exam, which replaced the old GCSEs in biology, chemistry and physics, saw 81 per cent of candidates scoring a pass (grades 4 to 9), but a continued 19 per cent failed. In comparison, the reformatted single science GCSEs had failure rates of around 10-12 per cent, depending on the subject. Critics, however, are unconvinced. Suella Fernandes, head of the National Council for Educational Achievement, described the response from Ofqual as “overly defensive.” She argued that while the higher standard was always the intention, the content and question design had been alienating for many students. “You can’t just shift to academically rigorous exams without ensuring the teaching and learning process evolves with it,” she said. “The gaps are too great for too many.” Some teachers have pointed to the lack of time given to prepare for the new exams.

Goal-line Technology Makes World Cup Debut as GoalControl Preps for 2014 World Cup in Brazil   German-based sports technology company GoalControl has been officially selected to provide goal-line technology (GLT) at the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, marking a historic first for the world’s most prestigious football tournament. The decision, announced by FIFA today, represents a significant step forward in the use of technology on the pitch—a move that has long polarised players, coaches, and fans alike but is now arguably seen as vital to the accurate resolution of high-stakes matches. After years of debate and test trials at major international tournaments, the introduction of GLT at the World Cup signals a definitive shift in the way football will be managed across the globe. GoalControl, one of two systems approved by FIFA, will work alongside the English firm Hawk-Eye, which was also given the green light for the tournament in June earlier this year. The system incorporated by GoalControl uses 14 high-speed cameras installed in each stadium to monitor the ball’s position in relation to the goal-line. Should the ball cross over, the system—set up with sensors, ball tracking, and a wireless communications network—will automatically notify the referee’s watch within a second, eliminating any ambiguity over whether a goal has been scored. FIFA President Sepp Blatter hailed the decision as “historic and necessary” in a statement, saying the governing body wanted to “ensure decisions on crucial positions are as accurate as possible.” The announcement comes after a heated campaign led by numerous coaches and fans demanding that referees be supported by technological assistance to counter the unfortunately frequent misjudgments that can impact the outcome of a game. The World Cup will see the system tested in 12 host stadiums in Brazil, including the iconic Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro. Matches such as the Group G opener between Germany and Portugal, and the highly anticipated Argentina versus Bosnia-Herzegovina clash, are expected to be among the first to benefit from the new addition. Supporters of GLT technology have welcomed the move as a long overdue solution to one of the most frustrating aspects of the beautiful game. The infamous “ghost goal” scored by Frank Lampard of England against Germany in the 2010 World Cup quarter-final—when the midfielder's shot clearly crossed the line but was not given—often cited as the catalyst for the push toward introducing technology.

NASA has delayed the first crewed flight of its long-awaited Orion Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle until at least 2023, according to the US space agency’s latest schedule update. The capsule, a cornerstone of the Artemis programme aimed at landing humans on the Moon and eventually Mars, has faced a series of setbacks in recent years due to technical and budgetary hurdles. The announcement was confirmed by NASA Administrator Bill Nelson during a public address on Thursday in Washington, D.C. “While this is a difficult timeline adjustment, it reflects the complexity involved in building a new deep-space spacecraft and the rigorous standards NASA must maintain when it comes to crew safety,” he said. The delay pushes back plans to launch astronauts aboard Orion as part of Artemis 2, the first crewed mission since the Apollo programme ended in 1972. Initially destined for a 2021 launch, Artemis 2 has already been postponed multiple times, with the latest setback primarily linked to the integration of Orion’s launch abort system with the powerful Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. The flight, which is expected to conduct a test orbit around the Moon, will now not begin until 2023, with the next planned Moon landing — Artemis 3 — likely to be pushed beyond its current target of late 2025. Industry experts say the delay is not unexpected for such a technically ambitious programme, but it has sparked renewed concerns among some members of Congress and the public about the pace and cost of NASA’s deep-space ambitions. Orion’s development — which began in 2011 — has also been complicated by the agency’s reliance on private sector partners, including Boeing and Lockheed Martin, both of whom have faced difficulties with their components under NASA’s scrutiny. The uncrewed Artemis 1 mission, which sent the capsule into the Moon’s orbit without passengers, is progressing as scheduled for this summer. This flight will test Orion’s systems, including its heat shield, to ensure the spacecraft can withstand the re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere at speeds of more than 24,000 miles per hour. Speaking to reporters, NASA Deputy Administrator Pam Melroy acknowledged the challenges. “We are learning as we go. These are space missions with no room for error. If we must go slower to go further, then that is something we are prepared to do,” she said. The delayed timeline has also prompted renewed questions about the US’s ability to maintain its space dominance, particularly as private firms like SpaceX continue to make rapid progress in crewed spaceflight.

Ukraine's win at this year’s Eurovision Song Contest has sent shockwaves through the bookmakers and stunned the commentating teams who had heavily favoured Russia or Australia as the likely victors. The Eastern European nation, which has long had a strong following at the event, claimed the top prize with its entry  1944  by Jamala, a haunting ballad that both impressed and divided fans and critics alike. The song, with its powerful lyrics and references to Soviet policy, managed to rack up top marks from both the public televote and the professional jury, securing Ukraine's fifth victory at the annual competition, the most of any nation after Sweden and Ireland. Jamala won with 534 points, edging out Russia's  You Are the Only One  by Sergey Lazarev, who narrowly missed the top spot by just 39 points, finishing in second place. Australia, the surprise entrant making its second appearance at Eurovision, had entered the conversation for a potential win early in the week following strong showings in the semi-finals and a blistering, high-octane performance of  Sound of Silence . The country finished in third, drawing loud cheers from both fans and the occasional orchestra in the Helsinki host city. Eurovision bookmakers initially predicted Russia as book-to-win favourites, with some early odds tipping Australia as a wildcard pick. The final result has left many stunned, not least in Ukraine, where the win has been embraced with national pride. Jamala, who has previously won the contest for Ukraine in 2016 and 2017, has now also added a new high to her already storied Eurovision career. The contest had taken on a different tone this year amid ongoing geopolitical tensions between Russia and Ukraine, with the political undertones in  1944  not lost on the audience or commentators. “Ukraine showed a tremendous amount of vision and strength with this performance,” said one Eurovision commentator, while another noted the tension in the room as the votes came in. The win marks a triumphant return to form for Ukraine at a time when the country continues to face intense domestic and international challenges. The national broadcaster has hailed the victory as not just a Eurovision achievement but a moment of unity and resilience. With the dust now settling, the Eurovision community turns its attention to Kyiv, where next year’s contest will go ahead. For now, Ukraine savours a victory none had expected—least of all, perhaps, the professionals who were placing their bets.

England’s football team etched a historic new chapter in their European journey with a grueling 2-1 victory over France in Deventer on Wednesday, ending a 43-year wait to beat their transatlantic neighbours and propelling themselves into the semi-finals of Euro 2017. The match, played under high tension and amid vocal support from thousands of travelling fans, was a thrilling encounter that kept supporters on the edge of their seats until the final whistle. Lesley Suchet’s early goal gave France a 16th-minute lead, capitalising on a defensive error to send England reeling in the tournament’s most anticipated quarter-final clash. But the Lionesses, led by captain Steph Houghton and manager Mark Sampson, showed remarkable resilience and composure, levelling the scoreline just before the break through a well-worked move finished by Darcy Baldwin. The game exploded into life after the interval, with both teams creating chances and the tactical jockeying intensifying. The breakthrough came in the 79th minute, thanks to a moment of individual brilliance from 22-year-old forward Emily Brunt, whose strike from the edge of the box sent the England dugout into raptures and sealed a dramatic turnaround for the tournament hosts. The win, which marks England’s first victory over France since 1973, is a testament to the growth of women’s football in the country and the journey of a squad that has consistently defied expectations. It also highlighted their newfound ability to perform under pressure—an essential trait for a team chasing their first major tournament success in decades. Speaking after the match, a visibly emotional Mark Sampson praised his players’ “unbelievable spirit.” He said: “To come out and beat a team like France in a European Championship quarter-final is something we will all remember for the rest of our lives. The belief they showed in the second half was extraordinary. I’m so proud.” The victory has already stirred immense national celebration, with social media platforms flooding with images of fans expressing their joy. Parents were spotted carrying young children wearing replica strip shirts, while supporters spontaneously formed a conga line outside the stadium following the final whistle. England now faces either reigning European champions Germany or Sweden in the semi-finals, a match that promises to test the limits of their progress. For fans, the run so far has rekindled the hope that the nation may finally see a generation of players end their long continental drought.

Virtual Reality (VR), once the stuff of science fiction and futuristic dreams, is now a tangible and rapidly evolving technology, with the power to transform the way we work, learn, play, and connect. Decades after the first VR headsets made their debut in the 1960s—most famously with the "Sensorama"—the technology is finally beginning to live up to the hype that has surrounded it for so long. What was once a niche curiosity is now poised to become one of the most influential innovations of the 21st century. According to industry experts, the VR market is set to grow considerably, driven by advances in processing power, the decline in hardware costs, and—most crucially—the increasing number of immersive applications being developed for both entertainment and industry. Major technology companies such as Meta, HTC, and Sony have each invested heavily in the space, while smartphones and gaming consoles have also turned to VR to offer users new ways of engaging with digital content. But the impact of VR is not limited to the home. Industries across the board, from healthcare and education to architecture and retail, are embracing virtual reality to enhance processes and improve user experiences. Surgeons, for example, are using VR to conduct preoperative planning, while trainees in high-risk professions such as aviation and emergency response are using it for realistic simulations. Educators, too, have harnessed the power of VR to create interactive, engaging, and highly visual learning environments. One of the most exciting developments has been the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning into VR experiences. This allows for the creation of adaptive environments in which users can interact with virtual objects in a more natural and intuitive way. As a result, the line between reality and the virtual world is becoming increasingly blurred—an idea once reserved for the pages of speculative fiction, now being tested in real life. Despite the promise of VR, challenges remain. Issues such as motion sickness, high costs for premium hardware, and the need for fast, stable internet connections have limited mass adoption. Yet, as technology continues to evolve and costs come down, the barriers are expected to fall. What was once confined to the imagination is now within our grasp—and the question is no longer whether VR will become widespread, but how fast it will change the world we live in. More importantly, it is not just a tool for entertainment, but a window into a new era of human experience.

Newcastle produced a sensational late comeback to inflict an agonising 26-25 defeat on Bath in a thrilling Premiership clash at Kingston Park on Saturday, ending the visitors’ poor run of form with a dramatic show of grit and determination. The hosts, who seemed set to suffer another season of inconsistency, seized upon a series of errors and a brave tactical switch to storm from 13 points behind and snatch victory in the dying moments of the game. Bath had appeared to have done enough to secure a third consecutive Premiership win, with a commanding first-half display and a resilient second-half performance. But Newcastle’s chase for points in the final 10 minutes, driven by a combination of clinical finishes and a last-gasp penalty, left the Robins’ fans stunned and the visitation coaching staff furious. The pivotal moment came in the 68th minute when Bath, on the cusp of what looked to be a deserved victory, lost possession at a ruck following a breakdown in communication between the forwards and backs. Handed a reprieve, Newcastle stormed downfield and set up a scrum near the Bath 22. Hooker Charlie Graham won the ball, and a well-executed move culminated in prop Damien Chouly powering over for the decisive try. The conversion, which gave Newcastle a three-point lead, was converted by captain Sean Long, who had earlier limped off with what initially seemed to be a serious knee injury but returned to the field to set up the winning line. Bath’s attempt to respond came too late as Newcastle made a last-ditch defensive stand at the tryline, with prop Kevin Thompson producing a sprawling tackle to deny Bath a consolation touch-down. The final whistle confirmed a stunning 26-25 victory for the home side, bringing an end to their five-game winless run in the process. This resurgence from the Tyne-based side will be welcomed by director of rugby Steve Borthwick, who has been under pressure for much of the season. The win put Newcastle back within reach of the top-half of the Premiership and shows that they still have the spirit and ability to trouble the very best. Bath, meanwhile, will be left to rue what might have been after being 12 points up with 20 minutes remaining and failing to protect their lead. Head coach Jake White, who has been under scrutiny since the team's away goalfest on 4 March, will be looking for answers after another slipping-up in the league.

The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised its economic growth forecasts for the eurozone amid promising developments in the region’s economy, yet it has opted to keep interest rates unchanged for now. The announcement came on Thursday after the bank's governing council concluded its latest policy meeting, underscoring a cautious but optimistic outlook on the path to recovery and inflation trends. According to the updated forecasts, the ECB now expects overall eurozone economic growth of 2.6% in 2024 and 1.7% in 2025, up from previous predictions of 2.3% and 1.5%. The revisions came as stronger-than-expected data from Germany, France, and Italy prompted the ECB to acknowledge an unexpected resilience among key eurozone economies. With growth underpinned by solid domestic demand, improved business confidence, and a rebound in the manufacturing sector, officials said the region faces little immediate risk of recession, at least for now. Despite this, the ECB decided against cutting interest rates, which have been maintained at a 22-year high of 4% since July. The decision was made due to lingering concerns over inflation, which, although slowing, is still above the ECB’s 2% target. Inflation is currently at 2.4%, having dropped from a peak of 10.6% in October 2022 but still requiring vigilance, particularly in areas such as energy and housing markets. The bank stressed that its decision to hold rates at 4% reflected a balancing act between supporting the recovery and remaining firm on its inflation-fighting mandate. ECB President Christine Lagarde highlighted the central bank’s commitment to acting decisively as and when needed. In a press conference following the meeting, she stated, “While there is a clear disinflationary trend, the path to our inflation target still requires caution. The Governing Council is attentive and ready to act if risks to price stability change materially.” The ECB also trimmed its inflation projections, forecasting that annual inflation will drop to 2.5% in 2024 and further to 2% in 2025, which aligns with its mandate. This outlook gives the bank room to consider rate cuts in the coming months, particularly if the inflation decline continues as expected and the economic expansion maintains its momentum. Analysts reacted to the ECB's decision with a mix of approval and caution. While the upward revisions to growth estimates have been welcomed as a sign of recovery, many remain concerned about the structural challenges facing the eurozone, including an aging population, energy vulnerabilities, and the uneven recovery within member states.

Liam Neeson and Graham Norton have thrown their weight behind calls for same-sex marriage to be legalised in Northern Ireland, in a high-profile show of support ahead of a planned protest in Belfast. The duo, both of whom are from Northern Ireland, have publicly condemned the region’s continued lack of legal recognition for same-sex marriage, which remains the only part of the UK where the practice is not permitted. Protests are scheduled to take place later this month, organised by the Equality Campaign in Northern Ireland, which has been pushing for legislative change for years. The cause has gained renewed momentum after the UK Supreme Court ruled in July that the decision to exclude Northern Ireland from the 2013 Same-Sex Marriage Act was unlawful, clearing the way for devolved governments to introduce their own legislation. However, Northern Ireland’s Assembly, currently unable to sit due to the political deadlock following the Stormont Collapse in January 2017, has yet to address the issue. In a statement released earlier this week, actor Liam Neeson said: “This isn’t just about marriage rights, it’s about equality and dignity. No one should be denied the right to love and be legally protected in that love because of where they were born.” The 68-year-old film star, who grew up in Belfast and is married to Northern Irish singer Natasha Richardson, added that it was “a disgrace” that his home region was still denying these basic rights to its citizens. Comedian and broadcaster Graham Norton, who was born in Northern Ireland and rose to fame internationally, echoed those sentiments in a statement to the BBC. “I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again – there’s no room for discrimination in a 21st-century society. Same-sex marriage should be a given, not a privilege reserved for those lucky enough to live south of the border,” said Norton. The presenter, a self-declared “ardent supporter of equality and justice,” has previously spoken up for LGBTQ+ rights on his award-winning TV show. Their interventions have added to growing pressure on the UK government to step in after a democratic solution appears distant. Prime Minister Theresa May has previously ruled out a Westminster bill to impose same-sex marriage in Northern Ireland, instead calling for political consensus in Belfast. However, with the Northern Ireland Executive yet to reach agreement on the issue, campaigners are growing increasingly frustrated.

The UK will take in more unaccompanied Syrian refugee children from Europe, Prime Minister David Cameron has announced, in a move seen as a shift in Britain’s often-criticised approach to the refugee crisis. Speaking during a visit to a primary school in Coventry, Mr Cameron said the government would begin accepting children who had been placed in temporary care in European partner countries, although he stopped short of providing a formal numerical commitment. The statement comes after a week of renewed international pressure following the tragic death of three-year-old Alan Kurdi, whose body was found washed up on a Turkish beach. Mr Cameron acknowledged the “terrible, sad image” of the boy and reiterated the UK’s position that it would not accept a “blank cheque” for uncontrolled refugee flows from the Middle East, but added that the situation required compassion and a sense of moral responsibility. Tens of thousands of children, including unaccompanied minors, have fled the conflict in Syria, often arriving in Europe by dangerous, often illegal routes. The UK’s current policy for Syrian refugees – under the Vulnerable Persons Resettlement Scheme – is separate from the ongoing European crisis, focusing instead on resettling over 20,000 Syrians over the next five years, primarily from refugee camps in the Middle East. The prime minister did not give a specific number of Syrian children who will be brought into the UK from European partner states, but said the government would work with the European Union and humanitarian agencies to identify and relocate vulnerable minors to “safe and legal” places in the UK. “Where children are alone and have no parents, where they are being cared for in emergency situations in Europe, then clearly we should do what we can to help,” he said. However, he stressed that the UK would not open its borders to uncontrolled migration and ruled out any policy that would allow refugees arriving from the Mediterranean to claim asylum in Britain. The announcement was welcomed by humanitarian groups, although some charities have called for more clarity on the specifics of the plan, including how the children will be selected, how many are expected to be brought to the UK, and how long any such process would take. Immigration Minister James Brokenshire told the House of Commons that the government remained "focused on preventing illegal migration and ensuring our borders are secure," while also “showing our humanity and support” for the most vulnerable individuals.

The distinctive patterns found on leopards and tigers are not just aesthetic features, but sophisticated forms of camouflage carefully adapted to the environments in which the big cats live, according to new research. Scientists have long been intrigued by the evolution of these striking markings, with new studies revealing the deep connection between such patterns and the animals’ survival in their natural habitats. In a paper published in the journal  Science Advances , researchers from the University of Bristol and a team of international biologists have mapped the distributions of big cat species across various ecosystems and matched them to their coat patterns. What they found was that the intricate designs serve more than just a decorative function—they are specially evolved adaptations to help these animals blend into their surroundings. Leopards, for instance, typically inhabit forests and bushland environments, where their spots mirror the dappled light and shaded foliage. The irregular, rosette-like shapes replicate the broken light patterns the cat encounters in wooded areas, breaking up its outline and making it difficult to detect by both prey and potential predators. In contrast, tigers, which are often found in dense reeds, mangroves, and open grasslands, have evolved vertical stripes. These, the researchers say, are particularly effective in grassy or narrow vegetated areas, where long stripes help to mask the animal’s body轮廓 (outline) against vertical backgrounds such as tall grasses or bamboo stalks. The study also highlights examples of transitional habitats, where species display a mix of pattern types. It notes that as environments shift due to climate change or human encroachment, the coat patterns may also evolve. This could have significant implications for conservation strategies, which have largely focused on habitat preservation without fully accounting for the biological adaptations tied to these patterns. Professor Martin Stevens, a lead researcher on the project, explained: "It's astonishing how closely these patterns reflect the specific conditions of the landscapes where these cats live. The evolution of these markings is not random—it's a calculated response to the need for concealment and survival." The research team used high-resolution images and geographical data to create a detailed mapping of more than 30 feline species across all continents. Using computational models, they simulated how these patterns would appear to other animals and how they might alter the perception of space or motion. The findings not only offer new insights into the evolutionary biology of big cats but also contribute to the growing field of biomimetics—where nature’s designs are studied to inspire human innovation.

Chancellor George Osborne has confirmed the UK government's support for a landmark £2bn investment deal between China and the UK that will see Chinese state-backed firms play a key role in the construction of the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station in Somerset. The £18bn project, long plagued by delays and uncertainty, is now set to move forward with backing from the Hinckley Point Development Company and China General Nuclear Power Corporation (CGN). The UK government has underwritten provisions of the deal to ensure it meets financial obligations, despite fierce opposition from some Conservative MPs and business leaders. Speaking at the Conservative Party conference in Manchester, Osborne revealed the guarantee as a cornerstone of the government’s plans to modernise the energy sector and transition to a low-carbon economy by 2035. "This is an historic step forward in our Ten Point Plan to decarbonise the economy and secure our energy future," Osborne said. "By working with responsible international partners such as China, we can deliver the safe, reliable and clean energy this country needs at a time of ever-growing global challenges, including rising energy costs and the climate emergency." The deal will see CGN hold a 33 per cent stake in Hinkley Point C, with the remaining shares owned by French energy giant EDF, which is also backed by the French state. The West Somerset project, expected to provide 7 per cent of Britain’s electricity, has been in the planning stages for over a decade and was repeatedly postponed due to cost overruns and political disputes. Last year, the previous prime minister, David Cameron, had resisted full government backing for the investment because of fears over foreign control of UK infrastructure. Now, with the backing of a £2bn UK guarantee and an assurance that the government maintains a key oversight role, the project has been given the green light. Energy minister Andrea Leadsom said the government had carried out a "comprehensive" risk assessment that showed the investment posed no threat to national security. The £2bn guarantee will cover potential shortfalls if energy prices do not meet a guaranteed level set at 92.5p per kilowatt-hour, which has been a point of contention among critics who argue it unfairly subsidises the project. Business Secretary Sajid Javid acknowledged the figures were "not the cheapest path", but he said it was a "tough but necessary price" to secure long-term energy security.

The United Kingdom faces a serious vulnerability to potential epidemics such as Ebola due to a significant shortfall in its domestic vaccine manufacturing capacity, according to a stark warning from a cross-party group of MPs. The Commons Foreign Affairs Committee has raised alarm over the UK’s reliance on overseas suppliers for the production of critical vaccines, highlighting the risks this dependency poses in the event of a global health emergency. In an urgent report released this week, the committee warned that the nation’s existing infrastructure is underprepared to respond swiftly to outbreaks of diseases like Ebola or even future pandemics. “We must not take for granted the essential role that vaccines play in protecting the public and underpinning our national resilience,” said one member of the committee. “The current gaps in supply and manufacturing capabilities must be addressed without delay.” Currently, the UK imports the majority of its vaccines from countries such as the United States and mainland Europe, a reliance that could be severely tested in times of crisis, supply chain disruption, or international travel restrictions. The committee has pointed to the lack of state-of-the-art virology and vaccine production facilities within the UK as a national security risk. One senior MP directly compared the vulnerability to the lack of domestic manufacturing highlighted in other critical sectors during the early stages of the coronavirus pandemic. The Foreign Affairs Committee cited the example of the Ebola outbreaks in West Africa and the Democratic Republic of the Congo as cases where rapid vaccine development and distribution起到了 a vital role in controlling the spread. However, the UK’s absence of robust home-grown vaccine manufacturing means it would be highly dependent on international collaboration and goodwill, which may not always be forthcoming in an emergency. The MPs have called on the government to increase investment in domestic production capabilities and to develop a long-term strategy to ensure the UK is better prepared for future health threats. They also urged for a public health system that is not only reactive but proactively resilient. Health Secretary Steve Barclay said in response that the government is “aware of the need to preserve and enhance the UK's vaccine capabilities” and that recent funding for new research and development projects will help strengthen resilience. However, critics argue that more urgent action is required, particularly in light of growing global health challenges and unpredictable international relations.

Andrew Mitchell has revealed for the first time that he felt he was "caught between the pincers" of the police and the media when he was accused of using his MP’s pass to bypass security barriers at Downing Street in 2012 — the row that eventually led to his dramatic resignation from the Cabinet. In a wide-ranging interview on Friday, the former Environment Secretary said he was never handed a formal caution by the Metropolitan Police despite being a "subject of a criminal investigation", and that this confused him during what became a public spectacle rather than a reasonable inquiry. "I'm not saying the media doesn't chase stories, but the decision by the police not to share details of their investigation forced me into a position where I was expected to fight two sides at the same time," he said. "You're accused of not cooperating with the police by behaving normally – like carrying on with your professional and family life — and then accused by the media for breaking the law." The so-called "Plebgate" affair began after a Downing Street policeman, Phillip Reevell, claimed that he had been abused by the Conservative MP for Sutton and Cheam when he was waved into the gates of the Prime Minister’s residence in 2009. Mr Mitchell strongly denied the allegation, and insisted that he had been waved through by a police officer who knew him from repeated visits. The matter – initially a minor workplace grievance between Mr Mitchell and Mr Reevell – erupted into national controversy in October 2010, when the then Environment Secretary published a letter in which he described Reevell as a "pleb". The term, which he later said he had used in an email rather than the letter itself, quickly became a symbol of class tension and led to fierce public reaction. Prime Minister David Cameron, then at the height of the expenses scandal, had publicly supported his ally, but withdrew his support when the police issued their report. Details of the report were not released at the time, and Mr Mitchell resigned on 10 October 2012, after his health had been undermined by the pressure of the events. Speaking now, he said that his decision to step down was not about principle, as he had expected to be cleared by the police inquiry. “I believed the process would have happened, but it never fully materialised," he said.

Margaret McGuckin has spent the past decade at the heart of one of the most sensitive and challenging campaigns in modern public life—fighting for justice for victims of historical institutional child sex abuse in Northern Ireland. As the public face of organisations such as   Marmot 139  , a survivors’ group named after a section of Ireland’s 1989 Adoption Act that was used to cover up abuse allegations in children’s homes, McGuckin has become a symbol of both resilience and moral courage. Her tireless work has brought a long history of institutional neglect and systemic secrecy into the public conscience, forcing successive governments and religious bodies to confront uncomfortable truths. The campaign has united survivors—many of whom were abandoned to harsh, often abusive environments in institutions like Letterkenny Industrial School, Goldenbridge, and the Nazareth House in Dungannon—under one voice. McGuckin, who has spoken openly about her own experiences, described the trauma of growing up in care and the decades of silence that followed. “We were not criminalised, we were not wrong,” she said in a recent interview. “But for years, we were told to stay quiet, to get on with our lives, and not make a fuss. What we’ve done is say: no, it has to stop. These children exist—and we have to be heard.” The movement gained national and international attention in 2014 when, following years of pressure, the Northern Ireland Executive set up the Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (HIA). The inquiry, which heard testimony from hundreds of survivors, was a major milestone in the campaign. McGuckin was a central figure in the push for its creation and continued to act as a liaison and advocate for survivors through its years of operation. More recently, Prime Minister Rishi Sunak offered his “deepest condolences” to survivors of institutional abuse in Northern Ireland during a visit to the region in March. His remarks followed a week of commemorations marking the final report of the HIA, published in 2022. Although the inquiry did not uncover new evidence of state collusion in abuse, as some had feared, it confirmed what survivors had long claimed: that the institutions had been rife with abuse, and that the authorities failed to act. The final report also acknowledged “catastrophic failure” in delivering justice for victims. McGuckin has welcomed the Prime Minister’s response but stopped short of calling it sufficient. “Words are important,” she said, “but we want to see action.

Turkey’s young voters, comprising nearly a third of the population, are pinning their hopes on the 1 November general election to restore stability after years of political upheaval. Many see the election as their chance to influence a future that has long eluded their generation – one built on peace, opportunity, and a shift away from the turbulence that has defined the country’s political landscape in recent years. The youth vote, often regarded as one of the most under-represented demographics in policy-making, has become a key focal point in this election as political parties increasingly turn their attention to young and urbanised populations. Issues such as employment, the cost of living, education, and the lack of political transparency have dominated conversations in university campuses and on social media, where hashtags like #YouthCanChangeTurkey have gained traction. In the cities of Istanbul and Izmir, two of the most populous and youthful provinces, political campaign posters now prominently feature promises of job creation, digital transformation, and a reform of universities. “We want more than just slogans in party manifestos,” said 22-year-old Kenan Yılmaz, a university student in Ankara. “We need real policies that show us we can have a place in this country’s future.” Political analysts suggest that younger Turks are more likely to vote for parties outside the country’s traditional left-right divide, such as the left-wing Social Democratic People's Party (SHP) or the centre-right Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), or even for new political actors pushing for a democratic transformation. However, the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), currently in power for 18 years, has a strong grip on institutions and a loyal base that still resonates with many young urbanites through its economic policies and social conservatism. Yet, as Prime Minister Binali Yıldırım and President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan continue to frame the election as a mission to “protect” Turkey from instability, younger voters increasingly argue that the real transformation they seek has yet to materialise. They point to stalled reforms in education, growing unemployment among graduates, and a stifling political climate as signs that their hopes have not yet been addressed. “The country is at a crossroads,” said Gülcan Demir, a young political campaigner from Istanbul. “This election is the moment we can tip the balance in favour of something different. We’re not the ones who got us here – it’s time others listened to what we have to say.”

The UK government has announced plans to hold a series of engagement sessions with key sectors in Scotland—including agriculture, energy, and fisheries—to assess the potential economic and operational impact of leaving the European Union. This comes amid growing concerns across Scotland, where support for remaining in the EU has historically been strong, and uncertainty over how Brexit might affect key industries that rely heavily on EU regulations, funding, and trade. The discussions, led by ministers in the UK government’s Scotland Office, are intended to provide a platform for stakeholders to highlight their specific concerns and propose policy adjustments or safeguards that could mitigate disruption. The Treasury has also been tasked with providing financial analysis to guide these conversations. One of the primary areas of focus is the farming community, with many warning of supply chain volatility and fears over losing access to agricultural subsidy programs such as the Common Agricultural Policy. Recent figures from Scotland’s Rural College show that the sector receives more than £300 million a year in EU funds, a lifeline for many small and medium-sized farms. The oil and gas industry, which has been profoundly affected by the collapse in oil prices, is another group set to participate. Scottish North Sea fields account for nearly one third of the UK’s total oil and gas production, much of which is exported to EU markets. Industry leaders fear that non-tariff barriers and regulatory divergence post-Brexit could further undermine the sector's already struggling recovery efforts. Whitefish fisheries, which represent a significant portion of Scotland’s seafood exports, have also been voiced as a potential casualty. The UK government has already pledged to maintain fisheries subsidies, but the lack of clarity on future trading rules and quotas has left many in the industry anxious. The UK government said the engagement process was part of a “consultative and responsible” approach to Brexit preparations, which it described as necessary for long-term economic stability. However, the move has drawn criticism from Scottish officials, including First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, who has reiterated that Scotland does not support Brexit and warned of the potential for economic harm and constitutional uncertainty. With the possibility of a second independence referendum once again on the table, the government’s initiative is also seen as an attempt to preemptively address concerns about the UK’s ability to manage regional differences in policy and economic planning.

Wayne Madsen has confirmed that he has stepped down as captain of Derbyshire to focus on his career and increase his chances of earning a call-up to the England national team. The 33-year-old left-handed batsman, who is in his final year of a six-season stint as Derbyshire’s skipper, made the announcement on Tuesday and will be replaced by Keaton Jennings, who has signed on loan from Durham until the end of the season. Madsen’s decision marks a significant shift in his career, as he now sets his sights firmly on international recognition. The Yorkshire-born player has never represented England, but his performances in domestic cricket have often drawn praise, including a recent score of 163 for Derbyshire against Glamorgan in the One-Day Cup, which helped underline his capabilities. In a statement, Madsen said the move would enable him to play more specialist roles in the team and allow him to focus entirely on his batting performance. “Being captain is a massive responsibility, and while I’ve enjoyed every minute of leading Derbyshire, I believe that stepping back to focus solely on my game will give me the best opportunity to force my way into the England set-up,” he said. Derbyshire’s managing director, Stevecroft, expressed support for Madsen’s decision, pointing out that the move could benefit both the player and the club. “Wayne is one of the most professional and experienced players in our squad, and we respect his decision to pursue international opportunities,” he said. “Keaton is stepping into the role with a wealth of experience at all levels, and we are confident he can provide strong leadership.” Jennings, a former England Under-19 captain, previously played as a central batsman for Derbyshire in 2021 and has been thriving at Durham this season. His promotion to captaincy is expected to bring consistency and a fresh outlook to the side as they continue their push up the County Championship table. Madsen’s career, which has seen him play for teams including Kent and Glamorgan, has been marked by a hunger to prove himself on bigger stages. After being disappointed to miss out on national team selection in previous years, the move to end his captaincy role may now finally provide the opportunity he has long desired. This decision also comes amid a growing trend of county captains stepping down or transferring roles to focus on individual game time in the run-up to major international cricket events.

Aston Villa found their feet at last as they emphatically ended their winless start to the Championship season with a hard-fought and thoroughly merited 2-1 victory over Norwich City at Villa Park. The win, which came after three frustrating opening matches, seemed to finally puncture the early-season nerves that had plagued Paul Lambert’s side and provided a timely boost as they aim to reclaim their place in the Premier League. The visitors started with a clean sheet intent, but it was the home side who struck first. Villa took the lead in the 28th minute when Nathan Baker, the centre-back who arrived from Arsenal in the summer, rose highest to power a header into the back of the net from a corner. The goal, only his second for the club, lifted the home crowd and seemed to settle the Villa players, who had struggled to assert themselves in their previous matches. Norwich responded in the second half with renewed intensity, and they were eventually rewarded with an equaliser in the 67th minute. Horsfall nodded in a cross from the right to bring the visitors level, but the home side had the stronger second half and regained the lead with just 13 minutes remaining. Christian Benteke, the Belgian striker who has endured a frustrating start to his Villa career, tapped in from close range after a smart move down the left. Benteke’s goal proved to be the decisive one, and despite a late push from the Canaries, Villa defended resolutely to pick up all three points. The victory could not have come at a better time for Villa, whose first three Premier League 2 matches had yielded just a single draw and suggested a side still adjusting to the rigours of top-tier football. Manager Paul Lambert praised his team’s resilience post-match, saying: "It was a good performance. We showed character, especially in the second half. The first goal helped settle things and the players are starting to enjoy playing together." The win lifted Villa to fourth in the Championship, two points behind the play-off places, while Norwich remain in the relegation zone with just a single point from their first four matches. Lambert, who returned to Villa Park in the summer to revive the club's ambitions of immediate promotion, knows this result will not be enough on its own. But he will also be heartened by a performance that suggested growing momentum and the prospect of a go-to victory on home turf if the players can maintain this form.

Liverpool will find out on Friday whether a disciplinary case will be brought against defender Joel Matip, who was involved in an on-field altercation with team-mate James Milner during the Reds’ 2-0 Premier League win over Watford on Sunday. The £25 million man, who has returned to full fitness after a lengthy lay-off, saw the incident unfold during the second half when tensions appeared to rise following a sequence of errors that temporarily compromised Liverpool’s lead. The Football Association has until this Friday to decide whether to formally investigate the exchange, which was captured briefly on live television and has since sparked debate among fans and pundits alike. The club confirmed on Tuesday that they were “aware of the incident and were in communication with the relevant authorities”. Matip, 26, has been a key part of manager Jürgen Klopp’s plans this season following an absence of almost six months due to injury. His return came with an added urgency as the Reds continue their relentless push at the top of the league table. However, the on-pitch dispute, which remains unexplained by the club or the players involved, has added uncertainty over his involvement in upcoming matches. Klopp refused to comment on the incident when questioned by reporters, saying only that he would “deal with it as it comes”. Relations within the squad have generally been strong this season, and the episode is seen as a rare moment of friction among a group known for its unity. There is also growing speculation over whether Matip will be rested for the visit of Manchester City at Anfield on Saturday — a mouth-watering fixture that currently sits in a 21:30 BST time slot. The timing of the potential disciplinary decision, which will be made just days before that weekend clash, has raised questions over whether Matip could face a suspension just as he is back in full stride. This season has already seen disciplinary action affect other Liverpool players, with Roberto Firminho receiving a three-match ban for a sending-off in December. Given the Reds’ current pursuit of the Premier League title and their growing ambitions on the Champions League frontier, any additional complications — on-field or off — could prove crucial. The waiting game will now continue. As fans and media speculate over what exactly transpired between two of their stars, the FA’s Friday decision will determine the next chapter in a season that has so far offered very few quiet moments for Liverpool.

In a tense session of questioning at the UK Parliament’s Treasury Select Committee, executives from some of the world's most recognisable firms faced a challenging and at times heated interrogation over the issue of tax avoidance. The session, held over two days and broadcast live, saw MPs lay bare their frustrations with multinationals that use complex financial structures to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, often at the cost of British taxpayers. Among those grilled was Sarah Wood, a senior executive from a major UK-based technology company, who insisted that her firm had “always acted in accordance with local and international tax laws.” However, Labour MP Ian Murray pressed her: “But at what cost? Your profits last year exceeded £10 billion, yet you paid less tax in the UK than some local councils,” he said, echoing the sentiments of cross-party members who accused the firm of behaving irresponsibly. The session, which was part of a broader government push to scrutinise the tax strategies of global corporations, drew on recent headlines that exposed how major Anglo-American companies have used offshore subsidiaries and fictitious headquarters to reduce their tax liabilities to near-zero. One such case involved a finance chief from a retail giant who outlined, under careful questioning, how profits from UK operations were legally routed through corporate entities registered in low-tax territories, such as Ireland and Luxembourg. The cross-examinations did not only focus on profits. Another PM, Tony Blair, earned £21million from a £3 million investment. The data for current and former PMs was obtained from company filings with the Companies House, a government register of public companies. scientists relied solely on question marks for their findings. After all the analysis, they had to admit they couldn't figure it out with any confidence. They wrote "This happened, but we don't know why," something akin to a scientist saying the sun is shining, but we need to figure if it's a regular or irregular action.

The US financial landscape is set for a new chapter as all five US financial regulators have formally approved the much-debated Volcker Rule, a key component of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. Designed in the wake of the 2008–09 financial crisis, the rule aims to prevent banks from engaging in speculative trading with their own money and to restrict relationships between banks and private hedge funds or private equity investment funds. The approval marks a significant moment in efforts to reduce risks within the financial system and to curtail the kinds of reckless behaviour seen before the economic collapse. The Volcker Rule is named after former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker, who first proposed the idea during the financial crisis. His suggestion was relatively simple: banks should not be in the business of making bets on their own accounts, a practice known as proprietary trading, which was blamed in part for precipitating the crisis by encouraging excessive risk-taking. The regulatory agencies, including the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), have worked collaboratively to finalise and implement the rule over the past several years. Each agency governs different aspects of financial institutions, from banking to market conduct, ensuring that the new restrictions are cohesive across the financial sector. Supporters of the rule argue that it will protect taxpayer money and prevent banks from engaging in activities that could destabilise the economy, particularly in times of crisis. They point to the crisis as a case study in the dangers of allowing financial institutions to operate without meaningful oversight, with many of the world’s largest banks involved in complex derivatives trades that ultimately collapsed under their own weight, requiring massive government bailouts. Critics, however, have long claimed the rule is a bureaucratic overreach that will stifle financial innovation and lead to job losses. Some industry leaders argued the rule, once finalised, could hamper banks’ ability to compete internationally, as many overseas financial institutions would not be subject to the same restrictions. Smaller banks, in particular, have pointed out the high compliance costs and burdens associated with the rule. With regulatory firms now backing the new measures, the financial sector braces for a transitional period where banks must adjust their investment strategies and ensure compliance with the Volcker Rule’s requirements.

Harry Kane marked his 100th appearance for Tottenham Hotspur with a decisive goal as the north London club moved into the Premier League's top four with a hard-fought 2-0 victory over struggling Southampton at St Mary's Stadium. The £150 million England captain, making his centuryth appearance since joining Spurs from Southampton in 2013, broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute with a composed finish that showcased his clinical touch. Kane's goal sparked a much-improved performance from Spurs, who had struggled for fluency in the first half, and set the tone for a dominant second. Spurs came into the match requiring a win to make up ground on the top four, and they emerged with another convincing display in a week that has seen Ange Postecoglou's side reflect a different team altogether from the one who missed out on European Qualification last season. Their 21st league win of the campaign lifted them back into the Europa Conference League places thanks in part to a lack of results at the top of the table. Kane, who showed both movement and intelligence in his goal, now stands as one of the most prolific forwards in Premier League history. His 18 league goals this season have made him a vital figure as Spurs continue to gear up for a potential Champions League return. Second-half substitute Brennan Johnson wrapped up the win with a late strike in the 83rd minute, his burst of pace and low cross finding the net as he finished off a flowing move. The goal reflected the attacking flair that Postecoglou has infused into Tottenham’s play this season. For Southampton, the defeat represented another sour evening on what has been a bleak campaign. Already relegated from the Premier League, Saints remain rooted to the bottom of the table and have now lost five of their last six games. Manager Owen Coyle, who took charge in March in an attempt to salvage some dignity from the season, will have had little to be optimistic about as his side struggled for energy and response. Postecoglou praised his side's perseverance after the game. "It was always going to be a tough place to come, but the players showed real character. We had to dig in after being a bit ragged in the first half, and it was good to see us grow with the game."

There is no question that India has the most positive economic story on the planet, with sustained growth, sweeping reform and a growing middle class that is reshaping the global economic landscape. In recent years, India has emerged as a beacon of opportunity and innovation, outpacing many developed economies and attracting unprecedented levels of investment. According to recent reports, the country is now the fastest-growing major economy in the world, driven by technological advances, youthful energy, and a rapidly digitising economy. This impressive performance has sparked a renewed interest in India, not just from global investors but also from business leaders and policymakers. The nation’s GDP is forecast to grow well above six percent this year, outperforming other major emerging markets. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has steadily increased, with companies across a range of sectors, from technology to manufacturing and renewable energy, setting up shop in the country. Driven by a demographic dividend of more than 600 million Indians under the age of 25, the Indian economy has seen a renaissance powered by entrepreneurship, digital inclusion, and the digitisation of public services. India’s smartphone revolution, coupled with the expansion of mobile internet, has transformed the way millions of Indians communicate, work and conduct business. At the heart of India’s success is the government's commitment to economic reform. The introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in 2017 marked a significant shift in the nation's tax structure, streamlining the process and reducing bureaucratic hurdles for businesses. Additionally, the government has accelerated efforts toward financial inclusion through initiatives such as the Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana, which has brought banking services to millions of previously unbanked citizens. India's continued economic growth also has a positive ripple effect across the globe. As a major consumer and producer, its influence is increasingly felt in global markets. The country’s green energy boom, for instance, is helping to meet rising demand for renewable power and laying the groundwork for a transformation in energy consumption. While challenges remain, including development disparities and the need for better infrastructure, there is no doubt that the future is bright for India. As the world continues to look for stability and opportunity, India’s story offers a compelling and resilient path forward. It is not only the 'world's fastest-growing major economy,' but also the embodiment of economic progress and a model for other developing nations seeking prosperity.

In a cruel twist of fate, the late Russian billionaire Elena Baturina, once dubbed the “Iron Lady of Russian real estate,” is finally being remembered with a degree of compassion that was largely absent during her lifetime. Her recent passing has prompted a wave of memorial tributes from the very circles—political and business—that once shunned or openly ridiculed her. While she was alive, Baturina was more often criticized for her self-serving political allegiances and the ostentatious wealth that sparked questions about corruption, but now, she is being described as a “woman ahead of her time,” and “a trailblazer in the new Russian economy.” Baturina, who amassed a fortune during Russia’s post-Soviet real estate boom, was among the wealthy few who managed to navigate the murky waters of privatization and political favor. As the first female deputy prime minister in Russia, and the wife of the former mayor of Moscow, Yuri Luzhkov, she wielded significant influence in both governmental and commercial affairs. However, in recent years, she found herself at the center of controversy after aligning aggressively—and perhaps opportunely—with President Vladimir Putin. Her relationships with both the government and media became increasingly contentious. After Luzhkov’s arrest in 2010 for alleged corruption, Baturina was accused of using her wealth and connections to undermine the Kremlin's agenda at the time. Years later, she shifted her approach, seeking to align more closely with Putin and the conservative tide that followed Russia’s Sillet Stones reforms. Her pivot, however, made her a target for public scorn and cast her as a suspicious political player rather than a reformer. Yet, in death, the narrative appears to have softened. State-backed media and influential figures have taken to praising Baturina’s resilience and business acumen. Her funeral, attended by a mix of old allies and new admirers, reflected what many see as a posthumous redemption. Former associates have spoken of her strength in overcoming the pressures of her complicated life, while commentators argue her ability to survive in the cutthroat world of Russian politics and business was something to be admired. Elena Baturina’s legacy remains a mosaic of contradictions: a woman who broke barriers as one of the first female business tycoons in Russia, yet was often reduced to a symbol of excess and political risk. Now, with the veil of controversy lifted in her absence, some see an opportunity to reflect on her contributions without the brashness of partisan rhetoric.

Britain’s Kell Brook has thrown open the gauntlet to middleweight legend Gennady Golovkin, branding the potential clash as a real-life “David versus Goliath” encounter. The Yorkshire boxer, who himself holds a record of 37 wins from 40 professional bouts—29 of them inside the distance—has made it clear that despite the gap in both weight and record, he believes he has what it takes to challenge the fearsome Kazakh. Golovkin, a name spoken with reverence and fear in boxing circles, is a three-time undisputed middleweight champion with a staggering 38 knockout wins in his 38 prior victories. Brook, who made his name at welterweight, concedes that stepping up in weight is the biggest challenge of his career, but remains undeterred. “I know the risks I’m taking,” Brook stated. “Golovkin is the most dangerous fighter in the sport at the moment. But I’ve always believed I can beat anyone, and in this case, I’m the oversized David.” Brook’s desire for the fight isn’t just driven by ambition, but by a personal quest to silence the critics who say he lacks the courage to test himself against elite opposition. “People say I’ve never stood toe-to-toe with the best, and I’m ready to show them I’m not just another name in another fight,” he said. “This is about legacy. This is about proving I’m not just a welterweight filler-in—I’m a world champion who can step up and take what someone like GGG is offering.” Steve Collins, Brook’s former trainer and a three-time world champion in his own right, has previously questioned whether the fight is even viable, citing the weight difference as a major concern. Brook refutes this. “People are always going on about my size versus GGG’s,” he said. “He may be bigger, but I’m not the untrained superhero in that comparison. I’ve got the techniques, the will, and the road map. The rest? That’s the show they want to see.” Unsurprisingly, Golovkin’s team has remained non-committal to the fight. Dzigao Ibragimov, his manager, recently hinted that GGG would only be interested in facing Brook after delivering a warning with another high-profile knockout. For now, the details remain in the murky waters of negotiation, but one thing is clear: Brook is no longer idly watching the middleweight scene from the outside.

Amid the sorrow and shock reverberating through the city of Boston, a broader political debate has erupted in the wake of the marathon bombing, as Massachusetts mourns its victims and pays its respects with a statewide minute’s silence. The tragedy, which claimed three lives and injured hundreds, has not only frightened a city renowned for its resilience but has also reignited heated discussions about gun control, national security, and civil liberties. The blasts, which occurred near the finish line of the Boston Marathon on April 15, were carried out by two brothers, who had evaded surveillance and prepared the devices in plain sight. Following the attacks, the manhunt that led to the capture of one suspect and the death of the other prompted national and international debate on how such events could be prevented in the future. While numerous vigils and memorials have been held by residents to show unity and withstand terror, the incident has also become the catalyst for renewed political tension in a state historically known for its strong liberal leanings. Calls to expand surveillance, restrict certain categories of firearms, and enable the government to detain individuals on suspicion of terrorism have clashed with the voices of those who argue that such measures could erode civil freedoms. MassachusettsSenator Elizabeth Warren, in a powerful speech at a local forum, warned of the dangers of “overreaction in the name of security.” She urged both federal and state lawmakers to consider the long-term impacts of new security measures, saying, “We must not respond to the fear of terrorism by surrendering the values that have always made us free.” Conversely, members of Congress from more conservative districts have lobbied for urgent changes in how potential threats are identified and acted upon. “The failures in the days before April 15 were not just mistakes,” said Representative Ted Wragg in a House debate about intelligence reform. “They were failures of the broken system we currently have. We must take what we’ve learned from this tragedy and plug those holes.” As Massachusetts unites in grief and celebration of resilience, the political fallout continues to ripple. Across the nation, the Boston Marathon bombing has reminded the country of a difficult balance all democracies must navigate—the need for security in the face of terrorism while safeguarding the freedoms that define them. And in Boston, with ashes still flying and memorials still standing, the debate is no less heartfelt than the city's resolve.

Survivors of ‘Dunkirk Miracle’ to Reunite for Final Remembrance   A small but brave group of veterans who played a vital role in one of World War Two’s most dramatic moments are to reunite this month for what is expected to be one of their last large-scale gatherings before the war generation passes from the scene. The event marks the 80th anniversary of the   Dunkirk evacuation  , an operation that saved the lives of more than 338,000 Allied soldiers under harrowing conditions as German forces advanced across France in May and June 1940. The ceremony, scheduled for late March in   Littlehampton, West Sussex  , is traditionally hosted by the   Dunkirk Association  , a group of surviving Little Myton Morpeth (LYM) Commando veterans — men who, decades earlier, volunteered to risk everything in Operation Dynamo. This year’s event is expected to draw about 80 survivors, many of whom are now in their nineties, marking one of the last major commemorations of their kind. For some of the veterans, the gathering will not just be a celebration of survival, but also a solemn chance to reflect on those they never saw again — fellow soldiers, crew members and civilians who did not return. As the years pass, the number of witnesses to history dwindles. “It's fading fast,” said one veteran who asked not to be named. “There used to be hundreds of us. Now, every year it gets harder to make the trip, but as long as we can, we will. This is one of the last chances to tell the truth.” The Dunkirk evacuation remains one of the most enduring symbols of British resilience and courage. Between May 26 and June 4, 1940, a flotilla of merchant ships, fishing boats and pleasure cruisers — famously known as the “Little Ships of Dunkirk” — crossed the English Channel under heavy fire to bring British and Allied troops back from the beaches of Dunkirk after their defeat in northern France. Thousands of civilians volunteered to take part in the mission, many risking their lives as they returned to the shore under constant threat from enemy aircraft and U-boats. The sustained bombing campaign by the Luftwaffe during what became known as the "Miracle of Dunkirk" cost around 500 civilian and military lives, leaving a legacy of heroism and tragedy. This year’s event will also see the unveiling of a new plaque in the town, dedicated to the memory of all those who took part in the operation.

The digital age proved to be both a new frontier and a powerful weapon in the unfolding of a high-profile sexual abuse case involving Adam Johnson, the former England international and Sunderland AFC winger. On Friday, Johnson was sentenced to six years in prison after being found guilty of sexual activity with a 15-year-old girl. At the heart of the prosecution’s case were conversations from social media platforms and private messaging apps that provided damning evidence of the relationship between the 33-year-old footballer and the teenager. Prosecutors revealed in court how records retrieved from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram offered a troubling insight into the communication between Johnson and his victim. The transcripts demonstrated not only the content of their exchanges but also tracked the timeline and frequency of the messages, reinforcing the gravity of Johnson’s actions. These digital threads, as investigators described them, were critical in establishing the nature and progression of their relationship. Although Johnson used multiple platforms to mask his identity—frequently using fake profiles and alternative accounts—to get around age-restriction protocols, the prosecution was able to trace his digital footprints using forensic phone and IP address data obtained through judicial warrants. The evidence demonstrated meticulous efforts on the part of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) to navigate the complexities of online anonymity. In their statements, grief counselors for the victim and her family described the emotional toll the ordeal had taken on the teenager. “It was unimaginably invasive for her to be forced to read out these messages in court,” one said, praising the efforts of staff at the CPS and police for ensuring the trial was sensitive to the girl’s emotional state. The case has cast an uncomfortable spotlight on the role of technology in modern crime and the challenges it presents for law enforcement. Advances in data science and real-time monitoring have allowed investigators to track online interactions in ways that would have been impossible just a decade ago. Yet they have also exposed the vulnerabilities of young people in an increasingly digital world and the need for greater awareness around online safety and consent. The sending of indecent photographs and inappropriate messages over platforms that many young people use daily has led to growing calls for more stringent regulation and education. Johnson was removed as a football coach at a primary school in 2017 while the case was being prepared for trial.

Labour has called on the government to abandon a controversial review of the Freedom of Information Act, warning that any changes could significantly weaken transparency and public accountability in the UK. The motion was raised by shadow culture, media, and sport secretary, Rushanara Ali, who argued that scrapping the review would protect the rights of the public to access information on how the state is run. The government was recently handed a formal recommendation by the all-party group on a Bill of Rights and Responsibilities to maintain the current FOIA, rather than reshape it. It was put together as part of a wider consultation on the government's proposed new Human Rights Bill. The decision has been welcomed by campaign groups and journalists alike who have long cautioned against potential amendments that could make it harder to uncover official wrongdoing or request public data. The current Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) was passed in 2000 and gives the public the right to access information held by public authorities, provided the information is not exempt. The law has been instrumental in exposing malpractice in areas such as criminal justice, public procurement, and health, with the UK’s national freedom of information service, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), receiving thousands of requests each year. Labour claims that the proposed changes could introduce loopholes and bureaucratic hurdles that would enable more public bodies to invoke secrecy. They argue that such a shift would undermine democratic oversight and public trust at a time when transparency is more important than ever. “In an era of deepening mistrust in public institutions and increasing demands for democratic accountability, any move to limit access to public information should be rejected outright,” Ms Ali said in a statement. The government insists the review is necessary to ensure FOIA remains “fit for purpose” in the modern age and is in line with its broader reform programme, which includes a new Human Rights Bill designed to replace the European Convention on Human Rights. However, critics fear the move is motivated more by political calculation than public interest. Suella Braverman, the justice secretary, claimed that the changes would ensure the law was “not used as a tool for partisan or inappropriate purposes”. In contrast, editor of the  Guardian , Katherine Viner, recently described the review as an “assault on transparency” and called for sustained public pressure to deter any meaningful amendments. The review has yet to be formally published, but voices across the media, opposition parties, and civil society remain united in their call for it to be abandoned.
