Haq’s ‘Unselectable’ Status Sparks Debate as Bradburn Vows Scotland Future    Scotland head coach Grant Bradburn has insisted Majid Haq still has a future in international cricket, despite the spinner being described as “deemed unselectable” for the forthcoming T20 World Cup. The remarks, made in a recent press conference, have ignited a debate among fans and pundits alike about the criteria used in selecting Scotland’s squad for the premier global tournament.  Haq, a 29-year-old leg-spinner and wicketkeeper, has long been a familiar face in the Scotland team during the 50-over and T20 formats. However, his omission from the World T20 shortlist, which sees 15 players selected for the event, has raised questions about his role within the national setup. Bradburn, who took charge of the team last year, explained the difficult decision. “Majid is a very talented player, and it was not an easy choice to say he was deemed unselectable for the World T20 squad, but we felt we had to prioritise players who fit directly into the T20 framework,” he said. The head coach quickly followed that up with strong reassurance to Haq and supporters. “Look, Majid is part of our future. He is a very capable player and is playing at a high level in New Zealand, with Horowhenua-Kapiti. His experience and his skills are vital for the team’s development, and he will definitely be considered for future fixtures,” Bradburn said. The comments come amid growing speculation over the structure of Scotland’s playing staff. With the World T20 set to be a shortened, compact tournament, selectors have opted for younger, more aggressive players who can dominate on smaller grounds. Bradburn added that “the shape of the competition this time meant we had to rethink our approach. This wasn’t about Majid not delivering, but about the tactical composition of the squad.” But Haq’s supporters argue that his all-round contribution – his ability to open the innings with his batting and provide late breakthroughs with his spin – is invaluable in unpredictable T20 conditions. Social media has already been flooded with fan support, questioning the 'unselectable' framing of the decision and highlighting recent performances that suggest otherwise. The debate has also spilled into the cricket media, with several columnists highlighting Haq’s seven wickets in two games during the recent Sahara Desert T20. Others note his adaptability across formats and emerging leadership potential.

Sweden’s ambitious experiment with six-hour working days aimed to boost productivity, mental health, and job satisfaction has concluded its most public two-year trial, leaving workplace experts and employees alike to debate whether the radical shift delivered on its promises. The trial, launched in 2015 in the city of Gothenburg, saw staff at a public care home work 20 per cent less than the standard eight-hour day—still full-time in Swedish terms—while being paid the same. The idea was to create a better work-life balance, reduce stress, and ultimately improve performance. But was the dream of a shorter working day, without the loss of pay or pension contributions, truly a success, or has it exposed cracks in the idea of condensing work hours without repercussions? Employees at the care home initially raved about the changes. Workers spoke of more time to spend with their families, pursue hobbies and even improve their mental health. Productivity in the early months reportedly rose by almost 30 per cent, thanks in part to a more alert and engaged workforce, reduced staff turnover and a team of 152 employees working the equivalent of 182 full-time places. Yet, as the trial stretched into its second year, frustrations began to emerge. Despite the early gains, managers noted that workload pressures increased due to the condensed hours. The same level of care needed to be delivered in less time, often leaving staff with less capacity to build meaningful relationships with residents or attend to complex patient needs. “It was like trying to run the same programme with a shrunken workforce,” one mid-level manager told local media. Critics of the experiment argued that the benefits came with a cost—job security, specifically. After the trial ended and politicians failed to extend the scheme nationwide, key workers reportedly left for other sectors where working hours were not as restricted. Employers, too, were reluctant to commit to what many described as an “untested model” in the long term. Business leaders in Sweden have claimed that without clearer structures and support for managing compressed working hours across all roles, the system could leave the most vulnerable sectors—such as healthcare and education—struggling under the pressure. Despite the mixed reception, the trial has sparked renewed conversations across Europe and beyond about the viability of a four-day work week. Some businesses in the UK, New Zealand, and the US are already experimenting with their own variations, drawing inspiration from Sweden’s controversial experience.

Sunderland manager Steve Bruce has emphatically denied claims he is considering quitting the post, despite facing intense abuse from fans following his side’s 2-0 defeat by Wigan at the weekend. Bruce, who was jeered by a section of supporters during and after the match, said in a tightly worded statement on Tuesday night that he “has no intention of walking away” from the club he has led since 2021. The defeat against Wigan, which leaves the side perilously close to the relegation zone, was met with visible frustration among fans at the Stadium of Light. Social media quickly filled with calls for Bruce to step down, while several fans were caught on camera chanting "who’s the traitor?" and "you’ve got to go" outside the manager's dugout. Bruce, however, is not new to adversity. Now in his 30th year as a manager, he has weathered storms for virtually every club he has been in charge of – from Birmingham to Celtic, Hull City to Middlesbrough, and now, again, at his boyhood club. In a post-match interview, he addressed the backlash head-on. "I’ve had some of the worst abuse I’ve ever had in a career that’s spanned over 30 years," Bruce said. "It’s heartbreaking. I give everything for this club. I’ve built this team with my own eyes, and I know the lengths I’ve gone to try and help this club get out of the situation we were in. There’s no way I’m walking away from this just because of a defeat. Clubs go through bad periods, and this one is no different." The 58-year-old, who previously guided Sunderland from being relegated from the Premier League back to the top flight, remains a fan favourite among many loyal followers. Bruce’s journey with the club has been an emotional one — his 2018 appointment was widely celebrated as the return of a ‘Sunderland man’ to the helm. Since then, he has overseen 53 matches and won 26 of them – not a stellar tally, but not uncommon for a team waiting on a transfer ban to be lifted and struggling financially. While supporters are right to express their frustrations, many within the football community have supported Bruce’s recent work, noting that his relationship with key players like Lyndon Dykes and Domenico Di Serio has contributed to a more settled first team.

Al Jazeera: The Media Giant That Put Qatar on the World Stage   For a nation smaller than London and with a population of just over three million, Qatar has long punched well above its weight on the global stage. While its vast financial resources, funded by the world’s largest natural gas reserves, have allowed it to build a skyline of futuristic towers and fund ambitious international projects, it is one entity that has truly put the kingdom on the map — a media network named Al Jazeera. Launched in 1996 under the patronage of then-Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, Qatar’s Al Jazeera Media Network has grown from a modest Arabic-language news channel into one of the world’s most powerful and controversial broadcast institutions. With its headquarters in Doha, the network now includes Al Jazeera English (AJE), Al Jazeera Arabic, and an array of news, sports and documentary platforms, the tiny Gulf state-controlled media giant has become synonymous with hard-hitting journalism, bold political commentary, and, frequently, global controversy. Al Jazeera’s rise has not been without turbulence, even within its own region. The network quickly became a thorn in the side of many of Qatar’s neighbours, particularly the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its investigative journalism and unflinching reporting on regional conflicts, from Libya to Egypt and – most notably – Syria, have drawn criticism, admiration, and accusations of bias. The network's coverage of the Arab Spring uprisings was particularly iconic, providing a platform for voices across the Middle East at a time when traditional powers were scrambling to maintain influence. Internationally, Al Jazeera has earned a reputation for challenging the mainstream Western narrative. Its English and Arabic arms have reported from war-torn zones, interviewed high-profile dissidents and offered alternative perspectives to the global story. While the network has been accused by some of being politicised, others praise it for its fearless approach and commitment to unearthing uncomfortable truths. The influence of Al Jazeera has helped Qatar play an outsized role in global affairs — from funding the English Football Association's St. George's Park training ground, to hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup and funding media outlets across Africa and Asia. Its power extends beyond the newsroom, with various arms of the network forming think tanks, digital platforms, and investigative units such as the respected Al Jazeera Investigations team.

In a move that is certainly not lacking in public interest—and perhaps a touch of levity—local councils in Wales are preparing to roll out new and improved public toilet facilities to cater for the needs of residents and visitors alike. With a long-standing reputation as a nation of green hills, breathtaking landscapes, and a unique cultural identity, Wales is now apparently beginning to place a more practical emphasis on one of life’s most mundane yet essential duties: making sure people can find a place to go when the call of nature is irresistible. The initiative comes in response to a growing awareness of the lack of public toilets in key tourist areas, shopping centres, and even some town centres across the country. Recent reports have highlighted the "toilet crisis" in parts of the UK, with Wales not immune to the issue. Councillors have taken note and are prioritising the installation of new, accessible, and well-maintained public lavatories as part of an extended civic infrastructure programme. Chairman of the Welsh Local Government Association, Councillor Steve Hennell, spoke on the matter, saying: “It’s not something many of us like to talk about, but it’s a key part of the visitor experience. If we want to continue attracting people from around the world to Wales, we need to make sure they can go on their walk, hike, or city trip without being anxious about where the next loo is.” He added that the new approach would also see an improved focus on accessibility and sanitation standards, ensuring that facilities are not only plentiful but clean and suitable for all. The toilets will be managed under a scheme in which local authorities will work closely with business improvement districts and community groups to install and maintain the facilities—especially in areas previously underserved. In Ceredigion and Pembrokeshire, for instance, popular coastal spots are seeing the introduction of "toilet hubs", which will also offer amenities like baby-changing facilities and even information kiosks. Beyond the straightforward practical benefits, the plan has also sparked something of a Twitter reaction. From local councils playfully warning residents about the weather and exercise, to the more traditional public health advice, it seems talking about toilets is becoming a little less taboo. Public reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. As one Twitter user eloquently put it: “At long last—Wales is taking the bathroom seriously.”

There is a distinct ‘back-to-school’ atmosphere in Whitehall as the government prepares to publish a series of detailed reports on Brexit timing and planning, just as A-level results are set to be released next week. The synchronicity has not been lost on analysts and journalists alike, who view the carefully timed releases as yet another effort by ministers to appear both in control and methodical in their handling of the country’s most complex political project in decades. The papers are expected to outline the policy changes that will be devolved to the devolved nations as the UK moves closer to triggering Article 50. They also promise clarity on how the government intends to manage the transition from EU membership to a system of independent trade and regulatory rules. The publication, however, has raised eyebrows among opposition MPs, who see it as more an exercise in political optics than a substantive contribution to the Brexit debate. Labour’s Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell described the releases as an attempt to dress up a ‘policy vacuum’ with administrative paperwork. “What happened to the negotiating objectives in the Brexit White Paper?” he asked in a statement, echoing criticisms from crossbench peers and EU law experts who have long questioned the government’s strategy. Despite the criticism, Prime Minister Theresa May has pointed to the “phased and structured” approach as essential to ensuring a stable and orderly departure from the European Union. Speaking from Chequers over the weekend, she stressed that the series of documents would act as a template for future negotiations and serve as a learning tool for civil servants and sector representatives alike. The timing, with young people across the country waiting anxiously for the results of their exams, has also sparked a degree of irony. As the government’s Brexit project appears to enter a new phase of practical consideration, it is juxtaposed with a key moment in the academic year, prompting calls from education unions for the government to focus more on the “crisis facing our schools” and less on “political theatre.” Education Secretary Justine Greening, meanwhile, has defended the timing, saying the Brexit papers are part of an essential road map for the future and that they will help ensure a stable environment for education and student life post-exit. Her comments, however, did little to dampen the growing sense of unease among teachers and unions, who worry that the long-term educational implications of Brexit are far from clear.

There is "no truth" in allegations that a former chief constable visited a children’s home to abuse boys, a court has heard. The claims, which have caused widespread alarm and anguish among victims of historical abuse, were dismissed by the defendant, Sir Alan Norton, who is the subject of a long-running criminal case in a hearing in Manchester. The court was told that the allegations against the retired senior officer, who played a prominent role in the police force for over 30 years before his retirement in 2012, were part of a broader pattern of false accusations circulating in the aftermath of recent abuse investigations in the care and education sectors. The hearing, part of a complex and sensitive legal process involving multiple complainants and civil lawsuits, marks the latest in a series of high-profile cases targeting public figures accused of historical misconduct. Sir Alan, who is now 73, is represented by a high-profile legal team and faces multiple civil claims relating to his conduct while in post, including allegations of abuse at a now-defunct state-funded residential school in the North West of England. During the session, Sir Alan’s legal team denied the details directly, arguing that the allegations lack credibility and are supported by no concrete evidence. A short, carefully worded statement read to the court on his behalf said: “Sir Alan Norton categorically denies any wrongdoing and will be seeking to prove that these claims are entirely false and motivated.” The school, which operated during the 1980s and 1990s, was closed several years ago following a series of internal and external investigations. Former resident boys and workers have since come forward to local authorities and the National Crime Agency with allegations of abuse and cover-ups. A specialist unit dealing with historical child abuse inquiries has referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service, with prosecutors currently reviewing evidence before deciding whether to bring criminal charges. The case has reignited public debate about the need for greater accountability in institutions that cared for vulnerable children in the past. Campaigners, including Survivors of Institutional Abuse (SIA), called for the active and thorough pursuit of all credible historical allegations. “We believe the system fell down on them for far too long," one campaigner said. "It is vital that we listen to survivors and that no effort is spared in seeking the truth, regardless of who may be involved.”

Amid a spate of high-profile fights in the business world, one New York hedge fund has thrown a lot of punches in recent weeks, making headlines not just for its investment strategies, but for its aggressive legal and public relations campaigns against rivals, former partners, and even industry regulators. Elliott Management, the well-known activist investment firm led by billionaire Paul Singer, has found itself at the center of a growing number of disputes involving major corporations, with critics calling its tactics ruthless—and supporters applauding its role as a corporate watchdog. Elliott Management, which manages over $30 billion in assets, has long been known for its no-holds-barred approach to activist investing. But in the past few months, its interventions have taken on a more combative tone. Most notably, the firm has launched aggressive campaigns against the board of directors at energy giant ConocoPhillips and Daimler, the German automaker. In both cases, Elliott is pushing for major restructuring efforts, including cost-cutting measures and shifts in leadership, which have in turn sparked fierce counterattacks from the companies involved. In the case of Daimler, Elliott accused the board of "delusional" benchmarking of rival automakers and sought three board seats, citing a lack of transparency and mismanagement. Daimler’s response was swift—dismissing Elliott’s strategy as out of touch with the automotive industry’s long-term challenges, including the transition to electric vehicles and self-driving technology. The resulting battle of public positions has exposed cracks within the German corporate establishment, with some shareholders siding with Elliott, and others defending Daimler’s leadership. ConocoPhillips has also borne the brunt of Elliott's pressure, prompting the company to launch a legal and communications counter-offensive. In a rare move, ConocoPhillips filed a countersuit against Elliott, alleging the fund had wrongfully interfered with its merger with ConocoPhillips and had engaged in misleading disclosures to investors. The suit, which could set precedents for future shareholder activism, underscores the growing escalation of corporate conflict in the post-pandemic business world. Elliott’s high-profile campaign strategy is not new, but recent events have raised concerns about the power such activist investors wield. Some industry observers fear that the weapons firms like Elliott use—threats of proxy battles, public shaming, and legal maneuvering—are becoming increasingly normalized in the boardroom. “This is the new frontier of corporate governance,” said one financial strategist in New York.

With a record-breaking number of Northern Ireland supporters making the journey to France for Euro 2016, the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office has been working closely with local authorities and supporters’ groups to ensure their safety and wellbeing during the tournament. The support for the team, led by manager Michael O’Neill, has been electric in both Ireland and the UK, and has culminated in thousands heading across the Channel for what many have described as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to watch their side in a major international competition. So far, Northern Ireland's journey in the championship has been nothing short of remarkable. Following a historic draw with world champions Germany in their opening match, the team defied the odds once more with a stunning 1-0 victory over Poland that sent the supporters into raptures. The win left the fans buoyed by the possibility of an emotional homecoming should the side progress in the knockout stages. With an estimated 20,000 loyal supporters travelling to France — many of them returning after years in which Northern Ireland’s national team failed to qualify for any major tournament — the demand for security, support, and assistance has been monumental. The FCO has highlighted that it is up and running with a 24-hour support line and a dedicated team based out of the UK’s embassy in Paris. Ambassador Jan MacGillivray has personally been ensuring that the needs of the fans, and any arising issues, are addressed promptly. This includes everything from passport and travel problems to medical emergencies or security concerns. Balbir Mehmi, the UK’s minister of state at the Foreign Office, acknowledged the significance of the occasion. “The passion of the Northern Ireland fans is a key reason why the team has captured the hearts of so many,” he said in a statement last week. “It is our responsibility to support these fans to ensure that their experience is positive and they can focus on enjoying the match without unnecessary obstacles.” Local authorities in areas hosting Northern Ireland supporters have also implemented additional safety measures. Lille, which will play host to one of the country’s matches, has extended police patrols and is working with FCO representatives to provide accurate information about waiting times, transport links, and medical support. As for the supporters themselves, the mood remains upbeat. Many have described the journey as “an adventure” and have set up informal groups around accommodation and fan zones, with the goal of creating a strong, united identity that mirrors the tenacity of the national side on the pitch.

Fresh doubts have emerged over EDF’s proposal to build a £18bn nuclear power plant at Hinkley Point in Somerset, with growing concerns over rising construction costs, delays, and questions about its economic viability. The UK government has previously committed to support the project as a cornerstone of the country’s energy strategy, but recent developments have cast a shadow over the future of the long-awaited facility. The French energy giant EDF – which plans to partner with China General Nuclear Power Corporation (CGNPC) on the Hinkley Point C project – has faced mounting pressure as construction timelines continue to stretch. Originally scheduled for completion in 2025, the site is now not expected to produce its first power before 2028, with EDF citing supply chain issues and the complexity of the first new nuclear plant to be built in the UK in decades. This delay, coupled with a recent announcement of increased projected costs from £18bn to nearly £23bn, has raised concerns among experts and critics. "The rising figures are a red flag," said Dr Emma Atkins, an energy policy analyst at the University of Exeter. "At this rate, it’s not clear how the project can be justified as a viable energy investment, especially with renewed focus on renewable energy and gas as alternatives." The UK Energy Secretary, Claire Coutinho, was consulted on the matter last week and was said to be "visibly frustrated" by the delays and cost overruns, according to insiders. A government spokesperson has since refused to comment on internal discussions but reiterated that the Hinkley Point project "remains an important part of the UK’s energy mix". The project is central to the ambition of replacing the UK’s aging nuclear and coal fleet with low-carbon energy sources. However, as EDF remains in talks with the French government for financial support, the role of state assistance is now under scrutiny. French President Emmanuel Macron has been an outspoken supporter of the project, but unconfirmed reports suggest that the French state may be cutting its financial contribution, which could further undermine confidence in the venture. Environmental groups have also stepped into the debate, with some questioning whether the money would be better spent on expanding wind and solar power as part of a more agile and sustainable energy strategy. "We need new nuclear plants to meet our climate goals, but delays and indefinite cost increases erode public trust and the credibility of the go-to-plan on energy security," said Nick Hughes of Greenpeace UK.

The British and Irish Lions kept their World Cup-winning momentum on track with a dominant display against a hard-pressed but outmatched Melbourne Rebels side in their warm-up match on Sunday, securing a 38-17 victory ahead of the second Test against Australia. The win, played out in front of a passionate yet noticeably smaller than expected crowd at AAMI Park, mirrored the Lions' relentless efficiency and physicality as they edged closer to making history in their ambitious bid to retain the ashes Down Under. From the outset, the Lions, brimming with confidence following their 24-21 victory in the opening Test in Brisbane, appeared well in sync as they exploited every gap in the Aboriginal-owned Melbourne outfit. Points came from the boot of fly-half Owen Farrell and tries from the ever-dangerous captain Sam Warburton and bursts of pace from Scotland’s Chris Murray who showed flashes of brilliance in the open field. The Rebels fought admirably in the face of the Lions’ tactical prowess, but moments of indiscipline and lack of cohesion in their back line were ruthlessly punished by the tourists, who showed no signs of letting up. Australia, who were defeated in the first Test, will hope to take note of the Lions' short attention span. With their backs against the wall in their bid to become the first team to complete a five-Test series against Australia since 1950, the Lions pressed their advantage, and by half time had already claimed a 23-point lead. The second half saw the Lions’ forwards continue their pressuring juggernaut, with scrum-half Ben Youngs disrupting the Rebels’ set pieces and forwards like Alun Wyn Jones and Jamie George tightening the screw at the breakdown. The victory was not without its own challenges for head coach Warren Gatland, whose side suffered a few late misfires and a frustrating period of the game when the coveted bonus point seemed out of reach. But with the match firmly攥ed in their grip, the Lions could afford to step back and rest some of their big names for the upcoming high-stakes encounter with the Wallabies in Sydney on Thursday. For any rugby fan, the performance was a reminder of why the Lions remain the darling of the international scene and why they are tipped to go all the way in what promises to be one of the most hard-fought series in recent memory.

Labour leader Ed Miliband has claimed the party is showing signs of recovery after coming second in the European elections, though he cautioned that significant work remains to restore trust with the British public. Despite losing ground in a number of key UK regions, Labour edged out UKIP to finish as the second-largest political force in the EU vote, a result that Mr Miliband described as "positive progress". However, he acknowledged that his party's performance "could have been better" and pledged to address policy and organisational weaknesses. The European elections, often seen as a barometer of broader political sentiment, were hit by a low voter turnout of just 34.4 percent – the lowest since the vote system was reformed in 1999 – and marked a mixed day across the political spectrum. While the Conservatives lost seats to the Liberal Democrats and Green Party, the real surprise was the collapse of UKIP’s influence, which managed just 13 percent of the vote nationwide – far below pre-election projections. Speaking at a post-election event in London, Mr Miliband said the result reflected both enduring challenges and the beginnings of a turnaround. “This is real progress,” he said, “but we know we have further to go. I’m under no illusions as to how high the bar is and how much we need to do to earn the trust of the British people again.” Mr Miliband’s comments came as new figures showed Labour performing least strongly in the north-east of England, a traditional Labour heartland that saw strong UKIP gains. In contrast, the party did better in London and the South, where it held key seats and saw higher voter engagement. The result will give some encouragement to Mr Miliband’s allies who have been urging the party to double down on its message of rebuilding public services and tackling inequality. But critics within his own party argue the performance was far from convincing and that Labour still struggles to project confidence and clarity. Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell, who has been openly unimpressed by the rhetoric of a ‘recovered’ Labour, told BBC Radio 4’s  Today  programme: “We need to show strength on the issues that matter to working people – not just talk about making progress. The trust is not there yet.” With a general election expected within the next 18 months, the European elections have set the stage for a crucial period of repositioning for the Labour Party.

This week promises a politically charged atmosphere as the UK’s longest-awaited public vote moves a significant step closer to reality. At the heart of it all is the decision to announce the date for the EU referendum, a moment that has been building since the 2015 general election, and which now holds the potential to reshape the country’s political and economic future. The Prime Minister is expected to unveil the chosen date on Monday following a government vote, a move that will mark the starting line in one of the most consequential political campaigns in recent British history. But as the referendum date looms, another matter of national security has also emerged into the public consciousness: the extent of the powers of the country’s intelligence agencies. In response to the increasing debate around surveillance and civil liberties following the global revelations by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden, the government is set to unveil further details of the proposed intelligence and security bill. The legislation has already stirred controversy among civil rights groups, legal experts, and even some members of the prime minister’s own party, raising questions about the balance between security and the protection of individual rights. Meanwhile, both the Leave and Remain campaigns are已经开始 laying the groundwork for their respective messages, with bookmakers and pollsters keeping a close eye on public sentiment as it shifts. The referendum, once seen as a distant possibility, is now less than a year away, and the implications for national policy – from trade deals to immigration – will be profound. With the political climate already tense and the potential for division looming, this week’s events mark the beginning of a period of intense scrutiny, debate, and public engagement that will define British politics for months to come. From the corridors of Westminster to the streets of London and beyond, the democratic process is set to be tested in a way not seen for decades. Prime Minister David Cameron, who has always been a reluctant campaigner, now faces the dual challenge of defending the EU and securing a date that satisfies both sides of the debate. For the public, the choice to remain within, or to exit, the European Union will become more than just a political decision – it will become a defining moment for the country’s future. As the votes for the date are cast this week, the eyes of the nation will be watching closely, anticipating the first move in the long and complex journey to Brexit – or no Brexit.

Leigh Halfpenny, one of Wales’ most celebrated rugby full-backs, has confirmed his move to French club Toulon, marking the latest chapter in his glittering career. The 33-year-old, who has earned over 100 caps for his country and is known for his sharp kicking and leadership on the field, will join the Top 14 side for the 2023-2024 season. Halfpenny, who has previously plied his trade in England with Bath and later Sale Sharks, is set to bring his extensive experience to the south of France. His arrival at the MTO stadium in Saint-Hône is expected to strengthen Toulon’s chances in the upcoming domestic and European campaigns. The Welsh international has endured a challenging period in recent years, including significant injuries and a dramatic early exit from the 2021 Rugby World Cup, which he called "the worst moment of my career." Despite these setbacks, he remained a key figure in Welsh rugby, playing in his fourth Rugby World Cup and continuing to be a pivotal player for both national and regional sides. Speaking of his decision to sign with Toulon, Halfpenny said: “It’s a new challenge and one that I’m excited to embrace. Toulon is a club with a proud history and a winning culture. I want to contribute to that success and help the team compete at the highest level.” Toulon head coach Gary Gold expressed his enthusiasm about the signing, saying: “Leigh is a world-class player with a wealth of experience at all levels. He brings a professionalism and composure that are vital to our squad. I’m looking forward to working with him and seeing the impact he can make.” Halfpenny’s move is also seen as a boost for Toulon’s ambitions in the Champions Cup, where they have struggled in recent seasons. With the likes of Blair Cowan and Billy Vunipola already bolstering the side, the addition of Halfpenny could create a formidable backline. The Welsh Rugby Union and Ospreys, Halfpenny's former club, have both wished him well in his new venture. Ospreys head coach Neil Doak said: “Leigh has been a fantastic ambassador for the Ospreys and Welsh rugby. We’re sad to see him leave, but we understand it's the right step for his career.” As he prepares to don the famous Toulon jersey, all eyes will be on Halfpenny to see if he can recapture the form that made him one of the game’s premier talents and bring European triumph back to the club that helped ignite his rise to rugby stardom.

A giant sixgill shark, suspected to be the largest of its kind ever caught on a fishing line in Europe, has been reeled in off the coast of County Clare, Ireland, sparking both excitement and superstition among anglers and marine biologists. The enormous creature, described as a "sea monster" by local fishermen, was estimated to weigh in excess of 1,000 pounds and measure approximately 11 feet in length. The shark was caught by a group of experienced anglers during a guided deep-sea fishing session, pulling it to the surface after a battle lasting nearly two hours. Sixgill sharks, also known as "cowsharks", are rarely seen by the public due to their preference for deep, dark waters where they can grow well beyond the size typical for most shark species found in temperate seas. They are known for their six gill slits and primitive features, which have earned them a reputation for being a "living fossil". However, no scientifically verified record of a sixgill caught in Western Europe on a rod and reel prior to this event provides the new catch with a unique status among angling circles. Initial assessments by local marine experts suggest the shark is a female, given the size and maturity of the specimen. Dr. Eilís Ní Laoire, a marine biologist based at Galway-Mayo Institute of Technology, confirmed that sixgills are not commonly targeted by fishermen and are often released after capture. In this case, the anglers and their guide followed responsible catch-and-release practices after removing the hook and examining the shark. The fish was then returned to the ocean unharmed, to the relief of conservationists. The catch has generated a flurry of interest on social media, with many using the term "monster" to describe the seemingly prehistoric beast. However, marine conservation groups are using the event to highlight the importance of sustainable fishing and the delicate balance of ocean ecosystems. "While this is an amazing catch for the anglers, it’s also a reminder of the hidden giants that inhabit our seas," said Fiona Mulholland, a marine protection officer with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group. "Species like sixgill sharks are important for maintaining healthy marine environments and should be treated with care and respect." Local folklore in County Clare has long spoken of sea monsters lurking in the Atlantic depths, with stories of leviathans dragged from the waves on fishing lines passed down through generations.

Serena Williams has brushed off the weight of history as she prepares for her Australian Open campaign, promising to focus solely on competing at her best without letting the prospect of surpassing Steffi Graf’s long-standing Grand Slam record dominate her mind. The 23-time major champion, who is currently level with Graf at 22 titles, is on the cusp of breaking the legendary German’s record, a feat that has not dented her focus. Speaking ahead of the tournament’s start in Melbourne, Williams, 40, expressed her unwavering determination. “I'm not going to let that take up space in my head. I came to play the Australian Open, not break records—those take care of themselves when I focus on my game,” she said. The 23rd Grand Slam win within her reach would solidify her place as the most successful tennis player in history, regardless of gender, given Graf and Margaret Court’s 24-title record is still widely regarded as one of the sport’s most unbreakable milestones. But for Williams, awards and accolades are not the driving force—victory is. “I’ve always approached each match like it’s my last,” she added. “I never think about points, titles, or records when I step on the court. I think about how I can beat my opponent, how I can play my best – that’s what gives me energy, not chasing numbers.” She also acknowledged the surreal nature of nearly matching Graf, whom she has always considered a role model and one of the greatest in the game. “Steffi is an icon—her legacy is forever in the sport. I want to do her legacy justice, not outshine her. I want to be remembered as someone who loved the game, as someone who fought for every point.” Williams is a two-time champion at the Australian Open, having claimed titles in 2003 and 2007. With her form unbroken despite her advancing age and a packed calendar of events since the US Open last year, fans remain hopeful that the 2024 edition could provide another chapter in her storied career. The 2024 Australian Open is widely being viewed not just as a chance to break the Grand Slam record, but also as the final chapter in Williams’ career road. “There will be a stopping point, but not because I want to break records or chase titles. If I feel I can still play and give my all, I’ll be out there,” she said.

The Labour Party is facing a moment of existential crisis, with one senior MP warning that it could “cease to exist” unless its leadership turmoil and deep internal divisions are resolved quickly. Wayne David, the MP for Caerphilly, described the party as “at a crucial point in its history,” appealing for unity in a bid to halt the growing fractures that have left its future uncertain. David’s comments come as the Labour leadership, embattled under Sir Keir Starmer, continues to face fierce criticism from both the left and right wings of the party. Shadow ministers have walked out of meetings and called for more influence, while the left has grown increasingly frustrated over issues such as Starmer’s approach to Gaza and the party's handling of anti-Semitism. On the other hand, right-wing MPs have also expressed dissatisfaction, particularly over the direction of the party on law and order, immigration, and economic policy. “We are in a state of crisis, and if we do not refocus, regain clarity of purpose, and re-establish a sense of unity across the party, the Labour Party as we know it may not be around in the way it is now in five years’ time,” David told BBC Radio Wales. “We are in danger — quite a real danger — of ceasing to exist as a credible, united force in British politics.” The row has drawn growing public attention, with media – and even Conservative politicians – increasingly questioning Labour’s viability after a catastrophic showing in the local elections in May. The party suffered major losses in key metropolitan areas such as London, Manchester, and Birmingham, where many Labour stronghold seats were either lost or badly underperformed. It marked one of the worst electoral results in the party’s history. David, a long-standing member of the party and former shadow attorney general, urged all factions to refocus on key issues — such as the economy, education, and the NHS — and to put aside ideological battles. “The public don’t care about our internal squabbles; they care about whether we can provide good schools, good hospitals, and a stable economy. If we don’t present a united front, we risk being swept aside,” he said. The calls for unity come amid growing speculation that some factions within the party are considering alternative strategies, including potential leadership challenges or even the consideration of forming an opposition-independent alliance for the next general election.

Police forces across the United Kingdom have paid a total of at least £22 million to informants over the past five years, according to figures disclosed in response to a freedom of information request by BBC Radio 5 live. The reveal has sparked fresh debate about the role and remuneration of those who assist police operations through intelligence gathering or inside information—many of whom operate in the most high-risk and underground parts of criminal networks. The payments, made by individual police forces, include cash compensation, benefits in kind, legal assistance, and even relocation for those in extreme danger. While the exact number of informants who received money or support remains unclear, the disclosed figures highlight the considerable financial outlay required to maintain such a vital part of policing, particularly in areas dealing with organized crime, gang violence, and drug trafficking. In Greater London, the Metropolitan Police was the largest single contributor, with reported payments of around £8.6 million. Other major contributors included the West Midlands Police, which paid £3.6 million, and Greater Manchester Police, which allocated over £2.2 million to its covert informants. These sums indicate the growing complexity of modern policing—especially in urban areas, where crime is often rooted in deeply embedded criminal groups with strong internal loyalties and few willing voices from within. One noteworthy aspect of the payments is that they are not limited to cash. Legal costs alone for informants have often reached tens of thousands of pounds, reflecting the dangers these individuals often face. It is not uncommon for informants to be targeted or threatened by criminals after betraying their organization. In some cases, full relocation to another part of the UK or even abroad has been arranged to protect them—though such measures are not disclosed in the figures and are likely under-recorded. The head of the Prime Minister’s Office, Cabinet Secretary Steve Bradley, has previously acknowledged the importance of informants in combating serious and organized crime. “Without inside information, many of these operations would have been impossible to execute,” he said in a recent speech on police intelligence gathering. “Such work requires not only exceptional courage but also a level of trust and support from the police and government.” However, critics argue that the sums could arguably be higher, as some payments are likely to be coded under different headings or not separately itemized in public disclosures.

Volvo's chief executive, Håkan Samuelsson, finds himself at the helm of a carmaker undergoing a dramatic transformation — and when asked directly about the brand’s future direction, he responds with a question of his own: “Do you believe car ownership will decline in cities over the next decade?” The motor giant’s top boss isn’t dodging the issue, as some might assume, but rather anchoring his strategy in shifting consumer habits — a crucial consideration as automakers across Europe grapple with questions of sustainability, shared mobility, and what it truly means to journey from A to B in the modern age. Samuelsson’s rhetorical gambit came during a tense but insightful session at the recent Geneva Motor Show, where he and other automotive leaders were quizzed about how the post-pandemic world might reshape the global transport landscape. Unlike many of his counterparts who delivered polished, formulaic responses, Samuelsson turned the question back on the audience — a move that quickly sparked debate, but ultimately underscored Volvo’s willingness to challenge convention in a fast-evolving industry. The Swedish automaker, now owned by the Chinese automotive giant Geely, has long positioned itself as a leader in sustainable design, safety innovation, and electric vehicle production — yet Samuelsson suggested that the greatest challenges for his company today might lie in something far less technical than battery range or carbon emissions. “We’re no longer just designing cars,” he said. “We’re designing experiences, and in some cases, we’re designing out journeys altogether.” This mindset is evident in the company’s growing collaboration with urban planners and mobility firms, all in an effort to understand how to thrive in an era where car ownership is no longer the norm in major metropolitan areas. Volvo has also been investing heavily in premium electric vehicles — with its Recharge line poised to dominate its model range by 2025 — but Samuelsson is quick to note that electrification alone isn’t the be-all and end-all. “It’s part of the picture, yes, but for every car we sell, we also have to consider how that customer will use it. Will they drive it every day, or will it be shared? Will it be autonomous or manually driven?” In this context, Samuelsson’s apparent deflection of a direct question on Volvo’s strategy becomes a masterclass in reframing expectations — delivering something more profound than a typical CEO’s soundbite.

Leeds United edge past Blackburn thanks to Wood’s last-gasp heroics in tense EFL Cup clash   In a tight and error-strewn EFL Cup third-round encounter at Elland Road, Leeds United preserved their FA Cup-style tradition of late drama to see off Blackburn Rovers 1-0 thanks to a stoppage-time winner from substitute Chris Wood. The goal, an acrobatic and comically fortuitous finish, encapsulated the frustrations and chaos of a match that will be remembered more for its tension than its quality. With just seconds remaining and the tie seemingly heading for extra time, Wood found himself in the thick of the action after a hopeful cross into the Blackburn box. A goalmouth scramble involving the Blackburn defenders and Rob Green left the ball bouncing at Wood’s feet, and with his first left-footed effort saved by goalkeeper Andy Lonergan, the striker bundled the ball in off the post. It was enough for the linesman to raise his flag, sparking scenes of late-night bedlam at a packed Elland Road. The victory moves Leeds into the next stage of the competition and keeps alive the memories of past giant-killing nights in the EFL Cup for Championship sides. Yet the match faltered under the weight of their own errors and misplaced hopes, with both teams struggling to find rhythm for much of the night. Leeds boss Daniel Farke made a flurry of substitutions in the final 20 minutes, a move that ultimately paid off as Wood picked up his fifth goal in as many games for the Rhinos since joining on transfer deadline day. Despite this, the full-time whistle also brought relief: not just for the players, but for the Elland Road faithful, who have continued to wonder exactly what they will make of their newly revitalised side as they make their long-awaited return to European football. Farke, the German who has transformed Leeds’ fortunes since taking charge in the summer, was philosophical in the aftermath. “We had a tough time in that game, but I’m happy with the result,” he said. “It was a battle at times, a very physical contest. But when it matters, I always believe our team can deliver.” For Blackburn, however, the night will end as one of sustained hope and missed opportunities. The Championship side, embroiled in an intense relegation battle, displayed admirable resilience throughout but were unable to turn early superiority in the opening 20 minutes into a breakthrough.

The developer of a heavy-lifting drone capable of carrying up to 500kg (1,100lb) has set an ambitious target to test its ability to navigate autonomously between trees and other obstacles by the end of this year. The £200,000 Nikomax VX-100, een ontwikkeld door het Duitse bedrijf Ayuun Robotics, is één van de zwaarste multirotor-dronen ter wereld, ontworpen om zware goederen te vervoeren in moeilijk toegankelijke gebieden. De plannen om de drone te laten vliegen zonder menselijke tussenkomst worden opgemerkt als een belangrijke stap voorwaarts in de technologie achter autonome vliegtuigen en openen de deur voor toepassingen op gebieden zoals defensie, logistiek, plantenteelt en noodgevallen. "De VX-100’s combinatie van kracht, duurzaamheid en geavanceerde navigatie moet ervoor zorgen dat hij ook in complexe omgevingen werkt — landingspleinen zijn niet altijd beschikbaar," zei een woordvoerder van Ayuun Robotics. "Als we deze missie succesvol afronden, wordt de drone een actief acteur in een gebied waar huidige technologie nog beperkt is." Op technologisch gebied zullen tests gebruiken maken van een complexe组合 van sensoren: cameras, lidar en een AI-taakafhandelingssysteem dat traint op grootschalige datasets van bossen, natuurreservoirs en onbebouwde gebieden. Deze dataset, gedeeltelijk gegenereerd via samenwerking met terreinherkenningsexperts, moet ervoor zorgen dat de VX-100 treedekkingen schat en haar route tussen de bomen kan minimaliseren. Een eerder sjabloonprototype, ontworpen voor stationair gebruik, toonde al aan dat sprite autonomie mogelijk is in gecontroleerd gebied. Het bedrijf doet al overleg met diverse sectoren over mogelijke toepassingen. In goederenvervoer, bijvoorbeeld, kan de VX-100 in complementaar gebruik treden met trucks en vliegtuigen in geografisch afgelegen regio's, zoals op weg naar gevoelige productiesites of tegelijk als medische logistiek in overstromingsgebieden of na aardbevingen. Ook krijgt het vliegtuig aandacht van defensiecontractanten, die het in overweging nemen voor transportsupport bij commandooperaties. "Zonder twijfel breekt dit de grenzen van wat wij kunnen aanbrengen op vliegtuigontwerpniveau," zegt Ayuun’s hoofd ingenieur, Markus Schaefer. “Als de VX-100 wordt ingezet voor vrachttransport in gevoelige natuurlijke gebieden, zullen we ook moeten zien tot welke mate deze technologie het snelheid en doeltreffendheid

A passenger jet flying into Heathrow Airport narrowly avoided a potentially catastrophic mid-air collision after it is believed to have flown into a drone on approach to the capital, triggering an urgent police investigation. The Airbus A320, operated by a major European airline, was coming in to land during the early evening on Tuesday when the crew reported what they believed to be a drone strike. The aircraft was carrying 135 passengers and five crew members on a flight from Aalborg, Denmark. While no injuries were reported, the plane made an emergency landing at a nearby airfield and was later inspected by aviation engineers. “There was an immediate vibration and a loud bang,” one of the passengers told the  Daily Mail . “The pilot announced we had hit something and would have to divert the landing.” The UK Airprox Board confirmed the incident is currently under review, and the Metropolitan Police has launched an inquiry into the presence of the drone. Heathrow Airport, one of the world’s busiest air hubs, has been at the centre of numerous drone-related incidents in recent years, prompting calls for stricter enforcement of no-fly zones near major airports. Transport for London, which oversees airspace regulations over the capital, said it is working with aviation authorities and the Met Police to determine whether the drone operator is known and, if so, whether they face prosecution. Under current UK law, it is illegal to fly a drone – even a small one – within 500 metres of an airport without prior permission. The penalty for breaching this regulation includes a maximum fine of £5,000, and in some cases, criminal charges. John Stewart, a spokesperson for the Airports Operators Association, said the incident was a stark reminder of the continued threat posed by rogue drones. “This demonstrates the very real hazards that unauthorised drone flights present to aircraft and to the safety of the public,” he said. “While the incident did not result in injury, it is a serious breach of aviation safety procedures and one that must not be taken lightly.” Meanwhile, Heathrow Airport has reiterated its commitment to working with the UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) and law enforcement to increase surveillance and enforcement around its perimeter. The airport has already deployed radar systems and trained drone-detection units to identify illegal flying activity. According to figures from the UK CAA, the number of drone-related alerts near airports has continued to rise in the past three years, with 2017 seeing over 110 incidents recorded at major UK airfields.

New combined Family Courts have come into being in England and Wales as part of a wide-ranging reform of the family justice system designed to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and streamline the often complex and emotionally fraught process of family law proceedings. The long-awaited change, introduced with the start of the new financial year on 1 April, unifies the previous family courts and county court family procedure rules into one single system. This marks the first major overhaul of the family justice sector in more than 40 years. The reform, spearheaded by the Ministry of Justice, aims to provide a more user-friendly, child-centric approach to cases involving divorce, child custody, domestic abuse, child protection, and adoption. In a statement, Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice, Alice Johnson, said the new system will help families resolve legal issues more swiftly and effectively. “By modernising the family justice system, we are ensuring it is fit for the 21st century, prioritising the needs of children and those seeking resolution to family disputes,” she said in a recent press briefing. The new Family Court will operate under a single set of rules and procedures, with all family law practitioners—solicitors, barristers, and mediators—required to apply for a “specialism designation” to be eligible to appear in the courts. This measure is intended to raise professional standards and ensure only those adequately trained and experienced in family law can deal with sensitive cases. The changes also introduce streamlined online processes for some applications, including making provisional arrangements for children or seeking financial support from a former partner. These digital services, piloted in selected regions, are expected to reduce delays and the need for face-to-face hearings in less contested cases. Supporters of the reform argue that it will help reduce the backlog of cases in the family court system, which has long been plagued by delays and a lack of consistency. However, critics, including advocacy groups and some legal professionals, have voiced concerns about the implications of merging procedures and the potential for further funding cuts. They argue that while the structure is being overhauled, ongoing underfunding risks undermining the very improvements the reform seeks to deliver. The Ministry of Justice has acknowledged these concerns but insists the reform is a crucial step forward in providing a more accessible and respectful system for those navigating the complexities of family law.

Another shooting, another solemn statement by President Barack Obama—and another call for action   The U.S. is once again reeling from gun violence. This time, it was a music festival in Las Vegas, left in chaos after a lone gunman opened fire from a hotel balcony, killing 58 people and wounding hundreds more. As emergency crews and relatives searched for survivors in the early hours of Sunday morning, the nation—and the world—paused once again to grieve. By early afternoon, President Barack Obama delivered what had become familiar rhetoric: a sombre condemnation of the violence and another plea for Congress to act on gun control. In a televised address from the East Room of the White House, Obama spoke with measured intensity. “This violence is not just an accident of history, it is not inevitable,” he said. “We cannot be numb anymore to the horror.” Dressed in a dark suit and flanked by first lady Michelle Obama, the President’s voice rose and fell, echoing the anguish felt across the country. “We are not at the mercy of the past,” he added, urging lawmakers to pass universal background checks, close loopholes that allow dangerous weapons into the hands of the inappropriate, and support research into gun violence. It was not the first time grief had shaped his words. Over the past decade, Obama has spoken after school shootings, church massacres and mass stabbings. Each time, his speeches became part of the national dialogue, but the legislative response has often fallen short. Following the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting that killed 26 people, including 20 children, Obama pushed for a federal ban on assault weapons and expanded background checks—only to watch Congress reject his proposals and let key provisions of the federal assault weapons ban expire in 2004. The same pattern has repeated itself time and again. This time, however, there is a growing sense of urgency. The shooting in Las Vegas—reported to be the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history—has left no community untouched. Victims are described as active and vibrant young people, music fans enjoying what was meant to be a fun weekend evening. The contrast between the hope of the event and the horror that followed has deepened public anguish. Political leaders across the ideological spectrum have been momentarily united in calls for change, but as with previous incidents, opposition from the National Rifle Association (NRA) appears to loom large.

No matter where you stand in the supporter spectrum, or which games make your heart race, the world of sports has something for everyone. Now, for the first time in digital media, a groundbreaking new development is giving sports fans the best of all worlds, all in one place. Cricket lovers had to swap screens for a round of golf and basketball enthusiasts had to toggle to rugby coverage. Myths like “football only” or “just cricket” rarely captured the full breadth of the average fan’s interest, and the challenge has always been how to bring them all under one digital roof. That problem is no longer an obstacle thanks to the launch of an innovative sports platform tailor-made for modern fans. Whether you follow the Grand Slam tournaments of tennis, the high-octane races of Formula 1, the grit of boxing, or the occasional cricket Test — your one-stop shop is now here. All the sports that matter to you, curated for you, appear on a single, unified page — no more tabs open, no more searches, no more scattered updates. This new era of sports coverage is set to appeal to both casual and hardcore fans alike. Casual viewers who don’t want to pay for multiple subscriptions will find value in one comprehensive hub. The platform features a user-friendly interface with customisable news feeds. You can select your favourite teams, athletes, and leagues — and the site learns from your preferences to bring you the most relevant content. No matter your allegiances, whether you’re a die-hard Liverpool fan or an impartial tennis lover, the coverage is designed to reflect the diversity of sports culture. This approach not only brings convenience, but also celebrates the global nature of sports. From grassroots matches to professional academies, from local leagues to international glory — it's all here.

Tottenham Hotspur kept the Premier League title race firmly alive on Monday night with a hard-fought 3-2 victory over Everton, moving to within seven points of leaders Chelsea, who were temporarily displaced by Liverpool after their game against West Ham was postponed. The win at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium marked another step in Mauricio Pochettino’s remarkable rebuilding of the north London club, who remain second in the table as their thrilling Premier League campaign continues to build momentum. This season has already seen Spurs top the league for a significant period, and as it stands, the title race appears wide open. The chase adds yet another layer of excitement to what promises to be one of the most unpredictable finishes to a Premier League season in years, with Manchester City, Liverpool and Manchester United also still in the mix. Harry Kane got the better of Jordan Pickford to give the hosts the lead, the England striker expertly controlling and firing in an inswinging free-kick from Gareth Bale, who was then at the heart of Spurs’ early dominance. The captain’s display was reminiscent of his enduring class, assisted both the first and the third goals, and was a constant presence for much of the evening. Everton, still reeling from Saturday’s relegation to the Championship and the sacking of manager Sean Dyche, provided little resistance for much of the first half. However, they found some respite when James Tarkowski headed in from a corner to reduce the deficit and restore some hope for their already mortal fans. Spurs responded through a sensational Liam Senses strike, which gave Pickford no chance with an arrowed effort from 20 yards out, before substitute Son Heung-Min capped the scoring with a clinical finish late in the game. Everton did manage to pull one back through a Tom Davies penalty late on, but by then the match was effectively beyond them. This result sets up a tantalising climax to the campaign for Spurs, who will face Liverpool, Chelsea, and both Manchester sides in their final four matches. If they are to secure their first league title in 60 years, it will require not just consistency, but also a repeat of the clinical performance they showed against Everton. As such, Monday night’s win will not only serve as a reminder of their capability but also as the spark that reignites the belief of fans who have come so close to glory before.

At least 27 migrants have died off the Turkish coast while attempting to reach the Greek island of Lesbos, according to reports from Turkish state media. The tragedy unfolded after the rubber dinghy carrying the migrants capsized in rough seas, leaving dozens thrown into the water and unable to swim to safety. Coast guard teams were quick to respond, but many were already missing by the time they arrived on the scene. The incident marks one of the most deadly recent crossings in the ongoing European migration crisis, as thousands continue to attempt the perilous journey in search of refuge or a better life in Europe. Lesbos, located just a few miles from the Turkish coast, is one of the main entry points into the EU for migrants, particularly those fleeing conflict and poverty in Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan. Turkish media have reported that the majority of the deceased were men between the ages of 18 and 35, but the exact nationalities have not yet been confirmed. Migrants often pay smugglers to transport them across the Aegean Sea in overcrowded and unseaworthy vessels, exposing them to the risk of drowning or other fatal incidents. This tragedy comes amid rising tensions between Greece, Turkey and the European Union over the influx of migrants. In recent months, Greece has taken steps to strengthen its border security, including erecting fences along its border with Turkey, following repeated attempts by migrants to cross on foot. Meanwhile, Turkey, still reeling from domestic political challenges and the aftermath of an attempted coup, has faced increasing demands from the EU to control the flow of people leaving its shores. The United Nations has warned that deaths among migrants making the journey to Europe have not decreased despite efforts by international bodies and governments to stem the tide. In 2023 alone, more than 1,700 people have been reported to have died trying to reach the EU, according to the UN’s International Organization for Migration. The capsize near Lesbos is a grim reflection of the continuing dangers faced by those who undertake the journey in pursuit of safety and hope. A representative from the Turkish Coast Guard told state television that they were recovering bodies and bringing the injured to hospital, but added that the search could take several days due to the difficulty of conditions. Greek and Turkish officials have begun to coordinate the response, though the full extent of the tragedy may not be known for some time.

A brutal attack on a vulnerable pensioner has shocked communities across the country after a man was convicted of her murder in a harrowing case that unfolded in a quiet residential home. Peter Morgan, 38, was found guilty by a jury at Birmingham Crown Court of entering the home of 84-year-old Edith Wilson, subjecting her to prolonged and cruel treatment, and then killing her with a kitchen rolling pin. The court heard that on a rainy Friday evening in March, Morgan forced open the door of Mrs Wilson’s home, bound her hands and feet with a scarf, and tortured her for upwards of four hours in an attempt to extract her bank card PIN number. Witnesses said Mrs Wilson, a well-regarded community member and former schoolteacher, had been left terrified and in excruciating pain as Morgan persistently demanded the code. Prosecutors told the court the elderly woman shouted for help and screamed in terror during the ordeal. When she was unable to recall her details, Morgan, driven by greed and a lack of conscience, resorted to violence. The prosecution described the final moments of the attack as “barbaric” and “inhuman,” with Morgan allegedly striking Mrs Wilson repeatedly on the head with a heavy rod. Forensic evidence showed that the victim sustained multiple concussive injuries, which were consistent with repeated blunt force trauma. Morgan was then seen calmly fleeing the scene, denying any involvement when questioned initially by responding police, but was later identified after a thorough investigation involving CCTV footage and forensic analysis. In their closing remarks, the Crown Prosecution Service painted Morgan as a predator who had targeted Mrs Wilson due to her vulnerability and age. defence argued that Morgan suffered from undiagnosed mental health issues at the time of the incident and was not in a stable frame of mind. However, the trial judge ruled out any claim of insanity as grounds for the acquittal of the charges. Speaking outside court, Mrs Wilson’s family described their grief as “immeasurable” and praised the dedication of the police, who pursued the case with “relentless determination” to bring justice. “Edith was a gentle soul. She lived alone, trusted the world, and never expected anyone to harm her. This is a tragedy that should never have happened,” said her nephew Richard, a local GP from Stoke-on-Trent. Morgan will be sentenced on Thursday after a pre-sentence report is prepared by the National Probation Service.

Worcestershire Captain Credits "Knack of Finishing Teams Off" for Strong Start   Worcestershire captain Joe Leach has credited his side’s ability to find the "knack of finishing teams off" as the key to their impressive start to the 2024 season. The county have been in sparkling form across all formats, beginning the campaign with a string of convincing victories that have sent shockwaves through the domestic cricketing ladder. Securing wins in both the T20 Blast and County Championship, Worcestershire have played with a cohesion and clinical efficiency rarely seen at the start of a season. Leach, the county’s vice-captain who leads when skipper Daryl Mitchell is absent, has been central to the team’s success, his seam bowling providing late wickets and bursts of momentum when needed most. Speaking after the recent victory over Yorkshire in the Championship — a match where Worcestershire’s bowling attack collapsed the visitors for just 167 to secure a historic win — Leach said his side had learned from previous years, where strong starts often failed to convert into consistent success. “It’s about finishing games when you get into positions of strength,” he said in a pre-match press conference ahead of their next fixture. “There have been times in the past where we've batted well, put the pressure on, and just missed out on taking the chance, and now we’re making sure we take the opportunity when it’s there.” Worcestershire’s win over Yorkshire marked their third Championship victory in a row, a feat not achieved in over a decade. The team has a mix of seasoned professionals and rising stars, with the bat and ball complementing each other in a way that has brought a new energy to the county. Leach, who has been a mainstay of the English Test team, is quick to deflect praise onto the rest of the squad. “You can’t take it all on the shoulder of one man,” he said. “When you’ve got lads like (captain) Daryl (Mitchell) playing with such consistency, and the lads in the middle and lower order getting those critical runs, it takes pressure off the seniors.” Head coach Steve Rhodes has also been instrumental in shaping the team’s mindset, with a focus on set-piece attacks and pressure-building bowler partnerships. The coaching staff's meticulous planning has seen improvements across all departments, particularly in the field, where the side’s catching figures are currently the best in the tournament.

Plans to restructure the entire state school system in England by making all schools academies will be presented by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in the upcoming Budget, government sources have revealed. The ambitious move comes as part of a broader long-term strategy to give individual schools more autonomy over their finances and curriculum, while reducing the role of local authorities in education funding and administration. The proposal will be unveiled   on Wednesday  , marking a major shift in the decade-long evolution of England’s academies programme. If implemented, it would see all schools – currently governed by local councils under a system known as “maintained schools” – converted into independently run academies over the next five to ten years. The government claims this will lead to improved performance, greater accountability, and a more dynamic system of education tailored to local needs. The policy is expected to be accompanied by substantial funding commitments, as the Treasury acknowledges the initial costs of transitioning the 16,000 remaining non-academy schools, often referred to as community schools. These figures have not yet been finalised, but officials have indicated that the funding windfall from the Higher Education and Research Bill will play a role in underpinning the change. Education Secretary Gillian Keegan has previously hinted at the reforms, stating in a recent speech that “the era of local authorities dictating standards and pacing in our schools is over. The future – and the best chance for our children – lies in giving headteachers the power they need to lead.” This has already been backed by a controversial government white paper in 2023 which proposed phasing out local authority-maintained schools over a decade. The move will likely reignite a fierce political and public debate. Opponents, including some within the Conservative Party, have raised concerns over the erosion of local democratic control, with fears that the centralisation of power to the Department for Education could exacerbate existing inequalities. Teachers' unions have also expressed reservations, particularly over the potential loss of support for smaller rural schools and less experienced staff without the backing of councils. Meanwhile, supporters argue that the system will reduce bureaucracy and encourage collaboration among schools through multi-academy trusts (MATs), which have shown mixed but in some cases improved results compared to local authority-run schools. With the Budget announcement set to define the next phase of education policy, all eyes will be on the Chancellor’s speech to see the scale of funding, the timeline for implementation, and how the government plans to manage inevitable pushback from educators, parents, and local councils.

ORACLE TEAM USA ELECTRIFY SAN FRANCISCO WITH DARING COMEBACK IN AMERICA’S CUP FINALE   In a nail-biting conclusion to the 35th America’s Cup, Oracle Team USA defied impossible odds to stage the most dramatic comeback in the 163-year history of the prestigious sailing event. Faced with a seemingly insurmountable deficit of 8-1 in the best-of-17 series, the underdog American team fought from the brink to overturn the deficit and defeat New Zealand’s Emirates Team by just 44 seconds in the deciding 17th race. The underdog victory saw the Kiwis, long considered America’s fiercest and most formidable challengers, left stunned and defeated in San Francisco Bay’s golden sunshine. Marco Ceresol, New Zealand’s team principal, addressed the Post-Race Press Conference, and said in a composed but visibly shaken tone, “We’ve put our team on breakfast, and we’ve lost this race. They did everything in the last few races, and we were pushed, and didn’t have the answers.” But for Oracle, the moment was seismic. Team captain Jimmy Spithill, who had proudly led the short-handed squad, described their victory as a culmination of “relentless grit, sheer belief, and a strategy that believed in the impossible.” The dramatic finale – watched by audiences in the hundreds of millions – saw the Oracle crew overturn a 33-point deficit after losing the first eight races. Oracle’s comeback began in earnest with an inspired, tactical change led by tactician Russell Coutts and crew sailing coach Dustin-Diamond. Relying on a revised racing strategy and the fury of a red-shirted crew being poured into action, the American team clawed back the deficit in about five days, finally fulfilling the improbable win on September 21. The first 14 races had gone badly for Oracle Team USA. After laying down marker after marker for the finals, New Zealand had appeared invincible. Enthusiastic fans had already celebrated on San Francisco’s shore as it looked like the event was all but decided. However, what followed was nothing short of extraordinary. As Oracle displayed unassailable speed and relentless zeal, their confidence grew, and the tide of public opinion gradually changed. Sailing fans took to social media to rekindle support for the Americans, goading them on with messages about their underdog status. And in the final line of the 17th and last race, the American boat crossed the San Francisco finish line at 19:23 local time, triumphing by those 43 seconds that gave life to a thrilling narrative of resilience.

Oldham director ‘has no regrets’ over Ched Evans transfer attempt   A top official at League One side Oldham Athletic has stated he has “no regrets” about the club’s failed attempt to sign ex-England international Ched Evans, despite the £250,000 fine the club now faces from the Football Association and widespread public condemnation over the move. Barry Owen, who has extensive experience in football as both a player and a director, defended the decision last night in a rare public statement, insisting it was made in good faith and that the club had no knowledge of the player’s pending legal issues at the time. The controversy dates back to June 2014 when Oldham, reeling from a poor start to the season and needing a striker, pursued a transfer for Evans. The Welsh forward, who was then captaining Sheffield Wednesday, had been charged with sexual assault in January of that year. It is now accepted that his trial – during which he was ultimately convicted and sentenced to five years in prison in October – was not made public knowledge to the club, who felt they had the legal and moral right to pursue the signing. Mr Owen, who served as director of football at the time, revealed yesterday that the club had made several human rights and welfare inquiries as part of its due diligence. "We have always been, and will remain, a club that does the right thing," he said in a statement published by the  Oldham Chronicle . “We entered into this process with the utmost professionalism and belief in the justice system. Ched’s case was not someone who had previously been convicted. We had no reason to believe otherwise at the time. As such, I personally have no regrets about the way the board acted.” The club’s decision to proceed, despite the significant reputational risk, has drawn sharp criticism from fans, former players, and civic leaders. Evans never made an appearance for Oldham after manager John Sheridan informed the media of the £3m deal. The news broke on the day Evans’ trial was set to begin, prompting his immediate withdrawal from the club. Last April, the FA ruled the club’s handling of the transfer was “a breach of the principle of good governance”, resulting in the fine and a two-point deduction. Local figures have urged the club to do more. Manchester-based human rights lawyer Amin Malik told the  Manchester Evening News : “Football is supposed to be about more than transfer windows and profit margins.

The rollout of a new £60million GPS tagging system for offenders in England and Wales is five years behind schedule and has delivered no measurable benefits to date, according to a recently published report by the National Audit Office. The initiative, first launched in 2014, aimed to modernise the way offenders were monitored by using real-time location data to track their movements. It was intended to replace the outdated electronic tagging system, making it harder for offenders to circumvent curfews and attendance requirements, while protecting the public and reducing recidivism. However, concerns over performance and value for money have now emerged after monitoring of the project has revealed serious delays and a lack of progress.
