According to the report, the system is still only partially deployed, and no data has yet been published to show whether it has achieved any of its stated benefits, such as increasing safety or reducing crime. Despite the vast financial investment, local probation services continue using older, less effective systems for a significant portion of cases. The lack of oversight and management in delivering the system’s roll-out is highlighted as a key issue, resulting in the costly and chaotic implementation of what was once heralded as a benchmark technology for public protection. Jonathan Dimbleby, former chair of the National Audit Office, expressed his frustration, saying: “For a scheme of such high financial and public importance, it is deeply concerning – even alarming – that five years in and there is no evidence to support its effectiveness.” He added that the delays have placed additional strain on an overstretched probation service, with resources being diverted from other critical public safety initiatives. Ministers have yet to respond to the report, but the findings are expected to intensify the debate about how the government administers justice through technology. The scheme had been contracted out to a private technology firm, who were responsible for the design, installation and maintenance of the system. Questions are now being raised about the decision to outsource such a critical national infrastructure project without sufficient safeguards in place. The report also reveals that the National Offender Management Service (NOMS), which oversees probation services in England and Wales, underestimated the complexity of the system and failed to establish performance metrics or realistic timelines from the outset. As a result of these missteps, the system remains a work in progress, with no clear schedule for when it will be delivering the results it was promised to deliver.

Rory McIlroy Shuts Down Social Media After Confrontational Exchange with Steve Elkington   World number one Rory McIlroy has confirmed he has stopped using social media following a highly publicised dispute with former US PGA champion Steve Elkington. The fallout, which spread across Twitter and prompted condemnation from golfing greats, has led the Northern Irish star to distance himself from the platform, citing the toxic nature of online discourse in professional sports. The controversy began after Elkington, a three-time PGA Tour winner, questioned McIlroy's commitment to training ahead of the U.S. Open. Elkington tweeted during the 2013 U.S. Open, suggesting that McIlroy, who had just won the U.S. Open two years earlier and made a career-high rise to world number one, appeared to be taking his fitness commitments "less seriously". Following the event, Elkington said in a press conference that he did not intend to imply that McIlroy was not a good athlete, but that he "could drive in his car and still be the best in the world, even if he's not working out as much". McIlroy was incensed by the remarks, later taking to Twitter to write: “Was quite surprised as to how quickly and easily people can forget how proud they were when others succeed—and then turn it around when they struggle. It's amazing – very human.” He initially considered responding further, but ultimately decided to step back from the growing online storm. Speaking to reporters after winning the British Open in July, McIlroy made it clear he had taken a break from social media altogether. “I read what a lot of people were saying at the time, and it is what it is,” he said. “I’ve removed all the social media apps from my phone and I just don’t engage with it anymore. It’s just too easy for people to say stuff they don’t even mean. I choose to focus on the things that matter.” McIlroy, 27, is no stranger to being in the public eye, with his meteoric rise to the top of world golf coming as he transitioned into his prime. However, he has pointed to the pressures of maintaining visibility in a professional landscape increasingly dominated by online interaction as a source of stress. “It’s hard when you want to be seen positively, but you're also under the magnifying glass for every little thing,” he explained.

Black Monday Again: NFL Shakeup as Three Coaches Lose Jobs    By Sarah Johnson  For the second time in four years, the NFL has returned to its grim tradition known as "Black Monday," a day synonymous with coaching changes and sweeping locker room overhauls. This year, as the dust settled on the 2023 season and playoff dreams faded for several teams, three head coaches found themselves suddenly jobless in what is a stark but routine reminder of the ruthless nature of professional football. The dismissals come amid a growing trend of teams opting for bold managerial changes in the hope of sparking a playoff resurgence. The three affected franchises – Buffalo Bills, Chicago Bears, and Washington Commanders – all failed to qualify for the postseason, despite significant investments in star players and front office restructuring. Yet, in the eyes of ownership, their failure was not deemed sufficient. Buffalo, which was the highest-profile loser of the day, dismissed head coach Sean McDermott after five seasons at the helm. The four-time Pro Bowl coach leaves behind a proud franchise that had become a staple of NFL dominance, having reached the AFC Championship Game in 2023 and 2022. Ownership, led by Teresa and Wellington Mara, said in a joint statement: “We are grateful for Sean’s commitment and passion for the Bills. We will now look toward a new direction as we build for the future.” In Chicago, Mitchell Trubisky’s short-lived coaching tenure came to an abrupt end as Bill Belichick’s former offensive coordinator, Matt Nagy, was let go. Despite overseeing a dramatic improvements in offensive output in 2023, Nagy was unable to secure a playoff birth, and Bears’ general manager Ryan Poles appears unshaken in his reform programme, stating: “It’s with deep respect for Matt’s work that we’re making this change. The Bears need a fresh voice and vision.” Meanwhile, Washington parted ways with Ron Rivera, a former head coach with the Carolina Panthers and Jacksonville Jaguars. Rivera, who had high hopes of revitalising his coaching career with a win-now approach in the nation’s capital, left disappointed but resolute. “I gave this team everything I had,” he said. “I'm proud of what we’ve built, and I’m looking forward to the next chapter.” Black Monday is a tradition deeply ingrained in the NFL’s annual cycle, drawing its name from a 1989 realignment that led to six head-coaching changes in a matter of days.

Innovative Sounds: Anna Meredith Claims Prestigious SAY Award with ‘ Varmints ’   Award-winning composer and producer Anna Meredith has been hailed as the latest winner of Scotland’s most coveted music prize, the Scottish Album of the Year (SAY) award, for her electrifying third album  Varmints . The announcement, made at a ceremony in Glasgow last night, marks a triumphant moment for the 35-year-old Ayrshire-born artist, who has long been recognized for her inventive approach to music, fusing classical training with contemporary electronic and pop influences.  Varmints , released in 2016 on the Mercury Prize-winning label Rough Trade, made a powerful impact with its dynamic, genre-defying soundscapes and intricate narratives. With bursts of frenetic energy and rich bursts of orchestration, the album was praised as a bold and fearless piece of contemporary composition. The title track, in particular, became an instant standout, incorporated into the 2018 BBC Proms and later repurposed for the 2020 Ken Burns documentary series  The Vietnam War . Meredith, who studied composition at the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland, takes pride in crafting music that leaves as much to the imagination of the listener as to the precision of the score. Over her career, she has worked closely with orchestras, operatic ensembles, and collaborating artists like Debi Nova and Dawn Reno, but  Varmints  has arguably been the most personal of her works yet. “Winning the SAY award for  Varmints  feels like a huge validation not only of the work itself, but of the path I’ve chosen as an artist,” said Meredith in a statement released after the ceremony. “This album is special because it really captures where I am creatively at the moment—pushing the boundaries of what classical and contemporary music can be and how they can be brought together.” The SAY Award, now in its tenth year, is voted for by 100 guest judges from across the music industry, and recognizes the best album of the year by a Scottish artist. Previous winners have included Mogwai, Elizabeth Fraser of Coctepe and Aldous Harding. The shortlisted artists were recently revealed in the “ SAY Award 2024 Shortlist ” list. Meredith's win is set against the backdrop of a growing spotlight on experimental and female-led music in Scotland, with the likes of Liz Cooper and Celestial, Scottish post-rock band KⅯ and rising queer artists like Lea Leah all helping to shift the boundaries of Scottish independent music.

In the middle of a narrow alley in Cairo's Ain Shams district, one shop stands out from the rest. Tucked away between a greengrocer and a local sweets stall, it offers no grand display or flashy lighting — just a plain wooden sign with the words “Sabah El-Kasr" (King of Dawn). But on any given morning, the line snakes out the door. Children sit on dusty cobbles clutching steaming plastic cups from Egypt’s most beloved breakfast stand — a place where tradition, comfort, and taste are as carefully crafted as the perfect khobz (bread) served warm from the oven. The shop has operated for three decades, surviving wars, revolutions and the shifting tides of urban development. Its loyal customers have followed successive generations of the El-Kasr family, whose name is synonymous with Cairo’s everyday hustle and bustle. But this unassuming stall has become more than just a breakfast destination — it’s a cultural monument, a humble guardian of Cairo’s past in a city rapidly transforming around it. Speckled with age but enduring, the kitchen’s stove has baked the same golden-brown khobz for decades, using a recipe passed down from Sabah El-Kasr’s late father to his son and current owner, Ahmed. The khobz is larger than most, brushed with olive oil and left to bake at just the right temperature to create a delightfully crisp exterior and a soft, almost sweet, interior. It is often served with koshary or ful medames, staples of Egyptian breakfasts, all for just a few Egyptian pounds. But the uniqueness of Sabah El-Kasr lies not only in its food, but in its community. The shop is crowded with elderly regulars, schoolboys, office workers and even foreign tourists who stumbled upon the gem during a wrong turn. Ahmed, who rarely speaks much beyond what is needed to serve another round of khobz and coffees, greets each one the same, with a warm smile and quiet pride. For Ahmed, it's not just about earning a living — it's about holding onto Cairo’s essence. “Cairo is changing too fast," he told The Times as he prepared a fresh batch of bread. "New glass towers, new shopping malls, new traffic — but our food, our habits, our traditions? They’re dying out. If even a little of it survives, if people like what we do here, then I have done my part.”

The De Karina chocolate factory, nestled in the scenic hills of the Golan Heights, has emerged as an unexpected yet beloved highlight on the sightseeing maps of thousands of tourists visiting the region each year. Known for its rich volcanic soil and stunning views, the Golan Heights offers visitors a blend of natural beauty, historical sites, and culinary delights — and at the heart of this gastronomic scene is De Karina. Founded in 2005 by Dani Karina, a local chocolatier and social activist, the factory quickly became a symbol of both local craftsmanship and political resilience. Located in the village of Am’ud, the factory has not only helped lift the local economy but also become a beacon for peace, employing workers from both Jewish and Arab communities in an area often polarised by political tensions. Tourists are greeted by the rich aroma of cocoa and the rhythmic hum of the machinery as they walk through the factory’s open production floor, where guided tours allow visitors to see the entire chocolate-making process — from bean to bar. De Karina’s signature product is its hides, filled with a smooth and creamy chocolate that has garnered a loyal international fanbase. The chocolate, made using fair trade practices and proudly powered by renewable energy, is as much a product of the Golan Heights as it is of local passion. Over the years, De Karina has expanded its range to include blends inspired by regional herbs and spices, such as sumac and za’atar, offering an edible snapshot of the local culinary landscape. Beyond chocolate, the factory hosts cookery classes, cultural events, and serves as a hub for cross-cultural dialogue. Its prominence in the region has been so profound that it was recently featured in a prominent documentary showcasing artisanal chocolate-making in underrepresented regions. As De Karina builds its reputation, its influence continues to grow — not just as a purveyor of taste but as a testament to the potential of local enterprise to bridge divides and foster understanding. For now, the chocolate factory remains a must-see for those venturing to the Golan Heights, offering a sweet respite from the complexities of the land beyond its walls. Visitors come for the chocolate, but they often leave with a deeper appreciation for the people behind it. Websites and travel agents have begun to add the chocolate factory to must-do lists, with some packages now termed “The Sweet Golan Tour.”

Xi Jinping urges global respect for 'cyber sovereignty' in internet governance   In a keynote address at an international forum on digital development, Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for nations to respect one another’s "cyber sovereignty" and varying models of internet governance. Speaking in Beijing, the president reiterated China's vision for a more regulated and state-guided internet, asserting that no single country should impose its policies on others. The call for mutual respect comes amid escalating global tensions over cybersecurity, data privacy, and the influence of tech giants. President Xi, who has long championed China's own model of internet control – often characterised as the "Great Firewall" – stressed the need for sovereign states to have "equal rights" in the digital world. “We must uphold the principle that cyberspace should be governed by an international order rooted in respect for each country’s sovereignty, interests, and special conditions,” said Mr Xi. “Diversity is the defining feature of human civilisations, and it is no different when it comes to internet governance models.” The message was widely interpreted as a rebuke to Western nations, many of whom have pressed for open, transparent, and rules-based internet governance, often underpinned by human rights principles. The U.S., in particular, has long advocated for a free and open internet, a stance that has sometimes drawn sharp criticism from Chinese officials. Mr Xi’s comments echo recent Chinese statements that have questioned the legitimacy of the U.S.-led Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which manages global internet addressing and domain names. China, along with Russia and other state-driven internet powers, has long pushed for a more multipolar system where countries have greater authority over their digital spaces. The Chinese president also urged a “collaborative approach” to key challenges such as cybercrime, online extremism, and misinformation. However, the emphasis on cyber sovereignty is likely to be a point of contention with Western allies who fear that it could be used to justify greater domestic surveillance and restrictions on online freedom. Commenting on the statement, a spokesperson for the European Union expressed support for a multilateral approach but caution over alignment with China’s vision. “We believe in a rules-based internet while safeguarding human rights. We are open to dialogue, but not at the expense of core freedoms.” This call from the Chinese leader follows a series of high-profile cyber disputes, including the ongoing negotiations around the export of surveillance technology and growing concerns over data security in trade and diplomatic relations.

A digital games programmer from Angus has claimed a unique place in sporting and gaming history by completing the iconic Land's End to John o'Groats cycling challenge – entirely in virtual reality (VR). Iain MacGregor, 33, is believed to be the first person ever to achieve what is traditionally one of the UK’s most challenging and rewarding endurance rides, but from the comfort of his living room and his gaming set-up in Forfar. The ambitious feat took him 17 days to complete, riding over 950 miles through a digital recreation of one of the most scenic routes in the country. Using a high-end VR headset and stationary smart trainer, MacGregor recreated the entire journey, with distances and real-world cycling conditions mirrored in real time. MyRoute-app, the popular cycling route platform used by cyclists around the world, provided the mapping and route data, while Strava tracked his progress and logged every pedal stroke for verification. MacGregor linked his indoor cycling trainer to the VR experience, using a combination of mapping overlays and immersive visuals to simulate the terrain, including the wind speeds and gradients of the real route. “For anyone who’s cycled the L-E-JOG, you know the impacts it has – your legs, the hills, and the real-time weather. I wanted to bring that same physical and mental challenge into a digital space,” MacGregor told BBC Scotland. “This isn’t just playing a game. It’s a real ride, just in a new form.” The undertaking was not just a personal challenge for MacGregor, who works in VR game development in Dundee, but also a way to test the boundaries of how immersive digital environments can mirror real-life adventures. “VR is often thought of as an escape – but I wanted to show how it can also bring tangible effort and real-life motivation back into the mix,” he added. The route simulation included major landmarks and even weather changes that reflected the actual weather experienced on the route in the first week of June, when MacGregor chose to base his virtual cycling on. Rain, wind, and even the notoriously hilly sections such as the Cairngorms and the Southern Uplands were all digitally recreated with as much realism as the technology could provide. Cycling enthusiasts and VR creators have hailed the challenge as a bold demonstration of how technology is evolving beyond entertainment. MacGregor's achievement has already go viral on cycling forums and social media, with some calling it the "VR line in the sand" between gaming and active fitness.

Plaid Cymru has thrown open the door to this year’s election campaign, launching its manifesto ahead of other major political parties and declaring itself the “decisive voice” for Wales. The centrepiece of the party’s proposals is a call for increased devolution and the protection of Welsh national interests, with a focus on restoring public services, boosting the economy, and confronting the challenges posed by Brexit and climate change. The manifesto, titled   “A Wales for the People,”   outlines a bold social and economic vision that reflects Plaid Cymru’s longstanding commitment to Welsh self-determination and democratic renewal. Ahead of the June general election, the party is seeking to capitalise on growing public discontent with Welsh Labour’s handling of key issues such as the NHS, education, and housing, while also positioning itself as the most credible alternative to UK Conservative policies. At the heart of the manifesto is a demand for the   full transfer of policing, civil service and economic development powers to the Welsh government  , reinforcing the party’s long-term drive for independence and a radical restructuring of Welsh governance. Leanne Wood, leader of Plaid Cymru, said that taking control over policing, for example, would allow Wales to better protect frontline services and reduce crime as local priorities were no longer shaped by UK-level objectives. The party is also pushing for a   10-year public services investment plan  , ensuring that health and education funding is not subject to cuts dictated by Westminster. Plaid Cymru proposes a new model for the Welsh NHS, including the establishment of a   NHS Wales Commissioning Authority  , designed to give patients more choice and to improve the efficiency of the health service. In the housing sector, the manifesto promises a   Welsh Homes and Development Corporation   to build thousands of new homes, particularly for key workers and first-time buyers. Given the ongoing housing crisis in the capital, Cardiff, and the rest of the country, this is expected to be one of the more popular policy pledges among Plaid Cymru’s supporters and the wider electorate. On the economy, Plaid Cymru proposes to increase the Welsh budget to provide   investments in green energy, rail infrastructure and digital connectivity  . The manifesto commits to   creating a Wales of work and skills  , with special attention given to upskilling the workforce and supporting small businesses, particularly in rural areas. The goal is to make Wales an attractive destination for investment without caving in to the kind of corporate tax cuts and deregulation often pushed by the UK government.

"Be careful what you wish for," the old saying goes – and this is exactly what the Russian leadership must be thinking right now. With Russia facing an unprecedented economic crisis, international sanctions, and a growing sense of isolation after its annexation of Crimea and support for separatists in eastern Ukraine, President Vladimir Putin and his inner circle might be realising the unintended consequences of their geopolitical ambition. What was once hailed as a strategy to reassert Russian influence on the global stage now looks increasingly like a self-inflicted wound, with oil prices collapsing, the rouble plummeting, and Western nations removing ties to key sectors of the Russian economy. Moscow has long prided itself on Russian resilience. The government made bold statements last year about the country’s ability to thrive "independent of the West," even as capital fled and the Central Bank raised interest rates to historic levels in an attempt to stabilise the sinking currency. Yet the reality of 2015 is far harsher than the rhetoric suggests. The World Bank has predicted that Russia's economy will shrink by around four per cent this year, with the IMF warning of the risk of a full-blown depression if oil prices do not rebound soon. The situation is compounded by demographic and structural weaknesses that have long plagued the Russian economy. For too long, Moscow has relied on commodity exports, especially oil and gas, to fund government spending and public services. With those revenues falling, the cheques that many ordinary citizens count on – including subsidies on food and utilities – are becoming increasingly hard to maintain. Last week, the government made headlines by announcing cuts to fuel subsidies in an attempt to reduce its deficit, a move that will likely hit households hardest in the months leading up to winter. At the same time, the isolation imposed by the West has forced Moscow into a deeper embrace of its old Soviet-style strategies. Russia has accelerated the development of its “Sochi 2.0” vision – a plan to transition key sectors of the economy away from foreign technology to domestic alternatives, including overhauling the construction industry, vehicle manufacturing, and even technology. But analysts question the ability of a state-dominated economy to innovate quickly enough to offset the losses. More troubling still is the growing sense of unease within the Russian public. While Moscow remains relatively stable, the cost of living continues to rise, with food prices set to rise by around ten per cent in the next month as govt subsidies on staples like sugar and sunflower oil are lifted.

In a final appearance at the despatch box during Prime Minister’s Questions, David Cameron has asserted that Northern Ireland is stronger now than it was when he took office six years ago, highlighting the progress made in a region long marked by political and sectarian tensions. The £20 million withdrawal from the children’s hospital project in Belfast, announced earlier this week, has triggered a storm of controversy both within the Westminster and Stormont legislatures. Cameron defended the move in the House of Commons, saying the government had explored “how best to support the project while staying within reasonable fiscal constraints and maintaining clarity around the role and responsibilities of the Northern Ireland Executive. “But I can confirm that the financial settlement of Northern Ireland is still intact. That has not changed, and the Chancellor will make that very clear at the Budget.” Despite the criticism, Cameron left PMQs on a positive note, saying: “Northern Ireland is stronger today in every area – whether it be in the economy, in terms of security, or in the political agreement that has now held for over a decade. When I came to office in 2010, the challenges in Northern Ireland were still immense, but I believe we can truly say that we have made significant progress.” His short, measured remarks did little to quell the commotion caused by the funding decision, which was met with fury from both Unionist and Nationalist leaders at the Assembly. First Minister Arlene Foster and Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness jointly condemned the cut as a “disregard for the will of the people of Northern Ireland,” while Sinn Féin TD Michelle O’Neill accused the government of “undermining investment in the health service at a time when it needs it most.” The Treasury previously stated that the central government would no longer fund the future operation and expansion of the new £200 million children’s hospital project, effectively shifting the financial burden to the Northern Ireland Executive. The hospital, expected to open in 2020, was one of the most high-profile projects for the Province since the Good Friday Agreement. Earlier in the week, Cameron told a charity event in Belfast that he was “deeply disappointed” about how the decision was communicated. However, he reiterated that the funding shift was not a cut to the overall budget for Northern Ireland but a “reallocation” aimed at ensuring that money was being spent “transparently and effectively.”

The UK House of Commons has voted to renew the Trident nuclear weapons programme, raising once again the contentious issue of the country’s stance on national defence and arms expenditure. The motion, passed by 356 votes to 245 on 18 July, maintained the government's £200 billion programme to replace the existing fleet of nuclear-armed submarines with new ones by the 2030s. The government of Prime Minister David Cameron, along with successive Conservative and Labour administrations, has continually defended Trident since its introduction in the 1960s, claiming it is essential for the UK’s national security. Labour has long grappled with the issue of Trident. While traditionally a proponent of the programme, divisions have grown among the party’s MPs, with several prominent backbenchers and left-wing activists opposing the renewal, citing cost, safety, and the push for global disarmament. On this occasion, 42 Labour MPs broke ranks and voted against the government, demonstrating deepening unease within the party over the renewal’s cost and necessity. In a floor speech, Labour leader Ed Miliband warned that the vote was taking place at a time of economic strain, saying: “We are in a struggle to keep as many public services and public jobs as we can in a time of austerity. We are voting to spend £200 billion on replacing – not improving – our nuclear weapons, and not because they are failing, but because they have nearly reached the end of their life.” Despite the internal dissent, the decision passed with the overwhelming support of Tory MPs. The Prime Minister said the programme was not a defence of the Cold War but a necessary guarantee against threats from hostile nations and non-state actors. “This is not a programme driven by panic or fear, it remains a vital part of our national security architecture,” he stated. Supporters of Trident argue that the programme is essential for maintaining the UK’s status as a global power and deterring acts of aggression that could befall the nation. They point to nuclear capabilities held by others, such as the United States, Russia, China, and France, as justification for the continued investment. The decision has drawn criticism from the opposition Green and SNP parties, as well as various disarmament campaigners. Campaign group CND (the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) called the vote a “missed opportunity to lead the world away from nuclear weapons.” They contend that the money could be better spent on public services like the NHS and education.

The explosive yet controversial batsman Kevin Pietersen has suggested he may hang up his England whites permanently after completing his participation in this summer’s T20 Blast with Surrey. Speaking in a recent interview, Pietersen hinted that he has little desire to return to the international scene, where he has long been a divisive figure among selectors, fans and team-mates alike. Pietersen, who remains one of the most feared and dynamic cricketers of his generation, is currently playing for Surrey in the T20 Blast but has not announced any further domestic or international plans beyond the competition. The 33-year-old, whose career with England came to a dramatic end in 2014 after a much-publicised and acrimonious rift with colleagues and the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB), has left the door open for a potential return – but only if all parties feel ready. “I think the history of my career in England is pretty clear,” Pietersen said. “We need to understand why cricket ended for me there and what’s changed. If people want to re-invent or bring back a relationship, I would expect that to be over the table, not under the bus.” Pietersen’s short but prolific spell as an England player saw him score two double hundreds in Test cricket and be named the Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 2009. However, his contributions were often overshadowed by his combative style and public feuds, including his famous split with former captain Andrew Strauss and team director Andy Flower. His omission from the 2015 World Cup squad marked his formal exit from the national team. Since then, Pietersen has enjoyed a continued career in various T20 leagues around the world, including in the Indian Premier League and South Africa's T20 Challenge. He has also played sporadically for Surrey and other county teams in England, but his presence in the game has remained more a reminder of his former self than a bridge to the past. This summer’s T20 Blast with Surrey represents a rare homecoming for Pietersen, who was once a central figure in English cricket. His performance could reignite talk about a potential return to the international fold, but both sides remain cautious. ECB chairman Colin Graves has previously stated the organisation is open to reflection, learning from past decisions, and the notion of reintegration. Whether on the field or off it, Pietersen has never shied away from making statements.

A Priest at South by Southwest: Bishop Paul Tighe finds music, faith, and humanity in the heart of Texas   As Bishop Paul Tighe sat down for our interview, he joked that not only is he probably the only priest at South by Southwest, but also the only person with grey hair. The Belfast-born prelate was in Austin for the event’s annual Faith + Spirituality conference, where theologians, preachers, and spiritual seekers rub shoulders with A-list musicians and Hollywood directors in a curious but fitting collision of genres. It was a far cry from the quiet of his role as the apostolic nuncio in the United States, a position that saw him represent the Holy See in America for over a decade. But the 74-year-old bishop, now semi-retired, is no stranger to cultural eccentricities. With a twinkle in his eye and a deep chuckle, he said of the world-famous music festival: “Where else can you have a breakfast keynote from a bishop and a mastering engineer in the same room, and no one blinks an eye?” Tighe’s presence at SXSW underlines a growing movement within the Church – one that sees faith being expressed in ways far removed from traditional pews and stained glass. The Faith + Spirituality programme, which has grown in prominence in recent years, invites religious leaders, from rabbis to Buddhist monks, to engage with evolving conversations on identity, purpose, and humanity in a digital and increasingly secular world. “I think what the Church needs to do is speak the language of our time, and that includes pop culture,” Bishop Tighe said. “I read books, I watch films, I listen to music – yes, sometimes it's a stretch – and being here allows me to speak more authentically to younger generations who are often far removed from religious institutions.” Tighe, who has published reflections on faith and music, was quick to praise the creative energy of the festival. “There is a genuine longing for meaning, for connection. I’ve heard that in young artists here, in people just discovering their voice. They may not use the language of the Church, but they are reaching for the same things we are: truth, beauty, love.” The bishop also spoke of the Church’s need to “humble itself” in the 21st century, something he has advocated for in the context of reform in the Vatican. His own Irish Catholic background, he said, has made him acutely aware of the need for change – from structural inflexibility to a deeper accountability for abuse scandals.

French former President Nicolas Sarkozy remains in custody as authorities continue questioning him over allegations of influence peddling, in what is shaping up to be one of the most significant legal cases involving a former head of state in modern French history. The 68-year-old ex-leader was placed under judicial control on Thursday, with French media reporting that he appeared before magistrates at the Évry judicial complex south of Paris. Sarkozy, who served as president from 2007 to 2012, is being investigated into allegations that he arranged to repay political debts to former interior minister Bruno Le Roux through his then-bodyguard, Christophe Goudal. The case, which dates back to 2013, relates to Goudal’s request for a promotion, which allegedly came after Sarkozy’s lawyer, Baroin, made appeals to Le Roux, a key figure in the Socialist Party at the time. The French government and institutions have been thrown into a fresh wave of political intrigue, with the scandal raising questions about the relationships between politics and personal networks, even at the highest levels of national power. It is the latest development in a series of legal battles for Sarkozy, who has already been convicted — though not in office — for illegally financing his 2012 re-election campaign. Magistrates have been examining whether Sarkozy committed the crime of influence peddling (“trafic d’influence”), which is a serious charge under French law carrying a maximum of 10 years in prison and a €150,000 fine. Officials have not revealed whether Sarkozy has confessed or denied the allegations, but his legal team has said he will “vigorously defend his integrity.” The investigation is part of a broader probe into alleged misuse of public funds and corruption surrounding Sarkozy’s former entourage. His wife, Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, is also under formal investigation in a separate inquiry linked to the same issues. Meanwhile, close allies have faced charges in recent months, adding to the steady erosion of Sarkozy's once-dominant political career. The holding of a former president under judicial questioning has rare legal and symbolic weight in France, where such actions usually signal that prosecutors have compelling evidence and are pursuing the case with unusual seriousness. It also raises concerns about the recent trend of legal proceedings against senior political figures, with some accusing the judiciary of overreach or political bias. Sarkozy’s legal woes have been made even more complex by his imprisonment between 2021 and 2022 for contempt of court, though this sentence was later suspended.

A deal that could secure the future of Tata Steel’s Scunthorpe plant is nearing the final stretch, with insiders suggesting a formal announcement could be made as early as Monday, the BBC has learned. The news has sparked a wave of cautious optimism among local residents and workers, many of whom have watched with dread as recent threats of site closures have loomed over the area. Scunthorpe, a town whose identity has been shaped by the steel industry for over a century, is now on the edge of a potential turning point. With thousands of local jobs and the stability of the broader region at stake, the deal has drawn attention from political leaders, trade unions, and even European Union representatives. The steel giant, once a cornerstone of British industry, has faced mounting financial pressures, including rising energy costs and global market fluctuations. India’s Tata Group, which acquired the British arm of the company in 2007, has itself been under intense scrutiny for its long-term British strategy following a controversial sale of Anglo-Dutch steel group Corus to the Japanese firm Liberty in March 2023. While the details of the deal remain under wraps, sources indicate that the new ownership is expected to be a UK-based buyer with strong backing from both public and private investors. Unions such as the Community and GMB have been vocal in their demand for guarantees that staffing levels at the works will be maintained and that no redundancies will immediately follow a change in ownership. Scunthorpe MP Nic Dakin described the possible deal as “the most critical moment for our town in many years.” He added, “This plant is not just a factory – it is the heart of our community. We cannot afford continued instability and uncertainty.” The region’s economic health has long been inextricably linked to the steelworks. Any disruption not only affects the 5,000 or so direct employees but also the local supply chains and small businesses that rely on the site as a major economic driver. The uncertainty over the plant’s future has already had a chilling effect on local services and investment. Public concern is further heightened by memories of the dramatic closure of the Redcar steelworks in 2015, which displaced over 1,500 workers and delivered a severe blow to the Teesside economy. That incident exposed the vulnerability of industrial communities and fueled a national debate about the govt’s capacity to protect key industries.

Two mothers whose daughters lost their lives to gang violence a decade ago are urging young people to think deeply about the consequences of their choices and the devastating impact of gang culture on local communities. Speaking at a community event in south London, Anaya Thompson and Maria Jones shared raw and emotional accounts of their children’s deaths, calling on families, schools and local leaders to work together to steer young people away from the lure of criminal activity. Anaya’s daughter, Aisha, was just 17 when she was shot during a street fight between rival groups in 2014. Maria’s daughter, Yasmin, was caught in the crossfire at the age of 18 during a dispute over unpaid debts. Both incidents sparked waves of grief across their communities, and now the two women are using their voices to prevent others from enduring the same pain. "Whatever problems you are facing, they are not worth taking another life," Anaya said, her voice breaking. "Once something is taken, it can never be given back. You can’t ever hug your child again, hold their hand, or even say goodbye. That is the reality of gang culture that no one tells the young people—until it’s too late." Maria echoed her words, adding that the legacy of grief only grows stronger with time. "Every year on the anniversary, we remember," she said. "We remember the funeral, the faces, the loss, and the families left behind. But we want others to remember too—not to suffer like we have." The event, held in a community centre in New Cross, was attended by local youth leaders, teachers, and police officers, all brought together to discuss ways of combating gun violence and the pull of criminal organisations. The two mothers also launched a new campaign, titled   "Choices Matter,"   which includes a series of local workshops and a short documentary featuring their daughters’ stories. Community leaders welcomed the campaign as a vital addition to the conversation about youth engagement. Councillor Sarah O’Reilly, who organised the event, said: "Too often, the victims of gang violence are the most vulnerable in our society. We need to give young people hope, resources and mentors. We hope Anaya and Maria can help lead the way." As their voices were met with standing applause from the crowd, the two women conceded that road ahead would not be easy but insisted that the time to act was now.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Filippo Grandi, has issued a stark warning about the escalating migrant and refugee crisis, declaring it to be a global phenomenon that cannot be tackled by traditional barriers or by simply turning people away at borders. Speaking at a recent emergency session in Geneva, Grandi stressed that the world is facing a historic surge in forced displacement, with more than one in every 113 people on the planet now a refugee or internally displaced person. “This crisis is too big, too complex, and too far-reaching to be solved by any one country or region alone,” he said. The remarks come as the Mediterranean migration route grows increasingly deadly, with more than 1,800 people reported to have died attempting to cross from North Africa to Europe since the beginning of the year. In the past week alone, over 500 men, women, and children were lost at sea after overloaded boats capsized off the coast of Libya. Europe, still reeling from the horrors of last year’s migrant influx, is under pressure to coordinate a more cohesive response, even as many national governments continue to grapple with rising anti-immigrant sentiment and political uncertainty. Grandi argued that sealing borders and adopting short-term containment policies would do little to address the real causes of the crisis: war, persecution, poverty, and climate change. “If we want to stop the cycle of desperation, we must not only save lives at sea but also address the root causes of displacement and support those who remain at home or are willing to return in safety and dignity,” he said. His statement was echoed by organisations on the ground, including the International Organisation for Migration, which has called for greater international cooperation and a scaling up of funding and resources to help host nations manage the growing numbers of displaced people. Figures about the scale of the crisis have continued to rise dramatically. In 2023 alone, more than 12 million new refugees and asylum applicants have been registered globally, with Syria, Afghanistan, and South Sudan remaining the top source countries. As the human toll mounts and political tensions rise, the UN continues to push for a more unified and long-term solution — one that recognises the shared responsibility of the global community. "Turning people away is not only morally indefensible," Grandi said. "It is also no longer a viable strategy in a world that is more interconnected than ever before."

The residents of Mexico City will be woken by an unusual alarm clock this weekend, as part of a bold new initiative designed to raise awareness of the risks posed by earthquakes. At 11am on Saturday, the city will participate in “Sismo Awareness Week,” with a timed simulation of what would happen if a major tremor struck again during the busy morning rush hour. The practice alarm, mimicking the intensity of a 7.0-magnitude quake, is part of emergency exercises that will see sirens blare across the city as government officials, students, and private-sector workers carry out mock drills in homes, offices, and public spaces. The move comes three decades after one of the worst earthquakes in Mexican history devastated the capital in 1985, killing more than 10,000 people and leaving much of the city in ruins. Following the disaster, Mexico City introduced one of the most sophisticated earthquake early warning systems in the world — a network of thousands of seismographs that can detect tremors in the ocean basins hundreds of kilometers away and provide advance notice to the city. On average, residents now have between 60 and 120 seconds to take cover before the impacts of a quake are felt. However, despite improvements in infrastructure and emergency preparedness, city officials say complacency remains a key challenge. “Many young people have never experienced a major quake, and some older residents may take the drills for granted,” said Sergio Obeso, head of Mexico City’s civil protection department. “Our goal is to keep the memory of past disasters alive and ensure people are never caught off guard.” The exercise will be coupled with workshops in schools and communities across the city, where volunteers will teach residents practical steps to take during and after an earthquake, as well as how to assemble emergency kits. Authorities are also using the event to test emergency response mechanisms, from hospital readiness to the coordination between local and federal agencies. Critics, however, argue that while such drills are important, they are not enough. “We need sustained investment in building codes, retrofitting老旧小区 (older housing), and investing in early warning technologies,” said Carlos Mendoza, a geologist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. “An alarm system is only as good as the people and structures it protects.” As the alarm is set to sound this Saturday, the city watches with a weary but resolute spirit. For Mexico City, where history and warning signs go hand in hand, the past is never far away.

The Crown Prosecution Service has confirmed that the late Labour peer Lord Greville Janner will not face sexual abuse charges due to his advanced state of dementia, which legal experts concluded rendered him unfit to stand trial. The decision, which ends a protracted legal and public inquiry into the allegations, brings closure to one of the most high-profile cases of historical child sexual abuse in recent British political history. Lord Janner, who died in 2019 at the age of 87, was a prominent figure in the Labour Party for over four decades, representing Leicester in Parliament from 1964 until his resignation in 1994. He was also a justice of the High Court and a Lord of Appeal in Ordinary, giving him considerable influence in both political and legal circles. The allegations against him were made by a number of men, some now in their 50s and 60s, who claimed he had abused them as children at his home in the 1970s and 1980s. The inquiry into the claims was reopened in 2020 following the publication of details from the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA). The IICSA report expressed strong concerns that the Labour Party and the Ministry of Justice, among others, had failed to act on credible allegations of abuse from staff and members. Despite the mounting evidence and public calls for accountability, the Crown Prosecution Service concluded in 2022 that there was insufficient opportunity to conduct a fair trial due to the mental state of the accused. A CPS spokesperson said in a statement: “Following a detailed assessment of the medical evidence, it has been concluded that the deceased is unfit to stand trial due to being in the late stages of dementia. The decision not to proceed with criminal charges is based wholly on the statutory test of fitness to plead, which is set out in the Mental Health Act 1983 and the Code of Practice issued under it.” The statement has been met with mixed reactions. Victims' groups have acknowledged the legal rationale behind the decision but expressed disappointment that justice could not be delivered through the courts. Jeremy Conway, a barrister representing some of the survivors, said: “This is clearly a tragic outcome for the victims, many of whom have been waiting for justice for almost 40 years. While the law does not permit the prosecution of the deceased or those unfit to stand trial, our clients are still waiting for truth, recognition and, in some cases, compensation.”

Universities Paid Out Hundreds of Thousands in Compensation to Students Over Complaints   Universities across England and Wales paid out more than £400,000 in compensation to students last year following a range of formal complaints, a figure that has sparked fresh debate over accountability, student welfare, and the handling of complaints within higher education institutions. The data, compiled from the Office for Students (OfS), reveals that the largest payouts were made by some of the country’s largest universities, including the University of Manchester, the University of Birmingham, and the Open University. While the exact nature of the complaints has not been fully disclosed, the OfS confirmed that many involved issues such as poor academic standards, inadequate pastoral support, and the mishandling of safeguarding and welfare concerns. The university sector, long under scrutiny for its handling of student welfare – especially in the wake of high-profile cases of mental health neglect and the rise of student activism – now faces renewed questions over whether enough is being done to address concerns at an institutional level. The figures also highlight a disparity in the way awards vary, with some students receiving £1,000, while others were awarded over £10,000 in compensation. Emma Revnell, deputy director of the Office for Students, said: “We expect all universities and colleges to treat students fairly and transparently. When things go wrong, redress must be available. These compensation figures remind us that while most institutions are delivering a high-quality experience for students, there is always more to do to ensure consistent standards across the sector.” One of the largest single compensation payouts was made by the University of Manchester, reportedly for £23,000 following a complaint related to a failure to support a student through a mental health crisis. The university, in a statement, said it was committed to continuous improvement and had implemented new mental health initiatives as a result of internal reviews. Meanwhile, reports suggest that the number of complaints has remained relatively stable in recent years, but the average award for each case has risen significantly. A whistleblower from a London-based university told The Times: “The culture is shifting. We are seeing a growing willingness among students to report issues, and while not all compensation cases are justified, they are vital to holding institutions accountable.” Critics of the sector have warned that the recent trend of monetary compensation, rather than structural or systemic change, risks masking deeper problems that continue to affect student wellbeing and academic standards.

Lee Smith has insisted there are no lingering tensions with his former club London Wasps ahead of his emotional return to Adams Park on Saturday. The Newcastle Falcons outside back will line up against his former employers for the first time since leaving the club in 2013, and he has dismissed any suggestion of a personal score to settle. "Here and now is my focus," Smith told reporters on Thursday. "I’ve played for London Wasps with a clean heart and a clean head, and I have no problem returning to Adams Park. It was a difficult decision to leave, but it was the right one at the time. I don’t see this as a personal matter, just a challenge to step up and produce a strong performance for Newcastle." The 33-year-old, who spent a decade with Wasps after joining from London Irish in 2003, was a key figure in their two Premiership title wins and a Heineken Cup victory in 2007. His exit from Wasps in 2013 was controversial at the time, as he was told his contract would not be renewed following the club’s takeover by Fortress Investment Group. Newcastle, who are currently eighth in the Premiership table, begin a run of crucial fixtures this weekend and will be eager for a strong result in a derby-like atmosphere against Wasps, who are just one place above them – ninth. Smith, who has helped bolster Newcastle’s backline since rejoining the club last season, will be vital in their efforts to climb the table toward the top-six. “We’ve got a big game against a rival in London Wasps,” said Newcastle head coach Dean Richards. “It's an occasion that brings added motivation for both sides and I want our players to relish that.” While Smith spoke of moving past the past, his return is not without controversy. Current Wasps players and fans have taken to social media in recent days to raise questions about why Smith left the club, with some accusing him of deserting a team that was reeling from financial uncertainty after the 2012 Heineken Cup win. For any hint of tension, however, Smith insists his mindset is purely professional. “I’m just looking to play well and help my team,” he said. “That’s what I’ve always done, wherever I’ve been." The match promises to be a fiercely contested encounter, not only in the battle on the pitch but also in the emotional stakes of a player returning to the home of his past.

Calls for the reintroduction of a post-study work visa system for international students in Scotland have been firmly rejected by the UK government, sparking disappointment and concern among university leaders and business groups. The proposal, which had been championed by a coalition of Scottish universities and industry representatives, aimed to allow international graduate students to remain in the UK for two years after completing their studies, providing a pathway to permanent employment and settlement. In a statement last week, a UK government source confirmed that no policy changes were under consideration, asserting that the current visa regime was “fit for purpose” and providing clarity for both employers and international students. The rejection marks the second time in recent months that the UK government has dismissed calls to reinstate flexible work permissions for graduates, following similar refusals across England and Wales. In Scotland, the issue has taken on added urgency due to the country’s increasing reliance on international students, who contribute significantly to the economy. Universities in cities like Glasgow, Edinburgh, and Aberdeen have reported a sharp decline in applications since the post-study work visa was abolished in 2012, with many prospective students opting to study in more student-friendly jurisdictions such as Canada and Australia. Caitlin Doran, director of Universities Scotland, expressed disappointment at the news. “International students play a vital role in our education and economy. They are not only future leaders and professionals but also key contributors to innovation and research in our universities,” she said. “Denying them the opportunity to work in the UK after they graduate undermines their investment in their education and fails to maximise the benefits they can bring.” Local businesses in key sectors also voiced concern. A business leaders’ group in Edinburgh warned that the decision could exacerbate skills shortages in science, technology and healthcare, industries that have historically benefited from the influx of international talent. The Scottish government, while not directly responsible for the UK’s immigration policy, had supported the call for reform and had urged the UK to reconsider. A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: “We remain committed to working with the UK government to promote Scotland as a leading international destination for students, and will continue to highlight the economic benefits of a student-friendly environment.” The decision comes at a time when the UK is seeking to project itself as a global leader in higher education and research.

Two men have been found guilty at the Old Bailey of plotting to smuggle firearms, including AR-15 assault rifles and Ingram MAC 10 sub-machine guns, into the United Kingdom from overseas, in what prosecutors described as a “dangerous and well-organised” conspiracy. Mohamed Islam, 31, and Daniel Baumbach, 38, were both sentenced to prison terms on Friday following a six-week trial that heard how the weapons were intended for use in the UK as part of an unspecified criminal enterprise. The firearms, worth an estimated £200,000, were being shipped from the United States under the guise of military memorabilia, with false customs declarations and false documentation used to evade detection at UK ports. Immigration officers at London Stansted Airport uncovered the first signs of the smuggling operation in December 2023, when a suspect parcel was flagged for further inspection. Inside were firearms listed in the US as “military-grade” and banned for civilian use in most jurisdictions, including the UK. A police investigation, codenamed Operation Spectre, revealed that the men had been in regular communication with a US-based supplier and had arranged for the guns to be split up into multiple packages, each destined for different UK addresses. The Old Bailey heard that Islam, of New Addington, south London, and Baumbach, from Slough – both of whom deny planning to use the weapons – had exchanged messages discussing “how to make the shipments discreet,” as well as their use of False identities and mail drops to reduce the risk of detection. Assistant Crown Prosecutor Emma White said the case exposed a worrying trend of firepower entering the UK undetected via the Americas, and warned that the potential consequences of these weapons falling into the wrong hands were catastrophic. "This was not about collecting old weapons or fulfilling a personal obsession," she said. "This was part of a commercial operation designed to supply high-powered guns to those who intend to use them unlawfully in this country." The court was told that intelligence links Islamic extremism were under investigation, but that no evidence of terror-related intent had been formally confirmed during the trial. During sentencing, Judge Sarah Payne QC described the pair’s actions as “a gross violation of the law and a serious threat to public safety.” She told them: “These were not the standard weapons used in serious crime. They were weapons of war.” Mohamed Islam was given a seven-year-and-nine-month sentence, while Daniel Baumbach received six years and six months.

The European Council president, Charles Michel, has called for a reform of in-work benefits for EU citizens arriving in the UK, in a bid to address concerns over record levels of migration since 2004. Speaking ahead of a major meeting of EU leaders, Michel suggested that the EU should respond to the unique situation in the UK by limiting access to certain state-funded benefits for recent arrivals from the continent. His remarks come amid growing political pressure on the UK government to manage the influx of migrants, with data from the Office for National Statistics showing over 6.5 million people from the European Union have moved to the UK since 2004. Michel’s comments reflect a nuanced position from Brussels, acknowledging the UK’s challenges while ensuring the reform does not breach EU free movement rules. Currently, EU citizens who move to the UK are entitled to claim a range of in-work benefits, including housing and child support, after a 12-month qualifying period. However, critics argue that this policy acts as a pull factor for migrants and places pressure on public services. The UK government has been exploring options to restrict access to such benefits for new arrivals, and Michel’s statement could pave the way for Europe-wide agreement on the issue. The immigration debate has become increasingly polarised in the UK, with the Conservative Party placing a strong focus on reducing net migration in domestic policy discussions. Chancellor Rishi Sunak has been at the forefront of pushing for stricter measures, stating that while the UK remains an open society, “we must ensure our system is not being unfairly exploited.” The Department for Work and Pensions is currently in discussions to reform the system, potentially limiting the time EU citizens can claim housing benefit and removing access to universal credit for recent arrivals. The proposed changes have been welcomed by some sectors, particularly in the property and public healthcare industries, which argue the costs of migration are disproportionately borne by communities. However, advocacy groups for EU citizens in the UK have raised concerns over the potential impact on vulnerable individuals and families.
