Lana the Labrador, once known as the "saddest dog in the world" for her long and lonely wait for a home, may be facing an unexpected third chapter in her life. After capturing hearts across the globe nearly a decade ago, the 13-year-old dog, who had lived at a care home in Leicestershire for over six years, has once again found herself in the spotlight — this time not as a beloved pet seeking a family, but as a candidate for one final act of adoration and care. Lana first came to public attention in 2007 when animal charity The Dogs Trust shared touching images of the grizzled but gentle giant sitting alone at the end of a ward bed at a residential care home. These photos went viral, and Lana became a symbol of loyalty and companionship, providing comfort to residents who had nowhere else to turn. Her devoted presence in the home lasted for years, becoming a fixture of daily life until she was adopted by a nursing couple in 2012 in what seemed to be the perfect happy ending. However, the couple’s sudden death in 2019 once again left Lana without a permanent home. Rather than returning to the care home, she ended up in temporary foster care and is now being rehomed by the same animal charity that first brought her international fame. “Lana is at the end of her second lease on life and needs one more act of kindness,” said a spokesperson for The Dogs Trust. “She’s still a beautiful, gentle soul and at this stage, she just needs a quiet place to rest and someone to show her a little love.” Animal lovers have once again flooded social media with messages of hope and encouragement, many recalling being moved by Lana’s story years ago. Her latest plight highlights a growing concern among charities about the vulnerability of pets to sudden change — especially as owners grow older or circumstances shift unexpectedly. As her chance to find new purpose and affection nears, many are reflecting on how, despite her hardships, Lana has always given more than she has ever taken. “She’s the kind of dog who gives you love without judgment, no matter how long you’ve been waiting to give it back,” wrote one fan on Twitter. Her story continues to be one of resilience and compassion, even as the curtain is beginning to fall on a chapter filled with remarkable adventures.

The man convicted of murdering a four-year-old boy in what a court described as an act of “incomprehensible brutality” has been found dead in his cell at HMP Lindholme, a Category C prison in South Yorkshire. Authorities confirmed that the individual, whose name has not been disclosed at the request of the family, was discovered unresponsive on Friday morning and was pronounced dead shortly after. The cause of death is yet to be determined, with an inquest expected to be held in due course. The tragic news comes more than two years after the child, named locally as Matthew, died as a result of severe, sustained abuse inflicted by his stepfather. The case shocked the nation and sparked renewed calls for urgent reform to safeguarding systems, especially for vulnerable children in the care of adults with criminal records. During the trial, the court heard how Matthew had suffered multiple, overlapping injuries, and had been subjected to savage beatings and sexual assault by the convicted man. His mother, who was present during much of the trial, expressed in open court the profound distress and anguish caused by the loss of her young son—and the horror of witnessing details of the brutal attacks laid bare. A woman who lived in the same housing estate as the family said the killings had left the community in “shock and disbelief” at the time. “He was such a little boy. You never think something like that could happen in your own street,” she said. The man, sentenced to a whole-life tariff after being found guilty of murder and sentenced to additional terms for sexual assault and child cruelty, never expressed remorse. Sources in the prison also said that his death was a surprise to staff, who described him as having had a “low-profile” and non-confrontational presence behind bars. No suicide note has been found at this stage. Justice Secretary Dominic Raab has not commented publicly on the man’s death, and a statement from the Ministry of Justice said that “any concerns will be fully investigated as part of the coroner’s process.” Meanwhile, the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) reiterated its call for urgent improvements to the background checks for people in contact with children—including step-parents and carers. "Matthew’s tragic death highlighted the critical gaps in the system that leave the most vulnerable children at risk," a spokesperson for the charity said.

The 2016 US presidential campaign brought an intensity to public discourse that split the nation along ideological, cultural, and personal lines in a way unmatched in modern political memory. Donald Trump’s divisive rhetoric, unfiltered negativity, and polarising approach dominated headlines and living rooms alike, deepening existing divisions among American voters and drawing stark contrasts in how citizens viewed the very fabric of the country they inhabit. While Trump celebrated his campaign as one of unprecedented popularity—boasting millions of supporters hungry for change—his opponents decried it as corrosive, pulling the nation toward a political impasse defined by mutual distrust and vitriol. From the first primary debates to the final presidential ballot, the tone and direction of Trump’s campaign stood out starkly amid a backdrop of historic social movements, a growing awareness of racial inequality, and bursts of populist rage over economic inequality and globalisation. His frontline strategy was as unconventional as the man himself—leading surrogates often at loggerheads with establishment figures, distancing himself from traditional Republican allies, and eschewing the diplomatic polish that has become a staple of presidential politics. With each tweet, each speech, and each unscripted exchange with the press, Trump reinforced a consistent image: one of a maverick unafraid to anger the political and media elite in pursuit of what he claimed was a mandate for a new America. “It's amazing – this is a new nation, people,” he declared on the campaign trail. “We have been failed for so long, and now we're going to turn it around.” Opinion polls, town hall footage, and social media trends reflected a society increasingly splintered. Support for Trump came not only from working-class voters in key swing states but also from a surge of disaffected individuals across the nation who felt excluded by the political and economic system. However, his verbal clashes with high-profile journalists, his insults toward political opponents, and his often controversial stances on race and religion left many Americans unmoored in their understanding of where they stood on the issues. To his supporters, he was a truth-teller, a blunt force casting a light on the rot he believed had infected Washington for decades. To his critics, he was a disruptor who threatened to undermine democratic norms and coarsen public life. “This campaign has left many Americans frustrated, anxious, and even ashamed,” said one Democratic strategist, who requested anonymity. “But it’s also energised a base that feels unheard and marginalised.”

Whole areas of the NHS in England are facing an unprecedented overhaul as the chief executive of NHS England has announced that failing services will be placed in special measures in a significant restructuring bid. In a bold move, NHS leaders aim to address systemic underperformance across a range of regions and services, from acute hospitals to mental health support and community care. The announcement comes amid growing concerns over delays in patient treatment, long waiting lists, and persistent staffing shortages that have strained the health service in recent years. Simon Stevens, the NHS England chief executive, confirmed the decision in a statement to the House of Commons, saying the measure would ensure lasting improvements are made to address underperforming services. “The NHS will not shy away from tough decisions,” he said, adding that placing areas in special measures would allow for a “rigorous review” and the introduction of specific targets to be met under the watch of independent oversight panels and regional leaders. The government has not released a full list of the regions or services affected, but it is understood that several hospitals with a history of poor inspection ratings, as well as areas struggling to meet emergency care benchmarks, will be the first to fall under the new regime. Special measures, a term usually applied to underperforming schools in England, would see local NHS trusts and providers subjected to external monitoring, mandatory action plans, and potential funding restrictions until improvements are seen. Concerns about the move have already been raised by some MPs and NHS staff, who argue that placing the system under such intense scrutiny could add pressure and reduce already stretched services. However, NHS leaders insist the step is necessary to restore public confidence in an institution facing its biggest test in decades. “Without intervention, some areas are at risk of failing the patients they exist to serve,” Stevens said. The announcement follows the release of a damning NHS performance report, which showed that key services across the country are operating beyond their safe capacity. A&E departments in particular have been highlighted for their alarming wait times, while delays in cancer diagnosis and treatment have sparked widespread concern. NHS Trusts have been told to prepare for stringent targets on reducing waiting times, improving effectiveness of care, and increasing workforce stability. The government has pledged additional funding to support the transformation, while urging trust chief executives to take immediate action.

For the first time in 400 years, a curious and distinctive moustachioed face is returning to Poole Harbour, where it once loomed over the waters like a silent sentinel of a bygone era. The long-lost figurehead of a 17th-century wrecked ship, now the subject of a major conservation project, is set to make a historic comeback as part of an ambitious restoration effort led by local heritage groups. The figurehead, which was once part of a merchant vessel that sank off the Dorset coast during the Stuart period, was recovered from the seabed decades ago by a local diver. But for many years, its identity remained a mystery, locked away in storage and cloaked in layers of salt, encrustation and time. Now, thanks to years of painstaking work by historians, marine archaeologists, and conservationists, the true face of this historical icon is finally beginning to emerge. The figure’s striking moustache and ornate details suggest it may have been Anglo-Dutch in origin — a style common in the 17th century as Britain’s ships ventured further into global trade. Identifying the exact ship it came from is proving elusive, but its return is being hailed as a symbol of Poole's long and proud maritime history. As a major port during the golden age of sail, Poole played a crucial role in the export of goods to the continent, and such ships would have been a common sight. Historian Dr. Emily Bell, who has been working on the project, said the figurehead's return will help bring that past to life for a new generation. "We are talking about a piece of history that was literally lost to the sea. Now, as we uncover its features, we are not just restoring a piece of wood — we are restoring a conversation between the past and the present." Local officials have confirmed that the figurehead will be displayed at Poole Museum as part of an upcoming exhibition exploring the town's connections with the sea. But the dream is grander than that. A growing campaign among residents and heritage enthusiasts wants it to be re-erected on a promenade facing the water — a fitting tribute to the ship it once adorned. While the figurehead has yet to find its new home by the waves, its path back is no less dramatic than the voyage of the ship it once commanded. After four centuries beneath the tides, this moustachioed legend is set to stand tall once more, gazing out over the same waters it disappeared from — a symbol of resilience, history, and the enduring pull of the sea.

Perhaps the sweetest part of Glasgow’s famous victory in Paris was that it was almost entirely unexpected. That, in itself, made it all the more triumphant—a shot of pure, unfiltered passion against a backdrop of widespread doubt and indifference. As the sun dipped over the Seine and the final whistle blew, the world watched in stunned silence as the underdog team from the West of Scotland claimed glory where few had thought possible. For many, the miraculous nature of the win carried echoes of Glasgow’s own past victories, but this one was arguably its most poetic. The tournament had been written off before it had even begun. Pundits dismissed the team as undertrained, out of form, and lacking direction. Fans, accustomed to years of near misses and heartbreak, had barely bothered to turn up for the opening matches. The stadium, when they finally made it through to the final, was half-empty in the first half. Yet, in the second half and especially in those final, nail-biting minutes, the crowd surged forward in a wave of defiance, planting the blue and gold of Glasgow deep into the Parisian night. What struck those who were there was not just the technical brilliance of the win, but the raw emotion that underpinned it. Younger players, many of whom still had traces of trepidation in their wide eyes, combined with veterans who had long given up on holding their breath. The coach, who had faced months of criticism and calls for her resignation, stood at the edge of the pitch, arms raised toward the heavens as if in silent defiance of all the naysayers. For the people of Glasgow, this wasn’t just a sports victory. It was a symbolic reclamation of pride in a year filled with setbacks—from economic hardship to climate disasters. There’s something deeply human about an underdog story, but there’s something even more powerful when it happens in a place like Paris, where sports are written in the grand narrative of history. This was not just a celebration of a win for Glasgow, but for every city, every community, every person who has ever believed in something before anyone else was willing to. Back home, as the streets came alive with cheers and the unmistakable sound of bagpipes being played out of control from bar lunches, a new kind of optimism settled in.

Turkey has called for an urgent meeting of NATO ambassadors in Brussels to discuss ongoing military operations against both the Islamic State (IS) terror group and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), as part of its broader strategy to address security threats on its soil and along its borders. The meeting comes amid heightened tensions in the region and growing concerns over Turkey’s military actions in northern Iraq and Syria, which critics argue risk further destabilising an already volatile area. The move signals Turkey’s continued determination to press its case within the alliance, seeking support and coordination as it escalates its fight against IS and the PKK. Ankara has accused the PKK, which the EU and the UN list as a terrorist organisation, of using areas in northern Iraq as a staging ground for cross-border attacks on Turkish security forces. turkey has carried out numerous airstrikes in the Kurdish-dominated region this year, including on civilian infrastructure, in a crackdown that has drawn widespread condemnation from human rights groups and political leaders. In a recent statement, Turkish Foreign Minister Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu said the meeting was necessary to align NATO’s strategic perspective with Turkey’s immediate security needs. “We are not excluded from the shared goals of the alliance, and we are determined to continue our operations in accordance with international law and as part of the broader global fight against terrorism,” he said. The meeting also follows a call by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for greater NATO involvement in the region, and for the alliance to establish a “no-fly zone” in northern Syria to prevent future attacks. However, several NATO countries have expressed concerns about the unilateral nature of Turkey’s operations, which they fear could undermine regional stability and inflame sectarian tensions. Germany, France, and the United States have all previously urged Turkey to co-ordinate more closely with coalition forces in its anti-IS efforts and to avoid actions that could alienate Kurdish groups, such as the U.S.-allied Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), who are also key in the fight against IS. The Pentagon has warned that Turkey’s recent operations near the strategic Islamic State-held city of Manbij — designated for liberation by the White House alongside the SDF — risk complicating efforts to defeat IS on the ground. However, Turkey insists that its operations are being conducted with regional partners and with the support of the international community.

Actress Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Hungarian-born Hollywood star who charmed audiences for decades with her glamour, wit, and a career spanning nearly 80 films, has died at the age of 99. Her husband, Frederic von Anhalt, confirmed the sad news following a heart attack. Known for her striking beauty and theatrical flair, Gabor was a fixture of the Golden Age of Hollywood and enjoyed a career that outlived many of her contemporaries. Gabor was born Zsa Zsa Gaborovna in Budapest in 1917 and began acting as a child during the rise of the Nazi regime in Germany. After fleeing Europe during World War II, she arrived in the United States and found fame in Hollywood during the 1940s and 1950s. She became a household name with roles in films such as  Queen of the Desert  (1948),  Two Cats from Lima  (1956), and  Catch-22  (1970). But Gabor's life was not only defined by her work. She became a tabloid sensation over the years, largely due to her string of high-profile marriages—nine in total. Her husbands were often young and wealthy, and her parties in Bel Air were the stuff of legend. She was also known for her personality – glamorous yet often sardonic, and fiercely proud of her Hungarian heritage. One of her most famous quotes, “I do not use a plastic face mask unless I’m faking a smile,” captured her self-assured and playful character. In recent years, Gabor had become a fixture at Hollywood’s Christmas tree lighting ceremony, a tradition she upheld for many years. She considered it her personal ballet, and her appearance in a feathered hat and glittering gold gown each December lit up the event. Her passing marks the end of not just another life well-lived, but the poignant closing of a chapter in Hollywood’s golden era. With the world mourning one of its most glamorous icons, tributes have poured in from fans, fellow actors, and those who knew her only from her larger-than-life public persona. Her legacy remains as vibrant as the sparkle of her emerald eyes and the confidence with which she told the world, “I am no aging beauty. I am a living work of art.” Ms Gabor is survived by her husband, Frederic von Anhalt, and her daughter Francesca, who has previously spoken about the deep bond they shared. Services and tributes will be planned in the coming days to celebrate the life of a woman who never stopped shining.

MPs face historic vote on Syria air strikes as divisions emerge over military action against IS   As the House of Commons prepares to cast a landmark vote on whether to extend UK airstrikes against so-called Islamic State (IS) targets in Syria, ministers, MPs, and commentators are sharply divided over the potential consequences — both on the battlefield and in public opinion. Prime Minister David Cameron has argued that the intervention is necessary to protect British citizens and break the “caliphate” established by IS in parts of Syria and Iraq, but opposition leaders and anti-war campaigners warn of the risks of escalation and the possibility of further destabilisation in the region. Cameron has made the case that air strikes in Syria are vital to degrade IS and to support the government’s fight against Ebola in West Africa by preventing the terrorist group from capitalising on the global distraction. In a dramatic speech to MPs, he warned that “the threat is not just to Syria — it is to the world.” Cameron highlighted the tactical successes of limited strikes in Iraq, where Anglo-American bombing campaigns in recent months have disrupted IS’s operations and reportedly led to the deaths of high-ranking militants. He also pointed to the threat posed by Syrian refugees, many of whom have fled areas under IS control and might spread the group’s ideology across Europe. Proponents of military action have also underscored the moral imperative. Writing in leading newspapers, senior Conservative MPs and Centrist figures have argued that the UK has a responsibility to act when humanitarian atrocities are underway. “It is not just about defeating IS,” wrote one commentator. “It’s about protecting civilians from the worst barbarity — people are being slaughtered in cold blood, just like they were in Rwanda, and the international community must not stand idly by.” However, politicians from across the political spectrum — including key members of the governing Conservative Party — have raised serious concerns about the lack of clear objectives and the potential for Britain to be drawn into prolonged conflict. The Liberal Democrats, currently in government, have unambiguously opposed the proposal, arguing that the mission lacks a coherent plan for success and risks exposing British service personnel to unnecessary danger. Their leader, Tim Farron, described the idea as “needlessly provocative” and warned that unilateral military action could end up being academically supported by the public, a new fact that could have major implications for future government decisions.

The knighthood awarded to Lynton Crosby, the chief strategist for the Conservative Party during the general election, has been described as “outrageous” by Labour’s shadow home secretary, Andy Burnham, as widespread outrage continues to mount over the controversial honour. Crosby, who has never worked in public service, was awarded a knighthood in the New Year Honours list handed down by the Queen on Thursday. The decision has sparked criticism from across the political spectrum, with many calling it a betrayal of the traditional values surrounding British honours. Burnham called the move “appalling” and said it undercut the image of fairness and merit associated with the system. The 65-year-old, who has been described as one of the most influential and controversial political strategists in British history, played a significant role in steering the Conservative campaign – including their use of microtargeted advertising in the final weeks of the election. While Downing Street and the Cabinet Office have declined to comment on the specifics of honours, Prime Minister Theresa May has defended the selection as being in line with the discretion of the monarch and the advisory body, the Honours Committee. “Crosby is a man of the people who has advised the Conservatives as their campaign director and has made a substantial contribution to the successful general election,” the Prime Minister reportedly said when consulted on the decision. “His efforts were vital to the outcome, and I take the view that such individuals deserve recognition.” Speaking after the list was published, Burnham accused the Conservatives of using the honours system to “pat themselves on the back” for their own political success. “Awarding a knighthood to an election strategist who has never held public office and worked for politicians who split this country along party lines is deeply unseemly,” he said. “This type of reward to those who benefited directly from an election they helped win sets a dangerous precedent.” The backlash has also come from members of the public and media. Prominent anti-Tory commentator and former guest on Question Time, Misha Glenny, told the BBC it was a “symptom of the corrosion of British values under Conservative rule”. Meanwhile, the Mirror has led a strong editorial condemning the decision, calling it “a slap in the face to the public servants who do the real work of running this country”. Crosby himself, who has largely kept out of the public eye since the end of the campaign, has made no public comment on the award.

Australia’s cricketers will not abandon a long-standing revenue-sharing agreement to resolve their ongoing pay dispute with Cricket Australia (CA), according to national captain Steve Smith. The announcement, made at a press conference in Sydney, comes as talks between the players’ association and CA continue to stall, raising concerns over the future of the national team’s participation in upcoming Test matches and key bilateral series. For decades, Australia’s cricketers have benefited from a deal that splits central contract revenues with CA, typically from broadcast, sponsorship, and ticketing income. Critics of the model argue it limits the players’ ability to demand higher earnings when compared to their counterparts in other international teams, but Smith said it formed the bedrock of a strong national team culture and long-term stability. “We are not looking to walk away from the revenue-sharing model,” Smith said. “This has been part of what has made Australian cricket so successful in the world for so many years. What we are looking for is a fair, modern agreement that better reflects the value cricket brings to CA, and the personal sacrifices our players make.” The central issue remains CA's demand that the players agree to a new financial arrangement that places a larger portion of match and player income into CA’s coffers, a move players and their representatives say would significantly reduce their earnings from tournament-based cricket, including Twenty20 internationals and one-day series. Players' Union boss David Boon, speaking separately, backed Smith’s position. “The cricketers are not opposed to CA having a level of financial control or involvement in our sport, but the current proposal is not in the best interests of the players,” Boon said. “The new CA model would reduce discretionary income and weigh heavily on the way players manage their careers, especially those with contracts in franchise leagues abroad.” CA, for its part, maintains the proposed changes are necessary to ensure long-term financial sustainability and a fairer approach between all levels of the sport. Chief Executive James Sutherland said the governing body was open to compromise but made it clear no agreement would happen at the expense of CA’s financial health. “Dialogue is ongoing, but all parties must come to the table with a shared understanding that cricket in Australia must continue to grow and prosper as a viable business,” Sutherland said. Without a resolution soon, the standoff risks disrupting the calendar, with particular concern over the upcoming three-Test series against India set to begin in November.

Roberto Mancini insisted on Monday that Manchester City had not surpassed Manchester United as the dominant force in English football, even after securing a record 6-1 victory at Old Trafford—the biggest margin of defeat by the Red Devils at their own home in Premier League history. The result marked a seismic shift in one of the biggest rivalries in world football and has reignited the debate over which club holds supremacy on the pitch. City’s emphatic performance saw Dani Alves, Edin Džeko and a Yaya Touré hat-trick dismantle a weakened United side stripped of key players due to European duty. The rout left the Red Devils rocking and highlighted the growing gulf in philosophy, budgets and results between the two Manchester clubs, who are now both among the wealthiest in the world, thanks to years of investment from Middle Eastern owners. Yet Mancini was careful to avoid declaring outright victory in the Premier League power struggle. “This is one game, and one team we defeated, but we are not saying we are better than Manchester United,” he said during his post-match press conference, which was delivered with the characteristic calm that has marked his tenure at the Etihad. The Italian manager, who took charge of City in June 2009 to great fanfare, stressed that success is measured in titles and domestic trophies, not by one-off games. “We want to build a strong team and compete every season, and we are on the right path. But to say we've taken over as the biggest power in the league—no, that’s not for me to say,” he added. Mancini also acknowledged the uniqueness of City's recent dominance, noting that the club’s investment had allowed them to attract world-class talent and create an attractive style of play that combines possession and intensity. He credited the efforts of his coaching staff and players, but stopped short of challenging City’s status as a generational force. The victory has triggered widespread debate among fans and pundits alike, many of whom have claimed that United are on the decline and that City have passed them in both on and off-field stature. However, Mancini insisted it was premature to draw such conclusions. “We need time,” he said. “We need to win things, and not just one game.” For the time being, City have shown the capacity to produce performances that would have once been unthinkable against their rivals.

A father from Hampshire has been charged with the murder of his six-year-old daughter, with prosecutors alleging that he orchestrated a "sophisticated charade" to cover up the crime, casting a grim light on the events leading up to her death. Dominic Perriam, 39, from Petersfield, appeared at Winchester Crown Court on Tuesday and was accused of killing his daughter, Ruby, on 21 August 2023. The court heard how Ruby’s body was discovered at a property in Warmington, Hampshire, following a 12-hour search operation involving local police and members of the public, many of whom had been led to believe the girl had gone missing. Perriam, who is the sole defendant in the case, was arrested that same day and has since been placed on remand. The prosecution alleges that Perriam fabricated the story of Ruby's disappearance as part of a calculated effort to divert attention from his involvement in her death. "This was not an accidental death or a tragic mistake," said Senior Crown Prosecutor, Lucy Lucas. "The evidence indicates that Ruby’s father was in the house at the time and actively planned and carried out actions to hide what had happened." Ruby, who attended a local primary school, is described in court documents as having been "healthy, active and full of life" before her death. Her mother is no longer in contact with Perriam, with school staff and neighbours unaware of the couple's estrangement. It is understood that Perriam attempted to create the appearance that Ruby had vanished without a trace. Mobile phone records and surveillance footage obtained during the investigation suggest he made a number of visits to the scene of the crime in the days before reporting his daughter as missing. The prosecution will assert that the search efforts—including appeals on social media and roadside inquiries—were a deliberate deception carried out using the resources of the police and the public. In a statement issued by Hampshire Police, Detective Chief Inspector Sarah Jones said: "We are committed to pursuing justice for Ruby and supporting her surviving family during this incredibly difficult time. The evidence we have gathered shows a deeply concerning pattern of behaviour by her father that we will present in full during the trial." As the case moves forward, investigators say they are continuing to examine Perriam’s communications and movements in the weeks prior to the incident for further clarity on the events that led to the tragedy.

The US government’s lead incident commander for the Deepwater Horizon oil leak has cast doubt on whether recent oil seepages detected on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico are directly connected to the ruptured oil well, raising further uncertainty about the origins and scale of the underground flow. Speaking during a brief media update, Rear Admiral Paul Zukunft, who is overseeing the federal response, said the seepage spots identified by remote underwater cameras as "flares" of oil rising from the seabed may in fact be long-standing natural oil leaks unrelated to the blown-out well that triggered one of the worst environmental disasters in US history. The comments come days after a new series of assessments by BP and environmental monitoring teams indicated that the leaking well is now spilling only around 5,000 to 10,000 barrels of oil per day – significantly lower than the initial, alarmingly high estimates of 210,000 barrels per day. However, while this apparent reduction in flow has been hailed by some as a sign that the capping operation and containment dome have been effective to some degree, the revelation that other oil seepages may be unrelated has sparked fresh questions about the full extent of the impacts of the disaster. Admiral Zukunft stressed that the government is working closely with BP to monitor the area using advanced sonar mapping and data from sea-floor cameras. "We are methodically identifying each flare and determining its source," he said. "Not all of them are associated with the Macondo well. Some are natural seepages that have been happening in the Gulf for decades." Natural oil seepage is not uncommon in the Gulf of Mexico, with petroleum occasionally rising from the ocean floor through existing fissures in the geological strata. These crude leaks are generally understood to have developed over millennia and are considered part of the region’s normal environmental dynamic. However, the fact that a new seep has emerged raises concerns that the recent drilling and the subsequent uncontrolled release of oil have disturbed underground geological structures. Some environmental scientists argue that high-pressure drilling operations can destabilise the seabed, triggering new fault lines or fractures through which oil and gas can escape. The possibility that the Deepwater Horizon leak has created new pathways for oil to flow has been a concern of environmental and regulatory bodies since the initial blow-out. The UK energy regulator Ofgem has issued a stark reminder to energy firms that they have no justification for raising standard tariffs without clear and compelling evidence, as rising costs continue to weigh heavily on consumers. In a recent statement, Ofgem reiterated that energy companies must ensure any price increases are proportionate and fully justified, warning against what it called “irresponsible” and “short-sighted” decision-making at a time when many households are already struggling with inflation and the cost-of-living crisis. This follows a summer in which numerous energy providers have announced or hinted at impending hikes to standard variable tariffs (SVTs), even as the price cap has recently been reduced. The regulator said it expects greater transparency and accountability from companies, and is closely monitoring complaints and data from across the industry to identify any patterns of unjustified increases. “Families and businesses are facing real financial pressure, and they deserve clear and honest communication from their energy suppliers,” said a senior Ofgem spokesperson. “We are committed to ensuring that any changes to energy prices are fair and based on real costs—not profit margins or poor planning.” The warning comes amidst growing public frustration over the fluctuating nature of the energy market and the lack of clarity around the impacts of short-term changes. Many customers still remain on standard tariffs, despite the availability of cheaper fixed-rate deals, and have little choice when their providers decide to raise prices – unless they actively switch. According to recent figures, the number of customers on the cheapest available tariffs in the UK has risen compared to previous years, but experts argue that the market remains dominated by the 'big six' suppliers and weaker competition. Many smaller firms have exited the energy sector amid financial challenges, leaving fewer options for price-sensitive consumers. Ofgem has also called on energy companies to make it easier for customers to compare and switch tariffs, and to ensure all marketing is clear and not misleading. “Tariff changes must be clearly communicated and explained,” the regulator added. “There is simply no excuse for increasing standard tariffs without a thorough assessment of the underlying costs and impacts on customers.” Industry analysts suggest that the message from Ofgem could have significant implications for the sector, particularly as it seeks to rebuild trust with a public already unfairly treated over the past few years. With winter fast approaching and energy usage on the rise, the call for responsible pricing has never been more urgent.

Wales prop Samson Lee has made a surprising personal sacrifice to stay fit and in peak condition ahead of rugby’s showpiece event: he has given up his hobby of ferreting for rabbits. The Ospreys forward, best known on the pitch for his powerful scrummaging and physicality at the set-piece, has put down his rabbits stick and terrier as he gears up for the 2019 Rugby World Cup in Japan. Ferreting, a traditional activity in Lee’s native Wales, involves using terriers to flush out rabbits from their burrows and was a weekend fixture for the 30-year-old. However, as the World Cup countdown intensifies, Lee made the tough decision to prioritise recovery and conditioning over his leisure time. "It’s a bit sad because I love the sport and I’ve been doing it for years," Lee told the Press Association. "But in the world of professional rugby, you’ve got to put performance first. I’m no longer allowed to do it. My trainers have made it clear: no more rabbits." The decision comes as part of a broader fitness plan overseen by Wales’ strength and conditioning coaches, who have placed a strong emphasis on injury prevention and longevity in the squad. Lee has enjoyed a stellar Six Nations campaign this year, starting in every match for Wales as they retained the title with a record win over England – a performance in which he was praised for his work rate and discipline. Having already represented his country in the 2015 World Cup, the Rhyl-born prop is determined to carry his form forward into the next four-year cycle. "I want to be a big part of the World Cup squad," Lee said. "I want to be as ready as I can possibly be. I’ve been doing everything I can in training and at home to ensure I’m not the problem come September." Wales head coach Warren Gatland has not commented directly on Lee’s new fitness regime, but the fly-half has previously stressed the importance of peak physical condition for the gruelling World Cup schedule. The tournament will test every player’s resilience and stamina, with Wales competing in intense matches against groups featuring formidable opponents such as Ireland, France, and possibly reigning world champions New Zealand. With two Six Nations titles under his belt and a World Cup appearance already marked in his career, Lee’s decision to make a small but meaningful lifestyle change reflects the growing professionalism within Wales’ rugby setup.

MPs have called for a “realistic timetable” for the High Speed 2 (HS2) rail project, warning that the current schedule is “overly ambitious” and at risk of falling further behind on both time and budget. In a recent report, the Commons Transport Committee said the government must re-examine the timing of future phases of the controversial £106 billion project if it is to avoid deeper delays and escalated costs. The committee said that while HS2 Phase One, which will connect London to Birmingham, is due for completion in 2027, extensions to Manchester (Phase Twoa) and Leeds (Phase Twob) are already facing uncertainty. Phase Twob is now not expected to open until the late 2030s at the earliest, a delay of more than a decade from the original timeline. The report highlighted the increasing risks of further delays, and said the government has not done enough to address the underlying issues affecting the project’s delivery. “The current schedule for HS2’s later phases appears overly optimistic and not built on the robust evidence we expect of large-scale infrastructure projects,” the committee warned. Committee chair Julian Sturdy said the government should take “a harder look at the assumptions that drive the projected delivery schedule to ensure it is based on realistic possibilities.” The MPs also raised concerns about the financial accountability of both the Department for Transport and HS2 Ltd, the company responsible for delivering the project. They called for more transparent reporting of costs and progress, and urged the appointment of a non-executive director with relevant infrastructure experience to the board of HS2 Ltd. The committee added that the government must not treat HS2 as a project that can operate without close parliamentary oversight. HS2 has been plagued by difficulties since its inception under the previous coalition government in 2010. The original cost estimate of £33 billion has more than tripled, and the project has faced fierce opposition from local communities, environmental groups and even some members of the government. The most recent cost update for the full development of HS2 stands at £106.2 billion, a figure which continues to rise as construction struggles with supply chain disruptions, environmental concerns and planning disputes. In response to the report, a government spokesperson said: “HS2 remains a vital piece of infrastructure to connect our great cities, creating thousands of jobs and boosting the economy by helping people and businesses travel faster.

Could the UK's Italian expats hold the key to their homeland's future?   Every day, as the morning sun rises over London’s bustling streets, thousands of Italian expatriates begin their routines—heading to offices in the financial district, teaching at local universities or running the family-run trattorias that dot towns across England. But as Italy faces an uncertain political and economic future, an increasing number of experts are suggesting that this community of around 350,000 Italians in the UK may play a crucial but often overlooked role in shaping their homeland’s destiny. From Leeds to London and Bristol to Belfast, Italian Britons have made a lasting impact on the UK, blending their culture, language, and entrepreneurial spirit into the very fabric of British society. But as the Italian economy struggles with high youth unemployment, mass emigration, and a shrinking population, the emotional ties these expatriates still maintain with the Bel Paese are being viewed by some as a potential lifeline. Dr. Elena Conti, a sociologist at the University of Manchester, has spent years studying the Italian diaspora’s influence. “We’re not just talking about money—although remittances are a factor—this is about ideas, culture and a strong network that spans both countries,” she explained. “Italians in the UK are often educated, aspirational, and have access to resources and perspectives that they can bring back.” The Italian government, under pressure to modernise the country and reverse the brain drain, has recently started to consider initiatives to better engage its expatriate community. One such idea is the introduction of a “passport to participation,” which would allow Italians living abroad to vote in referendums and local elections. Others are calling for more flexible repatriation policies, such as tax breaks for those returning to open businesses or develop skills in areas such as green energy and digital technology—sectors where Italy lags behind many of its European peers. London-born Anna Moretti, who runs a successful design company in Kensington and was born to Italian parents, told  The London Times : “I feel a huge sense of responsibility. I love the UK, but I also miss the country I was raised in. Italy needs people who are confident, educated and not afraid to challenge the status quo. If we do nothing, the next generations may be lost.” The idea of a “returning expat” go-to hub has also started to gain traction among Italian policy circles, with calls to create digital platforms that link professionals in the UK with opportunities in Italy.

The long-awaited Queen’s Speech has drawn widespread approval from across the criminal justice sector, with its promising announcement of new powers designed to give certain prisons the autonomy to shape their own rules, budgets and rehabilitation strategies. The proposals, outlined as a key part of the government’s commitment to reducing reoffending rates and tackling overcrowding, mark a significant shift in the approach to prison management in England and Wales. Under the new measures, select prisons will be given the freedom to determine how they allocate their budgets and implement rehabilitation programmes, with a greater degree of local discretion in decision-making. This marks a notable departure from the standardised model that has governed the prison system for decades, enabling governors and senior staff to tailor interventions to the specific needs and dynamics of their inmate populations. The reforms come at a time when the Prison Service is facing mounting criticism over failing to rehabilitate offenders and the increasing cost of incarceration. Despite the optimism surrounding the plan, some officials in the Ministry of Justice cautioned that the change would occur gradually, with only a small number of prisons in each region being granted the new powers in the coming year. “We want to encourage innovation and best practice at the frontline of the system,” said a government spokesperson. “These new powers will allow governors to make decisions that best suit their prisons and, ultimately, improve outcomes for prisoners and the public.” The announcement has been welcomed by prison reform charities and some senior prison staff, who argue that local authorities are best placed to respond to the unique challenges of their facilities. “Prisons have long been constrained by one-size-fits-all policies, which don’t always work in complex and often traumatic environments,” said Emma Frid, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust. “These powers will empower governors to think creatively and be more responsive to the needs of both staff and prisoners.” However, concerns remain about how the new flexibility will be implemented without the necessary safeguards to prevent poor practice or inequality between prisons. Some are also urging that the government provides sufficient support and resources for those piloting the reforms. Meanwhile, the response from senior prison officials has been cautiously optimistic. One senior governor, who wished to remain unnamed, said the initiative could lead to a “more human and effective” approach to managing prisons, provided that funds and training are sustained.

New rules that could severely limit the power of individuals and environmental groups to challenge government decisions on major infrastructure projects have come into force in England and Wales. The changes, introduced under the Environment Act 2021, require claimants to demonstrate that they have “a qualifying interest” before they can bring a judicial review in environmental cases. Campaigners say the move creates a high legal barrier for ordinary citizens and NGOs who have traditionally used the courts to challenge developments that threaten communities, wildlife or the climate. Critics argue that the changes are being used by the government to shield itself from legal action, particularly on projects that are deemed to be in the national interest — such as new roads, pipelines, or airports. Under the rules, the courts will only consider a case if the applicant has a direct interest in the outcome. For instance, a resident living close to a proposed waste site or a local organisation directly affected by a development might qualify. But in many environmental cases, the impacts are diffuse, and those most affected may lack the resources or legal standing to mount a challenge. The government says the new rules are not meant to restrict legal access but to ensure that judicial review is used responsibly and not misused for ideological or political purposes. A Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) spokesperson said: “The rules are standard across all areas of public law and help ensure that only legitimate claims are brought before the courts.” However, environmental lawyers and NGOs have expressed alarm at the implications of the ruling. “This is a significant shift that could severely hinder the ability of the public and civil society to hold the government and developers to account,” said Emma Howard, senior legal officer at Friends of the Earth. “Environmental law is often the last line of defence against reckless development and climate destruction.” The issue has come under scrutiny about high-profile developments such as the proposed third runway at Heathrow and the expansion of HS2. In both cases, environmental groups have used judicial review to argue that the government has failed to properly assess the environmental impact of the projects. With the new rules in place, activists fear that future challenges will be dismissed on technical grounds before scientists and communities can even present their evidence. The changes have also been highlighted as part of a broader trend of what some describe as the 'legal quietening' of dissent.

The United States remains the largest single donor of overseas aid in the world, despite ongoing political debates surrounding the value and purpose of such funding. According to the most recent data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the US is by far the largest bilateral donor, outpacing traditional European aid leaders such as Germany, the United Kingdom and France. In 2023, the Trump administration announced a record $165 billion in international aid, with provisions aimed at addressing human rights, poverty, climate change, and global health as part of a larger commitment to American foreign policy. The figure considerably outstrips the OECD’s definition of the 0.7 per cent target—where a country pledges to allocate at least 0.7 per cent of its gross national income (GNI) to aid—despite the US only contributing less than half a percentage of its GNI towards development assistance. Critics argue that the US often prioritises aid linked to military and geopolitical interests, rather than humanitarian need or long-term sustainable development. This approach has led to accusations of “neocolonialism” and a lack of transparency in how aid is distributed, particularly in conflict-affected regions. On the other hand, supporters of American aid shipments credit them with saving millions of lives in times of crisis—highlighting efforts in humanitarian relief, from the Ebola outbreak in West Africa to food insecurity in Yemen and, more recently, natural disaster support in Ukraine. The US Department of State and USAID have also been instrumental in global vaccine rollout efforts during the pandemic, including the COVAX scheme. However, the amount given often varies wildly with each administration, exposing the aid programme’s deep connection to internal political agendas. In contrast to many Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) nations, about half of which meet or exceed the 0.7 per cent GNI target for development assistance, the US continues to be the world’s largest donor while not adhering to this benchmark. The US’s role as the world’s top donor generates much controversy, with ongoing questions over where aid effectiveness ends and political influence begins. As the Biden administration revisits and reallocates foreign aid budgets—including an increased emphasis on climate funding and assistance to countries facing vaccine insecurity—the debate over how and to what end the US should be giving aid continues to be a polarising issue in Congress and the wider public discourse.

Falkirk maintained their position in third place in the Scottish Championship despite a frustrating 0-0 draw with Queen of the South at the Falkirk Stadium on Saturday. The result saw the Bairns fail to capitalise on Hearts’ win over Dunfermline, which left the gap at the summit unchanged at seven points. With Raith Rovers and Ross County triumphing on the same day, Falkirk remain just three points behind Hibs in second place, though a game behind the Edinburgh side. Manager Peter Houston, who took charge earlier in the season to stabilise the team, has guided Falkirk through a campaign marked by inconsistency but underpinned by a strong defensive record. The recent run of results, however, has seen them slip behind both Hearts and Hibernian, who are now vying for the automatic promotion spot. Ten-man Hearts made history on Saturday by becoming the first club to reach 100 points in a top-tier Scottish league campaign, while Hibs remain in prime position thanks to their 2-1 win at Easter Road. Saturday’s stalemate, however, showed both the resilience and the limitations of Falkirk’s current squad. Despite dominating possession and creating several chances, particularly in the first half, the hosts were unable to breakthrough a stubborn Queen of the South side. Falkirk’s best opportunity came in the 22nd minute when a curling cross into the box was not properly cleared, but the follow-up effort was blocked by visiting defender Declan McManus. Earlier in the week, Falkirk had beaten Berwick Rangers 3-0, with full-back John Baird netting a brace, but Saturday’s result left fans hoping for a finish to the season with a more commanding position. Queen of the South, positioned mid-table, remain in contention for a European qualification place and will be encouraged by the solidity of their defensive display. Manager Ally McCoist has often spoken of his desire to ensure the team finish the campaign on a positive note, and this result gives them just that. Despite their ability to cause problems for top-half teams, they will need to show more consistency if they are to secure a European spot. Falkirk’s next game is at home to Dumbarton, whose relegation from the Championship to League One was confirmed earlier in the week. Victory in that match could see the Bairns close the gap on their nearest rivals in the race for second place, though parity among the chasing pack means every point will be crucial in the final stretch.

A Northern Harmony: Estonia’s Cultural Ties Extend Beyond the Baltic Sea   Nestled between the vast expanse of the Baltic Sea and the forests of Eastern Europe, Estonia stands as the most northerly of the Baltic states, and is often described as a European country like no other. While it shares its region with Latvia and Lithuania, Estonia is unique in more than just geography — its language and culture set it apart as a nation with a distinctly Finnish soul. Estonian, one of the Finno-Ugric languages, mirrors Finnish in both structure and vocabulary, and the ties between the two countries run deep. The closest border between Estonia and Finland is just 60 nautical miles across the Gulf of Finland, and the connection between the two nations has been shaped by shared history, culture, and even folklore. It is not uncommon to see Estonian residents in major towns and cities who are multilingual in both Finnish and English, while Finland remains one of Estonia's most popular tourist destinations and a key source of investment. This linguistic bond has long positioned Estonia as a bridge between the Nordic countries and the rest of the Baltic region. During the Soviet era, the subtle cultural and linguistic links with Finland were maintained in coded ways — through folklore, literature and, famously, in music. Many Estonians draw strength from the notion that their heritage is unique, reinforcing national identity in the face of external pressures. Estonia became a member of the European Union in 2004, and later joined the Schengen Area in 2011 — a move that has deepened its integration with Europe and brought it closer to its Nordic neighbours. Tallinn, the capital, is now a hub for tech innovation and start-ups, drawing comparisons with Silicon Valley but with a distinctly Scandi aesthetic and charm. Its medieval architecture, smart technology solutions, and the warmth of its people provide a unique blend of old and new. The frosty northern climate and the long, dark winters may evoke the image of a remote European backwater, but for Estonia, it is a place of pride. Its geographical position is a strength, not a limitation. As the world focuses on regionalism and global cooperation, Estonia’s location and cultural affinity with Finland exemplify how small countries can play a significant role on the world stage — not by loudly asserting their presence, but by quietly and skillfully building their identity through culture, language, and innovation.

Old man found with crucifix shot dead by California police, sparking new wave of anger over use of force   A 73-year-old man with dementia has been killed by police in Merced, California, after officers opened fire following a report that he may have been carrying a gun. When officers arrived at the scene, they shot and killed Roy Cockroft, who was found to be holding a wooden crucifix instead of a weapon — a discovery that has now sparked outrage and deepening questions about the routine use of lethal force by law enforcement in the United States. Cockroft, who lived alone in a mobile home, had a long history of mental health issues and dementia, family members and local activists said. On the night of the incident, 911 operators received a call reporting that an eccentric man with a known history of behaving unpredictively had appeared in public, possibly carrying a firearm. A 911 caller was quoted as saying: “He doesn’t have a gun — he just carries a cross — but he’s not normal. Go carefully.” Despite this, responding officers confronted the man outside his home, where he was holding the crucifix, and fired seven shots, killing him. After the shooting, police said Cockroft had reached for a deadly object as he moved toward them, though no weapon was ever recovered from the scene. The incident has already triggered protests in Merced, with local civil rights groups condemning what they are calling a “routine senseless killing.” Videos and phone images of the scene, though not widely published for public safety reasons, appear to show the man being shot outdoors while not resisting officers, and not holding a gun at any point. “My uncle is a kind, peaceful man. He didn’t come at the officers with anything but a cross,” said a relative who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitive nature of the case. “He didn’t deserve this. No one does.” The Merced Police Department is now under investigation by both the California Department of Justice and the Merced County District Attorney. In a brief statement released on Monday, the department said a full internal affairs probe had begun, but offered no immediate assurances about whether officers who fired would face disciplinary action. This case adds to a growing list of incidents in the U.S. in which elderly and disabled individuals, particularly those with mental health conditions, have been shot and killed by police over concerns about potentially life-threatening objects or perceived threats.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a previously undisclosed conversation at a private dinner of world leaders in Germany earlier this month, according to multiple U.S. officials and European diplomats. The informal discussion, which took place during a G7 leaders' retreat in Taunus, has sparked fresh concern about the nature of Trump’s relationship with the Kremlin, as well as raised questions about transparency within the White House. The meeting reportedly occurred on June 8, during which Trump and Putin were said to have spoken for a number of minutes while other leaders were briefly absent from the table. Officials confirmed that the conversation was not part of the official G7 agenda and was not documented in publicly available records. This has prompted calls for greater clarity from both the White House and the G7 host, German Chancellor Angela Merkel. A senior U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, stated: “President Trump spoke privately with President Putin in the presence of other leaders. This was a brief and informal conversation.” When asked for details on the discussion’s content, the official declined to provide further information. The revelation follows a string of escalations in U.S.-Russia relations, particularly in the wake of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and the ongoing investigations by Special Counsel Robert Mueller into Russian influence during that election. The situation has also been further complicated by the recent barring of Russian diplomats from the U.S. under sanctions related to the poisoning of a former Russian spy and his daughter in the U.K. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, when informed of the report, did not confirm or deny the meeting but reiterated the administration’s focus on fostering a “positive and productive relationship with our allies.” However, lawmakers from both parties have expressed alarm at what they are calling another undisclosed Trump-Russia encounter. Democratic Representative Adam Schiff, the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said: “We have seen time and again that when the administration is not forthcoming about these meetings, the American public is left in the dark. There must be greater transparency about all contacts and conversations with foreign leaders.” The G7 summit, hosted by Germany, ended on June 9 with a final statement that notably omitted any mention of Russia’s controversial actions in Crimea or the conflict in eastern Ukraine. This has been interpreted by some analysts as a sign of Trump’s influence on U.S. foreign policy negotiations with its closest allies.

You have to feel the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) pain — especially if you’re trying to get any real clarity on Britain’s economic future. The independent body, tasked with assessing public finances and acting as the UK’s financial watchdog, finds itself in a position not seen since the early days of its creation in 2010: trapped between a Prime Minister demanding optimistic forecasts and an economy that simply refuses to deliver them. Downing Street has long had a problematic relationship with the OBR, which was set up to provide independent, data-driven analysis as a check on the Treasury. But under the current political landscape, the gap between political expectations and the financial reality is growing ever wider. A recent update from the OBR, reflecting another year of subpar growth and surging inflation, has placed the Chancellor in an unenviable position, forced to warn against rising borrowing and push for fiscal discipline — even as the Prime Minister continues to pledge a strategy of growth through breakfasts with entrepreneurs and “confidence-inspiring” rhetoric. The OBR finds itself at the heart of this maelstrom, its credibility under pressure from all sides. Month after month, its forecasts tell the same story: public finances are deteriorating faster than expected, tax as a proportion of GDP is trending higher, and economic momentum is weak. Yet the government refuses to align with the message. The most recent fiscal statement highlighted a significant shortfall in expected revenues, with the OBR noting that the Treasury is set to miss its borrowing target for the first time since the financial crisis. For an institution that is proud of its independence — and which has survived two major crises unscathed — the current situation must feel exasperating. The OBR’s role is to expose politicians when their numbers don’t add up, not to make them palatable. But with the economy performing below expectations, and the government refusing to acknowledge it outright, what choice does the OBR have but to highlight the worrying numbers, unvarnished and uncomfortable? The result for the public is confusion. Are things getting better or worse? Is the economic recovery on track or a distant mirage? The government says one thing, the Chancellor says another, and the OBR quietly lays out a third version of events — all with no consensus in sight. The OBR may not be a household name like the IMF or the Bank of England, but it is one of the most vital institutions in British public life.

The Shard, western Europe’s tallest building, has opened its observation deck to the public, offering breathtaking panoramic views of London’s skyline. Situated on the 72nd floor, more than 300 metres above ground level, the venue promises visitors an unrivalled vantage point of the capital, with the River Thames, St Paul’s Cathedral, and the Houses of Parliament all visible on a clear day. The observation deck officially opened its doors to the public earlier this week, drawing large crowds eager to experience the building’s dizzying height and sweeping vistas. Visitors can access the deck via the Shard’s high-speed elevators, which ascend at over 20 miles per hour, offering a smooth and swift journey to the top of the 95-storey glass spire, which was completed in 2012. Once there, they are greeted by floor-to-ceiling windows that provide 360-degree views of London’s landmarks and sprawling suburbs. The project, spearheaded by British developer Brian Johnson and designed by renowned architect Renzo Piano, is part of a broader £2 billion development in the London Bridge area, which has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. The Shard has long been a symbol of modern London, with its elegant tapering silhouette and mirrored glass design making it one of the city's most striking landmarks. The decision to open the public to its upper levels has been hailed as a way to bring even more of the building’s architectural grandeur to life. Visitors can also enjoy a curated exhibition on the building’s design and construction, as well as themed events and skyline cocktail experiences. According to a spokesperson for the Shard, the observation deck is open from 9 am to 10 pm and will remain so throughout the year, with special night-time lighting displays planned to mark key occasions. Given the anticipation surrounding the opening, ticket sales have already outpaced initial projections, and the venue is expected to become one of the city’s most popular tourist attractions. The Shard, which has hosted the world’s top restaurants and luxury hotels, now adds the experiences of a scenic getaway to its credentials, as it becomes a new highpoint for Londoners and visitors alike who are eager to experience the city from above. Websites and booking agents have begun to add the deck to "must-do" lists, as London continues to cement its status as a global tourism hub with an ever-expanding array of world-class attractions.

Northern Ireland's health system is facing a growing crisis in mental health care, with none of its five health trusts currently meeting waiting time targets for non-emergency mental health treatments. Patients suffering from common conditions such as anxiety and depression are experiencing long wait times, raising concerns among healthcare professionals, advocates, and frightened families. The issue has emerged as one of the most pressing challenges for the Department of Health, as recent data reveals that every trust in Northern Ireland is missing its Aneurin Bevan Waiting Time Standard, which requires that patients are seen by a specialist within 18 weeks. The standard, set under the previous Welsh Assembly but still used as a benchmark in the UK health sector, has become a critical measure of access to mental health services across the country. Public Health Minister Simon Hamilton has acknowledged the problem, expressing concern over the lack of progress in reducing waiting times for mental health patients, despite repeated pledges to address the growing backlog. "Mental health is an essential part of our health priorities," he said this week. "We are in discussion with the trusts to identify solutions and ensure that people who need support are not left waiting for help." Healthcare workers on the front line have spoken of the stress and strain imposed by inadequate staffing, limited resources, and the high demand for services, particularly as mental health demand has surged in the wake of the pandemic. According to NHS staffing data, mental health nurse vacancies in Northern Ireland remain unacceptably high, with some trusts reporting a vacancy rate of over 30%. Jayne Twinn, Chief Nursing Officer at the Department of Health, emphasized the need for improvements in both recruitment and retention: "We are facing significant challenges in filling vacant posts, and this has directly impacted our ability to meet the waiting time targets," she said. "We are working closely with trusts and NHS trusts across the UK to address these staffing issues and ensure that patients receive timely and effective care." Mental health campaign groups are calling for urgent government action. Mary White, Director of the Northern Ireland branch of Mind, warned that delays in treatment can exacerbate conditions and prevent people from leading fulfilling lives. "The longer someone waits for specialist support, the more their condition can deteriorate," she said. "Mental health conditions should not be treated as a 'last resort' but as an urgent and vital public health issue that deserves priority."

In a brazen act of wildlife theft, 101 Chinese box turtles were stolen from a temporary shelter in Kenting National Park in southern Taiwan during the quiet hours of the night. The incident, discovered by park staff early this morning, is believed to be the largest reported theft of the critically endangered species in recent years and has sparked alarm among conservationists and local authorities. The turtles, part of a conservation programme aimed at rehabilitating animals rescued from illegal wildlife trade, were housed in the shelter under 24-hour watch. The facility was secured with cameras and alarm systems; however, the thieves managed to bypass these precautions, leaving behind signs of forced entry and removing the animals with apparent ease. Police are currently investigating whether the theft was an inside job or carried out by well-organised poachers with inside knowledge of the shelter’s operations. Chinese box turtles – known for their hinged plastron which allows the shell to close tightly around the body – are among the most popular species in the illegal pet trade due to their unique appearance and hardiness. They are also considered a delicacy in some Asian countries and are highly valued in traditional medicine, which has severely driven down their numbers. Taiwan’s Wild Animal Conservation Act classifies the species as “fully protected,” and the penalties for trafficking such animals are severe, including lengthy prison sentences and heavy fines. Despite these measures, demand remains – particularly in mainland China and Vietnam, where trafficking routes are well established. Some local officials speculate that the stolen turtles were already tagged for transport, either through land borders or by sea, to be sold in underground markets at inflated prices. Conservationists have expressed deep concern over the theft, not only because of the loss of animals but also the impact on the park’s rehabilitation programme. Kenting National Park, a biodiverse and ecologically rich area in southern Taiwan, has been at the forefront of wildlife rescue and education for years. “This is a direct attack on conservation,” said Dr. Lin Mei-hui, a wildlife protection officer for the park. “We’re not just losing turtles – we’re losing progress in the fight to save an endangered species.” The park authorities have stepped up security and are working closely with the Taiwan Forestry Bureau and Interpol to monitor regional-trafficking patterns. Local wildlife detectives are also reviewing traffic surveillance and recent movement of vehicles in and out of the national park in the days leading up to the theft.

The pound has retreated to near 31-year lows against the US dollar and the euro after initial gains in the wake of a broader global markets rebound failed to hold. As of today, the British currency fell by 0.4% to $1.32 and 0.9% to €1.11 — hovering perilously close to levels last seen in the mid-1990s. The drop has been attributed to a fragile economic outlook, lingering policy uncertainty in the wake of the Brexit transition, and ongoing pressure from global markets as inflation and interest rate fears remain high. Sterling had briefly rallied earlier in the week following signs of stabilisation on Wall Street and European stock markets, fuelled by tentative optimism around supply chain resolution and hopes for a softer landing in the US economy. Investors also appeared to reflect on the UK government’s recent announcement of sweeping tax cuts, which sent bond yields soaring and raised concerns among many in the financial sector about the long-term stability of public finances. However, the Anglo-Saxon rout in morning trade saw the pound quickly lose these early gains, as traders remain unconvinced that Britain is heading for a recovery anytime soon. "The recent tax cuts and fiscal easing have not given the Sterling any sustainable momentum to push back against the dollar, especially as we continue to face domestic inflationary pressures and weak data from services and construction," said Davidborough Baptiste, senior currency analyst at Horwath FX. Economists are growing increasingly wary of the UK’s structural economic issues, with the Bank of England having raised interest rates 11 times in just over a year in a race against stubborn inflation. At the same time, the UK's recovery from the pandemic has been weaker than in comparator economies and Brexit-related trade frictions continue to weigh on investor confidence. "It’s not just about today’s numbers — it's the litany of uncertainty that persists from a combination of fiscal mismanagement, lack of agreement on the energy transition, and a fragmented domestic political scene," Baptiste added. The pound’s performance has also been exacerbated by the ongoing crisis at the UK’s financial debt ceiling, which raised concerns last week about the government’s ability to meet its obligations without an agreement with the opposition. Though the immediate danger has passed, the volatility surrounding the Autumn Statement and related policy measures is expected to keep markets on edge for the foreseeable future.

British businessman and former BBC chairman Sir Christopher Bland has died at the age of 78. A towering figure in public life and a fervent advocate for broadcasting excellence, Bland will be remembered for his distinctive voice, his unflinching integrity, and his commitment to the highest standards of journalism and public service. Deputies in-house and outsiders alike praised his formidable intellect and his ability to command a room with both eloquence and wit. Lord Hall, the current BBC director general, described Bland as “a man of principle, a champion of free speech and a deeply respected public servant.” tributes from across the media world highlighted how Bland’s influence extended far beyond the BBC, shaping the broader landscape of British broadcasting and public debate. Bland took over as chairman of the BBC in 1992 during a period of intense turbulence, following the infamous Newsnight affair, which had led to the resignation of then-director general Michael Checkland. He quickly became a steadying presence, working to restore confidence in the organisation and promoting a culture of accountability and objectivity that remains central to the BBC's ethos today. Under his leadership, the corporation was able to move beyond the crisis, and he was widely credited with saving the organisation. Even before his time at the BBC, Bland had already carved out a successful career in journalism and business. As the editor of The Tablet – a Catholic weekly publication – he helped establish its reputation for serious political and cultural commentary. His move into the world of business and commerce followed a natural trajectory, and he became a respected figure in the City, someone who could bridge the gap between media and finance with ease and authority. Bland was also known for his long and loyal service in the world of politics through his role as a Conservative peer in the House of Lords. Always measured in his opinions, but never afraid to speak the truth, he was a thorn in the side of complacency and mediocre governance. His crossbench independence allowed him to play a critical role in numerous parliamentary committees and inquiries, always advocating for greater transparency and public trust. As news of his death spreads, tributes are pouring in not only from within the BBC and the media world but also from across the political spectrum. His legacy is one of integrity, leadership, and an unwavering belief in the public good.

The police call centre tasked with handling the 999 emergency raised by a passerby who spotted a car crumpled in a ditch off the M9 has come under scrutiny today, after it emerged that staff were missing from their posts at a 10% absence rate the month before the tragic crash. The incident, which led to the deaths of Dinah McNicol and her four-year-old daughter Rachel, has already raised serious questions about the emergency response, and these latest details serve to compound concerns about the efficiency and staffing levels of Lanarkshire's local control room at the time. According to recent Freedom of Information requests reviewed by The Guardian Scotland, the control unit at Castle House handled over 40,000 calls in August 2018 — the month before the crash — with an average of 18 officers working each shift. However, during this period, absence rates in the department reached up to 10%, meaning at any one time, as many as two posts may have been unfilled. The crash itself occurred on the evening of 24 September 2018, when a family of four were taking a routine drive home, only for the car to veer off the motorway into a shallow ditch and ignite in a fire deadly enough to leave no survivors. The passerby, who saw the car from the central reserve, rang the 999 number at 5.29pm and claimed to the call centre staff that the vehicle “was burning and people were inside.” However, emergency services did not arrive at the scene until approximately forty-three minutes later, by which point the car had already been consumed by flames.
