The holder of the 999 call at the time was later replying: “I don’t know how we didn’t get there quicker,” while a control room representative from the nearby Strathclyde police headquarters said they were “gradually uncovering the truth” behind the delayed response. MSPs and local residents have already called for an independent review of the incident and are now insisting that the findings into staffing levels further underline a potentially flawed system. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, who recently ordered a full investigation into the response, has stated that safety of the public is paramount and that no effort must be spared to understand why such an avoidable tragedy took place. The deaths of Dinah and Rachel remain imprinted in the national consciousness — their names frequently recalled at vigils and charitable events — as the inquiry into that fateful September evening continues to unfold.

Power cuts and flooding linked to a series of severe winter storms have continued to disrupt lives across England, with some residents possibly without electricity until the end of the week. Over Christmas, thousands of homes were plunged into darkness as heavy rainfall and strong winds battered the UK, culminating in the flooding of as many as 1,000 homes and widespread disruption to energy services. Energy companies are struggling to restore full power amid challenging weather conditions that have hampered repair efforts and left engineers working in difficult and sometimes dangerous environments. In parts of the south-west, where the damage has been particularly acute, crews have been assessing the scale of the destruction caused by fallen trees, submerged transformers, and collapsed infrastructure. Network operators have warned that while the majority of customers could expect to have power restored within a few days, some properties may remain without electricity until later in the week. The Environment Agency has issued multiple flood warnings, particularly in the counties of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset and Somerset, where homes, roads and businesses were heavily impacted. Local authorities have reported isolated cases of people being evacuated as rising waters forced emergency services into action. One resident in Exeter, whose home was inundated with over 20cm of water, described the impact of the flooding as “devastating and entirely unexpected, especially during the holidays.” The country’s energy regulator, Ofgem, has urged patience from affected customers but has also pressed energy companies to prioritise repairs and improve communication with communities. The storms come as the UK braces for the first of what could be several severe winters following the record-breaking rainfall in 2023. With the climate emergency intensifying, experts have warned that such extreme weather events are likely to become more commonplace in the coming years. The government has been called upon to reassess infrastructure resilience and boost flood defences to protect vulnerable areas. Meanwhile, aid services and local councils have set up temporary shelters and provided food parcels to those displaced by the floods. Some communities have shown incredible solidarity, with neighbours helping each other clear wet debris and waters. As the nation continues to weather the storm, the effectiveness of the response is being scrutinised. Prime Minister Keir Starmer has pledged support for all affected households, while admitting that the scale of the disruption has highlighted the urgent need for long-term investment in the UK’s energy and environmental defences.

Two men accused of helping a US tourist hunt and kill a famous Zimbabwean lion have been released on bail, marking a brief but significant development in the case that has sparked international outrage. The lion, a well-known individual named Cecil, was shot dead by American dentist Walter Palmer in Hwange National Park, Zimbabwe’s biggest wildlife sanctuary, during a controversial hunt in July 2015. Video footage of the killing shared on social media quickly went viral, inciting fierce global condemnation and calls for legal action against those involved. According to reports, local guides Christopher Newton and Theo Bronkhorst, both arrested in the days following the incident, have now been freed on bail pending further legal proceedings. The two men are accused of unlawfully assisting Mr. Palmer in the hunt, which was allegedly carried out outside the boundaries of the official hunting permit. Zimbabwean authorities have stated that the case is still under investigation to determine if other parties were involved, including wildlife officials, and whether any laws were breached. The Hwange operations manager at the time, Dr. Charles Bwehenga, remains under scrutiny, though no criminal charges have yet been filed against him. The hunting permit system in Zimbabwe has been a point of contention both locally and internationally. The country, like many in Southern Africa, maintains a policy of controlled trophy hunting, from which national parks derive much-needed revenue. However, the killing of a known, named animal like Cecil — estimated to be around 13 years old and regarded as a breeding adult — has reignited debates about the ethics of such hunting practices. Cecil’s death not only sparked a rush of global protests and a backlash against the trophy-hunting industry but also prompted influential figures and organisations to reconsider their support for such activities. Prominent celebrities and conservationists joined calls to ban the trade in the remains of hunted animals, leading to changes in policies by airlines and auction houses that had previously facilitated the transport and sale of trophies. Many have claimed that the case exposed the vulnerabilities within Zimbabwe’s wildlife management system, with critics arguing that the involvement of local guides suggests widespread corruption and lax enforcement of hunting regulations. Others, including some within the conservation sector, have warned that such high-profile cases could affect the funding of conservation efforts, ultimately impacting the long-term survival of wildlife. As Christopher Newton and Theo Bronkhorst await the next legal proceedings, the case continues to loom large over the global conversation on conservation, trophy hunting, and the balance between environmental protection and local economic interests.

Parents face hurdles in accessing nurseries as eligibility gaps widen, report reveals   A significant number of parents across the UK are finding it difficult to access the childcare they are legally entitled to, according to a new report by the campaign group Childcare Choices. The study, published this week, highlights what it describes as a "complex and confusing" system, which leaves many families struggling to use the government’s childcare support schemes. The report reveals that most parents with eligible children are unaware of provisions in their area and are forced to search for information independently rather than receiving clear guidance. For some, the process of accessing funding or free hours is so convoluted that they decide not to apply at all, despite fulfilling the criteria. The 30 Hours Free Childcare Offer and Tax-Free Childcare are among the schemes being underutilised. Both are designed to alleviate the cost of early years education and support working parents in the UK. But the report finds that confusion over eligibility, discrepancies between local authority portals and national guidelines, and a lack of communication in hard-pressed social environments are creating obstacles that many families cannot overcome. The study looked at responses from over 1,000 parents, and of those, more than 25% reported difficulty in accessing childcare services despite supplying the correct information. Many cited a lack of nursery places, especially in urban areas, as a key issue. Others – particularly those from lower-income households, and/or families with mixed migration statuses – said they were not given accurate information by local authorities about their entitlements. Childcare Choices director, Sarah Dunbar, said the findings were "an alarming reminder that while the government may have good policies on paper, the implementation on the ground is failing families across the country." She added: “This is not just a financial issue – it affects parents’ ability to return to work, contribute to the economy, and take care of their mental and physical wellbeing.” The campaign group is calling for a national review of the eligibility process and for local councils to improve transparency and simplify the application process. They also suggest a centralised online portal where families can access uniform information regardless of their location. The government has responded, stating that it recognises the importance of good early childhood education and is doing all it can to expand availability. A spokesperson said: “We have invested over £5 billion in early years education in this parliament and will continue to prioritise making childcare more affordable for working families.”

The search for ripples in the fabric of spacetime is making rapid progress, with the Advanced LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) system now described as operating at an "amazing speed" by scientists involved in the groundbreaking project. The state-of-the-art instrument, designed to detect the faintest gravitational waves produced by cataclysmic cosmic events, has recently passed a major milestone in sensitivity and detection capability, promising a new era in astrophysical discovery. Advanced LIGO, which became fully operational in 2015, consists of two detectors located in Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana. These detectors use laser beams bounced between suspended mirrors to measure impossibly tiny distortions caused by gravitational waves—distortions so minuscule they are equivalent to a fraction of the width of a proton over a distance of several miles. It was this very technology that detected the first gravitational waves in September 2015, confirming a key prediction of Albert Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity in his 1915 formulation. According to scientists at the LIGO collaboration, the current observing run has dramatically increased the frequency and accuracy of detections. In just a few months, the instrument has detected a number of gravitational wave events, including mergers of black holes and neutron stars, at a pace far beyond expectations from just a year ago. This surge in detections has prompted experts to speak of an “observational revolution,” with the promise of uncovering new physics and deepening our understanding of the universe. Dr. Rana Adhikari, a leading researcher at Caltech and member of the LIGO collaboration, described the progress as “a paradigm shift in how we study the cosmos.” She added: “Advanced LIGO is now delivering results at a rate we did not expect to achieve for years. This is not just incremental science—it is rewriting the rules.” The rapid progress is attributed to extensive upgrades and ongoing improvements to the detectors, including noise-reduction technologies, enhanced laser power, and better mirror coatings. Plans are already in place to further refine the instruments as part of the planned “A+” upgrade, which will increase sensitivity even further, potentially allowing scientists to observe gravitational waves from as far as halfway across the observable universe. In the coming years, the data stream from Advanced LIGO is set to provide unprecedented insights into some of the most extreme phenomena in the universe, including the formation and evolution of black holes, the dynamics of neutron star mergers, and even the earliest moments of the universe itself.

Teenager raped on Glasgow bus as new inquiry launches   A teenage girl has become the victim of a horrific sexual assault by two men on a double decker bus in Glasgow, sparking outrage and prompting renewed calls for greater safety on public transport. The incident, which took place in the city centre at the weekend, is now under investigation by Police Scotland, who have launched a major inquiry to identify and charge those responsible. The assault occurred on a popular route through the city, just before the bus made a routine stop. Sources close to the investigation say that two men allegedly targeted the victim, subjecting her to a terrifying ordeal before fleeing the scene. The girl, who is in her mid-teens, was left with both physical and emotional trauma, and is currently receiving support from specialist officers. Police Scotland confirmed the ongoing investigation on Monday and assured the public that detectives are following a number of leads. "This was an absolutely shocking and unacceptable assault," a spokesperson said. "We are treating this as a high-priority case and are in contact with the victim, her family and witnesses, working to gather all the available evidence. We would urge anyone with information to come forward." Witnesses reported that the attack happened in broad daylight, yet it allegedly went unchallenged for a period of time before onlookers intervened. A local businessman who was nearby told BBC Scotland that the scene was "chaotic" and described hearing the girl scream before seeing the men flee. “It was horrifying,” he said. “You wouldn’t expect something like this to happen in the city centre in broad daylight — especially on a public bus. People are just in shock.” The incident has reignited concerns about safety for women using public transport and has drawn widespread condemnation from politicians and community leaders. Glasgow City Council has called for urgent action from both Transport Scotland and local busing companies to ensure that passengers are better protected. Sue Butler, Glasgow’s Convener for Safety and Communities, said: “This attack is a stark reminder that we must do more to provide women with safe spaces, both on and off public transport. I will be raising this with all the relevant authorities to ensure that steps are taken immediately.” Meanwhile, survivors' support groups have called for the victim to receive full anonymity and protection from the media while the case proceeds.

Daniel Radcliffe eyes Shakespearean stage role but admits he’s no scholar   Harry Potter’s Daniel Radcliffe has revealed his keenness to take on a Shakespearean role in the future, although he quickly admitted that he does not consider himself an expert on the Bard. The 33-year-old actor, best known for playing the iconic wizard during his teenage years, has continued to pursue an eclectic array of roles on stage and screen, from a conman in  The Woman in Black  to a humanised version of Robin Hood. Now he is setting his sights on one of the most prestigious—and challenging—genres in the acting world. Speaking at a recent theatre event, Radcliffe told reporters: “I would love to do something Shakespearean at some point. It’s always been a dream of mine to work on one of his plays. They’re so rich, the characters are so layered, and I think it would be a huge challenge in the best possible way.” However, when pressed on whether he has read all of Shakespeare or taken in every stage production, Radcliffe swiftly clarified that he is not looking to be the next great Shakespearean star off the back of his Hogwarts fame. “I’m not a scholar of the Bard,” he said with a grin. “I’ve seen a few of the plays in live production, and I’ve read a little of them—I’ve studied  Macbeth  in school, I think. So it’s not like I’ve done deep-dive analysis.” Radcliffe’s admission underlines his approachable and self-deprecating sense of humor, which has helped him navigate beyond his most famous role. While some might have worried he would struggle to escape the shadow of Potter, Radcliffe has instead worked hard to establish his own identity in the entertainment world, excelling most notably on the stage. In 2016, he received critical acclaim for his performance as Jonathan Holmes in the West End revival of  How I Learned to Drive , a role that earned him an Olivier Award for Best Performance in a Supporting Role in a Play. His experience in more modern works will likely stand him in good stead for the dramatic demands of Shakespeare, though he acknowledged there is a long way to go before that happens. “I know it’s not something you can just jump into—there’s a reason it’s considered hard,” he said.

India is in the middle of an extraordinary economic experiment — one that has sent shockwaves through its financial system, reshaped public life and forced millions to adapt to a new normal overnight. On November 8, 2016, in an abrupt and unprecedented move, the Indian government declared that the country’s 500 and 1,000-rupee notes — which accounted for 86 per cent of all cash in circulation — would cease to be legal tender. The stated aim of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s decision, which he described as a "surgical strike" against corruption and black money, was to eliminate illicit cash hoards, curb counterfeit currency and make the tax system fairer. But the real-world impact has been far more complex and controversial. With overnight sunset on high denomination notes left only a specific window for banks to return the old money for new, and no immediate replacement of sufficient volume to meet cash demand, the move effectively crippled India’s overwhelmingly cash-dependent economy. At a time when digital transactions in India remain relatively low, the sudden withdrawal of 90 per cent of the currency in circulation plunged businesses and households into chaos. Vending machines and taxis stopped taking cash, crop markets faltered, hospitals turned away patients and credit supplying informal lenders, who normally operated on demand-based cash, also withdrew. The tourism industry from humble hotels to national parks – all barring ones with credit facilities, became virtually crippled, while long queues formed at ATMs and bank counters. What followed was a national debate over the economic and social costs of the so-called “demonetisation” campaign. Critics argue that the government imposed a chaotic and top-down policy without an adequate plan for managing the fallout. Farmers and small traders, who rely heavily on cash transactions, were among the worst hit, and many communities in rural India — where less than 20 per cent of transactions are digital — faced prolonged hardships. The Reserve Bank of India reported that it took until late 2017 for the supply of currency to return to pre-November 2016 levels, by which time many small businesses had collapsed. Policy analysts remain divided over whether the move achieved its objectives. While there was a noticeable drop in the counterfeit currency circulating immediately after the announcement, data on long-term tax compliance and formalisation of the economy tell a mixed story. Meanwhile, the government claims the policy set the stage for a cashless India and spurred a digital revolution.

A Florida officer shot and injured an unarmed black therapist while responding to a request for help from a man with autism, according to local media reports. The incident, which has reignited debate over police use of force, occurred in Lakeland, where the 53-year-old therapist, identified as Marcus Smith, was helping a male client in an apparently non-threatening situation. The event began with the client’s family reporting his distress and possibly self-harming. The therapist, who is known to the family from previous appointments, was with the client when police arrived. Witnesses said the therapist was holding the client’s hand when the situation escalated, but the man made no movement towards the officers or any object that could be mistaken for a weapon. Initial police body camera footage, which has now been released, shows the officer firing after an apparent confrontation. However, the footage has sparked controversy, as the therapist is seen physically intervening in a moment of panic to calm the client, a move described by mental health experts as a standard technique to de-escalate situations in which a person with autism becomes agitated. Reacting to the incident, the Lakeland Police Department said it was taking the matter "very seriously" and is conducting a full investigation. A short statement from the department confirmed that the officer involved was on active duty and is in good health. No further comments were provided, and the department is cooperating with the Florida Bureau of Competitive Intelligence, which handles civil rights investigations. Autism advocacy groups and civil rights leaders voiced their concerns over the shooting. Reverend Brian Kelly from the Florida Justice Coalition, which has led protests against police violence in the state, described the incident as a "devastating example of failed de-escalation and a continued lack of training for officers when encountering people with disabilities.” Sandra Stoltenberg, president of the Florida Council for the Autistic, said the severity of the shooting highlighted a "deep lack of understanding about how people with autism react in stressful situations, and how unprepared many departments are to handle these calls appropriately.” This is the second major police shooting incident involving a Black man in the state in a matter of weeks, and it has added fuel to a national conversation on policing reform. As such, calls for renewed police academies to include specific training on disability awareness and crisis intervention are growing louder, particularly among parents of children on the spectrum.

Young man found guilty of hate crimes in school incitement case   A 19-year-old瑞典 (Swedish) university student, Anton Lundin Pettersson, has been convicted of hate crimes after dressing in provocative, extremist fashion and targeting students with dark skin at the technical university in Luleå, northern Sweden. The incident, which has shocked the academic and wider community, saw Pettersson clad in black combat-style clothing, a swordsman-like sword, and a mask that bore a striking resemblance to Darth Vader, while also wearing a Second World War-era German Nazi helm. Courts in Luleå today sentenced Pettersson to two months of home detention and ordered him to write a formal apology to the victims, who were reportedly left in fear and distress. The sentence also includes a prohibition on approaching the university grounds for a period of two years. Witnesses reported that on the day of the incident, Pettersson was seen parading through the campus corridors, often singled out students of ethnic minority backgrounds and threatening them while uttering racial slurs. His appearance, which included the use of the Nazi helmet, was widely condemned by both officials and members of the public for its overtly far-right connotations and the alarming Nazi symbolism it evoked. The Ministry of Education has since launched an investigation into how such an incident could occur in a space known for its commitment to inclusivity and diversity. University spokespersons expressed deep concern at the incident, describing it as “unacceptable and out of step with our values.” Luleå Technical University, which has a significant international student cohort, has announced new initiatives aimed at reinforcing a culture of respect and combating racism on campus. The case highlights the ongoing challenges faced by educational institutions in maintaining an inclusive environment in the face of rising extremism and lone actor radicalisation. While Petterson's actions appear to represent the views of a small and fringe element, the impact on victims and the university community has left many unsettled. “The most disturbing part was how calmly he moved through the building, as if he had planned it all,” one student told  Göteborgs-Posten . “It felt like something you only see in movies.” Psychologists have weighed in on the incident as well, suggesting that such behaviour can stem from a cocktail of resentment, psychological issues, and exposure to extremist ideologies via the internet. As the sentence is carried out away from the public eye, many are left wondering what more can be done to prevent such incidents in the future.

Scottish politicians are ramping up their campaign efforts this weekend as the countdown to the general election reaches its final five days. Candidates from all major parties are hitting the streets, attending local events and engaging directly with voters in a bid to secure support ahead of polling day on Thursday. With key seats across Scotland — including those in Glasgow, Edinburgh and the north-east — expected to play a crucial role in shaping the outcome of the national vote, candidates are leaving no stone unturned in their final push. From town halls to school gates, leaders of the Conservatives, Labour, the SNP and the Liberal Democrats are striving to connect with voters, outlining their visions for Scotland’s future and, more specifically, how they plan to address pressing issues such as the cost of living crisis, the NHS and the post-Brexit economy. The SNP, currently the largest party in Scotland, is seeking to hold on to its dominance amid widespread speculation that anti-Conservative sentiment could help reduce the Tories to almost no MPs in the region. Ruth Davidson’s returning Conservative slate in Edinburgh and Glasgow, however, is being viewed as a test of both the party’s appeal and the strength of the so-called red wall. Meanwhile, Labour is hoping to reclaim its traditional stronghold in the country by unseating SNP and Conservative candidates, with Keir Starmer pointing to municipal successes as a sign of momentum. The Liberal Democrats, too, are targeting specific marginal seats, with leader Dympna Haynes seeking to attract anti-Unionist and anti-SNP voters under the banner of “Common Sense for Scotland.” For voters, the final days of the campaign are shaping up as a whirlwind of promises, accusations and last-minute persuasion. Some community groups are expressing concern over the lack of engagement with older and more vulnerable members of the public, while others are delighted about the renewed attention to local issues brought by the high-stakes race. The weekend’s campaigning is likely to set the tone for the final days before the polls open, as candidates galvanise their bases and attempt to sway undecided voters. With high stakes and fierce competition, Scotland’s role in the UK general election is once again set to be intense — and potentially pivotal. The question now is whether these last-minute overtures will alter the trajectory of the campaign or merely seal the expectations already in place.

Facebook was the unlikely platform where one of the men who later killed Fusilier Lee Rigby five months prior to the brutal attack first publicly aired his violent rhetoric, the BBC has revealed. In a chilling prelude to the July 2013 murder in Woolwich, the social media giant hosted a post by Michael Adebolajo that appeared to glorify terrorism and Islamism, an incident that has now reignited debate about the responsibilities of online platforms in monitoring extremist content. According to BBC sources, Adebolajo, who was later sentenced to life in prison for his role in the killing, made the post during a time when Facebook's policies on hate speech and incitement were under greater scrutiny but still lacked the sophistication and real-time oversight that critics argue is now essential. The post, which has since been taken down or is no longer visible, reportedly contained graphic and inflammatory material, including threats against British soldiers and calls for violent action in the name of Islam. The revelation has drawn sharp criticism from experts in counter-terrorism and digital regulation. "This isn’t about politics," said one anonymous senior intelligence source speaking to the BBC. "This is about how platforms like Facebook enforce their own rules — or choose not to — when it comes to content that can directly feed into real-world violence." Facebook has defended its action at the time, stating that it was then reliant on user reporting to identify and remove content that violated its policies, and that it had significantly improved its content monitoring and AI-driven detection tools since 2013. A spokesperson said: “We have made major strides in identifying and removing harmful content in real time. If this post had appeared today, it would not have remained online for long.” Yet some remain unconvinced. Dr. Zeynep Tufekci, a technology and society researcher at New York University, said: “This is a classic case of looking back and seeing the warning signs that were there all along. The problem is not just Facebook’s response to the post, but the fact that it took a death before the system kicked in — and even then, the system was reactive, not preventive.” The story has particular resonance in light of ongoing discussions about tech giants' roles in amplifying extremist content. Websites and apps are increasingly scrutinised over their algorithms that can inadvertently recommend or promote violent material, sometimes leading users down a radicalisation funnel.

For once, that overused word turmoil is justified. The Greek government is at war with its creditors, its banks are shut, and its markets teeter on the edge of chaos. This is a situation that has left the world watching with bated breath as the fragile European project faces one of its most severe tests yet. Over the past week, Greece has moved from political stalemate to an all-out financial confrontation, with the potential consequences of a default and a possible exit from the eurozone sending shockwaves through global markets. The crisis started to unfold in earnest last week when Athens and its creditors—comprising the European Commission, the International Monetary Fund, and the European Central Bank—failed to reach an agreement on a new round of financial assistance. That failure left Greece needing to find €1.6 billion by Tuesday to pay the IMF, and without further aid from the eurozone, it is increasingly likely to collapse financially. In an unprecedented move, Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras called a national referendum for 5 July, asking the Greek people to accept or reject the financial terms that have been on the table. The decision has added uncertainty to an already volatile situation and pushed investors into a panic, with European stock markets plunging and the euro falling as buyers and sellers tried to grasp what would come next. Meanwhile, on the ground, the rhythm of daily life in Greece is grinding to a halt. Banks are closed, with cash machine access restricted to small withdrawals per day, and people are lining up to pull out their savings before the system completely fails. Smaller businesses, which form the backbone of the Greek economy, are already facing emergency liquidity issues, unable to pay wages or suppliers. Some reports suggest that rationing of hospital supplies and even fuel is under way as crude austerity measures come into force. The closure of the Athens stock exchange has not brought clarity but merely deepened the uncertainty. Greece’s government is clearly divided between those urging the public to accept the creditors’ terms and those backing Prime Minister Tsipras in his defiant stance. The European Union, for its part, has been at war with itself. France has called desperately for a last-minute solution, Germany remains resolute in its opposition to any compromise, and other European leaders are doing what they always do: waiting to see where the wind will blow.

Three years ago, Andy Murray arrived at the Roland Garros tournament in Paris with a significant cloud hanging over his participation. Suffering from a persistent and troubling back injury, the British tennis star had already seen his hopes dimmed after a flare-up in Rome just 10 days before the French Open began. The world number three was forced to withdraw from the Italian Open tournament in a sorely disappointing blow to his spring campaign—and potentially his prospects at the clay court grand slam. The injury had plagued Murray for months, with each tournament seemingly a test of whether it would flare up or allow him to compete at the peak of his powers. Back then, questions were being asked about whether Murray would be able to recover in time for the French Open, which began on May 27, 2013. Fans left Paris with uncertainty about whether their hopes for the world number three, and one of the few British grand slam champions of recent years, had died along with his injured back. He had spent much of the lead-up to the tournament in treatment, using the Rome tournament as a key marker for both his physical and mental fitness. Unfortunately for Murray, the combination of the injury and the aggressive nature of the clay courts in Rome proved too much as he was forced to pull out, with only minimal confirmation on when—let alone if—he would be ready for the French Open itself. At that point in his career, Murray was still basking in the afterglow of his U.S. Open victory in 2012, which had seen him defeat Novak Djokovic in a dramatic final. But the injury cast a shadow over a year that had already seen a mix of success and frustration. Critically, the absence from Roland Garros was considered a glaring omission in a player who had long been considered among the elite of the sport. With the 2016 French Open looming on the horizon, sports fans were reminded of how far Murray had come—and how far he still had to go. For the time being, it was uncertain whether he would even be fit to take to the Philippe-Chatrier Court, let alone reach the final, which had seemed inevitable just weeks before. As such, 2013 became a year defined by caution, treatment and the slow, painful process of recovery. But even in his absence, the buzz and support for the British No. 1 never died.

Australia is on the brink of losing one of its most cherished natural treasures to the United Nations’ list of “in danger” World Heritage sites, and the implications could be severe for both its environment and its economy. The Great Barrier Reef, a colossal coral ecosystem stretching over 2,300 kilometres and one of the seven wonders of the natural world, now faces the threat of a formal declaration by UNESCO if it is not shown to have made sufficient progress in addressing climate change and pollution threats. The Australian government has spent millions since 2018 as part of a five-year reef protection plan and has defended its efforts, but environmental groups and scientists argue these measures are inadequate in the face of escalating challenges. Coral bleaching caused by rising ocean temperatures has left large parts of the reef severely damaged, with mass die-offs occurring in 2016, 2017, and again in 2020. In recent years, the Reef 2050 Long-Term Sustainability Plan has been frequently delayed or only partially rolled out, planting the seeds for growing international concern. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is set to review the reef’s status in mid-2024, and as pressure mounts from human activity and environmental pressures, the World Heritage Committee is becoming increasingly frustrated by what it perceives as “business as usual” from the Australian government. Earlier last year, it warned the government that “repeated and systematic non-compliance” with the terms of the World Heritage Convention leaves the reef at greater risk and may lead to a “danger” listing. If such a listing is confirmed, it could trigger a profound backlash from the international community and weigh heavily on the Australian tourism sector, which currently generates around $6.4 billion annually and supports about 64,000 jobs. The reef is a major draw for overseas visitors, and a “danger” designation risks deterring tourists and damaging Australia’s image as a guardian of the natural world. Environmental scientists have described the current state of the reef as a crisis, with Dr. Terry Hughes, director of the Australian Research Council’s Centre of Excellence for Coral Reef Studies, stating: “We’re not seeing the scalability of effort needed to truly turn this around. It’s one thing to have funding, it’s another to deploy it where it’s most needed.” As the debate intensifies, Australia finds itself at a crossroads—not just for one of its most celebrated natural icons, but for its reputation on the global stage.

Celtic manager Ronny Deila has praised the performances of midfielders Callum McGregor and Scott Allan as the Glasgow giants claimed a 3-1 victory over Inverness Caledonian Thistle at Celtic Park. The win, which edged them closer to the Scottish Premiership title, saw both players play a pivotal role in maintaining control of the midfield and setting the tempo for the Light Blues. McGregor, the Scotland international, was a constant threat in central areas, providing both defensive cover and creative support, while Allan made his competitive Celtic debut in place of the suspended Nir Biton. The 23-year-old, whose £1.5m summer move from Dundee has united fans and critics alike, showed composure well beyond his years and proved an effective presence at the heart of the action. Deila left no doubt about the importance of the two midfield men in his post-match comments: "Callum and Scott had an excellent game. They both did what we asked, and more. It was a very important win for us, and they were big factors in that." McGregor assisted both of the first-half goals, with Sam Stanton scoring Celtic's opener and Bob McHugh doubling the advantage before the break. Stuart Armstrong added a third in the second half, before substitute Gary Mackay-Steven gave Inverness a measure of consolation with a late effort. While much of the pre-match talk centered around Celtic’s pursuit of the league title, Deila remained tight-lipped about their position in the league table. Instead, he focused on the performances of his younger players, many of whom have been included in the squad in recent fixtures ahead of key European fixtures. He said: “These are periods where we can test some of our young players under pressure. We need to continue to make sure we are technically at our highest level. We can do better still, but this was a solid performance.” Scott Allan, making his first appearance in the league since joining the club, appeared to thrive in the company of his experienced midfield partner. Deila revealed that he was impressed by the midfielder's composure and understanding of the game despite it being his first start for his new club. “Scott is a good kid, and I expected to see good things from him. He showed a lot of promise today,” Deila said. “He will be a big part of our future.”

Sudan’s youth are turning to poetry as a form of expression and protest in a nation still reeling from decades of political and economic turmoil. In Khartoum and across the country, a new generation of young poets are reclaiming the long-standing tradition of lyrical resistance, using spoken word and verse to challenge authority, voice discontent and celebrate the resilience of the Sudanese spirit. Yousra Elbagir reports that in an age where social media has become a powerful tool for activism, Sudanese poets are harnessing digital platforms to amplify their messages to a global audience. They recite and post their works on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube – often mixing Arabic, Sudanese dialect and English – bringing a unique, youthful energy to a centuries-old art form. The tradition of poetry in Sudan is deeply rooted. During the anti-colonial struggle, poets were the voice of a nation yearning for independence. They screamed of injustice and sang of liberation, and their words were passed on in universities, at community gatherings and in the streets. Now, under the oppressive regime of Omar al-Bashir’s government and the ongoing power struggle that followed his ousting in April 2019, young poets are once again standing at the frontlines of dissent. “The only thing we have more than injustice is poetry,” says 24-year-old Mohamed from West Darfur. “When we can’t protest in the streets, we take to the mic.” These young poets often gather in informal spaces – cafés, universities or makeshift studios in residential areas – to rehearse and perform in what have become known as “spoken word circles.” These gatherings are not just artistic but are also political, with each poem carrying a message of defiance, memory and hope. Some of the most powerful pieces are written by women, who are challenging norms while asserting their voices in the public sphere. Poets like Samia Elshafie and Dalal Almobarak have become local celebrities, their performances often going viral. Their words capture the complexities of being young, black and female in a patriarchal and authoritarian system. “Poetry is survival,” one young poet declared in a recent performance. “It gets us through the hunger, the fear and the silence of a country that knows only how to shout.” The government has long attempted to suppress dissent, but for these poets, silence is not an option. They are determined to write their truth, share their trauma and shape a future through the power of words.

Belfast Giants Makes Remarkable Comeback to Triumph Over Nottingham Panthers   A sensational third-period performance hurled the Belfast Giants to a dramatic 7-4 victory over the Nottingham Panthers in Saturday night’s Elite League encounter at the SSE Arena. The home side, who had trailed for much of the match, staged a heart-stopping finale that saw them score three goals in the final frame to steal the win and leave the Ulster crowd in raptures. With the game poised at 4-4 heading into the final stretch, the Giants, who are among the league’s heavyweights, displayed remarkable composure and clinical finishing to pull off a stunning turnaround. Not only did they even the score, but they added two more to seal a 7-4 triumph that will be spoken about for some time. The first half of the game belonged to Nottingham, who came into the SSE Arena with a game plan forged in recent success. The Panthers, traditionally a strong outfit, capitalized on early pressure and physical play to dominate the opening 40 minutes. Goals from key playmakers and strong team coordination gave them a 4-2 advantage over the Giants by the end of the second period. However, as the third period began, the tide turned dramatically. The Belfast backline began to settle, and the momentum quickly shifted in their favor. The Giants’ first of the period came from a slick power-play move, reducing the deficit and rattling the confidence of the visitors. The equalizer soon followed, as a sharp cross-ice pass set up a doorstep finish that made it 4-4. The final goal of the night was a moment of individual brilliance, a solo effort through the defense that sent the crowd into a roar and left the Panthers shell-shocked. John Phillips, head coach of the Giants, was full of praise after the match. “We had the belief right to the end. The lads stayed patient and stuck to the system. I’m so proud of them for pulling that off. It’s a massive three points for us.” Phillips also highlighted the resilience his players have shown this season. “We’ve had setbacks, sure, but this win is a huge shot in the arm. It shows we can come through in the pressure moments when it matters.” Nottingham Panthers’ coach Adam Keefe took the defeat in stride but acknowledged his side's struggles in maintaining consistency.

The national board of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has delayed a decision on whether to lift its long-standing ban on openly gay scouts and leaders, according to an announcement from the organization. This comes after years of mounting pressure from civil rights groups, parents, and even the organisation’s own membership to modernise its policies in line with broader societal and legal changes regarding LGBTQ+ rights. The postponed vote was expected to mark a decisive moment for a group that has played a significant role in shaping the lives of millions of American young people. It would have brought the BSA in line with the policies of rival youth organisations such as the Girl Scouts and the recent actions of several state and local councils who have already removed references to the anti-LGBTQ+ policies from their own charters. The BSA has long defended its stance by citing its constitutional rights, notably its right to religious liberty, and has said in the past that it must remain religiously affiliated to retain its tax-exempt status. The debate has deepened in recent years following the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark 2015 ruling legalising same-sex marriage, as well as the increasing visibility and acceptance of the LGBTQ+ community across the nation. According to two sources familiar with the board’s discussions, the decision to postpone the vote stemmed from disagreements among board members over how best to proceed without triggering a legal or public relations crisis. Some factions within the organisation still fear that lifting the ban could lead to a schism, particularly with more conservative units and chartered organisations withdrawing their support. For now, the BSA is expected to allow full discussions to continue in the new year, with the hope that a clearer path forward—ideally one that balances religious principles with modern values—can be charted. Organisations and individuals sympathetic to the LGBTQ+ community have expressed disappointment but not surprise at the delay. David Norris, executive director of the Equality and Scout Reform campaign, said: “We’re frustrated, but we understand this step has come at the urging of the most regressive elements within the Boy Scouts. The rest of America has moved on, and it’s time the Boy Scouts did too.” The organisation’s stance on LGBTQ+ inclusion has become a mirror of a broader cultural divide in the United States. While many youth councils and volunteers have supported change, others cling to traditional interpretations of the BSA’s foundational values, which historically have been rooted in Christian ideals.

A new Palestinian unity government has been sworn in, marking a pivotal moment in the long-standing political divide between rival factions in the West Bank and Gaza. The formation of the Cabinet is widely seen as a breakthrough in an effort to reunify the Palestinian territories under a single administration after years of acrimony between Fatah and Hamas — groups that have governed different parts of the divided nation with very different political and ideological agendas. The swearing-in of the unity government took place in Ramallah, the West Bank administrative capital, where senior officials and representatives from both Fatah and Hamas gathered to affirm the government's legitimacy. The new cabinet includes members from both political camps, signifying a rare moment of cooperation in a conflict-ridden political landscape. In his first address since the swearing-in, Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa — who is affiliated with Fatah — stressed the importance of national unity in the push for a lasting peace deal with Israel. "This unity is not symbolic; it is a foundation for a stronger and more respected Palestinian state," Mustafa said at the ceremony. The move is viewed by many as a direct response to increasing regional and international pressure for Palestinian factions to reconcile and present a united front in negotiations with Israel and the international community. In recent years, the divisions between the Hamas-led administration in Gaza and the Fatah-controlled West Bank have been a major obstacle to any meaningful progress in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and have often led to political stalemates and even outbreaks of violence. This new government aims to bridge that divide. The coalition includes senior Hamas figures, including the interior minister, who will be based in the Gaza Strip. However, the unity is not without challenges. Some hardline elements within both factions have expressed skepticism and concerns over compromises made during the coalition-building process. Meanwhile, the Israeli government has yet to respond publicly but has historically opposed any coalition that includes Hamas, which it officially designates as a terrorist organisation. Despite these obstacles, the new government has already moved quickly to establish basic communication channels between the West Bank and Gaza. A major task now lies ahead: implementing economic reforms and ensuring the protection of basic services for the estimated 5.5 million people living in the divided territories. The international community has welcomed the development, with the United Nations calling it a "diplomatic breakthrough" and the European Union offering support for a unified approach.

The UK government recently published the findings of an independent review into tidal lagoon energy, launching a renewed public debate over the potential and pitfalls of this emerging form of renewable power. At the heart of the discussion are the environmental impacts associated with constructing and operating tidal lagoons – large, artificial enclosures built on the shoreline to harness energy from the twice-daily tides. Proponents argue that the technology has the potential to deliver sustainable, predictable energy. However, environmental groups remain deeply concerned over the effects tidal lagoons could have on coastal ecosystems, marine life, and sediment dynamics. Tidal lagoons function by using the natural rise and fall of tides to generate electricity through turbines, offering a reliable alternative to intermittent sources like wind and solar. Supporters, including renewable energy industry leaders, see them as a clean and long-term solution to the UK’s climate goals, particularly in Wales, which was the focus of the government’s pilot projects in the Pembrokeshire lagoons, including the ill-fated Swansea Bay plan. The independent review, ordered by the Department for Business, Energy, and Industrial Strategy (BEIS), aims to assess the technical and economic viability of tidal lagoons, as well as their impacts on the environment. Among the key environmental concerns is the disruption caused by the construction phase. The process involves significant land and sea alterations, from building breakwaters to constructing reinforced infrastructure. This often involves large-scale dredging, which can disturb marine habitats and exacerbate erosion in already vulnerable coastal areas. Wildlife experts have raised particular concerns about the impact on migratory fish, birds, and invertebrates that depend on estuaries and tidal flats for feeding and breeding. Some studies suggest that tidal lagoons can alter the flow of water and sediment, potentially affecting key species such as salmon and flounder. Changes in salinity levels can also impact the fragile balance of estuarine ecosystems, leading to shifts in biodiversity that are difficult to predict and even more difficult to reverse. Additionally, the review will examine whether the carbon footprint of lagoon construction offsets the long-term benefits of reduced emissions from electricity generation. Environmental groups, including the National Trust and wildlife conservation bodies, have urged the government to approach such developments with caution. They argue that sustained environmental monitoring and rigorous impact assessments are essential before embarking on large-scale projects. As the UK seeks to meet its net-zero targets, the debate over tidal lagoons reflects a broader tension between innovation and sustainability.

South Africa Again Confronts the Rule of Law as Marikana Report is Released   President Jacob Zuma’s long-awaited release of the 600-page Marikana report has reignited a deeply national conversation over the state of the rule of law in South Africa, exposing tensions between political accountability, judicial transparency, and the public’s right to know. The report, compiled by judge Dunstan Mlambo following the fatal 2012 mining strike at Lonmin's Marikana platinum mine, in which 34 miners were killed by police, has been the subject of controversy, secrecy, and legal disputes. The timing of the report’s release has been deeply scrutinised, particularly after Zuma delayed the publication for nearly two years, citing national security concerns. Critics, including numerous civil society organisations and opposition parties, argued that the delay was an attempt to shield political and economic stakeholders in the mining sector from accountability. The final handover of the report last week, nearly a decade after the massacre, has been met with both cautious relief and widespread disappointment by victims' families, who accuse the government of a lack of genuine commitment to justice. At the heart of the report are uncomfortable revelations about police conduct during the two-day confrontation, as well as high-level interference in investigations by figures linked to then-country minister Pravin Gordhan and others. The document paints a picture of a breakdown in protocol, planning, and communication, with recommendations for legal and institutional reform. Civil liberties groups have urged the government to follow through on these recommendations, stating that the findings are a stark reminder of what can happen when the rule of law is not upheld. The Marikana killings had a profound impact on South Africa at the time, and the delayed publication of the report has only added to the national unease. “This is not about the past — it’s about the present and the future,” said Thembiso Nhlapo, a spokesperson for the Marikana Command, a group representing families of the slain miners. “We need to know that no one will be above the law and that no man will be president above any law.” Zuma, who has long been accused of undermining judicial independence and the principle of transparency, has faced mounting calls to resign over a separate corruption scandal involving the state procurement of security company services. Earlier this year, the country’s Supreme Constitutional Court ruled that the president must appear in court to justify his failure to repay public funds used for private upgrades.

In a spellbinding display of T20 batting, Alex Hales smashed a staggering 95 runs from just 30 balls to lead Nottinghamshire Outlaws to a record-breaking Powerplay score in a thrilling win over Durham Jets. The monumental knock not only earned Hales the accolade of the fastest to 95 in professional cricket but also helped Notts post the highest Powerplay total in the history of Twenty20 cricket. The game, held at Trent Bridge, was a showcase of explosive batting, with Hales single-handedly dismantling the Durham bowling attack in the first six overs of the innings. His innings featured ten towering sixes and a number of near-hits, each more audacious than the last. The crowd was left in stunned silence after each of his boundaries, as Hales continued to dominate with a brutal yet technically sound approach. Notts, aiming to push the boundaries of modern T20 batting, cashed in on the format’s tactical freedom, launching a blistering assault in the Powerplay phase. They scored a staggering 92 runs in the first six overs before eventually finishing with a mammoth 222 for 2, the highest opening Powerplay score ever recorded in the short-format game. Hales’ heroics set the tone for the rest of the innings, with fellow batters Ben Sanderson and Samit Patel adding crucial support to push the total past 220. Durham’s reply, while spirited, was ultimately out of their reach, as their batters struggled to cope with the Outlaws’ onslaught and the required run rate. Speaking after the game, Hales described the innings as "just going with the flow out there." He added: “You can’t get too bogged down in T20. You’ve got to have conviction and take your chance when it comes. Tonight, the scoreboard just kept ticking over and I was lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time.” The victory not only earned Notts a crucial win in the tournament but also sparked conversations about the evolving nature of T20 cricket. Experts have long argued that the Powerplay phase is where batting is most forgiving, but Hales' performance turned theory into practice on a historic scale. Notts' head coach, Glen Chapple, praised his side's fearless approach, saying: “Alex is one of the best finishers in the game, but it’s his adaptability and aggression early on that set the platform today. This team has bought into the T20 mentality, and what we saw was world-class.”

Middlesbrough have parted ways with manager Aitor Karanka after three and a half years at the helm, marking the end of a turbulent and ultimately unsuccessful tenure for the Spanish manager at the Riverside Stadium. The announcement came just days before the start of the 2016/17 Championship season, with the club having finished in 17th place last season – a position that narrowly avoided relegation but did little to lift the expectations of ambitious fans. Karanka, who took charge in 2013, was arguably the most successful Spanish manager in English football history at the time of his appointment. He led Real Betis to promotion to La Liga twice during his career and made a name for himself in the Eredivisie with FC Twente. Boro chairman Steve Gibson had high hopes for Karanka, believing his experience and credentials would bring stability and ambition to the club. In his first season at Middlesbrough, Karanka oversaw an impressive eighth-place finish in the Championship and guided the club into the FA Cup semi-finals for the first time in 48 years. However, the following campaigns saw a steady decline in form and results, despite a significant investment in the squad. After winning two FA Cup matches as a Premier League side during the 2015/16 season, Boro failed to beat a single Championship opponent in the knock-out rounds of cup competitions, with their opening EFL Cup game ending in a 3-2 home defeat to Championship rivals Brighton. Karanka's side also struggled with consistency in league football. Despite a strong pre-season which included a 1-0 victory over Manchester United at Old Trafford, the club flattered to deceive under pressure in the latter weeks of their titleless campaign. Unconvincing league performances and a lack of tangible progress disappointed fans who had anticipated the club taking a step closer to Premier League return. Reports suggest that Karanka had been under increasing pressure in recent weeks, with prominent supporters and local pundits calling for his replacement. The club's decision will now fall to managing director and chairman Steve Gibson, who is expected to appoint a new manager with relatable, results-driven credentials ahead of the new campaign. While Middlesbrough’s supporters are hopeful that this decision will breathe new life into the club, Karanka's departure marks the end of a chapter filled with promise, mixed results, and ultimately, unfulfilled expectations. His outgoing message thanked the players, staff, and fans for their support, acknowledging the challenges he faced while overseeing the club’s recruitment and development strategy.

Scotland were handed a heavy 3-0 defeat by Italy in a sweltering Rome on Saturday afternoon, marking yet another low point in Gregor Townsend’s tenure as head coach. Despite the comprehensive nature of their loss, there were moments where Scotland showed flashes of promise that left fans clinging to hope that the margin of defeat could have been greater. The Azzurri, runner-up in the 2023 Six Nations, were clearly a class above their visitors, but Scotland put in a spirited display, particularly in the attacking phases. However, their inability to convert chances into points proved costly once again. Italy opened the scoring after 15 minutes when number eight Simone Ferrari crashed over at the back of a powerful driving maul, with Carlo Canna adding the conversion. Scotland responded well, restricting Italy to limited opportunities and showing impressive resilience under the high tackles and physicality on offer in Stadio Olimpico. Owen Farrell was at the heart of Italy’s second, a well-constructed move involving Anglo-Italian lock Mariano Anduaga, setting up a try for captain Tommaso Casamento in the 30th minute. As the half progressed, Scotland had spells of possession and territory, particularly in the 20-minute period either side of half-time, as fly-half Finn Russell combined well with scrum-half Henry Pyrgos. Replacement number eight Zander Fagerson was denied a try by a slap-on-offside decision, and tight-head prop Tommy Bell displayed strong carries under pressure. Still, Italy’s greater experience shone through in the second half. A full-back intercept try from EmilianoCollectionView capped a thoroughly professional performance from the hosts, with Scotland unable to threaten a sustained comeback. Although Italy’s victory was deserved, Scotland had arguably come close to securing a try about half a dozen times during the game. Russell had the ball in his hands on the 50-metre line on more than one occasion but was up-ended unconvincingly by the Italian defence. Full-back Stuart Hogg was deployed high and wide, giving his side more width to work with, but was kept quiet for the majority. The defeat leaves Scotland waiting on results elsewhere in the European Nations League group. Though the 3-0 loss is a confidence blow, it is not the end of the road. Defeats by such a narrow margin suggest that the team is improving in certain facets, but their improvements must come at a faster rate if Scotland are to avoid further humiliation in the coming fixtures.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has issued an urgent appeal to the European Union, demanding that Syria’s neighbouring countries be granted €3 billion (£2.2bn; $3.4bn) in financial aid to address the crisis of displaced persons resulting from the ongoing civil war in Syria. Speaking at a European Council meeting in Brussels, Mr Orbán outlined his call as part of a broader strategy to manage the migratory crisis and ensure that humanitarian needs are met through regional cooperation. Mr Orbán, a long-standing critic of uncontrolled migration and a champion of EU border sovereignty, argued that the funding should be channelled through the bilateral and multilateral agreements of the European Union to avoid overwhelming European countries with continued mass migration flows. “We must not become the saviours of the entire world,” he said, echoing his oft-repeated stance that Europe should focus on aiding the countries immediately affected, rather than bearing the brunt of displacement within its own borders. In his address, Mr Orbán pointed to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Iraq—countries that currently host millions of Syrian refugees—as being on the front lines of the crisis. He claimed that providing substantial financial support would not only assist those nations in managing the humanitarian fallout but also serve as a disincentive for irregular migration across continents. “If we invest in stability on the southern rim of Europe, then people will not come here,” he asserted. Mr Orbán’s call follows months of tension within the EU over the issue of migration. Despite EU pledges of aid to refugee-hosting countries, the funds have often been delayed or insufficient in the eyes of those on the ground. Many member states remain divided over how to distribute responsibilities fairly, with Eastern European nations—including Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic—prioritising strict border controls and resisting quotas for refugee resettlement. The prime minister also reiterated his view that the EU must take “practical and not just symbolic” actions to stabilise the region and curb the flow of unauthorised migration to Europe. His comments are likely to provoke further debate among EU leaders, especially with ongoing disagreements over the management of the Schengen border system and the future of EU migration policy. While Mr Orbán’s proposal has gained support from certain EU members who share his concerns about migration, others have questioned the practicality and feasibility of the plan.

The chair of Kick It Out, the organisation dedicated to tackling discrimination in football, has called for sanctions against English Football League (EFL) clubs that fail to interview Black, Asian, and Minority Ethnic (BAME) candidates for coaching jobs. Kate Brook, who chairs the charity, said that as long as clubs can freely bypass the existing good practice guidance and avoid meeting basic diversity targets, progress on inclusion within the game will remain stalled. Brook’s comments come amid ongoing underrepresentation of BAME candidates in coaching and leadership roles across English football. Despite a Code of Practice introduced by the EFL in 2019, which encourages clubs to consider diverse candidates for head coach and senior assistant roles, there is no enforceable requirement to interview them. Brook stressed that unless that changes, the sector will continue to fall short of genuine parity. Speaking to the Evening Standard, Brook said: “It's sad but necessary to say that if you're a club that doesn't bother considering a BAME candidate when one is available and suitable, you should be punished. This isn't just about ticking boxes, it’s about changing the culture and giving people opportunities.” Her comments follow recent scrutiny over the low number of BAME managers across EFL and Premier League clubs. While the number of BAME managers in the Premier League has increased to 3, none currently lead a top-flight club. In the EFL, progress has been similarly slow, with only a handful of BAME appointments despite growing talent in positions such as assistant managers and first-team coaches. Brook’s proposal comes as part of a broader call for structural reform in how the game approaches diversity. She argued that the Football Association, the EFL, and the Premier League must shift from “good intentions” to “compulsory action” if they are to truly address the imbalance. The EFL has not yet commented publicly on Brook’s suggestion. However, in 2022, the league launched a pilot mentoring scheme aimed at supporting aspiring BAME coaches, and has made public commitments to boosting representation in coaching roles. Brook added: “In the modern world, any organisation that values equality should not be allowed to drag its feet. If a club wants to sit and hoard every opportunity for white men, then they must be prepared to face the consequences.” She said that potential sanctions could include points deductions, financial penalties, or the withholding of funding for academy or infrastructure projects.

The Premier League season is set to resume this weekend after a summer of swashbuckling transfers, managerial reshuffles and player retirements, and fans are bracing themselves for more high-speed action, dramatic goals and unforgettable moments. The 2023/24 campaign is widely being heralded as one of the most unpredictable in recent memory, with traditional powerhouses grappling with rebuilding and underdogs bolstered by smart signings. Among the teams making ambitious statements before the opening matches are Manchester City and Arsenal, both of whom are expected to dominate the title race. Manchester City, reigning champions, have retained most of their dominant squad and added a few key reinforcements, including midfielder Rodri, who made a world-record £100 million move from Getafe this summer. Arsenal, too, have spent big to reinvigorate their team, notably bringing in Declan Rice and Oleksandr Zinchenko. However, Chelsea, Liverpool and even Manchester United—who are still in the early stages of a restructure after their former owners' departure—have also spent heavily, causing some to question whether the so-called "big six" will continue to dominate the top table, or if Championship newcomers like Bournemouth and Nottingham Forest will land a shock blow. Mourinho and the Old Trafford Revival? One of the defining stories of the transfer window will be the appointment of José Mourinho at Manchester United. The Portuguese tactician, known for his flair for rebuilding clubs, takes over from Erik ten Hag and already has fans dreaming of a return to the team’s former glories. With the Red Devils investing in full-back Luke Shaw and defender Andreas Pereira, the hope is that Mourinho can bring fresh tactics and long-term stability. Meanwhile, across the city, Manchester United’s fiercest rivals, Liverpool, have suffered a summer of misfortune after a frustrating World Cup from their midfield trio of Thiago Alcântara and Jordan Henderson. Their manager, Jurgen Klopp, is uncharacteristically optimistic that the squad, despite their current injury list, will fight for the title. Off the field, too, the season is already shaping up as momentous. The Premier League will be launching new VAR technology this season to reduce controversial decisions. Though player unions have raised concerns about the system’s reliability and its impact on the “flow” of the game, clubs are optimistic it will make matches fairer. Broadcasters go head-to-head as well, with several major clubs sourcing deals with non-traditional platforms, prompting talk of a new era in how the league is watched.

Apple continues to face mounting scrutiny over its 30% commission fee on all purchases made through the App Store, with growing criticism from developers, businesses and even lawmakers who accuse the tech giant of leveraging its dominant market position to extract excessive revenue. The 30% cut, described by Apple as a "tax" on digital products and services, has long been a key source of income for the company and remains among the most controversial aspects of its business model. A developer selling a $19.99 app, for instance, pockets $13.99 after Apple deducts its standard fee. For in-app purchases or subscriptions, the same percentage is frozen until the product has been available for a year, after which the fee drops to 15%. While Apple has defended the cost as necessary for maintaining the App Store’s stability and security, critics argue the fees are unfairly high, especially given the lack of meaningful alternatives for most developers, who often rely on the App Store as their primary or only distribution channel. "Apple is in a unique position, thanks to the desktop-like shopping, ordering, entertainment and communication experience the App Store provides directly on users’ phones," said Bob Litterman, a former Apple board member and hedge fund executive. "It's like the real estate giants of decades ago: they own the prime land and charge a high rent." The controversy has escalated in recent months as high-profile companies, including Epic Games, Spotify and Match Group, have publicly challenged Apple’s fees as anti-competitive. Earlier this year, Epic Games launched a high-stakes legal battle after Apple removed its popular game Fortnite from the App Store following a dispute over payment rules. In response, Epic Games has been vocal in its calls for the App Store to allow third-party payment systems, which would let developers bypass Apple’s fee entirely. Meanwhile, Spotify, the music-streaming giant, claimed in a regulatory filing that Apple fails to provide equal access to users and treats it as a "second-class app," partly due to the burden of the 30% fee. On the regulatory front, the European Union is preparing a landmark law, part of its Digital Markets Act, restricting gatekeeper tech firms—including Apple—from unfairly exploiting their dominant market positions. Websites and apps will be allowed to add external links and payment systems, which could chip away at Apple’s control of the App Store ecosystem.

A man has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of 21-year-old Irish student Karen Buckley, whose body was discovered on a remote farm in Glasgow four days after she vanished from her home in the city. Rachel McCrone, 25, who had previously shown interest in Ms Buckley on social media and sent her unsolicited messages, was found guilty of the horrific crime following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The sentence, which includes a minimum term of 29 years before she becomes eligible for parole, was announced on Tuesday as the court heard how McCrone lured Buckley under false pretences, before attacking and killing her. The tragedy began on 9 June when Buckley, a law student at the University of Glasgow, left her south-side flat to meet McCrone after being invited to visit her home. What followed, the court heard, was a violent and premeditated attack. Buckley’s body was found in a disused boathouse on a farm in Bishopbriggs four days later after an extensive search by police, using the location data from McCrone’s mobile phone. Buckley’s family, who had flown over from Ireland, described the killer as a “monster” in a powerful victim impact statement. Her mother, Anne Hickey, said: “Every mother should live to see their daughter grow up, get married and have children – but we have had all that ripped away from us.” In a harrowing testimony, the court was told how McCrone sent Buckley a series of messages in the days leading up to the attack, many of which were disturbing and predatory in nature. Buckley had reportedly tried to block McCrone on social media and had expressed concerns about her unwanted advances to friends and family. During the trial, key evidence included phone records, messages and forensic findings from the scene of the murder. McCrone had claimed during her trial that Buckley had visited her home voluntarily and that the death was an accident, but the evidence quickly dismissed those assertions, leaving the court with little option but to deliver a guilty verdict. The sentencing has been met with widespread public support, with many calling for McCrone to spend the rest of her life in prison. Social media has become a platform of outpouring from the public, students and members of the Irish community in Glasgow, who have set up a memorial site with candles and flowers at the entrance to the university.

Are You Happy at Work? The Quiet Crisis in British Employment    By Sarah Johnson, Staff Writer  In an era typified by the pursuit of purpose and the rise of so-called "happiness economics", the UK is experiencing a silent but growing discontent among workers. According to recent surveys by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), nearly 34% of British employees report they are dissatisfied with their jobs. Yet, despite these figures, many remain in roles they would rather quit—stuck, unmotivated, and disconnected from their place of work. The question, "Are you happy at work?" has become increasingly central not only to employees but also to employers who are rethinking how to manage their most valuable resource: human capital. From the well-documented rise in "quiet quitting" to mass resignations dubbed the "Great Resignation", the workplace is undergoing a profound cultural shift. But what is making employees unhappy, and why are so many choosing, or feeling unable, to leave? For Hattie Morgan, a teacher from Newcastle, the answer lies in the overwhelming pressures of the education system. "After thirteen years of teaching, I can truly say I loved this job—until I didn’t. Now it’s exhaustion and anxiety. I fear something will break either me or my students," she said. Morgan is far from alone. The education sector – alongside health, social care, and retail – continues to report among the highest levels of stress and job dissatisfaction. At the same time, the pandemic has changed expectations. Many younger workers, in particular, are no longer willing to tolerate toxic cultures, micromanagement, or work-life imbalance. A YouGov poll from earlier this year found 72% of employees under 35 would leave a job if it didn’t support their mental health. Yet the same poll found that 43% had considered quitting in the past year but decided to stay due to financial concerns and housing insecurity. “The problem isn’t just with the job itself,” says Dr. Samuel Greene, organisational psychologist based at the University of Manchester. “It’s about how work fits into a broader picture of life stability. People today aren’t just looking for a wage. They want dignity, flexibility, and the chance to develop both professionally and personally.” In workplaces across the country, conversations once reserved for the water cooler or the staff room are now go-to topics on social media, forums, and even policy debates in Parliament.

Kodjia Inspires Villa’s Fourth Consecutive Win with Seven-Game Magic   Aston Villa made it four victories on the bounce as Jonathan Kodjia continued his staggering run of form, netting his seventh goal in seven matches to secure a 2-1 win against Queens Park Rangers at Villa Park on Saturday night. The emphatic result moved Steve Bruce’s men one place closer to the Championship summit and further dented QPR’s fading hopes of survival. Kodjia, who has taken the league by storm since signing from Stoke City in January, once again was the star of the show. The 29-year-old Gabon international needs just one more goal to equal the record for scoring in seven successive matches, a feat last achieved by prolific forwards such as Alan Shearer and Thierry Henry. Villa took the lead in the 23rd minute when Kodjia showcased his predatory instincts. A neat through ball split the QPR defence and allowed the striker to run onto the pass before slotting past goalkeeper Joachim Andersen. The goal was a carbon copy of his previous efforts this month, once again underlining his exceptional positioning and composure in front of goal. QPR responded 15 minutes later through a deflected effort from Nathan Wood, who found space on the edge of the box before unleashing a first-time shot that rattled the back of the net. However, the visitors' momentary hope was short-lived as Villa sealed the win in the 84th minute. A well-worked move down the right saw Jack Grealish deliver a pinpoint cross to the back post, where Kodjia rose highest to head the ball past Andersen and spark wild scenes of jubilation in the home stands. Steve Bruce, whose future in charge of the club remains about as secure as any Villa manager has been in recent years, praised his skipper’s remarkable form in the post-match press conference. “I’m amazed by Jonathan. To do this in seven games is unheard of at this level,” Bruce said. “He’s a true goalscorer, a leader. He’s not just scoring goals—he’s changing the way we play when he gets the ball. It gives everyone around him a lift. And tonight, he was special again.” For QPR manager Ian Holloway, whose side drop further into the relegation scrap, the defeat was a bitter one. “We gave them life in that first goal, and then we made it hard on ourselves,” Holloway admitted.

The European Commission has abandoned proposals to impose new time limits on surcharge-free roaming for European Union citizens using mobile phones abroad, in a shift that has been welcomed by consumer groups and operators alike. Under the original plan, the current cap on unlimited roaming within the EU—introduced in 2017—would have been reduced from three months to 15 days annually.
