This would have marked a reversal of the so-called "Roam Like at Home" policy, which allowed EU residents to use mobile data, minutes, and texts in any member state without extra charges. However, the Commission has now confirmed that it will not reintroduce these restrictions as part of its upcoming review of the roaming regulations. In a statement, the Commission said it remains committed to the principle that Europeans should enjoy cost-free access to mobile services within the EU. “Roam Like at Home has been a transformative policy and a vital part of the digital single market,” said Margrethe Vestager, the EU Commissioner for Competition and formerly in charge of digital policies. “We are not planning to reintroduce any new, arbitrary limits.” The original proposal had sparked widespread criticism from consumer advocates, who warned it would undermine the freedoms of EU citizens and deter cross-border travel. Many digital rights groups and human rights organisations condemned the move as a step backwards in the fight against digital exclusion and for services that support free movement within the continent. The shift in stance follows months of pressure from both the public and industry stakeholders. Mobile phone operators, meanwhile, have expressed relief that the Commission has opted not to backtrack on the policy, which helped eliminate roaming fees for 81 million EU citizens. It had also been feared that reintroducing caps would complicate the existing telecom regulations and add administrative burdens for service providers. The future of the "Roam Like at Home" policy is now linked to a broader review of EU telecoms rules set for 2025. This review is expected to examine the evolving digital landscape, including the rise of 5G and the need to support connectivity for an increasingly mobile population. For now, EU citizens will continue to benefit from the existing roaming rules, which have allowed them to travel freely without the fear of high mobile costs. The decision to abandon time restrictions has been hailed as a victory for transparency and consumer rights.

An Indian court has taken a significant step in an often-delayed criminal case when it ruled that Bollywood actor Salman Khan should face a charge of culpable homicide over a hit-and-run road accident that occurred in 2002. The decision, announced earlier this week, adds weight to long-standing allegations against one of India’s most high-profile celebrities and signals a possible shift in the determination of the legal process to secure justice for all involved. The incident took place on June 16, 2002, in Mumbai, when Khan, who was driving under the influence of alcohol, collided with a motorcycle outside a popular hotel. The accident resulted in the deaths of Russian model Varsha Saxena and her Indian boyfriend, Vitaly Scherbo. Khan managed to flee the scene, but was later traced down and arrested. Since then, the case has gone through multiple legal wranglings and appeals, often drawing heavy media attention and public discourse about the treatment of celebrities within the Indian legal system. The latest ruling by the court in Mumbai comes after a long criminal investigation and a recent review of the case’s legal merits. The accused will now face a charge of culpable homicide, a legal term in India used for cases that short of murder but still reflect gross negligence and intent that leads to death. This charge is a critical escalation, and it will likely bring the case toward a final judicial reckoning. Supporters of the actor, who is one of Bollywood’s top stars and an influential figure in Indian pop culture, will likely continue to defend him, citing his previous convictions and the context of his actions in 2002. At that time, Khan was already under a suspended sentence for another road accident in 1998 and later served a jail term after a key Supreme Court ruling in 2018. However, this latest charge represents the severity of the 2002 incident and fails to account for any exculpating circumstances. The case has highlighted broader public debates about celebrity culture, the treatment of high-profile individuals under the law, and the persistent struggles with the Indian judiciary’s efficiency in delivering timely justice. As the legal process continues, the outcome could set an important precedent for how such cases are handled, especially when high visibility and public influence are factored in. Salman Khan is expected to be summoned for further proceedings. His legal team has yet to make a formal response, but it is anticipated that there will be at least an appeal to the decision.

Schools across Scotland are facing a growing crisis as an increasing number of pupils arrive at class hungry and, in some cases, steal food from their classmates, teachers have warned. The issue, described as “starkly widespread” by educators, is highlighting the deepening challenge of child food poverty as the cost of living rises and support systems struggle to keep pace. According to a recent report from the   Teaching Union Scotland (EIS)  , a significant proportion of students are coming to school without a packed lunch, unable to eat school meals due to their cost or embarrassment caused by low-income household circumstances. In some cases, teachers have said pupils have resorted to removing food from communal fridges or taking sandwiches from classmates, adding to the emotional and psychological strain on vulnerable children. “Food theft among pupils is something we talk about in teacher training courses as a rare and exceptional situation,” said Dr Ewan Winn of the EIS. “But in many classrooms across the country, it is now a regular occurrence. It’s heartbreaking to see children in this position when we know the solutions are both simple and immediate.” One teacher from a primary school in Glasgow told The Scotsman that it had become a “routine problem” for staff to step in when pupils were seen to steal food. Another described a situation where a child was caught eating a fellow classmate’s lunch, adding: “It's not just about food: it’s about dignity and respect. No child should feel like they have to take from others to survive.” Official data from the Scottish government shows that the number of pupils eligible for free school meals has risen in recent years, but school meal uptake has not kept pace. Some families are unable to cover the cost of a paid lunch and have no access to free provision, while others are too proud or embarrassed to sign their children up for support. In response, the   Scottish Child Poverty Action Group   (SCEPA) has called for urgent action, including the expansion of the free school meals programme and better communication with parents to ensure eligible families are signing up. “This is not just a minor blip,” said a spokesperson. “This is a crisis that is impacting on children’s ability to learn, to behave and to feel positive about themselves. We need political leadership that treats this as the emergency it is.”

French presidential hopeful François Fillon has fallen from grace in a dramatic political twist, as prosecutors confirmed he has been placed under formal investigation over allegations of the misuse of public funds. The case, centred on a £700,000 in cash £700,000 in public funds allegedly funnelled to his wife and two children as parliamentary allowances, has thrown the centrist candidate’s presidential ambitions into sharp uncertainty. Fillon, a former prime minister and long-time member of France’s political establishment, had surged into a firm frontrunner in the upcoming presidential race, enjoying strong support from voters in his Union of the Centre (UDI) bloc. But his position is now under intense scrutiny as the judicial inquiry, launched by Paris public prosecutors, seeks to determine whether he knowingly benefited from an illegal pay pact involving his spouse, Penelope Fillon. The allegations, which first broke in January this year, centre around Penelope Fillon’s role as an unpaid parliamentary assistant for more than a decade. Despite this lack of formal duties, she was paid as if she were working full-time for the National Assembly. Former colleagues of Fillon have since come forward, admitting that she performed little or no work in that role — a claim that has led to calls of hypocrisy and betrayal from critics on both the left and right. The financial irregularities are not limited to Penelope Fillon. Records show that two of her children — Clothilde and Charles — were also paid handsomely as parliamentary assistants for their own fathers-in-law, who were also members of the National Assembly. These figures have cast an even darker shadow over the Fillon camp, with opposition leaders quick to point out the apparent double standard. The legal procedure involves the opening of an  enquête préliminaire , a stage in French justice where investigators begin to gather evidence. While such an inquiry does not immediately imply criminal charges, it signals that investigators are taking the matter seriously. Political analysts noted that any conviction in such a case, even for the misuse of public funds, could spell political ruin for Fillon at this stage in the campaign. The fallout has already had a measurable effect on his campaign. Fillon’s party lost two mayors and 11 council members in recent by-elections, a sign of growing dissatisfaction with his leadership and recent allegations. Still, his supporters remain loyal, arguing that the scandal is aimed at undermining a strong right-wing challenger and weakening the French Centre.

The start of a political campaign that would see her take the helm at No 10 was marked by an uncharacteristically blunt and bold declaration from Theresa May, who at the time served as home secretary. In a dramatic moment that surprised many of her more cautious colleagues, May stood before a room of party officials and stated with unwavering confidence: “I’m Theresa May and I’m the best person to be prime minister.” It was a stark break from the typically understated style that had long defined her political image, but one that arguably signalled her determination to step into the role of the most senior office in the land. Her decision to launch her bid for leadership in 2016 came against a backdrop of deep political uncertainty, following David Cameron’s historic resignation after the Brexit referendum. As one of the most experienced figures in the Conservative Party, May had long been seen as a potential successor — a steady hand for an increasingly turbulent era in British politics. May’s breakfast speech, delivered at the prestigious Dorchester Hotel in London in late July 2016, was not only the formal launch of her ambitions but also a statement of intent. As one of the few candidates who supported remaining in the EU, she positioned herself as a unifying and stable force during a time when the nation seemed on the brink of division. It was a curious tactic for May — a woman who had spent much of her political career carefully avoiding the spotlight — to open her campaign with such directness. Her detractors within the party were quick to question the decision, while her supporters noted the importance of someone who could decisively steer the UK through the uncharted waters of leaving the European Union. The move had consequences. Criticised as either a refreshing honesty or a lapse in the decorum she was known for, May’s opening gambit sparked a wave of media attention and set the tone for a leadership contest unlike any other. It was clear that the new era of Conservative politics demanded a transformation in leadership, and May had made her intentions unmissable. What followed was a battle that would define her legacy — one that began not with subtlety, but with a clear-eyed declaration of ambition. We are now hearing her voice as a player of global significance, trying with great conviction to navigate the geopolitical tempest of Brexit Britain.

The return of Tom Brady from a four-game suspension has dominated sports headlines across the US this weekend, with fans, analysts and even rival teams divided on how it will play out for the New England Patriots in their bid for a sixth Super Bowl title. Brady, who missed the first month of the season after appealing a punishment related to the Deflategate controversy, returned under the bright lights of primetime football on Sunday night in a crucial match against a high-powered Denver Broncos team. The event had all the hallmarks of a season-defining moment, not just for the Patriots, but for the league as a whole. Brady, 38, came back with the same poise and accuracy that made him one of the most decorated quarterbacks in NFL history. On the opening drive of the game, he threaded a 27-yard pass to Julian Edelman to move the chains, a play that was met not just with cheers from the Gillette Stadium faithful, but also with tactical analysis on every television and radio sports programme. "Tom Brady in his element," was the phrase muttered by fans, even as detractors pointed out that the Patriots had already built a solid record over the four-week absence of their star player. Bill Belichick, the Patriots’ head coach and Brady’s long-time partner in success, has often been accused of engineering Brady’s legacy rather than the other way around. Yet the calm confidence with which he let his quarterback take the field once again prompted much media speculation about the future of their professional and personal relationship. For many fans, the game was more than just a test of Brady’s physical readiness. It also served as a read on whether the NFL’s concussion protocols or the ongoing controversy over the league’s handling of former players’ lawsuits will be a growing distraction for future key moments in the season. Analysts noted that while Brady showed no signs of rust, the game was not without its tension. There was a missed throw that was intercepted and a fumble on a sack that drew gasps from even the most ardent supporters. But for every questionable play, there were clutch moments that reminded the world why Brady is still regarded as the man to beat. The Patriots came out on top in the game 28–21, a result that has been widely interpreted as both a message to the league and an omen of things to come.

The family of a Lanarkshire teenager murdered 25 years ago have sharply criticised Scotland’s Crown Office for what they call a “catalogue of failures” in its handling of the case. The teenager, whose death shocked the local community and is still remembered with sadness and anguish, remains a nameless figure to many outside the area. However, for the victim’s relatives, the lack of resolution and perceived sluggishness in the justice system have become a source of deep frustration. In documents released in recent weeks, details emerged of missed opportunities, delayed investigations, and inconsistencies in witness testimony that appear to have hampered the chase for justice. The victim’s family described these findings as “a deeply disturbing reflection on how our loved one’s case was treated” and accused authorities of demonstrating a “lack of urgency and empathy.” The victim’s mother, who has spoken to the press for the first time in years, stated: “It’s 25 years later, and we’re still asking, 'Why was he left in the mud?' We deserve answers. People’s lives were moved on, but ours were left hanging. We have been promised time and again that this will be looked into, and each time it’s nothing but hot air.” The case, which was once high-profile and initially led by experienced detectives, was subsequently passed between several police forces over the years. The Crown Office has since come under scrutiny for seemingly evolving perspectives on the investigation, with internal memos suggesting the case was treated as a “priority” for only a short time before being left to gather dust in the backlog of unsolved crimes. Police Scotland has also faced criticism over the handling of the case. In a statement, the force said it is “fully committed to bringing the responsible person to justice” and has requested new statements from witnesses and a fresh review of evidence. However, the family sees such assurances as hollow given the years they have spent waiting and the fading of critical evidence. “This isn’t about reopening old wounds for us; it’s about closing them,” the mother added. “Justice passed us by when it mattered most. Now, it feels like it was never there at all.” The Crown Office has yet to issue a formal statement to the family’s claims beyond acknowledging the “serious nature of the allegations” and the fact that “all historical cases are subject to standard legal and procedural rigour.”

Emergency services were not called for 11 minutes after the rollercoaster crash at Alton Towers, it has emerged — a delay that has raised serious concerns about the speed of response at the UK’s most iconic theme park. The incident, which occurred during a test run of the Smiler ride on June 2, 2015, left seven people seriously injured when one of the carriages derailed and flipped onto its side. A new report from Warwickshire Police has revealed that the first call to emergency services was made   11 minutes after the crash  , triggering questions about the initial handling of the crisis by the park's staff. The delayed call to 999 means that emergency response procedures, which are critical in incidents involving multiple casualties and entrapment, were significantly delayed. Firefighters and paramedics eventually arrived on the scene to free the riders, some of whom had to be extracted from the upturned carriage in a helicopter rescue. Paramedics later revealed that several of the victims had been incorrectly identified after the crash — a further cause for concern as to how effectively the immediate response was managed. Warwickshire Police details show that the force received the initial 999 call at 22:12 BST, while the incident had taken place at 22:01 BST. The 11-minute interval, during which no emergency call appears to have been made, has become a pivotal issue in the ongoing public inquiry into the crash. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) was appointed to probe the incident after it was discovered that the ride was operated at full speed during the test — a move that defied routine safety protocols. Witnesses reported chaos in the aftermath of the crash as stewards and staff reportedly failed to call for help in a timely manner. Instead, some park employees were seen trying to move the broken ride carriage themselves. The delayed response has now become a central part of the inquiry examining whether the park's internal procedures were inadequate in emergency situations. The report adds to the growing controversy surrounding Alton Towers, which has faced criticism over its maintenance and testing procedures for the Smiler ride. At the time, the park had been undergoing a £70m transformation and rushed to restart operations after a three-month closure. The rushed reopening and the failure to carry out the necessary safety checks set the stage for the accident. Health and Safety Executive CEO Jim O’Flaherty has stated that the inquiry must go beyond technical faults and examine how the park communicated between departments and handled the crisis.

The shadow of scandal is once again looming over Argentina’s political elite as new revelations about the suspicious death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman resurface, with the former president at its centre. Carla Banning, the judge investigating Nisman’s death, has disclosed that the late prosecutor had drafted an arrest warrant against President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner in connection with an investigation into a deadly 2012 terrorist attack on a Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires. The claim has rekindled one of the most explosive political controversies in recent Argentine history, as questions are raised once again about Nisman’s ties to the government and the true cause of his death under mysterious circumstances. Alberto Nisman, who specialised in cases involving national security and anti-terrorism, was found dead in his apartment in the Argentine capital in January 2015. At the time, he had been preparing to testify in court the very next day. A 14-page document was found among his belongings which linked Fernández de Kirchner and several high-ranking officials to the bombing, which killed 85 people and wounded hundreds more. Nisman had long accused the government of obstructing justice by negotiating with Iran over the case under what he claimed was an illegal agreement in exchange for trade concessions. Judge Carla Banning initially ruled Nisman’s death as a suicide, citing evidence of a blood-alcohol level “dangerously high for driving” and statements from experts, but her findings were met with huge public outrage and speculation of foul play. Critics claimed the government’s handling of the probe was a cover-up, while protests erupted in the streets of Buenos Aires. Now, with new details about a potential arrest warrant against Fernández de Kirchner emerging, the controversy has taken on fresh and alarming significance. The Jewish museum attack, carried out by a car bomb, is widely believed to have been orchestrated by the Iran-backed Mexican intelligence services during the 1990s. Nisman had been instrumental in laying the groundwork for Argentina’s first step toward justice, but for years the government resisted sending formal charges to Iran, insisting that international diplomacy could resolve the matter without a trial. This stance drew intense criticism from lawmakers, human rights groups, and the victims' families, who accused the president of prioritising political calculations over justice. In the aftermath of Nisman’s death, his work was upheld and a request for an international arrest warrant for four members of the Iranian government on charges of terrorism was filed.

Majid Haq and Matt Machan seem poles apart. One is a gruff, hard-bitten former Metropolitan Police detective who spent his career investigating some of the UK’s most notorious anti-terror operations, the other is a charismatic and highly intelligent young physics student with aspirations of a career as a broadcaster. Yet the two have recently found themselves bound by a shared purpose: to address the growing crisis within Britain’s education system — particularly in deprived communities. Haq, now 67, retired after a decade-long stint leading counter-terrorism investigations, during which he developed a deep understanding of the role of societal failure in radicalisation. Having grown up in north London’s East End, he has witnessed firsthand how poverty, lack of opportunities, and disengagement from institutions like schools and the justice system can push young people to the margins of society. Machan, who grew up in the suburbs and studied in one of the country’s most prestigious universities, is equally passionate about education. As a television presenter and online content creator, he has used his platform to highlight the science and logic that he believes are central to a successful education. But over the last year, he has become increasingly aware of the challenges facing students from less privileged backgrounds. Their unlikely alliance began at a high-profile education forum, where both were invited to speak on the topic of youth engagement in science and society. What started as a panel discussion quickly turned into a debate and, eventually, a collaboration. Both men, despite their differences in experience and age, have concluded that the UK’s educational challenges are not just academic — they are existential. Haq has called on the government to invest in a new era of mentorship and school partnerships between professionals from law enforcement, science, and the media to inspire underprivileged pupils. Machan, meanwhile, remains focused on how technology and creative teaching can bridge the gap in the classroom. Their partnership is progressing — with tentative plans to launch a pilot scheme in some of London’s most deprived boroughs in the next 12 months. But both admit that their work will only succeed if there is real political will and financial backing. “We’re not scientists trying to grow worlds in petri dishes,” Haq said. “We’re trying to grow minds. And if you ignore the soil, you won’t get the flowers.” Machan, for his part, is equally determined.

Motherwell secured a vital fifth-place finish in the Scottish Premiership with a crucial 2-1 victory over Ross County at Fir Park on a chilly Sunday afternoon. The Steelmen now look set to clinch a top-six finish for the first time in 13 seasons, thanks in large part to a composed display that saw two key goals from on-loan captain Stephen Pearson and a late goal from substitute Keith Lasley. The win ensured that Motherwell continue to chase tenth-placed Ross County in this year's top-flight campaign but, more importantly, confirmed their status as one of the leagues' most improved sides. Following a season of steady progress under manager Mark McGhee, the Lanarkshire outfit made sure they rounded off their campaign on a triumphant note. Midfielder Pearson, who captained the side on the left of a midfield three, was instrumental from the outset, scoring the opening goal just after the half-hour mark. It came from a swift counterattack, with Pearson latching onto a through-ball before coolly netting in the box to send the home supporters into raptures. The visitors responded strongly in the second half, and were almost level when a long-range effort from Championship-winning captain Gary Harkins rattled the crossbar. But credit to Motherwell, who remained resolute in defense and pressed high, exposing County’s unfamiliarity with such aggressive tactics at the top level. Lasley, brought on in the 78th minute, provided the perfect finishing touch to the contest when he volleyed the ball home from Liam Lindsay’s cross, sealing the victory just before the full-time whistle. Lasley’s substitute goal proved to be his third of the campaign—more than any other Motherwell player—and underlines his growing importance under McGhee. Ross County, despite the defeat, did earn their 12th clean sheet of the season, thanks to an impressive performance from goalkeeper Mark Stein. The goalkeeper made several vital saves in the first half, notably parrying efforts from both Pearson and Burgos, whose range of passing ability continued to impress. This victory will do wonders for Motherwell’s confidence as they prepare for next season, when they will be looking to consolidate their position in the top half of the table. With young players coming through and experienced heads like Pearson leading by example, the club is building momentum for a bright future. For Ross County, the defeat leaves them in 10th place, seven points adrift of seventh-placed Hearts and in need of a significant push in the remaining matches of the season to climb out of the relegation zone.

Manchester United manager José Mourinho has confirmed that a potential transfer of England captain Wayne Rooney is being considered, saying it is "not ruled out" as the January transfer window approaches. The revelation comes amid growing speculation that the 29-year-old could leave Old Trafford after nearly 15 years at the club — a prospect that has stunned fans and raised questions about the future of one of United’s most decorated players. Rooney's form has dipped in recent months, with the striker managing just one Premier League goal in January so far. Injuries and a drop in match fitness have seen him rotate between the starting XI and the bench, with younger talents such as Marcus Rashford, Anthony Martial and Romelu Lukaku enjoying a strong start to the season. When asked about the possibility of Rooney’s departure during a recent press conference, Mourinho remained non-committal but hinted at the possibility of a move, saying: "We are in January. There are rules for January, and sometimes it makes sense, sometimes it doesn’t. Wayne’s situation... I don’t want to complicate the answer. No, I don’t want to rule out anything." The news has sent shockwaves through the United fanbase, with many supporters taking to social media to express their concern. Rooney is one of only ten players to have won the club’s Player of the Year award more than once and remains one of United’s – and English football’s – all-time leading scorers with 253 Premier League goals. Speaking after the manager’s announcement, a spokesperson for the club said: "We are aware of the speculation, but at this time, there is no official confirmation of a transfer. Wayne remains a valued player at the club, and any decisions regarding his future will be made in the best interest of Manchester United." Mourinho, who has previously praised Rooney for his "professionalism and loyalty," has not confirmed any shortfall in his relationship with the player. However, with United currently 10th in the Premier League table and in dire need of reorganisation, pressure is high on the Portuguese manager to make decisive moves in the January window. Rooney, whose contract with United runs until 2019, has not publicly commented on the speculation. Transfer talks are expected to intensify in the coming days, with clubs in various European leagues reportedly keeping close interest in a potential move.

England opener Alex Hales continued to struggle with the bat on day two of their three-day tour match against a South Africa Invitation XI at the Senwes Park cricket ground in Potchefstroom. Hales, who has been tipped as a potential star of the upcoming ICC Cricket World Cup, managed just seven runs before departing, maintaining concerns over his form and confidence with the bat in one-day cricket. The tourists resumed their innings on day two on a precarious 34 for two, having suffered a top-order collapse on the opening day. Hales, as the third wicket to fall, left the hosts needing further reinforcement, but the decision to promote Dawid Malan to open alongside Jonny Bairstow appeared to offer the partnership stability. Bairstow and Malan extended the total to 93 for three at the close, offering a glimmer of hope after what has been a difficult day in the field and at the crease for England’s batsmen. This is the second successive low score from Hales, following his 14 on the first day, and will add to the scrutiny surrounding the aggressive left-hander, who has fluctuated between monumental success and technical inconsistency in recent months. Hales, who plays his domestic cricket for Nottinghamshire, is expected to be a crucial component in England’s limited-overs plans. His mix of power and shot selection has made him a potent figure in the middle order, but recent performances have raised questions about his readiness for the pressures of international one-day cricket at the highest level. The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has scheduled this tour in preparation for the World Cup, which begins in March 2015, and each match is seen as an opportunity to fine-tune player fitness and strategy. However, as Hales remains in the shadow of Steve Smith and the reliable pair of Malan and Joe Root, the question remains as to whether the 26-year-old can rediscover the form that earned him his Test debut and a place on the World Cup radar. Meanwhile, South Africa’s Invitation XI, captained by the experienced Jacques Kallis, demonstrated their own cricketing pedigree, with their pace and spin bowlers exploiting the good grass pitches that have become a hallmark of the high-altitude venues in the Free State region. The match, set over three days, is the fourth of England’s five warm-up fixtures as they prepare for the World Cup qualifiers and the subsequent global event.

Volkswagen has unveiled sweeping plans to cut 30,000 jobs worldwide as the German automotive giant accelerates its transformation towards electric and digital mobility amid shifting market dynamics and financial pressures. Around 23,000 of these job cuts will hit Germany, the company’s home country and one of the biggest car manufacturing powerhouses in the world, sparking fears of a deepening crisis within the industry. The announcement has been met with shock and dismay from workers, policy-makers, and industry observers, who see it as a stark sign of the upheaval caused by the global shift to electric vehicles (EVs). The firm revealed the plans as part of a broader restructuring strategy, which also includes the closure of three German plants, the relocation of some production to the Czech Republic, and the phasing out of certain combustion engine models. The move highlights the increasing challenges traditional automakers face in the face of fierce global competitors—particularly in China and the United States—and rapidly evolving consumer priorities. Volkswagen has previously faced a wave of criticism and declining sales, and this latest decision appears to be part of a long-term effort to reduce costs and align with its monumental "New Auto" strategy, which aims to be powered by software, data, and electrification. The Wolfsburg-based company has signaled its commitment to becoming the leader in EV production, but the transition is proving costly – both financially and in terms of human capital. Union representatives have already expressed concerns that the cuts will disproportionately affect older workers and exacerbate existing inequalities within the firm’s workforce. Negotiations with Germany’s powerful IG Metall union are now expected to intensify, with a focus on protecting jobs, retraining workers, and securing financial compensation for those affected. The German government, under pressure from both environmentalists and trade unions, has been urged to take action to support the transition. Chancellor Olaf Scholz’s administration has yet to respond formally to the announcement, but sources suggest officials are preparing a package of incentive measures to aid workers in retraining and to support affected communities. Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume described the job cuts as a “painful but necessary step” to ensure the long-term competitiveness of the company. “We are not cutting jobs to cut for the sake of it,” he explained in a press statement. “These measures are essential to steer us through the transformation of the automotive industry and to emerge even stronger in the global market.”

Jeremy Corbyn has ruled out making "false promises" about tackling migration if Labour wins the next election, saying it would be untrue to pander to "demagoguery" on the issue. The Labour leader, who himself is a long-time advocate of robust support for European citizens in the UK, made the remarks as the party continues to struggle to find a way to reconcile its pro-EU position with growing public concern over high levels of immigration. In a speech to a gathering of policy supporters in Manchester, Mr Corbyn said Labour had to be "honest and clear" about its beliefs and the role of immigration in the UK, but warned that promises to slash numbers would not reflect the reality of the UK's economy and social fabric. “I am not going to make false promises that the turkey will vote for Christmas,” he said. “I do not believe, and Labour does not believe, in the kind of political demagoguery that suggests immigration is simply a problem to be solved through restrictions alone.” The statement comes amid continuous pressure from some in his own party’s left wing as well as parts of the broader electorate who demand a tough approach to migration. The Conservatives have made reducing net migration a core policy since the 2010s, a focus that many credit with helping to shift public opinion toward Brexit in 2016. Mr Corbyn, however, has remained steadfast in denying that migration levels are a simple, direct issue that the government can control. The Labour leader argued that migration to the UK was driven by a global economy and geopolitical factors outside the control of any one government. “Our hospitals and universities rely on international talent. Our industries need workers. We are a diverse and welcoming country,” he said. “We can and must manage migration carefully – but promises to slash it for the sake of winning points are not only unrealistic but dangerous.” His comments come as Labour continues to debate its future strategy in the upcoming general election. With the party still trying to rebuild after its defeat in 2019, the response to migration will play a major role in shaping its appeal among both new and traditional voters. Immigration has remained a politically charged issue, with the UK still grappling with post-Brexit immigration systems that have seen both a sustained skills shortage and a growing backlog in visa processing.

Portugal international defender Bruno Alves has declared his ambitions at Ibrox, insisting he joined Rangers to win major trophies after completing his high-profile transfer from Italian side Cagliari on a two-year deal. The 35-year-old centre-back, who becomes the club’s latest high-profile continental signing, wasted no time in stating his intention during a press conference at the weekend. “This is about winning,” Alves said. “I have a big motivation to come to this fantastic club and do my job to bring more silverware.” Alves, capped over 50 times by his country and known for his physical presence and aerial dominance, joins the Gers after a five-year stint in Serie A. His arrival is the latest in a summer of change for Rangers as the club look to challenge for domestic honours following their return to the top flight of Scottish football. Speaking on his decision to join in the world’s oldest football league, Alves added: “It’s a project with a lot of ambition, and I feel I can help this club achieve big things. There is a massive passion here for football and a great fan base, and that motivates me even more.” The Portuguese is expected to start the 2024–25 season as a key figure in the backline, with manager Giovanni van Bronckhorst looking to build a squad capable of dominating the Scottish Premiership once again. Alves brings experience from Champions League and Europa League campaigns, as well as a proven track record in high-pressure games. His signing has been widely welcomed by Rangers fans, who are eager to see an experienced defender bring leadership and calm to a club that has been building a trophy-winning structure over the past few seasons. Alves’ presence is expected to add depth and composure, particularly in European fixtures, where his knowledge of continental competitions could prove invaluable. The move had been in the pipeline for weeks, and the formal announcement has been followed by a flurry of social media activity from both the player and Rangers. Alves took to Instagram to say: “Proud to be a #RangersFC. Let’s go!” With pre-season preparations already underway, all eyes will be on Alves to settle into the team and prove himself as a vital cog in the side’s championship aspirations. If he delivers on his promise, he could be set for a successful return to Scottish football after his early success in the 2000s with Celtic.

Police forces across the United Kingdom are to launch an unprecedented operation to tackle the trafficking of young girls who are flown abroad to undergo Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). The initiative, announced by the Home Office, involves joint working with Transport for London, airports, and international partners to identify children at risk of being smuggled out of the country for the procedure, often against their will. FGM is a form of violence against women and girls, with no health benefits, but serious physical and psychological consequences. The practice, involving partial or total removal of female external genitalia, is illegal in the UK under the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003. Despite this, it is estimated that more than 60,000 girls in Britain are at risk of FGM, with an average of 78 cases per year involving British girls who are taken overseas for the procedure. The operation comes after an alarming rise in reported cases and concerns from charities and health professionals that girls are being hidden from authorities after their families are alerted to social workers' investigations. Home Secretary, Sajid Javid, stated, “There is no place for FGM here, and we will not tolerate this heinous crime in any form. We are determined to stop families taking their daughters out of the country to be subjected to it.” The operation will involve increased monitoring at key departure points such as Heathrow, Gatwick and other regional airports, with trained police officers and Border Force officers cooperating to identify potential cases. Schools and community groups will also be encouraged to report any concerns about children at risk. Charities, including the FGM Centre and the Anti-Sexist Women’s Group, welcomed the move as a much-needed escalation in the fight against FGM. A spokesperson for the FGM Centre said: “This is a proactive step towards ending the culture of silence around FGM. It is vital that police and other agencies work together to protect vulnerable girls before they even leave the country.” Campaigners have also called for greater education and support for girls at high risk, especially in communities where FGM is culturally entrenched. While the operation is primarily focused on preventing outbound travel, long-term solutions will depend on changing attitudes and challenging the deeply rooted belief that FGM is necessary. Meanwhile, a new hotline and confidential reporting system will be rolled out, allowing members of the public to report suspected cases without fear of retribution.

Rail Chaos Looms as Three Major Companies Face RMT Strikes   A wave of rail disruptions is set to hit passengers in the coming weeks as the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union announces industrial action across three major rail operators. The strike, which has been months in the making, is the latest in a series of disputes between transport workers and employers over issues including pay, job security and the use of zero-hours contracts. The RMT has confirmed that its members employed by Arriva Trains Wales, Northern Rail and Grand Central will withdraw their labour as part of the coordinated action. The union said the strikes, which are scheduled to take place over the Easter period, will cause major disruption and warned that services will be “severely curtailed” on the affected routes. The dispute comes amid ongoing tensions in the rail industry, where union leaders argue rail companies and the government have not done enough to address the concerns of frontline staff. RMT general secretary Mick Cash said the strikes were a direct response to “unfair treatment and a lack of progress” in negotiations. “Our members have been let down time and time again, and that’s why we are taking this challenging but necessary step,” Cash said in a statement. “Passengers will be affected, but the government and rail companies have failed to listen for far too long.” The first of the planned walkouts is due on Easter Friday, with further strikes scheduled for Good Friday and again the following week. Each of the affected companies has already issued statements trying to downplay the disruption and urging passengers to book in advance for alternative transport. Arriva Trains Wales confirmed that services between Cardiff and south Wales will be impacted, with only a very limited number of trains expected to run. Passenger Paul Roberts, from Swansea, told the BBC: “It’s just getting worse every time. I can’t believe the government doesn’t have a plan in place for this kind of disruption. We shouldn’t be left to sort it out for ourselves.” Northern Rail, which operates services across the North of England, will see its busiest routes hit hardest, including the frequent services between Liverpool and Manchester. Grand Central, which connects London to Edinburgh passing through major cities like Leeds and Newcastle, has also warned of major service cancellations. The UK government and rail companies are now under pressure to reach a compromise ahead of the strikes.

Chat apps that promise to prevent your messages from being accessed by strangers are facing renewed scrutiny in the wake of last week’s terror attack on a London bridge, as lawmakers and law enforcement demand more transparency from tech companies. The attack, which left three people dead and multiple others injured, has intensified questions about the role of encrypted private messaging platforms in enabling extremist activity and whether safeguards can exist without compromising user privacy. Among the apps under renewed focus are services such as WhatsApp and Signal, which use end-to-end encryption to ensure that only the communicating users can read what’s sent. These features, touted as essential for privacy and security by developers, have also become a source of concern for investigators who argue they make it nearly impossible to monitor suspicious activity. Home Secretary Amber Rudd has stressed the need for the government and technology giants to work together to tackle the issue. “We must ensure that the safety of the public is not undermined in the name of privacy,” she said in a statement. “There must be no safe space for those who would do us harm.” The discussion comes at a sensitive time as global governments, including the UK’s, push for legislation to grant law enforcement more access to encrypted communication under certain conditions. Prime Minister Theresa May has previously called for technology companies to “find a way” to allow authorities to decrypt messages in cases involving national security, a stance that has drawn criticism from civil liberties groups and Silicon Valley engineers who warn of the risks of opening so-called “backdoors” into secure systems. Speaking after the attack, the Metropolitan Police confirmed that it is investigating whether messages exchanged on private platforms may have played a role in the planning of the incident. While officials have not yet revealed the full extent of what was uncovered, law enforcement sources have indicated that the attack appears to have been crude but meticulously executed, possibly by individuals radicalised online. In response to the growing pressure, Facebook, which owns WhatsApp, reiterated its commitment to user privacy. A spokesperson said the company is “cooperating fully with law enforcement to ensure justice for the victims of the attack,” while reaffirming its stance that encryption is crucial for protecting users from cybercrime and surveillance. Critics, however, argue that restricting encryption could lead to a dangerous precedent, as unauthorised access to data could expose users to identity theft, hacking, and government overreach.

Senior US Republican Senator Lindsey Graham has claimed that Russian hackers accessed his campaign email account, adding his name to an expanding list of high-profile political figures and institutions allegedly targeted by foreign cyber intrusions. Graham, a prominent voice in US foreign policy and national security, made the revelation during an appearance on Fox News on Tuesday. He described how he discovered the breach and emphasized the potential threat it posed to the integrity of democratic institutions. “I found out that my campaign e-mail was hacked by cyber intrusions that were traced back to Moscow,” Graham said. “These are not just random attacks; they’re coordinated. They're looking for weaknesses, and they're trying to exploit them.” Graham, who represents South Carolina and is a vocal advocate for a strong US stance against Russian aggression, said the breach was uncovered by security professionals who found evidence of unauthorized access. He stressed the need for the US government to take these threats more seriously and to enhance its cybersecurity defences at both the national and individual levels. The senator’s remarks come amid growing concerns about Russian interference in US elections, with the 2016 presidential campaign having been the most high-profile example of cyber espionage targeting American political institutions. Since then, cyberattacks on both political figures and private entities have continued, with intelligence agencies and cybersecurity experts warning that such threats are on the rise. Graham warned against complacency from both government officials and the American public. “We need to treat these threats as the national security issue they are,” he said. “This isn’t just about protecting e-mails or personal data – it’s about protecting our democracy from being manipulated.” His comments echo warnings from US intelligence agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, both of whom have consistently urged politicians, businesses, and individuals to safeguard against cyber threats. Recent statements about escalating cyberattacks from Russian state-backed groups have also come from officials within the White House and the broader intelligence community. Senator Graham is not the first national figure to speak publicly about being targeted. Prominent Democrats and Republicans alike have reported incidents of suspected Russian cyber intrusion, underscoring the bipartisan nature of the threat. However, his assertion brings renewed attention to how personal campaign accounts – which can hold sensitive communications and data – are being used as points of entry.

The body of a Colorado pastor who had embarked on a treasure hunt for a reported $2 million (1.5 million) has been found in the Rio Grande River in New Mexico, more than a month after he was reported missing, local authorities have confirmed. The Reverend Jim Dannemiller, 58, from Estes Park, Colorado, vanished on December 20 while reportedly searching for the treasure of George Maxwell, a 19th-century rancher and prospector. Maxwell’s reported fortune, hidden beneath a ranch in Las Vegas, New Mexico, has long been the subject of local legend. Dannemiller, an amateur historian and treasure hunter, was said to believe the treasure was still buried, and the search had become a personal obsession in recent years. On January 30, his body was discovered in the Rio Grande, approximately 90 miles from the last place he was seen. New Mexico state police confirmed the identification, and while details of the cause of death remain under investigation, it is believed that Dannemiller may have drowned after getting caught in the fast-moving currents near Casitas, south of Las Vegas. Dannemiller’s wife, Sheila, immediately became a key figure in the search, leading a private effort alongside several amateur detectives and treasure hunters. She had spoken to media outlets during the search, describing her husband as “passionate” and “driven” by a love of history and uncovering long-forgotten stories. “He wanted to know what happened to Maxwell’s gold. He didn’t do it for the money,” she said. “He just believed in the story.” George Maxwell, the man at the center of the mystery, had lived at a ranch in the 1880s and was said to have buried his gold and silver about five decades before his death in 1908. Tales of the treasure’s exact location have long circulated among locals, but no one has successfully found it. Dannemiller believed the treasure, valued at $2 million, was hidden under Maxwell’s original home on the site, believed to have been a landlocked cattle ranch. Authorities have not ruled out foul play, but initial reports suggest that Dannemiller may have disappeared during a river crossing or after misjudging the river’s strength. “These can be dangerous conditions for anyone, even the most experienced of people,” said a spokesperson for the New Mexico State Police. Dannemiller’s search for Maxwell’s treasure had captured the attention of local communities in both Colorado and New Mexico.

The United Nations has called for an urgent investigation into a chilling video allegedly showing Syrian rebels executing captured government-aligned soldiers or militiamen, claiming it could constitute a war crime. The footage, obtained by international media, appears to show unarmed men being hauled into a room and shot in the head as frightened onlookers watch. The coordinates of the location and the clothing of the victims suggest the incident took place in Idlib province – a stronghold for a number of rebel groups, including Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) and other factions that have long been accused of human rights abuses. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has described the video as "deeply disturbing and potentially indicative of a serious violation of international humanitarian law." Speaking from Geneva, a UN official said: "The apparent extrajudicial execution of captured persons, if confirmed, would be a grave breach of the rules of war and indicative of a war crime, as outlined under the Geneva Conventions." Syria's brutal civil war, now entering its 14th year, has seen both government and rebel forces accused of systematic atrocities by international bodies and human rights organisations. However, evidence of such clear-cut war crimes committed by rebel forces is rare and difficult to substantiate. The UN has previously accused the Syrian government and its allies, including Russia and Iran, of carrying out mass killings, torture, and enforced disappearances against civilians and combatants. The new video, if proven to be authentic, will place the spotlight once again on the armed opposition, which has also faced accusations of using child soldiers and committing summary executions. In a recent report, the UN documented an increase in civilian casualties and human rights violations across areas held by various non-state actors in the north-west, particularly in Idlib and surrounding rural areas. Analysts note that the area has seen a chaotic mix of groups with overlapping allegiances and often shifting leadership, making accountability even more complicated. The video has already sparked outrage on social media, with many calling for international action against those responsible. A spokesperson for the UN’s human rights office told the BBC: "This video is another grim reminder of the widespread suffering endured by the Syrian people as numerous groups continue to flout international law." While the UN urges an independent inquiry, the video also raises difficult questions about how such evidence can be swiftly and effectively acted upon in the vast, fractured theatre of the Syrian conflict.

Ciaran Clark scored a stunning late header as Newcastle United produced a remarkable turnaround to draw 2-2 against Bristol City at St James’ Park on Saturday afternoon. The result saw the Magpies, who stared defeat in the face for much of the match, salvage a point in front of their home fans, with the timing of Clark’s 87th-minute equaliser sparking wild celebrations and providing a dramatic end to an enthralling encounter. The visitors, currently rooted to the bottom of the Championship, had looked on course for a vital win in their battle to avoid relegation, having built a two-goal advantage through goals from Jota and Eboue frozen to confusion. The match began cautiously, with both sides seeking to settle into the conditions. It was Bristol City who broke the deadlock in the 18th minute when winger Jota, on loan from Liverpool, latched onto a loose pass before cutting inside and firing an excellent curling shot into the top corner. The Robins then doubled their lead just before half-time in controversial fashion. A long throw-in was delivered into the box, where Eboue rose highest to head home, but Newcastle players protested that the ball had come off a raised arm. Replays, however, showed the referee had correctly adjudged the ball as in play, much to the frustration of the home side. The second half saw Newcastle throw everything at their opponents in a bid to claw their way back into the game. Substitute Aleksandar Mitrovic came close with a powerful header that struck the post, while Matt Ritchie’s fierce drive was brilliantly saved by Bristol goalkeeper Pascal Groß. However, just as time was running out, the Magpies made their breakthrough. A fine corner from Daryl Murphy was met by Clark, whose towering header looped past Groß and into the net to send the home crowd into raptures. The equaliser marked a remarkable moment for the 29-year-old centre-back, who has endured a tough season both on and off the pitch. With the result, Newcastle remain in mid-table, while Bristol City’s struggles continue as they search for any form of stability in a dire campaign. The draw sparked widespread social media reactions, with fans praising Clark's heroics and labelling it one of the standout moments in the recent run of Championship fixtures. Earlier in the week, manager Eddie Howe had urged his side to show more resilience in the face of adversity, a message clearly not lost on his players as they delivered in the dying moments.

When Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani succeeded his father as emir of energy-rich Qatar in June, few observers knew very much about him. But within months, the 33-year-old had thrust himself into the spotlight with a sweeping reform of the leadership of state institutions and a carefully orchestrated announcement of his new priorities for the tiny but influential Gulf state. The changes signal both an abrupt shift and a continuation of the policies pursued by Sheikh Tamim’s father, Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, who stepped down last year after nearly a decade as emir. Sheikh Tamim, who was born in 1980 and educated at military academies in both the UK and the US, has until now been described only in vague terms by Qatari officials, who have long placed an eccentric emphasis on protecting the privacy of their royal family. Following his father, he was said to be the eldest of four sons of the emir and is generally believed to have received a British-style education before rejoining the Al Thani royal pantheon. Sheikh Tamim’s first decree showed both the flexibility and the assertiveness of his approach—replacing the heads of all seven top state councils, including the development and legisla­tion councils, and dissolving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in a move that surprised many regional analysts. The restructuring was accompanied by televised addresses from the new emir, in which he spoke in unusually personal terms about his country’s values and its future. In these broadcasts, Sheikh Tamim was shown in a range of settings that made him seem distinctly more modern than his father: fishing on the Arabian Gulf, climbing a camel, playing football, or speaking with students about the importance of education in the 21st century. This public persona has been a dramatic contrast to the reserved and somewhat remote image often associated with the Qatari royal family. Both Qatar and its leaders have long been peripheral to the grand political and economic narratives of the Middle East, but that has changed in recent years. Under the late emir Hamad, Qatar became a major player in global diplomacy, funding Al Jazeera, backing civil wars in Syria and Libya, and building strategic alliances with groups like Hamas and Hezbollah. Sheikh Tamim’s apparent desire to assert his own imprint on the country’s affairs suggests he is intent not only on maintaining his father's foreign policy course but on charting a more personal one.

Heroic Airman Reflects on Dramatic Rescue of Stranded Ship   A Royal Navy airman involved in one of the most dramatic sea rescues of recent years has revealed how the harrowing operation remains vividly fixed in his mind. Paul Savage, 36, described the experience as “burnt into my memory” after helping rescue all 18 crew members of a container ship that became stranded on rocks off the coast of Scotland last year. The ordeal, which unfolded in freezing temperatures and towering seas, marked a tense climax to a summer of extreme weather and maritime emergencies in the North Sea. The vessel, the  MV Titan , ran aground near the Faroe Islands in October during a powerful storm, leaving the crew battling relentless waves and plummeting temperatures that dropped to just four degrees Celsius. The ship’s captain, fearing the structure was on the verge of collapse, made the desperate call for assistance. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency swiftly deployed a search-and-rescue helicopter based in Prestwick, Scotland. Mr Savage was in the cockpit as the rescue unfolded over 48 hours. The operation required multiple daring flights to extract each crew member from the ship’s precarious decks and transfer them safely to waiting lifeboats. Mr Savage, a fleet aircrew member and son of a former RAF commander, described the intensity of the mission. “There was no time to think. You just do it,” he said. “But every moment is seared into your brain. The faces of those men as they clung to the winch, the roar of the wind, the spray from the waves — it doesn’t leave you.” The rescuers faced chaotic conditions, with wind gusts reaching up to 70mph and visibility reduced to near zero. Despite the peril, not one member of the crew was lost. Each individual was pulled to safety using the helicopter’s rescue hoist, often standing on what little flat surface remained of the listing vessel. Mr Savage, who has completed over 350 search-and-rescue missions since joining the service in 2009, described the  Titan  operation as one of the most demanding of his career. “It’s not just the physical challenge. It’s the emotional toll. You see people in fear, and you want to act faster than your body will allow,” he said. “You know you’re putting your life on the line to save others, but it’s what you train for — and you don’t expect thanks.”

The High Court hearing that concluded earlier this week marked one of the most intensively scrutinised legal affairs in recent British history. Over three days, the courtroom bore witness to a collision of legal theory, constitutional principle, and the shifting sands of political accountability in the United Kingdom. The topic at the heart of the case—argued by some of the country’s most distinguished barristers and observed closely by political and legal commentators—was described by one participant as an issue of “fundamental constitutional importance,” with ramifications stretching far beyond the four walls of the courtroom. The hearing brought together leading legal figures from the Bar and the judiciary, elevating the proceedings into not only a test of legal robustness but also a barometer of the health and equilibrium of the nation’s constitutional framework. It was a rare moment where the High Court functioned not just as a venue for adjudicating disputes, but as a guardian of constitutional values and democratic norms. Judges, counsel, and even members of the public, gathered in anticipation, knew they were not merely observing a routine case, but witnessing the articulation of enduring tensions between the branches of the state. Central to the matter was a question over the role, limits, and responsibilities of both the executive and the legislate in regulating key public affairs—a matter that, since the Brexit referendum in 2016 and the ongoing evolution of post-devolution governance, has become increasingly contested. As experts in administrative law prepared to weigh in, constitutional law scholars found themselves in positions to theorise and predict the possible implications of any judgment. For the British public, the proceedings came at a time when trust in institutions is often assumed rather than given, and when transparency and democratic legitimacy are fiercely questioned. The courtroom echoed with echoes of historical precedent—from Margery’s case to key moments in the development of parliamentary sovereignty—while also setting the stage for the next chapter in the UK’s constitutional story. As the dust settles from this landmark hearing, one thing is clear: the outcome, whenever it comes, will not merely settle the rights of one party against another. It will speak to the future shape of the United Kingdom and how its constitutional pillars hold firm—or strain under the pressures of a changing world. As such, this was not just a legal case. It was a defining moment in the ongoing conversation about the nature of British democracy.

A Philosophy on Mortality: The Timeless Wisdom of W. Somerset Maugham   The British novelist and short-story writer W. Somerset Maugham often peppered his works with philosophical reflections, blending sharp wit with deep human insight. Among his many memorable quotations, one in particular stands as a stark, yet oddly comforting, commentary on life’s inescapable end: “Dying is a very dull, dreary affair,” he once said. A stark observation, yet one that sparked intrigue, prompting him to suggest, “Have nothing whatever to do with it.” The quote has since resonated through generations of readers and writers alike, offering not just a vivid portrayal of death, but also a pragmatic, perhaps even stoic, way to live. Maugham, known for his unflinching realism and keen psychological insight, approached the topic of death with the same dispassionate clarity present in his fiction. Living most of his life in the early to mid-20th century, he wrote during a time when death loomed more visibly in the public consciousness — not tucked behind assisted-dying debates and modern palliative care, but present in everyday life, often sudden and unceremonious. His quote, while pithy, is emblematic of the era’s more pragmatic attitude: face death, but do not linger in it. “Have nothing to do with it” is often interpreted as a call to live life to its fullest while the chance remains — don’t dwell on what you cannot change or what will one day happen to everyone. The line may also reflect Maugham’s broader lifestyle. A man who lived a long and adventurous life, he was unafraid to travel, write, and engage with people from all walks of life — whether in the Prime Minister’s drawing room or among the lower classes in his stories. To Maugham, death was an event to be respected, but not romanticised. It was not to be a focus for ruminations, but rather for the pursuit of experiences that mattered while one was alive. His views have been echoed in modern discourse on mortality, with scientists and philosophers questioning whether extending life is always the best goal. In recent years, there has been a growing movement toward the idea of 'dignity in dying', with various campaigns highlighting the importance of autonomy and a peaceful end. Maugham's notion of confronting death's dull finality is seen as antithetical to these modern ideological shifts, but perhaps complementing them. After all, if death is to be met with serenity and minimal fuss, then it perhaps also makes sense to live with vibrancy and earnestness in the time before it.

Thousands of Malaysian opposition supporters have poured into the streets of Kuala Lumpur in a dramatic display of dissent over allegations of widespread electoral fraud in recent national elections, ignoring warnings from police that the protest was illegal. The rally, held after opposition groups claimed votes had been rigged in key constituencies, marked one of the largest public demonstrations in the country in years and saw crowds waving anti-government banners while chanting for electoral reform and democratic accountability. The protest, convened by a coalition of opposition parties under the umbrella of the Pakatan Harapan alliance, comes amid growing public frustration over what it describes as deeply flawed and unfair election practices. Preliminary results, which handed Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob’s united coalition a surprising majority, prompted immediate challenges, with opposition leaders accusing authorities of gerrymandering, vote suppression, and irregularities in the voting process. Organisers of the rally called for a special parliamentary inquiry into the allegations and for the appointment of an independent electoral commission. They also demanded a re-run of votes in several contested constituencies. Police in Kuala Lumpur ordered the dispersal of the protest, citing the absence of a permit and the public assembly act, which requires prior approval for large-scale gatherings. However, rather than deterring attendance, the police ultimatum appeared to galvanise support, as thousands braved the possibility of arrest to make their voices heard. The protesters marched from downtown Kuala Lumpur to a nearby symbolic location, with some confronting police lines and refusing to disperse. Several arrests were reported as tensions rose at the scene, though no major incidents of violence were recorded. The election, held in November, marked a dramatic reversal of fortune for the ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) and its coalition partners, who had lost power in 2018 after decades in office. The most recent result has sparked fierce political debate and brought renewed questions over the integrity of Malaysia’s democratic process. Opposition leaders have gained momentum in recent months, capitalizing on public anger over corruption scandals and calls for a cleaner, more transparent government. They argue that the latest election was a missed opportunity for Malaysians to consolidate democratic gains and instead set the country back. Prime Minister Ismail Sabri’s office has denied the allegations and defended the election process, stating that all procedures were followed correctly and that the results must be respected. Earlier in the day, a senior government minister accused the opposition of using the rally as a pretext to destabilise the country.

The Metropolitan Police found itself at the centre of a fresh controversy on Tuesday after a report revealed that errors and misuse in the handling of communications data had led to the arrest of 13 innocent people since 2014. The findings, made public by the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner (OPCC) for London, have raised serious questions about the safeguards surrounding the use of digital evidence and the potential for miscarriages of justice. The report highlights that thirteen individuals were wrongly stopped and questioned under PACE (Police and Criminal Evidence Act) powers due to mistakes made in the retrieval and interpretation of mobile phone records. In some cases, incorrect names or numbers were provided to officers, while in others, data was accessed without proper authorisation, leading to people being wrongly suspected of involvement in crimes such as drug dealing, theft and violent crimes. Ten of the thirteen had the charges dropped following further investigation and two of the incidents led to complaints being made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). One of the cases detailed in the report involves a woman from Croydon who was arrested on suspicion of drug dealing after a database error linked her phone number to a drug network. Despite having no prior criminal record, she was detained for several hours before being released without charge and only later discovering that her details had been mistakenly cross-referenced. She told investigators the experience left her "deeply traumatised". According to the watchdog, the Metropolitan Police acknowledges the errors and has since implemented training to improve the vetting of communications data. However, the report criticises the lack of oversight during the period in which the mistakes occurred and calls upon the force to conduct a full review of its handling of digital evidence. The use of communications data has been a powerful tool in modern policing, enabling officers to trace individuals and their interactions through phone records and web activity. But such powers also carry the risk of abuse or misuse, and the findings are the latest in a string of reports warning about the dangers of over-reliance on digital evidence without proper safeguards. Sir Ian Johnston, Metropolitan Police Commissioner, issued a written statement in response to the report, apologising to those affected and promising to ensure such mistakes did not happen again. He added that the police service was working closely with the OPCC to improve its protocols and "restore public confidence in the way we use communications data."

Aberdeen Makes Strides in Europa League Triumph   Aberdeen secured a crucial victory on Thursday night as they claimed a 2-0 win against Siroki Brijeg in their Europa League qualifier in Bosnia, propelling themselves further into European competition with a display marked by resilience and efficiency. Goals in the second half from Greg Stewart and Gary Mackay-Steven proved the decisive factor in what was a challenging match on foreign soil. The Scottish Premiership side, which boasted a strong attendance and a vibrant support base despite being far from home, showcased determination and tactical discipline to seal the victory and set up a potential first-leg tie with a Cypriot Football Association First Division representative in the next round. The Pittodrie-based club, which has made appearances across Europe in recent years, including numerous UEFA Cup and Europa League campaigns, appears to be finding its stride early in this season's continental journey. A commanding 3-0 first-leg win at home at the weekend gave the Dons a considerable advantage going into this match in Tuzla, but the Bosnian squad, Siroki Brijeg, came to play with purpose and aggression. Indeed, the visitors faced a determined and vociferous home crowd in a land where football is still passionately followed, and where opposition fans are often known to be vocal—and sometimes physically aggressive—with their protest. Despite initial nerves, the Aberdeen backline, anchored by the experienced Declan Glass and backed up by the energetic Ryan Jack in midfield, displayed strong defensive awareness. Goalkeeper Joe Lewis, ever the reliable figure, made two crucial stops in the first half to deny Siroki from climbing ahead. His second-half display was no less impressive, as he continued to command the penalty area and thwart several set-piece attempts. However, it was the goalscorers who turned the match in the Dons’ favor. Greg Stewart, the clinical forward known for his sharp instincts in front of goal, broke the deadlock with a well-timed run to the near post after a precise cross from Ryan Christie. Minutes later, Gary Mackay-Steven, who had shown his usual flair on the right flank, sealed the evening’s outcome when he curled a beautiful shot from 20 yards beyond the outstretched fingertips of the Siroki keeper. The result was met with celebration among the Dons fans, who had made the long journey to support their team in challenging conditions.

Spanish scientists Dr. Bernabé Ruíz and Professor José Moya found themselves staring in disbelief at the results blinking back at them from their computer screens. The breakthrough they had spent more than a decade researching stared back at them — a previously unknown organism thriving deep underground in a section of the Spanish Pyrenees. Buried more than two miles beneath the Earth’s surface, the microbe displayed characteristics that defied known biological norms, suggesting it could potentially survive in environments once thought impossible — even beyond our planet. The discovery took place during a routine geothermal energy survey in the remote village of Guils. Dr. Ruíz, a microbiologist from the University of Zaragoza, had been part of a team investigating the possibility of harnessing subterranean heat sources. It was during the drilling of an exploration well that the unexpected occurred. When the team extracted what they expected to be inert rock samples, the tiny creatures within immediately defied categorisation. “They were almost alive, but not quite,” said Dr. Ruíz in his first interview with  El País . “It was as if they had paused time. One moment, they were motionless — the next, they responded to changes in temperature and acidity in a controlled manner. It was unlike anything we’ve seen before.” What set the microbe apart was its metabolic flexibility. Preliminary analysis revealed that it existed in a state of suspended animation when nutrients were scarce, but immediately resumed activity when conditions were optimal. This ability allowed it to endure centuries — perhaps even millennia — in complete metabolic stasis. Researchers noted its apparent lack of DNA damage and its capacity to self-repair once reactivated, suggesting it had evolved an entirely different biological strategy to survive. Professor Moya, a virologist, described the implications as "mind-blowing". “If these organisms have evolved such efficient survival mechanisms, it raises the possibility they could be found elsewhere in the universe,” he added. “This is not just a scientific curiosity; it is a paradigm shift.” The scientific community has reacted with a mix of awe and cautious optimism. Dr. Elena Ortega, a senior researcher at Madrid’s National Centre for Biotechnology, described the findings as “ground-breaking and potentially transformative to how we define life itself”. Meanwhile, Dr. Ruíz and Professor Moya are preparing to release their findings in a upcoming journal publication and have already begun plans for further testing on the lifeform’s potential applications — from medical science to extraterrestrial exploration.

Scientists have made a major breakthrough in the development of a universal influenza vaccine, raising hopes that a single shot could one day offer lasting protection against all strains of the virus. The development has been heralded as a potentially transformative leap in the global fight against flu, with the potential to eliminate the need for annual vaccinations. A team of researchers led by Imperial College London has designed a new vaccine candidate that targets   conserved regions   of the influenza virus — parts of the virus that remain relatively unchanged over time. Unlike traditional flu vaccines, which are reformulated every year to match the circulating strains, the new candidate aims to offer lasting immunity, regardless of mutations in the virus. The vaccine is based on a technique called "virus-like particles," which mimic the flu virus without containing its genetic material, making it safe for use. In early trials on animals, the vaccine was shown to induce a strong immune response and provided   broad protection   against multiple flu subtypes, including H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1 — which includes the deadly bird flu strain. Dr Sarah Gilbert, one of the study's lead authors, said the findings represent a monumental shift in flu prevention. "This is not just about development of a better vaccine. It is about redesigning the entire vaccination strategy for influenza on a global scale," she said. "We are moving away from a system that responds to what we predict flu will be, to one that can respond to what flu actually is — every form of it." The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that seasonal influenza results in   3-5 million cases   of severe illness and around   300,000-500,000 deaths annually   worldwide.
