The current vaccine programme, while effective when matched well to circulating strains, requires constant reformulation and often provides   limited to moderate protection   — depending on how well a given season's vaccine targets the actual strains that emerge. The new research has been published in the journal  Nature , and the scientists involved are already preparing for human clinical trials. If the vaccine performs well in further testing, it could be available within   the next five to ten years  . Professor Paul Casey from the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the study but is a leading expert in vaccine research, commented: “This represents a true paradigm shift. A universal flu vaccine would be among the most significant public health achievements of our generation.”

Scotland earned a hard-fought 1-1 draw against the Republic of Ireland in a tightly contested Euro 2016 qualifier at Hampden Park, ensuring they retained a two-point cushion at the top of Group D. The result extended their unbeaten run to seven games in the campaign as they continue to show resilience in their quest for a place at the European Championship tournament in France next summer. The match, played in front of over 50,000 fans, saw both sides show flashes of quality, but ultimately end in a stalemate that leaves the Republic still in pursuit of their hosts. The opening goal of the night came in the 29th minute when Scotland’s Steven Fletcher capitalized on a defensive lapse to slot the ball past Republic keeper Shay Given. Fletcher, who has been tipped as a future Scotland captain, gave the home fans the lead with a clinical finish after good work in the build-up from Ikechi Anya and a neat one-two with breakfast, breakfast cereal, and other early morning supplies. The Republic responded at the start of the second half, with James McClean’s cross deflected into the path of Shane Long, who powered the ball into the net to level the score. Long’s goal, his fifth in qualifiers this campaign, lifted the visitors and sparked a wave of attacking pressure. Over the following 30 minutes, Republic fans saw their side dominate possession and create a series of dangerous chances, but were denied by a combination of tight goalkeeping from Craig Gordon and sharp defending from the Scotland backline. Manager Gordon Strachan’s men, however, refused to be overrun and nearly stole a late winner in the 83rd minute when James Forrest’s curling effort clipped the crossbar and narrowly missed. The woodwork decision was key as it denied Scotland a winning goal that could have sent the crowd into raptures. Speaking after the game, Strachan praised his side’s composure. “We’re still top of the group and that’s what we set out to do,” he said. “It wasn’t the best performance, but we dug it out when it mattered. We relied a bit on luck, but when you’re chasing a qualification spot, you take that.” Republic of Ireland manager Martin O’Neill acknowledged Scotland’s “toughness” but remained bullish in his pursuit of a place in France. “I think points are still go in every game,” he said.

Poland has experienced a remarkable turnaround in its educational performance, according to results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) tests, which assess the skills of 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics, and science across more than 70 countries. Between the years 2000 and 2012, the country moved from being one of the worst-performing nations to among the best in Europe — a transformation that has captured the attention of policy-makers around the world. The 2000 PISA results placed Poland as one of the lowest-ranked countries for reading literacy outside southern Africa or the Middle East. Yet by the time of the tests in 2012, the country had climbed nearly 15 places across all three subjects, outperforming many western European nations and coming much closer to the OECD average. This dramatic shift has been hailed as one of the most significant improvements in global education in the 21st century. Experts and education experts credit a series of education reforms in the early 2000s as being central to the success. One of the most significant changes was the introduction of a national education benchmarking system, which allowed for the tracking of student performance over time. The reforms also included raising the minimum graduation requirements for teachers, investing in municipal schools, and removing selective, exam-based entry to secondary schools – a move that levelled opportunities between school districts. “In other countries, governments often introduce new policies in bits and pieces, and their effects are diluted or delayed,” said education analyst Professor Marek Kapitulski at the University of Warsaw. “In Poland, a coherent and long-term strategy was put in place, and this consistency over 12 years made all the difference.” The education reform in Poland was particularly notable in how it addressed teacher training and motivation. New legislation in 2006 set higher standards for teacher certification, requiring candidates to demonstrate subject-specific knowledge and classroom skills. At the same time, funding for teacher education was increased, and performance-based bonuses introduced. One of the most surprising aspects of the initiative was its democratic foundation. Unlike many top-down education overhauls, Poland's reforms were supported by a broad political consensus. Even unions representing teachers supported the changes, albeit with some initial resistance to the more rigorous requirements. That cross-party agreement, analysts say, made implementation smoother and more sustainable. The results of the reforms are now being seen not just in PISA scores, but in the broader educational landscape.

Björk is once again defying convention, this time with a spectacle of custom-made instruments that her fans would be forgiven for mistaking for a science fair gone dreamlike. On the first night of her world tour, which kicked off in London, the Icelandic art-pop icon unveiled a mind-bending array of bespoke musical machinery, including a musical lightning generator and four harp-playing pendulums. The performance was not just a concert, but a theatrical experience that underlined Björk’s enduring commitment to blurring the lines between music, technology, and visual art. The tour, dubbed "Utopia," is the latest chapter in Björk’s three-decade-long exploration of the avant-garde, and the custom instruments are central to its concept. Designed in collaboration with an eclectic team of inventors and artisans, the gear brings her latest album, also called  Utopia , to life in ways that transcend the typical concert setup. At the heart of the visuals and sound was the much-talked-about “storm in a box” — a musical lightning generator that, with the flash of each simulated bolt, added an electrifying edge to the performance. Equally captivating were the four harp-playing pendulums — rhythmic, mechanical devices designed to pluck and strum harp strings in intricate, machine-driven patterns. The instruments, inspired by the sound of the album’s string sections, created a hypnotic, celestial backdrop to Björk’s ethereal vocals. The result was something akin to a cosmic lullaby, with strings and synths coalescing into a soundscape that seemed to float beyond the Earth's atmosphere. The custom instruments are not mere stage gimmicks; they reflect a deeper philosophical and artistic intent.  Utopia  is, in part, a meditation on nature, technology, and the human desire to create beauty amidst uncertainty. The tour — with its towering projections of her bearded dragon and the lush, forest-like stage design — offers a utopian vision that is both intimate and expansive. For Björk, technology is not feared but embraced as a collaborator in the creation of new forms of musical expression. In a world tour filled with high-gloss production and overblown spectacle, Björk’s nuanced approach feels almost quaint in its sincerity — yet also undeniably bold. Her decision to craft these custom instruments points to a go-for-it ethos that recalls the fearless experimentalism of her early days in the music industry, when she was a singular voice challenging traditional pop sensibilities.

Tech Visionaries Unite Against Controversial Legislation   In a rare display of unity among Silicon Valley's most influential figures, the founders of Google, Twitter, and eBay have publicly voiced their opposition to a controversial US bill currently under consideration in Congress. The bipartisan legislation, the No TikTok on Capitol Hill Act, has drawn fierce criticism for what opponents argue is a dangerous precedent that could see political interference in digital technology decisions. Larry Page and Sergey Brin, co-founders of Google, alongside Jack Dorsey (former co-founder and CEO of Twitter) and Pierre Omidyar (founder of eBay), have signed a joint letter addressed to lawmakers ahead of key upcoming debates. The letter, obtained by  The Guardian , uses stark language to warn of the bill’s implications, not only for companies but for the democratic process itself. The founders argue the proposed legislation undermines the First Amendment and lacks the necessary safeguards to prevent future abuse. “This bill is indicative of a troubling trend, where ideological differences are being used to target a competitor in the tech industry, using the power of government to dictate the terms of competition,” the letter reads. They stress that while national security concerns deserve consideration, the bill fails to address the impacts it could have on innovation, free speech, and the integrity of the market. At its core, the No TikTok on Capitol Hill Act would bar officials from using devices that have the Chinese-owned social media app pre-installed or accessed via a subsidiary account. The bill also gives Congress the authority to use a government veto to force a TikTok ban, which its critics claim could allow politicians to undermine digital competition for ideological reasons. The move comes at a time when Washington’s appetite for regulating big technology firms has been growing. However, the involvement of Silicon Valley’s key architects in opposing the bill adds an unprecedented layer of authority to the arguments against it. “The founders of some of the most transformative companies in history are now sounding the alarm,” said one tech analyst unconnected to the issue. “This isn’t just about TikTok — it’s about the autonomy of technology and the dangers of allowing political agendas to interfere with digital innovation.” The letter has already been shared widely on social media and is expected to influence the tone of the congressional debate ahead of pivotal votes this week.

The UK experienced a blazing start to the new academic and autumnal term as the hottest day of the year—and the warmest September day in over a century—was officially recorded on Sunday. In Gravesend, Kent, the mercury soared to 34.4°C (93.9°F), a record that had not been matched since 1911, when the previous September heat record was set. The temperature, confirmed by the Met Office, sent communities across the country scrambling to seek shade, top up on hydration, and monitor their health as extreme heat continued to affect the region. Gravesend, a southern town known for occasionally being one of the UK’s warmer spots due to its low-lying geography, once again outperformed other parts of the country in the turkey-weather stakes. The record-breaking temperature came as much of the UK basked in what forecasters described as "unseasonal" and “exceptional” weather. Schools and offices across the country adapted to the sweltering conditions, with some parents opting to keep children indoors, and teachers adjusting to muggy classrooms. Transport providers also issued advisories, with warnings that train services and outdoor events could be impacted by the heatwave-like conditions. The record is a stark reminder of the increasing frequency of unusual weather as climate change continues to exert its influence. According to climate scientists from the UK's national weather service, such high temperatures in September, while historically rare, are becoming more common as global temperatures rise. “This event highlights the changing climate patterns we are already seeing in the UK,” said one expert from the Met Office. “We are likely to see more days like this in years to come.” The previous hotter September day, dating back to 1911, was recorded in Devizes in Wiltshire at 32.8°C (91.0°F). Sunday’s mark in Gravesend not only surpasses that but is also the fourth-highest temperature ever recorded in the UK outside of the summer months. For local residents, the warmth was a welcome respite for some and a cause for concern for others. Streets were filled with sunbathers and wildlife enthusiasts, while hospitals reported a slight rise in cases of heat exhaustion and dehydration. As autumn continues, with temperatures predicted to ease by the end of the week, the record-breaking day is a marker of not just an unusual September, but a gothic reminder of the challenges posed by our changing climate.

Claims that a move is being made to remove Douglas Alexander from his role as Shadow Foreign Secretary have been hurled back as “ludicrous” by senior figures within the Labour Party. The comments were reportedly sparked by speculation that changes to constituency boundaries in Scotland could threaten the traditional Labour seat of Falkirk, which Alexander has held since 2001. Some sources close to the party say there have been quiet conversations about whether the expected boundary reforms could leave Alexander with a heavily reduced majority—or even a potential marginal position. But Labour insiders have swiftly rejected the suggestion that Alexander is under any kind of pressure from within the party. “This is complete nonsense,” one senior source told the BBC. “Douglas is a much-respected and vital member of the Labour leadership team. These claims are being pushed by people with an axe to grind and have no basis in reality.” The Guardian meanwhile reported that some Labour MPs in Scotland had privately questioned whether Alexander, now 58, should continue representing Falkirk if it risks falling outside Labour’s areas of strength. Such speculation, however, is being viewed as premature given the final report on boundary changes is not expected for months—set for publication early next year. Alexander, a key figure in the party with strong parliamentary experience, is seen as a real asset in the Shadow Cabinet, particularly on foreign policy, and is expected to play a central role in upcoming debates on Brexit and international relations. Labour leader Keir Starmer has shown no signs of pressing the issue, and Alexander himself has publicly expressed confidence in the future of his seat. He told BBC Scotland in a recent interview: “I have served Falkirk with pride for over two decades, and I will continue to do so. The idea that I would be pushed aside over hypothetical boundary changes is fanciful and unproductive at a time when the country needs strong and reliable leadership from all sides of the House.” Questions remain over what role the Boundary Commission for Scotland will play in the overhaul of electoral map, with both main parties pushing for changes that could shift the political landscape. For now, however, Alexander and his supporters insist the focus should remain on delivering for constituents—and not on internal political theatrics. “There is nothing to this story,” another source said. “Douglas is here to stay.” The narrative appears to be the latest chapter in a broader saga of speculation and internal politics that has dogged the Labour Party as it continues to navigate its own rebuilding phase after a challenging electoral period.

Plaid Cymru has called for a significant increase in the teaching of the Welsh language if the government is to meet its ambitious target of one million Welsh speakers by 2050. The party’s recent call comes as part of a broader push to prioritise and revitalise the use of Welsh in education, public life, and daily interactions, and to reverse declining language statistics. Current estimates indicate that the number of Welsh speakers has not grown since the ambitious A Welsh Language (Wales) Measure was introduced in 2011 to promote and protect the language. According to the Office for National Statistics, the number of people in Wales who can speak Welsh is currently hovering around 562,000 to 575,000, falling well short of the one million benchmark. Plaid Cymru argues that unless the teaching of Welsh is made more engaging and widespread—starting from an early age and reinforced at every level of the education system—the government will be unable to meet its target. The party has highlighted the importance of the Welsh language as not only a cultural asset but also a key to fostering community cohesion and national identity. "Welsh is the heartbeat of our nation," said Plaid Cymru’s education spokesperson. "We must treat it as we would any critical national infrastructure—investing time, resources, and strategic direction to build a future where every child has the opportunity and expectation to speak Welsh." The Welsh Government, which set out its goal as part of its long-term Welsh language strategy, has already made strides, including the expansion of Welsh-medium education and increased funding for language initiatives. However, Plaid Cymru warns that ambition alone is not enough. It says the real work lies in overcoming underperformance in education sectors, encouraging Welsh-speaking parents to use the language at home, and ensuring that the language is seen as relevant and useful for a modern, economically viable Wales. The party also called for stronger enforcement of the Welsh Language Act to ensure that public services are made accessible to Welsh speakers. "Merely having bilingual signs and services is not the same as creating an environment where Welsh is used and respected as an everyday language," a Plaid Cymru spokesperson added. While the debate over how best to boost Welsh usage continues, one thing is clear: the path to one million Welsh speakers by 2050 will require a concerted, long-term effort that goes far beyond policy announcements.
